items.label: 1A
items.claim: A near-new used NovaSeq 6000 is being marked down to about half of the $200K resale anchor, so the second-hand market is oversupplied.
items.detail: REUZEit lists an 'Excellent', 'very little prior use' NovaSeq 6000 with UPS and 15 S4 buffer cartridges at $99,000 (51% off a $200,000 anchor). A search-result snippet of the same site showed $150,000 (25% off $200,000), so the ask appears to have been cut by about a third. The instrument launched at $985K. The listing is undated, and the page is inconsistent on whether it has sold.
items.quote: Near-new, with very little prior use and minimal cosmetic wear.
items.why_new: No resale-market prices for the 6000 are in the known list; this is the first used-instrument price datapoint.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: A university-retired NovaSeq 6000 has been halved from $60K to $30K, which points to a tail of unwanted, retiring 6000 units.
items.detail: MSU Surplus Store lists a retired NovaSeq 6000 (includes 2 APC UPS units; drive wiped) at a $30,000 sale price vs a $60,000 regular price. An earlier search snippet showed $60,000. That is about 3% of the $985K launch price. A flat-to-falling resale value suggests institutions are retiring 6000s rather than keeping them indefinitely. It is one unit, so it says nothing on pace.
items.quote: It came from a working environment and was retired from use
items.why_new: The known list names core retirements (Dana-Farber, Georgia) but has no resale-price evidence.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: A core's own price sheet shows an explicit volume-tier discount of about 9% on 25B flow cells for 2 or more, a sign that larger accounts get cheaper $/Gb.
items.detail: Pitt internal rates effective 6/2025: 25B-300 is $21,393 for one flow cell and $19,533 each for 2 or more. On 8,000 Gb, that is $2.67 and $2.44/Gb. The 10B-300 tier is $12,792 versus $11,680 (also about 9% off), and 25B-100 is $15,640 versus $14,280. The tier is built into the list, so the discount comes from the lab's own pricing structure, not a negotiated deal.
items.source_name: Pitt Health Sciences Sequencing Core price list
items.why_new: Pitt is not in the known core list, and the 2+ flow-cell tier discount is new.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: A core still carries the NovaSeq 6000 in mid-2025 at roughly 4x the X's price per Gb, so the 6000 is still a high-price tail at some cores.
items.detail: Pitt 6/2025 internal: 6000 S2-300 full flow cell $14,030 (about $11.2/Gb on about 1,250 Gb), SP-300 $4,571 (about $9.1/Gb). 25B-300 is $2.67/Gb, so the ratio is about 4.2x. This is a core's price, not Illumina revenue, so the ratio runs higher than the roughly 3.4x revenue-per-Gb ratio derived from Illumina's disclosures. The S4 300-cycle line is not in the fetched text.
items.source_name: Pitt Health Sciences Sequencing Core price list
items.why_new: This gives a 6000 versus X per-Gb ratio at a core that is not in the known list. It is the first sheet found with both on one page.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: A US academic core sells an all-in 30x human genome on Ultima UG100 for $192 internal / $221 external.
items.detail: UMGC (2026 page) lists 30x on UG100 at $192 (UMN) and $221 (external) including prep, QC and variant analysis. 60x costs $238/$274 and 90x costs $329/$379. This is a real service price, which makes it a concrete reference for what large accounts can demand from Illumina. The headline $199 genome is already known, but this is the full batch-size price grid.
items.why_new: Known list has only the '$199' headline and ~$12/50M reads. This adds the full 30x/60x/90x grid by platform and batch size.
items.verify_note: Verified on the UMGC page: 30x UG100 costs $192 / $221 (batch of 24), 60x $238 / $274 (batch of 18), 90x $329 / $379 (batch of 12). The 30x price includes QC, PCR-free prep, sequencing and DeepVariant/GATK calling. The page is undated. It lists no NovaSeq X genome price at all, which suggests this core now prices WGS only on Ultima and Element. New as a full grid; the ~$200 Ultima genome headline is already known.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: On the same core's price list, AVITI costs about 2x the Ultima genome, so Element is not yet a price threat at this core.
items.detail: UMGC lists 30x on AVITI at $407 internal / $469 external (batch of 4) and on AVITI Ultra Q at $1,015 / $1,168 (batch of 2), against $192 / $221 for UG100. Ultima is the price threat at this core and AVITI is not. This partly cuts against the Element-specific part of the discounting thesis.
items.why_new: Gives an all-in AVITI 30x genome price, which the known list lacks (it only has per-Gb AVITI costs from Northwestern/UMN).
items.verify_note: The numbers check out: AVITI $407 / $469 (batch of 4), Ultra Q $1,015 / $1,168 (batch of 2). The direction is wrong, though, and should be 'against' the Element-specific part of 1B. The comparison is also not like-for-like, because a batch of 4 vs 24 inflates AVITI's per-sample cost. The known list already has conflicting UMN/Northwestern AVITI $/Gb, so this adds little.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: The UMGC page lists no NovaSeq X per-genome price, only a link to standalone X+ sequencing.
items.detail: Its human-genome offer is built around UG100 and AVITI, with Illumina X Plus only a standalone lane service. A core steering its human-WGS offer to non-Illumina platforms is a datapoint on where Illumina's volume could leak. The core does still run X Plus for other work.
items.why_new: Observation on platform steering at a core, not in the known list.

items.label: 2A
items.claim: One academic core sells external customers X flow cells at a 55% premium to internal ones, which does not look like a price-fighting research buyer base.
items.detail: KUMC: 25B-300 full flow cell $37,002 external versus $23,872 internal. 10B-300 lane is $1,794 versus $1,157. External academic users therefore pay about $4.63/Gb, close to the top of the known core range (Rush $4.20-4.62/lane). The page has no date, so this is a single snapshot.
items.why_new: KUMC is not in the known core list, and it adds a wide internal/external gap.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: Azenta promotes a 25B lane at $2,799 for ~950 Gb (about $2.95/Gb) and a partial 375 Gb at $1,500 ($4.00/Gb).
items.detail: Search snippet says $2,799/lane (950 Gb); the opened page shows 375 Gb for $1,500. Illumina's own 25B kit list is roughly $2.30-3.02/Gb, so the provider's selling price is at or above Illumina's per-Gb list and the provider margin is thin. This shows commercial providers' resale prices are not far below Illumina list.
items.why_new: Known list has Novogene/UMN/core prices but no Azenta lane or partial-lane prices. The 25B figure is from a search snippet only.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: Azenta advertises NovaSeq X Plus WGS 'as low as $488/sample' (search snippet; coverage and species unclear).
items.detail: Snippet only. If this is 30x human, it would be well below the roughly $650 cores charge. It may be non-human or reduced depth. Needs the page opened.
items.why_new: Not in known list.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: Cores are retiring 6000s and replacing them 1-for-1 with X Plus, so conversion at research cores is largely done, which cuts against research-side 6000 pricing tail risk.
items.detail: UW-Madison announced (27 Jun 2024) the replacement of a NovaSeq 6000 with a NovaSeq X Plus, citing expanded capacity and lower consumable costs. This is a search-result snippet that I did not open. It adds to Dana-Farber (Oct 2024) and Northwestern (Jan 2024), which are already known.
items.why_new: UW-Madison and Duke are not on the known list of retired-6000 cores.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: Commercial resale prices for the 25B lane look flat: Admera (2024 promo) and Azenta (current promo) both show $2,799.
items.detail: Admera 25B was $2,799 for 937.5 Gb in the H1'24 promo. An Azenta promo snippet shows $2,799 for 950 Gb now. A $/Gb of about $2.95 that has not fallen in two years cuts against the idea that large-account discounting is already feeding through to service-provider prices. Both are promotions and not contracts, so this is weak.
items.why_new: Time-series comparison of provider lane prices is absent from the known list.

items.label: 2B
items.claim: More academic cores (UC Davis, Cornell) now offer AVITI as a standard service at prices that undercut a 25B lane on a per-read-batch basis.
items.detail: UC Davis DNA Tech core: AVITI 300-cycle PE150 run $2,000 (UC rate). Cornell: AVITI24 lane (400M reads) $799 internal, $999 external. Both are undated snippets; per-Gb comparison needs run yields I did not verify. Adds two named cores to the known Northwestern and UMN AVITI list.
items.source_name: UC Davis DNA Technologies Core; Cornell BRC
items.why_new: UC Davis and Cornell AVITI rates are not in the known list.

items.label: 2A
items.claim: Admera offered up to 50% off (WGS $600/sample for 8+ samples), which shows research buyers get discount-led offers.
items.detail: The March 2024 promo had 'up to 50% off' and an 8-sample WGS minimum at $600 (about 90 Gb, about $6.67/Gb including prep). It shows discounting is the normal route to winning research volume.
items.why_new: Not in known list.

items.label: 2B
items.claim: A large US academic core (Michigan AGC) is an Ultima UG 100 service provider, which adds an in-house low-price alternative to Illumina for research work.
items.detail: The AGC says it is among the first academic facilities worldwide to install the UG 100 and will offer 'significantly lower-cost sequencing' to internal and external investigators. The vendor cites $1.00/Gb or $0.30 per million reads (vendor figure, not a core price). I did not open the page, so the date and any core price are unverified.
items.source_name: University of Michigan Advanced Genomics Core
items.quote: significantly lower-cost sequencing for both internal and external investigators
items.why_new: No Michigan or other US academic Ultima core is in the known list; known Ultima share data is from a Georgia core.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: Barcelona's FRCB-IDIBAPS issued new 2026 tenders for outsourced sequencing on NovaSeq X Plus 25B lanes, so public buyers are now shopping for 25B lane capacity (search-result snippet only).
items.detail: TED notices 528143-2026 and 536530-2026 cover sequencing services on a NovaSeq X Plus 25B, and the second is a change notice to the first. The ted.europa.eu PDFs did not load, so the values, bidders and awardee are unread. These are follow-ons to the known IDIBAPS 2025 award at about €2.00/Gb. They could reveal whether the 2026 price per lane is lower than 2025.
items.why_new: These are 2026 follow-on notices to the known 2025 IDIBAPS award. Their price has not been read.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: An all-in 30x human genome costs about $650 on NovaSeq X at TCAG and JHU, against $192-221 on UG100 at UMGC.
items.detail: TCAG (April 2025) $650 including prep for 90-100 Gb. JHU GRCF $650 on X Plus (internal). UMGC UG100 $192 internal / $221 external. The roughly 3x all-in spread is the evidence for Ultima undercutting at the whole-workflow level, which supports pressure on large-account pricing. Prep and analysis inclusion differ across providers, so the comparison is imperfect.
items.why_new: Known list has per-Gb and lane prices, not all-in genome prices on the X vs UG100.
items.verify_note: I could not verify the JHU page (403). TCAG is already in the corpus and may be quoted in CAD. UMGC's $192 includes variant calling, while TCAG and JHU include prep, so the ~3x all-in spread is directional only. The more robust version is derived item D2 below.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: JHU GRCF keeps separate pages for 6000 WGS and X Plus WGS, so a price history exists for the 6000 to X per-genome step.
items.detail: Pages grcf.jhmi.edu/sequencing/whole-genome-sequencing (6000) and grcf.jhmi.edu/?p=15308 (X Plus, $650). The 6000 page price was not opened. Comparing them gives a direct per-genome conversion step for a research core.
items.why_new: JHU is not in the known core list.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: UKHSA committed up to £12.0M to Illumina proprietary consumables through Aug 2028, a large, locked-in public-sector volume (the figure comes from a call-off ceiling).
items.detail: The notice was published 3 Dec 2025 and updated 19 Jun 2026. The supplier is Illumina Cambridge Ltd, and the procedure is a call-off from a framework. No separate direct-award justification is given. At roughly £4.4M a year, the ceiling is a cap, not spend. It shows continued public-sector reliance on Illumina consumables, which tempers a view that volume is rolling off.
items.quote: provision of its proprietary consumables
items.why_new: No UK public procurement award appears in the known list.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: Federal buyers keep justifying sole-source Illumina reagent buys as 'only one responsible source', which shows lock-in that limits extra discounting in the public sector.
items.detail: NIH (27 Apr 2026, 25B kits), the Naval Medical Research Command (23 Jul 2026) and others cite FAR 13.106-1(b)(1) and proprietary chemistry. This reduces competitive price pressure from rivals in that channel. It does not rule out volume discounts at large commercial accounts. The wording is from search-result summaries, not from opened notices.
items.why_new: Federal sole-source notices were not in the known list. Only SKU pages from distributors were.

items.label: 2B
items.claim: A Canadian federal research lab (NRC) chose to upgrade its existing Element AVITI platform in 2026 rather than add Illumina capacity.
items.detail: The value was CAD 122,000, posted as a single-source Advance Contract Award Notice on 29 May 2026. The upgrade is to AVITI24, with installation due by 31 Jul 2026. It is a small deal, but it is a government research buyer using Element as a standard platform. Illumina is not named. This was read only as a search-result summary.
items.why_new: No known item shows a government research lab choosing Element.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: Used NovaSeq 6000 asking prices in the US span $30K to $99K, a long way below the ~$985K new price.
items.detail: MSU Surplus Store lists a used 6000 at $30,000 (regular $60,000, 50% off), local pickup only, with 2 APC UPS units, a wiped PC and no year given. REUZEit asks $99K for a ~2021 unit. Parts-or-repair units in the UK (Unigreen Scheme) are £7,950–8,000. Against the CASRAI reported launch range of $985K–$1M, the US asks are 3–10% of new. Asking prices are not sold prices, and the units differ in age and warranty.
items.source_name: MSU Surplus Store; Unigreen Scheme; CASRAI price guide
items.why_new: Adds a cross-listing price band, the percent-of-new arithmetic and the UK parts-only floor. F002 had only the MSU markdown.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: A European dealer still asks €200,000 for a used NovaSeq 6000, and a 2022-build unit on Exapro is marked 'Sold'.
items.detail: Labprocure GmbH, via the Labexchange shop, lists a used 6000 at €200,000 excluding VAT (€238,000 with 19% VAT). The listing gives no year or serial. Exapro shows a 2022 US-located 6000 as 'Sold', 'no longer available', with the price on request and seller activity as of 10 Apr 2026. This argues the 6000 is not uniformly worthless. Some buyers still want units, which fits a persistent tail. The dealer ask is the opposite of the US markdowns, so resale prices are dispersed and the signal is noisy.
items.why_new: Resale data that cuts against the 'oversupplied' reading in F001/F002. It shows a demand floor and a regional price gap.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: Faulty 6000s are listed in the UK at about £8K each, which sets a floor for the used-6000 price.
items.detail: Unigreenscheme lists two 2018-manufactured NovaSeq 6000s in Wales: ITEM-49972 at £8,000 ex VAT (software fails to initialise at 94%) and ITEM-49973 at £7,950 (pump, XY-stage and tip-tilt motor failures). Both are sold for spares or repair, with a PAT test dated 24 Nov 2025. The source is 'a laboratory where it was surplus to requirements', and no university is named. A 2018 unit is roughly 1 year after launch, so first-generation boxes are already being scrapped for parts. Listed price is about 0.8% of the ~$985K launch price (£8,000 is roughly $10.5K at ~1.3 USD/GBP; the FX rate is my assumption).
items.quote: removed from a laboratory where it was surplus to requirements
items.why_new: These are fault-state UK units with a dated PAT test. The known list has only US surplus items.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: Unigreenscheme's sequencer catalog shows older Illumina platforms valued at near-scrap levels, which gives the end-state for the 6000 tail.
items.detail: Of the 47 rows I parsed on page 1 of 2, prices run: NextSeq 2000 £90,000 (2020), NextSeq 550 £15,000, NextSeq 500 £5,090-6,000 (six listings), MiSeq £1,000-5,000, HiSeq 1000 £1,000 and Genome Analyzer IIx £2,100. The HiSeq 1000 appears elsewhere on the same site at £15,000, so the same model ranges from £1,000 to £15,000 depending on condition and listing. This shows prior-generation Illumina boxes have near-zero resale value once an upgrade cycle completes. The 6000 listings at £8K already sit in the NextSeq 500 price band. This is a UK reseller sample with mixed condition, not a market index.
items.why_new: This is a priced cross-section of used Illumina platforms, which the known list does not include.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: MSU applies stepped markdowns to its other retired Illumina box, so the 6000 price cut follows store policy rather than a 6000-specific signal.
items.detail: Two MSU MiSeq listings (created 30 Mar 2026) carry tags 'Markdown Date_06-15-2026' and 'Markdown Date_09-16-2026'. Both now sell at $1,575 against $3,000 (-47.5%). Both listings carry a '30 Days' tag. The 6000 has the same tag structure and a single recorded markdown (20 Jan 2026). The inference is mine: markdowns look like a scheduled cycle. That weakens the 6000 cut as a demand signal. It still shows the unit failed to sell at $60K for 258 days.
items.why_new: This is a caveat on the 6000 data point and was not in the known list.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: A university core's Ultima UG 100 wafer price now looks higher than its earlier listing, so the Ultima price gap is not widening at this core.
items.detail: The UMN Genomics Center's search-result snippet showed full wafers (10-12B reads) at $2,909 internal / $3,212 external. The page I opened now shows $3,204 / $3,688 on the 'Savings' tier. That is +10.1% internal and +14.8% external, so Ultima is not cutting price at this core. The earlier snippet is undated, and the opened page shows no effective date; it carries a 2026 footer and links to 'lower FY 2024 rates'. Per read, $3,204 / 10-12B reads is about $0.27-0.32 per million reads.
items.source_name: University of Minnesota Genomics Center rate page, plus search snippet
items.why_new: The exclusion list has a UMN-style evaluation of about $12 per 50M reads but no wafer price trend and no increase.
items.verify_note: The chronology is not established. The 'earlier' $2,909 / $3,212 comes from an undated snippet. The current Savings/Speed/Priority tiers date from UMN's 'lower FY2024 rates' announcement (1 Dec 2023, Savings ~10% below FY23). The snippet could therefore be a pre-tier or different-tier price, not an older version of today's price. The external/internal markup also moved from 1.104 to 1.151, which points to a core overhead/IDC change rather than an Ultima pass-through change. This cannot support '

items.label: 1B
items.claim: UMN offers three Ultima delivery tiers, and the cheapest tier is about 5% below the 'Priority' price, so Ultima is priced by speed at this core.
items.detail: Full wafer: Savings $3,204 / Speed $3,356 / Priority $3,508 internal, and $3,688 / $3,863 / $4,038 external. Half wafer (5-6B reads): $2,107 / $2,206 / $2,305 internal. The full wafer lists as up to 3.6 Tb, which is about $0.89/Gb at the Savings internal rate if the full 3.6 Tb is delivered. This is a lower-bound cost per Gb, because it assumes the maximum output. It is the sort of benchmark Illumina's 25B lane price of about $2.9/Gb at UCSD is measured against.
items.why_new: Gives a per-Gb Ultima core price with 3.6 Tb output stated, not the genome-level or per-read figures already known.
items.verify_note: Prices verified. Correction: the half-wafer external price is $2,425 / $2,539 / $2,653. A 5% speed-tier spread is not evidence of discounting. The page's own overview says '≥2.5–3.0 Tb' per run against an 'up to 3.6 Tb' spec. Realistic $/Gb at the Savings internal rate is ~$1.07–1.28, not $0.89. The main value here is as an input to D1.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: Cost per Gb at one core is roughly 3x lower on Ultima than on the Illumina X at current core rates.
items.detail: UCSD IGM's 25B-300 lane is $2,800 UC / $3,836 outside. At the spec of 3.2B read pairs, which is about 960 Gb, that is about $2.92/Gb UC and $4.00/Gb outside. UMN's Ultima full wafer is $3,204 internal for up to 3.6 Tb (about $0.89/Gb). I used two different cores, so the ratio is only indicative: about 3.3x internal and about 3.9x outside by my arithmetic on the output specs, which are maximum figures.
items.source_name: UCSD IGM rate card; UMN Genomics Center
items.why_new: UCSD's rate card is not on the core-level list; the cross-core per-Gb ratio is new.
items.verify_note: Verified on the UCSD IGM PDF (created 14 Oct 2025, 'some rates pending committee approval'): 25B-300 lane $2,800 UC / $3,836 outside; 25B-100 $1,900 / $2,603; 10B-300 $1,700 / $2,329; 1.5B-300 $3,200 / $4,384. Using realistic Ultima output (2.5–3.0 Tb, not 3.6), the ratio is ~2.3–2.7x internal and ~2.9–3.6x outside, not 3.3x / 3.9x. UCSD is a new core datapoint, and it sits in the known $2.5–3.1/Gb 25B band.

items.label: 2B
items.claim: UMN gives $500 off per wafer (about 16% of the $3,204 price) for 10x Genomics projects on Ultima, so research counting work is being courted by price.
items.detail: Preferred pricing: $500 off a full wafer and $250 off a half-wafer (about 16% and 12% off the internal Savings price) for compatible 10x single-cell and spatial libraries. It applies to UMN and external users. That makes about $2,704 per full wafer for a 10x project, about $0.76/Gb at 3.6 Tb. The announcement is undated, with only a 2026 footer.
items.why_new: Shows a targeted Ultima discount on 10x work, the segment where 10x's CEO said price per read has dropped.
items.verify_note: Verified: $500 off a full wafer and $250 off a half wafer, for 10x single-cell/spatial libraries, open to UMN and external users. Undated. Effective price is $2,704 internal, or ~$0.90–1.08/Gb at realistic 2.5–3.0 Tb output. It is new as a concrete, core-level price incentive aimed at counting work. The known list has only 10x's CEO crediting Ultima/Roche pricing.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: Other cores' 25B-300 lanes sit at $2,317-$2,595 at the low end, below some prior core figures.
items.detail: Search snippets showed MD Anderson at $2,595 per 25B-300 lane and Missouri at $2,317 (no dates). UConn is $2,933.99 from 1 Jan 2026 including a 5% tariff surcharge, and UCSD UC is $2,800. At about 960 Gb, Missouri is about $2.41/Gb and MD Anderson about $2.70/Gb. These are snippets only, and Missouri's $2,317 may be an older or internal rate.
items.source_name: MD Anderson ATGC and Missouri core (search snippets)
items.why_new: MD Anderson is new; I opened its page and it listed no prices, so the figure is snippet-only. The Missouri figure differs from the $2.70 in the known list.

items.label: 2B
items.claim: MD Anderson's core advertises 'up to 60% reduction in sequencing price' on its X Plus service page.
items.detail: The page gives no baseline and no dates, only a 2026 footer. It still shows a large cancer center marketing steep reductions in sequencing price to internal researchers, in line with the X conversion price step. I could not turn this into a per-Gb figure.
items.source_name: MD Anderson Advanced Technology Genomics Core
items.quote: Up to 60% reduction in sequencing price
items.why_new: New named core; its X Plus page still points to the NovaSeq 6000 for differently sized libraries.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: UKHSA's successor Illumina consumables ceiling implies only about 33% more spend per year than the prior contract, which is well below 25-30% annual Gb growth compounded over the gap.
items.detail: The prior UKHSA direct award (National Microbiology Framework Lot 2) ran 17 Jan 2022 to 16 Jan 2025 with a total value of £9.8M, or about £3.27M/yr over 3.0 years. The successor call-off (28 Nov 2025 to 30 Aug 2028) is £12.0M over about 2.75 years, or about £4.36M/yr, which is +33%. The midpoints are about 3.5 years apart (mid-2023 to early 2027), so the ceiling grows about 8.6%/yr ((1.333)^(1/3.5) -1). That is far below Illumina's 25-30% Gb growth, which implies flat-ish volume, lower unit prices, or a conservative ceiling. Caveats: ceilings are not spend, the contract is a public-health lab covering all Illumina platforms (not NovaSeq X specifically), and the Jan-Nov 2025 gap period is unknown.
items.quote: awarded a contract to Illumina Cambridge Limited for the provision of its proprietary consumables
items.why_new: F019 gave only the £12M figure; this adds the £9.8M predecessor and the per-year growth arithmetic.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: A UK NHS-area buyer in Leeds signed a NovaSeq 6000 maintenance call-off for calendar 2026, so 6000s are still being kept in service there.
items.detail: A Contracts Finder notice published 11 Feb 2026 records a £119,360.40 call-off from a framework for maintaining a NovaSeq 6000, running 18 Jan 2026 to 17 Jan 2027, awarded to Illumina Cambridge Ltd. This is a 12-month renewal of service on a 6000, not a retirement. It is a single-site data point, and the notice does not say how many 6000s are covered or their consumables use.
items.why_new: This is a dated public-sector 6000 service renewal in 2026; the known 6000 evidence is mostly company statements and core price sheets.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: Public buyers are still buying NovaSeq X Plus systems and are replacing sequencers, which points to conversion continuing in UK public labs.
items.detail: A March 2024 award for a NovaSeq X Plus system totalled £1,115,627, with a term to 19 Mar 2025, and the buyer is at a Leeds address. UKHSA awarded £323,929.84 (20 Feb to 31 Mar 2026) to replace sequencing equipment across its Genomics laboratory networks. APHA awarded £354,823.10 for high-throughput NGS sequencers (Dec 2025, to 31 Dec 2026). These support the idea that UK labs refresh onto new hardware, not that they stay on old 6000s.
items.why_new: Dated UK public-sector hardware refresh awards with values; none are in the known list.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: UK public buyers award Illumina consumables by direct award on a sole-supplier basis, so there is no tender competition on price.
items.detail: The 2021 AFBI MiSeq award (£230K ex-VAT, 5 years, concluded 5 Jul 2021) was a direct award because Illumina is the sole supplier of servicing and reagents for its machines. NHS Grampian's £198,846 genetics reagents award (Feb 2026) cites only 'Direct Award to existing supplier'. UKHSA's £9.8M and £12M contracts are also direct awards or call-offs. This shows lock-in for existing platforms, which cuts against pricing pressure on installed machines. The tender mechanics also mean discounts are negotiated privately, which is consistent with large accounts getting bigger extra discounts, but no discount figure is published.
items.source_name: BidsFactory (UK FTS 018331-2026) and Find a Tender 015684-2021
items.quote: Direct Award to existing supplier
items.why_new: Gives the stated justification text for the UK direct awards; the known list has none of it.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: The UKHSA 'framework' structure contains a competitive layer for Illumina platforms, but the latest notice shows no price concession disclosed.
items.detail: APHA's Aug 2024 call-off 'Sequencing Reagents and Consumables (Illumina, UKHSA Framework Call-off)' was £1,598,054, so smaller UK agencies buy Illumina consumables off the UKHSA framework. That pooled buying gives volume leverage to a central buyer. The notices show no discount schedule, so the evidence cannot show whether the pricing falls over time.
items.why_new: Adds an extra £1.6M call-off from the UKHSA framework not in the known list.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: Combined UK public-sector Illumina awards on the bidsfactory company page are small and do not show strong volume acceleration.
items.detail: BidsFactory shows 20 awards (12 service, 8 supply) to Illumina Cambridge. The itemised ones are UKHSA £12.0M (Nov 2025), AFBI £2.7M (Jul 2026, benchtop sequencer plus consumables and servicing over ten years) and a UKRI sequencer relocation at £11K (Sep 2026). The 10-year AFBI deal is about £0.27M/yr, which is a tiny run rate, and the page's own totals conflict (£3.1M vs $17.5M). Treat this as a size check on UK public demand, not a trend.
items.why_new: AFBI £2.7M ten-year award and the company-page tally are not in the known list.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: Federal labs are still buying service plans for NovaSeq 6000s in 2025-26, so the 6000 tail is being kept alive. This is the opposite of the rapid-retirement pattern at research cores.
items.detail: The Naval Medical Research Command (NMRC) posted a sole-source notice on 22 Dec 2025 for a one-year Silver Support Plan on NovaSeq 6000 S/N A01716 (CAT# 20019988). A separate NMRC listing shows a Silver Support Plan award of $141,313 for a 6000. NIEHS (June 2025) renewed a 6000 Bronze agreement for 29 Jun 2025-28 Jun 2026. NICHD (Feb 2025-Feb 2026) and CDC (Dec 2024-Dec 2025) renewed 6000 service as well. Each of these is a government 6000 that still has a service contract and is probably still running consumables. Because these are annual renewals, they act as a dated check on whether federal 6000s are retired. Aggregator text is not the SAM.gov record. Four agencies renewing is an anecdote, not a count of the base.
items.source_name: GovContractFinder / SweetSpot mirrors of SAM.gov notices (NMRC, NIEHS, NICHD, CDC)
items.quote: intends to award a sole source contract to, Illumina Inc., San Diego, CA
items.why_new: Prior notes list only Novogene, Dana-Farber and cores retiring 6000s. No federal 6000 service renewals or Silver plan value were captured.
items.verify_note: I verified only the NMRC notice: posted 22 Dec 2025, 6000 S/N A01716, Silver plan CAT# 20019988, one year, sole source to Illumina, no dollar value stated in that notice. NIEHS, NICHD, CDC and the $141,313 award are unverified. These are federal research/public-health labs, not the clinical regulated tail that 1A depends on, and a service contract does not prove consumables use. It is anecdotal but new.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: Illumina holds a sole-source federal framework for reagents, so the largest federal account is not forcing extra discounts through competition.
items.detail: NIH OLAO awarded IDC 75N98026D00035 to Illumina on 21 May 2026, funded by NHGRI. It is a 5-year vehicle ending 21 May 2031 with a $90M ceiling, i.e. $18M a year at most. It was not competed (1 bid) and was justified as 'unique capabilities'. Obligations on it rose from $1.30M to $5.35M (about 6% of ceiling) between the first aggregator snapshot and the 8 Oct 2026 page. The page shows no unit prices (pricing is 'order dependent'). Federal demand is therefore small against Illumina's roughly $3B of sequencing consumables, and the buyer has no competitive tension. It is a modest watch-out for the idea that large accounts extract bigger discounts.
items.why_new: The 2026 NHGRI sole-source IDC, its $90M ceiling and its obligation growth are not in the known sources. The known federal item is only the 'only one responsible source' notice pattern.
items.verify_note: Verified: 75N98026D00035, NIH OLAO for NHGRI, start 21 May 2026, end 21 May 2031, $90M ceiling, $5.35M obligated, 1 bid, 'Not Competed / unique source'. The title cites EO 14398. The page contradicts itself ('full & open' in its narrative text). A sole-source vehicle says nothing about unit price, since federal buyers can still get GSA/negotiated pricing. The main takeaway is that federal demand is small (≤$18M/yr). Weak against.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: Federal NovaSeq X 25B purchases are sized in single orders, not volume-ramp programs.
items.detail: NIH OLAO solicitation 75N98026Q00260 (posted 27 Apr 2026, responses due 7 May 2026, NAICS 325414, PSC 6550, Bethesda) is a one-off notice for 25B kits, with no quantity or award found. The 5-year NHGRI vehicle is capped at $90M, and only about $5.4M was obligated in its first 4.5 months, which annualizes to roughly $14M. That is under 0.5% of Illumina's annual sequencing consumables of about $3.1B (consensus FY26). This federal demand is tiny and slow-ramping.
items.why_new: This adds a quantified obligation pace for the federal Illumina vehicle. No earlier source gave one.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: A European university replaced both a NovaSeq 6000 and a NextSeq 500 with one X Plus, showing the typical conversion is consolidation, not extra volume.
items.detail: The University of Copenhagen awarded Illumina Denmark ApS a NovaSeq X Plus sequencer for USD 2,878,114 on 28 Feb 2025, to replace the older NovaSeq 6000 and NextSeq 500. Two boxes consolidating into one X Plus means the old 6000 revenue stream moves to X prices in one step. The figure is a contract value for the instrument, not consumables.
items.why_new: The known tenders cover only CIBER and IDIBAS consumables. No instrument-replacement tender was cited.

items.label: 2B
items.claim: A federal buyer in New Mexico solicited an Element AVITI24 system in Aug 2026, one sign of competitive systems entering public purchasing.
items.detail: A federal combined synopsis/solicitation for an 'Element Biosciences AVITI 24 sequencing and spatial' system was released 11 Aug 2026 and closed 27 Aug 2026, run by the Indian Education Acquisition Office (New Mexico). Quantity, value and justification are not visible because the attachments are restricted. The buyer is an education agency, so it is weak evidence. It shows Element is being bought by name by federal buyers, in contrast to Illumina's 'only one responsible source' justifications.
items.why_new: This is the first federal procurement of a non-Illumina sequencer. The known federal items are all Illumina sole-source buys.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: NIH's intramural sequencing center was renewed on proprietary-reagent grounds in 2025, which shows lock-in at a large federal research account.
items.detail: NHLBI posted a non-competitive modification (75N92025R00033) on 4 Jun 2025 for Illumina reagents at the NIH Intramural Sequencing Center. It extended performance from 3 Sep 2020 to 2 Mar 2026, a 5.5-year run with no competition. The stated reason was that switching reagents 'could jeopardize research outcomes'. The Intramural Sequencing Center is one of the largest federal users, and its follow-on is the 2026 NHGRI $90M vehicle. This shows a research account that has not used a rival to force a re-bid.
items.quote: Illumina's proprietary systems require specific reagents
items.why_new: The Intramural Sequencing Center contract history and the continuity into the 2026 vehicle were not in the known sources.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: Even DoD buys of Illumina reagents are being routed through overseas distributors on sole-source grounds, which adds channel margin rather than discounts.
items.detail: DHA posted a special notice (PANDHA25P0000028745) on 7 Jan 2026, amended 13 Jan, for a BPA for brand-name Illumina reagents, kits and consumables for AFRIMS/WRAIR in Bangkok. The intended sole-source awardee is Bio-Active Co., Ltd (Thailand), a distributor, not Illumina. No value or discount is stated. This is the same distributor-channel pattern as the IDIBAPS tender. It is weak evidence, but it suggests that overseas federal buyers pay distributor prices.
items.quote: validated compatibility with Illumina sequencing platforms
items.why_new: This distributor-based DoD BPA is not in the known list.

items.label: 2B
items.claim: A Canadian federal research lab bought an Element AVITI in mid-2025, citing lower reagent costs, then paid to upgrade it 11 months later instead of adding Illumina capacity.
items.detail: NRC's Human Health Therapeutics centre posted Advance Contract Award Notice 25-58071 on 20 Jun 2025. It sought an NGS instrument using avidite base chemistry to 'increase throughput and reduce reagent costs'. NRC then posted notice 26-58031 on 14 May 2026 for an AVITI24 upgrade, awarded to Element on 2 Jun 2026 as contract 1043467 for CAD 141,250. The upgrade gives +50% output with 'existing consumables' unchanged and adds in situ multiomics. Correction to the probe note: the notice estimated CAD 122,000, and the award came in 15.8% higher (141,250 / 122,000 = 1.158). The notice was published 14 May and awarded 2 Jun, not 29 May.
items.quote: seeking the purchase of a NGS instrument that increases throughput and reduces reagent costs
items.why_new: The known list shows only the Element AVITI24 hardware and the NRC's choice. It lacks the 2025 first-purchase notice, its stated reagent-cost motive, and the awarded value.

items.label: 2A
items.claim: A federal animal-disease genomics lab ran an open lowest-price tender for a benchtop sequencer and awarded it to Element for CAD 315,000.
items.detail: The CFIA National Centre for Foreign Animal Disease (Winnipeg) published RFP 39903-260455 on 24 Dec 2025. It closed on 19 Jan 2026 and used 'Lowest Price' as the only selection criterion. Contract CW2434465 went to Element Biosciences (CAD 315,000) on 18 Feb 2026. The number of bidders is not stated and Illumina is not named, so we cannot say whether Illumina bid. It does show a government research buyer choosing a supplier by price in a competitive process.
items.why_new: A competitive, price-only government tender won by Element was not in the known list. The known items are mostly sole-source or core price sheets.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: A Canadian university genomics core that still runs NovaSeq 6000s is moving to the X as a 'replacement and expansion', which shows 6000-to-X conversion continuing at research and clinical cores in 2026.
items.detail: The University of Calgary (Centre for Health Genomics and Informatics) posted Advance Contract Award Notice AB-2026-04518 on 16 Jun 2026, closing 23 Jun 2026. It describes the NovaSeq X as the 'next-generation replacement and expansion' of its Illumina ecosystem, which includes 'NovaSeq 6000 instrumentation'. It calls the buy 'a continuation of an existing platform strategy'. The notice does not say whether the 6000 will be retired, and it gives no value or quantity.
items.quote: continuation of an existing platform strategy rather than the introduction of a new technology
items.why_new: This is a named Canadian university 6000-to-X migration notice, dated Jun 2026. The known list has no Canadian procurement of this kind.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: Calgary's internal NovaSeq 6000 S4 lane and kit prices rose about 4–5% from mid-2024 to 2025, so list pricing on the 6000 tail is not being cut at this core.
items.detail: The CHGI internal list for the S4 v1.5 300-cycle one-lane option (PE150, ~750 Gb spec) was CAD 5,600 in June 2024 and CAD 5,820 in the 2025 list, a rise of 3.9%. On the 750 Gb spec that is $7.47 and then $7.76 per Gb. The full S4 300-cycle kit went from CAD 21,371 to CAD 22,420, up 4.9%. The same core is now buying an X, so it is reselling 6000 capacity at higher prices while it migrates. These figures come from search-result snippets, because the PDFs could not be rendered. They contrast with the Salk and EPFL 6000 price cuts already known, and are similar to the CNAG ~4% rise.
items.source_name: University of Calgary CHGI internal price lists (June 2024, 2025)
items.why_new: This gives a dated two-point 6000 price series at a core not previously used. It shows increases, which cuts against 6000 price erosion.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: Government buyers keep justifying Illumina purchases as sole-source on compatibility grounds, which limits how much extra discount they can extract.
items.detail: Calgary's notice says Illumina Canada ULC is the 'sole Canadian distributor' and that the system is proprietary. PHSA's 2023 notice (BCPHSA_12658) was a one-year, non-volume direct award of up to CAD 4.3M to Illumina Canada for NovaSeq 6000 and X Plus consumables at BC Cancer. Its stated reason was 'compatibility with existing products/systems', and it gave no unit prices. PHSA also issued a notice for CAD 2.9M of Infinium arrays over four years (closing 13 Mar 2026). I found no 2025–26 renewal of the PHSA NovaSeq consumables award. Public buyers are not running price-based competition for the installed Illumina base, though that applies to instruments and arrays, not necessarily to HT flow cells.
items.quote: to ensure compatibility with existing products/systems
items.why_new: The known list covers US federal 'only one responsible source' use. These are Canadian provincial and university notices, with the PHSA $4.3M consumables ceiling as a baseline.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: Canadian federal labs are still buying Illumina mid-throughput instruments on non-competitive awards in late 2025 and early 2026.
items.detail: Illumina Canada ULC received directed contracts for a NextSeq 1000 (CW2414712, CAD 276,132, Sep 2025–Mar 2026), and for NextSeq 2000 systems (CW2431423, CAD 404,866.81, Dec 2025–Mar 2026, Ontario, and CW2436812, CAD 404,860.78, Jan 2026–Mar 2027, National Capital Region, Health Canada). These are small amounts, about CAD 1.09M in total. They show mid-throughput demand holding up at government labs, which weakens the claim that mid-throughput and research demand is eroding to Element. They also add placements to Illumina's instrument base.
items.source_name: CanadaBuys award notices CW2414712, CW2431423, CW2436812
items.why_new: The known list has no Illumina mid-throughput government award data. This is a small offset to the AVITI-win items above.

items.label: 2A
items.claim: Canada's agriculture department set up a six-provider competitive sequencing-services pool, so government research demand is being steered to outsourced, price-competed providers.
items.detail: AAFC's Request for Supply Arrangement 01R11-231050 awarded places to the University of Toronto, UBC Life Sciences Institute, Génome Québec, Edinburgh Genetics, Metagenom Bio and GIFS AG Tech. Terms are 48–54 months, ending Mar 2030, and the first awards began 29 Sep 2025. Contract values are listed as CAD 0, so there are no spend figures and the platforms are not named. The structure is as-and-when work competed among providers, the outsourced model that the known core and Novogene evidence says is price-led.
items.source_name: CanadaBuys award notices CW2444034, CW2419630, CW2419637, CW2419641, CW2430293, CW2419634
items.why_new: This is a new government outsourcing channel, with a dated Sep 2025–Mar 2026 award wave. It is not a price or volume figure.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: Canada's public-health lab has run a sole-source Illumina reagent standing offer with a very large ceiling, though the record is internally inconsistent.
items.detail: PHAC's National Microbiology Laboratory standing offer CW2237770 (WS3625214747) is a non-competitive 'Exclusive Rights' award to Illumina Canada ULC for genomic-sequencing reagents. The page shows an amendment value of CAD 30,000,000 but a total of CAD 0 and conflicting amendment dates (2022, 2024, 2026). A ceiling is not spend, so it cannot be used as volume evidence. I treat it as a possible sign of large public-health sequencing demand and flag it for follow-up.
items.why_new: A government sequencing-reagent standing offer with a CAD 30M amendment ceiling was not in the known list.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: At UCLA the premium of 10B over 25B per read shrank from about 58% to about 26% because 10B was cut and 25B was held.
items.detail: Assuming lane output scales with flow-cell cluster count (25B:10B = 1:0.4), 10B-300 cost (2,234/0.4)/3,538 = 1.58x the 25B per unit of output in the 2024 sheet. On the 2026 page it costs (1,765.67/0.4)/3,512.47 = 1.26x. The lane-output assumption is mine, not UCLA's. Equivalently, the 25B discount per Gb versus 10B narrowed from about -37% to about -20%. The 25B price barely moved while the 10B price fell, so the within-X price ladder has been flattened by cuts to the lower tiers.
items.why_new: Known data had the 10B to 25B step at -24% to -37% per Gb at cores; UCLA's own time series shows it narrowing as the 10B tier reprices.
items.verify_note: Verified: 10B-300 non-profit $2,234 (Aug 2023 and Mar 2024) → $1,765.67 external (1 Jul 2026), −21%. 25B-300 $3,538 → $3,512.47. Using Illumina's output specs (10B-300 ~3 Tb / 8 lanes = 375 Gb; 25B-300 ~8 Tb / 8 lanes = 1 Tb, ratio 0.375, not 0.4), the 10B per-Gb premium falls from ~68% to ~34%. UCLA marks X lanes as 'material pass-through at cost', so this tracks UCLA's purchase price. It largely quantifies the known 'harmonised cost per read across 5B/10B/25B' (late 2025), so it is incremental

items.label: 1B
items.claim: UCLA's 25B-300 lane price was essentially unchanged across nearly three years, which cuts against fast discounting on the flagship flow cell at this core.
items.detail: The external non-profit price was $3,538 in Aug 2023 and again in Mar 2024 (the 6/18/2024 revision is identical), and is $3,512.47 on the 1 Jul 2026 page (-0.7%). Internal 25B-300 was $3,168 in 2023-24. Core rates are pass-through plus labor and policy, not Illumina's net price. Library prep at the same core rose over the period: stranded mRNA prep $63 to $68.14 (+8%), DNA prep $61 to $68.90 (+13%).
items.why_new: This is a three-point time series for the 25B at one major core; the 25B-300 was known only as a $3.51 snapshot.
items.verify_note: Verified: 25B-300 $3,168 internal / $3,538 non-profit / $3,933 profit in both the Aug 2023 and Mar 2024 sheets; $3,512.47 external on the 1 Jul 2026 page. The footnote says X lanes are 'Material Pass Through rates… at cost', which makes this a better proxy for UCLA's Illumina purchase price than a policy rate. Prep rises verified: mRNA $63 → $68.14, DNA $61 → $68.90. Consistent with the known Harvard +17.8% FY27 move. List-anchored pass-through at a mid-size core; large-account net prices could

items.label: 1A
items.claim: The 6000 lane price at UCLA fell 10-16% from Jul 2022 to Aug 2023, before the 6000 was withdrawn, so list-price erosion on the 6000 started well before conversion.
items.detail: Internal S4-300 went $5,356.20 to $4,817 (-10.1%) and SP-300 $2,765.55 to $2,406 (-13.0%). S1-300 went $4,069.50 to $3,719 (-8.6%) and S2-300 $6,655.35 to $6,407 (-3.7%). External S4-300 was $6,014.15 in 2022 and $5,057 non-profit in 2023 (-15.9%); the 2022 external column may not match the 2023 non-profit column. Cuts came while X was still new, consistent with 6000 pricing being pushed down.
items.why_new: Known 6000 list cuts were Salk and EPFL; this is a 2022-23 UCLA series for all four 6000 flow cells.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: On Aug 2023 UCLA rates the 6000 S4 lane cost about 1.9x the X Plus 25B lane per Gb, and the 1.5B X lane was priced above the SP lane.
items.detail: Taking spec yields of ~750 Gb per S4 lane (3 Tb over 4 lanes) and ~1 Tb per 25B lane, S4-300 at $5,057 gives $6.74/Gb against 25B-300 at $3,538 giving $3.54/Gb (ratio 1.9x). Yield figures are my approximations. Against the 10B-300 ($2,234 per ~375 Gb = $5.96/Gb) the S4 premium is only about 13%. So the 25B, not the 10B, carried the large per-Gb price gap that drives conversion drag.
items.why_new: Gives a same-core 6000-vs-X per-Gb ratio at a point in time; known 3.4x is the revenue-per-Gb ratio on Illumina's own data.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: UCLA's price for rival MGI DNBseq T7 flow cells fell 36-37% between the Mar 2024 sheet and the Jul 2026 page.
items.detail: T7-300 fell from $4,736 to $3,043 (-35.7%), T7-200 from $4,248 to $2,688.95 (-36.7%), and T7-150 now lists at $3,651.20. These are the 2024 non-profit and 2026 external columns. The same core's Nanopore GridION run fell $2,644 to $1,951.33 (-26%). A university core is therefore passing through falling low-cost-rival run prices while the Illumina 25B stayed flat.
items.why_new: Known MGI evidence was unit counts and a T7+ cost claim; this is a priced time series at a US core.
items.verify_note: Verified on the Mar 2024 sheet: T7 non-profit 50c $3,643, 200c $4,248, 300c $4,736. July 2026: 200c $2,688.95 (−36.7%), 300c $3,043 (−35.7%), 150c $3,651.20 (a new SKU, oddly priced above 200/300c, so it may be a different flowcell format). The ONT −26% is not like-for-like: the 2024 row was 'Library Construction & Sequencing' per flowcell, while the 2026 row is GridION per flowcell. Drop the ONT figure or caveat it. The T7 cut is MGI pricing, not a Ultima/Element/Roche effect, but it supports t

items.label: 2A
items.claim: UCLA Illumina X Plus lane-price cuts of ~20-29% on 10B and 1.5B hit a research-heavy core, while its non-sequencing items rose or were mixed.
items.detail: UCLA's own 10X 3' GEX fresh prep fell $2,093 to $1,810.81 (-13.5%). Visium HD rose $6,977 to $7,725 (+10.7%), and MiSeq v3 PE150 fell $1,814 to $1,791 (-1.2%). Sequencing lines on the Illumina X tiers fell most. This suggests the research buyer base sees larger per-run reductions on Illumina's X flow cells than on other services.
items.why_new: No prior comparison of UCLA 2024 vs 2026 lines; this contrasts X-lane cuts with other services.

items.label: 2B
items.claim: UCLA now carries a 5B lane and a 25B-100 lane at tiered prices, adding more X price points that make cheaper capacity available to research buyers.
items.detail: New 2026 lines are 5B-100/200/300 at $1,210.42/$1,351.61/$1,462.87 per lane, 25B-100 at $2,164.94 and 25B-200 at $3,202.38. The 2024 sheet had only 25B-300. Per unit of output (assuming 5B = 0.2 of a 25B lane), the 5B-300 costs about 2.1x the 25B and the 10B about 1.26x, so the 25B stays the cheapest per Gb. Added mid-size SKUs let smaller research projects move to X at lower ticket price.
items.why_new: Gives the full UCLA 5B/25B-100/25B-200 ladder; only the 25B-300 was known.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: At MD Anderson's core, the 6000's S4 lane cost about 2.5x the X Plus 25B lane per Gb, a ~61% step down. The 6000's own lane price was flat to rising before the X.
items.detail: MD Anderson ATGC FY2022/23/24 schedules (search-result summary; my direct fetch of the files returned 404) show the S4-300 Xp lane at $4,933 (FY22), $4,901 (FY23) and $5,167 (FY24) for MDA members. That is +4.8% FY23→FY24. External users paid $8,475, $8,430 and $8,805 (+4.4% FY23→FY24). The current X Plus page (opened) lists the 25B-300 lane at $2,595, 3.2B read pairs per lane. At ~750 Gb per S4 lane, the member 6000 price is ~$6.89/Gb. At ~960 Gb per 25B lane, the X Plus price is ~$2.70/Gb, so ~−61% (6000 = ~2.55x X). The user class for the $2,595 is not stated, and the S4 and X Plus prices are not the same fiscal year. The page's own 'up to 60% reduction in sequencing price' fits this.
items.source_name: MD Anderson Advanced Technology Genomics Core (ATGC) price schedules and X Plus page
items.quote: Up to 60% reduction in sequencing price (depending upon sequencing type)
items.why_new: MD Anderson is not in the known core list. It gives a named 6000-to-X per-Gb step (~−61%) and shows 6000 list prices were rising into FY24.
items.verify_note: A search snippet of the MDA X Plus page confirms the $2,595 price for a 25B-300 lane (3.2B read pairs per lane). When I opened the page directly I got the read table but no prices, and no user class is shown. The S4 figures ($4,933/$4,901/$5,167 member) come from FY22–24 PDFs that I could not open. The page's claim of 'up to 60% reduction' does not name the 6000 as the baseline. The comparison also crosses fiscal years. The ~2.5x gap is below the known blended 6000/X revenue-per-Gb ratio of ~3.4

items.label: 1A
items.claim: Where 6000 lanes were still sold in FY24, their price was held or raised, which is consistent with the tail being less price-elastic.
items.detail: MD Anderson S4-300 Xp lane prices ran $4,933 → $4,901 → $5,167 across FY22–FY24 for members (+4.7% over two years). The external rate went $8,475 → $8,430 → $8,805 (+3.9%). Salk and EPFL cut 6000 prices, and CNAG raised them ~4%. MD Anderson's 6000 pricing therefore looks like the 'raise on the tail' pattern, not the 'cut' pattern. The figures come from a search-result summary of the schedules, so they are unverified at file level.
items.source_name: MD Anderson ATGC FY2022, FY2023 and FY2024 price schedules
items.why_new: Adds a third core's 6000 price direction (up ~4–5% in FY24) next to the known Salk cut and CNAG rise.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: Core price ladders imply each larger X flow cell cuts per-read price by ~33–35%. A 35B with +40% output priced on the same ladder would cut per-Gb price by about 14%.
items.detail: TCAG (Apr 2025, CAD): 10B-300 C$2,080 and 25B-300 C$3,470 per lane, ratio 1.67x. MD Anderson: $1,523 vs $2,595, ratio 1.70x. Output per lane is 1.25B vs 3.2B pairs (2.56x), so price rises only ~1.68x for 2.56x output. That gives a price-to-output exponent of ln1.68/ln2.56 ≈ 0.55. Per M pairs: TCAG C$1,664 (10B) vs C$1,084 (25B), −35%. MD Anderson $1,218 vs $811, −33%. A 35B with 1.4x the output of the 25B would then cost ~1.4^0.55 ≈ 1.20x per lane, ~−14% per Gb. That is smaller than the ~20% estimate from the ex-Illumina AD. If Illumina prices more aggressively than the historical ladder, the cut would be larger.
items.source_name: TCAG NGS Price List Apr 2025 and MD Anderson ATGC X Plus page
items.why_new: First ladder-based derivation of the 35B per-Gb cut from two core price lists. It brackets the single ex-AD figure of ~20% from below.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: Mid-throughput X flow cells carry far higher per-read prices than the 25B, so the mid-throughput tier is the most exposed to cheaper rivals.
items.detail: TCAG Apr 2025 (opened): the 1.5B-300 lane is C$2,485 for ~0.8B pairs (C$3,106 per M pairs/1000). The 10B-300 is C$2,080 for 1.25B (C$1,664). The 25B-300 is C$3,470 for 3.2B (C$1,084). The 1.5B per-read price is 2.9x the 25B and 1.9x the 10B. At MD Anderson, 1.5B-300 is $2,166 for 0.8B ($2,708 per B pairs) vs $811 for the 25B, 3.3x. The 1.5B lane costs more than a 10B lane at TCAG. A lab needing small runs pays 3x per read, which is the segment where Element, MiSeq i100 and others compete.
items.source_name: TCAG NGS Price List; MD Anderson ATGC X Plus page
items.why_new: Quantifies the per-read premium on the 1.5B flow cell at two cores. The known corpus covers only the 10B-to-25B step.

items.label: 2A
items.claim: Johns Hopkins GRCF charges the same $650 for a 30x human genome on the 6000 and on the X Plus. The reagent saving of roughly $450 per genome is kept by the core, not passed on to users.
items.detail: The GRCF 6000 WGS page and the separate X Plus WGS page both list $650 per genome (30x), with a saliva surcharge of 25% on the older page and 20% on the X Plus page. At ~100 Gb per genome, S4 reagent at ~$6.9–7.2/Gb is ~$690–720, and 25B reagent at ~$2.6–2.7/Gb is ~$260–270, a gap of ~$430–460 per genome. TCAG prices the same product at C$650 and NGI at ~6,000 SEK. Research end-customers are not seeing price falls, so cores are not passing savings on and are not a price-fighting buyer base here. The JHU page text was read via search snippets because direct fetch returned 403. The 6000 page may be stale.
items.source_name: JHU Genetic Resources Core Facility (GRCF) WGS pages
items.quote: Price per Sample $650* *Saliva samples require a 20% additional charge
items.why_new: The known corpus notes only the existence of two JHU pages. This compares them and puts a dollar figure on the unshared saving.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: At research cores, sequencing reagent is still about half of a retail 30x genome's price, so sequencing cost is not yet a minor line in research WGS.
items.detail: TCAG Apr 2025: human 30x including prep, 90–100 Gb, is C$650. PCR-free prep is C$140 (22%). Sequencing is ~95 Gb of a ~960 Gb 25B lane at C$3,470, or ~C$343 (53%). The remaining ~C$167 (26%) is handling, QC and margin. NGI's 6,000 SEK all-in includes bioinformatics, and its 25B lane example is 32,000 SEK, so ~3,200 SEK of sequencing per genome on the same maths (~53%). This cuts against 'sequencing cost no longer binds' for research WGS. The known 5–10% share applies to clinical workflow cost, not research core price.
items.source_name: TCAG price list; NGI Sweden price examples
items.why_new: Decomposes a retail core genome price into prep, sequencing and margin. This is a watch-out for the 'cost not the constraint' claim.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: Johns Hopkins cores price by sample count, and the discounts are steep: exome tiers fall 53% from small to large projects, and WGS is cheaper above 192 samples.
items.detail: GRCF exome pages list $950 per sample for 1–23 samples and $450 for 128+, a 53% fall. The JHU CIDR sheet (updated 1 Feb 2024) lists 30x WGS at $500–600 scaled by sample count above 192 samples, with a 25% saliva surcharge. The $500–600 range is a ~17% spread, and the sheet notes lower prices can be negotiated by project. The figures are search-result snippets. This is core-level pricing, not Illumina's own, but it shows large-project buyers get materially lower unit prices and pass that pressure upstream. It also adds a second, larger volume tier to the known ~9% 25B 2+ flow-cell tier at another core.
items.source_name: JHU CIDR price sheet and GRCF exome pages
items.why_new: Provides a quantified large-account tier (−53% exome, −17% WGS) from JHU. The known list has only a 9% flow-cell tier at another core.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: Sweden's national sequencing infrastructure (NGI) still charges about 32,000 SEK per 25B lane. That is above US core lane prices and shows no sign of a collapse.
items.detail: NGI price examples (last updated 24 Jun 2026; prices flagged 'as of 2025-02-01') cost one 25B-300 lane (~3B read pairs) at 32,000 SEK. Library prep is 1,200 SEK per sample. A human 30x PCR-free genome is ~6,000 SEK all-in with bioinformatics. At an assumed 9.5–10 SEK/USD (my assumption), the lane is ~$3.2–3.4K vs MD Anderson $2,595 and TCAG C$3,470. NGI also moved to unit pricing: 600M read pairs per unit, with 5B = 1, 10B = 2 and 25B = 5 units (announcement dated 2025/11), which removes any flow-cell-size discount. The lane price may be stale relative to the page date.
items.quote: approx. 6000 SEK total/sample
items.why_new: NGI is not in the known core list. It is a European national-infrastructure price point and a flat per-read pricing unit.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: University of Turku (FFGC) ran a tender in Oct 2024 to upgrade a NovaSeq 6000 bought in 2019 to a NovaSeq X, so the replacement cycle is landing on ~5-year-old boxes.
items.detail: The Mercell notice (published 31 Oct 2024) covers one NovaSeq X system plus a separate DRAGEN server. It says the existing NovaSeq 6000, purchased in 2019, must be upgraded to 'the newest instrument version'. Value and award are not stated. A five-year-old 6000 being swapped fits the retiring-tail narrative, though it was a core-style centre, which is the cohort already largely converted.
items.why_new: A Nordic 6000 replacement tender with the 2019 purchase year is not on the known list.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: Third-party service contracts show 6000s still being maintained in Europe, and one costs more than the service on a newer X Plus.
items.detail: Motol University Hospital (Prague) awarded GeneTiCA s.r.o. a CZK 13,000,000 ex-VAT 'repair, maintenance and service of the NOVA Seq 6000D' on 5 Nov 2024 (about €0.53M at ~24.5 CZK/EUR; term not stated). Charles University 1st Medical Faculty's X Plus post-warranty service was listed at CZK 9,750,000 (Oct 2025, same vendor), about 25% lower, though terms may differ. Aachen University Hospital also tendered NovaSeq 6000 maintenance in Mar 2026 (search-snippet level). The hospital keeps paying for a clinical-genetics 6000 into 2026+, consistent with the long tail management describes.
items.source_name: Publications Office of the EU; BidSonar (Charles University)
items.why_new: Czech 6000D service award and the X Plus service comparison are not in the known list. Only a Leeds NHS 6000 call-off was found earlier.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: European hospitals are adding NovaSeq X Plus capacity on top of existing instruments, which supports clinical volume growth.
items.detail: Region Hovedstaden (Rigshospitalet, Copenhagen) bought an 'additional' NovaSeq X Plus for whole-genome analyses to 'extend existing capacity' and let the two instruments back each other up, final value DKK 8,500,000 ex-VAT (~€1.14M at ~7.46 DKK/EUR; award date not shown). Region Syddanmark (Odense Clinical Genetics) awarded a NovaSeq X Plus by negotiated procedure on 5 May 2026 (value not seen). Graz Medical University (human genetics diagnostics) awarded a X Plus system to Illumina Austria for €954,498 on 16 Dec 2024, on price alone. Hospital genomics labs are still buying sole-source Illumina capacity. This cuts against the thesis that volume is plateauing, though the dates are 2024–2026 and the volume impact is unquantified.
items.source_name: Publications Office of the EU / TED (Rigshospitalet, Odense, Graz)
items.quote: extend existing capacity
items.why_new: Specific European hospital capacity-add awards with euro values were not previously listed.

items.label: 2B
items.claim: A Chinese-owned sequencing service provider (BMK GmbH) keeps winning Spanish public-research sequencing contracts, which supports low-cost outsourcing pressure.
items.detail: The Spanish award aggregator lists 28 awards to Biomarker Technologies (BMK) GmbH in the last three years. Five were visible, from Jun to Sep 2026: CSIC (10 Jun, NovaSeq X Plus, 7 Tenebrio genomes plus ancient-DNA pool), FRCB-IDIBAPS (29 Jul, Illumina sequencing for project PI24/00982), CSIC RNA-seq (13 Jul), CSIC (14 Aug, 100 reptile RNA samples on NovaSeq X PE150) and Universidad de Málaga (16 Sep, Iso-seq). Amounts are hidden. The workload runs on Illumina X flow cells but is priced at a low-cost provider's rates, so Illumina's lane price is set by the aggregator's price, not the end buyer's. IDIBAPS also posted a separate 2026 lane-based service tender (528143-2026) with lots of 12 25B flow cells at 100 cycles and 100 independent 25B-300 lanes over 760 days; estimated values were not retrievable.
items.why_new: BMK's repeated Spanish awards are new. Earlier work found Novogene-type outsourcing at cores but no named EU public-tender winner.

items.label: 2B
items.claim: Public hospitals and universities in Europe are buying Element AVITI systems at roughly $320–390K, well below the ~$500K list in the known file, often by sole-source justification.
items.detail: Innsbruck Medical University (Institute of Pathology, ref V24-18r) listed a final contract value of €293,439.34 for an AVITI system with ancillary services, described as 'mandatory for patient therapy'. The Edinburgh notice shows a total value of £290,640. The Natural History Museum (London) made a £157,544 direct award for an upgrade (3-year term, options to 2030). Leiden UMC published a voluntary ex-ante notice (7 Nov 2025) to award an AVITI24 to Element Biosciences Netherlands. A German university hospital's negotiated award (TED 318692-2026, Jan 2026) found only Element could supply the required service. These are small, but clinical-genetics labs are choosing Element in public procurement, which gives rivals a price-signal foothold.
items.source_name: Publications Office of the EU; TED; Find a Tender (search snippets for Edinburgh, NHM, LUMC, UKA)
items.why_new: Named EU/UK public AVITI purchases with values (Innsbruck, Edinburgh, NHM, LUMC) were not in the known list, which only has NRC Canada.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: Czech and Baltic public buyers use framework or distributor structures for NovaSeq X kits, hiding Illumina's net price. Estimated values give a sizing, not a unit price.
items.detail: Charles University 1st Medical Faculty (TED 301608-2026, OJ 4 May 2026) ran a framework for 'sequencing kits compatible with NovaSeq X Plus' with an estimated value of CZK 12,000,000 (about €0.49M) for Q4 2025 supplies, open procedure Z2023-059058. The University of Tartu concluded a €1.0M framework (Mar 2026) for Illumina consumables across iScan, MiSeq, NextSeq 2000 and NovaSeq, awarded to distributor Nova natura OÜ. Riga Stradiņš University awarded an NGS platform to Nova natura for €109,671 (Apr 2026). Distributor intermediation and open competition at the reseller level are consistent with large-account discounting being negotiated outside Illumina's own disclosures. No unit prices.
items.source_name: BidsFactory (TED mirror); TED 301608-2026 via search result
items.why_new: The Estonian, Latvian and Czech consumable and platform awards are new. The known list has only Spain and Germany.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: A UK public lab and European public labs continue to commit sizeable multi-year budgets to Illumina X-series consumables.
items.detail: Tartu's €1.0M Illumina consumables framework (Mar 2026) and Charles University's CZK 12M kit framework (~€0.49M per quarter-year of supply, estimate) show institutions budgeting for flow cells beyond 2026. CIBER's 225-flow-cell tender (€2.88M) at one centre alone equals roughly 225 × 8 Tb nominal 25B output, about 1.8 Pb if 2×150 (derived from the Illumina spec cited by the search tool). That shows demand for dense capacity from public research consortia, not saturation.
items.why_new: The Gb equivalent of the CIBER buy and the cross-country framework budgets give a volume context the known list lacked.

items.label: 2A
items.claim: Part of European research sequencing spend is funded by one-off recovery money (NextGenerationEU / ISCIII), a funding-cliff risk for 2026–27 research consumables.
items.detail: The IDIBAPS 25B kit order (project PMPER24/00011) was funded by Instituto de Salud Carlos III and NextGenerationEU. NextGenerationEU spending must be committed by 2026 under EU rules, so similar grants will roll off. Single example, so only a directional signal for EU research consumables.
items.why_new: The EU recovery-fund source of research flow-cell money is not in the known 2A funding evidence, which is US-focused.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: Many public buyers are locked into Illumina through sole-source justifications and notices with token values, which limits visible discounting.
items.detail: Helmholtz Munich's 'div. Nova Seq X Kits' (ref 4500217555, 6 Dec 2024) was awarded to Illumina GmbH at a placeholder €1.00. Warsaw's Children's Health Centre awarded PLN 3,823,656.20 of Illumina reagents (18 Dec 2024) to exclusive distributor Analityk Ewa Kowalczyk, with the title itself noting the distributor is exclusive and award on price (100%). Illumina's exclusivity in the channel means open price competition on consumables is rare.
items.why_new: The Warsaw PLN 3.82M exclusive-distributor award is new. Helmholtz is known but not the Polish pattern.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: Per-Gb price paid for the NovaSeq 6000 S4-300 kit at one university core is still about 2x the X 25B rate at the same core, so no sign the gap is narrowing there.
items.detail: UConn's Center for Genome Innovation rate page (updated Jan 2025, 'current through Feb 2025') lists the NovaSeq 6000 S4 v1.5 300-cycle kit at $16,578 internal contract price, plus 6.5% shipping. At the roughly 3,000 Gb nominal S4 output (my assumption) that is about $5.5/Gb. UConn's X 25B price of about $2.94/Gb is already in the known list. The page shows no earlier 6000 prices, so there is no change over time. Rutgers' 2022 sheet showed S4-300 at $15,230 (from a search snippet; the PDF was unreadable), which would be +8.9% by Feb 2025 across two different institutions. That is a weak comparison.
items.source_name: UConn Center for Genome Innovation service rates
items.why_new: UConn's X 25B price is known; the S4-300 $16,578 and the Rutgers $15,230 (2022) pairing are not in the exclusion list.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: BillionToOne's prenatal revenue is still growing +55% in Q2'26, and oncology is up +176%, so the NIPT-maturation drag is not visible at this lab.
items.detail: Prenatal revenue was $94.2M versus $60.9M in Q2'26 (+55%). H1 prenatal was $190.8M (+63%). Oncology was $13.7M versus $4.9M (+176%). Total revenue was $109.4M (+64%), gross margin was 70% versus 65%, and FY26 revenue guidance of $450–465M was reiterated. The company is a share gainer and is expanding its panel (the 130-gene Unity Fetal Risk Screen), so this is a watch-out for the NIPT-maturation argument. Part of the growth is price: ASP is up 21%.
items.why_new: The known list has only 'BillionToOne +35%' (tests). This adds the segment revenue split, H1 figures and gross margin.
items.verify_note: The press release confirms the numbers: prenatal $94.2M vs $60.9M, oncology $13.7M vs $4.9M, total $109.4M (+64%), gross margin 70% vs 65%, and FY26 guidance of $450–465M reiterated. Total tests accessioned grew only 33% (197K vs 148K), and that figure includes fast-growing oncology. The +21% ASP gain explains most of the gap between revenue growth and test growth. Prenatal test growth is not split out and is probably below 33%. Test growth of about 35% is already on the known list, so only the

items.label: 2A
items.claim: A published university-wide Illumina consumables contract shows only a modest 10% minimum discount floor, not 'insane' discounts, at least for Oxford.
items.detail: Oxford's finance procurement page lists an agreement with Illumina Cambridge Ltd. It sets a minimum 10% off published list on consumables and 20% on equipment, with no delivery charges. The page gives no date, no tiers and no actual realized discount, so it is a contractual floor and weak evidence of research discount depth. It was read via search-result snippet only, because the page redirected.
items.source_name: University of Oxford Finance, Sequencing equipment & services
items.quote: minimum discount of 10% from published list price on consumables
items.why_new: Not in the known list: no Oxford or other university contract discount floor has been captured.

items.label: 2A
items.claim: The University of California system renegotiated a UC-wide Illumina agreement in 2024 covering instruments, reagents and research services, which shows a consolidated buyer using purchasing leverage.
items.detail: UCOP announced a new systemwide Illumina agreement (CalUsource #2023003585) on 9 Apr 2024. It covers sequencing instruments, reagents, discounted service agreements (25% off) and research services. No reagent discount percentages or renewal dates are public, so depth and trend cannot be measured from this page.
items.source_name: UC Office of the President, Procurement
items.why_new: The UC systemwide contract and its 25% service-agreement discount are not in the known list.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: Element's scale is still small (about 450 systems, $58–85M FY25 revenue), which limits how much price pressure it alone can put on Illumina in the near term.
items.detail: Element ended 2025 with more than 450 AVITI systems (+60%), against about 40 units to 190 in the prior 12-month comparison. Revenue was about $85M per GenomeWeb or $58M per a Substack summary of the JPM talk, missing the $100M target. For scale, Illumina's sequencing consumables run about $775M a quarter. Illumina's X had 352 placements in its first year, versus Element's 112 (known list).
items.source_name: Element JPM 2026 / Rhymes with Haystack / GenomeWeb (search snippets)
items.why_new: It gives the year-end 2025 installed base (450+), the FY25 revenue miss versus the $100M target, and the clinical mix (>25%). The known list does not have these.
items.verify_note: Vilella's Substack confirms the >450 AVITI base and $58M of 2025 revenue. GenomeWeb's ~$85M was not verified, so treat revenue as a $58–85M range from conflicting sources. The '40 units to 190' comparison in the detail is garbled and should be dropped. The 450-system base and the miss against the $100M target are not on the known list.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: Ultima says about half of its customers sign long-term minimum-consumable contracts, a structure that locks large buyers into non-Illumina volume.
items.detail: From search snippets of the JPM 2026 remarks: the installed base doubled in 2025, is split about half research and half clinical, and about half of customers have long-term contracts with minimum utilization. Named customers are Arc, Myriad, Quest, Broad and Mayo. This is a vendor statement and not independently verified. It supports the idea that big accounts use rival commitments as leverage. Quest and Myriad were already known as development-stage collaborations.
items.source_name: Ultima Genomics JPM 2026 (search-result snippet; primary not opened)
items.why_new: It gives installed-base doubling, the research/clinical split and the share of contracted customers. The known list has only collaborations and prices.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: A one-million-biospecimen multi-omics program (Precure) picked Ultima's UG200 Ultra, so new population-scale volume is landing outside Illumina.
items.detail: Ultima announced on 22 Sep 2026 that UG200 Ultra was selected for Precure, the Mayo Clinic initiative with Thermo Fisher. It is rated up to 60,000 30x genomes a year. This is volume Illumina does not get, although Precure's Gb size and start date are undisclosed. One report names Helix as the sequencing operator, which conflicts with the Unite.AI account.
items.why_new: Precure (22 Sep 2026) is not in the known list, which has only UK Biobank/Truveta proteomics on Ultima.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: At one pass-through-priced core, the per-Gb price gap between Illumina's 25B and MGI's T7 widened from ~1.1x to ~1.7x between Mar 2024 and Jul 2026, because the T7 was cut ~36% while the 25B stayed flat.
items.detail: UCLA TCGB non-profit/external rates: 25B-300 lane $3,538 (Mar 2024) → $3,512.47 (Jul 2026), ~1 Tb per lane at spec, so ~$3.54 → $3.51/Gb. T7-300 flowcell $4,736 → $3,043. At an assumed ~1.5 Tb per T7 PE150 flowcell (our assumption from the ~6 Tb / 4-flowcell run spec), that is ~$3.16 → ~$2.03/Gb. Illumina's per-Gb premium over MGI at this core therefore rose from ~12% to ~73%, while the rival cut its price and Illumina held list. Output-per-flowcell assumptions drive the level but not the direction.
items.source_name: UCLA TCGB rate sheets (Mar 2024 PDF; Jul 2026 page)
items.quote: Material Pass Through rates are at cost
items.why_new: The known list has a UCLA 25B point price only. No MGI price trend or Illumina-vs-MGI gap over time is in the corpus.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: A core sells an all-in 30x Ultima genome for less than the Illumina 25B reagent pass-through alone would cost for the same data at another core.
items.detail: UMGC sells a 30x UG100 genome (prep, sequencing, QC and DeepVariant/GATK calling) at $192 internal / $221 external. At UCSD IGM the 25B-300 lane is $2,800 UC / $3,836 outside (~$2.92 / $4.00 per Gb at ~960 Gb). A 30x genome needs ~100–120 Gb, so that is ~$290–350 internal / ~$400–480 external for sequencing only, before prep. Ultima's full workflow price at a core is therefore ~35–55% below Illumina's sequencing-only cost at research-core rates. Two different cores, and Illumina's large-account net prices are lower than core pass-through.
items.source_name: UMN Genomics Center; UCSD IGM rate card
items.why_new: The known list compares $/Gb or $/read. This compares a rival's all-in genome with Illumina's reagent-only cost, which undercuts the 'total workflow cost' defense.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: Using realistic output instead of spec maximums, Ultima at UMN is ~2.3–2.7x cheaper per Gb than an Illumina 25B lane at UCSD (internal rates) and ~2.9–3.6x cheaper at external rates.
items.detail: UMN UG100 full wafer, Savings tier: $3,204 internal / $3,688 external. UMN's own overview says ≥2.5–3.0 Tb per run (spec 'up to 3.6 Tb'), so ~$1.07–1.28 / $1.23–1.48 per Gb. UCSD 25B-300 lane: $2,800 / $3,836 at ~960 Gb, so $2.92 / $4.00 per Gb. Ratio ~2.3–2.7x internal, ~2.7–3.3x external (up to ~3.6x on spec). This is tighter than the 3.3–3.9x in F029.
items.why_new: It corrects the source's $/Gb ratio using the core's stated realistic output. The known list has Broad Clinical Labs ~$0.85 vs $0.50 per M reads only.

items.label: 2B
items.claim: For 10x single-cell counting work, Ultima at UMN costs ~$0.23–0.27 per million reads after the 10x discount vs ~$0.88 per million clusters on a UCSD 25B lane, ~3.2–3.8x cheaper for read-count-driven research.
items.detail: UMN wafer $3,204 internal minus the $500 10x preferred discount = $2,704 for 10–12B reads, or $0.23–0.27 per M reads. UCSD 25B-300 lane $2,800 for ~3.2B clusters, or ~$0.88 per M clusters (outside rate $3,836, ~$1.20). Counting assays depend on reads, not bases, so this is the relevant unit. It sits between the known Roche list claim ($0.06 vs $0.68 per M) and Broad Clinical Labs ($0.50 vs $0.85). Different cores, and discount dates undisclosed.
items.why_new: This is the first actual research-core price per read for single-cell work on a rival vs Illumina. The known list has only list-price or clinical-lab comparisons.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: At UCLA, which passes Illumina reagents through at cost, the 10B-300 lane fell 21% while the 25B was flat, cutting the 10B per-Gb premium over the 25B from ~68% to ~34% between 2023–24 and Jul 2026.
items.detail: 10B-300 non-profit $2,234 (Aug 2023 and Mar 2024) → $1,765.67 (Jul 2026); 25B-300 $3,538 → $3,512.47. At spec output of 375 Gb per 10B-300 lane vs 1,000 Gb per 25B-300 lane, $/Gb went $5.96 vs $3.54 (2023–24) → $4.71 vs $3.51 (2026). Illumina's price cuts reached the mid-volume 10B (pricing for users who can't fill 25B lanes), not the flagship 25B. The blended $/Gb falls when 10B users stay on 10B, even with 25B list flat.
items.quote: Material Pass Through rates are at cost
items.why_new: It quantifies the known qualitative 'harmonised cost per read across 5B/10B/25B' with a dated, pass-through-at-cost price series.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: Genomics England's biggest 2025 WGS award went to a services vendor (Revvity) after the open tender failed, at an all-in price of roughly £650 per sample.
items.detail: Award notice dated 6 Mar 2025, ref GEL-HE-596-23, covers extraction, WGS and storage of 44,500 Generation Study newborn samples at £29.2M ex-VAT, about £656 per sample all-in (derived). This is below the 2023 estimate of £40.5M (about £910 per sample), a 28% lower value. The open procedure produced no suitable bidder, so the award was negotiated with a single supplier. The sequencer is not named in the snippets. The lower-than-estimated value is consistent with buyer pricing leverage, but it includes extraction and storage and cannot be turned into a clean Illumina $/Gb figure.
items.source_name: Find a Tender (Genomics England award notice)
items.why_new: Genomics England's 2025 WGS award value and the 28% drop vs the 2023 estimate are not in the known list.

items.label: 1B
