items.claim: Genomics England buys long-read WGS as per-sample services from non-Illumina-centric vendors, at roughly £1.3-2.2K per sample.
items.detail: Babies in Focus (tender published 8 Aug 2025) awarded Lot 2 to Eurofins Genomics UK at £1.288M ex-VAT (26 Sep 2025). Lot 1 went to Cambridge University Technical Services at £2.206M ex-VAT (20 Nov 2025). Lot 1 covers 1,000 samples, sequenced 5 Jan-31 Mar 2026, so about £2.2K per sample. The lot 2 sample count was not seen. The buyer had estimated Lot 1 at £1.4M. Newborn WGS spend is being routed to long-read services, which may take some volume away from Illumina short-read. The scale is small, about £3.5M.
items.source_name: Find a Tender (Genomics England, Babies in Focus)
items.why_new: Genomics England's 2025 long-read award values and winners are not in the known list; NHS rare-disease WGS volume is, but not tenders.

items.label: 2B
items.claim: Public research sequencing runs on the NovaSeq 6000 are still rising and far outnumber NovaSeq X runs, so the 6000 research tail is not visibly shrinking in open data.
items.detail: ENA runs first made public on 'Illumina NovaSeq 6000' were 372,853 in 2024Q2, 457,581 in 2025Q2 and 582,347 in 2026Q2 (+25% and +27% y/y). In 2026Q2 the X models were about 68K ('X Plus') and 72K ('X'). The 6000 is therefore roughly 80-89% of NovaSeq-family public runs by count, depending on whether the two X strings overlap. Release lag of 1-3 years means this mostly reflects 2023-25 sequencing, not current mix. It is a weak counter to the idea that the research tail is already converted.
items.source_name: EMBL-EBI European Nucleotide Archive portal API
items.why_new: ENA run counts by sequencer model were never used before.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: Public AVITI and DNBSEQ-T7 run releases are small next to Illumina, but DNBSEQ-T7 is already about 2x AVITI, and the X Plus count has grown fast.
items.detail: ENA 2026Q2 first_public counts: Element AVITI 14,110 runs, DNBSEQ-T7 31,738 runs, against the 6000 at 582,347. AVITI is about 2.4% of the 6000 count. 'Illumina NovaSeq X Plus' went from 0 (2024Q2) to 25,784 (2025Q2) to 68,110 (2026Q2), +164% y/y. Challengers are therefore still a rounding error in public run data, but the lag hides how much current volume they carry.
items.source_name: EMBL-EBI European Nucleotide Archive portal API
items.why_new: First quantified open-data read of AVITI and DNBSEQ-T7 against the 6000 and X Plus.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: BillionToOne's cost per test has stopped falling, which suggests sequencing and reagent cost deflation is not what drives its volume.
items.detail: Derived cost of revenue per accessioned test (cost of revenue / tests): FY23 $54.4M/272K = ~$200, FY24 $71.7M/410K = ~$175, FY25 $96.7M/616K = ~$157. Management-reported COGS per test was $152 in Q1'26 and $161 in Q2'26. Q2'26 is +3% y/y on oncology mix. Over six months the company calls cost per test 'relatively stable'. The decline went from -13% (FY24) to -10% (FY25) to flat. Average selling price rose +21% in Q2'26 and +25% for H1, so gross margin gains come from pricing and payor contracts, not cheaper sequencing.
items.why_new: Known list has BillionToOne cost per test only as 'relatively stable'; this adds the FY23-FY25 series, Q1/Q2'26 figures and the arithmetic.
items.verify_note: This mostly restates known items ('BillionToOne cost/test relatively stable', 'cost declines plateaued'). The Q2'26 release says cost per test 'increased slightly' on oncology mix. Cost of revenue covers much more than sequencing, so a flat cost per test does not show that sequencing deflation fails to drive volume. I folded the useful arithmetic into a derived item.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: BillionToOne's COGS drivers are labor, supplies, phlebotomy and shipping. The company says it cuts cost per test through automation and supplier negotiations, not cheaper sequencing.
items.detail: Q2'26 cost of revenue rose $9.2M y/y (to $32.3M from $23.1M, +40%). Of that, testing samples, supplies, phlebotomy and shipping added $4.9M and labor and consulting added $4.3M. That is a 53%/47% split of the rise, and none of it is a sequencing-price line. Variable costs were 56% of COGS in Q2'26 and 57% in H1'26 (54% in H1'25). Management cited 'successful negotiations with suppliers' without naming any. Sequencing cost is therefore not described as the constraint on volume.
items.quote: successful negotiations with suppliers
items.why_new: The cost-of-revenue driver breakdown has not been used; the known list cites only the cost-per-test sentence.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: BillionToOne reports oncology COGS per test fell more than 10% sequentially in Q2'26, a sign that a Gb-heavy product is getting cheaper to run.
items.detail: Per the Q2'26 call summary, COGS per test was $161 (vs $152 in Q1). Prenatal COGS was roughly flat sequentially and oncology COGS declined by more than 10%. The 10-Q says cost per test fell for both oncology and prenatal vs Q1'26 and Q2'25. Management aims to hold gross margin at or above 70% through pricing and further oncology cost cuts. The source does not say how much came from Illumina pricing versus workflow changes. Lower oncology cost per test, if reagent-driven, means less revenue per test for the supplier.
items.source_name: MarketBeat Q2'26 call summary (via search result)
items.quote: oncology cost of goods sold declined by more than 10% sequentially
items.why_new: Known list has no sequential oncology-vs-prenatal COGS split for BillionToOne.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: BillionToOne relies on sole/single-source sequencers and reagents but keeps only about three months of inventory and says a supplier switch takes 1-9 months.
items.detail: The FY25 10-K says it relies on limited or sole/single-source suppliers for certain sequencers, reagents and blood tubes. It aims to 'keep, at least, a three-month inventory' of most materials. It estimates replacing a supplier 'could take approximately one to nine months.' No Illumina purchase commitment appears in the pages read. Illumina is named only as an NIPT competitor (via Verinata), and Illumina sued BillionToOne on 7 May 2026. A customer that competes with its supplier and has no stated minimums has leverage and a reason to diversify.
items.quote: could take approximately one to nine months
items.why_new: The known list has only the Illumina patent suit; the supplier-dependence language and the inventory and switching timeline are new.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: Reimbursement and payer limits, not sequencing cost, are the stated gating factors for NIPT and oncology volume at BillionToOne.
items.detail: The FY25 10-K lists CMS rates of $759 for aneuploidy NIPT, ~$1,825 for the carrier PLA, ~$2,920 for Northstar Select and ~$1,644 for Northstar Response. It says overall ASP is below these code rates and out-of-network pay may be 'a small fraction of the CMS rate'. Third-party payors are more than 90% of revenue. State Medicaid coverage gaps exist (carrier screening not covered in Alabama, Michigan and Nevada; aneuploidy not covered in Nebraska or Utah). It has 250M in-network covered lives. Growth is described as coverage- and contract-driven.
items.quote: Coverage and reimbursement by third-party payors ... can be limited and uncertain.
items.why_new: Known list has the generic 'adoption is the binding constraint' expert view; this gives filed CMS rates, state coverage gaps and the 250M-lives count.
items.verify_note: This is new as a named-customer filing datapoint, but it is generic 10-K risk-factor and reimbursement language. It supports the known expert view that reimbursement is the binding constraint. It does not show that volume is gated today, since the company grew tests 33%.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: NIPT penetration at BillionToOne is rising slowly while it describes the prenatal market as commoditizing.
items.detail: The FY25 10-K says it tests 'approximately 1 in 11 babies'. The Q2'26 10-Q says 'more than 1 in 10', so share of US births moved from ~9.1% to above 10% in about five months. The 10-K cites 'increasing commoditization' in prenatal testing and says competitors launched recessive-condition NIPTs and RhD NIPTs in 2024. Prenatal revenue is still +55% y/y in Q2'26, but it grows mainly through ASP (+21%) and payor contracts rather than volume alone, and oncology mix adds to cost per test.
items.quote: we test more than 1 in 10 babies
items.why_new: The 1-in-11 to 1-in-10 penetration datapoint and the commoditization language are new.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: BillionToOne's capex is rising: purchases of property and equipment were $8.5M in H1'26 vs $5.2M in H1'25 (+63%).
items.detail: Net PP&E was $24.9M at 30 Jun 2026 vs $20.4M at 31 Dec 2025 (+22% in six months). Non-cash capex in payables was $2.1M vs $1.4M. The 10-Q does not break out sequencers. It is still small in absolute terms: a NovaSeq X-class system costs about $1M, so this is at most a handful of instruments.
items.why_new: Not in the known list: the capex step-up at a growing Illumina customer.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: BillionToOne's gross-margin gain is price-led (ASP +21-25%), so a growth-rate slowdown is plausible once price gains annualize.
items.detail: Gross margin was 70.4% in Q2'26 vs 65.3% in Q2'25 and 71.7% in H1'26 vs 64.9% in H1'25. FY25 was 68% vs 53% in FY24 and 24% in FY23. Overall ASP was +21% in Q2'26 and +25% in H1'26, driven by more payor contracts and the proprietary PLA code. Revenue per accessioned test was ~$264 (FY23), ~$372 (FY24) and ~$495 (FY25). Volume growth (35%) is below revenue growth (64%), so about 2/3 of growth is price/mix and not Gb.
items.why_new: The price-vs-volume decomposition of BillionToOne growth is new; the known list has headline revenue growth only.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: Ultima's instrument price per annual genome capacity is only about $21-28 per genome, which supports its sub-$100 genome claims.
items.detail: Arithmetic from list prices and rated capacity: UG200 Ultra $1,250,000 / 60,000 genomes a year = about $21 per genome in year-one instrument cost. UG200 $850,000 / 30,000 = about $28. On the same basis a $689K VITARI would need to run well over 6,000 genomes a year to match, and the figures exclude reagents, service and labor. Solaris 2.0 Max is planned for H2'26 at up to 20B reads per wafer. This lets a high-volume buyer such as Helix or a large clinical lab use rival capacity as leverage when negotiating Illumina consumables. This is derived arithmetic, not a vendor-published all-in cost.
items.source_name: CLP Magazine / Ultima UG200 launch coverage (via search results)
items.why_new: The known file has the UG200 list prices and the '$80 genome' claim. The capacity-normalised instrument cost and the Solaris 2.0 Max 20B-read target are new.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: Element's installed base grew >60% to >450 AVITI systems in 2025 while consumable kit shipments more than doubled, so rival short-read volume is scaling faster than its box count.
items.detail: Deck (JPM, Jan 2026) says the base passed 450 systems in 40+ countries, up >60%. Back-solving gives roughly 280 systems at end-2024 and ~170 net adds in 2025. Kit shipments and connected runs >2x vs a >1.6x base implies utilisation per system up by roughly 25%+ (2.0/1.6). Element is still small next to Illumina's installed base, but the usage trend is the new datapoint.
items.source_name: GenomeWeb / Element JPM 2026 deck (search summary, not read in full)
items.why_new: Known list has ~450 systems only via F082 and no utilisation or kit-shipment growth for Element.
items.verify_note: I did not verify the claim that kit shipments more than doubled; the Substack does not mention it, and the GenomeWeb summary was not read in full. The back-solved end-2024 base of ~280 (450/1.6) is arithmetic only. The utilisation inference rests on an unverified figure.

items.label: 2B
items.claim: AVITI24 multiomics was >35% of Element's new instrument bookings in 2025, with biopharma bookings reportedly +175% y/y.
items.detail: GenomeWeb and the Substack both cite >35% of new bookings for AVITI24. The Substack adds biopharma AVITI24 bookings +175% y/y. Counting-application run settings are priced below $1 per million reads. That is a research and pharma counting-application wedge, the area the thesis says is price-exposed.
items.source_name: Rhymes with Haystack (Vilella) on Element JPM26
items.why_new: Known list has Element price points and the VITARI launch but not the bookings mix, the +175% pharma growth or the sub-$1 per million reads claim.
items.verify_note: The Substack confirms both figures: AVITI24 at >35% of new instrument bookings, and biopharma AVITI24 bookings +175%. Counting-application pricing is described only as 'below one dollar per million reads', with no exact figure. AVITI24 is largely an in-situ multiomics instrument, and the bookings are on a small base, so this is only a weak link to research sequencing price pressure on Illumina.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: Element's clinical-research revenue passed 25% of its total in 2025, up from ~20% in 2024, so a rival is moving into Illumina's clinical-adjacent base.
items.detail: The deck says clinical research is >25% of revenue vs ~20% in 2024. On ~$85M revenue that is >$21M, vs ~$12M on $60M in 2024, roughly +80% (derived). Element also plans an IVDR AVITI Dx for late 2026 and has ISO 13485 certification (Jun 2026). The base is still small.
items.source_name: Element JPM 2026 deck via search summary
items.why_new: Known list has Medicover and PathoNext as AVITI clinical users but not Element's clinical revenue share or the AVITI Dx timeline.
items.verify_note: Not verified; the Substack does not mention the clinical-research share. If revenue was $58M rather than $85M, clinical research is about $15M, not $21M. Either way it is under ~1% of Illumina's ~$1.9B clinical consumables, so this shows direction, not material pressure.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: Element's FY25 revenue of ~$85M missed its own $100M projection, which tempers the pace of rival share gain.
items.detail: GenomeWeb says ~$85M, +40% from $60M, below the $100M projected at JPM 2025. The $85M is a company estimate. The Substack's $58M conflicts with it and I could not resolve it. If $58M were right, growth would be about -3% on $60M, which is implausible next to a >60% base increase, so $85M looks more credible. Element's installed base and revenue are both small next to Illumina's.
items.why_new: F082 cites $58-85M without the missed $100M projection or the 40% growth math.
items.verify_note: Duplicate of F082, which already covers the revenue miss against the $100M target. It is also mislabeled: Element's revenue speaks to competitive price pressure (1B), not Illumina's volume growth (1C). The $58M vs $85M conflict is unresolved, and the Substack, which I opened, says $58M.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: Public 6000 run releases are still growing y/y, not declining, which undercuts a fast-shrinking tail on the research data side.
items.detail: 6000 runs released: Q2'24 324k, Q2'25 456k (+41%), Q2'26 578k (+27%). Q1'26 was 452k vs 351k in Q1'25 (+29%). Only Q4'25 (351k vs 422k, -17%) and Q3'25 (421k vs 389k, +8%) were soft. Release lag means this reflects 2023-25 sequencing, so it cannot show current conversion.
items.why_new: Quantifies y/y growth in 6000 releases by quarter; the known file only says the count is rising.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: The X family grew far faster than the 6000 in public releases, so the mix shift in public data is still early.
items.detail: X + X Plus runs: Q2'25 62.9k to Q2'26 138.8k (+121% y/y), against 6000 +27%. Q2'24 was 5.9k. If the X family keeps taking share of new data, the 6000 share of future releases keeps falling, but it is still ~80% of runs. This matches a mix shift that is not complete.
items.why_new: Gives the growth rates of the X vs 6000 public-data series; not previously computed.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: Rival-platform public data is growing fast off a small base, led by DNBSEQ-T7 and AVITI.
items.detail: Runs released in Q2: DNBSEQ-T7 14,813 (2025) to 31,576 (2026), +113%; Element AVITI 6,413 to 10,004, +56%. Ultima (instrument_platform=ULTIMA) has only 2,887 runs in total, and 88 in Q2'26 vs 391 in Q2'25, so it is not visible in ENA yet (it mostly goes to other archives or is unreleased). T7 is about 3x AVITI and about 5% of 6000 run volume.
items.why_new: Adds y/y growth rates for T7, AVITI and Ultima releases; F088 only gave a rough ratio.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: Rival platforms are still tiny relative to Illumina in public data, so competition is not yet visible in volume.
items.detail: Q2'26 AVITI 10.0k and T7 31.6k runs vs Illumina 6000+X+X Plus 716.6k, so the two rivals together are about 5.5% of the combined total. Ultima is ~0.01%. Public-data share lags any commercial price pressure, and run counts do not capture Gb.
items.why_new: Quantifies the rival-to-Illumina ratio in public archives.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: Genomics England's own long-read award prices the option tranche of PromethION flow cells at less than half the per-unit price of the initial tranche, showing how hard this large public buyer negotiates on volume.
items.detail: Award 039504-2024 (6 Dec 2024, Oxford Nanopore, single-operator award) is £5,234,229 for 3,900 flow cells plus consumables, about £1,342 each. The option for a further 4,400 flow cells is capped at £2,774,772, about £631 each, which is 53% lower per unit. The notice says 'associated consumables' without a split, so the per-unit comparison is approximate. This is a non-Illumina platform, so it only shows the buyer's leverage and that a national genomics programme gets steep volume tiers.
items.source_name: Find a Tender (OCDS API), Genomics England notice 039504-2024
items.why_new: The known list covers only the 2025 Babies in Focus long-read awards, not the Dec 2024 ONT flow-cell award or its tiered unit prices.
items.verify_note: The per-unit comparison is approximate. The initial £5.23M covers flow cells plus unsplit 'associated consumables', while the option is a cap, so the 53% lower unit price is likely overstated. The platform is not Illumina's, so the item shows only that a public buyer gets volume tiers. It is tangential to Illumina's large-account discounting.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: Genomics England's newborn programme is buying outsourced WGS capacity with no committed volume, and the cap implies about 7,000 samples per quarter, a modest run-rate of about 0.7-0.9 Pb per year.
items.detail: The Revvity contract (008121-2025, signed 5 Mar 2025) covers about 44,500 samples over 21 months, up to 7,000 per quarter from Jul 2025 to Mar 2027, with no minimum. At 30x (about 100-125 Gb per genome) that is about 4.5-5.6 Pb in total, or 2.6-3.2 Pb per year, against an HT base of about 800 Gb per quarter in the known file's scale. It is a small, capped programme rather than a volume driver. The contract status field is also inconsistent: the lot shows 'cancelled' and the award 'active'.
items.why_new: The known file has NHS rare-disease WGS volumes but not the Generation Study's capped quarterly volume or the no-minimum term.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: Genomics England's newborn WGS contract came in 27% below its 2023 estimate of £40.5M, a sign that planned public-programme genome volume or price was scaled back.
items.detail: The December 2023 notice estimated £40.5M for 30,000-65,000 genomes in the accelerated stage. The March 2025 award was £29.2M for about 44,500 samples, which is 28% below the estimate (29.2/40.5 = 0.72). It is unclear whether the cut comes from lower price per genome or lower volume, because the award sits inside the volume range. The award has a 12-month extension option that could add spend.
items.why_new: The known file does not compare the estimate with the award for this programme.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: NHS and UK public labs keep buying Illumina consumables on direct awards that name the older MiSeq and NovaSeq platforms, not the NovaSeq X, so the legacy installed base is still being fed.
items.detail: Northumbria University's 3-year, £300,000 award (signed 13 May 2025, 1 bid, Illumina Cambridge) covers consumables for a new MiSeq i100 Plus and 'existing NovaSeq and MiSeq instruments'. A buyer notice dated 1 Sep 2026 for the Illumina MiSeq (£156,201 net, 15 Sep 2026 to 15 Sep 2027) names no NovaSeq. A search snippet attributes that same value to the Northern Ireland HSC Business Services Organisation, so the buyer is unclear. These are small values and not clearly NovaSeq 6000.
items.source_name: Find a Tender (OCDS API) Northumbria T24/0068; ocds-h6vhtk-06ef73
items.why_new: The known list does not include these specific awards or their platform wording.

items.label: 2A
items.claim: Ultima is priced by turnaround at UMN, and the cheapest tier needs a wait of up to 21 business days. This is the kind of price-for-delay trade research buyers make.
items.detail: The full wafer costs $3,204 (Savings, 6-21 business days), $3,356 (Speed, 4-12 days) or $3,508 (Priority, 4-7 days). Savings is therefore 4.5% below Speed and 8.7% below Priority. A research buyer who accepts a wait of up to 21 days pays about 9% less. The internal rate is also about 13% below external at every tier ($3,204 vs $3,688).
items.why_new: The tier percentages are derived here; the found list notes the tiers exist (F028) but not the full grid or the 13% internal/external gap.

items.label: 2B
items.claim: Public research buyers are using open, price-weighted competition for sequencing services that can go to non-Illumina platforms, with 7 bids per lot on Babies in Focus.
items.detail: Babies in Focus (GEL-RE-25161) used an open procedure, quality 70% and price 30%, and drew 7 bids and 7 final-stage bids per lot. It was split by technology (ONT vs PacBio) rather than by Illumina equivalence. This shows UK public research funders are willing to buy outsourced sequencing in competitive lots, which adds price pressure on research consumables over time, even though the work is not short-read.
items.why_new: The known list does not cover the Babies in Focus bid counts or the 70/30 award weighting.

items.label: 2B
items.claim: UMGC makes Ultima its primary WGS platform and uses AVITI 'where appropriate'. Illumina's NovaSeq X+ is not offered for WGS on the page.
items.detail: The WGS page lists only Ultima UG 100 ($221 external), AVITI ($469 external) and AVITI Ultra Q ($1,168 external). NovaSeq X+ appears only in the site navigation, with no WGS price. A flagship research core has therefore routed its human-genome product away from Illumina's high-throughput platform. This is consistent with F007 but confirms the exclusion on a second UMGC page.
items.why_new: Adds the platform-priority statement and the full AVITI/Ultra Q ladder. F007 notes only the missing X price.
items.verify_note: Opened the page. It confirms the Ultima UG 100 is the primary WGS platform, AVITI24 is used 'where appropriate', and no Illumina platform is offered for WGS. Correction: this page lists only $221 (external, 30x on UG100). The AVITI prices come from the other UMGC page, which is already on the list as F005/F006. Only the fact that Illumina is excluded from the WGS service is incremental.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: Genomics England's 2024-25 Oxford Nanopore awards were sole-source on 'technical reasons and scalability', so the programme's long-read spend carries no competitive discounting.
items.detail: Both the May 2024 award (015641-2024, £3,067,524 for 1,000 cancer participants, about £3,068 per sample including flow cells) and the Dec 2024 award (039504-2024, £5.23M) were made without competition under the single-operator exclusion. The earlier award covered the 3rd year of the Cancer programme through FY24/25 and had no option. This indicates the programme's non-Illumina volume is lock-in, not price competition.
items.quote: only provider able to meet the justified requirements
items.why_new: The known list does not include the ONT sole-source awards or the £3,068 per-cancer-sample figure.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: In the NIH Genetic Testing Registry, a phrase search finds about 10x more clinical test records naming the NovaSeq 6000 than the NovaSeq X.
items.detail: On 12 Oct 2026, esearch on db=gtr returned 130 records for "NovaSeq 6000" and 12 for "NovaSeq X". AVITI returned 11. The 6000 count may include records that also name the X, and the search may be loose. The ratio nonetheless points to a clinical documentation tail that is still mostly 6000. This is directional only, not a volume measure. GTR entries are self-reported and often not refreshed.
items.why_new: First registry-level count of clinical tests naming the 6000 versus the X; earlier notes used job postings and FDA PMA files only.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: At UMGC, Element AVITI is priced at about 2.1x Ultima per 30x genome, and AVITI Ultra Q at about 5x. Element is not a price threat at this core.
items.detail: External 30x prices are $221 (Ultima), $469 (AVITI) and $1,168 (AVITI Ultra Q). The ratios are 469/221 = 2.1x and 1,168/221 = 5.3x. Internal prices are $192, $407 and $1,015, or 2.1x and 5.3x. Small batch sizes (4 and 2 samples) likely explain part of the premium. Element's low-price challenge is therefore weaker than Ultima's at this core. This partly cuts against the 1B claim about Element.
items.why_new: The Ultra Q price and the internal/external ladder are new; F006 gives only the AVITI 2x ratio.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: Ultima's coverage ladder shows very low marginal cost for depth: 90x costs only 1.7x the 30x price.
items.detail: External prices are $221 (30x), $274 (60x) and $379 (90x). Tripling coverage raises price 71%: ($379-$221)/$221. The 60x genome costs +24% for 2x depth. Ultima therefore lets a buyer reinvest savings in depth cheaply. Customers buying depth at this cost would lift Gb per dollar but lower Illumina's revenue per Gb. Compared with the ~$650 X genome elsewhere, a 90x Ultima genome ($379) is still 42% cheaper than a 30x one on the X.
items.why_new: The 60x and 90x ladder and the 90x vs X-30x comparison are not in the known or found lists.
items.verify_note: Restates F005, which already lists the 30x/60x/90x prices of $221/$274/$379. The ratio is simple arithmetic. The step that more depth bought on Ultima 'lowers Illumina's revenue per Gb' is not supported.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: UMGC's headline price rose from '$199 human genome' (search-snippet title) to '$221' external now, but it is still far below the Illumina X benchmark.
items.detail: A search result titled 'Offering the $199 human genome' points to the same URL, while the live page headlines the '$221 human genome'. That is +11% ($221/$199). It may reflect a switch from an internal to an external headline, or a tariff or cost pass-through. Ultima pricing is rising slightly and is not collapsing, which is a watch-out for any claim that rivals' prices are still falling. The history could not be verified, because the Wayback Machine was blocked.
items.quote: Offering the $199 human genome
items.why_new: The $199 to $221 move is flagged only in the probe notes, not in the known list.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: UMGC launched Ultima service on 2 Jan 2025 at '$100 raw reagent cost', which it described as a 50% cut versus the cheapest sequencing then available.
items.detail: UMGC's news item (28 Oct 2024) said the UG 100 service starts 2 Jan 2025, with about 16 genomes per wafer and up to 20 wafers a week, or about 320 genomes a week. It calls $100 a '50% decrease' relative to the cheapest prior option. Ultima capacity at one core is therefore about 16,600 genomes a year, which is a rival short-read platform scaling inside a large academic buyer. The claim is the core's own marketing, not an invoice-level comparison.
items.why_new: The launch date, capacity and 50% claim are new; the known list has only UMN-style evaluation prices.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: Tempus xT (a large oncology lab test) is still registered on the NovaSeq 6000, with the lab last reviewed in Nov 2025.
items.detail: The GTR record for Tempus xT, offered by Tempus AI - RTP, lists 'Novaseq 6000' in the Methodology Instrument column for both the DNA and RNA workflows. It was registered 2024-11-06 and the lab's last annual review was 2025-11-12. This is consistent with the known Tempus job posting that mentions both the 6000 and the X. It shows the 6000 named in a current-year registry entry, but not that the lab has no X capacity.
items.quote: on an Illumina NovaSeq 6000
items.why_new: Registry-level confirmation that Tempus's flagship panel is documented on the 6000 as of Nov 2025; earlier evidence was a job posting only.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: A Wisconsin core page says NovaSeq X Plus delivers more data per dollar than AVITI, and that groups negotiated only about 15% off list.
items.detail: This comes from a search-result snippet only. The page could not be opened and its date is unconfirmed. The snippet says the NovaSeq X 25B list is $16,480 at 2x150, negotiated discounts are around 15%, and X Plus gives 60% more data than Element AVITI per dollar. The 15% negotiated discount is small next to the 'insane' discounts for large accounts. It also suggests Illumina still wins on price per read at some academic cores.
items.quote: groups negotiated discounts around 15%
items.why_new: The $16,480 list price and the 15% negotiated-discount figure are not in the known list, but the claim is unverified.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: Natera's non-oncology volume, mostly NIPT and women's health, grew only about 10-12% y/y in H1'26 while oncology grew 54-57%.
items.detail: Derived from Natera's press releases. Q2'26: total tests of about 1,043.9K less oncology of 296.7K gives about 747.2K non-oncology, against 664.3K in Q2'25 (853.1K less 188.8K), so +12.5%. Q1'26: total of 1,013.6K less oncology of 258.9K gives about 754.7K, against 687.4K in Q1'25 (855.1K less 167.7K), so +9.8%. Non-oncology fell sequentially from Q1 to Q2'26 (754.7K to 747.2K). Oncology is now about 28% of tests, up from about 22% a year earlier. The non-oncology line is the bulk-volume, low-Gb NIPT base, so mix is moving toward MRD while the NIPT base matures at roughly 10% growth. That supports the NIPT-maturing drag. The category also includes organ health, so this is not a pure NIPT figure.
items.why_new: The known list cites total +22% and oncology +57% but not the derived non-oncology y/y of about +10-12% or the sequential dip.
items.verify_note: Totals and oncology counts check out against the Q2'26 8-K (1,043.9K / 296.7K vs 853.1K / 188.8K). However, 'only ~10-12%' is an ACCELERATION from +5-7% through 2025 (see F131), not a slowdown. The known list already has Q2'26 non-MRD ~+13% and H1'26 ~10-12%. The non-oncology line also includes organ health, so it is not pure NIPT. The only new support is the small sequential dip (754.7K→747.2K).

items.label: 1C
items.claim: Natera's oncology tests are growing fast and are gaining share of the mix, which gives Illumina volume support.
items.detail: Oncology tests processed were about 296.7K in Q2'26 (+57.2% y/y) and 258.9K in Q1'26 (+54.4%). Sequentially that is +14.6% q/q, and clinical MRD units rose 34K q/q, the largest sequential increase to date. Q2 total tests of about 1.04M were up 22.4%, against +18.5% in Q1, so total test growth accelerated. Natera raised FY26 revenue guidance to $2.85-2.91B. This cuts against the claim that NTRA is not seeing MRD become a meaningful share of its mix. Oncology went from about 22% to about 28% of tests in a year. The caveat is that tests are not Gb, as the known list already notes.
items.why_new: This quantifies the oncology mix share (22% to 28%) and the Q1'26 oncology figure of 258.9K, which are not in the known list.
items.verify_note: Restates known facts: Natera tests +22% (1.04M), oncology +57%, MRD 283K (+56%). The +34K q/q MRD figure is confirmed but marginal. The oncology share move (22%→28% of tests) is trivially derivable, and tests are not Gb.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: At BillionToOne, a fast-growing Illumina clinical customer, all of the Q2'26 gross-margin gain came from price, and cost of goods per test rose about 4% year over year.
items.detail: Q2'26 ASP was $551 at a 70% gross margin, which implies COGS of ~$165 per test. Q2'25 ASP was $455 at 65%, which implies ~$159 per test, so COGS per test rose about 4%. Gross profit per test rose from ~$296 to ~$386 (+30%), entirely because ASP rose 21%. Tests accessioned grew 33% while revenue grew 64%. This customer's volume and economics are being driven by reimbursement and price, not by falling sequencing costs; COGS includes far more than Illumina reagents.
items.quote: overall cost per test rose slightly year over year
items.why_new: The known list has only 'cost per test relatively stable'. The implied COGS per test and the split of the gain into price vs cost are new.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: Element's implied consumables-and-service revenue per AVITI system is at most ~$100K a year, mid-throughput scale, so near-term pressure on Illumina's high-throughput consumables is limited.
items.detail: Element reported $58–85M of 2025 revenue (sources conflict) on a base that rose from ~280 to >450 systems, ~365 on average, with ~170 net adds. At an assumed blended instrument price of ~$290–500K, the 170 adds would bring in ~$49–85M of instrument revenue. That leaves ≤~$36M of non-instrument revenue even on the $85M figure, or ≤~$100K per average system. That compares with Illumina's guided NextSeq 1k/2k pull-through of $80–100K and NovaSeq X pull-through of ~$1.24M. The instrument price is our assumption (list was ~$289K at launch; an expert said ~$500K).
items.source_name: Rhymes with Haystack / GenomeWeb on Element JPM 2026
items.why_new: No implied Element pull-through or scale comparison is on the known list.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: At MD Anderson's core, Illumina's 10B-300 lane costs ~50% more per Gb than the 25B-300. That is about double UCLA's ~26% premium, so within-X price steps still have room to compress at cores that have not cut the 10B.
items.detail: MD Anderson's X Plus page (search snippet, 2026) lists 10B-300 at $1,523 per lane (1.25B read pairs ≈ 375 Gb, so ~$4.06/Gb) and 25B-300 at $2,595 per lane (3.2B read pairs ≈ 960 Gb, so ~$2.70/Gb), a ratio of ~1.50x. UCLA's ratio fell from 1.58x to 1.26x after its 10B price cut (D005). If MD Anderson follows UCLA, the 10B price would fall ~16%. MD Anderson's 25B price of $2.70/Gb is in line with UCSD ($2.92) and UConn ($2.94).
items.source_name: MD Anderson ATGC NovaSeq X Plus page
items.quote: Up to 60% reduction in sequencing price
items.why_new: MD Anderson's X lane prices and its 10B/25B ratio are not on the known list.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: Mayo Clinic Laboratories, a top US reference lab, still lists only the NovaSeq 6000 on about 104 of the 130 GTR records that match 'NovaSeq 6000', with none on the X.
items.detail: An esearch for "NovaSeq 6000" returned 130 test records. Adding AND "Mayo Clinic Laboratories" returned 104, or about 80%, though GTR free-text tokenizes loosely so the count is approximate. The same Mayo query with "NovaSeq X" returned 0. Spot-checked Mayo records (hereditary renal cancer, Ehlers-Danlos, epilepsy, muscular dystrophy) list only 'Illumina NovaSeq 6000' (the epilepsy panel also lists a capillary sequencer). Lab review date is 28 May 2026, so the listing is current. Mayo's inpatient/reference germline panels are exactly the 'old assays stay on 6000' cohort. Registration dates for the checked records run from Jun 2020 to Dec 2022 with no sign of re-registration on the X.
items.why_new: Names a specific large clinical lab and quantifies its 6000-only listings, rather than only the 10x aggregate ratio already known.
items.verify_note: Counts confirmed via E-utilities: 130 records for 'NovaSeq 6000', 104 for AND 'Mayo Clinic Laboratories', and 0 for 'NovaSeq X' AND Mayo. But the whole GTR has only 12 records naming 'NovaSeq X' (4 of them one Labcorp NIPT family), against ~78% clinical X Gb share. GTR instrument fields are therefore stale, and a 6000 listing is weak evidence of actual 6000 use. The 28 May 2026 review date is lab-level, not test-level.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: Across all GTR records naming either sequencer, no lab or record lists both the 6000 and the X, so there is no dual-running signal and the 6000 labs are not converting.
items.detail: The query "NovaSeq 6000" AND "NovaSeq X" returned 0 records. Both lists are self-reported. The 6000 list holds 130 records and the X list 12. The 6000-only labs found are Mayo (about 104 records), Tempus AI-RTP (Tempus xT, registered Nov 2024, lab reviewed 12 Nov 2025) and an Indian molecular genetics division (reviewed Apr 2026). Labs listing only the X are Labcorp's Integrated Genetics, Univ. of Michigan and an Indian institute. Labs are therefore split into converted and not converted, with none in transition on paper.
items.why_new: Adds a lab-level split (6000-only vs X-only, zero both). Earlier GTR work gave only a ~10x record-count ratio.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: Labcorp's Integrated Genetics (Sequenom) lists its MaterniT NIPT family only on the NovaSeq X Plus, which confirms that large NIPT volume has already moved to the X.
items.detail: MaterniT21, MaterniT GENOME and the two MaterniT21 Genome Add-On records (IDs 501985, 569955, 593063, 593064) all list 'Novaseq X Plus' as the only instrument. The lab's last annual review is 22 Oct 2025, so the listing is recent. Registration dates go back to 2013 and 2020, so the instrument was updated in place rather than newly registered. The NIPT cohort (Thaysen's cohort 4) is therefore mostly converted, consistent with the known '<20%, mostly moved' view. This limits the remaining NIPT repricing risk for 2027.
items.why_new: Names the Labcorp NIPT lab as X-only; the known file has no per-lab NIPT instrument evidence.
items.verify_note: Confirmed: IDs 501985, 569955, 593063 and 593064 all come back for an esearch on 'NovaSeq X'. The esummary does not show the instrument field or the review date, so those were not re-verified. This largely confirms the known 'NIPT <20%, mostly moved' cohort view, so it adds little.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: The University of Michigan Molecular Genetics Laboratory lists seven germline gene tests on the X Plus only, so an academic clinical reference lab has converted.
items.detail: Records for BRCA1/2, TP53, CFTR, ATP7B, CHD7 and GDI1 (IDs 509980, 508735, 508734, 508371, 507003, 506862) are all in the 12-record 'NovaSeq X' result set. The BRCA record shows the instrument as 'Illumina NovaSeq X Plus' with the lab last reviewed 25 Jun 2026. These tests were registered back in 2021, so the lab updated them from an older platform. This is a counter-example to the idea that every germline panel lab stays on the 6000.
items.why_new: Shows an academic clinical lab fully on the X, with a dated review.

items.label: 2B
items.claim: GTR shows 11 tests naming AVITI (Element), mostly registered long ago at a few small labs, so Element's clinical footprint is tiny and often stale.
items.detail: An AVITI search returned 11 records (IDs include 613429, 558563, 558561, 332665 and others). The one record opened, a retinal dystrophy panel at a Laboratory of Human Genetics, was registered 25 Oct 2024. It is the only instrument listed, and the lab's annual review (31 Jan 2025) is marked 'Past due'. An 'Ultima Genomics' phrase search is unusable because it matched on the single token 'Genomics' (31,252 hits). Rival short-read platforms are close to invisible in clinical test registrations, and that cuts against fast clinical share loss near term.
items.why_new: Gives a count of registered clinical tests on AVITI and a dated example.

items.label: 2B
items.claim: UIUC's Carver Biotechnology Center sole-source Illumina reagent ceiling for 2024-29 averages about $5M/yr, the same as its 2019-20 estimate.
items.detail: Search-result snippet, not opened (the .docx would not parse). The May 2024 Illinois trustees report sets the FY2025-FY2029 Illumina reagent contract at about $25M (about $5M/yr), with one 5-year renewal option, for six Illumina sequencers. The March 2019 report estimated $5M for FY2020. A flat ceiling is not actual spend, and it covers only one large public research core. It gives no sign of a research price cut or of a volume change.
items.source_name: University of Illinois Board of Trustees purchase recommendations
items.why_new: Not in the known list; the corpus has no Illinois trustees procurement data.

items.label: 2B
items.claim: UIUC approved a NovaSeq X Plus purchase of about $1.08M in March 2023 while keeping a sole-source reagent contract.
items.detail: Search-result snippet, not opened. The March 2023 trustees report recommended a NovaSeq X Plus system at an estimated $1,078,438. This shows a large public research core adopting the X while its reagent ceiling stayed near $5M/yr. That fits flat reagent dollars on higher capacity, which is consistent with falling $/Gb.
items.source_name: University of Illinois Board of Trustees purchases and renewals
items.why_new: Not in the known list; the corpus has no Illinois university procurement data.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: GRAIL's Illumina royalty (suspended since 2024) resumes 24 Dec 2026 unless GRAIL changes control, with a 7% effective floor and a 5% rate after $1B cumulative.
items.detail: The Q2'26 10-Q says the 9% oncology royalty is suspended until 24 Dec 2026. Anti-stacking can lower it to a 7% floor, which GRAIL expects to be its effective rate. This is a new Illumina revenue stream starting in Q1'27, but it is a royalty, not consumables pricing, and it is small relative to the scale of the thesis. It does not show price pressure and is more neutral than supportive. Q2'26 Galleri volume rose 35% y/y while ASP fell 8%. Cost of screening revenue was $23.3M in Q2'26 and $44.6M for H1'26, which is roughly $380 per test on about 61K tests, including all lab costs.
items.quote: suspended until December 24, 2026 or any earlier change of control
items.why_new: The royalty restart date and the screening cost per test are not in the known list. The volume figures are already known.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: Natera's non-oncology test volume (mostly NIPT/women's health) slowed sharply from +21% y/y in Q4'24 to about +5-7% through 2025.
items.detail: Non-oncology = total tests minus oncology tests. Q4'23: 626.8K-97.5K = 529.3K. Q4'24: 792.8K-150.8K = 642.0K (+21.3%). Q2'25: 853.1K-188.8K = 664.3K vs Q2'24 634.9K (+4.6%). Q3'25: 893.6K-211.0K = 682.6K vs 638.7K (+6.9%). Q4'25: 923.6K-233.3K = 690.3K vs 642.0K (+7.5%). FY24 non-oncology was 2,536.4K (+17.7% vs 2,155.1K). FY25 was 2,724.7K (+7.4%). This is a quarterly series for the NIPT-maturation drag, where the known list has only Q2'26 non-MRD ~+13% and H1'26 ~10-12%.
items.source_name: Natera 8-K Ex. 99.1 (Q4'25, Q4'24 and 2025 quarterly releases); derived
items.why_new: Eight-quarter non-oncology series and the 2024-to-2025 deceleration are not in the known list. Only the H1'26 point is.
items.verify_note: Verified from the Q4'25 8-K: Q4'25 923.6K/233.3K, Q4'24 792.8K/150.8K, FY25 3,525.5K/800.8K, FY24 3,064.6K/528.2K, so FY non-oncology +7.4%. Caveat: growth re-accelerated to +9.8% (Q1'26) and +12.5% (Q2'26). The 'maturing' signal is 2025-specific and partly reversed in 2026.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: Oncology growth has been about 46-57% for eight straight quarters, but oncology share of tests rose only to about 28% and the non-oncology base is flat-ish in absolute terms.
items.detail: Oncology tests (K): Q1'24 114.8, Q2'24 125.4, Q3'24 137.1, Q4'24 150.8, Q1'25 167.7 (+46.1%), Q2'25 188.8 (+50.6%), Q3'25 211.0 (+53.9%), Q4'25 233.3 (+54.7%), Q1'26 258.9 (+54.4%), Q2'26 296.7 (+57.2%). Oncology share of total: 15.6% (Q1'24), 25.3% (Q4'25), 28.4% (Q2'26). Non-oncology moved from 621K (Q1'24) to 747K (Q2'26), +20% over 9 quarters. Total growth is therefore carried by oncology tests, which are mostly low-Gb classic MRD tests (<1 Gb per draw per the known list). Oncology test counts overstate Gb growth.
items.source_name: Natera 8-K Ex. 99.1 releases Q4'24 to Q2'26, plus search-snippet results for Q1'25 to Q3'25 and Q1'26; derived
items.why_new: The known list has only the Q2'26 oncology figure. The full 10-quarter table and share-of-mix path are new.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: Natera's total test growth was lowest in Q2'25 (+12.2%) and was +16% to +22% in the next five quarters, driven by oncology mix.
items.why_new: The known list gives only Q2'26 total +22%. FY24 to FY25 total deceleration (+22.8% to +15.0%) is new.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: Natera's Q2'26 sequential oncology jump (+37.8K tests) was partly weather-inflated from a Q1 suppression, so the run-rate may be overstated.
items.detail: Clinical MRD units rose 34,000 sequentially (record) to 283K. Analysts probed sustainability on the call, and management said Q1 was partly suppressed by weather. Oncology tests went 258.9K to 296.7K (+14.6% q/q) in Q2'26, after +11.0% in Q1'26 and +10.6% in Q4'25. Sequential increments: Q2'25 +21.1K, Q3'25 +22.2K, Q4'25 +22.3K, Q1'26 +25.6K, Q2'26 +37.8K. A normalised increment (~+26-28K) would imply Q2 oncology of about 285-287K.
items.source_name: GuruFocus Q2'26 call highlights; Natera 8-K; derived
items.why_new: The weather-suppression catch-up and sequential increment series are not in the known list. They affect any extrapolation of 57% growth.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: Natera says MRD is only at mid-single-digit penetration, and its Signatera ASP uplift (~$150-200) depends on MolDX approvals 12-18 months out. Volume is not limited by sequencing cost.
items.detail: Q2'26 call Q&A themes: MRD market penetration described as mid-single-digit; MolDX submissions could add ~$150-200 to the ~$1,275 Signatera ASP over 12-18 months; SIGNAL-ER 101 study for CDK4/6 use. The stated gating factors are reimbursement, evidence and guidelines. This is consistent with the thesis that adoption, not $/Gb, is the constraint, though low penetration also means long runway (against).
items.why_new: The MolDX $150-200 ASP uplift timeline and MRD penetration statement are not in the known list.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: Natera's Q2'26 revenue guidance raise of $100M to $2.85-2.91B (+31% ex true-ups) and Q1 guide raise to $2.74-2.82B show no demand slowdown at Illumina's biggest clinical customer.
items.detail: Guidance rose twice in 2026: $2.74-2.82B (Q1 release, 7 May) then $2.85-2.91B (Q2 release, 6 Aug), with Q2 revenue $752.8M (+37.7%) and Q1 $696.6M (+38.8%). Revenue is up much more than tests (+22%), so ASP drives part of it. Q1'26 and Q2'26 gross margin were 64.7% and 64.5%.
items.source_name: Natera press releases Q1'26 and Q2'26 (search results)
items.why_new: The known list has no Natera guidance path. This is a watch-out that the main Illumina customer is still accelerating.
items.verify_note: Verified: guide $2.74-2.82B → $2.85-2.91B, Q2 revenue $752.8M (+37.7%), GM 64.5% vs 63.4%. This is revenue, not volume. Revenue per test rose ~12.5% (37.7% vs 22.4%), so it is ASP-led. It does not directly show Illumina Gb demand.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: Natera's Q2'26 gross margin of 64.5% was flat q/q and about 50bp up ex true-ups, well below its 70%+ target, which suggests sequencing cost savings are being absorbed.
items.detail: Gross margin by quarter: Q1'24 56.7%, Q4'24 62.9%, Q1'25 63.1%, Q2'25 63.4%, Q4'25 66.9%, Q1'26 64.7%, Q2'26 64.5% (FY24 60.3%, FY25 64.7%). Margin gained 8.9 pts from Q4'23 to Q4'25 (51.4% to 66.9%) but has fallen 2.4 pts since Q4'25. Product revenue per test, using 6M'26 product revenue of $1,441.8M and cost of $511.8M, shows cost of revenue is growing in step with volume. Gross margin is not expanding alongside volumes, which is consistent with deeper-not-cheaper testing and the reinvestment point (against a $/Gb cost-pass-through story).
items.why_new: The gross margin time series from Q4'23 to Q2'26 and the post-Q4'25 reversal are new.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: Caris more than doubled its lab supplies (reagents) balance in H1'26, consistent with capacity and volume build-out rather than a volume slowdown.
items.detail: The Q2'26 10-Q balance sheet shows supplies of $123.8M at 30 Jun 2026 vs $63.6M at 31 Dec 2025. The H1'26 operating cash outflow for supplies was $61.6M vs $2.6M in H1'25. Molecular profiling revenue was $252.3M in Q2'26 vs $162.9M in Q2'25 (+55%), while cost of services fell from ~40% to ~32% of revenue. The excerpt does not say whether the supplies are Illumina flow cells, and could reflect pre-buying ahead of price rises or tariffs. Laboratory equipment (gross) rose from $106.2M to $138.2M.
items.quote: Supplies consist primarily of laboratory items and reagents used by the Company
items.why_new: The known list covers Caris case growth and cost per case but not the H1'26 supplies build ($61.6M cash outflow vs $2.6M) or the cost-of-services ratio.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: Michigan State's genomics core bought an AVITI to replace its NovaSeq 6000, with retirement planned for late December.
items.detail: From a search-result snippet of an MSU RTSF seminar flyer (Fall 2024 schedule). The year of the late-December retirement is not confirmed, and the page fetched empty. The flyer is vendor-influenced and claims ~2% duplication on AVITI vs >20% on NovaSeq. It is an example of a core taking 6000 volume to a rival platform, not to the X.
items.quote: to replace our NovaSeq 6000
items.why_new: MSU is not in the known core list. It shows a 6000 retirement that went to Element, not the X.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: UMN's genomics core cut AVITI prices ~40% in Jul 2024 and a further ~20% in Dec 2024, putting AVITI below the X Plus 25B on a per-1B-read basis.
items.detail: UMGC page dated 19 Dec 2024 says the average cut was 20% on top of the ~40% cut announced in Jul 2024. It says AVITI is now cheaper than the NovaSeq X Plus 25B, which had been its lowest-cost option. It installed five AVITIs in Jun 2024, and most users moved to AVITI over the prior six months. The page text gives no absolute prices; those are only in figures.
items.quote: sequencing on the AVITI is less expensive than on the Illumina NovaSeq X Plus 25B
items.why_new: The known list holds UMN's 62-71% AVITI fall to $2.6-3.6/Gb. This adds the dated 40%+20% step sequence and the five-instrument volume migration, plus the crossover below the 25B.
items.verify_note: Verified wording (~40% cut Jul 2024, a further ~20% average cut Dec 2024, AVITI now cheaper than the 25B). This largely overlaps the known 'UMN says AVITI costs fell 62-71% since FY24'. The new parts are the timing and the explicit 'below 25B' statement. It is a 2024 datapoint, so possibly stale.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: A practitioner write-up reports typical negotiated discounts of only ~15% off the $16,480 25B list price, a modest concession for a small buyer.
items.detail: From a search snippet, which I did not open in full. It reports a 25B 2x150 list price of $16,480 (~$2.06/Gb on stated output) and negotiated discounts 'in the range of 15%', with yields meeting or exceeding the advertised 26B read pairs. This suggests small and mid buyers get limited discounts and that real output is at or above spec. Date and author were not verified.
items.quote: we've seen groups negotiate discounts in the range of 15%
items.why_new: The known list has core-level $/Gb and the large-account 'half or a quarter' claims, but not a 15% small-buyer discount observation or the $16,480 list figure.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: A European university list shows Element AVITI Cloudbreak FS High Output 2x75 at about €7.19/Gb (€1,077.75 for 150 Gb).
items.detail: The Tampere University-hosted Element EURO 2025 price list (V7, modified 2 Apr 2026) prices kit 860-00015 at €1,077.75 for 1B reads and 150 Gb. That is about €7.19/Gb and €1.08 per M reads. The 2x75 kit is Element's priciest per-Gb format, so it is a ceiling point, not the headline. The full table (2x150 and larger-output kits) is unread. The comparison with Illumina 25B €/Gb is therefore incomplete.
items.source_name: Tampere University-hosted Element AVITI EURO price list
items.why_new: The corpus has only US core AVITI rates and no Element euro list price.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: Guardant Shield added ~50K tests y/y (66K vs 16K) and ~22K q/q, and the FY26 guide was raised to 270-285K tests, a large new sequencing-volume source.
items.detail: Shield tests were ~66K in Q2'26 vs ~16K in Q2'25 and 44K in Q1'26. FY26 test guide rose from 230-245K to 270-285K, which implies H2 tests of roughly 160-175K if H1 is ~110K. UnitedHealthcare coverage began 1 Aug 2026 (~70M lives, ~60% of the addressable market). Shield is a low-depth assay (the Guardant Shield COGS figure of ~$410 is known), so Gb per test is likely modest. Even so, the volume trajectory runs against the 'volume slows' view.
items.source_name: Motley Fool transcript of Guardant Q2'26 call
items.why_new: Raised FY26 Shield test guide, UHC coverage start and implied H2 run-rate are not in the known list (only ~66K and 4x are).
items.verify_note: Verified in the 8-K: Shield ~66K vs ~16K; FY26 Shield guide 270-285K (prior 230-245K). The ~66K (4x) was known; the guide raise is new. Shield is a low-Gb assay, so the Gb impact is modest.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: Personalis clinical (NeXT Personal) tests reached 10,384 in Q2'26, +199% y/y and +33% q/q, with new Medicare coverage in two indications.
items.detail: Derived Q2'25 was ~3,470 tests (added ~6,900 y/y) and Q1'26 was ~7,800 (added ~2,600 q/q). More than 1,400 physicians were ordering the test, and Medicare coverage was added for immunotherapy monitoring and for neoadjuvant TNBC/HER2+ breast cancer. Personalis is being acquired by Tempus, so guidance and calls are suspended. The per-test Gb is large (whole-genome-based MRD), so a small test count may still matter for Gb. The known list has only the Tempus deal and a gross margin figure.
items.why_new: Gives the Personalis clinical test count (10,384) and growth; only gross margin and the Tempus deal are known.

items.label: 2B
items.claim: AXELIOS 1 is already commercially launched (RUO, 29 Jun 2026) in North America plus select Europe/APAC markets, so research price pressure begins in 2026–27, not later.
items.detail: Roche announced the global launch on 29 Jun 2026. The initial geographic focus is North America and select markets in Europe and Asia-Pacific, and the platform is research-use-only. Trade press says Roche declined to disclose a full list of early-access customers. Hartwig Medical Foundation, Broad Clinical Labs and 10x Genomics (kits for single-cell and spatial) are named collaborators. This fixes the launch date, which the exclusion list does not state, but it adds no new price or customer data.
items.why_new: Gives the exact 29 Jun 2026 commercial launch date and the NA/select-markets scope; the exclusion list has only the May 2026 Investor Day pricing and the placement counts.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: Observed 25B output beats the advertised spec, so the effective $/Gb is lower than the list price implies, which is hidden deflation.
items.detail: The post's measured averages are 29.4B read pairs (about 8,800 Gb, n=37 runs at BCL) and 27.2B (about 8,200 Gb, n=4 at MU). Both are at or above the 8,000 Gb spec (+10% and +2.5%). At list, $16,480 / 8,800 = $1.87/Gb, against $2.06/Gb on spec, so customers get about 9% more data per dollar than the price sheet shows. Older MU runs were about 20% lower, which suggests yield rose over time, so effective price per Gb fell with no list-price cut.
items.why_new: The known list gives only spec-based $/Gb and a Texas A&M '30% more output' anecdote; this adds measured per-run yields (n=37 and n=4) and a ~20% older-run lag.
items.verify_note: Verified: BCL 29.4B read pairs (8,800 Gb), n=37 'samples' (not runs); MU 27.2B, n=4; spec 26B pairs/8,000 Gb; list $16,480 per flow cell. The post also says groups negotiate ~15% discounts (new). This is conceptually similar to the known Texas A&M '~30% more usable output'. It is a 2025 post.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: Yield on 25B flow cells has been rising over time, a second source of unpriced $/Gb decline.
items.detail: The author says older MU runs were about 20% below the current 27.2B read-pair average, which implies roughly 21.8B pairs earlier. The 25% gain from 21.8B to 27.2B is a de facto price cut of 1 - 1/1.25 = 20% per Gb at an unchanged list price. This is a small sample (n=4 at MU) at one sequencing center, so treat it as directional.
items.why_new: Gives a quantified, dated yield improvement on a single core, extending the known 'hidden $/Gb deflation' point.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: Usable data per flow cell is only about 60% of raw output in a real workflow, so adjusted cost per usable Gb is much higher and the real constraint is not raw sequencing price.
items.detail: Adapter trimming keeps about 60% of raw bases, because median read length falls from 300 bp to about 170 bp. That lifts cost from $1.87/Gb raw to $3.30/Gb usable (the post's figure, about 1.8x). For this wastewater use case, the cost lever is sample prep and read design more than flow-cell price. That is consistent with the thesis that sequencing cost is no longer the sole constraint, but it is one non-clinical, non-Illumina-revenue-representative workload.
items.why_new: Quantifies the raw-to-usable gap (60%) for a metagenomic workload, not previously in the file.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: Illumina's cost advantage over nanopore is large (about 100x per Gb in this use case), which limits switching pressure from ONT.
items.detail: On PromethION flow cells at $900 in bulk, the author observed only 3.3 Gb per flow cell (n=25), against marketed '>200 Gb', or about $272/Gb. Illumina 25B at $1.87-3.30/Gb is therefore nearly two orders of magnitude cheaper for wastewater metagenomics. This cuts against the idea that every rival platform is eroding Illumina pricing, at least in metagenomics and on this author's protocols.
items.why_new: The known list covers ONT's per-genome pricing, not observed wastewater yield versus claims.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: At UCLA the NovaSeq 6000 S4 lane price per read fell about 62% from Nov 2019 to the Mar 2024 X Plus 25B lane. The 6000 itself fell 27% in 3.75 years, so the X step is a further large cut on top.
items.detail: Internal S4 2x150 lane: $6,603.67 (Nov 2019) → $5,356 (S4-300, Jul 2022, −18.9%) → $4,817 (Aug 2023, −27.1% cumulative). The Mar 2024 X Plus 25B-300 internal lane was $3,168, −34% vs Aug 2023 S4 and −52% vs 2019. Assuming ~2.5B reads per S4 lane and 3.125B per 25B lane (spec), cost per M reads is $2.64 → $2.14 → $1.93 → $1.01. The 2022 and 2023 S4 figures come from my earlier probe of those sheets, not re-read this session. The 2019 anchor and the per-read series are new.
items.source_name: UCLA TCGB rate sheets (Nov 2019, Mar 2024; Jul 2022 and Aug 2023 from earlier probe)
items.why_new: The 2019 S4 anchor and the 2019→2024 per-read series are not in F054–F062; those start in 2022.
items.verify_note: Not verified: the UCLA 2019 PDF is compressed and unreadable via fetch, and the 2022/2023 S4 figures come from an earlier, unre-read probe. The 6000→X per-read step (~−48 to −62% on spec yields) overlaps the known ~3.4x revenue/Gb ratio and the MDA ~2.5x. The new part is the 6000's own ~27% core-price decline in 2019-23.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: Each Illumina high-throughput generation reprices per read by 60–75% at this core, a precedent for the 35B step. HiSeq 3000 to NovaSeq S4 was about −73%, and S4 to X 25B about −62%.
items.detail: HiSeq 3000 2x150 lane was $2,933.56 (Nov 2019 internal). Assuming ~300M reads per lane, that is ~$9.8 per M reads. S4 2x150 lane was $6,603.67 at ~2.5B reads, or $2.64 per M (−73%). The Mar 2024 25B-300 internal lane was $3,168 at ~3.125B reads, or $1.01 per M (−62% vs 2019 S4). Read counts per lane are spec assumptions, since the sheets carry no yields. Under this ladder a 35B priced like the 25B would be a large per-Gb step, not the ~20% in the known file.
items.why_new: The HiSeq 3000 price point and the two-generation per-read ladder at one core are new. The known file only covers the HiSeq precedent via revenue/Gb.
items.verify_note: Overreach. A HiSeq→NovaSeq→X platform-generation ladder at one core does not predict a within-X flow-cell step (35B). The known 35B estimate is ~20%, and within-X 10B→25B steps (−24 to −37%) are the relevant analog. Lane prices include core overhead, the yields are assumed, and the 2019 PDF is unverified. Generation-level repricing is already known (two-thirds cut, HiSeq precedent).

items.label: 1B
items.claim: Long-run per-Gb deflation at UCLA is about −17% a year, in line with management's mid-teens. It is not accelerating, because the 25B has been flat since 2024.
items.detail: A 30x genome (~100 Gb, assumed) on the external S4 lane in Nov 2019 was ~$12.15/Gb ($9,113/750 Gb assumed) plus $237 DNA prep, or ~$1,452. In Jul 2026 it is ~$3.51/Gb (25B-300 external lane $3,512.47/~1,000 Gb) plus $68.90 prep, or ~$420, a 71% fall. Over 6.67 years that is ln(0.289)/6.67 ≈ −18.6% per year, or −17% compounded. The external column in 2026 may be the non-profit rate, so the comparison to the 2019 external rate is approximate. The 2024 non-profit 25B-300 lane was $3,538 vs $3,512 in 2026, about flat.
items.source_name: UCLA TCGB pricing page and 2019 sheet
items.why_new: The seven-year all-in genome-cost CAGR at one core is new.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: Mid-throughput and benchtop run prices at UCLA rose from 2019 to 2024 while 6000 and X lanes fell. Illumina list-price increases are being passed through where there is no rival.
items.detail: Internal rates, 2019 approved → Mar 2024: NextSeq 500 Mid-Output 2x75 $1,505.86 → PE150 $2,116 (+40.5%), and Mid-Output 2x150 $2,331.75 → PE300 $3,074 (+31.8%). NextSeq High-Output 2x75 $3,876.10 → $4,210 (+8.6%). MiSeq v3 2x75 $1,389.68 → v3 PE150 $1,619 (+16.5%), and MiSeq v2 2x150 $1,534.28 → v2 PE300 $1,804 (+17.6%). Cycle-count mapping between sheets is my inference, and internal rates also carry core overhead. Over the same period the HT lane (S4 to 25B) fell about 52%.
items.why_new: The known file has only 2024+ mid-throughput ladders (F064). The 2019→2024 mid-throughput price increases are new.

items.label: 2A
items.claim: UCLA's pass-through X lane prices imply per-flow-cell costs at or above Illumina list. That shows no deep research-side discount at this UC core.
items.detail: The Mar 2024 internal lane prices carry the footnote 'Material Pass Through rates are at cost'. 25B-300 at $3,168 × 8 lanes = $25,344 vs list $24,155 (+4.9%). 10B-300 at $1,962 × 8 = $15,696 vs list $14,493 (+8.3%). By Jul 2026 the external 25B-300 is $3,512 × 8 = $28,100 (+16% vs list). This assumes 8 lanes per flow cell and the list prices from the known file (Jan 2025), and lane prices may include handling and PhiX. The external premium over internal fell from 38% (2019: $9,113 vs $6,604) to 11.7% (2024 non-profit: $3,538 vs $3,168), consistent with the move to pass-through pricing.
items.quote: Material Pass Through rates are at cost and are subject to change
items.why_new: Comparing pass-through lane prices to Illumina list at a research core is new. F080 is a different (Oxford) data point.

items.label: 2B
items.claim: At this research core, sequencing has stayed about a quarter to 30% of per-sample RNA-seq cost since 2019 because library prep fell as fast. Further sequencing price cuts, such as Roche's, move counting-work economics less than a per-read comparison suggests.
items.detail: External rates, 2019 → Jul 2026: DNA prep $237.28 → $68.90 (−71%), stranded RNA prep $255.91 → $68.14 (−73%), exome prep (NimbleGen) $406.91 → $123.88 (−70%). The 2026 prep prices are the page's external column. Take a 25M-read RNA-seq sample. In 2019 sequencing was 25M × ~$3.65 per M = ~$91 vs $256 prep, or 26% of the total. In 2026 it is 25M × $1.12 = ~$28 vs $68 prep, or 29%. The share has not fallen, so the lab still faces the prep cost and cutting sequencing price by half moves total cost ~14%. Reads per lane are spec assumptions.
items.why_new: A same-core 2019→2026 library-prep series and the sequencing share of per-sample cost are new. This quantifies the workflow-cost defense in the known file.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: Rush University's genomics core (GMCF) reportedly discontinued NovaSeq 6000 service by Dec 2025, steering users to the X or the MiSeq i100+.
items.detail: This comes from a search-result snippet of the Dec 2025 GMCF update. It says the core discontinued NovaSeq 6000 service, including SP 2x250 flow cells, and offers the X or the MiSeq i100+. I couldn't open the PDF to confirm the date, reason or price change. A second search summary found no 6000 mention in the Rush sources, so treat it as unconfirmed. If it is confirmed, it dates a mid-size US core exit from the 6000 in late 2025.
items.quote: has discontinued service for the NovaSeq6000
items.why_new: The corpus has Rush's rate card but not this retirement note.

items.label: 2A
items.claim: Illinois's negotiated discount from Illumina was only 5%, 10% and 12% on most items in the 2018-19 contract, a baseline for judging later 'insane' discounts.
items.detail: The Mar 2018 trustees agenda for the $5M/yr Illumina reagent contract says negotiation produced 5%, 10% and 12% discounts on the majority of items. A 2012 purchase had a 10% volume discount. This is a low historical research-core discount tier against which expert claims of 'half or even a quarter' pricing for large accounts can be measured. The 2024 entry's discount language has not been confirmed because the .docx was not read.
items.source_name: University of Illinois Board of Trustees, Mar 2018 Purchases Renewal Report
items.quote: 5%, 10%, and 12% discount on the majority of items
items.why_new: The known corpus has no university board discount tiers; this is a dated baseline for research-core discount levels.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: Guardant raised its FY26 oncology volume growth guide from about 35% to about 50% after Q2'26 oncology tests accelerated sharply from Q1.
items.detail: Guardant's reported oncology tests were ~74K (Q3'25), 86K (Q1'26) and ~104K (Q2'26, +63% y/y). I derived the earlier quarters from the stated growth rates: Q1'25 ≈58.5K (86/1.47), Q2'25 ≈64K (104/1.63), Q4'25 ≈79.5K (FY25 ~276K less the other three). Q2'26 added ~18K tests q/q (+21%), versus ~6.5K (+8%) in Q1. FY26 at +50% on 276K implies ~414K tests, so H2 needs ~224K (~112K/qtr), still above Q2's 104K. This is a large Illumina clinical customer accelerating, which is a watch-out for the 1C volume-slowdown call. Test counts are not Gb: Reveal and the Shield cohort differ in depth, and Guardant360 Liquid moved to the X in May.
items.source_name: Guardant Health 8-K Ex. 99.1 (Q2'26); Q3'25, Q4'25 and Q1'26 8-K exhibits and snippets
items.quote: Oncology volume growth is now expected at about 50% (prior about 35%).
items.why_new: The known file has Q2 oncology +63% and ~104K but not the guide raise from 35% to 50%, the derived quarterly series or the q/q acceleration.
items.verify_note: Restatement: the known list already has Guardant oncology +63% (~104K) and the FY26 oncology volume guide raised to ~50%. The derived H2 implication is moved to a derived item below, which actually implies H2 deceleration.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: Guardant's Shield FY26 test guide has been raised twice, from 210–225K to 270–285K. That implies H2 volumes of 80–88K per quarter, against 66K in Q2.
items.detail: Shield tests were ~9K (Q1'25), ~16K (Q2'25), ~24K (Q3'25), ~38K (Q4'25), ~44K (Q1'26) and ~66K (Q2'26, +22K q/q). The FY26 guide went 210–225K (Feb) → 230–245K (May) → 270–285K (Jul). H1 is ~110K, so H2 must be 160–175K, or 80–88K per quarter (+21% to +33% above Q2). Combined Guardant oncology plus Shield tests were ~170K in Q2'26 against ~80K a year earlier (+112%). FY26 implies ~690K tests against ~363K in FY25 (+~90%). Illumina's clinical consumables grew only ~15% ex-China, so test growth and Gb are far apart. Shield depth is undisclosed, so I did not convert to Gb.
items.source_name: Guardant Health 8-K Ex. 99.1 (Q2'26); Q4'25 and Q1'26 releases; GenomeWeb/360Dx
items.why_new: The known file has Q2 Shield ~66K and the raised FY guide, not the full six-quarter series, the three-step guide path or the implied H2 per-quarter run-rate.
items.verify_note: This mostly repeats F143, which already covers the guide raise to 270–285K and the implied H2 of 160–175K, and the known Shield figure of ~66K (4x). The only new detail is the original Feb guide of 210–225K. The combined oncology-plus-Shield FY26 total of ~690K (+~90%) follows directly from D009 plus F143. Merge into F143 rather than keep it as a separate finding.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: Guardant is cutting Shield cost per test by ~15% in 2026 and ~51% by 2028, and the cuts depend on a new FDA-approved higher-throughput workflow that went live in August 2026.
items.detail: The CFO put Shield cost per test at ~$410 against an ASP of ~$800. He said it falls ~15% (≈$61, to ~$350) by year-end 2026 and reaches $200 in 2028 (−51%), dependent on scale and automation. The higher-throughput, lower-COGS workflow was FDA-approved and goes into production in August. At ~165K H2 Shield tests, 15% is roughly $10M of H2 cost. Sequencing consumables are probably a large share of Shield COGS, though no source breaks it out. This is a large customer treating supplier cost as the main lever and gives it a reason to push for volume-tier concessions. The ~$200 saving from moving Guardant360 Liquid to the X is separate and already known.
items.source_name: Guardant Health Q2'26 earnings call transcript (Webull)
items.quote: Shield cost per test will reduce by roughly 15% from the current level of approximately $410.
items.why_new: The $410 and the 2028 target of $200 are known. The 15% cut by year-end 2026, the August production go-live of the FDA-approved workflow and the dollar arithmetic are new.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: Guardant is raising lab capacity spending ahead of volume, adding $10M to its FY26 free-cash-flow burn, which supports near-term demand for Illumina capacity and consumables.
items.detail: The FY26 free-cash-flow burn guide rose to $195–205M from $185–195M. Management attributes the increase to accelerated investment in laboratory capacity for Shield volume. The co-CEO said the company is building lab capacity 'ahead of rapidly increasing volume'. This supports the known view that capacity may be bought ahead of volume, but it also means a big customer is adding sequencing capacity in H2'26.
items.source_name: Guardant Health Q2'26 call and 8-K Ex. 99.1
items.quote: build our lab capacity ahead of rapidly increasing volume
items.why_new: The known file has Natera's Austin capacity and Caris reagent build. Guardant's FY26 burn guide raise for lab capacity is new.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: Personalis's NeXT Personal volumes are scaling quickly: 10,384 tests in Q2'26 (+199% y/y, +33% q/q). The FY26 guide of 43–45K tests needs about 25–27K in H2.
items.detail: Quarterly tests are 7,815 in Q1'26 (+258% y/y, +26% q/q) and 10,384 in Q2'26. Derived quarters: Q1'25 ≈2,180, Q2'25 3,478, Q4'25 ≈6,200, and Q3'25 ≈4,140 as a residual against 16,000 tests in FY25. H1'26 is 18.2K, so H2 must be 24.8–26.8K (12.4–13.4K per quarter, +19% to +29% above Q2). Clinical revenue per test is ~$250 (Q2'26) against ~$144 (Q2'25). It is a small Gb contribution, and Tempus is acquiring Personalis (merger announced 20 Jul 2026, $16.25 per share cap noted in the 10-Q), which ends separate calls and guidance. Because Tempus will absorb the volume, it is a data point on large-account concentration (1B) more than on Illumina Gb.
items.source_name: Personalis Q2'26 and Q1'26 releases; Q1'26 call (MarketBeat)
items.quote: extremely confident in our 2026 annual volume estimate of 43,000-45,000 tests
items.why_new: The known file has only the Q2 tests and the +199%/+33% figures. The six-quarter series, the FY guide with the H2 hurdle and the revenue per test are new.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: Exact's Oncodetect MRD test is not broken out of Abbott's results, so MRD is not yet a visible share of a large cancer-diagnostics mix.
items.detail: Abbott closed its Exact Sciences acquisition on 23 Mar 2026. Q2'26 cancer diagnostics sales were $919M, +13.3% comparable, with H1 +13%, and the growth was credited to Cologuard (mid-teens). No Oncodetect test count appears in the Q2 coverage. The next-generation MAESTRO-based Oncodetect was planned for 2026. I could not open Exact's own filings, so this is an absence of disclosure in the sources I reached, not proof of immateriality.
items.why_new: The known file has Exact only as an Ultima supply agreement (2022). The Abbott acquisition and the absence of an Oncodetect breakout are new.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: Aug 2026 Illinois rates put the 25B at $3.61/Gb. Ultima wafers are about 3-4x cheaper per read, and bulk discounts are only 6-15%.
items.detail: Carver Biotech (rates effective 1 Aug 2026): NovaSeq X Plus 25B 2x150 lane $3,380 ($3,180 at 8+ lanes, -5.9%); 10B 2x150 $2,000 ($1,710 at 8+ lanes, -14.5%). Assuming 25B = 3.125B reads/lane x 300 bp = ~937 Gb, that is $3.61/Gb; the 10B (375 Gb) is $5.33/Gb. The same core lists a full Ultima wafer at $3,310 for about 10-12B reads, or $0.28-0.33 per M reads versus about $1.08 per M clusters on the 25B lane. That is a 3.3-3.9x per-read gap. Library prep and read-length caveats apply.
items.source_name: UIUC Carver Biotechnology Center DNA Services pricing
items.quote: All pricing is updated, effective Aug. 1, 2026.
items.why_new: Illinois is not among the core rate cards already used. The Ultima-vs-25B per-read gap inside a single core's price list, plus the tier discounts, are new.
items.verify_note: Fetched the page and confirmed the 1 Aug 2026 rates: 25B 2x150 lane $3,380 ($3,180 at 8+ lanes) and 10B 2x150 lane $2,000 ($1,710). These look like internal rates; external users pay +30.8% overhead (25B ≈ $4,421). The 25B works out to ~$3.4–3.6/Gb, which sits inside the known core range ($2.63–3.51), so it adds a data point, not a new conclusion. Corrections: (1) The 8+ lane discounts are the core's own volume tier, not Illumina discounts. (2) The page gives no read count for the 'Full Wafer $3

items.label: 1B
items.claim: NCI Frederick's price ladder gives about a 33% per-Gb cut at each larger flow cell, and non-NCI users pay exactly 2x. A 35B on the same ladder implies another step down.
items.detail: NovaSeq X Plus 300-cycle NCI rates per flow cell: 1.5B $2,794, 5B $6,831, 10B $10,275, 25B $17,196. Using reads x 300 bp as Gb (450 / 1,500 / 3,000 / 7,500 Gb), $/Gb is $6.21, $4.55, $3.43 and $2.29. The 10B-to-25B step is -33%, and 5B-to-10B is -25%. Non-NCI rates are exactly 2.0x NCI for every run type, so list price is policy rather than cost. This is the same ladder logic Illumina would apply to a 35B.
items.why_new: NCI Frederick is not among the cores in the known list; it adds a full four-step $/Gb ladder including the 5B, and a federal 2x external premium.
items.verify_note: Confirmed the numbers: 1.5B/5B/10B/25B-300 cost $2,794 / $6,831 / $10,275 / $17,196, which is $6.21 / $4.55 / $3.43 / $2.29 per Gb. Non-NCI users pay exactly 2x. But the 10B→25B step of −33% is a restatement of the known within-X step (−24% to −37% at cores). The 2x non-NCI multiplier is a federal cost-recovery policy and says nothing about Illumina's pricing. Saying a 35B 'follows the same ladder' is speculation. The page is undated. It is used in a derived item below.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: At KU Medical Center the 25B costs about the same per Gb as the 10B, which suggests room for a 25B price cut.
items.detail: KUMC internal 300-cycle prices: 10B full flow cell $9,255 ($1,157/lane), or about $3.09/Gb on 3,000 Gb. The 25B is $23,872, or about $3.18/Gb on 7,500 Gb. Externally the 10B is $14,346 ($4.78/Gb) and the 25B is $37,002 ($4.93/Gb). Other cores show the 25B at 25-37% below the 10B per Gb (NCI -33%, Illinois -32%, UChicago -34%), so KUMC's 25B is priced too high by about 25-35% relative to peers. The 25B remains the unadjusted price layer at this core.
items.why_new: KUMC is not in the known core list. It shows a core that has not passed the 25B cost advantage through, a latent discount.

items.label: 2A
items.claim: UChicago charges commercial users only about 5% more than academics on the 25B-300 lane, so research prices are compressed toward a common low price.
items.detail: UChicago Genomics Facility: 25B-300 lane is $2,461 for internal, affiliated and academic users, $2,530 for start-ups and $2,599 for commercial. That is +2.8% and +5.6% versus academic. The 10B-300 is $1,499 vs $1,624 commercial (+8.3%). Per Gb that is about $2.62 on the 25B and $4.00 on the 10B (-34%). The $2,599 commercial price matches Novogene's 25B promo. Providers are therefore pricing near one narrow price, which limits Illumina's room to hold higher prices on any customer class.
items.why_new: UChicago is not in the known core list. The very narrow internal-to-commercial spread contrasts with NCI (2x) and KUMC (+55%).

items.label: 1B
items.claim: 10B lane prices at pass-through cores look flat from Jul 2023 to Aug 2026, so cheaper rivals have not yet forced visible cuts at these cores.
items.detail: UW Biotechnology Center quoted a 10B 2x150 X+ lane at $2,050 in Jul 2023. Georgia (GGBC, 12 Mar 2025) lists $2,000, and Illinois lists $2,000 effective 1 Aug 2026. Over 3 years that is about -2.4%, and it is flat Mar 2025 to Aug 2026. The Georgia 25B lane was $3,000 in Mar 2025 and Illinois is $3,380 in Aug 2026 (different cores, +12.7%). UW noted its X+ prices had since changed, so the series is not clean. Hidden gains such as extra usable output and cuts to other flow cells are a caveat.
items.source_name: Georgia Genomics & Bioinformatics Core news; UW Biotech Center (2023); UIUC (2026)
items.why_new: Known list covers CWRU, Harvard, UCLA and others. This is a cross-core flat-lane-price series that cuts against fast list-price erosion.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: UNMC's Genomics Core still lists only a NovaSeq 6000 as its Illumina platform, next to an AVITI24 and with no NovaSeq X. This is a research 6000 holdout adding the rival instead of the X.
items.detail: The 2026-dated page lists AVITI24, Illumina NovaSeq 6000, Chromium X, nCounter and library robots. It describes the 6000 as the high-capacity platform for large projects, with no X listed and no end-of-life date. Together with MSU (AVITI installed Aug 2024 'to replace our NovaSeq 6000', second AVITI Jan 2025) and UNMC, some research 6000 replacements are going to AVITI rather than the X. That lowers Illumina's capture of the conversion.
items.why_new: UNMC is new. MSU's AVITI is known (F139), but the leakage-to-AVITI pattern across two cores is new.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: Core throughput gains are huge per instrument, so one X Plus replaces more than one 6000, which supports flat consumable dollars after conversion.
items.detail: Duke's SGT core (3 Oct 2023) says the X Plus runs 128 human 30x genomes in the time its predecessor ran 48 (2.67x) and 'does more for half the cost'.
