UW-Madison (27 Jun 2024) replaced its 6000 with an X Plus, citing expanded capacity and lower consumable costs. UW (Jul 2023) said a Visium project costing a full S4 on the 6000 costs about half on the X+ lane. A 2.7x capacity gain at half the cost means flat spend only if the core's volume rises about 2x in Gb terms.
items.source_name: Duke SGT core; UW-Madison Research news; UW Biotech Center
items.quote: does more for half the cost
items.why_new: Quantifies the 2.67x per-run genome throughput gain and the 'half the cost' claim at named cores; dated 2023-24, so trend only.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: The UIUC Carver Biotechnology Center, a large public core, runs the NovaSeq 6000 alongside its NovaSeq X Plus and keeps the 6000 for a use case the X cannot serve.
items.detail: The Carver DNA Services instrument page (search-result text, Oct 2026) lists both the NovaSeq X Plus, labelled new, and the NovaSeq 6000. It notes the 6000 runs 2x250nt reads, which the X Plus does not offer. Carver bought the X Plus in Mar 2023 for $1,078,438, and the May 2024 trustee item says it owns six Illumina sequencers, so the 6000 has been kept for 3+ years after the X purchase. Read length is a reason for some 6000 volume to stay beyond a price-driven conversion. I did not verify the number of 6000s.
items.source_name: Carver Biotechnology Center, DNA Services (search-result text)
items.why_new: Gives a technical, read-length reason for 6000 persistence at a research core, which is not among the known tail cohorts.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: A public university core has had a sole-source reagent contract with Illumina since at least 2009, and its annual ceiling stayed flat in nominal terms from 2018 to 2024.
items.detail: Trustee filings show about $3.0M/yr (2012–13, renewed 2015 and 2017), then $5.0M/yr from Jul 2018 with renewal options to Jul 2024. The May 2024 item sets $25.0M over Jul 2024–Jun 2029 with one five-year renewal option, i.e. $25M ÷ 5 = $5.0M/yr. The ceiling rose 67% ($3M→$5M) in 2018, then 0% from 2018 to 2029, even though Gb per dollar has risen sharply. A ceiling is an authorization, not spend, so it signals a budget cap rather than a price. The contract uses Illumina sole-source language with no competitive rebid.
items.source_name: Univ. of Illinois Board of Trustees purchase recommendations (2012–2024; search-result summaries)
items.why_new: The known list has only the 2024 ceiling and the 2018 discounts; the full $3M→$5M→$5M/yr series is new, though it is a ceiling and not spend.

items.label: 2B
items.claim: The Carver instrument list shows no Element AVITI or Ultima, and I found no trustee item for a non-Illumina sequencer at Illinois.
items.detail: Carver's DNA Services page lists Illumina X Plus, 6000, MiSeq i100 and MiSeq, plus PacBio Revio and an ONT GridION, but no AVITI or Ultima as of the search results. The search found no 2025–26 trustee purchase item for a competitor. This is a watch-out: in this large Big Ten core, price competition from new short-read rivals has not yet reached the instrument list.
items.why_new: This is a negative check on a Big Ten flagship core, which is not covered by the known core cards.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: Guardant's raised ~50% FY26 oncology volume guide implies H2'26 oncology test growth slows to ~+46% y/y from +63% in Q2, with sequential growth near ~8%.
items.detail: FY25 oncology ≈276K tests, so +50% gives ≈414K for FY26. H1'26 was 86K + 104K = 190K, leaving ≈224K for H2 (≈112K/qtr, +8% vs Q2's 104K). H2'25 was ≈74K (Q3) + ≈79.5K (Q4) = ≈153.5K, so H2'26 implied growth is ≈+46%, versus +47% (Q1) and +63% (Q2). Shield's 270-285K guide implies H2 of ≈160-175K (80-88K/qtr) vs 66K in Q2. Even raised guides embed sequential deceleration at a top clinical customer. Test counts are not Gb.
items.quote: Oncology volume growth is now expected at about 50% (prior about 35%).
items.why_new: The known list has the guide raise but not the implied H2 deceleration math.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: Natera's non-oncology (mostly NIPT/women's health) test growth bottomed at ~+5-7% in 2025 and re-accelerated to ~+10-12.5% in H1'26, so the NIPT-maturation drag is not deepening at the largest NIPT lab.
items.detail: Non-oncology = total minus oncology tests. Q4'24 +21.3% (642.0K) → Q2'25 +4.6% → Q3'25 +6.9% → Q4'25 +7.5% (690.3K) → Q1'26 +9.8% (754.7K) → Q2'26 +12.5% (747.2K). FY25 was +7.4% (2,724.7K vs 2,536.4K). Oncology's share of tests rose from ~22% to ~28% (Q2'25→Q2'26). Organ health is included in non-oncology, so this is not pure NIPT, and sequentially Q2'26 was down slightly vs Q1.
items.why_new: Combines F121 and F131 into one trend. The 2026 re-acceleration contradicts the 'slowing' framing of both items.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: At negotiated reagent-level prices, the Illumina 25B costs ~$1.59/Gb, so the per-Gb gap to Ultima at UMN is ~1.2-1.5x, not the ~2.3-3x seen at core rates.
items.detail: List $16,480 per 25B-300 flow cell less the ~15% negotiated discount cited by Kaufman (2025) gives ≈$14,008. On measured output of ≈8,800 Gb that is ≈$1.59/Gb (≈$1.75 at the 8,000 Gb spec). UMN's Ultima full wafer is $3,204 internal for ≈2.5-3.0 Tb, ≈$1.07-1.28/Gb (D003), a gap of ≈1.2-1.5x. Core 25B rates of $2.50-3.50/Gb (UCSD ≈$2.92) include core overhead, so core-to-core comparisons overstate Ultima's raw reagent advantage. This still sits below the known 'no core reaches $2.00/Gb'.
items.why_new: First net reagent $/Gb for the 25B using measured yield and a stated discount, set against Ultima's core price.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: NIH GTR instrument fields lag reality badly: only 12 records name the NovaSeq X vs 130 naming the 6000, despite ~78% of clinical HT Gb being on the X, so registry 6000 listings (e.g., Mayo) say little about actual tail size.
items.detail: E-utilities esearch on 12 Oct 2026 returned 130 for 'NovaSeq 6000' and 12 for 'NovaSeq X'. Four of the 12 are one Labcorp/Sequenom MaterniT family, so the X has ~8% of instrument-named records. Illumina reports clinical X share of HT Gb at 78% (Q2'26). Most labs evidently do not update instrument fields after switching, so F123's 104 Mayo 6000 records are a weak tail indicator.
items.why_new: Calibrates the GTR as a source. No known item measures registry staleness.

items.label: 2A
items.claim: Michigan State University's genomics core bought an AVITI to replace its NovaSeq 6000, an example of a research core moving volume to Element.
items.detail: A fall 2024 MSU core seminar listing says the AVITI 'will replace our NovaSeq 6000' (retirement late December). The same search snippet lists AVITI 2x150 300 Gb flow cell pricing of about $2,089, or roughly $6.96/Gb, which is not cheaper per Gb than the 25B. Switching here looks driven by quality and by instrument and service costs. This is a snippet-level read, the page predates Jan 2025, and the switch may overlap with the known Dana-Farber and Novogene 6000 retirements.
items.quote: This instrument will replace our NovaSeq 6000
items.why_new: Named MSU core retiring its 6000 for AVITI is not in the known core list. Evidence is snippet-level and pre-2025.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: GeneDx's exome and genome revenue is growing much more slowly than its volume, so revenue per test is falling.
items.detail: Q2'26 exome and genome volume was 30,785 (+32% y/y) but exome and genome revenue was $100.3M (+17%), so revenue per test fell about 11% y/y (our calc). Q1'26 volume was 27,488 (+34%) against revenue of $90.6M (+27%), about −5% per test. This is GeneDx's own price and mix deflation. It shows even the largest US clinical exome/genome lab is not turning volume into proportionate dollars. That fits the thesis that large clinical accounts push for $/test and $/Gb cuts, and the lab reinvests only part of any sequencing savings. The release does not say whether the cause is payer mix, genome mix or a customer sequencing price. Adjusted gross margin was 70% versus 71% a year earlier.
items.source_name: GeneDx Q2 2026 earnings release (Business Wire); Q1 2026 release
items.why_new: The Q2'26 32% volume figure is known. The quarterly revenue-per-test arithmetic and the Q1'26 27,488 data point are not.
items.verify_note: Checked the numbers against the 8-K: exome/genome revenue $86.0M→$100.3M (+17%) and volume 23,246→30,785 (+32%), so revenue per test fell from ~$3,700 to ~$3,258 (−12%). Q1 was −5%. The FY guide (volume ≥30%, revenue ≥20%) implies about −8%. However, this is GeneDx's payer reimbursement (blended ARR, outpatient genome collection falling 43%→32%). It is not evidence of Illumina $/Gb discounting, so it does not support 1B. It belongs to the reimbursement-gating point in F188 and the derived item b

items.label: 1C
items.claim: Natera's clinical MRD unit adds were steady at +20K to +24K per quarter, and the Q2'26 record +34K was flattered by weather-suppressed Q1 volumes, with management guiding no new record in Q3.
items.detail: Clinical MRD units: Q1'25 161K, Q2'25 ~181K (+20K), Q3'25 202K (+21.5K), Q4'25 225K (+23K), Q1'26 249K (+24K), Q2'26 283K (+34K). The sequential growth rate is 12.4%, 11.9%, 11.4%, 10.7%, then 13.7%. Over the two quarters Q4'25 to Q2'26, units rose 283/225 = +25.8%, about 12.2% a quarter. That is in line with the prior trend, so the Q2 record is catch-up, not acceleration. On the Q2'26 call management said Q1 weather suppressed volumes, the 34K prior record was 25K, and it does not expect a record in Q3. If adds revert to ~25-29K, the y/y rate drifts from +56% toward the high-40s%, still strong.
items.source_name: Natera Q2'26 call (GuruFocus summary), Q3'25/Q4'25/Q1'26 call summaries and 8-Ks
items.why_new: The known file only has the Q2'26 level (283K, +56%); this adds the full sequential-add series, the q/q % trend and the explicit weather and Q3 caveat.
items.verify_note: The new piece is the sequential analysis plus management's comment that Q2 was weather catch-up and Q3 will not set a record (from the GuruFocus summary, not checked against a transcript). It supports 1C only in the narrow sense that MRD is not accelerating. MRD still grows ~+45–50% y/y, and MRD tests carry little Gb each except Signatera Genome. Low weight.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: Natera's accrual for 'testing and laboratory materials from suppliers' more than doubled in H1'26, a consumables-spend signal that points to rising volume at Illumina's largest customer.
items.detail: The Q2'26 10-Q shows the accrual at $30.9M against $12.4M at 31 Dec 2025 (+150% in six months). Over the same period inventory of supplies rose from $68.4M to $80.3M (+17%). Gross machinery and equipment rose from $170.6M to $214.8M, and construction-in-process from $94.0M to $131.1M. The accrual is not split by supplier, so it is not Illumina-specific.
items.why_new: Balance-sheet capacity and supplies data not in the known file; it corroborates the Austin build-out already noted.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: Natera's total material supplier purchase commitments fell to $220.5M at 30 Jun 2026 from $256.9M, with the largest block ($120.3M) running to Nov 2030. That is consistent with no growing hard commitment to a single sequencing vendor.
items.detail: The 10-Q lists total material commitments of $220.5M: material suppliers $120.3M (to Nov 2030), other material suppliers $48.3M, lab instruments $13.4M (Dec 2027), cloud $22.7M and application services $15.9M. The known FY25 10-K figure is $256.9M, so commitments fell about 14% while tests grew 22% y/y. The line does not name Illumina. Commitments below volume growth mean Natera is not locking in volume-based pricing through commitments, which leaves its leverage with the supply-agreement terms (the Eleventh Amendment).
items.why_new: Updates the known $256.9M commitment figure to Q2'26 and shows the 2030 maturity of the largest block.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: Women's health at Natera is gaining share after the enhanced Panorama launch, so NIPT looks less like a maturing drag at the largest NIPT lab.
items.detail: On the Q2'26 call the CFO said women's health grew high-single-digit on a seasonally adjusted basis versus Q2'25, helped by new account wins and early results from the enhanced Panorama test. The test cuts the no-call rate to 0.5%, and Fetal Focus adoption helped. The CEO said Natera is 'definitely benefiting from share gains in women's health'. Share gains at one lab mean some of the volume is taken from other NIPT labs (Labcorp, BillionToOne), so the market itself may be growing more slowly.
items.source_name: Natera Q2'26 earnings call (GuruFocus and Fool summaries)
items.quote: definitely benefiting from share gains in women's health
items.why_new: Adds management's seasonally adjusted women's health growth rate, the 0.5% no-call figure and the share-gain framing, none of which are in the known file.
items.verify_note: Natera's women's health HSD growth and the re-acceleration are largely covered by D010. What is new is management saying the growth comes from share gains. Share gains among Illumina-based NIPT labs (Natera, Labcorp, Myriad, BillionToOne) are roughly neutral for Illumina Gb, so this cuts against 1C only weakly. It actually hints that the market is growing more slowly than Natera's own rate (see the derived NIPT item).

items.label: 1C
items.claim: The largest US clinical exome/genome lab guides to a volume slowdown, with Q3'26 volume of 33,200 tests and FY26 growth of at least 30%.
items.detail: GeneDx cut its FY26 revenue guide in May 2026 to $475-490M and reiterated it in August, with exome and genome volume growth of 'at least 30%'. Q3'26 guidance is 33,200 tests, only about +8% q/q from 30,785. Y/y growth ran 34% in Q1 and 32% in Q2. Revenue missed the Street by about $10M in Q1 (Seeking Alpha summary). Test growth near 30% is a rare-disease volume engine, but it is a single customer. It is a modest tailwind for Illumina clinical Gb, and roughly a third of its growth is price-offset. The release does not name the cause of the May guide cut, and the call transcript should be read for it.
items.source_name: GeneDx Q1 2026 earnings release; Q2 2026 release (guidance section)
items.quote: exome and genome volume growth of at least 30%
items.why_new: The Q3'26 volume guide (33,200) and the FY26 guide cut are not in the known list. Only Q2 test growth is.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: Illumina is building a new Enterprise Pricing and Financing function and hiring a senior pricing lead to run personalized, segmented pricing.
items.detail: The 28 Jun 2026 Associate Director, Pricing Transformation posting (base $170.6K–$255.8K) is described as a critical hire to build out Enterprise Pricing and Financing. It sets pricing at the customer-type level under a 'pay for ownership, pay for consumption, and pay for performance' vision. It also calls for 'personalized pricing' by region, tier or channel, competitive-intelligence-driven pricing scenarios, and approval-workflow governance. This is consistent with more bespoke discounting for large accounts. The posting does not mention discounting or large accounts, so the link to the thesis is inferential.
items.source_name: Illumina job posting via resumegeni (xtalks copy also exists)
items.quote: Implement advanced customer segmentation and personalized pricing strategies
items.why_new: The known list has management quotes on application-specific pricing but no posting showing a new enterprise pricing and financing organization.

items.label: 2B
items.claim: Roche is hiring customer-facing bioinformatics, applications and field-service staff to support AXELIOS adoption, consistent with a push into counting and research workflows.
items.detail: A Santa Clara Sr. Manager, Bioinformatics ($171K–$317K) leads a customer-facing software team 'to drive adoption' of the Axelios XOOS ecosystem. A Sweden Field Service Specialist role keeps SBX systems running at customer labs. Roche also lists application-development scientists building assays on AXELIOS. This is qualitative. It shows Roche resourcing a customer-adoption push but gives no unit counts.
items.why_new: The known list covers AXELIOS buyers and pricing but not Roche's commercial and field hiring.

items.label: 2B
items.claim: A major academic core (Northwestern NUSeq) staffs an Illumina X Plus alongside AVITI, Complete Genomics T1+, Revio and ONT, and its job asks for evaluating new sequencing technologies.
items.detail: The NUSeq Senior Core Technologist posting lists six platforms from five vendors. Complete Genomics T1+ (the MGI DNBSEQ line) is new relative to the known Northwestern pricing. The role's duty is 'evaluating and implementing sequencing technologies', so the core is actively shopping. The page has no date and no volume data, so this is weak adoption evidence.
items.why_new: The known list has the NUSeq rate card but not the Complete Genomics T1+ presence or the technology-evaluation mandate.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: Myriad's prenatal volume (NIPT/carrier) shrank double digits in H1 2026, a second NIPT-adjacent datapoint showing maturity or share loss.
items.detail: Prenatal Health test volume was 144K in Q2'26 vs 159K in Q2'25 (−9%), and 297K in H1'26 vs 332K in H1'25 (−11%). Q1'26 was 153K vs 173K (−12%) (search snippet of the release). Prenatal revenue fell 16% in both Q2 and H1 ($39.8M vs $47.6M; $81.7M vs $96.9M). Myriad cut FY26 revenue guidance to $770–790M, citing 'lower Prenatal Health test volumes'.
items.source_name: Myriad Genetics Q2 2026 earnings release (8-K Ex. 99.1)
items.quote: lower Prenatal Health test volumes
items.why_new: The known list had only 'Myriad prenatal −9%'. This adds Q1 −12%, H1 −11%, absolute volumes and the revenue decline.
items.verify_note: Confirmed in the 8-K: Q2 volume 144K vs 159K (−9%), H1 297K vs 332K (−11%), and prenatal revenue −16% in both periods. FY26 revenue was cut to $770–790M 'due to lower Prenatal Health test volumes and more conservative assumptions regarding average revenue per test.' The −9% is already in the known list; the H1, revenue and guide-cut detail is new. This most likely reflects share loss to Natera and BillionToOne, not market contraction, so it shows NIPT maturity only when netted against the gainer

items.label: 1C
items.claim: Prenatal revenue per test is falling at Myriad, so NIPT volume is shrinking and pricing is eroding at the same time.
items.detail: Prenatal revenue fell about 16% against a volume decline of 9–11%, so revenue per test fell roughly 6–7% in Q2'26. In Q2'26 revenue per test was about $276 vs about $299 a year earlier. Management said guidance now assumes 'more conservative assumptions about average revenue per test'. Management attributes part of the volume weakness to payer friction and a Q2'25 order-system change, so some of this is company-specific rather than market-wide.
items.source_name: Myriad Genetics Q1 and Q2 2026 earnings releases
items.why_new: This is a revenue-per-test calculation on a prenatal peer. The corpus has no Myriad prenatal pricing datapoint and no read-through on prenatal Gb demand.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: GeneDx's quarterly volume series shows sequential stalling: Q1'26 fell 1% q/q before Q2 recovered.
items.detail: Quarterly volumes: Q1'25 20,562; Q2'25 23,246; Q3'25 ~25,702 (derived); Q4'25 27,761; Q1'26 27,488 (-1.0% q/q); Q2'26 30,785 (+12.0% q/q). Y/y growth went +34.3% (Q4'25), +34% (Q1'26), +32% (Q2'26). The Q1 dip came while the company says it added sequencing capacity, so capacity was not the limit.
items.why_new: The 2025-26 quarterly series was untabulated. The known list has only Q2'26 (30,785, +32%).

items.label: 1C
items.claim: GeneDx's genome mix is falling, which lowers sequencing Gb per test just as it adds fleet capacity.
items.detail: Genomes were 45% of the exome/genome portfolio in Q1'26. In the insurance outpatient channel they were 32% in Q2, down from close to 40% in Q1 (15% in 2025). Management expects about 30% or slightly less in H2, and reflex volumes exceeded genomes in July 2026 for the first time. Illustratively, Q1 had ~12,370 genomes at ~100 Gb (~1.24 Pb) and ~15,120 exomes at ~10 Gb (~0.15 Pb). Genomes are ~89% of Gb, so a few points of mix move Gb faster than test counts.
items.quote: reflex volumes exceeding genomes in the month of July
items.why_new: Known list covers Gb per test by test type but not GeneDx's genome-mix reversal, which is a Gb-per-test drag at a large Illumina customer.
items.verify_note: Confirmed on the Webull transcript: genomes were 32% of insurance-based outpatient volume in Q2, down from close to 40% in Q1; ~30% or slightly lower is expected in H2; reflex volumes exceeded genomes in July for the first time. Corrections: (1) The 45% figure is the whole exome/genome portfolio in Q1 (from the deck), while 32% and 40% are the insurance outpatient channel only, so don't put them on one series. (2) The '15% in 2025' figure is unverified. (3) Many GeneDx tests are trios, so absolu

items.label: 1C
items.claim: At GeneDx, payer collection and coverage, not sequencing cost, limit genome growth.
items.detail: Outpatient genome collection rate is ~32%, flat versus Q1 and down from 43% a year earlier. Management's mature-test goal is ~70%. It expects Q3 collection flat, with improvement in Q4 and the larger uplift in 2027. Genome cost is nearly 2x exome, mostly reagents, yet management does not call cost the constraint. This fits the thesis that volume is gated outside sequencing.
items.why_new: Known list has BillionToOne and Tegus expert versions of the constraint. This is a named large customer with a measured collection rate.
items.verify_note: Confirmed: outpatient genome collection is ~32%, flat q/q and down from 43% in Q2'25, and Q3 is expected roughly flat. The ~70% mature-test goal and the Q4/2027 uplift timing were not seen in the fetched excerpt. The statement that cost is not the constraint is the agent's inference, not management's words.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: A large Illumina customer is planning on lower reagent prices: genome reagent cost is ~2x exome, expected to fall as manufacturers advance technology.
items.detail: On the Q2'26 call the CFO said whole-genome production cost is nearly double exome, "almost entirely" reagents. He expects it to fall with utilization and manufacturer technology advances. Cost per test is said to stay "relatively flat for the second half of 2026" with step improvements in 2027. The 2027 timing matches the roadmap 35B flow cell (H1 2027). The customer is therefore budgeting a reagent price cut, which is the leverage the thesis describes.
items.quote: The difference there is almost entirely higher reagent costs.
items.why_new: Known list has GeneDx cost/test of about -14% (directional) but not the 2027 step-improvement guide or the reagent attribution.
items.verify_note: Confirmed quotes: genome costs 'nearly twice as much to produce than exome… almost entirely higher reagent costs,' expected to come down 'as utilization for genome grows and manufacturers advance their technology'; cost per test flat in H2'26 with 'step improvements in 2027.' Linking this to the 35B is our inference, since the CFO named no vendor or product. Part of the expected saving comes from utilization, not from supplier price. This shows a large customer budgeting for lower reagent cost;

items.label: 1C
items.claim: GeneDx is spending ahead on sequencing capacity, which shows near-term demand for Illumina consumables.
items.detail: Purchases of property, equipment and internal-use software were $16.6M in H1'26 versus $8.5M in H1'25 (+95%). The CFO said the company "significantly increased the sequencing fleet" to keep pace with genome volume, and expects capex to level off. Equipment and software purchase commitments were $41.5M at 30 Jun 2026 versus $33.5M at 31 Mar 2026. Inventory was $17.8M versus $13.95M at year-end 2025 (+28%).
items.why_new: Known list has BillionToOne capex (+63%) and Guardant capacity, not GeneDx.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: GeneDx's revenue per exome/genome test fell about 12% y/y in Q2'26, so its own price per test is falling, which keeps pressure on its sequencing cost.
items.detail: Revenue per test was $3,258 in Q2'26 ($100.3M / 30,785) versus about $3,699 in Q2'25 ($86.0M / 23,246), or -11.9%. Q1 was about $3,296 versus $3,473 (-5%). Q3 guidance is ~$3,343 ($111M / 33,200). The company says contracted pricing is unchanged and the cause is genome mix, so it has less room to absorb a flat reagent price. It reported adjusted gross margin of 70.4% versus 70.6% a year earlier.
items.quote: There have been no meaningful changes to our contracted pricing.
items.why_new: The known list has GeneDx revenue growing slower than volume. The quantified per-test series and Q3 guide arithmetic are new.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: GeneDx's FY26 guidance cut was driven by reimbursement mix, not volume, but its volume guide was also lowered from 33-35% to at least 30%.
items.detail: FY26 revenue guidance was cut from $540-555M (23 Feb) to $475-490M (4 May), a ~$65M or ~12% cut at the midpoint. Exome/genome volume growth went from 33-35% (128-131K tests) to at least 30%. Of the Q1 revenue shortfall, ~$5.5M was lower blended ARR and ~$6.5M was weakness in Fabric and biopharma. The CFO said the initial guide "proved to be too aggressive".
items.source_name: GeneDx Q1'26 deck and release (call summary via search snippets)
items.quote: proved to be too aggressive
items.why_new: The known list has only Q3 volume. The guide-cut sizing, its causes and the prior volume range are new.
items.verify_note: Confirmed in the Q1 deck: revenue guide $540–555M → $475–490M; volume growth 33–35% → ≥30%; exome/genome revenue growth 33–35% → ≥20%. Most of the cut is price and ARR, since the revenue-growth guide fell ~13–15 pts against ~3–5 pts for volume. The volume cut is modest and volume still grows ≥30%. The Q1 shortfall split ($5.5M ARR / $6.5M Fabric and biopharma) and the 'too aggressive' quote come from snippets and were not verified.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: Payer coverage is widening for GeneDx's exome/genome tests, which supports clinical Gb growth into 2027.
items.detail: Texas Medicaid exome coverage began 1 May 2026. Medi-Cal genome pricing at 100% of the Medicare rate began 1 Jul 2026. Carelon outpatient genome coverage began 14 Jun 2026 (up to 56M lives). Mississippi Medicaid started 1 Jul 2026, bringing state Medicaid programs covering outpatient exome and/or genome to 39. Genome tests run ~100 Gb each, so each approved payer adds Gb.
items.why_new: These dated payer expansions are not on the known list. They are a watch-out for the volume-slowdown claim.
items.verify_note: Confirmed in the Q2 8-K: Texas Medicaid exome coverage from 1 May 2026; Medi-Cal genome pricing at 100% of Medicare from 1 Jul 2026; Carelon outpatient genome from 14 Jun 2026 (up to 56M lives); Mississippi Medicaid from 1 Jul 2026; 39 state Medicaid programs. Two things offset it: genome mix is falling (F187) and collection rates are flat at ~32% (F188), so near-term Gb gains from new coverage are slow.

items.label: 2B
items.claim: By Mar 2026 Roche had posted installation and field-service roles for AXELIOS in the Nordics and the UK/Ireland, so a customer-facing build-out was under way before the 29 Jun 2026 launch.
items.detail: A Field Service Engineer (SBX sequencing technology) role, listed for the Nordics and posted 2026-03-03, covers installing and commissioning new platforms 'from checking the customer's technical infrastructure through final handover'. It also covers travel across EMEA-LATAM. A separate UK/Ireland 'Technical Specialist' field-service post for the 'new Axelios Sequencing System' (NHS, university labs, private service providers) was removed 28 Feb 2026. Neither post states unit counts. This is directionally supportive for 2B only, and it shows Roche investing ahead of revenue.
items.source_name: jobbsafari.se mirror of Roche posting; builtinlondon.uk mirror
items.quote: the guarantor of maximum system uptime in our customers' laboratories
items.why_new: Known file lists Roche hiring generally (F182). This adds dated, country-level field-service posts (Nordics, UK/Ireland) tied to SBX/AXELIOS.

items.label: 2B
items.claim: Roche is building a customer-facing bioinformatics organization around AXELIOS and is hiring a senior manager at $170.5K–$316.6K.
items.detail: A Roche Sr. Manager, Bioinformatics post was dated 18 Jun 2026, 11 days before launch, and has since expired. It pays $170,500–$316,600 in the US. Aggregator text says the hire is the 'primary executive-level technical contact for new customers' and manages customer-facing bioinformatics scientists and solutions architects. The role is based in Santa Clara or San Diego and is tied to the XOOS open-source tool ecosystem. A senior-manager-level customer-facing team implies Roche expects enough accounts to need a managed team.
items.source_name: jobrxiv.org (Roche posting mirror); Built In SF
items.quote: Serve as the primary executive-level technical contact for new customers
items.why_new: Adds the post date (18 Jun 2026), the salary range and the team-management scope. Prior notes only name Roche bioinformatics hiring.

items.label: 2B
items.claim: Roche has posted a Global Technical Product Manager role for AXELIOS inside Global Customer Support, which signals an on-market product support structure.
items.detail: The Bay Area post pays $109,300–$203,100 and is described as supporting 'on-market products' with second-level troubleshooting. A Wilmington, MA 'Technical Customer Experience Manager' role runs customer visits and proof-of-concept studies showing AXELIOS 1 with KAPA library prep. Together they point to a support layer for post-launch customers and for converting evaluators. Neither post gives counts. These are search-result snippets, and the jobboardly page returned 404 when I tried to open it.
items.why_new: Names two further AXELIOS support and pre-sales roles (Global TPM, Technical Customer Experience Manager) that are not in the known file.

items.label: 2B
items.claim: Roche's research and early-development hiring is aimed at single-cell, spatial and protein-by-sequencing applications, which are the counting workloads where AXELIOS price per read would hit Illumina research volume.
items.detail: The Pleasanton Principal Research Scientist II role (removed 21 Oct 2025; CA pay $108.4K–$201.2K) builds 'the application ecosystem for the Axelios Sequencing platform'. Desired experience is single-cell sequencing, protein detection by sequencing and spatial sequencing. A parallel Principal Scientist I Molecular Lab role develops assays on AXELIOS. The lead time shows Roche was building counting-type applications about 8 months before launch. It is qualitative and says nothing about pricing.
items.quote: build the application ecosystem for the Axelios Sequencing platform
items.why_new: The known file cites the 10x and single-cell partnership. This adds the dated job-description evidence that Roche is staffing single-cell, spatial and protein applications.

items.label: 2B
items.claim: Roche's open AXELIOS roles are few, clustered in R&D, support and the US, and mostly not sales, so the roles I found do not show a mass-market commercial push.
items.detail: Across about 8 searches I found roughly 8 distinct Roche postings tied to AXELIOS or sequencing. They split by function as follows: R&D or applications 2, bioinformatics 1, field service 2 (Nordics, UK), product or customer support 2, sales 1 (Seoul, not AXELIOS-specific). The main sales roles found were not AXELIOS-tagged. Reuters-cited analyst Stefan Schneider expects a gradual ramp because of institutional tenders. This is a thin and incomplete aggregator sample, so it is a weak counterpoint.
items.why_new: This is the first function-by-function tally of AXELIOS-related postings. Prior notes list roles without a count.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: Illumina's launch-date comparator shows its own list price is far above Roche's: NovaSeq X at about $985K–$1.25M against AXELIOS at $750K.
items.detail: GenomeWeb and Reuters snippets give the AXELIOS 1 US list as $750,000 and about $150 per 30x duplex genome in a 16-genome run, with the sensor reused up to 20 times or for 90 days. Reuters puts NovaSeq X list at about $985K–$1.25M. The instrument is about 24% cheaper than the low end of the X range ($750K vs $985K). Analysts say the recurring consumable cost matters more than the instrument price. CNAG is reported as an early commercial customer.
items.why_new: The known file has the $750K and $150 figures. It does not have the X instrument price range, so the 24% discount to the low end is new arithmetic.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: GeneDx's falling genome mix means its sequencing Gb grows much more slowly than its ≥30% test-volume guide; a 5-point portfolio mix drop roughly halves Gb growth.
items.detail: Illustrative Gb per test is ~100 Gb for a genome and ~10 Gb for an exome (singleton; trios scale both). At the Q1'26 portfolio genome share of 45%, the average is ~50.5 Gb per test. At 40% it is ~46 Gb (−9%), and at 35% it is ~41.5 Gb (−18%). So ≥30% test growth turns into roughly +18% Gb (40% mix) or +7% (35% mix). Management is guiding the insurance-outpatient genome share down from ~40% (Q1) to 32% (Q2) and ~30% (H2'26), with reflex exomes outrunning genomes in July. The largest US clinical exome/genome lab therefore adds far less Illumina volume than its test counts suggest.
items.source_name: GeneDx Q2'26 call (Webull) and Q1'26 deck (SEC); our calc
items.quote: hovering at around approximately 30%, maybe slightly lower
items.why_new: The known list has GeneDx test growth (+32%) but no Gb-per-test or mix-adjusted Gb estimate for GeneDx.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: Netting Natera's NIPT-heavy gains against Myriad's prenatal losses, combined volume at the two labs grew only ~+8% y/y in Q2'26, so most of Natera's women's health growth is share shift.
items.detail: Natera non-oncology tests were 747.2K in Q2'26 vs 664.3K (+82.9K). Myriad Prenatal Health was 144K vs 159K (−15K). Combined that is 891.2K vs 823.3K, or +8.2%, against Natera's own +12.5%. For H1, Myriad was 297K vs 332K (−35K). Both labs run on Illumina, so the share shift between them is roughly neutral for Illumina NIPT Gb, and the underlying pool is growing at a high-single-digit rate. Caveats: Natera's non-oncology line includes organ health, Myriad's prenatal line includes carrier screening, and Labcorp and BillionToOne are not netted.
items.source_name: Myriad Q2'26 8-K Ex. 99.1; Natera Q2'26 release; our calc
items.quote: lower Prenatal Health test volumes
items.why_new: The known list has Myriad −9% and Natera non-oncology separately, but no combined net NIPT-pool growth rate.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: GeneDx's statement that a genome costs ~2x an exome, almost all reagents, implies an incremental reagent cost of roughly $2.4–9 per extra Gb, well above negotiated 25B levels (~$1.6–2.3/Gb). This gives it a strong motive to seek supplier price cuts in 2027.
items.detail: With the known blended cost per test of ~$1,176 and a ~45% genome mix, the cost split is 0.55C + 0.45×2C = 1.45C. That gives an exome cost C of ~$810 and a genome cost of ~$1,620. The ~$810 difference buys ~90–115 extra Gb per singleton (~$7–9/Gb) or ~270–345 Gb per trio (~$2.4–3.0/Gb). Even the trio case sits above the ~$1.6–2.3/Gb negotiated or GSA 25B estimates. The difference probably includes genome library prep, so Illumina's sequencing share of the gap is smaller. The CFO is budgeting 'step improvements in 2027' as manufacturers advance their technology. Heavy assumptions apply: the mix and cost periods differ, and the trio share is unknown.
items.source_name: GeneDx Q2'26 call (Webull); known GeneDx cost/test; our calc
items.quote: almost entirely higher reagent costs
items.why_new: No known item converts GeneDx's genome-vs-exome cost gap into an implied reagent $/Gb.

items.label: 2A
items.claim: NCI Frederick's internal recharge for a 25B-300 flow cell ($17,196) is ~4% above Illumina's $16,480 list, so this large federal research user does not appear to pass through deep discounts.
items.detail: NCI Frederick's undated rate page lists the 25B-300 at $17,196 per flow cell for NCI users (non-NCI users pay 2x, $34,392). Against the $16,480 list price (F146), that is +4.3%. Unless overhead and labor are large, the implied reagent cost is near list. This fits the sole-source, uncompeted NIH reagent IDC (F040; $90M ceiling over 5 years). Both cut against the 'insane discounts' picture for government research accounts, though Broad-type large academic centers may differ. Caveat: the recharge rate includes labor and QC, so the actual reagent discount cannot be backed out.
items.source_name: NCI Frederick Sequencing Facility pricing; F146 list price
items.why_new: No known item compares a federal facility's flow-cell recharge with Illumina list price.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: At GeneDx, revenue per exome/genome test fell ~12% y/y in Q2'26, and the FY26 guide implies ~−8%. Payer economics, not sequencing capacity, gate the lab's growth.
items.detail: Exome/genome revenue was $100.3M on 30,785 tests in Q2'26, or ~$3,258 per test, vs $86.0M on 23,246 (~$3,700) in Q2'25: −12%. Q1'26 was ~$3,296 vs ~$3,472, or −5%. The FY26 guide of volume ≥30% and revenue ≥20% implies at least −8% per test. Outpatient genome collection fell from 43% to 32% over the same period, and management cut the revenue guide by ~$65M while trimming volume only 3–5 points. A key Illumina clinical customer is therefore limited by reimbursement, which caps how fast it can expand genome (high-Gb) volume.
items.source_name: GeneDx Q2'26 and Q1'26 8-K/deck; our calc
items.why_new: The known list has GeneDx volume (+32%) and cost per test, but not its revenue per test or the guide-implied ARPT decline.

items.label: 2B
items.claim: UMGC, a historically Illumina-heavy core, now lists no in-house Illumina high-throughput sequencer; its in-house fleet is 5 Element AVITI24s plus 2 Ultima UG200s, and the NovaSeq X Plus is outsourced to partners.
items.detail: The current UMGC core-facility page lists 2 Ultima UG200 (the services menu still says UG100), 5 AVITI24, 1 Nanopore P2 Solo, and PacBio Revio and NovaSeq X Plus only via 'partnered outsourcing'. The Dec 2024 price-drop post says AVITI was installed in Jun 2024 and 'most users' moved to AVITI within about six months. The post reports two cuts, ~40% (Jul 2024) then ~20% (19 Dec 2024), so the AVITI price is about 0.6 x 0.8 = 0.48 of its launch level (-52%). It says AVITI then undercut the NovaSeq X Plus 25B, previously the center's cheapest option. An older UMGC job posting named HiSeq, so the core's Illumina footprint has shrunk from in-house HiSeq to none for high throughput. Earlier UMGC pages listed one UG100; the page I read now lists two UG200. The page has no install dates, and the UG100/UG200 labelling is inconsistent.
items.source_name: University of Minnesota Genomics Center (core facility page and AVITI price-drop post)
items.quote: most users moved their work to AVITI
items.why_new: Known items cite UMGC's Ultima/AVITI prices; the fleet count (5 AVITI24 + 2 UG200, no in-house Illumina HT) and the 'most users moved in six months' share shift are not in the known list.
items.verify_note: Checked on the live page (12 Oct 2026). In-house there are 2 Ultima UG200, 5 AVITI24 and 1 Nanopore P2 Solo. NovaSeq X Plus is offered only through 'partnered outsourcing' and Revio only through Mayo. The services menu still says UG100. The AVITI price cuts (~40% then ~20%) are already known from F140 and the known list ('UMN AVITI costs fell 62–71%'). Only the fleet composition is new: the core has no in-house Illumina high-throughput instrument. Outsourced X Plus lanes still earn Illumina cons

items.label: 2B
items.claim: UNMC's genomics core has added Ultima to a fleet that is only AVITI24 plus NovaSeq 6000, so a research core is now stacking two non-Illumina short-read platforms next to a legacy 6000.
items.detail: The UNMC services page (copyright 2026) lists Element AVITI24, Illumina NovaSeq 6000, an Ultima platform 'for selected projects', and 10x Chromium X. For RNA-seq it says the platform is chosen by scale: AVITI24 or NovaSeq 6000. F169 recorded this core with only the 6000 and AVITI24. The Ultima line is new here. There is no NovaSeq X. No share or price data are given.
items.why_new: Prior notes recorded UNMC as 6000 plus AVITI24 only; the Ultima addition and the scale-based choice rule are new.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: At Northwestern NUSeq the NovaSeq X Plus 25B remains the cheapest platform per read and the core calls it the most cost-effective at <$3/Gb, so AVITI and T1+ are not undercutting Illumina there; only the 10B lane price looks cut.
items.detail: The FY27-labelled pricing page shows 25B PE150 at $3,000 internal ($3,750 external) for 2,500-3,000M read pairs, or about $1.09 per M pairs at the 2,750M midpoint. AVITI high-output PE150 is $2,096 for 800-1,000M pairs, about $2.33 per M pairs, roughly 2.1x the 25B. The 10B PE150 lane is $1,499 internal, against $1,600 in the FY26 PDF (search snippet) and $1,660 on the older web page. That is about -6% to -10%, and the 25B did not move. The technologies page says the 25B is 'most cost effective among all NUSeq sequencers at <$3 per Gbp'. The page header says FY26 while the linked file is 'fy27-prices', so year labelling is uncertain. Yields are quoted as ranges, so per-read figures are midpoint-based.
items.source_name: Northwestern NUSeq pricing and technologies pages
items.quote: most cost effective among all NUSeq sequencers at <$3 per Gbp
items.why_new: Known Northwestern AVITI $/Gb range is a conflict item. The 10B-only cut with a flat 25B, the 2.1x AVITI per-pair ratio, and the core's own '<$3/Gb' statement are new.
items.verify_note: Prices confirmed. 25B PE150 is $3,000 internal for 2.5–3.0B pairs, 10B PE150 is $1,499, and AVITI PE150 high-output is $2,096 for 0.8–1.0B pairs. The page says FY26 but the PDF is named fy27. The core-level fact (25B cheaper than AVITI at Northwestern) is already known ('Northwestern AVITI ~$10.8–19/Gb vs 25B $3.2–5.0'). The '<$3/Gbp' marketing line does not match the card: $3,000 for 750–900 Gb is $3.33–4.00/Gb. Only the small 10B lane cut (−6% to −10%) is new.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: UC Davis's DNA Technologies Core says its AVITI per-base cost is only 'similar' to the NovaSeq X 10B flow cell, so rival short-read cost parity, not a large gap, is the claim at a major core.
items.detail: The current AVITI page says it delivers higher-quality data faster 'at similar per-base cost' to the X 10B flow cell. The 'significantly lower costs' wording is relative to Illumina sequencers generally. Older versions compared AVITI to the biggest 6000 flow cell at the same per-base cost. Prices are $2,000 for a PE150 run and $1,400 for a PE75 run at UC rates. So the cost position vs Illumina has not moved from parity in about two years at this core, and the 25B is not mentioned.
items.source_name: UC Davis Genome Center DNA Technologies Core
items.quote: similar per-base cost NovaSeq X 10B flowcell
items.why_new: The probe note quoted only 'significantly lower costs'; the actual per-base parity claim vs the X 10B and the UC-rate run prices are new.
items.verify_note: Not verified: the page returned HTTP 403. Parity with the 10B means AVITI costs roughly 1.25–1.5x the 25B per Gb, which is consistent with Illumina staying cheapest at high throughput. The claim that parity is unchanged over about two years rests on 'older versions' the agent did not cite.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: Complete Genomics' DNBSEQ-T7+ began shipping in Feb 2026 with a '$1 per Gb / $100 genome' claim, and several US/Canadian cores already list DNBSEQ T7 service, adding a third low-price short-read option.
items.detail: Complete Genomics says the T7+ is available for immediate sale in the US and Canada, with 'high single-digit' installations already in place. Its provider list shows University of Colorado Anschutz (G400 and T7), McGill (G400 and T7), Vancouver Prostate Centre (G400 and T7) and UNC HTSF with a DNBSEQ-T7. The $1/Gb figure is a vendor claim, not a core rate. It compares with core 25B rates of about $2.5-3.1/Gb in the known list. No university core announced T1+ or T7+ service in 2025-26 in what I found.
items.source_name: Complete Genomics news and service-provider list; UNC HTSF page
items.why_new: The known file covers MGI units and UCLA T7 flow-cell prices, not the T7+ US launch, the $1/Gb claim, or the list of US/Canadian core providers.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: NovaSeq 6000s are still listed in core and lab fleets in 2026 (Bonn NGS core, UNMC, Queen's Belfast technician posting), which suggests the legacy tail has not disappeared outside the US.
items.detail: The University of Bonn NGS core lists NovaSeq X Plus, NovaSeq 6000, MiSeq and AVITI LT. A Queen's University Belfast Genomics & Cytometry Core technician posting (closing 20 Jul 2026) names MiSeq, NextSeq 2000 and NovaSeq 6000, with no X or AVITI. A University of Warsaw core posting also names the 6000. OIST's sequencing specialist posting lists X Plus and no 6000. Counts and dates are not given, and pages are often stale. This is anecdotal, not a measure of volume.
items.source_name: Univ. Bonn BTC NGS core; jobs.ac.uk Queen's Belfast posting; search results
items.why_new: Prior notes list US/Canadian/UK public-buyer 6000 holdouts, not Bonn, Belfast or Warsaw postings.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: Dated core retirement notices show 6000s going out in 1-for-1 swaps, with Northwestern's 6000 unavailable from Jan 2024, MSU's retiring in Dec 2024 and UW-Madison's replaced in Jun 2024, so research-side conversion is largely complete.
items.detail: UW-Madison's DNA Sequencing Facility posted on 27 Jun 2024 that a 6000 was replaced by one X Plus, citing 'expanded capacity' and lower consumable costs. This is consolidation (one X replaces the 6000), not extra boxes. UW-Madison also reported its 10B flow cell was 30% cheaper and gave 60% more data per dollar than AVITI (snippet, date unclear), which cuts against Element pressure there. Together with the known Dana-Farber, Rush and Novogene exits, the dated cases sit mostly in 2024, so they are not new tail data after 2025. Use these as watch-outs for the 1A tail size at research cores.
items.source_name: UW-Madison Research news; cgsi.wisc.edu 'Sequencing's best bang for the buck'
items.why_new: UW-Madison's replacement and its 10B-vs-AVITI 30% cheaper / 60% more data claim are not in the known list.

items.label: 2A
items.claim: Vendor-subsidised free sequencing is reaching academic users: Arizona Genetics Core ran an AVITI grant giving up to 4 awards of one free flow cell (up to 1B 2x150 reads) plus free library prep.
items.detail: Published 11 Sep 2024, applications ran 12 Sep-11 Oct 2024 with awards by 25 Oct 2024. Each award is one Element flow cell and library prep and labor at no charge. The AZGC pages disagree on whether NovaSeq is routine or by request. No prices are published (quotes only) and the pages carry a 2026 copyright. This is about Element seeding adoption in research, not about Illumina price cuts.
items.source_name: University of Arizona Cores / Arizona Genetics Core
items.quote: free sequencing from Element Biosciences
items.why_new: Known Arizona items are expert channel checks; the free-flow-cell grant program is new.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: A federal HHS/NIH sequencing procurement (presolicitation 17 Jun 2026) targets Ultima for high-throughput DNA sequencing, a sign that a large federal sequencing center is testing a non-Illumina platform.
items.detail: A search-result snippet describes an NIH Intramural Sequencing Center presolicitation posted 17 Jun 2026 to use Ultima Genomics technology; a related closed solicitation is numbered 75N98026Q00652 (titled 'Ultima Genomics, Opentrons Flex'). I did not open the notice, so scope and value are unknown. F044 recorded the same center renewing on Illumina proprietary-reagent grounds in 2025, so this would be a change of posture. Treat as a lead until the notice is read.
items.why_new: F044 and F040 cover Illumina lock-in at NIH; the June 2026 Ultima presolicitation is not in the known list.

items.label: 2B
items.claim: The University of Chicago genomics facility positions AVITI only for small, specialised projects and calls the NovaSeq X the 'lowest cost per base', so Element has not displaced Illumina for bulk research work there.
items.detail: The NGS page lists only NovaSeq X (10B, 1.5B and 25B flow cells; 25B is 8 lanes at ~3-3.2B reads per lane) and the AVITI. It says AVITI is for smaller projects needing flexible scheduling, and that NovaSeq X offers the lowest cost per base with up to 25B reads per flow cell. Pricing examples are dated 2024. No 6000 is listed. This is a counterexample to the Minnesota pattern.
items.quote: lowest cost per base
items.why_new: The known file has UChicago's commercial-vs-academic 25B premium only, not its fleet or the AVITI-as-niche positioning.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: Illumina advertises 6000 lease pricing at about 79% of the X's, so the 6000 is still being actively financed and sold.
items.detail: The 3-year lease starting prices are $32,700/month for the NovaSeq 6000 and $41,500/month for the NovaSeq X Series. The 6000 is therefore 79% of the X: 32.7 / 41.5 = 0.788. The 6000Dx (IVD) is $35,900/month. The page shows no end-of-life language for the 6000, consistent with the live 6000 product page. Leasing is a fixed payment with no reagent commitment, so it does not lock in tail consumables.
items.why_new: These instrument lease price points are not in the known list. They add a data point that the 6000 is still offered and financed in 2026.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: A Singapore Senior Contracts Analyst posting shows commercial contracts and tenders in APAC and Greater China are being worked as dedicated headcount.
items.detail: The role (APAC and/or Greater China) covers reviewing, drafting, negotiating and managing contracts, tenders and order-related terms, working with Legal, Finance, Sales and account managers. Tender work is where price competition is most visible in Asia, including against MGI. I could not verify the posting date, the asset-financing or reagent-rental scope, or any increase over 2024-25 headcount.
items.why_new: The known list has no contracts-role evidence.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: Myriad's prenatal test volume has fallen about 17% from its Q1'25 peak, with four straight y/y declines through Q2'26.
items.detail: Quarterly prenatal tests (thousands) were: Q1'24 172, Q2'24 ~173, Q3'24 162, Q4'24 160, Q1'25 173, Q2'25 159, Q3'25 155, Q4'25 150, Q1'26 153, Q2'26 144. Q2'26 is 144/173 = -16.8% versus the Q1'25 peak and -9% y/y. Y/y changes ran +1% (Q1'25), -8%, -4%, -6%, -12% (Q1'26), -9% (Q2'26). The prior corpus held only 'Myriad prenatal -9%'; the full series and the four consecutive declines are new.
items.source_name: Myriad Genetics 8-K EX-99.1 (Q2'26), with Q1'26, Q4'25, Q3'25 and Q1'25 exhibits
items.why_new: Known file has only the Q2'26 -9%; the 10-quarter volume series and the Q1'26 -12% are new.
items.verify_note: Q2'26 (144K vs 159K) and H1 (297K vs 332K) are confirmed in the EX-99.1, but they are already known via F184. The new part is the earlier series (Q1'24–Q4'25), which I did not verify. Correction: Myriad's 'Prenatal Health' segment includes carrier screening (Foresight) as well as NIPT (Prequel), so this is not a pure NIPT series.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: Myriad's prenatal revenue per test peaked in 2025 and is now falling, and the 10-Q blames reimbursement declines.
items.detail: I derived revenue per test as revenue ÷ tests. The series is: Q1'24 $44.3M/172K = $258; Q2'24 ~$44.4M/173K = $257; Q3'24 $43.5M/162K = $269; Q4'24 $44.9M/160K = $281; Q1'25 $49.3M/173K = $285; Q2'25 $47.6M/159K = $299; Q3'25 $44.5M/155K = $287; Q4'25 $44.9M/150K = $299; Q1'26 $41.9M/153K = $274; Q2'26 $39.8M/144K = $276. Q2'26 is -8% y/y and -7.7% from the $299 peak. The 10-Q says Q2 revenue fell $7.8M 'due to a 9% decrease in volume and an 8% decrease in revenue per test'. H1'26 fell 11% in volume and 6% in revenue per test. Q2'24 revenue is backed out of the 9-month total less Q1 and Q3.
items.source_name: Myriad Genetics 10-Q for the period ended 30 Jun 2026, MD&A
items.quote: an 8% decrease in revenue per test
items.why_new: The known file has no NIPT revenue-per-test series; this one is derived and dated.
items.verify_note: Confirmed in the 10-Q MD&A. Q2 had a 9% fall in volume and an 8% fall in revenue per test; H1 had −11% and −6%. Both are explicitly 'due to declines in reimbursement.' Q2 revenue per test is $39.8M/144K = $276, versus $47.6M/159K = $299, which is −7.8%. Part of the 2025 peak came from carrier-screening coverage mix. This is pricing pressure on the lab, not a direct Illumina datapoint.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: Myriad cut FY26 revenue guidance by $90M, citing lower prenatal volume and more conservative revenue-per-test assumptions, and expects no H2 rebound.
items.detail: Guidance moved to $770-790M, about $90M below the prior outlook. The release says it reflects 'lower Prenatal Health test volumes and more conservative assumptions regarding average revenue per test'. H2 revenue is assumed to roughly match H1, Q3 flat to slightly up, and the outlook excludes new products and the expanded sales team. Q1'26 had said management expected 'improved performance' and a return to growth in H2 from reactivation and FirstGene; Q2 walked that back. A NIPT lab that cannot re-accelerate even with a launch is a maturity datapoint, though the company blames execution.
items.source_name: Myriad Genetics Q2'26 press release and call summaries (GuruFocus, Quartr)
items.quote: more conservative assumptions regarding average revenue per test
items.why_new: The guidance cut and the reversal of the Q1'26 H2-recovery language are not in the known file.
items.verify_note: The new guide of $770–790M and the CEO's reason (lower Prenatal Health volumes plus more conservative revenue-per-test assumptions) are confirmed in the EX-99.1. The release does not state the prior range, so the '$90M cut' is unverified. Management attributes much of the weakness to company-specific execution (see F215).

items.label: 1C
items.claim: Myriad's prenatal decline is mostly company-specific execution, not market-wide NIPT maturity.
items.detail: Management ties the volume loss to the Q2'25 order-management-system change, SneakPeek demand (Q3'25 release), a salesforce expansion lag and 'competitive dynamics'. Revenue rose 7% in the 9 months of 2025 and 5% in FY25 ($186.3M vs $177.1M) on payer coverage of expanded carrier screening. Meanwhile BillionToOne's prenatal revenue was $94.2M in Q2'26 (+55%), 2.4x Myriad's $39.8M. Share is moving between labs while the total market keeps growing.
items.source_name: Myriad Q4'25 8-K EX-99.1; BillionToOne Q2'26 release (search snippet)
items.quote: transition dynamics following the second quarter 2025 implementation
items.why_new: The known file calls Myriad prenatal -9% a maturity signal; this isolates the company-specific causes and the winner comparison.
items.verify_note: The reasoning about share shift is fair. However, the BillionToOne +55% figure is already known (F079), and D014 already nets Natera's gains against Myriad's losses (combined +8%). The incremental value is small.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: Myriad's prenatal volume loss is immaterial to Illumina's Gb base.
items.detail: Myriad ran 637K prenatal tests in FY25. At 1-2 Gb per NIPT (from the known file), that is roughly 0.6-1.3M Gb a year. The 35K fewer tests in H1'26 (297K vs 332K) is about 35-70K Gb, a rounding error against the ~800M Gb HT base the known file uses. Myriad's NIPT slowdown therefore says nothing quantitative about Illumina volume growth; only the share-shift and pricing signals matter. The Gb-per-test figures are the known-file assumptions, not Myriad disclosures.
items.why_new: Quantifies how little of Illumina's Gb base this lab's NIPT swing represents.
items.verify_note: The arithmetic is correct: 637K × 1–2 Gb ≈ 0.6–1.3M Gb a year, and 35K × 1–2 ≈ 35–70K Gb. Carrier-screening panels use somewhat more Gb per test than NIPT, but the total is still immaterial against an ~800M Gb base. This is a sizing caveat, not new evidence.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: Myriad's 2025 prenatal revenue per test rose about 10% on coverage and then reversed in 2026, so NIPT pricing gains were not durable.
items.detail: FY24 was $177.1M/666K = $266 per test and FY25 was $186.3M/637K = $292 (+10%) while volume fell 4%. Q3'25 revenue grew 2% 'reflecting ongoing expansion of payer coverage, particularly for Foresight Expanded Carrier Screen' even as volume fell 4%. Q1'26 revenue per test dropped to $274 (-4% y/y) and H1'26 to $275 (-6% y/y). In April 2026 a national payer broadened carrier-screen coverage, yet Q2 was still down. Per-test price pressure on the customer side is a pointer that labs will keep pushing suppliers on cost.
items.quote: ongoing expansion of payer coverage
items.why_new: The known file has no NIPT revenue-per-test path for this customer.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: A Q1'26 prenatal revenue drop of 15% on volume -12% shows the decline accelerated into 2026.
items.detail: Q1'26 prenatal volume was 153K vs 173K (-12%) and revenue $41.9M vs $49.3M (-15%). That compares with Q4'25 at -6% volume and flat revenue, and Q3'25 at -4% volume and +2% revenue. The y/y volume decline widened from -4% to -6% to -12%, then eased to -9% in Q2. Management said the decline stems from a 'difficult year-over-year comparison' and the order-system disruption, but also guided to a H2 return to growth that Q2 then dropped.
items.quote: a difficult year-over-year comparison
items.why_new: The Q1'26 figures and the deceleration path are new.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: Payer coverage for prenatal tests is widening, which supports future volume.
items.detail: In April 2026 a national payer updated its medical policy to cover expanded carrier screens such as Foresight Universal Plus. The 10-Q forward-looking language still flags 'reducing reimbursement rates'. Myriad's launch of FirstGene (July 2026, 14-day turnaround) and a fully staffed prenatal sales team are not in guidance. If these lift volume, the Myriad decline is transitory.
items.why_new: The April 2026 payer-coverage change and the excluded upside are new to the file.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: A government reseller lists the NovaSeq X 25B 100-cycle kit at $13,650, but Illumina's published Jan 2025 price is $11,700.
items.detail: Government Scientific Source lists NovaSeq X 25B 100-cycle (20125967) at $13,650 and 25B 300-cycle (20104706) at $24,155.04. The 300-cycle price matches the known GSA price. The 100-cycle price is ~17% above the Illumina-published figure the analyst already has. This could be reseller markup or a stale price. If the Illumina figure is the true price, the X kit price paid by small and government buyers sits above the list, which shows how much of the gap to large accounts' prices is negotiated rather than list.
items.why_new: The $13,650 100-cycle GSA price differs from the known $11,700 Illumina list, and no earlier source in the exclusion list gives it.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: Element's own AVITI list prices (Nov 2025, EUR) are about €5.6-11/Gb, so Element is not undercutting Illumina's 25B at list price on its Cloudbreak kits.
items.detail: Element AVITI EURO price list V7 (Nov 2025, modified Apr 2026, list includes shipping): 2x150 FS High Output €1,676.51 for 300 Gb (€5.59/Gb). 2x75 High is €1,077.75 for 150 Gb (€7.19/Gb). 2x300 High is €1,876.09 for 180 Gb (€10.42/Gb). Ultra Q 2x150 is €2,674.43 for 240 Gb (€11.14/Gb). Library prep (Elevate €648.65) is excluded. Compare Illumina's 25B list of about $2.1-4.5/Gb and core-level $2.5-3.1/Gb, and the Broad Clinical Labs claim of Ultima at about $0.50 per M reads. Element's discount leverage therefore depends on VITARI (H2'26, about $1.00/Gb claimed) and negotiated deals, not on current list prices. This suggests the AVITI pricing gap that large accounts can use is mainly a promise about future products.
items.source_name: Tampere University (tuni.fi) hosted Element AVITI EURO 2025 price list V7
items.why_new: This is a primary Element list-price table with a $/Gb calculation per kit. The known list had only core-level AVITI figures (Northwestern, UMN).
items.verify_note: Not verified. The PDF's metadata (V7, created 12 Nov 2025, modified 2 Apr 2026) is confirmed, but the price table could not be extracted. AVITI is a mid-throughput box, so the fair comparison is NextSeq 2000, not the 25B. The known list already shows AVITI costing more per Gb than the 25B at cores. The claim that 'list includes shipping' is unverified.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: TGen's academic price for a NovaSeq X Plus 25B-300 lane rose about 8.8% from the 2024 list to the Jul 2026 list, with no sign of discounting on the flagship flow cell.
items.detail: The 25B-300 lane was $2,883.16 on the list revised 13 Sep 2024 (the April 2024 original showed $2,883.17). It is $3,136.63 on the list valid 22 Jul 2026 to 31 Mar 2027. That is 3,136.63/2,883.16 = +8.8% over about two years. At a nominal 3.125B clusters per lane, the price per million clusters went from about $0.92 to $1.00. The 2026 PDF itself was unreadable here, so the 2026 figures come from the live sequencing-costs page and a search snippet of the PDF. The 2024 figures come from search snippets only.
items.source_name: TGen Collaborative Sequencing Center academic price lists
items.why_new: This is the first TGen price pair across 2024 and 2026. The known list only has TGen at $3.14/Gb with no time series.
items.verify_note: The live page shows 25B-300 at $3,136.63 per lane, but its heading says '2025 Academic Price List' while the linked PDF is named 08-2026. So the price may date from 2025, and the 2024 price ($2,883) is from a search snippet only. Core lane rates sit about 50% above Illumina's per-lane list (see derived item), so a core rate rising does not show Illumina's net price rising.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: At TGen the 10B-300 lane price fell about 16% while the 25B rose, so the 10B per-Gb premium over the 25B shrank sharply.
items.detail: The 10B-300 lane was $1,678.74 in 2024 and $1,413.47 in the 2026 list, which is -15.8%. On a nominal 375 Gb per 10B lane and 937 Gb per 25B lane, the 10B went from about $4.48/Gb to $3.77/Gb. The 25B went from about $3.08/Gb to $3.35/Gb. The 10B premium over the 25B therefore narrowed from about 45% to about 13%. This matches the within-X flattening seen at UCLA, and it implies the 10B is being cut toward the 25B. The 10B figure is from a search snippet, and the cycle count and nominal outputs are my assumptions.
items.why_new: This is a new core data point on mid-throughput repricing, and it is independent of UCLA and MD Anderson.
items.verify_note: The math checks out: $4.48 vs $3.08/Gb (1.45x) in 2024 and $3.77 vs $3.35/Gb (1.13x) in 2026. But no 10B lane price is shown on the live TGen page, so both 10B figures rest on snippets. The direction matches UCLA (D005) and Northwestern.

items.label: 2A
items.claim: TGen added a 5B lane at $904.69 in the 2026 list, a new cheap entry tier for research buyers that was not in the 2024 list.
items.detail: The live TGen page lists a NovaSeq X Plus 5B-300 lane at $904.69, stocked for immediate use. No 5B appeared in the 2024 snippets. The 10B at $1,413.47 and the 5B at $904.69 mean a smaller-run user can now pay under $1K per lane. The 5B's per-Gb price is unknown because the page does not give a nominal output.
items.why_new: The known list has CWRU's 5B at about $3.20/Gb. TGen's 5B lane price is new, and it adds to evidence of falling price points.

items.label: 2B
items.claim: TGen's Oxford Nanopore PromethION flow cell price rose about 29% year over year, and the Revio SMRT cell fell about 1.4%, so TGen's long-read list shows no uniform price war.
items.detail: PromethION R10.4.1 went from $1,494.63 in 2024 to $1,927.83 in 2026, which is +29.0%. The Revio SMRT cell went from $1,834.85 to $1,809.43 (-1.4%), and the new SPRQ-Nx cell is $1,798.93. Long-read vendors are not discounting here. This is a watch-out for any thesis that rivals cut price everywhere.
items.why_new: No TGen long-read series is in the known file.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: The 2026 TGen live price page shows no NovaSeq 6000 rows at all, so the 6000 is gone from this large core's price list.
items.detail: The live 2026 page lists only X Plus 5B and 25B lanes (10B appears in the PDF snippet), plus Revio and PromethION. It does not list S4 or S2. I did not confirm that the 2024 list carried 6000 rows. The page says Element AVITI is 'Coming Soon', with no price.
items.why_new: This is a new core's 6000 absence, and it fits the research side of the 6000 being converted.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: The University of Minnesota Genomics Center is not scrapping its retired NovaSeq 6000. It is sending the unit back to the medical school for clinical sequencing.
items.detail: The UMGC page says that from 2 Jan 2024 it no longer accepts new NovaSeq 6000 projects. The instrument is 'returning to the UMN Medical School for critical clinical sequencing'. Researchers needing high output are sent to the X Plus. So at least one research core's 6000 moved to clinical use, not to the scrap heap. That fits management's claim of a permanent clinical 6000 tail and the 'legacy assays stay' cohort. It does not support fast retirement. No date for the clinical move and no price change are given.
items.quote: returning to the UMN Medical School for critical clinical sequencing
items.why_new: Prior items cover UMN's Ultima and AVITI pricing but not this redeployment of a retired research 6000 into clinical work.
items.verify_note: The page confirms 'retiring… and returning to the UMN Medical School' and that new projects stopped on 2 Jan 2024. The exact phrase 'critical clinical sequencing' did not appear in my fetch, so the clinical-use detail is unverified. One instrument redeployed is anecdotal.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: Emory's primate-center genomics core still lists the NovaSeq 6000 next to its NovaSeq X Plus, each bought with its own NIH S10 grant. The same core has also asked NIH to fund replacing the 6000.
items.detail: The ENPRC services page lists the X Plus (S10 OD038274), the NovaSeq 6000 (S10 OD026799) and a MiSeq, with no retirement note or date. A search snippet says a 2025 NIH request states the core 'requires replacing' its 6000 with an X Plus to shorten turnaround and cut costs. I did not open that grant text. Net: the research-core 6000 still runs while a replacement is being funded, so dual running is slow rather than instant.
items.date: 2025-2026 (undated page; grant request 2025 per search snippet)
items.source_name: Emory National Primate Research Center genomics core
items.why_new: Emory is not in the known list of cores, and the dual-instrument S10 funding history is new.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: The Rochester Genomics Center, the Cornell BRC and other cores still list or sell NovaSeq 6000 runs alongside the X. None posts a retirement notice.
items.detail: Rochester's instruments page (footer 2026) lists the NovaSeq X Plus as a 'New Addition' and the NovaSeq 6000 with no retirement note. The only replacement note there is for the NextSeq 550 on 1 Jan 2024. Cornell's BRC (14 May 2024) advertises 'NovaSeqX and NovaSeq6000 sequencing runs' through contracted external sequencing. It says shared lanes will bring 'lower pricing' to projects under 1 billion reads, with no price listed. Together with the Emory, UMN and UNMC examples already in the file, this shows most cores have no public 6000 sunset date.
items.source_name: University of Rochester Genomics Center; Cornell BRC Genomics Facility
items.why_new: Rochester and Cornell are not in the known core list.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: The University of Missouri core said its move to the X cut user sequencing rates by 40%. It calls the 6000 the 'previous' instrument.
items.detail: A Sept 2024 Missouri research-news item says the XLEAP-SBS chemistry lets the core 'reduce sequencing rates by 40%'. It describes the 25B flow cell as giving 2.5x the output of the NovaSeq 6000, and it calls the 6000 the 'previous NovaSeq 6000'. No dollar rates are given on the page. Known Missouri pricing ($2.70/Gb on the 25B) is a level, not a pass-through of the cut. This item adds the size of the user-facing step-down at the time of conversion: 40% in one move.
items.source_name: University of Missouri Office of Research
items.quote: reduce sequencing rates by 40%
items.why_new: The known file has Missouri's $2.70/Gb level only. This is the stated user-rate cut at conversion.
items.verify_note: Checked: Missouri news item, 6 Sep 2024, quotes director Nathan Bivens: X chemistry is 'allowing the core to reduce sequencing rates by 40%' and the 25B gives '2.5-fold' the 6000's output. The conversion step itself is known, but this is the first like-for-like user-price step for a single customer. A 40% cut equals a ~1.67x ratio, well below the ~3.4x revenue-per-Gb gap (~70% cut). That makes the per-customer conversion hit smaller than the known calc assumes. So it cuts against the size of 1A,

items.label: 1B
items.claim: Natera's historical Illumina price schedule ties discounts to trailing-12-month spend and exclusivity, so a large customer's discount rises automatically as its spend rises.
items.detail: Natera re-filed the 2015 Second Amendment as Ex. 10.2 to its Q2'26 10-Q. 'Consumable Spend' is recalculated quarterly from the prior 12 months of Illumina invoices plus NIPT test fees. Separate TG and non-TG percentage tables apply, and the discounts are conditioned on Natera using Illumina exclusively. The percentages are redacted. This is the base mechanism on which the later Tenth and Eleventh Amendments (known) were layered, and it shows that volume growth by itself gives a large account a deeper discount.
items.why_new: Not on the known list: the spend-recalculation and exclusivity-linked discount mechanics, and the 2026 re-filing of the early amendments.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: Natera's agreement lets Illumina raise base prices only within limits whose size and frequency are redacted, and a rival undercut could be matched only by concession.
items.detail: The Third Amendment (June 2016, Ex. 10.3) lets Illumina adjust base prices 'in the usual course of its business', subject to limits on timing, frequency and size that are redacted. Any increase 'remains in Illumina's sole discretion'. This is the 2016 baseline that the Eleventh Amendment (known) later changed with its §7(k) bar on inflation-adjusted increases. It shows that the 2026 price-protection terms are a reversal of the original terms, not a continuation.
items.quote: remains in Illumina's sole discretion
items.why_new: The known list covers the Eighth, Tenth and Eleventh Amendments. The 2016 baseline that makes the Eleventh Amendment a reversal is not on it.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: Natera says its tests are validated only on Illumina and that alternative platforms need significant time, which limits how fast large accounts can leave.
items.detail: The FY25 10-K (filed 27 Feb 2026) says Illumina is the sole supplier of sequencers and reagents for Panorama, Horizon, Signatera and Prospera. It says the tests are 'currently only validated to perform on Illumina's sequencing platform' and that the supply agreement runs to August 2033. This weakens the threat of rapid switching to Ultima or Element at the largest account, although the pricing leverage can still be used in negotiation.
items.quote: only validated to perform on Illumina's sequencing platform
items.why_new: The known list has the contract terms and the 2033 term. This is the FY25 10-K statement that no alternative platform is validated, which sets the switching limit.
items.verify_note: Restates known facts. The corpus already uses Natera's 10-Ks FY23–FY25, the supply agreement to Aug 2033, and the finding that none of nine large US clinical customers has a verified production test on Roche, Ultima or Element.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: Caris's FY25 10-K says its Phoenix labs run both NovaSeq 6000 and NovaSeq X, so parallel running continues at a large clinical customer.
items.detail: Caris's 10-K for FY25 (filed 3 Mar 2026) says the Phoenix labs use NovaSeq 6000 and NovaSeq X systems. It also restates that the Open Offer agreement has no minimum purchase requirements, offers volume discounts, cannot be revoked by Illumina before August 2033, and lets Caris terminate on 90 days' notice. Running both models at year-end 2025 is consistent with a 6000 tail at a regulated customer whose PMA names the 6000.
items.quote: does not contain any minimum purchase requirements
items.why_new: The Caris PMA naming the 6000 and the Open Offer terms are known. The FY25 10-K confirming that both platforms run in the Phoenix labs is a new, dated datapoint.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: At Calgary's core in 2025, the NovaSeq 6000 S4 cost about 1.6-1.7x the NovaSeq X 25B per Gb.
items.detail: Calgary CHGI 2025 internal list: S4 v1.5 300-cycle flow cell $22,420 for 3,000 Gb gives $7.47/Gb. The S4 single lane is $5,820 for 750 Gb, or $7.76/Gb. The NovaSeq X 25B lane (300 cycles) is $4,100 for 900 Gb, or $4.56/Gb. The ratio is 1.64x for the flow cell and 1.70x for the lane, well below the roughly 3.4x ratio in Illumina's revenue per Gb. At core level the 6000 premium is smaller, which suggests the 41%-of-revenue skew comes from list-price and discount structure at clinical and large accounts.
items.source_name: University of Calgary Centre for Health Genomics and Informatics, Internal Price List 2025
items.why_new: Gives a same-sheet 6000 vs X $/Gb ratio (1.6-1.7x) from the Gb column. Prior notes had Calgary only as a source name and had no per-Gb ratio.
items.verify_note: Checked the PDF directly. S4 v1.5 300-cycle is $22,420 for 3,000 Gb ($7.47/Gb). The S4 one-lane is $5,820 for 750 Gb ($7.76). The 25B one-lane is $4,100 for 900 Gb ($4.56). The ratios are 1.64x and 1.70x. Corrections: (1) prices are probably CAD, which doesn't change the ratio; (2) the 25B lane is run by a partner, BC Genome Sciences Centre, not in-house. The direction must be 'against'. A core-level gap of ~1.7x means the like-for-like step is ~40%, not ~70%. The 3.4x revenue gap therefore refl

items.label: 1A
items.claim: The core-level 6000 premium over the X is far smaller than the roughly 3.4x in Illumina's reported revenue per Gb.
items.detail: Calgary's 25B lane is a partner-run (BC Genome Sequencing Centre) lane with a longer turnaround and no custom primers. This makes it a discounted tier, so the ratio may be understated. The X 25B at $4.56/Gb is also above the roughly $2.5-3.0/Gb seen at other cores. So 1.6-1.7x is a lower bound for the premium. The 41%/17% skew probably reflects clinical or large-account pricing rather than academic core rates.
items.why_new: Quantifies a watch-out: core user prices do not reproduce the 3.4x gap, so the gap must come from the customer mix.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: Across five US cores with 2026 rate cards, the X 10B lane now carries only a ~1.13–1.50x per-Gb premium over the 25B. Where the history can be tracked (UCLA, TGen, Northwestern), the premium shrank because 10B lanes were cut 6–21% while 25B lanes held flat or rose.
items.detail: 2026 $/Gb at nominal 300-cycle output (10B ≈ 375 Gb, 25B ≈ 937–1,000 Gb per lane): TGen $3.77 vs $3.35 (1.13x, down from 1.45x in 2024); UCLA 1.26x (from 1.58x); Northwestern internal $1,499/330 Gb = $4.54 vs $3,000/825 Gb = $3.64 (1.25x, 10B lane −6% to −10% vs FY26); MD Anderson 1.50x; Carver $2,000/375 = $5.33 vs $3,380/937 = $3.61 (1.48x). The cuts are concentrated in the mid-tier X flow cell, which is per-Gb deflation that headline 25B prices don't show. TGen's 10B figures are snippet-based.
items.source_name: Northwestern NUSeq, TGen CSC, UCLA TCGB, MD Anderson ATGC, Carver Biotech rate cards
items.why_new: Known items cover single cores (UCLA, MD Anderson); this is a five-core cross-section, with Northwestern and TGen newly added.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: Core rates for a 25B-300 lane run ~26–70% above Illumina's per-lane list, so flat or rising core prices (TGen +8.8%, UCLA flat) mostly reflect core overhead and cannot show that Illumina's net price is holding.
items.detail: $16,480 list per 25B-300 flow cell ÷ 8 lanes = ~$2,060 per lane. Core lane rates: MD Anderson $2,595 (+26%), UCSD $2,800 UC (+36%), Northwestern $3,000 internal (+46%), TGen $3,136.63 (+52%), Carver $3,380 (+64%), UCLA $3,512.47 external (+70%). A 15% cut in Illumina's net price on a lane priced 50% above list would move the core rate only ~10% if the core passed it through, and pass-through is discretionary. Core rate cards are therefore a weak read of Illumina's net pricing in either direction.
items.source_name: Core rate cards vs Illumina 25B-300 list (F146)
items.why_new: No known item measures the markup of core lane rates over list, which is how core price moves should be interpreted.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: At list price, Element's AVITI 2x150 kit costs ~3x Illumina's 25B-300 per Gb, so Element's pricing pressure at high throughput depends on VITARI and negotiated deals, not on today's AVITI list.
items.detail: AVITI 2x150 High Output at €1,676.51 for 300 Gb is €5.59/Gb, or ~$6.5/Gb at ~1.17 USD/EUR (Element EURO list V7, Nov 2025). Illumina's 25B-300 at $16,480 for ~8,000 Gb spec is $2.06/Gb, or $1.87 at measured output, which is ~3.2–3.5x cheaper. Northwestern's internal AVITI rate of $2,096 for 240–300 Gb ($7.0–8.7/Gb) is consistent with this. The Element list figures could not be re-verified (the PDF was unreadable).
items.source_name: Element AVITI EURO price list V7 (tuni.fi) vs Illumina 25B list
items.why_new: The known list has only core-level AVITI $/Gb; this is a list-to-list comparison of vendor reagent prices.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: Myriad's prenatal revenue decline splits roughly evenly between volume (−9%) and reimbursement-driven price (−8%), so NIPT-adjacent labs face both volume and pricing pressure at the same time.
items.detail: Q2'26 Prenatal Health revenue was $39.8M vs $47.6M (−16%) on 144K vs 159K tests. Multiplying 0.91 × 0.92 = 0.837 gives −16.3%, which matches. In H1'26, 0.89 × 0.94 = 0.837, matching the reported −16% ($81.7M vs $96.9M). The 10-Q attributes the per-test decline to 'declines in reimbursement.' Lower revenue per test squeezes lab margins, which may add pressure on reagent spend. That last point is our inference, not a disclosure.
items.quote: due to declines in reimbursement
items.why_new: The known list and F184 have the volume and revenue declines but not the split into volume and price, or its reimbursement attribution.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: NCI's internal recharge for a NovaSeq X 25B-300 flow cell is at or slightly above Illumina list ($16,240-$17,196 vs $16,480), so large federal users show no discount.
items.detail: Three NCI pages (fetched Oct 2026) list the NCI/NIAID rate for X Plus 25B-300 at $16,240, $16,702 and $17,196. The 25B-200 is $14,718-$15,131 and the 25B-100 is $11,876-$11,911. Against the known $16,480 list price, the 25B-300 spread is -1.5% to +4.3%. The 10B-300 is $10,275, and the 1.5B-300 is $2,794. Non-NCI users pay exactly 2x: $34,392 for the 25B-300.
