This is a federal intramural facility that does not use extra volume discounts, and the facility's recharge covers its overhead. It cuts against the idea that every large institutional buyer gets deep discounts.
items.source_name: NCI CCR Frederick sequencing facility pricing page
items.why_new: This is the first NCI recharge table, giving 1.5B/10B/25B rates by cycle count and an exact 2x non-NCI multiple; not on the known list.
items.verify_note: Duplicate. The $17,196 NCI rate for the 25B-300 is already D016. The other pages' $16,240 and $16,702 were not verified (the fetched page shows only $17,196). F247 carries the new ladder.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: Natera's 2016 Fourth Amendment, re-filed as Exhibit 10.4 to the Q2'26 10-Q, shows Illumina earns a per-test fee from Natera in addition to consumable revenue.
items.detail: Section 3(b) sets an 'NIPT Test Fee' per NIPT test performed in whole or in part in a quarter. For structural-anomaly tests the fee is the greater of two redacted amounts. The Second Amendment counts NIPT Test Fees inside the trailing-12-month 'Consumable Spend' that sets the volume-discount tier. The fee amounts and tiers are redacted, and the amendment predates 2016 (the signature dates are blank in the filed copy). Whether this fee survives in the current agreement is unverified. If it does, part of Illumina's take from the largest NIPT customer is per test and not per Gb.
items.why_new: The known file covers the Eighth, Tenth and Eleventh Amendments. This is the per-test fee mechanism from the Fourth Amendment, newly re-filed.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: GeneDx's FY25 10-K says it has not validated an alternative sequencing platform, which limits its leverage to extract extra discounts.
items.detail: GeneDx writes that it has 'not, to date, validated a viable alternative sequencing platform' for commercial use. It also says its 'significant supply contracts' are short-term and 'may face material price increases upon renewal'. This is a large clinical exome and genome customer that is not threatening to move to Ultima, Element or Roche, and it expects renewal price rises. That cuts against the thesis of accelerating extra discounts for large accounts, at least for GeneDx.
items.quote: not, to date, validated a viable alternative sequencing platform
items.why_new: The known file lists no GeneDx statement on alternative-platform validation or renewal price increases.
items.verify_note: Quote not re-fetched. GeneDx's 10-K is a known source (R9). The 'material price increases upon renewal' wording is standard risk-factor boilerplate, so it is weak evidence about actual pricing. Still, it is a large exome/genome customer that does not claim switching leverage.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: Guardant's FY25 10-K says switching sequencers is 'time-consuming and expensive' and names Ultima only as a general market participant.
items.detail: Guardant names Illumina as sole supplier of sequencers and sole provider of maintenance and repair. It says switching may require revalidating tests and that equipment 'can take several months or more to procure, setup and validate'. Ultima appears only in the competitor list, not as an alternative Guardant is using. The supply agreement runs to Jan 2033 on 90 days' notice from Guardant. This tempers the idea that large accounts can quickly shift volume to rivals.
items.quote: time-consuming and expensive
items.why_new: Updates the known 2020 Guardant exhibit with FY25 10-K wording on switching cost, procurement lead time and Ultima.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: Tempus's average oncology NGS reimbursement per test is rising, which gives large labs room to absorb costs and keep sequencing volume growing.
items.detail: Tempus's FY25 10-K gives average oncology NGS reimbursement of about $1,450 (2023), $1,510 (2024) and $1,600 (2025). That is +4.1% in 2024 and +6.0% in 2025. This is revenue per test, not sequencing cost. It shows the lab's economics are not tightening while its sequencing cost per Gb falls, so volume is not limited by cost.
items.why_new: The known file has Natera's ASP and the Medicare Signatera cut but no Tempus per-test reimbursement series.

items.label: 2B
items.claim: Complete Genomics put the T7+ on US sale at an $800K list price in Feb 2026, with no published per-Gb cost.
items.detail: The release (24 Feb 2026, seen only in search snippets) says the T7+ is available for immediate sale in the US and Canada at $800K. It outputs up to 3,600 Gb per run. The company pitches it as well below comparable high-throughput systems. A vbdata report says the company would not give a reagent cost per Gb at launch, so the price gap versus Illumina consumables cannot be measured. US customers are unnamed.
items.why_new: The known list covers MGI units and the T7+ cost cut, but not the US $800K list price or the 3,600 Gb/run spec.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: UNMC, a research core still running only a NovaSeq 6000 on the Illumina side, charges about 4x the going 25B-lane rate per Gb for 6000 runs, and its own AVITI24 runs undercut the 6000 by 30–50%.
items.detail: UNMC internal 6000 prices (v1.5): S4-200 $19,905, which is $9.95–12.44/Gb on 1.6–2.0 Tb spec. S2-300 is $14,785, or $11.83–14.79/Gb on 1.0–1.25 Tb. External rates are 1.5x higher (S4-200 $29,858). In-house AVITI24 2x150 High Output costs $2,601 internal, or $5.78–8.67/Gb on 300–450 Gb. Peer-core 25B-300 lanes run ~$2.5–3.0/Gb (e.g. Pitt $2,907/~975 Gb = $2.98, eff. 1 Jun 2025). Holdout research users are paying tail prices to Illumina. But the core's in-house alternative is Element/Ultima, not the X, so the conversion revenue may go to rivals.
items.source_name: University of Nebraska Medical Center Genomics Core pricing
items.why_new: UNMC was known as a 6000 holdout (F169/F201), but its 6000 and AVITI prices and the per-Gb gaps were not.
items.verify_note: Checked: S4-200 v1.5 is $19,905 internal / $29,858 external; S2-300 is $14,785; AVITI24 2x150 High Output is $2,601 internal. No NovaSeq X price is listed, but the page does not say whether there is an in-house X, so 'running only a 6000' is unconfirmed. Correction: AVITI24 High Output is ~300 Gb, giving $8.67/Gb vs S4-200 at $9.95/Gb (2,000 Gb spec). AVITI is only ~13% cheaper, not 30–50%. The Pitt 25B comparison is cross-core. Value of the item: a research core is still selling 6000 runs at ~$

items.label: 2B
items.claim: MSU's 6000 retirement went to AVITI at a per-Gb price ~12% below its last 6000 lane price, not to an X.
items.detail: MSU's NovaSeq 6000 by-the-lane sheet (19 Jul 2023, search snippet; PDF now 404) lists the S4 lane at $5,953 and S1 lane at $4,204. At ~2.5B reads × 300 cycles = 750 Gb, the S4 lane is ~$7.94/Gb (cycle count assumed). The Element deck MSU posted (10 Sep 2024, snippet) prices 2x150 High (1,000M read pairs, 300 Gbp) at $2,089, or $6.96/Gb. MSU then retired the 6000 for AVITI (known F139). This quantifies that the swap happened at similar or lower per-Gb cost with no Illumina capture.
items.source_name: Michigan State University RTSF Genomics Core (search-result snippets)
items.why_new: This is the first per-Gb quantification of MSU's 6000→AVITI swap. The known file only notes that the swap happened.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: UChicago's newer price sheet drops all NextSeq and NovaSeq 6000 SP lines and replaces them with X 1.5B lanes, so mid-throughput research work moved to cheaper-per-Gb X lanes, a form of hidden deflation.
items.detail: The older 'fees' page lists NextSeq runs from $1,499 (150bp Mid) to $5,499 (300-cycle), plus a NovaSeq SP-500 lane at $3,191.97 and flow cell at $6,051.25. The newer page has no NextSeq or SP rows. It has 1.5B lanes at $1,325 (100c), $1,750 (200c) and $1,775 (300c), each ~750M reads, i.e. 300-cycle ≈ $7.89/Gb on 225 Gb. Any NextSeq run carrying under ~330 Gb (P3-class or lower) costs more per Gb than this ($5,499/$7.89). Illumina's NextSeq 1k/2k pull-through ($80–100K) is being swapped for 1.5B lanes on the X.
items.quote: NextSeq-300-cyc ... $5,499
items.why_new: This NextSeq→1.5B substitution at a named core is not in the known file.

items.label: 2A
items.claim: UChicago's 'NoReagents' lane rows imply a 10B-300 reagent cost of about $9.0K per flow cell, ~38% below Illumina's GSA price, so a mid-size research core gets well under catalog prices.
items.detail: The NoReagents rows are exactly 25% of the full lane price ($374.75/$1,499; $293.75/$1,175; $368.75/$1,475). The implied reagent share is $1,124.25 per 10B-300 lane, or ×8 = $8,994 per flow cell, against the known GSA 10B-300 price of $14,493 (−38%). On a 3 Tb spec that is ~$3.00/Gb of reagent. This is our derivation and assumes the 75/25 split is a cost basis, not just a policy formula.
items.quote: NovaX-10B-300-ln (PE150) - NoReagents $374.75
items.why_new: This implied core-level net reagent price for the 10B is new. Known items cover 25B core rates and GSA prices only.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: NCI's full X Plus rate ladder shows per-Gb prices that fall with flow-cell size but sit at or above Illumina's published list. A large federal account is not getting deep discounts.
items.detail: NCI-rate flow cells (crtp.ccr.cancer.gov, undated, opened Oct 2026): 25B-100 $11,911, 25B-200 $15,131, 25B-300 $17,196. Illumina's Jan 2025 published prices are $11,700 (100-cycle) and $14,500 (200-cycle), so NCI pays about +1.8% and +4.4% above them. 25B-300 is about +4.3% above the $16,480 list. Extending the ladder to the 100 and 200 cycle kits supports the 'no extra discount at big public accounts' reading.
items.source_name: NCI CCR Frederick Sequencing and Genomics Core rate card
items.why_new: Known file has only the 25B-300 NCI figure; the 100 and 200 cycle comparisons against published list are new.
items.verify_note: Checked the full ladder (no date on the page). 25B-100 is $11,911, 25B-200 $15,131, 25B-300 $17,196, 10B-300 $10,275, 1.5B-300 $2,794; non-NCI users pay 2x. The comparison to the $11,700/$14,500 Jan-2025 published prices holds (+1.8% / +4.4%). The 25B-300 point duplicates D016. An internal recharge near list is ambiguous: it could be list with no overhead, or a discounted price plus overhead. See the derived item for the uniform-discount reading.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: Within the X family at NCI, each smaller flow cell costs more per read, so mid-throughput buyers carry the largest premium. A 35B priced on this ladder would cut per-Gb prices a lot.
items.detail: Per-read, 300-cycle, NCI rate: 25B $17,196/25,000M = $0.688/M; 10B $10,275/10,000M = $1.03/M (+49%); 5B $6,831/5,000M = $1.37/M (+99%); 1.5B $2,794/1,500M = $1.86/M (+171%). Per Gb at spec (25B 8,000 Gb; 10B ~3,000 Gb): $2.15 vs $3.43, so the 10B is +59% per Gb. The 25B is only about $0.69/M clusters, in line with the UBS $0.68 figure. Rivals priced at $0.06–0.25/M would still be 3–11x cheaper.
items.source_name: NCI CCR Frederick Sequencing and Genomics Core rate card
items.why_new: Adds a federal-lab ladder with the arithmetic; the 10B premium is higher than the UCLA/TGen figures in the file. Spec outputs are my assumption.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: The NCI Frederick core now lists only NovaSeq X Plus on its rate card and instrument list, with no 6000 row. This is a government core that has fully converted, and the 6000-vs-X gap cannot be computed there.
items.detail: The rate card has NovaSeq X Plus (1.5B/5B/10B/25B), NextSeq XLEAP, iSeq, Revio and PromethION rows only. The OSTR provider page lists 'Illumina NovaSeq XPlus' as the only NovaSeq. The 6000 was probably retired and its S4 history is not on public pages. Archive.org was blocked in my environment, so the old snapshots were not read.
items.why_new: Confirms the NCI core's conversion status; no 6000 price found.

items.label: 2A
items.claim: NCI's Frederick core dropped full-service routine Illumina NGS on 1 Oct 2025. Routine work is routed to the CCR Genomics Core in Bethesda, which suggests consolidation of routine research sequencing.
items.detail: The FSGC page says that from 1 Oct 2025 it stops full library-prep-plus-sequencing for routine RNA-seq, WES and WGS on renewable cell-line and animal samples. Ready-to-sequence library sequencing continues via the CCR Genomics Core. This points to consolidation of intramural routine volume, but it gives no volume data.
items.why_new: Dated service change at a federal research core.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: Instrument capital cost per Gb on the T7+ is very low, so a low-price rival can sustain aggressive reagent pricing.
items.detail: Genohub lists $800K and up to 3,600 Gb/run with 14-24h runs. At one run per day for 330 days that is ~1,188,000 Gb/yr, so $800K is $0.67/Gb in year one, or ~$0.13/Gb over a 5-year life. Genohub shows no reagent cost per Gb, and the company declined to give one at launch, so only the capital side can be derived. Peak utilization is assumed.
items.why_new: Derives capital $/Gb from the specs; the known list has only the price.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: The previous-generation T7 was already sold in the US at a $1.5/Gb promotional reagent price in 2023, which shows MGI sets reagent prices well below Illumina.
items.detail: A 2023 Complete Genomics US promo set reagents at $1.5/Gb for the original T7 (a ~$150 genome), and the 2026 T7+ claim is ~$1/Gb. That is a one-third fall in three years. Over the same period the 25B stayed flat at many cores (UCLA, TGen). The $1.5/Gb is a promo figure and the T7+ figure is a claim, so neither is a transaction price.
items.why_new: Gives a dated MGI price series ($1.5 to $1/Gb) not in the known list.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: UCLA's DNBseq T7 per-flow-cell rates sit at $2.7-3.7K, which makes the T7 a credible alternative to Illumina lanes in US research cores.
items.detail: UCLA TCGB lists the T7 at $3,651 (150 cycles), $2,689 (200 cycles) and $3,043 (300 cycles) per flow cell. Per-flow-cell output is not published here (T7 PE150 is 1.7-7 Tb across 1-4 flow cells), so $/Gb needs an assumed output of ~1.75 Tb per flow cell, which gives ~$1.5-2.1/Gb. That is a derived estimate. It is below the same core's 25B pricing of $3.51/lane per the known list. The earlier F058 finding that T7 prices fell 36-37% is the same page.
items.why_new: Gives the T7 flow-cell prices and a derived $/Gb; F058/D001 cover only the change.

items.label: 2B
items.claim: The 1260H list now includes Novogene alongside BGI, Complete Genomics and MGI, which hits the main low-cost outsourcing channel for US research.
items.detail: A law-firm note dated 12 Jun 2026 says the 2026 list update (PDF dated 8 Jun 2026) includes BGI Group with subsidiaries (Complete Genomics), MGI Tech and Novogene. Listing alone does not make a firm a covered 'biotechnology company of concern'. OMB must designate it, and the first restrictions on new federal contracts and grants are expected in late 2028. If designated, this would limit US-funded research and cores that outsource to Novogene or buy MGI. That cuts against 2A/2B pricing pressure on the 6000/X from the cheapest providers, but only from 2028 onward. The known list notes MGI's 1260H listing, but not that the Novogene listing is combined with the late-2028 timing.
items.why_new: Confirms Novogene is on 1260H and gives the late-2028 timing for the federal restrictions.
items.verify_note: Checked: the HLC note of 12 Jun 2026 lists BGI (including Complete Genomics), MGI Tech and Novogene. Restrictions are 'first expected to occur in late 2028', and OMB designation is still required. Direction corrected to 'against': it would restrain the lowest-cost research channel and reduce pressure on Illumina pricing. It is weak because the timing is after 2027 and Novogene runs Illumina X Plus anyway. The Novogene listing is new versus the known MGI-only mention.

items.label: 2B
items.claim: BIOSECURE became law on 18 Dec 2025 without named entities, so MGI/Complete Genomics face no immediate US federal-grant ban, leaving the threat to Illumina in US academic markets slow-building.
items.detail: Arnold & Porter and the FDA Law Blog say the enacted law dropped the named-company list and relies on 1260H or OMB designation. Restrictions apply only to new federal contracts and grants and are expected from late 2028 for particular companies. Until then US-funded cores can buy T7+ systems. The 1260H route may still make academic compliance offices cautious, and Complete Genomics said it was 'disappointed' with the bill.
items.why_new: Gives the enactment date and the statutory mechanism and timing; the known list has only 'BIOSECURE affects federal purchases (list due Dec 2026)'.
items.verify_note: Mostly restates the known 'BIOSECURE (NDAA FY26)… list due Dec 2026'. The late-2028 timing is captured in F254. Source is a search summary only.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: A US service lab, Gene by Gene (Houston), agreed to be an early adopter of several T7+ units, so MGI capacity is being placed with service providers that compete for sequencing work.
items.detail: The Complete Genomics release (Oct 2025, via a search summary) says the lab has processed more than 40,000 genomes on DNBSEQ and will take multiple T7+ units. This is a commercial service lab, not a core. Its price is not given. Illumina's own list does not name US MGI service providers. MGI launched the T7+ in Sep 2025 at >14 Tb/day, a figure that conflicts with the 3,600 Gb/run spec and probably counts all four flow cells.
items.why_new: Names the first US T7+ buyer (Gene by Gene) and its scale; no US customers are named in the known list.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: Rush's June 2026 core fee sheet prices the NovaSeq 6000 S4 2x150 lane at exactly the same $6,615 / $6,945.75 as its October 2021 sheet, so the 6000 price has not been cut in about five years.
items.detail: Search-engine text of both Rush GMCF PDFs shows the S4 2x150 lane at $6,615.00 (internal) and $6,945.75 (external): once in the fee schedule dated 20 Oct 2021 (file metadata July 2022) and once in the 15 Jun 2026 sheet. The tail is therefore priced as a fixed, high-price product. This conflicts with the earlier finding that Rush discontinued 6000 service by Dec 2025 (F156). The 2026 sheet still lists the S4, though a leftover sheet row does not prove the service is still offered. I could not read the PDFs directly (compressed binary), so the numbers come from search-result text.
items.source_name: Rush University GMCF fee schedules (Jun 2026 vs Oct 2021)
items.why_new: The probe note and exclusion list cite only Rush's $4.20-4.62 X lane price; the S4 price's five-year constancy is new, and so is the conflict with F156.
items.verify_note: Numbers come only from search-snippet text of compressed PDFs and could not be verified. A row unchanged from Oct 2021 to Jun 2026 looks like a stale template row. It also conflicts with the earlier finding that Rush discontinued 6000 service (F156), and with the known 6000 cuts at Salk (−24%) and UCLA (−27%).

items.label: 1A
items.claim: At Rush the 6000 S4 lane costs only about 1.9-2.0x the X 25B lane per Gb, far below the ~3.4x gap in Illumina's reported revenue per Gb.
items.detail: Rush June 2026: 25B lane (930 Gb) is $4,200 / $4,620, which is $4.52 / $4.97 per Gb. The S4 2x150 lane is $6,615 / $6,945.75; at the 750 Gb per lane Calgary lists for an S4 lane, that is $8.82 / $9.26 per Gb. Ratio = 8.82/4.52 = 1.95x internal and 9.26/4.97 = 1.86x external. Rush prices both near list, so the core gap understates what large-volume customers see.
items.why_new: Rush's S4 lane price and the computed per-Gb ratio are new; the probe flagged this but had not resolved the unit (per lane) or computed it.
items.verify_note: Rests on the unverified, possibly stale Rush S4 row (F257) plus Calgary's lane output. The ratio point is better made with the verified Calgary and Missouri data in the derived item.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: UConn's 2026 rate cards put the 6000 S4 only about 1.8-1.9x the X 25B per Gb, again well below the 3.4x revenue-per-Gb gap.
items.detail: UConn Center for Genome Innovation lists an S4 v1.5 300-cycle kit at $15,938.08 per flow cell, 'current through Feb 2026'. With 4 lanes of ~750 Gb (3,000 Gb), that is $5.31 per Gb, or $5.66 after the 6.5% reagent shipping charge. The 25B 300-cycle lane (start 1 Jan 2026) is $2,933.99 including a 5% tariff surcharge, or ~$3.01 per Gb at ~975 Gb per lane. Ratio = 1.76x ex-shipping, 1.88x with shipping. The S4 figure is my own per-lane arithmetic and the 25B lane output is my assumption.
items.source_name: UConn Center for Genome Innovation service rates (+ Honeycrisp 25B lane listing)
items.why_new: UConn was only listed with its X 25B lane price in the exclusion list; the same-core S4 price and the ratio are new.
items.verify_note: Not re-fetched. UConn rate cards are a known source, but the 6000-vs-25B ratio of ~1.76–1.88x is new. Caveats: the S4 rate is 'current through Feb 2026', so it may already be retired; the 25B lane output is assumed; the 25B rate includes a 5% tariff surcharge. Consistent with Calgary (1.64–1.70x) and Missouri (40% cut).

items.label: 1A
items.claim: At UCSF CAT the S4-300 lane costs about 2.6x the X Plus 25B lane per Gb at every user tier.
items.detail: UCSF CAT (page undated, X 100/200-cycle labelled 'Coming Nov. 2024', so ~late 2024 or 2025) lists S4 300-cycle at $5,778 internal / $7,281 external non-profit / $9,101 for-profit, with 2.5B reads per lane (~750 Gb). The 25B 300-cycle lane is $2,850 / $3,591 / $4,448 with 3.25B reads (~975 Gb). Internal: $7.70 per Gb vs $2.92 = 2.6x. External non-profit: $9.71 vs $3.68 = 2.6x. The page does not say whether prices are per lane or per flow cell. I read them as per lane because the 25B price matches other cores' per-lane prices.
items.source_name: UCSF Center for Advanced Technology sequencing rates
items.why_new: UCSF CAT is not among the cores in the exclusion list or the F-items.
items.verify_note: I checked the page. S4 lanes are $5,778, $7,281 and $9,101 at 2.5B reads per lane. The 25B-300 lane is $2,850, $3,591 and $4,448 at 3.25B reads per lane. The page is undated: the 25B 100- and 200-cycle rows still say 'Coming Nov. 2024'. The 2.6x ratio is correct. It is a mixed signal, not a clean 'against'. It is below Illumina's 3.4x revenue gap, but at the high end of core ratios, the same as MD Anderson's 2.5x. A tail lab converting here would still pay about 62% less per Gb.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: Emory's primate-center core (page updated 11 Dec 2025) charges $20,700 per 6000 S4-300 run and $22,500 per X 25B run, which is about 2.4-2.8x less per read on the X.
items.detail: One cost-per-run column covers both platforms. S4 PE150 gives 8-10B reads for $20,700 ($2.07-2.59 per million reads). 25B PE150 gives 26B reads for $22,500 ($0.87 per million). That is 2.4-3.0x per read. The 200-cycle 25B run ($18,600, 26B reads) costs about the same as an S4 200-cycle run ($18,100, 8-10B reads), so the X gives ~2.6-3x the data for the same bill. Single-lane S4 is $4,600. This confirms F228 (Emory lists both platforms) and adds the actual prices and the 2025-26 price level.
items.source_name: Emory National Primate Research Center genomics core rates
items.why_new: F228 noted only that Emory lists both instruments; the prices and the dated ratio are new.
items.verify_note: I confirmed the page, last updated 2025-12-11. S4 PE150 is $20,700 for 8–10B reads. The 25B PE150 is $22,500 for 26B reads. The 25B 200-cycle is $18,600 vs the S4 200-cycle at $18,100. Correction: the $4,600 single S4 lane is the 200-cycle price. The 2.4–3.0x per-read ratio is like-for-like (both in clusters). Like F260, this sits closer to the revenue gap than the Calgary and UConn ratios do, so it is only weakly 'against'.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: Core S4-300 flow-cell prices at five cores sit close to Illumina's ~$21.7K list, so the legacy tail is being resold at or above list rather than discounted, while one large institutional account pays about a third less.
items.detail: S4-300 flow cell (~3,000 Gb, 4 lanes) versus the $21,683 list (already known): MIT BioMicro FY25 (7/1/2024) $5,400 per lane = $21,600 (-0.4%); Oregon GC3F internal $5,070 per lane = $20,280 (-6%, undated); Calgary 2025 $22,420 (+3%; $21,371 in Jun 2024, +4.9%); UCSF internal $23,112 (+7%); LJI affiliate $23,431 (+8%, undated); Rush $26,460 (+22%, frozen since 2021). Partners/MGB (Mass General Brigham) internal is $14,400 (-34% vs list) with non-MGB academic $20,736 and industry $22,896. Most cores add a margin to reagent cost; only the big internal buyer gets a real discount. The dates mix 2024-26 and some pages are undated.
items.source_name: Partners MOGI, MIT BMC, Oregon GC3F, UCSF CAT, LJI, Calgary CHGI rate pages
items.why_new: MGB, LJI, Oregon, UCSF and MIT S4 rows are new. The exclusion list has only Salk/Calgary 6000 prices and F049/F062 (Calgary, UCLA, MD Anderson).
items.verify_note: Core rates include each core's overhead, so they do not show what Illumina actually charges. The $21,683 benchmark is a GSA distributor price. GSA marks X flow cells up about 1.41–1.47x over list (25B: $24,155 vs $16,480; NCI pays 71% of GSA). So S4 core rates sitting near $21.7K may be well above Illumina's net price, not 'at list'. The claim that the tail is sold without discounts is not supported. The real takeaway is that core S4 rates cluster at $20–23K across 2024–26.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: The same 4-lane S4-300 flow cell sells for $14,400 to Mass General Brigham labs but $52,098 on Salk's external list, a 3.6x spread, which shows size and affiliation drive the price.
items.detail: Partners MOGI lists the S4-300 4-lane flow cell at $14,400 for MGB labs, $20,736 for non-MGB academic and $22,896 for industry, all per flow cell. The known Salk external non-profit price is $52,098 and Illumina's list is $21,683. MGB's $4.80 per Gb (3,000 Gb) is 34% below list. This gives a real-world marker for how far a large institutional account can sit below list, and the discount applies to a legacy product that is supposedly premium priced. The MGB column is my reading of an internal rate, and the page is undated.
items.why_new: MGB's S4 flow-cell prices are not in the exclusion list; the 34%-below-list marker for a large internal account is new.
items.verify_note: I verified the prices: S4-300 4-lane flow cell $14,400 (MGB), $20,736 (non-MGB academic), $22,896 (industry); S4-200 2-lane $12,925. The page has no date. The 3.6x spread is a bad comparison: Salk's $52,098 is an old external rate that has since been cut to $39,701, and it carries core markup. MGB's $14,400 is about what you get by applying NCI's 71%-of-GSA ratio, and close to UConn's $15,938. So it looks like a standard academic net price, not proof of large-account leverage. I re-labelled it '

items.label: 1A
items.claim: Pitt's June 2025 rate sheet shows the 6000 pricing 3.7-4.2x the X on a like-for-like per-Gb basis, and its S4 menu is cut down to one configuration.
items.detail: Pitt HTGC (internal rates, effective 6/1/2025): S2 300-cycle full flow cell $14,030 for ~1,250 Gb = ~$11.2 per Gb. X 25B 300-cycle at $21,393 per full flow cell (about 7,500-8,000 Gb) = $2.7-2.9 per Gb, or $2,907 per lane (~$3.0). Ratio = 3.7-4.2x. The fetched S4 rows listed only the 35-cycle option ($14,381); no S4 300-cycle row appeared, and the fetch could be truncated. This is the one core found where the gap approaches or exceeds Illumina's 3.4x. The S2 is a smaller flow cell than the S4, so this exaggerates the 6000 gap, which is why the S4 would give a lower ratio.
items.source_name: University of Pittsburgh Health Sciences Sequencing Core (HTGC)
items.why_new: Pitt HTGC is not in the exclusion list, and the S2-versus-25B per-Gb ratio is new.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: Natera's unit costs per test have barely moved over seven quarters, and its rising cost per test is explained almost entirely by the shift toward oncology tests. That shows no visible pass-through of falling Illumina prices at Illumina's largest NIPT/MRD customer.
items.detail: Cost of product revenue divided by tests processed gives ~$216 (Q3'24), ~$216 (Q1'25), $234 (Q2'25), $232 (Q3'25), ~$237 (Q4'25), $242 (Q1'26) and $255 (Q2'26). A two-segment fit with fixed unit costs (solved on Q2'25 and Q2'26) gives ~$500 per oncology test and ~$158 per non-oncology test. With no change in unit costs, that fit reproduces Q3'24, Q1'25, Q3'25, Q4'25 and Q1'26 within +1% to +4%. Example for Q1'26: 754.7K×$158 + 258.9K×$500 = $248.7M vs $245.2M actual. So unit costs fell at most ~2–4% over two years, a period in which Illumina's per-Gb pricing fell mid-teens a year. Either Natera reinvests the savings in depth or its Illumina price is not falling much.
items.source_name: Natera 8-K Ex. 99.1 earnings releases (Q3'25, Q4'25, Q1'26, Q2'26)
items.quote: continued progress in reducing cost of revenues associated with tests processed
items.why_new: The known file has only the two-point $255 vs $234 cost per test. This adds an 8-quarter series and a mix decomposition showing flat unit costs.
items.verify_note: I re-checked the arithmetic. Q2'26: 747.2K×$158 + 296.7K×$500 = $266.4M vs 1,043.9K×$255 = $266.2M. The fit uses two equations for two unknowns, so the back-tests carry the evidence. Predictions run 1–4% above actuals, which means unit costs fell only slightly. Caveats: cost of product revenue includes fixed and non-reagent costs. The $500 oncology figure mixes tumor exomes into the MRD draws. This fits the known depth-reinvestment pattern (Signatera Genome).

items.label: 1C
items.claim: Clinical MRD blood draws make up 94–96% of Natera's oncology tests, so its headline oncology growth is almost all low-Gb Signatera draws. Non-MRD oncology tests (tissue/CGP/other) are only ~6–14K a quarter.
items.detail: Oncology tests minus clinical MRD units: Q3'24 137.1K−130K=7.1K; Q4'24 150.8K−145K=5.8K; Q1'25 167.7K−161K=6.7K; Q2'25 188.8K−181K=7.8K; Q3'25 211.0K−202K=9.0K; Q4'25 233.3K−225K=8.3K; Q1'26 258.9K−249K=9.9K; Q2'26 296.7K−283K=13.7K. The +57% oncology growth is therefore MRD draws at ~0.16–0.24 Gb each (known per-draw Gb), not Gb-heavy CGP. On that basis the record +34K q/q MRD add in Q2'26 is only ~5–8 TB of draw sequencing a quarter (34K × 0.16–0.24 Gb).
items.source_name: Natera Q2'26 earnings deck (8-K Ex. 99.2) and Ex. 99.1 releases
items.quote: Clinical MRD oncology units (Signatera plus Latitude)
items.why_new: The known file has oncology test growth and MRD totals but not the MRD share of oncology tests or the tiny non-MRD residual series.
items.verify_note: The share calculation is new and correct. Two cautions. First, a 'unit' and a 'test' may be defined differently. Second, the 5–8 TB draw figure understates Gb: per the known data, the one-time tumor exome per new patient carries about 80–90% of Gb per patient-year. Natera's Gb therefore tracks new-patient adds, not draws, and Signatera Genome draws run 10–15x deeper.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: Natera's clinical MRD unit growth has held at +52–56% y/y for six straight quarters with no deceleration, and sequential adds keep rising.
items.detail: Clinical MRD units (Signatera + Latitude) per the Q1'26/Q2'26 decks: 106K, 118K, 130K, 145K (2024); 161K, 181K, 202K, 225K (2025); 249K, 283K (H1'26). Y/y growth: Q1'25 +51.9%, Q2'25 +53.4%, Q3'25 +55.4%, Q4'25 +55.2%, Q1'26 +54.7%, Q2'26 +56.4%. Q/q adds: +12, +12, +15, +16, +20, +21, +23, +24, +34K. Management notes Q2 was partly weather catch-up, but even ex-Q2 the y/y rate is not slowing.
items.source_name: Natera Q1'26 and Q2'26 earnings decks (8-K Ex. 99.2)
items.quote: Fastest unit growth quarter at ~24K volume growth
items.why_new: The known file has the Q2'26 +56% point and the q/q adds (F176). The full 10-quarter level series and the flat y/y growth trend are new.
items.verify_note: The y/y math checks: 51.9%, 53.4%, 55.4%, 55.2%, 54.7%, 56.4%. It largely restates the known 283K (+56%) and the q/q series in F176. The only new element is the steady y/y rate. MRD draws are low-Gb, so this cuts only weakly against the thesis.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: Natera's new single-gene NIPT, Fetal Focus, was nearing ~200K orders a year by Q1'26. That is a new prenatal sequencing product that partly offsets NIPT maturation.
items.detail: The Q1'26 deck says Fetal Focus is nearing an annualized pace of ~200K orders (~50K a quarter), after a 2026 launch milestone in the Q4'25 deck (21-gene single-gene NIPT). For scale, ~50K a quarter is ~7% of Natera's ~747K non-oncology tests in Q2'26. A gene-panel cfDNA test likely carries more Gb than SNP-based aneuploidy NIPT (our inference, undisclosed). Women's health had a 'record quarter… second fastest growth since 2019' (Q1'26). Management cites Fetal Focus as a driver of women's-health share gains.
items.quote: Record quarter for Women's Health, second fastest growth since 2019
items.why_new: Fetal Focus order volume is not in the known file or the found list.
items.verify_note: Confirmed: on the Q1'26 call Natera said it was 'approaching' an annualized run rate of about 200K orders. The 21-gene version launched 5 Jan 2026. Fetal Focus is mainly a reflex test for Horizon carrier-positive patients when the father is unavailable, so it adds tests on women already tested, not new pregnancies. Orders are not the same as tests processed. These tests are already inside the known non-oncology counts (+12.5%), so this does not add volume beyond what is known.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: Texas building records show Natera is building a dedicated 'Natera Sequencing Core' in Austin, due by 31 Dec 2026, on top of ~$23M of other 2025–26 Austin lab build-outs. Large new sequencing capacity at Illumina's biggest NIPT/MRD customer comes online for 2027.
items.detail: TDLR TABS2026019294, 'Natera Sequencing Core': $6.0M, 12,048 sq ft, lab remodel plus an extra make-up air unit, 13011 McCallen Pass Bldg A, registered 4 May 2026, start 8 Jun 2026, completion 31 Dec 2026. Earlier projects: TABS2025012493 'Pista – Level 3 South', $9.9M, 24,000 sq ft of new lab, Apr–Dec 2025; 'Enzo' (TABS2025018660), $9.4M, office/lab/warehouse; 'Daytona' (TABS2026008903), $4.0M, 43,960 sq ft office→lab, 2026 (the last figure is from a third-party tracker snippet). The 'largest sequencing capacity in the world' claim (May 2026) fits a ~12K sq ft room, so the core houses dozens of high-throughput boxes, not hundreds (our inference). Model unnamed.
items.source_name: Texas Department of Licensing and Regulation, TABS project registry
items.quote: Partial demolition and remodel of existing interior space for lab use
items.why_new: The known file has only the May 2026 Austin press release with no size, cost or timing. These permit records add dollars, square footage and a Dec 2026 completion date.
items.verify_note: Verified in TDLR. The owner is 13011 McCallen Pass Holding LLC, the landlord, with Natera named in the project title. Cost $6.0M, 12,048 sq ft, start 8 Jun 2026, completion 31 Dec 2026. Scope is a remodel plus an extra make-up air unit. The other Austin projects were not checked. Capacity is not volume, and the sequencer vendor is unknown. This adds detail to the known May 2026 Austin facility announcement.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: Natera says its newest products (Signatera Genome, Fetal Focus, Latitude) are not yet cost-optimized and that it has a COGS-reduction roadmap. That is the Gb-heavy launch where it will push hardest on sequencing input costs.
items.detail: On the Q2'26 call (6 Aug 2026), management blamed the slight COGS rise on volume from recently launched products not yet optimized for cost. It said it leaves 'substantial room' for COGS improvement as volume scales and is working through that roadmap. The CFO said cost projects pay off over the next 12–18 months (GuruFocus summary). In Q1'26, ~2 pts of 'transient' gross-margin impact included COGS tied to volume acceleration (a higher receive-to-report ratio). Signatera Genome is the ~10–15x Gb-per-draw product (known), so its cost-down is where Illumina's per-Gb price is most exposed.
items.source_name: GuruFocus Q2'26 call summary; Natera Q1'26 deck
items.quote: not yet optimized for cost efficiency
items.why_new: The known file has Natera's cost per test but not management's naming of Signatera Genome and Fetal Focus as unoptimized-COGS products with a 12–18-month cost roadmap.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: Natera's Q2'26 10-Q re-filed its 2013–2016 Illumina supply-agreement chain (Ex. 10.1–10.4). The re-filed exhibits show Illumina's grants are non-exclusive and that NIPT test fees count toward Natera's discount tiers.
items.detail: Ex. 10.1 is the 2013 Supply Agreement (TG Consumables), which includes a 4-month termination-for-convenience right for Natera. Ex. 10.2 (Second Amendment, Sep 2015) defines 'Consumable Spend' as trailing-12-month Illumina invoices plus NIPT Test Fees, with discounts capped at a redacted top tier. Ex. 10.3 (Third Amendment, Jun 2016) adds clinical oncology testing (including LDTs) and organ-transplant monitoring as non-exclusive fields, with a redacted revenue share on Natera IVD kits and Subject Tests. It also ran 10 years (to ~Jun 2026), with Illumina able to end NIPT/clinical rights on 2 years' notice after year 5. The supply agreement now runs to Aug 2033 (known), so these terms were extended. Filing the old chain in Aug 2026 may reflect an SEC review or a new amendment; unverified.
items.quote: the non-exclusive, non–transferable
items.why_new: F238 covers only Ex. 10.4. The re-filing of Ex. 10.1–10.3, the 2016 oncology/transplant field grant and the 10-year term are new.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: On per-test Gb, Natera's MRD draws are probably a fraction of its NIPT Gb, so even +56% MRD unit growth adds little sequencing volume unless Signatera Genome scales.
items.detail: Q2'26 draw-level Gb: 283K × 0.16–0.24 Gb ≈ 45–68 TB. Non-oncology tests (1,043.9K − 296.7K = 747.2K) × 1–2 Gb ≈ 0.75–1.5 PB. Draw Gb is therefore ~3–9% of non-oncology Gb before one-off tumor exomes; if exomes are 80–90% of MRD Gb per patient-year (known), total MRD Gb is ~0.2–0.7 PB, ~15–90% of NIPT Gb. Caveat: Panorama is a targeted SNP-amplicon assay whose reads per sample are undisclosed, and the May 2026 'SNP-informed deep sequencing' upgrade may raise NIPT Gb per test.
items.source_name: Natera Q2'26 release (tests processed); our calc using known per-test Gb
items.why_new: The known file gives per-test Gb but has no Natera-specific MRD-vs-NIPT Gb split.

items.label: 2B
items.claim: At UChicago's core, the AVITI 300-cycle flow cell is priced below the X 25B lane and about level with the X 10B lane.
items.detail: UChicago's genomics facility lists AVITI 300bp flow cell at $1,475 internal / $1,999 commercial. The NovaX 10B PE150 lane is $1,499 / $1,624. The NovaX 25B PE150 lane is $2,461 / $2,599. The 25B lane carries much more output than the 10B lane, so Illumina still has the lower cost per Gb on the 25B. Read this as a research-core price ladder. AVITI is priced to compete with the 10B, and the commercial rate for X 25B ($2,599) is only about 30% above AVITI's ($1,999). No date and no prior-year price were found, so direction over time is not established.
items.source_name: University of Chicago Genomics Facility price list
items.why_new: UChicago is not among the core rate cards already used, and it shows a same-table AVITI vs X lane comparison.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: William Blair's Feb 2026 survey of 169 OB-GYNs and MFMs reports near-universal use of chromosomal condition testing, which implies aneuploidy NIPT is already saturated.
items.detail: The firm's own summary page says the survey shows 'near-universal use' of chromosomal condition testing, and it gives no percentages. The wording suggests little room for further penetration in average-risk NIPT, in line with the 1C maturing argument. The numbers (percent offered, expected ordering change) are inside the PDF and were not extracted.
items.source_name: William Blair Dx Trends: Prenatal Genetics
items.quote: near-universal use of chromosomal condition testing
items.why_new: Known list cites experts (70-80% reached) and ACMG, not a physician survey from a broker.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: The same survey summary stresses strong momentum for single-gene NIPT, which is a growth driver for prenatal sequencing volume.
items.detail: William Blair says single-gene NIPT momentum is strong, and that removing paternal sampling would be 'game changing' and could speed adoption across the sector. BillionToOne's UNITY test is the beneficiary. This is expansion in prenatal testing beyond aneuploidy, so it could offset the maturing of standard NIPT. It is qualitative and a search snippet only, with no volume or Gb figures.
items.source_name: William Blair Dx Trends: Prenatal Genetics
items.quote: game changing
items.why_new: Known list covers BillionToOne's 35% growth but not a physician-survey view that single-gene NIPT adoption could accelerate.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: GeneDx genome production cost is nearly 2x exome from reagents, and management expects flat cost per test in H2'26, so genome adoption keeps consuming Illumina reagent dollars while it is capped by payers.
items.detail: CFO Feeley said whole genome costs nearly twice as much to produce as exome, 'almost entirely' from higher reagent costs. He expects cost per test to stay 'relatively flat' in H2'26, with step improvements in 2027 as genome utilization grows 'and manufacturers advance their technology'. This implies that a reagent price cut from Illumina (35B) is an assumed lever for GeneDx's margin. That is mildly relevant to 1B, because a large account is counting on supplier price cuts. Q2 capex rose because GeneDx 'significantly increased the sequencing fleet', and spending is 'leveling out'.
items.quote: Whole genome cost us nearly twice as much to produce than exome.
items.why_new: The known list has GeneDx cost per test (-14%, directional) but not the genome:exome cost ratio, the flat H2 cost guide, or the fleet-capex plateau.
items.verify_note: Duplicate of F189 and D015, which already cover the genome ≈2x exome cost, mostly reagents, and the flat H2 cost per test. The fleet-capex remark is too minor to stand alone.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: GeneDx's sequencer fleet build has plateaued after a Q2'26 capex step-up, suggesting capacity was bought ahead of volume at one major clinical customer.
items.detail: The CFO said capex rose in Q2 to expand the sequencing fleet for genome volume and has 'reached a point of leveling out'. Genome mix is guided down to ~30% in Q3. Together these point to instrument and consumable pull-through at this customer normalizing. The sequencer model was not stated in the material I read.
items.why_new: The known list has capacity bought ahead of volume only as a generic estimate. This is a named customer's capex statement.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: Caris's first clinical WGS product (ChromoSeq, myeloid) only just received a Medicare rate ($3,228), so WGS is not yet a meaningful share of Caris's mix.
items.detail: On the Q2'26 call (5 Aug 2026) the CFO said Caris received its first Medicare reimbursement for ChromoSeq at $3,228. The product launched recently, and the search snippet gave no volume. Caris cases were 59.2K in the quarter, +18%. WGS at Caris is therefore a nascent addition to the volume base, not a driver of the current volume run-rate. This is based on a search-result snippet only.
items.why_new: The known list has Caris case growth and cost per case, but not the ChromoSeq WGS launch or its reimbursement rate.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: Tempus's new rare-disease WGS offering (GenomeNext) has a single month of data and 'small' early volume, so WGS remains immaterial to its mix.
items.detail: On the Q2'26 call (~30 Jul 2026) the CEO said demand exceeded first-month expectations but the volume is small, with one month of data. Tempus's core testing volume grew 31%. WGS cannot yet explain any of the volume acceleration at this customer. This is based on a search-result snippet only.
items.source_name: MarketBeat Tempus Q2 call highlights (search snippet)
items.why_new: The known list has Tempus oncology +31% and the Personalis deal, but not GenomeNext.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: Like-for-like core prices put the 6000→X per-Gb step at only ~40–50%, against the ~70% implied by Illumina's 3.4x revenue-per-Gb gap, so a near-list tail lab converting may cost Illumina ~30% less per point than the known ~$24M/yr per clinical point calc.
items.detail: Core 6000/25B per-Gb ratios: Calgary 1.64–1.70x (S4 $7.47–7.76/Gb vs 25B lane $4.56, 2025), UConn 1.76–1.88x (2026), Missouri '40%' rate cut at conversion (≈1.67x, Sep 2024); MD Anderson 2.5x (known) is the high end. Stripping an assumed ~$1,000–1,500 per-lane core overhead (cores run 26–70% above per-lane list, D019) from Calgary leaves ($5,820−O)/750 vs ($4,100−O)/900, or ~1.9–2.0x, a ~48–50% step. The known calc implies ~$34M/yr of 6000 revenue per clinical Gb point at a ~70% cut (=$24M); at a 45–50% cut that is ~$15–17M per point, so 5 points ≈ $75–85M vs the known $112M. Caveat: the 3.4x may be real for large clinical accounts that move onto deeply discounted X pricing; this matters only for tail labs that pay close to list.
items.source_name: Calgary CHGI 2025 price list; UConn CGI rates; Univ. of Missouri Office of Research
items.quote: reduce sequencing rates by 40%
items.why_new: The known file has only the revenue-ratio-based conversion cost; no like-for-like single-customer step has been sized or set against it.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: NCI's X Plus recharge is a uniform ~71% of the GSA distributor schedule across 25B, 10B and 1.5B flow cells, consistent with a flat contract discount and no extra discount scaled to flow-cell size at this sole-source federal account.
items.detail: NCI rate ÷ known GSA price: 25B-300 $17,196/$24,155 = 71.2%; 10B-300 $10,275/$14,493 = 70.9%; 1.5B-300 $2,794/$3,928 = 71.1%. Identical ratios to within 0.3 pts point to a single percentage off the GSA schedule, likely via the NIH sole-source reagent vehicle (F040, $18M/yr ceiling, awarded May 2026). Per Gb at spec, the 25B-300 is ~$2.15 (8,000 Gb) vs the 1.5B-300 at ~$6.21 (450 Gb), so small-volume users at the same account pay ~2.9x per Gb. The page is undated, and the uniform ratio is our inference.
items.source_name: NCI CCR Frederick Sequencing Facility rate card; GSA/Government Scientific Source SKU pages
items.why_new: Known items compare only the 25B-300 to list; the uniform 71%-of-GSA pattern across the ladder is new.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: A research core still selling 6000 runs pays ~4.6x the NCI 25B rate per Gb, and its in-house alternative is AVITI at only ~13% below the 6000, so this tail's conversion is contestable by Element rather than captured by the X.
items.detail: UNMC internal S4-200 v1.5 is $19,905 for ~2,000 Gb ($9.95/Gb), and S2-300 is $14,785 for 1,250 Gb ($11.83/Gb). AVITI24 2x150 High Output is $2,601 for ~300 Gb ($8.67/Gb). NCI's 25B-300 is ~$2.15/Gb at spec. UNMC lists no NovaSeq X pricing, though the page does not confirm the absence of an X. Single core, page undated.
items.source_name: UNMC Genomics Core pricing; NCI CCR rate card
items.why_new: First live 2026 research-core 6000 price paired with an in-house Element alternative instead of an X.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: Caris's Q2'26 revenue per case rose about 31% y/y while cost per case rose only about 5%, so a big sequencing customer's gross-margin gain came from price and mix, not from more sequencing volume per case.
items.detail: Molecular profiling revenue was $252.3M on about 59.2K cases, or about $4,261 per case. In Q2'25 it was $162.9M on about 50.2K cases (59.2K/1.18), or about $3,245. Revenue per case is up about 31%. Molecular profiling cost of services was $81.3M vs $65.3M, or about $1,373 vs $1,301 per case (+5.5%). Molecular profiling gross margin is about 67.8% vs 59.9%. The 59.2K cases are +18% y/y, below the +55% revenue growth, so sequencing demand is not the swing factor. The 50.2K prior-year case count is derived from the +18% rate, not read from a filing.
items.why_new: The known file has cost per case ($1,373 vs $1,301) but not revenue per case (+31%) or the molecular profiling margin expansion.
items.verify_note: The cost per case ($1,373 vs $1,301) and cases (+18%) are already known. The only new part is revenue per case of about $4,261 vs $3,245 (+31%). The prior-year case count is derived. This shows the customer's growth comes from ASP and mix (reimbursement), which is only loosely tied to Illumina Gb.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: Caris's FY26 clinical therapy-selection volume guide is only about +20%, while case growth has already slowed from +22% to +18%.
items.detail: Caris reaffirmed clinical therapy-selection volume growth of about 20% for 2026. Q2 cases were +18% y/y, and the CEO said they were up more than 12% sequentially. The known file records Q1'26 case growth as +22%. Caris is one of Illumina's larger oncology customers, with over 50 NovaSeqs. Its volume is growing in the high teens, not accelerating toward the street's clinical bar of mid-teens or better in Gb.
items.why_new: The 20% FY26 volume guide, reaffirmed in Aug 2026, is not in the known list.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: Caris tripled its capex and capitalized software in Q2'26, which is a sign of capacity build, but its gross margin is expanding, so it is capturing sequencing savings rather than passing them on.
items.detail: Capex and capitalized software were $22.1M in Q2'26 vs $1.4M in Q2'25. Gross margin was 68% vs 63%. Free cash flow was only $6.4M vs $5.9M. Cost of services grew 28.8% total (84.1M vs about 65.3+2.4=67.7M) against revenue +45%. Per-case sequencing cost is rising slightly, so Caris is not seeing falling $/Gb flow into a lower cost per case.
items.why_new: The Q2 capex of $22.1M vs $1.4M and the cost-of-services growth are not in the known file.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: GeneDx's largest supplier fell to about 14% of Q2'26 spend from 20% in Q2'25, while the company says alternative suppliers exist for most reagents.
items.detail: The 10-Q says one supplier was about 14% of spend in Q2'26 vs 20% in Q2'25. For six months it was 23% vs 22%, which implies a very lumpy Q1'26 of roughly 30% or more. GeneDx does not name the supplier. It says it has no multi-year purchase commitments with suppliers and that alternatives are available for most reagents. Together these point to little lock-in, and so to bargaining leverage, at a large clinical customer. The Q2 share drop may be timing of purchases, so this is weak to medium.
items.why_new: Known list covers GeneDx's 10-K on not having validated an alternative platform, not the quarterly supplier-share series or the no-commitments language.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: GeneDx's six-month capex doubled and cost of services grew faster than revenue, while it expects reagent cost to fall as manufacturers advance technology.
items.detail: Six-month capex was $16.6M vs $8.5M (+95%), with construction in progress $11.7M vs $7.4M at year-end 2025. The 6M cost of services was $70.2M vs $60.4M (+16.2%) against revenue +14.2%, and gross margin was 67.6% vs 68.2%. Depreciation in cost of services was $1.73M vs $1.39M in Q2 (+24%). Management expects genome cost (nearly 2x exome, mostly reagents) to fall as genome utilization grows and manufacturers advance their technology. That is an explicit customer expectation of lower $/Gb in 2027.
items.why_new: Adds exact 6M capex, CIP, depreciation and cost-of-services figures; the known list has the qualitative capex step-up only.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: Nationwide Children's Hospital's clinical genomics lab (IGM) lists both the NovaSeq 6000 and NovaSeq X Plus in a Sept 2026 job posting, so it is still running the two side by side.
items.detail: A Sept 2026 Indeed posting for a Genetic Technologist I in a clinical NGS lab (genome, exome, RNA-seq, Sanger, FragileX) names 'MiSeq, NovaSeq 6000, NovaSeq X+, SeqStudio Flex'. A hospital genomics lab is a clinical 'mid-conversion' cohort, and it still staffs for the 6000 about 11 months after its peers' stated end-2026 target window began. This is one lab, so it does not show the pace of conversion. It fits the existing view that the clinical tail is converting slowly. The posting is hiring for the 6000 skill set.
items.source_name: Indeed via Apify misceres/indeed-scraper (A02.json); employer Workday req R-27891-1
items.quote: MiSeq, NovaSeq 6000, NovaSeq X+, SeqStudio Flex
items.why_new: A children's-hospital clinical lab with both instruments is not among the named dual-running examples (Tempus, Natera, Caris, Mayo, Siena, Providence).

items.label: 2B
items.claim: At four cores that list both platforms, AVITI costs about 1.7–3.0x the NovaSeq X 25B per Gb, so a visible AVITI price attack on research is not there yet.
items.detail: I assumed 25B ≈ 3.125B pairs/lane (≈940 Gb at 2x150) and AVITI high-output ≈ 1B pairs per flow cell (≈300 Gb at 2x150). UChicago internal: AVITI 300bp flow cell $1,475 → $4.92/Gb vs 25B-300 lane $2,461 → $2.63/Gb (1.9x) and 10B-300 $1,499 → $4.00/Gb. UC Riverside (rates eff. 17 Apr 2025): AVITI 300-cycle $2,000 → $6.67/Gb vs 25B-300 $3,168 → $3.38/Gb (2.0x). Northwestern FY26 internal: AVITI HO PE150 $2,096 → $7.0–8.7/Gb vs 25B PE150 $3,000 → $3.3–4.0/Gb (1.75–2.6x). Salk (eff. 1 Jul 2025, nonprofit): AVITI HO-300 flow cell $3,610 → $12.0/Gb vs 25B-300 $42,560/7,500 Gb = $5.67/Gb (2.1x) and 10B-300 $8.61/Gb. This is a per-Gb view. UChicago's flow-cell sticker prices (AVITI $1,475 < 25B lane $2,461, F273) hide the difference in output.
items.date: 2025-2026 (UCR 17 Apr 2025; Salk 1 Jul 2025; Northwestern FY26; UChicago undated)
items.source_name: UChicago Genomics Facility; UC Riverside IIGB; Northwestern NUSeq; Salk IGC rate sheets
items.why_new: Known list has Northwestern AVITI at $10.8–19/Gb and UMN at $2.6–3.6/Gb. This adds a same-core AVITI-vs-X ratio at UChicago, UCR and Salk, plus a per-read re-derivation of Northwestern, with the output assumptions stated.
items.verify_note: The Northwestern figure is already known (AVITI ~$10.8–19/Gb vs 25B $3.2–5.0). UChicago, UC Riverside and Salk are new. The output assumptions are reasonable: AVITI HO about 300 Gb, 25B about 940 Gb per lane. This is consistent with D020 (AVITI list ~3x the 25B). UMN (F140) is the counter-example. VITARI is not yet on rate cards.

items.label: 2B
items.claim: UMN's AVITI24 'Savings' tier, at about $2.6/Gb, sits at or below 25B prices at three of four other cores. Research buyers who accept a wait can already get X-level or cheaper $/Gb on AVITI.
items.detail: UMN internal 300-cycle High lane (1.5B reads) is $1,175 Savings / $1,416 Speed / $1,617 Priority. At 1.5B pairs × 300 bp = 450 Gb that is $2.61 / $3.15 / $3.59 per Gb. Savings turnaround is 3–12 business days. Against internal or pass-through 25B: UChicago $2.63 (parity), UCR $3.38 (AVITI 23% lower), TGen $3.14 (17% lower), Illinois Aug 2026 $3,380/937 Gb = $3.61 (28% lower). The 450 Gb figure is my assumption. UMN's external Savings price is $1,352, only 15% above internal.
items.source_name: University of Minnesota Genomics Center AVITI24 rate page
items.why_new: Known list has UMN's $2.6–3.6/Gb, but not the cross-core comparison to X 25B at four other named cores or the Savings-to-Priority spread (+38%).

items.label: 2A
items.claim: Several research cores now charge external academics the same as internal users, or a small premium. That is a price-compressed customer base.
items.detail: UChicago AVITI flow cells cost $1,175 / $1,475 / $2,699 for internal, affiliated and academic non-profit alike (0% premium); only commercial pays more (+58% on 150bp). UChicago 25B-300 is $2,461 for non-profits vs $2,599 commercial (+5.6%). UMN AVITI external vs internal Savings is +15% (150-cycle High: $1,380 vs $1,199). UCR external-educational vs internal UC is +28.8% on AVITI ($2,576 vs $2,000). Northwestern external is +25% on every row. These sit well under the 55% premium in F008 and the 3.6x Salk/MGB spread in F263.
items.source_name: UChicago; UMN; UC Riverside; Northwestern rate sheets
items.why_new: F167 covers only UChicago's 25B commercial premium. This adds the AVITI rows and UMN, UCR and Northwestern premiums as a spread.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: At Salk the NovaSeq 6000 S4-300 costs 2.3–3.1x the X 25B per Gb, and a 2025 AVITI high-output run is cheaper than the 6000.
items.detail: Salk rates (eff. 1 Jul 2025, nonprofit): 6000 S4-300 flow cell $39,701 for 2.4–3.0 Tb (8–10B pairs × 300) = $13.2–16.5/Gb. X 25B-300 flow cell $42,560/7,500–8,000 Gb = $5.32–5.67/Gb. That is 2.3–3.1x, the highest core-level ratio seen, closer to Illumina's reported 3.4x than most cores (1.6–2.0x in F235/F258/F259). AVITI HO-300 at $12.0/Gb undercuts the 6000 S4 by 9–27%. A 6000 user at Salk therefore saves more by moving to the X (−57%) than to AVITI (−9% or more).
items.source_name: Salk Institute Integrative Genomics core rate page
items.quote: Rates effective as of 07/01/25 and are subject to change.
items.why_new: Known list has Salk's S4 price cut, not the per-Gb 6000:X ratio or the AVITI comparison on the same sheet. Flow-cell read counts are the sheet's ranges.
items.verify_note: Verified on the Salk page (eff. 1 Jul 2025, external nonprofit; the page has no internal tier). S4-300 is $39,701 for 8-10B pairs (2.4-3.0 Tb), or $13.2-16.5/Gb. The 25B-300 flow cell is $42,560, ~$5.32-5.67/Gb at 7.5-8 Tb. Ratio 2.33-3.11x. AVITI HO 300-cycle is $3,610 for 1B reads (~300 Gb), or ~$12.0/Gb. The S4 price itself is already known ($52,098→$39,701); the cross-platform ratio is new. Caveat: Salk marks up both platforms heavily (25B is +158% vs the $16,480 list and +76% vs GSA; S4 is

items.label: 1A
items.claim: MIT's BioMicroCenter pricing sheet from July 2024 lists the NovaSeq 6000 and AVITI but no NovaSeq X, so it is a possible 6000 holdout.
items.detail: The FY2025 page ('PRICING UPDATE 7/1/2024', last edited 12 Jun 2024) lists 6000 SP/S1/S2/S4 and AVITI rows only. S4-300 is $5,400 per lane (Core Lab), $5,940 (MIT) or $7,560 (non-MIT). That is about $7.2/Gb at 750 Gb per lane. The AVITI 150 PE lane (~400M reads) is $1,375, about $11.5/Gb if reads are pairs. Several 6000 SP/S1/S2 rows carry a 'minimal inventory maintained' footnote, a sign the lower-volume 6000 flow cells were being run down. The page is stale, and a later sheet may have added an X.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: Indian and Canadian public buyers are still buying 6000 S4 reagent kits and awarding 6000 sole-source work in 2026.
items.detail: Tenderkart lists an Indian tender (28 Aug 2026 close) for the NovaSeq 6000 S4 Reagent Kit v1.5 (300 cycles), item 20028312, with one bid. Alberta (2026RSS0064) and CanadaBuys (AB-2026-04518) have 2026 direct-award or compatibility-justified notices naming the 6000 'workflows'. Contract Finder (UK, Aug 2026) shows a 6000 maintenance contract (quote 4759535). The 6000 S4 kit is the current-generation kit, which suggests continued kit demand.
items.quote: NovaSeq 6000 S4 Reagent Kit v1.5 (300 cycles)
items.why_new: The known list covers Canadian 6000 buyers in general terms. This adds an India S4 kit tender and a count of 3 non-US 2026 kit/service notices.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: Illumina's 6000 S4 and SP kits are still cited in 2026 publications, and multiple 2026 papers benchmark the 6000 against rivals, showing installed-base inertia.
items.detail: CiteAb shows the NovaSeq 6000 SP Reagent Kit v1.5 cited in July 2026 publications. Wiley (Nov 2025) and MDPI Genes (2026, 17(8):853) compare the 6000 with GeneMind SURFSeq 5000, Salus Evo and MGI G400, which treat the 6000 as the incumbent benchmark. This is a weak sign of use, not purchase.
items.why_new: Not in the known list. Publication-citation evidence of 6000 kit use is new, though the signal is weak.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: Only about 10% of Tempus's sales force sells MRD, and MRD volume is still ~9K tests a quarter.
items.detail: MRD ran ~6,500 tests in Q1 and ~9,000 in Q2'26 (+38% q/q). Management says 'only about 10% of our sales force is selling MRD today' on reimbursed indications. Against Natera's 283K MRD tests in Q2'26 (known), Tempus MRD is ~3% of Natera's volume. That supports the thesis point that MRD is not yet a meaningful share of lab mix beyond Natera. Management says MRD is a '$20 billion plus market' and wants scaling timed to break-even ASPs, so ramp spending is deliberately paced.
items.quote: only about 10% of our sales force is selling MRD today
items.why_new: The 9K figure is known. The 10% sales-force coverage, 38% q/q growth and break-even-ASP pacing are new.
items.verify_note: Tempus MRD ~9K/qtr is already known. Only the '10% of sales force' quote is new, and it comes from a third-party transcript I did not check. It cuts both ways: limited sales coverage also means large untapped upside if Tempus scales the sales force (Personalis deal pending).

items.label: 1B
items.claim: Tempus Diagnostics gross margin rose about 3.8 points y/y, which suggests falling unit cost at a big oncology lab.
items.detail: Diagnostics GAAP gross margin was 62.6% vs 58.8% in Q2'25 (non-GAAP 63.9% vs 59.4%). Diagnostics cost of revenue rose only 8.5% ($108.2M vs $99.8M) while oncology volume grew 31%. Cost per unit therefore fell on rough math: 1.085/1.31 = 0.83, about −17%, though the mix includes hereditary and other tests. Sequencing cost is not broken out. Lower unit cost at a large customer supports the thesis that price and productivity gains are being kept by labs, which feeds their pricing leverage over Illumina.
items.why_new: The known file has Tempus oncology volume and a job posting but no unit-cost or margin series.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: The US birth cohort shrank 1% in 2025, so NIPT volume growth must come from penetration or share, not more pregnancies.
items.detail: NCHS provisional data show 3,606,400 births in 2025, down 1% from 2024, with the general fertility rate at 53.1 per 1,000 (about -1%). Earlier coverage called the 2024 uptick short-lived. With NIPT already reaching an estimated 70-80% of US pregnancies (known list), a falling denominator is a structural drag on prenatal Gb. Natera's Q2 2026 women's health growth was described as high single digit.
items.why_new: The known list has NIPT penetration and ACMG guidance but no birth-denominator data from CDC/NCHS.
items.verify_note: Verified: 3,606,400 provisional 2025 births, −1% y/y, GFR 53.1. Real but small. A −1% denominator matters much less than penetration and share shifts (Natera non-oncology +12.5%, Myriad −9%). The Natera women's-health HSD figure is already known (F179).

items.label: 1C
items.claim: Natera's women's health (NIPT/carrier) growth was only high single digit in Q2 2026, against total tests +22%, so the mature NIPT base is a volume drag.
items.detail: A Canaccord conference summary dated 13 Aug 2026 gives women's health growth as high single digit year over year, attributed to Fetal Focus and an enhanced Panorama. Total Natera tests grew 22% to 1.04M and oncology +57%. This is the largest NIPT franchise, and it is growing far slower than the clinical Gb growth that Illumina needs. The source is an AI-generated summary and the figure is unverified against the transcript.
items.source_name: Quartr (AI summary) of Natera at Canaccord
items.quote: high single-digit year-over-year growth
items.why_new: The known list has Natera total, oncology and MRD growth, but not women's health growth. It says only that NIPT is maturing.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: MolDX widened Medicare MRD coverage repeatedly in 2026, which supports MRD volume growth.
items.detail: Versions R17 to R19 of billing article A58454 (Mar to Aug 2026) added NSCLC for Signatera and NeXT Personal, neoadjuvant breast, and TrueMRD for bladder. They also added the Personalis whole-genome-designed assay. Wider indications and more approved competitors raise MRD draws and WGS-based MRD, which cuts against the thesis that MRD volume is too small to matter. This is from search snippets only, and the posted dates are inconsistent.
items.why_new: The known list covers NCCN and the bladder indication, but not the 2026 A58454 revision trail: NSCLC, neoadjuvant breast, TrueMRD, and the NeXT Personal WGS assay.
items.verify_note: Built from snippets only and the dates conflict, so the R-version contents are unverified. Directionally consistent with known coverage expansion (NCCN bladder, Signatera Genome). Adding WGS-based MRD (Personalis) is the most thesis-relevant piece.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: Medicare Part B spending on genetic tests grew 20% in 2024, which shows strong demand for genomic testing.
items.detail: OIG reports genetic tests were 43% of 2024 Part B lab spend ($3.6B of $8.4B), up 20% on 2023, with 10 of the top 25 tests genetic. This points to continued growth in clinical genomics test volume in the Medicare population. It is aggregate spend, not MRD-specific or Gb, so it only mildly cuts against the volume-slowdown label.
items.why_new: The known list cites only the OEI report number among its sources, not these aggregate spend and growth figures.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: Payer coverage for rapid WGS is still limited to 17 Medicaid programs, and fiscal pressure is blocking further expansion.
items.detail: As of Sep 2025, 17 state Medicaid programs covered rapid WGS, mainly for critically ill infants. A few states widened it to under-21s in pediatric intensive care. The brief says the OBBBA makes new benefit expansions improbable. This backs the view that clinical WGS volume is limited by reimbursement and adoption, not by sequencing cost. It is a secondary policy brief with no volume data.
items.quote: improbable due to potential fiscal ramifications
items.why_new: The known list has no Medicaid rWGS coverage count or the OBBBA constraint on payer expansion.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: Newborn genomic screening costs about £963–£1,208 per infant, and most of that is not sequencing.
items.detail: A May 2026 Genetics in Medicine micro-costing across six NHS Trusts puts total cost at £1,208 per infant including research activity, and £963 for routine delivery. The study covers recruitment through confirmatory testing. That fits the thesis that cost beyond sequencing is the constraint. I only saw this in a search snippet and did not read the sequencing share.
items.why_new: The known list only has the Generation Study enrollment (52K/100K), not this per-infant cost split.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: Adding UCSF and Emory widens the core-level 6000-to-X per-Gb ratio to 1.6–3.0x, with a median of about 2.5x. Converting labs therefore get a cut of about 60% per Gb, not the 40–50% D022 inferred from Calgary and UConn alone.
items.detail: S4-300 vs 25B-300 per Gb at cores: Calgary 1.64–1.70x (2025), UConn 1.76–1.88x (2026), MD Anderson 2.5x (FY24), UCSF 2.6x at all three tiers (undated, ~late 2024–25), Emory 2.4–3.0x (Dec 2025). The median of about 2.5x is a ~60% step down. Illumina's revenue-per-Gb ratio is 3.4x, so the core evidence closes much of the gap D022 used to argue against the thesis. These are core rates with overhead, not Illumina invoices.
items.source_name: Emory ENPRC, UCSF CAT, Calgary CHGI, UConn CGI, MD Anderson ATGC rate cards
items.why_new: Corrects D022's 40–50% step using two new cores that sit at 2.4–3.0x.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: Applying NCI's uniform 71%-of-GSA ratio to the GSA S4-300 price gives an academic net price of about $15.4K. MGB's $14,400 and UConn's $15,938 sit close to that, so MGB's low S4 price looks like a standard academic net price, not extra leverage from a large account.
items.detail: NCI pays 71.2%, 70.9% and 71.1% of GSA on the 25B, 10B and 1.5B (D023). The same ratio on the known GSA S4-300 price of $21,683 gives about $15,400. MGB internal is $14,400 (−7%) and UConn is $15,938 (+4%). On that consistent net basis the S4 is about $5.13/Gb (3,000 Gb) vs NCI's 25B at about $2.15/Gb (8,000 Gb), roughly 2.4x. That is below Illumina's blended 3.4x revenue gap. The rest of the gap would have to come from clinical mix (higher 6000 clinical prices, or deeper X discounts at large clinical accounts) or from Gb shipped differing from Gb consumed. That last step is our inference.
items.source_name: MGB Research Cores MOGI; NCI CRTP; UConn CGI; GSA schedule
items.why_new: Links NCI's GSA ratio to the S4 and recasts F263's 'large-account' discount as normal academic net pricing.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: Cores mark up the 25B more than the S4 relative to GSA prices, so core-level 6000/X ratios understate the vendor-level gap, though only by about 10–15%.
items.detail: Emory's S4-300 run is $20,700, −5% vs the $21,683 GSA price. Its 25B-300 run is $22,500, −7% vs the $24,155 GSA price but +37% vs the $16,480 list. UCSF's internal S4 flow cell (4×$5,778 = $23,112) is +7% vs GSA, while its 25B (8×$2,850 = $22,800) is −6% vs GSA. Against GSA the markups are similar, so the about-2.4–2.6x ratio is robust at both the GSA and core level. This leaves the 3.4x revenue gap mainly to clinical pricing.
items.source_name: UCSF CAT; Emory ENPRC; GSA schedule
items.why_new: First comparison of S4 and 25B core prices with both measured against the same GSA basis.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: Medicare Part B genetic-test spending grew 20% in 2024, with the per-enrollee payment up 26%, so government-paid demand for genomic testing was still accelerating.
items.detail: Genetic tests were $3.6B in 2024 (43% of $8.4B Part B lab spend), up from about $3.0B in 2023 ($3.6B / 1.20). The OIG work plan puts the increase at about $500M. Average Part B genetic payment per enrollee approached $800, up 26%, while enrollees receiving any lab test fell 15% from 2018 to 2024. This is dollars of a fee-for-service payer, not Gb. It includes pathogen and non-sequencing molecular tests, so it overstates Illumina-relevant growth.
items.source_name: HHS-OIG data snapshot OEI-09-25-00330 (via CLP Magazine)
items.why_new: The known list has only the '20% growth' headline. This adds the per-enrollee +26%, the implied 2023 base and the +$500M increase.
items.verify_note: Verified via CLP: $8.4B total (+5%); genetic $3.6B, up 20% from $3.0B; 43% of spend but 5% of tests; per-enrollee ~$800 (+26%); enrollees receiving lab tests −15% from 2018 to 2024 (possibly a shift to Part C). The OIG report is in the source list, but these figures are not in the known findings. These are payer dollars from 2024, including price. Ex-87798 growth is ~17% (see derived).

items.label: 1C
items.claim: The biggest single genetic line in Part B is a pathogen test (CPT 87798), not human sequencing, so the headline $3.6B overstates Illumina-relevant spend.
items.detail: Code 87798 (infectious organism detection) was the top-spending lab test at $442.5M, a median payment of $447 per claim, up 51% vs 2023. The top 10 genetic tests total $1.5B. Excluding 87798, the other nine genetic tests total about $1.06B, roughly $118M each on average. Because OIG's 'genetic' class includes infectious-disease molecular assays, the 43% share cannot be read as sequencing-heavy demand.
items.source_name: HHS-OIG OEI-09-25-00330 (via CLP Magazine and MedTech Dive)
items.why_new: Not in the exclusion list. It qualifies the Medicare 'genetic tests +20%' datapoint (F298), which was presented as a demand signal.
items.verify_note: Verified: 87798 is $442.5M (+51%, median $447/claim) and the top-10 genetic tests total $1.5B. The arithmetic is right. It mainly qualifies F301 rather than supporting the volume-slowdown thesis directly.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: Medicare's rate-setting for genetic tests was static through 2024, so 2024 spend growth was volume and mix, and the 2027 CLFS cuts are a new price headwind for the test volume that feeds Illumina.
items.detail: CLP Magazine says fee schedule rates have been unchanged since 2020, so the 20% rise is not price-driven. That means about 20% growth in volume or mix, a measure of pre-cut demand. The known CMS preliminary CY2027 CLFS cuts (genomic sequencing codes −23%) break this regime. Generic panels are the most exposed, while branded MRD/CGP is largely protected.
items.why_new: It links the 2024 volume-driven growth to the CMS 2027 cuts, which the known list covers only separately.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: Medicare genetic spend is concentrated in a small set of high-priced tests, and OIG is opening a fraud and waste probe that could chill volume.
items.detail: 346 labs were paid more than $1M each for genetic tests and 55 labs more than $10M. Most genetic tests in the top 25 grew 30% or more. OIG announced a follow-up project, OEI-09-26-00270, on 15 Jun 2026, to find tests vulnerable to fraud, waste and abuse, and to compare MolDX and non-MolDX jurisdictions. A crackdown would be a risk to volume growth, not a certainty.
items.why_new: The known file has the CMS cuts and an OIG report cite (OEI-09-25-00330), but not this active 2026 OIG audit or the lab concentration counts.

items.label: 2A
items.claim: University of Iowa's genomics core says its NGS sequencing has moved to Element AVITI, citing lower cost.
items.detail: The page says NGS sequencing 'has been migrated' to AVITI, which runs Illumina-prepared libraries at lower sequencing cost. NovaSeq X is kept only for large projects or whole-flow-cell purchases. The page gives no date, no prices and no list of retired instruments. Routine academic volume appears to have left Illumina flow cells while a niche remains.
items.quote: NGS sequencing has been migrated to the Element AVITI sequencing platform
items.why_new: Iowa is a whole-core default move to AVITI, not a dual-platform core like the ones already logged.
items.verify_note: The migration statement is real, but the page is undated and the instrument is AVITI24. NovaSeq X is still offered for large projects and full flow cells ('inquire for pricing'). Read it together with F320: the 'lower cost' claim is not visible in the published $/Gb.

items.label: 2B
items.claim: A vendor-published Cornell epigenomics-core claim puts AVITI at $0.90 per million reads against $7.85 on Illumina.
items.detail: Per the Element blog (4 Jun 2024), the director estimated 2023 Illumina sequencing at $130K versus $15K on AVITI for the same reads. The prices are for an outsourced Illumina provider, not Illumina's list prices. The source is Element marketing and predates 2025, so it shows a trend only.
items.why_new: This is the first named academic buyer with a before/after cost figure, though a vendor-sourced one.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: BillionToOne's test volume growth decelerated about 10 points in one quarter, from roughly +45% in Q1'26 to +35% in Q2'26. Illumina has few higher-growth NIPT customers than this one.
items.detail: Derived from the release. Tests delivered were 384K in H1'26 and 196K in Q2'26, so Q1'26 was 188K. H1'25 was 275K and Q2'25 145K, so Q1'25 was 130K. Q1 growth was 188/130 = +44.6% and Q2 growth was 196/145 = +35.2%. Accessioned tests also slowed: Q1 189K vs 137K (+38%) became Q2 197K vs 148K (+33%). Sequential delivered tests rose only about 4% (188K to 196K). Management said Q2 prenatal volume was 'in line' and that volume dipped in accounts where it captures all test volume.
items.why_new: The known file has only the Q2'26 +35% and the +55% prenatal figures. The Q1→Q2 deceleration derived here, and the fall in accessioned-test growth, are not in it.
items.verify_note: Verified from the 8-K: delivered 196K/145K (Q2) and 384K/275K (H1), so Q1 was 188K vs 130K (+44.6%) and Q2 +35.2%. Accessioned 189K/137K (+38%) vs 197K/148K (+33%). Caveat: Q1'25 was a soft base (130K, then +11.5% q/q to 145K), so part of the slowdown is comps. Drop the 'few higher-growth NIPT customers' assertion as unsupported.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: BillionToOne's revenue growth was driven by price and mix more than volume. Excluding true-ups, ASP rose about 22% against 35% volume growth.
items.detail: Q2'26 revenue was $109.4M with true-up revenue of $2.8M (call), leaving $106.6M. Q2'25 revenue was $66.6M with true-ups of $2.1M, leaving $64.5M. Ex-true-up revenue per delivered test was $106.6M/196K = $544 vs $64.5M/145K = $445, or +22%. Ex-true-up revenue growth was about +65% against +35% test growth. So about 65% of the revenue growth rate comes from price, mix and payer coverage rather than sequenced volume. Illumina's consumable pull is tied to the 35%.
items.why_new: The known file says the gross-margin gain was price-led (F096, D006), but it does not give the true-up-adjusted ASP growth or the true-up amounts.
items.verify_note: This substantially restates D006 (ASP $551 vs $455, +21%; the margin gain was price). The true-up figures ($2.8M/$2.1M) come from an unverified call summary; the 8-K release mentions no true-ups.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: Management's guide of 48-52% revenue growth implies H2'26 revenue growth slows sharply, and Q2 had true-up and payer-claims noise in it.
items.detail: FY26 guidance is $450-465M and H1 was $217.8M. H2 is therefore $232.2-247.2M, or $116-124M per quarter. That is +6% to +13% above Q2's $109.4M run rate. Against H2'25, which is implied at about $450/1.50 = $300M for FY25 less H1'25's $125.5M, or about $175M, H2'26 growth is +33% to +41%, versus +74% in H1. That is a guide to slower growth, and it excludes any further true-ups. The deceleration in the guide is mostly price and payer-contract timing, but test growth is also slowing (see the 1C deceleration item).
items.why_new: The guide was reiterated, not raised, after a Q1 raise. The arithmetic of the H2 deceleration (+33-41% vs +74%) is not in the known file. FY25 revenue of about $300M is my back-out from the 48-52% guide.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: Management says health-system integration is a new growth channel, with each onboarded system adding roughly 1-3K tests per quarter. Volume may re-accelerate from Epic Aura onboarding.
items.detail: On the Q2'26 call, management said it is fully integrated with Epic Aura, and that other labs take six months or more per health system. BillionToOne's first integrations took two to four weeks. The onboarding funnel began in May or June, with growth 'slow at first, then accelerate', and no 2027 quantification. Unity Confirm is ordered on more than 50% of eligible high-risk Unity Aneuploidy patients and is described as reducing account splitting between labs. At 1-3K tests per system per quarter, 20 systems would add 20-60K tests per quarter, a 10-30% lift on the 196K base. This is a counter-argument to NIPT maturity for the share-gaining lab.
items.why_new: The known file lists BillionToOne only as a customer with slow penetration gains. The Epic Aura per-system volume figure and the Unity Confirm attach rate (>50%) are new.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: Volume at BillionToOne carries a seasonality or account-capture dip that management did not model. Prenatal volume is therefore not accelerating at the margin.
items.detail: On the Q2'26 call, management said Q2 test volume dipped in accounts where BillionToOne captures all test volume, and that fewer patients were tested in existing accounts. Excluding true-ups, prenatal revenue rose only about $4.5M sequentially, roughly 5%, from both volume and ASP. Total delivered tests rose about 8K sequentially (+4%). Management said the effect 'tends to be relatively small' but could grow with scale. Together with the US birth cohort shrinking 1% in 2025 (known), prenatal volume is increasingly share-driven, not market-driven.
