items.why_new: The known file has no sequential prenatal ex-true-up growth (+5%) and no seasonality or fully-captured-account saturation comment.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: BillionToOne is a captive, platform-locked account, so it is not a source of extra Illumina discounting. It is raising ASP and holding gross margin at 70%.
items.detail: Gross margin was 70.5% (70% in the release) vs 65.3% a year earlier, and management said it expects to 'maintain 70% gross margin regardless of the mix'. Each product is designed for 70-80% long-term gross margin. Gross profit was $77.1M on $109.4M of revenue. The earlier known items say the company relies on single-source sequencers and keeps about three months of inventory (F092). The company says nothing in the call about a second sequencer or a supplier negotiation. This is a customer that is expanding margin without pointing to lower reagent prices.
items.quote: we expect to maintain 70% gross margin regardless of the mix
items.why_new: Prior items cover the gross margin gain being price-led. The explicit 70% floor 'regardless of mix' and 70-80% product design target are new, and imply no planned reliance on supplier cost cuts.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: BillionToOne's receivables jumped 80% in six months to $74.9M, with more than $10M of claims held by national payers. Billing friction is a gating item for volume, not sequencing cost.
items.detail: Accounts receivable were $74.9M at 30 Jun 2026 vs $41.6M at 31 Dec 2025, +80%, against H1 revenue of $217.8M. On the Q2 call, more than $10M of claims were held by mutual agreement while national payers implement in-network codes, which affected cash collections and possibly true-up revenue. Resolution is expected in H2. Free cash flow was $5.1M in Q2 and capex $4.0M (known). Payer behaviour, not sequencer cost, gates how fast this customer grows.
items.why_new: F093 names reimbursement as a gating factor in general terms. The receivable balance, its 80% six-month growth and the $10M held-claims figure are new.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: Free cash flow and operating margin at BillionToOne fell sharply from Q1 to Q2, which constrains how fast it can buy sequencers and consumables.
items.detail: Operating margin fell from 16% in Q1 to 5% in Q2'26. Management said over half of the decline was lower true-ups ($9.2M in Q1 vs $2.8M in Q2, or $49 vs $14 per test). Operating income was $5.5M in Q2 vs $17.8M in Q1 (H1 $23.3M less Q2 $5.5M). SG&A was $54.3M, +63% y/y, as it hires sales staff. A lab with 5% margin and a payer backlog is unlikely to ramp lab capacity beyond the current plan.
items.why_new: The true-up series ($2.8M, $9.2M, $2.1M) and the per-test true-up ($14 vs $49) are not in the known file.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: BillionToOne's Q2 prenatal ASP reading was held down by true-up timing. Underlying ASP rose about $15 sequentially, and payer contract wins were a record, so price and volume could still lift in H2.
items.detail: Reported ASP fell about $20 sequentially because of true-up timing. Excluding true-ups, ASP rose about $15 sequentially, so the drop is a timing effect, not a price cut. A record number of payer contracts were signed in the quarter. Management also said it sees 'no prenatal payer friction' because most tests bill under its PLA codes (effective January 2025). A competitor (unnamed) cited payer friction in carrier screening. This is evidence against the view of a maturing NIPT market at the share-taking lab.
items.why_new: The ASP sequential bridge (-$20 reported, +$15 underlying) and the PLA-code explanation are not in the known file.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: The Generation Study micro-costing says sequencing is 58% of the £1,208 per-infant cost, which contradicts the known note that most newborn-screening cost is not sequencing.
items.detail: Genetics in Medicine (2026) puts gNBS at £1,208 per infant, with sequencing 58% 'mainly consumables'. 0.58 × £1,208 ≈ £700 of sequencing and lab supplies per infant (my arithmetic; the paper's own split was not readable). The authors say costs may fall with throughput and automation. This is a UK-specific research estimate, not a consumables spend figure. If screening scaled, sequencing would still be the binding cost, so a fall in Illumina's price per Gb would unlock more volume. That cuts against the thesis point that sequencing cost is no longer the constraint, at least for population screening.
items.source_name: Genetics in Medicine (Vu et al.), via Omnicuris summary and search snippets
items.quote: sequencing comprising 58% of total costs, mainly consumables
items.why_new: The known list (F300) says most of the £963–£1,208 is not sequencing; this gives the opposite split of 58%.
items.verify_note: Secondary summary only; the paper's split was not read. The framing needs correcting: the known list says sequencing is 5-10% of workflow cost below a ~$100 genome. A 58% share at ~£700 per infant reflects UK research-scale costs well above that level, so it is consistent with, not contradictory to, the 'constraint only binds at high $/genome' view. Its relevance is limited to population screening (Generation Study is ~52K babies).

items.label: 1C
items.claim: Even in the study's own routine-care scenario, a £963 per-infant cost with a £700 sequencing share means volume depends on public funding and price, not on technology readiness.
items.detail: Removing research-only recruitment and consent activities cuts the cost 20%, from £1,208 to £963. If the £700 sequencing cost (58% × £1,208) is unchanged, sequencing is about 73% of the routine £963. That is my inference, because the paper may allocate sequencing differently. A figure like £963 is far above the roughly £100–250 sequencing cost per genome cited elsewhere, so the programme's costs are mostly non-sequencing or per-sample overheads. The paper's split could not be read in full, so the 73% needs checking.
items.why_new: This adds an inference, with arithmetic, on the sequencing share of the routine-care scenario.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: The Generation Study tender Lot 2 (PacBio) was awarded at a price 8% below the £1.4M estimate, but Lot 1 (ONT) came in 58% above it, which does not suggest broad price deflation.
items.detail: Lot 1 estimate £1.4M against award £2,206,318: +57.6%. Lot 2 estimate £1.4M against award £1,288,000: −8.0%. The Lot 1 figure includes option volume, so this is not a clean comparison. I found no short-read tender in this notice set, and the study's short-read sequencing supplier remains unidentified.
items.why_new: The known list has only a 27% newborn contract discount (F108), a different tender.

items.label: 2A
items.claim: A Georgia academic core cut library-prep prices in March 2025, citing UGA researcher demand for cheaper genomics, and now lists X Plus lanes at $2,000 (10B) and $3,000 (25B).
items.detail: The GGBC post of 12 Mar 2025 (modified 20 Feb 2026) lists UGA rates of $20/sample for full-plate DNA-Seq ($1,920) and $50/sample for full-plate stranded RNA-Seq ($4,800). Small batches cost $40-45 for DNA and $70-80 for RNA. It cites surveys of UGA researchers showing 'a strong demand for more cost-effective genomics options'. The 10B lane (1.25B reads) is $2,000, about $5.3/Gb by my calc. The 25B lane (3.125B reads) is $3,000, about $3.2/Gb by my calc. The post gives no prior prices, no survey data, and no subsidy-versus-vendor-cost explanation, so the size of the cuts is unquantified.
items.source_name: UGA Georgia Genomics and Bioinformatics Core (WordPress REST API)
items.quote: strong demand for more cost-effective genomics options
items.why_new: It is a dated, public record from the core behind the Georgia expert call. Its 25B lane price ($3,000, ~$3.2/Gb) is not among the known core prices.

items.label: 2B
items.claim: Iowa's Genomics Division moved routine sequencing to AVITI, but its published AVITI lane rates are well above 25B Illumina core rates per Gb.
items.detail: Fees effective 1 Apr 2026: AVITI 2x150 High lane is $1,042 internal and $1,245 external for 150–225 Gb. That is $4.63–6.95/Gb internal and $5.53–8.30/Gb external. Known 25B core prices are about $2.0–3.5/Gb, so the 'lower sequencing cost' claim cannot be a $/Gb advantage at list. The 2x75 High lane is $688 internal for 75–112.5 Gb, or $6.1–9.2/Gb. The migration therefore looks like a service-mix and turnaround choice rather than a headline price attack.
items.source_name: Univ. of Iowa Genomics Division fee page
items.why_new: Gives the first actual Iowa AVITI lane rates. The known list only had a snippet that Iowa moved to AVITI.
items.verify_note: Verified (eff. 1 Apr 2026). The AVITI24 2x150 FS-High lane is $1,042 UI / $1,245 external for 150-225 Gb ($4.63-6.95 and $5.53-8.30/Gb). 2x75 High is $688 for 75-112.5 Gb. Iowa lists no X price ('inquire'), so the comparison is to other cores' 25B rates, not Iowa's own. Note the per-flow-cell AVITI rate ($2,083 for 300-450 Gb, ~$4.6-6.9/Gb) is well below Salk's AVITI (~$12/Gb), so AVITI core pricing varies ~2x.

items.label: 2B
items.claim: The Iowa Microbiome Core's 2026 AVITI24 per-sample rates fall steeply with batch size.
items.detail: Library prep plus sequencing is $45 internal and $56.30 external per sample for <92 samples. It falls to $24 internal and $30.30 external for 285–380 samples. That is a 47% internal drop (45 to 24) and 46% external, which shows volume-tier discounting on a rival platform at a second Iowa research core. The page's date header (Jan 2024) conflicts with its '2026 Prices' label.
items.why_new: The AVITI24 per-sample tier table at Iowa is not in the known list.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: Iowa's AVITI lane rates carry little volume incentive and sit far above Illumina's 25B cost per Gb.
items.detail: A whole 2-lane High 2x150 flow cell is $2,083 internal, exactly 2 x $1,042 less $1. There is no flow-cell discount. Lower-output lanes cost more per Gb: Med 2x150 is $751 for 75–125.5 Gb ($6.0–10.0/Gb). Element is not a $/Gb threat at this core at list.
items.source_name: Univ. of Iowa Genomics Division fee page
items.why_new: The flow-cell versus lane arithmetic and Med-output $/Gb at Iowa are new.

items.label: 2B
items.claim: Rockefeller added AVITI in Nov 2024 as its first non-Illumina platform to cut costs, and its news page shows no later Illumina change.
items.detail: The 26 Nov 2024 post says it was adopted for efficiency and cost, used for DNA-Seq, RNA-Seq, ATAC-Seq, CUT&RUN and single-cell. The page has no 2025–26 news and no NovaSeq 6000 retirement. The price list is now FY27 but is behind a restricted redirect, so rates were not read.
items.why_new: Confirms the lack of follow-up news. Rockefeller was previously only a lead.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: The Georgia core's own X Plus price ladder puts the 10B lane about 67% above the 25B per Gb, so within-X price steps are steep and mid-throughput buyers carry the premium.
items.detail: The core's 12 Mar 2025 post lists 10B at $2,000 per lane (1.25B reads) and 25B at $3,000 per lane (3.125B reads). At PE150 (300 bases per read pair), that is about 375 Gb vs about 937 Gb. The price is about $5.33/Gb on the 10B vs $3.20/Gb on the 25B, a 67% premium. The 25B carries a 40% lower price per read: $0.80 vs $0.96 per million reads, or 17% lower when calculated per read. This is my arithmetic on nominal read counts, not measured yield. This extends the known 10B-to-25B gap at other cores to a Georgia core.
items.source_name: UGA Georgia Genomics and Bioinformatics Core (WordPress REST API)
items.why_new: The known list gives only the lane prices. The per-Gb conversion and the 10B premium at this core are new.

items.label: 2A
items.claim: The Georgia core has discontinued single-cell, Visium spatial and PacBio services, and dropped them in a single 27 Jan 2026 edit. It has narrowed its menu to short-read bulk work.
items.detail: The REST API shows three pages relabelled 'Discontinued': Single Cell Genomics, Visium Spatial Genomics, and PacBio Single Molecule Sequencing. All three were modified on 2026-01-27. Single-cell library prep was priced at $2,758 for 1 sample and $16,333 for 8 (UGA rate). The pages give no reason. Consistent with thin core margins and a retreat from the counting applications, which fits the research-funding story.
items.quote: Single Cell Genomics: Discountinued
items.why_new: Prior notes only cover the Mar 2025 library-prep price cut at this core, not the Jan 2026 service closures.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: The Georgia core does not run X Plus in-house. It ships pools off campus twice a week and says library prep is 'significantly higher' if sequenced elsewhere. This is the outsourcing channel that cuts out Illumina's core-level pricing.
items.detail: The Mar 2025 post says pools for off-campus sequencing ship Tuesdays and Thursdays. The library-prep page (modified 18 Sep 2025) says prices are significantly higher if libraries are prepared at GGBC but sequenced elsewhere. The post names no vendor, so the provider's identity and price remain unknown.
items.quote: Prices are significantly higher if libraries are prepared at GGBC but sequenced elsewhere
items.why_new: The known list notes the Georgia core's outsourcing and promised-discount complaints, not the twice-weekly off-campus pooling or the library-prep surcharge.

items.label: 2A
items.claim: The Georgia core's library-prep rates show no evidence of 'insane' research discounts. Prices are essentially unchanged from the 2023 table, and its core history shows annual list rises.
items.detail: The Mar 2025 'lower prices' post gives DNA-Seq at $45 (1–12 libraries), $40 (13–47) and $20 per sample on a full plate ($1,920). The 2023 library-prep table shows the same numbers ($45/$40, $1,920 plate, Stranded RNA $80/$70, $4,800). The 2023 page was edited in Sep 2025, so it may have been overwritten, and the size of the cut cannot be determined. In 2018 and 2019 the core raised Illumina run prices about 5% a year when Illumina raised list prices, and passed the increases on.
items.why_new: The Wayback Machine was blocked, so the pre-cut prices could not be recovered. This sets a 2018–19 baseline of pass-through list increases of about 5% a year.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: Japan's PMDA package insert for FoundationOne CDx reportedly names the NovaSeq 6000 as its only sequencer, with no NovaSeq X.
items.detail: This comes from a web-search summary of the PMDA inserts, not a PDF I read myself. A Feb 2024 version (the 22nd edition) reportedly listed 'HiSeq 4000 or NovaSeq 6000', and a later version reportedly names only the NovaSeq 6000. That would show a regulated test staying on the 6000 as of the later versions, which supports a sticky 6000 tail outside the FDA. The edition number and date of the later version are unverified.
items.date: 2026-09-18 (insert date per PMDA list page; sequencer text unverified)
items.source_name: PMDA package insert, FoundationOne CDx (search-result summary)
items.why_new: It is a datable Japan regulatory record of the HiSeq 4000 to NovaSeq 6000 change, but it is unverified against the PDF text.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: Clinical genomics labs face a measured shortage of technologists, a non-sequencing-cost limit on volume.
items.detail: Survey of US CLIA molecular and cytogenetics lab directors (fielded Jul 2022, published Mar 2023, 70 labs answered). About 10% of molecular positions went unfilled, against 31% in cytogenetics and 44% in combined labs. Average time to fill was 16.5 weeks. Only 8 accredited molecular programs exist, so the pipeline is thin. The survey reports no direct effect on test volume, and it predates 2025.
items.source_name: CAP Today / Genetics in Medicine Open (Leung et al.)
items.why_new: The known list has the 'samples/library prep' constraint but no lab-staffing vacancy data.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: PMDA's list page shows FoundationOne CDx and Liquid CDx were revised in 2024–26. The latest FoundationOne CDx insert is dated 2026-09-18, and the page shows no X-related approval record.
items.detail: FoundationOne CDx has revisions dated 2026-04-21 and 2026-08-26 and a current insert dated 2026-09-18. FoundationOne Liquid CDx has a revision dated 2024-05-27 and a current insert dated 2026-09-18. The Guardant360 CDx insert is dated 2026-07-16. The list page does not state the sequencer, so this is only a map of which documents to extract.
items.source_name: PMDA medical device search, generic name list page
items.why_new: It gives PMDA revision dates for the CGP tests that were not in the known list. It does not yet show what changed.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: Prior authorization and reimbursement, not sequencing cost, are the top-cited barriers to NGS in oncology.
items.detail: A US physician survey (n about 200, published 2025) found reimbursement challenges were the top barrier at 87.5%. Prior authorization was the most common reimbursement challenge at 72%. A Yale Pathology USCAP 2026 review, known only from a blog summary, found 20% of 1,392 NGS tests were denied (2022-23). It attributed most denials to administrative coding errors. The data are old and from one center.
items.source_name: PubMed (US physician survey); Discoveries in Health Policy (Yale/USCAP 2026 summary)
items.why_new: The known list has a Tegus expert and CMS pricing, but no quantified prior-authorization or denial data.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: UK public buyers are buying Illumina consumables on sole-source 'proprietary' terms, not in competitive tenders that pull price.
items.detail: UKHSA awarded Illumina Cambridge £12,000,000 for 'supply of proprietary Illumina consumables' (3 Dec 2025), the largest of 36 contracts on the supplier page. The Animal and Plant Health Agency also took £1.60M of sequencing reagents (Aug 2024) through a UKHSA framework call-off. This suggests large UK public accounts are still contracted with Illumina, with no visible rival competition.
items.quote: Supply of proprietary Illumina consumables
items.why_new: The UK UKHSA £12M consumables award and the framework call-offs are not in the known corpus.

items.label: 2B
items.claim: A UK university research core bought an Element AVITI at £290,640, showing that rival instruments are winning research awards.
items.detail: The University of Edinburgh's Find a Tender notice 003074-2025 (30 Jan 2025) is worth £290,640 ex VAT for an Element AVITI for its Genetics Core. It argues AVITI is the only system suited to 2-12 samples at high quality and throughput. This is a justified direct award, not a competitive price bid. It is comparable to Aston's £282,662 Illumina box (11 Feb 2026) and UKHSA's £323,929 replacement of a MiSeq i100 Plus and NextSeq 2000 (Feb 2026), so Element is priced in line with Illumina mid-throughput and not at a discount.
items.quote: only system on the market that can fulfil this requirement
items.why_new: This UK AVITI award at £290,640 and its box-price comparison with Illumina are not known.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: Molecular labs face a looming retirement wave: 29.5% of molecular staff are expected to retire within 5 years, the highest of any lab department, up from 8.9% in 2022.
items.detail: ASCP's 2024 Vacancy Survey (AJCP vol. 164 no. 5, 2025; 1,027 responses covering more than 18,626 employees) reports the expected 5-year retirement rate for Molecular Pathology/Diagnostics at 29.5%, against 8.9% in the 2022 survey. That is about 3.3x (29.5/8.9). Staff-only retirement was 30.1% vs 7.8%. Cytogenetics rose from 12.0% to 25.3%. This is a non-sequencing-cost limit on clinical volume that builds over 2026-2030. It is a staffing-supply signal, not a measured volume effect. An AI summary of the full text gave these figures, and I could not open the table myself.
items.source_name: American Journal of Clinical Pathology / ASCP 2024 Vacancy Survey
items.why_new: Known notes cite only a 'technologist shortage' (F329, from the 2022 survey); this is the 2024 retirement series by department, with a 3.3x jump.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: Molecular lab vacancies are easing: the overall rate fell from 13.4% in 2022 to 10.4% in 2024, so the staffing constraint on volume is weakening.
items.detail: ASCP 2022 Table 10 puts Molecular Biology/Pathology/Diagnostics at 13.4% overall (staff 13.2%, supervisor 14.8%), up from 7.3% in 2020. The 2024 full text shows 10.4% overall (staff 10.5%, supervisor 8.2%). That is a drop of 3.0 points, or about 22% relative. Time to fill for molecular staff stayed at 3-6 months in both survey years. In 2024 cytogenetics had the lowest vacancy rate of any department at 7.7% (staff 6.7%). This undercuts a thesis that labor binds clinical NGS volume now. Overall vacancies fell vs 2022, but retirements are rising.
items.source_name: American Journal of Clinical Pathology / ASCP Vacancy Surveys 2022 and 2024
items.why_new: Gives the 2022-to-2024 molecular vacancy trend (13.4% to 10.4%) that the known notes lack. It is a watch-out against a labor-constraint argument.
items.verify_note: Not verified (AJCP full text not opened). The known thesis names library prep, interpretation, reimbursement and samples as constraints, not labor specifically, so this rebuts a weak strand. 2024 is still above the 2020 level of 7.3%.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: UKHSA's Dec 2025 £12M Illumina consumables award is roughly 22% above the prior £9.8M framework award, with a longer term and no disclosed concession.
items.detail: The Contracts Finder notice (3 Dec 2025, awarded 28 Nov 2025) lists £12.0M for Illumina proprietary consumables, running to 30 Aug 2028. The prior UKHSA National Microbiology Framework Lot 2 award (Jan 2022) was £9.8M and ended Jan 2025. £12.0M / £9.8M = 1.22, so the ceiling rose 22% in total. The notice is a ceiling, not spend, and the unit price schedule is not published.
items.why_new: Adds the prior-contract £9.8M baseline and term to the known UKHSA ceiling (F019, F033).

items.label: 1C
items.claim: In the Leung/Akkari genomics-lab survey, labs averaged 4.24 open positions, took 16.5 weeks to fill them, and left 44% of combined-lab openings unfilled.
items.detail: The survey went to more than 330 CLIA lab directors in July 2022, with 70 labs answering workforce questions. Time to fill averaged 16.5 weeks (125 positions). Molecular roles drew 6.73 applicants each, against 3.38 for cytogenetics. Molecular technologists stayed an average of only 3.68 years, vs 9.5 in cytogenetics. Salaries were $61.6K at entry, with $78.7K in the West and $49.1K in the South. Only 8 molecular and 2 cytogenetics NAACLS programs exist, vs more than 240 MLS programs. The article does not mention NGS or any volume effect, and the data are stale and from a small sample.
items.source_name: CAP Today (Carpenter) on Leung et al., Genetics in Medicine Open
items.why_new: Adds the survey's quantified pipeline figures (16.5 weeks, 3.68-year tenure, 8 molecular programs) to the known one-line shortage note.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: No 2025-26 genomics-specific staffing follow-up exists, and no published source links the staffing shortage to lower NGS volume.
items.detail: Searches of CAP Today, ASCP, ASCLS and CLN (published 22 Jun 2026) found only generic lab-workforce pieces. ASCP's 2026 Vacancy Survey was launched in April 2026, its deadline was extended to 31 May 2026, and results are not yet out. The CLN article describes turnaround times that 'inch upward' but gives no numbers. Customer data point the same way: Natera's tests grew +22% and Guardant's oncology grew +63% in Q2'26, with no staffing limit cited. So the staffing channel is unproven as a volume brake.
items.why_new: Establishes that the labor-constraint evidence is absent from 2025-26 literature and flags the ASCP 2026 survey as a future datapoint.
items.verify_note: This only shows that no evidence was found, which is weak in either direction. It does not cut against the thesis's 'limits elsewhere' claim. It only says that staffing specifically is unproven as a volume brake. The CLN date (22 Jun 2026) was not independently checked. It pairs with F335 (vacancies easing).

items.label: 1C
items.claim: Illumina Cambridge UK public awards in 2025-26 are broad-based across 16+ buyers and include new instruments, which shows continued demand.
items.detail: Page 1 of the supplier list shows 25 awards from Oct 2024 to Jun 2026. Late-2025/2026 instrument awards include APHA 'High Throughput NGS Sequencers' £354,823 (16 Dec 2025), UKHSA MiSeq i100/NextSeq 2000 £323,929 (Feb 2026), Aston Next Generation Sequencer £282,662 (Feb 2026), Environment Agency two MiSeq i100 £154,861, and Dstl MiSeq i100 £43,645. These are small, mid-throughput boxes.
items.why_new: Gives a dated award-by-award list; the known file has only fragments.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: NHS Leeds signed 6000 and mixed MiSeq/NovaSeq maintenance in Feb-Mar 2026, so the 6000 tail is being serviced into 2027 and beyond.
items.detail: Leeds Teaching Hospitals: 'Maintenance contract for NovaSeq 6000' £119,360 (11 Feb 2026) and 'MiSeq & NovaSeq' £705,125 (19 Mar 2026). Leeds had bought a NovaSeq system for £1,115,627 on 8 May 2024. The 2024 purchase is consistent with an X, but the notice does not say so. Combined 2026 maintenance of £824K shows the 6000 still sits in the fleet alongside the newer box.
items.why_new: Adds the £705K Mar 2026 Leeds contract and the 2024 £1.116M purchase, not just the F034 6000 call-off.
items.verify_note: ukspending confirms both Leeds Teaching Hospitals maintenance contracts: NovaSeq 6000 £119,360 (published 11 Feb 2026, contract 97575) and MiSeq & NovaSeq £705,125 (published 19 Mar 2026, contract 101270). The May 2024 £1.1M purchase was not on page 1 and is unverified. The £705K contract may cover an X rather than the 6000, so only the £119K contract clearly services a 6000. This is the UK NHS analog of the known NMRC service plans (F039). Contract length was not seen, so 'into 2027 and beyond'

items.label: 2B
items.claim: Natural History Museum bought an Element AVITI system in Mar 2025 for £658,756, then added a £157,544 upgrade direct award in May 2025.
items.detail: Per search-result snippets of Find a Tender notices, the contract was awarded to Element Biosciences Netherlands B.V. (concluded 11 Mar 2025, 2 tenders received). A follow-on upgrade was direct-awarded on 16 May 2025, term to Aug 2028 with extension to 2030. This was a competitive award with two bidders, so a UK public research buyer picked Element. The notice is a snippet, not opened in full.
items.why_new: The NHM award is not among the known UK Element wins (Edinburgh £290,640 only).
items.verify_note: Confirmed via Find a Tender summaries. The award notice (2025/S 000-014412, published 10 Apr 2025) shows the contract concluded 11 Mar 2025 for £658,756 ex VAT, with 2 tenders received. The upgrade was a £157,544 direct award (decision 15 May 2025; runs 4 Jun 2025 to 31 Jul 2028, plus a 2-year option). The notices say only 'DNA Sequencer'. That it is an AVITI, and that the upgrade is AVITI to AVITI24, are inferences. £659K is well above an AVITI list price, so the award probably bundles consumab

items.label: 1B
items.claim: A UK 2024 NHS Blood and Transplant HLA sequencing award split volume across six suppliers including Oxford Nanopore, so a large public buyer ran a competitive multi-vendor award.
items.detail: NHSBT published a £4.499M total-value award (12 Aug 2024; 1 Aug 2024 to 31 Jul 2028, quality 60 / cost 40 weighting). Illumina Cambridge is listed at £4.499M on one aggregator and £2.0M with ONT at £0.88M on a preview listing, so Illumina's share is unresolved. ukspending lists the Illumina entry at £4,499,000.
items.why_new: The known file lacks the NHSBT HLA multi-supplier structure and the conflicting values.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: UK public Illumina consumables are bought through framework call-offs, with APHA paying £1.6M in Aug 2024 under the UKHSA framework.
items.detail: APHA 'Sequencing Reagents and Consumables (Illumina, UKHSA Framework Call-off)' was £1,598,054 (14 Aug 2024). This is a call-off under the same UKHSA framework, which adds a second buyer to the sole-source structure. Net unit pricing is not shown, so discounting cannot be measured.
items.why_new: Quantifies the APHA call-off at £1.6M, which is not in the exclusion list.

items.label: 2A
items.claim: UK research buyers keep paying Illumina for consumables and service, not shifting wholesale.
items.detail: Research-side 2025 awards: Northumbria 'Sequencing System Consumables' £300,000 (9 Jun 2025), Bristol consumables £182,134 (31 Jul 2025), Birmingham 4-year service £589,058 (6 Jan 2025), CEH HTS suite £214,896 (Nov 2025), UKRI MRC LMS kits/system £35,626 and £39,280. The sum of these seven awards is £1,361,000 (rounded). The values are modest and show steady spend rather than price fights.
items.why_new: Lists named UK research awards and values.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: A 2020 US physician survey (published Jan 2025) finds nearly all NGS-ordering oncologists, surgeons and pathologists report barriers, led by reimbursement rather than sequencing cost.
items.detail: Future Oncology 2025;21(2):231-239, n=200 US physicians surveyed Oct–Dec 2020. 99.5% reported barriers. Reimbursement challenges were cited by 87.5%, knowledge gaps about methods by 81.0%, and limited clinical-utility evidence by 80.0%. Cost per Gb is not among the top-ranked barriers in the summaries I found. I read this from a search-result summary because PubMed itself returned a cookie wall.
items.why_new: Gives the actual percentages (87.5/81.0/80.0) behind the known qualitative 'reimbursement, not sequencing cost' point.
items.verify_note: Figures verified: n=200, fielded Oct–Dec 2020, published online Nov 2024 in the Jan 2025 issue. 99.5% reported barriers: reimbursement 87.5%, knowledge 81.0%, clinical utility 80.0%. The data predate the X and the current coverage expansions, so they are stale. The thesis point is directional only. F346 is folded in here: prior authorization was 72.0%, new fee codes 68.0%, paperwork 67.5%.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: Prior authorization is the single most-cited reimbursement obstacle to NGS ordering, so demand is gated downstream of the sequencer.
items.detail: In the same 200-physician survey, prior authorization for NGS was cited by 72.0%. Uncertainty about new fee codes was cited by 68.0% and paperwork/administrative duties by 67.5%. All three are non-sequencing constraints, consistent with the thesis that cheaper Gb does not unlock volume. The data are from 2020, so they are stale.
items.why_new: Quantifies prior-authorization burden (72%) for NGS ordering physicians; not in the known list.
items.verify_note: Same survey as F345, so it is redundant. The figures are verified and were merged into the F345 note.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: Payer denials of lab, molecular and genomics claims rose sharply in 2025, a rising non-sequencing-cost brake on clinical volume.
items.detail: XiFin's 2026 Payor Denial Impact Report (published Apr 2026) analyzed more than 30M claims. The blended denial rate for clinical lab, molecular and genomics claims was 11.2% in 2025 vs 8.0% in 2024, a 40% relative rise. Traditional Medicare was the lowest at 3.4%. The rate is blended across segments, not molecular-only. XiFin sells revenue-cycle services, so its sample reflects its own customer base.
items.source_name: XiFin 2026 Payor Denial Impact Report via CLP Magazine
items.why_new: Claims-based 2025 denial series (8.0%→11.2%) is not in the known file, which has only the CMS price-cut and HHS-OIG items.
items.verify_note: Verified: 11.2% (2025) vs 8.0% (2024), >30M claims, Traditional Medicare lowest at 3.4%. Date correction: the CLP article is dated 8 Oct 2026, not Apr 2026. The rate is blended across clinical lab, molecular and genomics, and bundling edits drive 59% of clinical-lab denials. So the rise is not mostly about NGS-specific demand gating. XiFin's client base may not be representative.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: Prior authorization's share of molecular and genetic testing denials more than doubled from 2021 to 2025.
items.detail: In XiFin's data, prior-authorization denials were 13.1% of molecular/genetic denials in 2021 and 27.6% in 2025 (×2.1 in four years, about 20% per year compounded: (27.6/13.1)^(1/4)=1.205). The figure is a share of denials, not a denial rate. It shows payer friction is growing in exactly the high-Gb clinical categories Illumina's customers sell. XiFin's trade summary said payers had pledged to ease prior authorization, but this data does not show it.
items.source_name: XiFin 2026 Payor Denial Impact Report via CLP Magazine
items.why_new: Time-series quantification of prior-authorization friction for molecular testing; new.
items.verify_note: Verified: prior authorization was 13.1% of molecular/genetic denials in 2021 and 27.6% in 2025. The 2024 value was not reported. This is a share of denials, not a rate. Date correction: 8 Oct 2026. The compounding arithmetic (~20%/yr) is correct.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: Bundling edits, which pay nothing separately for lab procedures, now account for most lab denials, a pricing and volume headwind for labs.
items.detail: 'Procedure not paid separately' bundling was 59% of clinical-lab denials in the 2026 report vs 33% in 2018. It exceeded 61% of denials at hospital outreach labs. This is a payer-side revenue squeeze on test volume that has nothing to do with sequencing cost. It also makes customers more price-sensitive on COGS.
items.source_name: XiFin 2026 Payor Denial Impact Report via CLP Magazine
items.why_new: Adds a payer-edit time series (33%→59%) for lab claims; not in the known file.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: A Yale single-center analysis finds 20% of solid-tumor NGS tests were denied, and most denials were administrative, so friction caps volume independent of Gb cost.
items.detail: Korie et al., USCAP 2026 (Lab Invest supplement), via Bruce Quinn's AI-drafted blog summary of 27 Mar 2026. Of 1,392 solid-tumor NGS tests from 2022–23, 275 (20%) were denied. By cancer type, lung was 30%, head and neck 11% and colorectal 8%. 78% of denied cases carried incorrect ICD-10 codes. Of denials, 34% had no prior authorization and 25% were 'not medically necessary'. This is one center and a secondary summary; I could not open the original abstract.
items.why_new: Gives first claims-level NGS denial rate (20%) and its drivers; the known file has none.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: The Yale authors frame denials as fixable with coding and workflow changes, so the denial drag may be removable rather than structural.
items.detail: The blog summary says 96% of ordering-clinician coding was correct and 100% of pathology-report coding was correct. 78% of denials traced to ICD-10 errors downstream in billing, and 80% of tests were physician-ordered rather than reflex. If labs fix coding, about 20% of tests are recoverable, which would support volume. The data are from 2022–23.
items.why_new: Watch-out: the denial friction is operational and fixable.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: Successful appeals of molecular claims recover large dollars per case, which gives labs a path to retain volume and revenue despite denials.
items.detail: XiFin 2025 data show an average recovery of $1,684 per successful molecular/genetic appeal vs $235 for pathology, $171 for clinical lab and $48 for hospital outreach. Appeals take two to three cycles at 20+ minutes of staff time each. High-value molecular claims therefore justify the effort, so denial friction is more likely to delay than to destroy volume.
items.source_name: XiFin 2026 Payor Denial Impact Report via CLP Magazine
items.why_new: Appeal-recovery economics for molecular claims; not in the known file.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: Natera's CEO said 30–35% of Signatera volume is for indications not covered by Medicare's MolDX program, which limits how fast MRD volume can monetize.
items.detail: On the Q4'25 call (Feb 2026), Natera said it has a 'full suite' of Signatera submissions under MolDX review. About 30–35% of Signatera volume is in indications not yet covered. FY25 oncology tests were ~800,800 vs ~528,200 in FY24 (+51.6%). Coverage, not sequencing cost, sets the ASP and the economics of that volume. This is from a search-result snippet; I did not open the call transcript.
items.source_name: Natera Q4'25 call via search summary; FY25 10-K
items.why_new: The 30–35% uncovered share is a number the known file lacks; the known file only has the ASP-uplift timing.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: A genomics-assay denial benchmark shows how severe payer friction can be for newer high-Gb tests: a 64% initial denial rate for HRD/BRCA testing.
items.detail: A FinThrive white paper reports a 64% initial denial rate for HRD and BRCA testing, on 2023–24 claims. These are genomic assays, not MRD or ctDNA tests, so the transfer to MRD is indirect. The paper also notes that coverage by the plan does not stop a 'not medically necessary' denial.
items.source_name: FinThrive EXECLS white paper (search snippet only)
items.why_new: A claims-level denial rate for a genomic assay; the known file has none.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: Older ctDNA coverage policy data show liquid-biopsy MRD coverage was narrow, which is the same gating that limits MRD's share of mix.
items.detail: A 2020 JNCCN study (UCSF and City of Hope) of policies through mid-2019 found 65% of 20 MRD policies provided coverage and 28% of 40 progression-monitoring policies did. Among policies with ctDNA coverage, 91% restricted it to patients without available tissue or with a contraindicated biopsy. The data are old. Medicare coverage has since widened (known file: MolDX and NCCN bladder), so this shows the starting point only.
items.source_name: JNCCN via Discoveries in Health Policy (search snippet)
items.why_new: Historical coverage-share datapoints (65%/28%/91%) for ctDNA; not in the known file.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: Pittsburgh's clinical high-throughput genome effort launched in 2018 with five NovaSeq 6000s. The Pitt HTGC, which looks like a related Shadyside CLIA lab, now lists one 6000 and two X Plus, so most 6000 capacity there has gone but one unit survives.
items.detail: UPMC's June 2018 release says the UPMC/Pitt Genome Center opened with 'five next-generation NovaSeq 6000 systems' as a CLIA whole-genome center. The current HTGC equipment page lists one 6000 and two X Plus, and HTGC calls the 6000 'the first of HTGC's sequencing instruments.' That fits roughly 4 of 5 6000s gone with 2 X Plus added, about 2 X per 4 retired 6000s, which is consolidation. The link between the two entities is not confirmed: the UPMC Genome Center domain now redirects to the UPMC Enterprises portfolio page.
items.source_name: UPMC press release; Pitt HTGC equipment page
items.quote: five next-generation NovaSeq 6000 systems
items.why_new: A 2018-to-2026 fleet count at a US academic/clinical genome center is not in the ledger. The entity link is unverified.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: Pitt HTGC cut its internal NovaSeq X 1.5B lane prices by about 8% to 20% between the 11/01/2024 sheet and the 6/01/2025 sheet.
items.detail: A search-result snippet of the 11/01/2024 Pitt internal sheet shows 1.5B lanes at $1,854 (100-cycle) and $2,554 (200-cycle). The 6/01/2025 live sheet shows $1,714 and $2,054. That is -7.6% (1,714/1,854) and -19.6% (2,054/2,554) in seven months, on the mid-throughput X flow cell. It matches the UCLA cuts on 10B/1.5B lanes (F059) at a second core. The 25B and 10B rows for Nov 2024 were not visible, so it is unknown whether the flagship held.
items.source_name: Pitt HTGC internal price sheet (2024 values from search-result snippet)
items.quote: Pitt/UPMC Internal prices effective 6/01/2025
items.why_new: The first time series for Pitt, which the ledger had only as a single June 2025 snapshot.
items.verify_note: The live page confirms the 6/01/2025 internal 1.5B prices: $1,714 (100-cycle), $2,054 (200-cycle), $2,191 (300-cycle). The Nov 2024 values come from a search snippet only. Pitt's 1.5B price exceeds its 10B lane price ($1,309 / $1,633 / $1,738), so the 1.5B is probably a whole 2-lane flow cell. The snippet comparison is like-for-like only if the 2024 unit was the same. Core rates mix pass-through and overhead (D019).

items.label: 1B
items.claim: Pitt's X ladder carries one of the steepest within-X premiums seen: the 10B costs ~1.5x and the 1.5B ~3.1x the 25B per Gb. A 35B on the same ladder would cut flagship per-Gb prices further.
items.detail: Internal full flow-cell prices at 300 cycles (output = reads x 300 bases): 25B $21,393 / 7,500 Gb = $2.85/Gb ($0.86 per million reads); 10B $12,792 / 3,000 Gb = $4.26/Gb (+49%); 1.5B $4,032 / 450 Gb = $8.96/Gb (+214%). The 10B premium of 1.49x sits at the top of the 1.13–1.50x range across five US cores (D018), well above UCLA's ~26%.
items.why_new: Adds Pitt's X-ladder data point. F264 covered only the 6000 vs X ratio.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: Pitt's '2 or more flow cells' discount is a flat ~8.7% applied to every product, including the NovaSeq 6000 and the MiSeq. It is a core recharge rule, not evidence that Illumina's volume discounts reach the buyer.
items.detail: The ratio of the 2+ price to the single price is 0.913 on every row checked: 25B-100 $14,280/$15,640, 1.5B-100 $2,879/$3,154, 6000 S4-35 $13,131/$14,381, MiSeq Nano $643/$705. Buying a full flow cell instead of 8 lanes saves a further uniform 8.0% (25B-100 8 x $2,125 = $17,000 vs $15,640; 10B-100 8 x $1,309 = $10,472 vs $9,632). The total lane-to-2+ ladder is about -16%, and it is identical across the X, the 6000 and the MiSeq, so it reflects core policy. This weakens reading core tier discounts (F003) as a sign of vendor discounting to large accounts.
items.quote: 2 or More Full Flowcells
items.why_new: Shows the tier is uniform across platforms, which F003 did not test.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: Pitt's internal 25B prices sit 27–34% above Illumina's published kit list at every cycle count. Even the 2+ tier is ~18.5% above list, so this core passes no visible discount through to research users.
items.detail: Pitt full 25B flow cell vs Illumina's published Jan 2025 list: 100-cycle $15,640 vs $11,700 (+34%); 200-cycle $18,400 vs $14,500 (+27%); 300-cycle $21,393 vs $16,480 (+30%); 300-cycle 2+ tier $19,533 (+18.5%). The markup is consistent across cycle counts, which fits a fixed overhead uplift on a contract cost. It matches the 26–70% core markup in D019, now with every cycle length at one core.
items.source_name: Pitt HTGC internal price sheet vs Illumina published list (known)
items.why_new: A Pitt-specific markup across all three 25B cycle kits. D019 used other cores.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: At Pitt's sister core (HSSC, Oct 2025) a NextSeq 2000 P4/P3 300-cycle run costs 4.2–5.7x the HTGC X 25B per Gb, and 1.35x even the X 1.5B. The mid-throughput Illumina tier is the most exposed to cheaper rivals, even inside one university.
items.detail: HSSC (UPMC Children's) Oct 1, 2025 rates: P4-300 $6,540 for 1.8B reads (540 Gb) = $12.11/Gb ($3.63 per million reads); P3-300 $5,880 for 1.2B reads (360 Gb) = $16.33/Gb. HTGC 25B-300 costs $2.85/Gb and the 1.5B-300 $8.96/Gb. Users who stay on benchtop runs pay a 4–6x per-Gb premium for turnaround and convenience. That is the price umbrella AVITI, MiSeq-class rivals and pooled X lanes can attack.
items.source_name: Pitt Center for Advanced Genomics, Health Sciences Sequencing Core pricing
items.quote: All PITT/UPMC prices below are effective October 1, 2025
items.why_new: A new same-institution comparison of NextSeq 2000 P4/P3 and X pricing. The HSSC sheet was not in the corpus.

items.label: 2B
items.claim: A Pitt research center (Pittsburgh Liver Research Center) offers members AVITI 600-cycle sequencing at $8 per million reads. Its leaders co-authored an Element-sponsored AVITI evaluation, so Element is present in Pitt's research channel even though HTGC is all-Illumina.
items.detail: The PLRC service-charge sheet (Jan 2025) lists custom bulk/single-cell RNA and DNA sequencing at $1 per million reads (150 cycles) and $2 per million reads (300 cycles), and '600 cycles AVITI sequencing' at $8 per million reads. It also lists bulk RNA-seq at $24/$44 per sample and WES/WGS at $30/$50 per sample, which look like subsidized sequencing-only member rates. A 2024 bioRxiv preprint on AVITI chemistry lists the PLRC directors (Luo, Liu) with Element co-authors. Taking 300 cycles as 2x150 per pair, $2 per million reads is ≥$6.7/Gb, above HTGC's 25B internal rate (~$0.93 per million reads per lane), so the PLRC price is not an undercut.
items.source_name: Pittsburgh Liver Research Center service-charge sheet
items.quote: For 600 cycles AVITI sequencing, the cost is $8 per million reads.
items.why_new: A new Pitt AVITI user and price point, not in the ledger.

items.label: 2B
items.claim: None of Pitt's three sequencing cores (HTGC, HSSC and the Single Cell Core) lists an Element, Ultima, MGI or Roche sequencer as of late 2026. Research sequencing at this large academic medical center is still all-Illumina at the core level.
items.detail: HTGC equipment: 2 X Plus, 1 NovaSeq 6000, 1 MiSeqDx, plus arrays and mass spectrometry. The HSSC price sheet (Oct 2025) lists only NextSeq 2000 and MiSeq runs. The Center for Advanced Genomics pricing hub lists no non-Illumina sequencer. AVITI appears only at a departmental center (PLRC). This contrasts with the Iowa, MSU and UMN moves to AVITI or Ultima (F305, F139, F200).
items.source_name: Pitt Center for Advanced Genomics pricing hub; HTGC equipment page
items.why_new: A whole-institution fleet check at Pitt, not in the ledger.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: At one core's rates the NovaSeq 6000 costs 2.3-3.1x the X 25B per Gb on S4 flow cells but ~4-10x on the smaller S2/SP flow cells, so a tail made up of small users would explain Illumina's 3.4x revenue-per-Gb gap without any X repricing.
items.detail: Salk (eff. 1 Jul 2025, external nonprofit) prices per Gb are: S4-300 $13.2-16.5, S2-300 $24,938 for 3.3-4.1B pairs × 300 (~0.99-1.23 Tb) = $20.3-25.2, and SP-300 $10,175 for 0.65-0.8B × 300 (195-240 Gb) = $42-52. The 25B-300 is $5.32-5.67. That is a 6000/X ratio of ~2.3-3.1x (S4), ~3.6-4.7x (S2) and ~7.5-9.8x (SP). The GSA S4-300 vs 25B-300 ratio is ~2.4x ($7.23 vs ~$3.02/Gb), so Illumina's reported 3.4x suggests the remaining 6000 volume skews to smaller flow cells and lower-volume, higher-price users. Those users are the least volume-elastic, which fits the thesis that they convert slowly and that each conversion is a big price step.
items.source_name: Salk IGC rate page; GSA prices (known)
items.quote: Rates effective as of 07/01/25 and are subject to change.
items.why_new: Prior core ratios compared only S4 to 25B; this adds the flow-cell-mix explanation for the 3.4x vendor gap.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: If 6000 and X users both paid NCI-like ~71%-of-GSA prices, the 6000/X revenue-per-Gb ratio would be ~2.4x. Illumina's reported 3.4x therefore implies converted X volume is realized ~30% below that academic net rate, near the ~$1.5-1.6/Gb negotiated level.
items.detail: GSA S4-300 is $21,683 for ~3,000 Gb ($7.23/Gb) and the 25B-300 is $24,155 for ~8,000 Gb ($3.02/Gb), a ratio of ~2.4x. At the uniform 71% NCI ratio (D023/D026) these become ~$5.13 and ~$2.15/Gb. To reach the 3.4x reported in Q2'26, X would need ~$5.13/3.4 ≈ $1.51/Gb, about 30% below the NCI-type rate. That matches D011's ~$1.59/Gb (list less ~15%, measured output). So the big gap rests on deep X discounts to large converted accounts, and further large-account conversions land at those prices.
items.source_name: Derived from GSA schedule, NCI recharge, Illumina Q2'26 deck
items.why_new: Reconciles the vendor-level 3.4x ratio with the list/GSA ratio to back out an implied realized X price.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: With NIPT already reaching ~70-80% of US pregnancies and births falling 1% in 2025, total US NIPT test volume has only ~24-41% of cumulative headroom left, even at full penetration.
items.detail: Full penetration from 70% or 80% gives at most +43% or +25% more tests. Applying the 2025 births decline (0.99) gives ~+41% and ~+24%. Spread over 4-5 years that is ~5-9%/yr at most before share shifts. Natera's +12.5% non-oncology growth therefore comes mainly from share gains, consistent with the D014 combined Natera+Myriad figure of ~+8%.
items.source_name: CDC NCHS provisional births 2025 plus known NIPT penetration
items.why_new: Converts the penetration estimate and the new birth data into an explicit ceiling on NIPT volume.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: Excluding the pathogen code 87798, Medicare Part B genetic-test spending still grew ~17% in 2024, and 87798 alone was ~25% of the dollar increase.
items.detail: 87798 was $442.5M in 2024 after +51%, so ~$293M in 2023 (+$150M). Total genetic spending was $3.6B vs $3.0B (+$600M). Ex-87798 it was ~$3.16B vs ~$2.71B, or +16.6%. These are 2024 payer dollars and include price and non-sequencing PCR assays, so they are only a loose proxy for sequencing volume.
items.why_new: Nets the pathogen code out of the headline genetic-spend growth.

items.label: 2B
items.claim: NIH's own Intramural Sequencing Center operates an Ultima sequencer and is making a follow-on single-source purchase from Ultima (Jun 2026).
items.detail: A presolicitation posted 17 Jun 2026 and due 27 Jun 2026 uses single-source authority (FAR 13.106-1(b)(1)) with a value under the $350K simplified acquisition threshold. The justification is accuracy for mosaic DNA, and the notice says the Ultima sequencer gives 'rapid high-volume sequencing at low cost'. This is a small buy, but it shows a federal genome center adopting Ultima next to Illumina. It does not give a price comparison or quantity.
items.source_name: cleat.ai mirror of SAM.gov notice 75N98026Q00652 (NIH OLAO)
items.quote: rapid high-volume sequencing at low cost
items.why_new: The exclusion list has no NIH or federal intramural Ultima procurement.

items.label: 2A
items.claim: A University of Nebraska core cut internal subsidies twice in about a year, shifting more cost onto investigators.
items.detail: BORC cut the subsidy for non-NPOD NU investigators from 20% to 10% effective 31 May 2025 (search snippet). A second notice effective 1 Jun 2026 cuts NPOD members and pilot grantees from 40% to 30% and the NPOD-unrouted tier from 20% to 15%. BORC cites its MOU with UNL and sustainability after NIH Phase 3 funding ends in 2029. This is not a sequencing core, and the page gives no user-response data.
items.source_name: University of Nebraska BORC fee page
items.why_new: Dated, quantified core subsidy cuts at a university core, not in the known core-rate-card list; but not a sequencing core, so weak read-across.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: Myriad's FY25 prenatal volume fell 4% (666K→637K) while revenue rose 5%, so the 2025 'growth' was price-led, and volume decline began a year before the 2026 reimbursement cuts.
items.detail: FY25 prenatal revenue was $186.3M vs $177.1M (+5%). Volume was 637K vs 666K (−4%). The 10-K reports revenue per test up 10%, partly offset by volume, 'mainly' lower SneakPeek testing. Revenue per test is $292 vs $266 (my arithmetic). Q4'25 volume was 150K vs 160K (−6%) on flat revenue of $44.9M. Management tied the Q4 drop to transition dynamics after a new order management system in Q2'25. Volume has therefore fallen y/y in every period from FY25 onward, which is the period the Natera non-oncology and BillionToOne data show as strong for others.
items.source_name: Myriad Genetics FY25 10-K MD&A; Q4'25 earnings release
items.why_new: Adds the FY24→FY25 annual baseline and the stated causes. Earlier items start at Q1'25.
items.verify_note: This restates known items. F212 already has the quarterly series (FY25 173+159+155+150 = 637K vs FY24 ~667K) and four straight y/y declines. F213 already has revenue per test peaking in 2025. F215 already covers the order-management-system and SneakPeek attribution.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: Myriad pays Illumina a royalty on Prequel volume under a non-exclusive Illumina IP licence. As Myriad's prenatal volume falls, Illumina's per-test fee income falls with it, on top of consumables.
items.detail: The FY25 10-K licence table says Myriad pays 'a royalty based on the volume of Prequel testing administered by us'. No rate or dollar amount is given in the sections read. Prenatal volume is −17% from the Q1'25 peak, so this royalty stream is shrinking. This parallels the Natera per-test fee (F238). Illumina's NIPT-linked revenue is therefore not only consumables.
items.quote: royalty based on the volume of Prequel testing administered by us
items.why_new: A new Illumina-royalty datapoint at a third NIPT lab; the amount is undisclosed, so only the direction is known.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: Myriad's FY25 10-K credits lower reagent and supply costs, not volume, for the fall in its cost of revenue. This is consistent with falling consumables prices paid by a large Illumina user.
items.detail: FY25 cost of revenue fell $4.3M (−2%) to $247.9M while staying at 30.1% of revenue. The filing attributes this 'mainly' to a lower cost per test from reduced laboratory reagent and supply costs. It does not name Illumina or give a prenatal cost split, so this is indicative only. Tariffs are flagged as a risk in the Q2'26 10-Q.
items.why_new: Earlier customer cost-per-test items covered Natera, Caris, GeneDx and BillionToOne, not Myriad.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: Myriad's Q2'26 cost of revenue per test rose ~5% y/y, and the 10-Q blames fulfillment and personnel, not sequencing price. Myriad shows no visible sequencing-price relief.
items.detail: Q2'26 cost of revenue was $63.7M vs $61.3M (+3.9%). Total tests were 379K (−1%, so ~383K in Q2'25). Derived cost per test is ~$168 vs ~$160, about +5%. The 10-Q cites 'increased fulfillment costs and personnel-related costs'. Adjusted gross margin fell to 66.9% from 71.5%, but this is driven by lower revenue per test (−9% company-wide, including $11.0M of collections adjustments). It is not an Illumina price effect.
items.source_name: Myriad Genetics Q2'26 10-Q MD&A and 8-K EX-99.1
items.quote: increased fulfillment costs and increased personnel-related costs
items.why_new: A cost-per-test datapoint that cuts against the 1B pricing-relief story.

items.label: 2A
items.claim: UC Davis DNA Tech Core markets AVITI as significantly cheaper than Illumina, at $2,000 per 300-cycle run.
items.detail: Per a search snippet, the core lists UC rates of $2,000 for a PE150 (300-cycle) run and $1,400 for PE75. It says AVITI offers 'significantly lower costs' than Illumina sequencers and accepts existing Illumina libraries. This shows research cores are repricing around Element. Output per run was not verified.
items.quote: significantly lower costs compared to the long-time standard Illumina sequencers
items.why_new: UC Davis is not in the core rate-card list already used; this is a snippet-level read.

items.label: 2A
items.claim: A UC-wide Illumina contract publicly shows only a 25% discount on service agreements, and no deep reagent discount percentage.
items.detail: UC Systemwide Procurement announced its Illumina agreement on 9 Apr 2024 (CalUsource #2023003585). The agreement covers instruments, reagents, service agreements and research services. The only stated percentage is 25% off service agreements, and the page gives no reagent discount or term. The UC system is one of the largest public research buyers, so the missing reagent percentage fits the idea that deep consumables discounts are not formalized in public contracts.
items.quote: 25% discount on service agreements
items.why_new: UC's Illumina agreement and its 25% service discount are not in the known list.

items.label: 2A
items.claim: The UC package covering sequencing and synthesis (Illumina included) saved only about 5.6% on $98M of annual spend.
items.detail: UC procurement reported on 2 Jul 2024 that the sequencing and synthesis contracts cover $98M of annual spend. They save $5.5M a year, or $26M over five years, on an 8-year term (5+3). That is about 5.6% in blended savings, derived by us. It covers several suppliers and has no Illumina-specific figure, and the source may be counting savings against a different baseline. It suggests that discounts at a large academic buyer were modest in a headline sense, not 'insane'.
items.why_new: UC procurement spend and savings figures are not in the known list.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: The NISC Ultima buy was justified on capability (accuracy), not on price, so it is not evidence of price-driven switching away from Illumina at a large federal account.
items.detail: The only stated reason is deep, accurate sequencing of mosaic samples. No cost-per-Gb or per-genome comparison with Illumina appears in the notice text I could read. The full justification sits in a DOCX attachment that I could not open. This is a watch-out: the Ultima win at NIH rests on a use case Illumina can compete in on accuracy grounds, per its own 6x/22x error claims.
items.why_new: It reads the justification for price content and finds none, which the known list does not.

items.label: 2B
items.claim: Element is becoming an established federal vendor: the CDC filed a sole-source notice for AVITI service in 2026.
items.detail: A CDC notice of intent names Element as the only vendor with trained, certified service engineers for AVITI instruments and reagents. I saw it only as a search-result summary. Together with the USDA-ARS AVITI upgrade request (closed 3 Jul 2026), this shows rival platforms moving from pilots to support contracts. The notices are small and carry no price data.
items.source_name: samsearch.co (USDA-ARS 1232SA26Q0805; CDC notice via search result)
items.why_new: The CDC service-vendor notice is not in the known list. USDA-ARS and Canadian AVITI buys are already known.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: Illumina may still be shipping NovaSeq 6000 control software in 2025, which would be consistent with a supported long tail.
items.detail: A single unverified page summary of the NovaSeq 6000 downloads page lists NVCS/Installer 1.8.2 dated 25 Aug 2025 (the last 1.8.1 notes were 6 Nov 2023). No end-of-support statement was seen, and no v1.9 was found. Search snippets and the indexed v1.8 page show nothing newer than 2023, so the 1.8.2 date is unconfirmed. Even if real, it is a patch release, not a new feature version.
items.why_new: The known list shows no 6000 software cadence data; the known evidence only notes that the 6000 product page is live.

items.label: 2A
items.claim: A major US university genomics core says outsourced NovaSeq X Plus lanes are now cheaper and faster than running them in-house.
items.detail: UMN Genomics Center's NovaSeq X Plus service page (2026 copyright) says it has partnered with unnamed outside sequencing facilities because outsourcing is cheaper and faster for now. This shows a core that owns Illumina capacity routing research volume to lower-cost providers. It gives no price or volume figure and no date for the statement.
items.quote: access to the NovaSeq X Plus will be both faster and less expensive when outsourced
items.why_new: The known list names UMN only for AVITI cost declines, not its own admission that outsourcing X Plus is cheaper than in-house.
items.verify_note: F200/F112 already record that UMGC offers the X Plus only via partnered outsourcing. The only new part is the stated reason (cheaper and faster outsourced). The statement is undated and gives no price.

items.label: 2B
items.claim: A University of Chicago core is stopping sequencing services and sending users to Novogene and other low-cost providers.
items.detail: The DFI Microbiome Metagenomics Core stopped taking new sequencing projects from 11 Aug 2026 and recommends the UChicago Genomics Facility, Plasmidsaurus and Novogene. No reason is given. It is a small, microbiome-specific core, so it is an anecdote and not a trend.
items.quote: phasing out sequencing services
items.why_new: The known list has one Georgia core sunsetting its 6000 and Dana-Farber's retirement, but not a core exiting sequencing for Novogene.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: Natera's 10-Q commitments show a small lab-instrument supplier obligation ending Dec 2027, plus the large material-supplier block to Nov 2030, so long-dated purchase commitments remain thin.
items.detail: The Q2'26 10-Q contractual commitments table lists $120.3M for material suppliers (expiring Nov 2030) and $13.4M for a laboratory instruments supplier (expiring Dec 2027). Together that is $133.7M of named blocks, against ~$753M of quarterly revenue. The instrument commitment ends in about 14 months, leaving Natera free to rebid sequencer purchases.
items.why_new: The $13.4M instrument-supplier block to Dec 2027 is new; the $120.3M block is already known.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: Wayne State's genome sciences core describes the NovaSeq 6000 as its latest platform and lists no X, AVITI or Ultima.
items.detail: The page calls the 6000 'the latest' platform the core has 'operationalized' and names no other sequencer. The page has no date, so it may be stale. If current, it is a pure 6000 holdout with no conversion plan visible.
items.why_new: Wayne State is not in the known core list.

items.label: 2B
items.claim: UMN Genomics Center lists AVITI24, NovaSeq X+, NextSeq 2000, MiSeq, Nanopore, Revio and Ultima UG 100, with no 6000.
items.detail: The page names the AVITI24 as newly installed. Illumina is down to the X+ and mid/low-throughput boxes. A research core with three non-Illumina or non-short-read additions and no 6000 shows research capacity being rebuilt around rivals. The known notes already hold UMN pricing, but not this fleet snapshot.
items.why_new: Gives the full fleet list; known notes cover UMN pricing and UMGC primarily.
items.verify_note: Duplicate of F200, which already gives the UMGC fleet in more detail (2 UG200, 5 AVITI24, Nanopore P2, Revio and X Plus via outsourcing).

items.label: 2B
items.claim: Northwestern's NUSeq now lists only the X Plus, AVITI and Complete Genomics T1+ for short-read, a three-vendor fleet with no 6000.
items.detail: NUSeq's technology page lists NovaSeq X Plus, Element AVITI, DNBSEQ-T1+, NextSeq 500 and MiSeq. Search results note the X Plus has been offered since Sep 2023 and the DNBSEQ-G400 was added. The 6000 is not mentioned. Three vendors in one research core at mid-throughput shows broad rival entry.
items.why_new: Adds the T1+ addition to the known Northwestern pricing notes.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: Of the cores whose pages loaded, most research cores no longer list a 6000, which cuts against a thick research 6000 tail.
items.detail: Count of 10 cores with readable fleet pages: 6000 listed at Yale, UNMC, Wayne State, MD Anderson (4 of 10, 40%). No 6000 at UMN, EMBL, NUSeq, plus Bonn and UMGC from earlier notes (6 of 10). Page fetches for Stanford, Princeton, Penn, Vanderbilt, HudsonAlpha, WashU and Baylor did not give fleet lists. This is a small, non-random sample.
items.why_new: First tally of 6000-retention across cores in this scrape.

items.label: 2A
items.claim: NIH funded about 3,000 fewer projects in FY2026 than in FY2025, even though it obligated its full ~$34B extramural budget.
items.detail: STAT (2 Oct 2026, via secondary summary) says NIH funded ~58,000 projects in FY26 versus ~61,000 in FY25 and ~63,700 before 2025. Average obligation per project was ~$586K versus ~$534K at baseline. The count may rise a little as database lags clear. Fewer, larger, front-loaded awards mean fewer labs funded, which is consistent with thin research volume.
items.source_name: Granted AI blog summarizing STAT 'Analyzing FY 2026 NIH grants'
items.why_new: The known list has only FY26 data through 20 Mar 2026 ($5.8B, 10,327 grants). This is the first full-year FY26 count.
items.verify_note: This is a secondary blog summarizing STAT. The STAT article was not found directly. AAMC showed $30.2B (89%) obligated entering September, so 'fully obligated' is unconfirmed. CRS attributes the lower project count partly to forward-funded multiyear awards. Fewer projects therefore overstates the drop in active funded labs, though new-lab funding is still down. The per-project arithmetic is consistent ($34B/58K ≈ $586K; $34B/63.7K ≈ $534K).

items.label: 2A
items.claim: Multiyear (up-front) funding is crowding out new awards and has been capped by law at the FY25 level.
items.detail: AAMC data through 31 Aug 2026 show $1.6B of multiyear funding to competitive RPGs, versus $556M in FY25 (per a July–Aug snippet of $1.1B). Public Law 119-75 (Feb 2026) reportedly caps multiyear obligations at the FY25 level. Per AAMC and the AAU, new awards were 12% of all awards through 20 Mar versus 18–22% normally, and 66% fewer grants through February than in FY21–24. Because competitive RPG counts are down 8% versus FY24, researchers see fewer new projects that would buy sequencing.
items.source_name: AAMC Tracking NIH Awards FY2026; STAT; Granted AI
items.why_new: The known list has no multiyear-funding dollars and no statutory cap. It also has no FY26 count of competitive RPGs versus FY24.
items.verify_note: Partly a duplicate and partly unverified. The 12% new-award share is already known. The multiyear figures ($1.1B / $1.6B vs $556.4M) are covered more precisely by F405. The AAMC Jul and Aug briefs do not mention the Public Law 119-75 cap on multiyear funding, and the claim of '66% fewer grants through February' could not be verified. Merge into F405.

items.label: 2A
items.claim: NIH is still spending its full budget and has a continuing resolution (CR) through 11 Dec 2026, so there is no funding cliff.
items.detail: The ~$34B extramural budget was fully obligated, and total obligations exceed FY25. Public Law 119-103 (signed 2 Sep 2026, per a secondary source) funds NIH at the FY26 enacted level to 11 Dec. The House FY27 Labor-HHS bill keeps NIH roughly flat to +2%. Award counts are down, but dollars are not. This is a watch-out for the idea that research pricing power is the only issue: research customers have funds even if grant counts are low.
items.why_new: The known list had a CR 'through 11 Dec', but not the full-year 'fully obligated' fact or the P.L. 119-103 citation.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: At KUMC the internal 25B-300 flow cell is priced at 99% of Illumina's published list, while the 10B-300 is priced at 64% of list, so the discount lands on the smaller flow cell and not on the flagship.
items.detail: Internal 25B-300 is $23,872 against the known list of $24,155 (98.8%). Internal 10B-300 is $9,255 for a full 8-lane flow cell against the known list of $14,493 (63.9%). The 1.5B-300 is $5,225 against list $3,928 (133%). The ratios are against already-known list prices and assume the KUMC lines are full-flow-cell prices, as the page states. NCI's uniform 71%-of-GSA ratio is already logged. This core instead shows a 25B at list and a 10B at about two-thirds of list. That fits a core that passes through the vendor's net price on the 10B, and the 25B may have little discount to pass through.
items.source_name: KU Medical Center Genome Sequencing Facility
items.why_new: Gives separate list-relative ratios for the 25B (99%) and the 10B (64%) at one core. The known list only gave 'near list' for the 25B.
items.verify_note: Correction: $24,155 / $14,493 / $3,928 are GSA distributor prices, not Illumina list. Against the $16,480 list (F146), the KUMC internal 25B-300 ($23,872) is about 145% of list. Verified on the page, which shows full-flow-cell internal prices of $9,255 (10B-300), $23,872 (25B-300) and $5,225 (1.5B-300), with no effective date. Restate the claim: the 10B is priced at about 64% of GSA while the 25B is at about 99% of GSA, so per Gb the 10B is roughly at par with the 25B (see derived item).

items.label: 1B
items.claim: KUMC's 25B-100 cycle flow cell is $19,917 internal, about 1.7x Illumina's published $11,700 list, so cycle-count pricing here is compressed and the long-read configuration carries all the discount.
items.detail: Internal 25B prices are $19,917 (100-cycle), $21,805 (200-cycle) and $23,872 (300-cycle). Against the known Jan 2025 list ($11,700 / $14,500 / $24,155), the ratios are 170%, 150% and 99%. Moving from 100 to 300 cycles adds only +20% at KUMC, against +106% on Illumina's list. Either the core is not passing through Illumina's net prices on the short-cycle kits, or Illumina's short-cycle kits are priced much lower than the core's recharge. This suggests the core's recharge policy, not Illumina's net price, drives the short-cycle prices.
items.source_name: KU Medical Center Genome Sequencing Facility
items.why_new: The cycle-count ladder (+20% from 100 to 300 cycles) and the 1.7x-of-list markup on the 25B-100 are not in the known core data.

items.label: 2B
items.claim: The House FY27 bill cuts NSF by ~20%, and the White House asked for a ~55% cut, adding a second federal research-funding squeeze beyond NIH.
items.detail: The House CJS bill (committee vote 13 May 2026) funds NSF at $7.0B versus $8.75B enacted for FY26. R&RA falls 10.3% to $6.4B. The request was ~$3.9B. Illumina's known list covers NIH only, but the SC core said 2027 risk is a 'huge reduction of NSF and NIH'. Final outcomes are unresolved, and the Senate is expected to be higher.
items.why_new: The known list has no NSF FY27 numbers and no White House request level.

items.label: 2A
items.claim: Congress is rejecting deep NIH cuts: the House bill holds NIH roughly flat to +2%, versus a proposed ~$5B cut.
items.detail: The White House FY27 request cuts NIH by ~$5B. The House Labor-HHS bill keeps NIH near FY26, and institutes like NEI are held at FY26 levels. Senate language also tells NIH to fund as many meritorious new awards as possible and to brief Congress on multiyear funding. This lowers the tail risk for research demand in 2027.
items.source_name: BPS in the Beltway / Internet2 update (search snippet)
items.why_new: The known list has the House NIH level but not the Senate directive on new awards and multiyear reporting, nor the ~$5B request cut.

items.label: 2A
items.claim: UC Berkeley's QB3 genomics facility owns no NovaSeq X and sends all lanes to the UCSF CAT lab, so a major UC core has consolidated rather than buying capacity.
items.detail: The QB3 rates page (effective for work after 1 Jun 2026) says 'UCB does not have a NovaSeq X, all lanes are sent to the UCSF CAT Lab at this time.' It lists internal prices for 10B 150PE ($1,535) and 25B 150PE ($2,600 for ~875 Gb, about $2.97/Gb). It lists no NovaSeq 6000. The sequencing is done at another core on a pass-through basis, so the volume stays on Illumina but one fewer buyer is making its own purchasing decisions. This is consolidation, not price-driven loss to a rival platform.
items.quote: UCB does not have a NovaSeq X, all lanes are sent to the UCSF CAT Lab
items.why_new: Not among the cores already known; consolidation of purchasing into one UC hub.
items.verify_note: Relabelled from 2B. Consolidation onto Illumina at UCSF is evidence neither of worse research pricing from Roche nor of flat volume. Verified on the page: rates are effective 1 Jun 2026, and the move of all lanes to UCSF CAT ('from all other partners') happened in summer 2026. The 25B 150PE lane is $2,600 UC for 875 Gb ($2.97/Gb). The page says specs are conservative and real output runs 25–30% higher (~$2.3/Gb). Weak support for buyer aggregation: volume pools at a larger core with more purchas

items.label: 2A
items.claim: Cornell's BRC Genomics Facility runs no NovaSeq in house and sells externally sequenced lanes at 'low rates' with about 3-week turnaround.
items.detail: A Cornell BRC spotlight post dated 14 May 2024 says the facility 'contracted for external sequencing at low rates'. Orders go through the BRC portal with no quote or PO, and NovaSeq turnaround is about 3 weeks after QC. The facility keeps MiSeq and NextSeq instruments for fast work. The partner is not named and no prices are given. The pattern is a research core that prices on speed against an outsourced low-cost supplier, which makes it a price-for-delay trade of the kind research buyers accept.
items.quote: We do not load the instruments in house
items.why_new: Dated, named core with an explicit outsourced-for-cost model; no earlier item records Cornell's NovaSeq lanes as outsourced.
items.verify_note: Relabelled from 2B. The source is from May 2024, so it is stale. It names no partner and gives no prices, and it repeats the known pattern of cores outsourcing to low-cost providers. The 'price-for-delay' reading is our interpretation, not the source's.

items.label: 2A
items.claim: The University of Mainz sequencing core routes all sequencing to Novogene Munich and owns no sequencers, a cheap-provider model inside a German university.
items.detail: The Mainz core page (last updated 18 Jul 2024) says 'All sequencing takes place at our sequencing partner Novogene (Munich)'. It adds that the core has worked with Novogene for several years and handles shipment, forms, data processing and analysis. It names Novogene's NovaSeq X Plus, with two systems in Munich. No prices are listed. Volume therefore stays on Illumina hardware, but the buyer is a pass-through core with no purchasing leverage of its own and Novogene sets the price. It is a European example of the outsourced-core structure.
items.quote: All sequencing takes place at our sequencing partner Novogene (Munich)
items.why_new: Not in the known list of core outsourcing examples; pure Novogene pass-through with no in-house instrument.
items.verify_note: A European example of the known pattern of outsourcing to Novogene. The page was last updated Jul 2024 and lists no prices. The volume stays on Illumina X Plus hardware, so this is a pricing-channel point, not volume loss.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: University of Oregon's GC3F core still sells NovaSeq 6000 runs at prices that work out to about 2.3x the X 25B per Gb at UC Berkeley, so a research 6000 tail persists at some cores.
items.detail: GC3F lists S4 300-cycle at $5,070 internal and $6,903 external. S4 output is roughly 2.5B read pairs, about 750 Gb at 2x150, giving about $6.8/Gb internal. UC Berkeley's 25B 150PE lane is $2,600 for 875 Gb, or about $2.97/Gb. The ratio is 6.8 / 2.97, about 2.3x, which falls inside the earlier core range of 1.6-3.0x. The GC3F SP 100-cycle run is $1,683, so small-flow-cell 6000 buyers pay far more per Gb. The page is undated.
items.why_new: Oregon was not in the known core list; the 6000/X ratio is derived across two different cores, with output assumed.

items.label: 2A
items.claim: UMass Chan closed its Deep Sequencing Core on 1 Jul 2025 and its Molecular Biology Core Labs and PacBio core on 22 May 2026, a run of academic core closures.
items.detail: The UMass Chan NEMO site says the Deep Sequencing Core closed on 1 Jul 2025 and queued samples would be completed. Library-building help was to continue through the Molecular Biology Core Labs. A later search snippet says the MBCL and PacBio core closed on 22 May 2026. Two of the three pages returned 403, so the 2026 closures rest on a search snippet. No reason (cost, funding or outsourcing) is stated, and there is no volume data.
items.source_name: UMass Chan NEMO core pages (search snippet)
items.why_new: Not in the known list; reasons unstated, so it only shows consolidation.

items.label: 2A
items.claim: Edinburgh Genomics, a large UK academic sequencing facility, stopped taking projects on 31 Oct 2025 and is being folded into the Genetics Core after a review.
items.detail: The University of Edinburgh post of 7 Nov 2025 says projects ceased on 31 Oct 2025, with staff and equipment moving to the Genetics Core. It cites consolidating genomics expertise after a college-level review. The post gives no cost or price rationale and does not mention outsourcing. The closure date in the post reads 4 Jan 2025, which is probably a typo for 2026. It is a consolidation datapoint, not price-driven attrition.
items.why_new: Edinburgh Genomics is a large European core that is not in the known list.

items.label: 2A
items.claim: Searches of .edu pages, minutes and annual reports found no published core volume-loss numbers tied to Novogene or other outsourcing in 2025-26.
items.detail: About 17 searches and fetches found no committee minutes with a sequencing-revenue decline, no 2025-26 core exit citing Novogene, and no outsourced-versus-in-house price column. The UChicago Genomics Facility pages found still list in-house instruments, and the earlier claim that UChicago is exiting sequencing for Novogene could not be confirmed. The 'outsourcing wins on price' claim therefore rests on a few pass-through pages, with no quantified volume shift.
items.why_new: Documents that the quantified version of this evidence is not available on the open web.
items.verify_note: A negative search result. It is useful as a caveat: there is no quantified shift of core volume to outsourcing. The unconfirmed claim that UChicago is exiting sequencing should be dropped from any ledger.

items.label: 2A
items.claim: Novogene's FY25 sequencing-platform-service gross margin fell 1.88 pts to 32.50% on revenue of only +0.63%, consistent with research sequencing price pressure.
items.detail: Novogene is the largest research sequencing-service provider and a major Illumina customer. FY25 platform-service revenue was RMB 1.062B (+0.63% y/y) with gross margin 32.50% (-1.88 pts), as reported in the 14 Apr 2026 annual report summary. Basic life-science research services grew +10.36% at a 54.17% margin (-0.69 pts). Per-unit price was not given in the summary. The 33% data-output growth already known implies a steep fall in revenue per Gb.
items.source_name: Jiemian (summary of Novogene FY25 annual report)
items.quote: 毛利率仅32.50%,同比下降1.88个百分点
items.why_new: The known list has Novogene volume and revenue growth but not the segment gross margin of 32.50% or the -1.88 pt change.

items.label: 2A
items.claim: The House Labor-HHS bill is a modest cut of 2.9% overall, and NIH is described as flat to slightly up.
items.detail: CRS reports H.R. 9260 at $189.3B in regular discretionary Labor-HHS appropriations. That is $5.6B (−2.9%) below the FY26 enacted $194.9B. Adjusted appropriations are $192.5B vs $198.0B. AAAS's House analysis says ARPA-H is flat, matching the intent for NIH. I could not read the NIH line itself, so the 'NIH flat to +2%' claim rests on the known file. The cut to the parent bill is small and NIH is not singled out, so a deep NIH cut is not in prospect via the House.
items.why_new: Quantifies the parent Labor-HHS bill (H.R. 9260, −2.9%), which the known file does not give.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: At Pitt's core (internal rates, Jun 2025) the NovaSeq 6000 S2-300 costs ~3.7x the X 25B-300 per Gb and the SP-300 ~6x, which replicates Salk's small-flow-cell pattern (D028) at a second core.
items.detail: Pitt/UPMC internal rates effective 6/01/2025: S2-300 flow cell $14,030 for 4.1B clusters × 300 bp ≈ 1,230 Gb = ~$11.4/Gb. SP-300 $4,571 for 0.8B × 300 ≈ 240 Gb = ~$19.0/Gb. The X 25B-300 lane is $2,907 for ~3.125B × 300 ≈ 937 Gb = ~$3.10/Gb, so the ratios are ~3.7x (S2) and ~6.1x (SP). The 10B-300 lane is $1,738/375 Gb = $4.63/Gb (1.49x the 25B, in line with D018). Pitt lists the S4 only at 35 cycles, so its S4 ratio cannot be computed. Unlike the S4-based core ratios (1.6–3.0x, D025), the smaller-flow-cell 6000 users pay far above X levels per Gb.
