That is consistent with the high-price, low-volume tail behind Illumina's 3.4x revenue-per-Gb gap. The Pitt 25B lane is also ~41% above the ~$2,060/lane list ($16,480/8), consistent with D019's core markups.
items.quote: Pitt/UPMC Internal prices effective 6/01/2025
items.why_new: Pitt's 6000 S2/SP-vs-X per-Gb ratios are not in the known list; D028 had only Salk.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: XiFin's data imply that prior-authorization denials on molecular/genetic claims rose roughly 2.5–3x from 2021 to 2025 as a share of claims, if molecular denial rates moved like the blended rate.
items.detail: Prior authorization's share of molecular/genetic denials rose from 13.1% (2021) to 27.6% (2025), ×2.1. The blended lab/molecular/genomics denial rate rose from 8.0% (2024) to 11.2% (2025), ×1.4 in one year. If the molecular denial rate rose at least that much since 2021, prior-auth denials per claim rose ≥2.1 × 1.4 ≈ 3x (2025: ~27.6% × 11.2% ≈ 3.1% of claims vs ≤~1% in 2021). This is illustrative only, because XiFin gives no molecular-only rate and no 2021 rate. Payer friction rising this fast is a non-sequencing brake consistent with the 2020 survey, where 72% of physicians cited prior authorization.
items.source_name: XiFin 2026 Payor Denial Impact Report via CLP Magazine; Future Oncology 2025
items.why_new: Combines the new XiFin share and rate data. No payer-denial trend is in the known corpus.

items.label: 2A
items.claim: Terminated or frozen NIH grants are mostly a one-off 2025 shock, and only part of the dollars are still lost, so they are a weak driver of 2027 research consumables.
items.detail: Late-2025 search snippets say Grant Witness counted 5,464 NIH projects 'impacted' (terminated or temporarily frozen), with about $2.3B of estimated loss still halted or unfunded as of Nov 2025. In Sep 2025 it had 5,100+ impacted, about $4.5B lost, and only 1,295 reinstated. On those numbers the cumulative total stayed roughly flat while the still-lost amount fell, so the shock is not growing. I could not open live counts: grantwitness.org loads its counters by JavaScript and returned 'Loading…'. The snippets come from secondary press, so treat the dollar figures as approximate.
items.source_name: Maryland Matters / Grant Witness (via search snippet)
items.why_new: The known file has NIH obligation and award-count data, but not Grant Witness's impacted, reinstated and still-lost dollar series.

items.label: 2A
items.claim: Terminations were concentrated at large research universities, which are Illumina's biggest academic accounts (Columbia, Harvard, Johns Hopkins).
items.detail: A JAMA letter covering 28 Feb–8 Apr 2025 found the most terminations at Columbia (157), then Johns Hopkins (19), Yale (14), Emory (14) and Michigan (14). A less authoritative tally for 28 Feb–27 May 2025 lists Harvard Medical School 340 awards, Columbia Health Sciences 163, Harvard School of Public Health 158 and Harvard University 139. These are big multi-instrument buyers who negotiate discounts. They are an early 2025 snapshot, and the current still-terminated dollars by institution were not retrievable.
items.why_new: It names the specific large academic accounts hit, which the known file does not.

items.label: 2A
items.claim: Courts have restored many terminated grants, which limits lasting damage to academic sequencing budgets.
items.detail: On 16 Jun 2025 Judge Young (D. Mass.) ordered NIH to restore 367 grants worth nearly $3.8B. In May 2026 the Ninth Circuit upheld reinstatement of grants cut under DEI and environmental-justice executive orders. NIH also reinstated UCLA awards suspended from 31 Jul 2025 under a court order. HHS is still appealing, so the restored list is not final. Restoration does not mean normal operation, because projects stalled and some are slow to restart.
items.why_new: The known file has the indirect-cost cap ruling but not the grant-termination reinstatement rulings.

items.label: 2A
items.claim: NIH funded about 1,924 fewer grants through Aug 2026 than at the same point in FY25, even though dollars obligated are near the full budget.
items.detail: AAMC's brief (data through 31 Aug 2026, published 9 Sep 2026) reports $30.2B obligated, about 89% of the ~$34B extramural budget. It also reports 1,924 fewer grants than at the same point in FY25 and 9,714 fewer than FY24. Dollars are roughly intact but spread over fewer awards, so fewer labs have grants to spend on consumables. This quantifies the 'tight funding' point at the unit level. The ledger has F383 (~3,000 fewer projects) but not this monthly count.
items.source_name: AAMC Tracking NIH Awards FY2026 (data through 31 Aug)
items.quote: 1,924 fewer grants than at the same point in FY 2025
items.why_new: Gives the AAMC Aug-2026 award-count gap vs FY25 and FY24 as a dated series point; the known file only has aggregate NIH obligation and award shares.
items.verify_note: Verified in the AAMC brief with data through 31 Aug, published 9 Sep 2026: $30.2B obligated (89% of ~$34B), 1,924 fewer grants than FY25 and 9,714 fewer than FY24. This is an interim count; F383 gives the full year (~3,000 fewer).

items.label: 2A
items.claim: The FY24 award-count gap has stayed near 9,000-10,000 all year, so there has been no catch-up.
items.detail: The gap vs FY24 is 'nearly 9,000' at 30 Jun, about 10,000 at 31 Jul and 9,714 at 31 Aug. The gap is not closing even as obligations jump from $18B to $30.2B. The FY26 award base is therefore structurally about 10K awards smaller than FY24. That fits a research-customer base that is spending less on consumables than in FY24.
items.source_name: AAMC Tracking NIH Awards FY2026 (Jun/Jul/Aug briefs)
items.quote: approximately 10,000 fewer grants compared to this point in FY 2024
items.why_new: Builds the Jun/Jul/Aug monthly series of the gap to FY24 (~9.0K / ~10.0K / 9.7K), which is not in the known file.
items.verify_note: The Jul (~10,000) and Aug (9,714) gaps vs FY24 are verified. The Jun 'nearly 9,000' was not rechecked. This is a comparison to FY24, which was a high-count year.

items.label: 2A
items.claim: Competitive new-award activity is down sharply: through 31 Jul 2026, competitive R01s were down 14% and competitive research project grants (RPGs) down 8% vs FY24.
items.detail: The AAMC brief with data through 31 Jul 2026 (published 5 Aug) gives these as comparisons to the same point in FY24. R01s are the bread-and-butter investigator grants that fund reagent purchases. The 14% fall in competitive R01s is steeper than the 8% fall in all competitive RPGs, which shows the damage sits in the core academic grant type. The brief gives no FY25 comparison.
items.source_name: AAMC Tracking NIH Awards FY2026 (data through 31 Jul)
items.why_new: The known file has a secondary 'R01-equivalents -24% y/y' claim; this is the primary AAMC count vs FY24 (-14% R01, -8% RPG).
items.verify_note: Verified: through 31 Jul 2026, competitive RPGs are −8% and competitive R01s −14% vs FY24. No FY25 comparison is given. Counts are cumulative to date.

items.label: 2A
items.claim: Multiyear (up-front) funding of competitive RPGs rose from $769M (30 Jun) to $1.1B (31 Jul) to $1.6B (31 Aug), vs only $556.4M at 31 Jul FY25.
items.detail: At 31 Jul the FY26 figure was about 2x the FY25 figure at the same date ($1.1B vs $556.4M). By 31 Aug it was $1.6B. Each up-front dollar pays for several years of work at once, which crowds out new awards and cuts the number of labs with fresh money for reagents. This is the likely mechanism behind the fewer-grants-but-full-dollars pattern, and it argues for weak new-project reagent demand into 2027. It extends F384, which only noted the crowd-out qualitatively.
items.why_new: Gives the three-month MYF dollar series and the FY25 comparator, not previously quantified.
items.verify_note: $1.1B (31 Jul) and $1.6B (31 Aug) are verified. Caveat: the Jul brief compares to '$556.4 million in FY 2025' without clearly saying it is the same date, so the ~2x comparison may be to all of FY25. The Aug brief gives no FY25 figure. The $769M at 30 Jun was not rechecked.

items.label: 2A
items.claim: NIH obligations are catching up in dollars: $18B at 30 Jun to $30.2B at 31 Aug, 89% of the ~$34B extramural budget.
items.detail: Cumulative obligations went from $18B (53% of $34B) to $23.3B (69%) to $30.2B (89%). The implied monthly obligations are about $5.3B in July and $6.9B in August, though the brief itself states $6.6B for August (the two don't reconcile). Only $3.7B remains for September. At 30 Jun the total was above FY25 but $2.6B below FY24. So the dollar flow is large and should reach labs by year-end. That undercuts a funding-cliff argument for Q4'26, though not for award counts.
items.why_new: Builds the cumulative-dollar monthly series (18.0 / 23.3 / 30.2) with percent of budget; the known file only has the Mar-2026 $5.8B/34%-below-FY24 point.
items.verify_note: Verified: $23.3B (69%) at 31 Jul and $30.2B (89%) at 31 Aug, with $3.7B left. The Aug brief states $6.6B obligated in August. The Jul brief gives no July dollar figure, so the implied $5.3B is our derivation. The $6.6B vs $6.9B gap is likely revision or rounding.

items.label: 2A
items.claim: The NIH catch-up ($5.3B in July, $6.6B in August) means a big wave of award money reached institutions in Q3'26, which could support a Q4'26 research consumables rebound.
items.detail: Thermo says funding takes 2-3 quarters to reach spend (known). Heavy obligations from July to August 2026 would therefore flow into lab spending from roughly Q4'26 to Q1'27. This runs against Illumina's FY26 guide of a mid- to high-single-digit research decline with no recovery assumed. It is a watch-out for Q4'26 R&A and for the 2027 base (research consumables flat to up), rather than a refutation of price pressure.
items.why_new: Links the dated obligation surge to the lag-to-spend mechanism and the Q4'26 R&A guide; the known file does not contain Jul/Aug obligations.

items.label: 2A
items.claim: The comparison to FY25 is weak: through 30 Jun 2026 obligations only 'surpass' FY25, and by 31 Aug the grant count was still 1,924 below FY25.
items.detail: FY25 was the year Illumina's R&A fell about 7% on a US academic cut it had assumed at -15%. FY26 is still below FY25 in grant count, so FY26 NIH-funded activity is no better than that low base. A mid- to high-single-digit R&A decline in 2026 is consistent with this. A 2027 recovery needs award counts to rebound, and nothing in the AAMC series shows that yet.
items.source_name: AAMC Tracking NIH Awards FY2026 (30 Jun brief)
items.why_new: Tests the R&A guide directly against the primary award series rather than secondary commentary.

items.label: 2B
items.claim: A US academic core sells a 30x human genome on Ultima UG100 at $221 external, with 60x at $274 and 90x at $379.
items.detail: The University of Minnesota Genomics Center page lists a 30x minimum-coverage human genome at $221 for external users and $192 for UMN users, on the Ultima UG 100 platform. The page also lists NovaSeq X+ as a service but gives no price for it. The page is undated, so this is a current-state snapshot with no year-over-year comparison. It shows a research core marketing an Ultima genome as its headline price, which suggests rival platforms are setting reference price points in research.
items.why_new: The known list has UMN Ultima evaluations at ~$12/50M reads, not the $221/$192 headline 30x genome price or the 60x and 90x tiers.

items.label: 2B
items.claim: Canadian federal research agencies are buying Element AVITI-class equipment: two NRC purchases and one CFIA purchase from Jul 2025 to Jun 2026.
items.detail: Canada's proactive contract disclosure lists Element Biosciences contracts with NRC ($337,265.31 on 30 Jul 2025 and $141,250 on 1 Jun 2026) and CFIA ($300,000 on 18 Feb 2026). These are all equipment categories, which is consistent with sequencer or accessory purchases. They show government labs adopting a rival short-read platform alongside continued Illumina reagent buying. A second NRC purchase in 11 months suggests repeat adoption, and the descriptions do not confirm the product.
items.source_name: Government of Canada Proactive Disclosure of Contracts over $10K
items.why_new: Named government customers buying Element equipment are not in the known corpus, which lists only core facilities and tenders.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: Federal Illumina reagent orders in Canada are frequent and continuing in 2026, including a large order.
items.detail: The 1,692 Illumina Canada ULC rows run through Jun 2026, and PHAC placed about 8 orders between 11 May and 29 Jun 2026. Sizes were $12K-$22K, plus one $150,879.56 order on 13 May 2026. NRC ($27,963 on 9 Jun) and AAFC ($13,495 on 12 May) also bought. This is a small sample of a mostly small-dollar stream, but it shows no abrupt stop in demand from these buyers. Yearly totals and the price trend are not yet computed.
items.source_name: Government of Canada Proactive Disclosure of Contracts over $10K
items.why_new: Dated, buyer-level federal contract values for Illumina were not in the known sources.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: Europe PMC full-text mentions of 'NovaSeq 6000' were still rising in 2025 and early 2026, and still far outnumbered 'NovaSeq X' mentions.
items.detail: Papers mentioning 'NovaSeq 6000' were 8,565 in 2023, 11,122 in 2024 and 15,228 in 2025, with 13,011 already in 2026 YTD. 'NovaSeq X' mentions were 20, 382, 2,235 and 3,436 in the same periods. The X share of 6000+X mentions was 12.8% in 2025 and 20.9% in 2026 YTD. These are any-section full-text mentions, not methods-only, and papers lag the sequencing run by 6 to 18 months.
items.why_new: Publication-count proxy for platform share has not been used before, and it shows the 6000 is still the main platform in the research literature.

items.label: 2B
items.claim: Competitor platforms are still very small in research papers: AVITI and Ultima mentions were below 2.5% of NovaSeq 6000 mentions.
items.detail: AVITI mentions were 53 (2024), 219 (2025) and 292 (2026 YTD), versus 6000 mentions of 11,122, 15,228 and 13,011. Ultima/UG100 mentions were flat at 64 (2024) and 70 (2025). DNBSEQ is the larger rival, at 1,398 (2024) and 2,352 (2025), up 68%. The lag means this understates the current share of competitors.
items.why_new: This is the first quantified publication-share view of rival platforms, and DNBSEQ's size relative to AVITI and Ultima is not in the known list.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: Medicare fee-for-service Signatera billing is a small share of Natera and of total genetic testing, so Medicare cannot carry MRD volume alone.
items.detail: CMS Part B provider-and-service file (apparently data year 2024) shows Natera billing 25,746 services of code 0340U (Signatera) to 11,922 beneficiaries, about 2.16 draws per beneficiary, at an average Medicare payment of $3,519 (~$90.6M allowed). Natera's Q2'26 MRD volume was 283K tests in a single quarter, so the FFS Medicare slice is a modest share of one year's volume. OIG counts about 18M Part B genetic tests in 2024, so Signatera is about 0.14% of that count.
items.date: 2024 data year (inferred from file name), file released May 2026
items.source_name: CMS Medicare Physician & Other Practitioners by Provider and Service
items.why_new: First hard Medicare claims count for Signatera (0340U); not in the known list, which has only Natera-reported test counts.
items.verify_note: The record is verified: Natera NPI 1558672279, 0340U, 11,922 beneficiaries, 25,746 services, average allowed $3,518.68. The record has no year field, so the 2024 data year is an inference. The period comparison is mismatched (one year of Medicare data against one quarter of Natera volume). Compared with Natera's ~499K clinical MRD units in 2024 it is ~5%. The file is fee-for-service only and excludes Medicare Advantage, and Natera may bill some Signatera under other codes, so this understates Me

items.label: 1C
items.claim: Medicare FFS NIPT billing is negligible, so there is no public claims read on NIPT maturity from this file.
items.detail: Code 81420 (fetal aneuploidy cfDNA) shows only LabCorp with 39 services and Quest with 11 services in the file. Nothing came back for 81507. NIPT is mostly commercial or Medicaid, so the file is uninformative for the NIPT-maturing leg of the thesis.
items.source_name: CMS Medicare Physician & Other Practitioners by Provider and Service
items.why_new: Establishes that Medicare data cannot test NIPT; avoids wasted effort.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: GUARDIAN enrollment reached 30,000 newborns by 7 Oct 2026, well ahead of the 4,000 in the JAMA interim, so a new genome-volume source is real but pacing below the 100K target.
items.detail: GeneDx's 7 Oct 2026 ICoNS release says GUARDIAN 'has now enrolled 30,000 newborns', with 72.3% consent. Earlier datapoints: 4,000 (Sep 2022–Jul 2023, ~360/month), 15,000 (first follow-up cohort, Oct 2025), 17,000+ (lab insights, Oct 2025). The run-rate is about 1,250/month (15K to 30K in ~12 months). Reaching 100K by the Sep 2029 primary completion needs ~70K in ~35 months, or ~2,000/month, about 60% faster. At ~110 Gb per 30x genome (midpoint of the known 100–125 Gb range), 30K babies is ~3.3 Pb cumulative, and ~1.4–1.65 Pb/yr at the current pace (~0.2% of the ~800 Pb HT base cited in the known file). This is immaterial to Illumina's Gb growth.
items.quote: has now enrolled 30,000 newborns
items.why_new: The known file has only the 4,000-baby JAMA interim and Generation Study; the 30K enrollment count and run-rate are new.
items.verify_note: Confirmed in the release: 'has now enrolled 30,000 newborns' and a 72.3% consent rate. The release does not name the sequencing method, so the ~110 Gb per genome figure is an assumption. The item's own arithmetic (~1.4–1.65M Gb/yr, ~0.2% of the ~800M Gb HT base) shows the volume is immaterial. That makes it another 'public/newborn programs are too small' datapoint, which supports 1C rather than cutting against it. Direction changed to supports.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: A multi-state NIH-funded newborn genome program (BRIDGES-NBS, up to 30,000 babies, GeneDx sequencing, Illumina in-kind) begins enrolling in Oct 2026, adding a small new Gb source in 2027.
items.detail: BRIDGES-NBS is funded with $14.4M from the NIH Common Fund. Illumina and GeneDx give in-kind support. It uses a 746-gene panel covering 777 conditions and plans to enroll up to 30,000 newborns over 2–3 years. Sites are reported as seven programs (Iowa, Minnesota, New York, Oregon, Puerto Rico, South Carolina, Texas); GeneDx says eight states and territories. That is ~10–15K babies/yr, or ~1.1–1.65 Pb/yr at ~110 Gb. The sequencing is GeneDx's, and Illumina's role is in-kind, so the revenue contribution to Illumina is likely small.
items.source_name: Oregon Health Authority / GeneDx release (search-result snippets)
items.why_new: BRIDGES-NBS, its size and its in-kind Illumina support are not in the known file.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: Statewide scaling of GUARDIAN-type screening in New York would be material to Illumina volume only if mandated, which no source shows.
items.detail: My arithmetic uses ~200K NY births/yr (my recollection, unverified) × ~110 Gb = ~22 Pb/yr (22M Gb), about 2.7% of the ~800M Gb HT base cited in the known file. At ~$2.5/Gb consumables that is ~$55M, or ~2.6% of ~$2.1B clinical consumables. No NY State program has been announced beyond the research partnership, and NYSDOH is a partner of the research study only. Florida's Sunshine Genetics pilot (target 100,000 over five years, GeneDx a partner, first 1,000 tests free) is the only state-backed program found. At 20K/yr it would be ~2.2 Pb/yr.
items.why_new: The known file covers only Generation Study and NHS volumes, and has no state-backed US newborn program sizing.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: Newborn genome screening is reimbursement- and study-funded, and its yield is low, which limits how fast it can become a volume lever.
items.detail: The JAMA interim (Oct 2024) found 3.7% of newborns had early-onset genetic conditions, and only ~10 of ~120 flagged babies would have been caught by standard screening. Funding is philanthropic, NIH and in-kind (Illumina, GeneDx). GeneDx's own programs total only ~22,000 newborns as of Oct 2025. There is no payer coverage, and the Florida pilot's first 1,000 tests are free. This fits the thesis that adoption, not sequencing cost, is the constraint.
items.why_new: The known file has no GeneDx newborn-program enrollment or funding structure.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: In open-literature methods text, NovaSeq X mentions are rising fast from a small base but still trail the 6000 by roughly 3-4x in 2026, which fits a 6000 tail that is far from gone.
items.detail: Europe PMC full-text hitCounts for 'NovaSeq X' vs 'NovaSeq 6000': 2023 20 vs 8,565 (0.2%); 2024 382 vs 11,122 (3.4%); 2025 2,235 vs 15,228 (14.7%); 2026 year to date 3,436 vs 13,011 (26.4%). The X/6000 ratio roughly doubled each year, but the X would still be only about a quarter of the 6000's mention count. Papers lag instrument use by 1-2 years, so this measures the research-lab fleet that existed in 2024-25, not the current fleet. Counts were read through WebFetch summaries, not raw JSON.
items.why_new: This is a quantified time series of publication mentions by sequencer. The known file has only the Europe PMC 2025-26 qualitative note (F412).
items.verify_note: Publication mentions measure the research-lab fleet with a 1–2 year lag. Research is already 92% on the X, and the 6000 tail is ~80% clinical, which rarely publishes methods. The ratio of mentions cannot be mapped to the Gb or revenue mix. D012 already establishes that public instrument text lags the fleet. This item adds no usable signal on the clinical tail.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: The 6000's annual paper mentions have not yet turned down in the open literature through Oct 2026.
items.detail: 'NovaSeq 6000' mentions: 2022 6,081; 2023 8,565 (+41%); 2024 11,122 (+30%); 2025 15,228 (+37%); 2026 year to date 13,011 through about 12 Oct. Annualizing 2026 by 0.78 of the year gives about 16,700, roughly +10% vs 2025. Publication lag means the 2026 papers describe 2023-25 data. This confirms the research 6000 installed base ran heavily through 2025, and says nothing about the 2026 run-rate.
items.why_new: This adds the 2022-2024 series and growth rates. F102 and F412 give only direction.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: Quarterly 2026 data show the X share of mentions climbing, from 23% of the 6000 count in Q1 to 31% in Q3, so mix shift in the literature is still moving.
items.detail: By first-publication date: Q1 2026 NovaSeq X 1,089 vs 6000 4,686 (23.2%). Q3 2026 (1 Jul to 30 Sep) X 971 vs 6000 3,158 (30.7%). The Q3 totals are depressed by incomplete full-text indexing of recent papers, so the ratio is more reliable than the levels. The share trend is consistent with Illumina's X share of Gb rising, but the 6000 is still about 3x the X in what is published.
items.why_new: The quarterly split has not been run before; it was listed as 'not run' in the probe.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: Roughly one in six 2025-26 papers that cite the X also cite the 6000, which points to parallel running (dual-fleet labs).
items.detail: Papers mentioning both 'NovaSeq 6000' and 'NovaSeq X': 2025 389 of 2,235 X papers (17.4%); 2026 year to date 543 of 3,436 (15.8%). Co-mention could also mean comparisons or data reuse, so it is a ceiling for true dual running. It still shows many labs are not fully converted, consistent with the thesis that the 6000 tail persists. This is a literature proxy only, since the clinical X share of Gb is already 78%.
items.why_new: F124 found no dual listing in the GTR. This is a counter-signal from papers and is quantified.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: Illumina-related literature volume is flat to falling, which fits no acceleration in research-side usage.
items.detail: Papers mentioning 'Illumina': 2024 50,514; 2025 60,909 (+20.6%); 2026 year to date 47,492 (annualized about 60,900 at 0.78, so about flat vs 2025). Sequencer-specific growth of 6000 plus X mentions (2025 17,463 vs 2024 11,504, +52%; 2026 annualized about 21,000, +20%) outpaces the Illumina denominator, so the slowdown in 2026 is partly a lag artifact. It is weakly consistent with research Gb growth decelerating, not conclusive.
items.why_new: A denominator series for the literature was not in the file.

items.label: 2B
items.claim: AVITI mentions are growing about a third faster than NovaSeq 6000 mentions in 2026, so a low-cost rival is gaining share of published methods, though from a small base.
items.detail: AVITI went from 219 (2025) to 292 year to date 2026, about 375 annualized (+71%). The 6000 went from 15,228 to about 16,700 annualized (+10%). The X went from 2,235 to about 4,400 annualized (+97%). AVITI is growing faster than the 6000 but slower than the X. Share of 'NovaSeq 6000' count: 1.4% in 2025 vs 2.2% in 2026.
items.why_new: This gives growth rates for AVITI vs 6000 vs X, not just a static share.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: At KUMC the internal NovaSeq X 10B-300 flow cell costs essentially the same per Gb as the 25B-300 (~1.03x), the narrowest 10B premium yet seen, extending the within-X price compression on smaller flow cells.
items.detail: KUMC internal full-flow-cell prices (undated, 2026 page) are 10B-300 $9,255 for ~3,000 Gb (8 lanes × ~375 Gb), or ~$3.09/Gb, and 25B-300 $23,872 for ~8,000 Gb, or ~$2.98/Gb, a ratio of ~1.03x. The 1.5B-300 is $5,225 for ~450 Gb (~$11.6/Gb). Measured against GSA prices, KUMC charges ~64% for the 10B, ~99% for the 25B and ~133% for the 1.5B. The other cores span 1.13–1.50x (D018), and TGen and UCLA showed the 10B being cut while the 25B was held.
items.source_name: KU Medical Center Genome Sequencing Facility
items.why_new: Adds a new core with a 10B/25B ratio below the known 1.13–1.50x range.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: UC Berkeley's pass-through rates (Jun 2026) put the 10B 150PE lane at ~1.38x the 25B per Gb, and the 25B at ~$2.3/Gb on the realized output the core states, near the low end of US core 25B pricing.
items.detail: QB3 UC rates effective 1 Jun 2026 are 10B 150PE $1,535 for 375 Gb ($4.09/Gb) and 25B 150PE $2,600 for 875 Gb ($2.97/Gb), a ratio of 1.38x and inside the D018 range. The page says output runs 25–30% above the stated specs, which gives ~$2.29–2.38/Gb for the 25B, close to Harvard's $2.06–2.43. These lanes are run at UCSF CAT, so they reflect UCSF's pricing passed through.
items.quote: data returns are generally 25-30% higher
items.why_new: A new 2026 core datapoint, with realized-output $/Gb stated by the core itself.

items.label: 2A
items.claim: NIH's growth in multiyear (up-front) funding is roughly large enough to explain the FY26 shortfall in grant counts versus FY25.
items.detail: Through 31 Aug 2026, NIH put $1.6B of competitive RPG money into multiyear awards. If those awards pre-fund ~4–5 years, roughly $1.2–1.3B of it pays for future years rather than FY26 work. At ~$586K average obligation per project (F383), that money would fund ~2,000–2,200 one-year-funded awards, close to the 1,924-grant shortfall vs FY25 at the same date. Total dollars are near full (89% of ~$34B), so the funding squeeze shows up as fewer labs with new money, not fewer dollars. The assumptions (award length, using a per-project average that includes multiyear awards) are ours.
items.source_name: AAMC Tracking NIH Awards FY2026; STAT via F383
items.quote: 1,924 fewer grants than at the same point in FY 2025
items.why_new: Links the multiyear-funding dollars to the grant-count gap; earlier items stated these separately.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: Medicare fee-for-service Signatera billing averages ~2.2 draws per patient per year, below the 3–4 draws a year that experts assume for MRD Gb modelling.
items.detail: The CMS provider-and-service file (Natera NPI, code 0340U; data year not stated, likely 2024) shows 25,746 services for 11,922 beneficiaries, or 2.16 per beneficiary per year, at ~$3,519 average allowed (~$90.6M). Patients starting mid-year depress the ratio, but it still sits below the expert 3–4x/yr cadence in the known list and near the Medicare CRC 'same frequency as CEA' rule (~2–4/yr). With ~0.16–0.24 Gb per classic Signatera draw, a fee-for-service patient-year uses only ~0.35–0.5 Gb.
items.source_name: CMS Medicare Physician & Other Practitioners by Provider and Service
items.why_new: First observed claims-based MRD draw cadence; the known cadence figures are trial protocols or expert estimates.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: Natera's combined Medicare FFS billing across 0340U and 81479 grew roughly 47% in dollars in 2024, so the MRD volume engine is intact.
items.detail: Services across the two codes were 36,295 in the prior-year file (13,783 + 22,512) and 56,069 in 2024 (25,746 + 30,323), +54.5%. Medicare payment dollars are services times average payment. In 2024 that is 25,746 × $3,518.68 = $90.6M for 0340U plus 30,323 × $3,460.65 = $104.9M for 81479, or $195.5M. In the prior-year file it is 13,783 × $3,837.98 = $52.9M plus 22,512 × $3,562.91 = $80.2M, or $133.1M. That is +46.9%. The dollars are Medicare FFS only; Medicare Advantage is excluded.
items.source_name: CMS Medicare Physician & Other Practitioners by Provider and Service
items.why_new: Derives Natera's Medicare FFS dollar run-rate and growth from claims, which the file does not have.
items.verify_note: Verified against both CMS files. 2023: 0340U 13,783 services at $3,837.98 and 81479 22,512 at $3,562.91. 2024: 25,746 at $3,518.68 and 30,323 at $3,460.65. Totals are $133.1M → $195.5M (+46.9%). Caveats: this is CY2024 data, so it is stale against the known 2026 Natera MRD growth of +52–56%, which it mostly restates. 81479 is an unlisted code and may include non-MRD Natera tests such as transplant or tissue. Growth in test counts and dollars is not growth in Gb.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: MRD draw cadence per Medicare patient barely rose, so MRD volume growth is coming from more patients, not more draws per patient.
items.detail: For 0340U, services per beneficiary were 13,783/7,028 = 1.96 in the prior-year file and 25,746/11,922 = 2.16 in 2024, a 10% rise. Beneficiaries rose 69.6%. For 81479 it was 22,512/15,483 = 1.45, then 30,323/20,898 = 1.45, flat. A cadence of about 2 draws per patient-year is well below the 4-9 draws per year in the known trial protocols, so the high-Gb-per-patient scenario is not showing in claims. Counts cover the year's billed claims, and patients enrolled mid-year would bias the ratio down.
items.source_name: CMS Medicare Physician & Other Practitioners by Provider and Service
items.why_new: Known notes cite protocol cadences (every 6 weeks or 3 months), not observed real-world claims cadence.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: Medicare's average payment per Signatera (0340U) test fell 8.3% in 2024, so price pressure is already reaching MRD at Illumina's largest customer.
items.detail: The average Medicare payment per 0340U service fell from $3,837.98 in the prior-year file to $3,518.68 in 2024 (−8.3%). The 81479 payment fell from $3,562.91 to $3,460.65 (−2.9%). Average submitted charge in 2024 was $4,944. A shrinking per-test price supports Natera pushing for lower reagent costs under its supply-agreement re-openers. The known file already has the Jan 2026 rate cut ($3,920 to $3,590), so this adds the 2024 step. It could reflect a changed code or test mix.
items.source_name: CMS Medicare Physician & Other Practitioners by Provider and Service
items.why_new: Adds an earlier observed per-test payment decline; only the Jan 2026 cut is known.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: Guardant360 liquid CGP volume in Medicare FFS was essentially flat in 2024, consistent with a saturated therapy-selection market.
items.detail: Guardant's 0242U plus 0326U services were 21,416 + 16,798 = 38,214 in the prior-year file and 20,206 + 19,695 = 39,901 in 2024, +4.4%. Beneficiaries were 36,091 and 37,300 (+3.3%). 0242U fell 5.7% while 0326U rose 17.2%, so part of the change is code migration. Adding 0334U (1,941 to 2,759, +42%) gives 40,155 to 42,660 (+6.2%). Against Guardant's +63% oncology growth in Q2'26 in the known file, which is mostly Reveal and Shield, the legacy genotyping line is mature. This is Medicare FFS only.
items.source_name: CMS Medicare Physician & Other Practitioners by Provider and Service
items.why_new: Known notes call CGP 'quite saturated' from experts only; this gives claims-based growth of +4% to +6%.
items.verify_note: Verified. 0242U 21,416→20,206 and 0326U 16,798→19,695 (+4.4%); with 0334U, 40,155→42,660. Also new: the 0326U average Medicare payment rose from $3,533 to $4,892 (+38%), so Guardant's Medicare dollars grew ~20% on ~5% more services (see derived item). The data is Medicare FFS only and CY2024.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: Foundation Medicine's Medicare FFS CGP billing fell 7.8% in 2024, which adds a data point that comprehensive genomic profiling is not accelerating.
items.detail: FoundationOne CDx tissue (0037U) services were 15,551 in the prior-year file and 13,787 in 2024 (−11.3%); beneficiaries went 15,460 to 13,693 (−11.4%). FoundationOne Liquid CDx (0239U) was flat at 7,188 and 7,181. Combined: 22,739 to 20,968 (−7.8%). Average payment was unchanged at about $3,420. Part of the fall may be a shift to Medicare Advantage, so this is not proof of falling total Foundation volume.
items.source_name: CMS Medicare Physician & Other Practitioners by Provider and Service
items.why_new: Quantifies CGP stagnation at a Roche-owned lab using claims; no Foundation Medicare volumes are in the known file.

items.label: 2A
items.claim: Greater China revenue fell about 11% y/y in Q2'26 and about 20% in H1'26, and the sequencer import ban is no longer the cause.
items.detail: Q2'26 Greater China revenue was $56M against $63M in Q2'25. H1'26 was $108M against $135M. China is about 4.8% of revenue. The import ban was lifted in Nov 2025 but revenue is still falling, which points to domestic substitution and not just the ban. The 10-Q figures were seen in a search snippet, not on the page. The effect on the global research-pricing thesis is indirect.
items.why_new: The known list has only the Q2'26 Greater China organic change of -19%. The dollar levels and H1 comparison are not in it.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: MGI won 47% of Chinese government contracts for newly installed sequencers in 2023-24, against Illumina's 16%.
items.detail: This comes from local media citing a data platform (reported in a search summary). It shows that domestic-preference procurement already moves share away from Illumina. Illumina's share of China new installs was about 26.5% in 2024. The primary dataset was not opened, so treat it as an unverified secondary claim.
items.why_new: The known list has no China procurement share data.

items.label: 2B
items.claim: MGI instrument revenue fell 6% and installs fell in H1'26, so the domestic-substitution threat to Illumina's research volume is slowing.
items.detail: MGI installed 410 sequencers in H1'26 against about 600 domestic units in H1'25 (the two counts are not like-for-like). Instrument revenue fell 6% while reagents rose 16%. Overseas revenue was +34%. MGI's momentum is in reagents and overseas, not new China boxes, so this is a watch-out for anyone arguing for large share loss to MGI.
items.why_new: The known list has MGI overseas +33.8% and 1,470 units in 2025. The install decline and instrument -6% are not in it.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: Aston University awarded an NGS sequencer contract to Illumina for £282,662 on 12 Jan 2026, with a term to March 2031.
items.detail: The contract is a single-supplier award to Illumina Cambridge Ltd for a teaching sequencer in the medical and biological sciences. The model is not named. It shows a UK university choosing Illumina on a multi-year contract with no visible discounting pressure. The scale is tiny.
items.why_new: The known tenders are CIBER and IDIBAPS (2025). No UK university instrument awards are listed.

items.label: 2B
items.claim: Charles University (Prague, First Faculty of Medicine) bought NovaSeq X Plus-compatible kits through a TED-published award of about CZK 12M excluding VAT (published 4 May 2026).
items.detail: The notice covers successive deliveries of kits for a NovaSeq X Plus to be installed by the buyer. CZK 12M is roughly $0.5M. The CZK 12M is an estimated value, and the winner and unit prices were not retrieved, so it is not a confirmed award price. It is a European academic buyer committing to the X Plus (against the thesis), but it is too small to matter and the snippet is unclear on dates.
items.why_new: The known tenders are CIBER and IDIBAPS. This Czech kit framework is not listed.

items.label: 2B
items.claim: University of Osaka's Sept 2026 tender bundles about 78 line items (about 2,873 sets) including Illumina NovaSeq X kits and MGI DNBSEQ sets in the same procurement.
items.detail: Published 24 Sep 2026, bids due 16 Nov 2026, delivery Dec 2026 to May 2027. Line items span NovaSeq X 1.5B, 5B, 10B and 25B kits and MGI G400, G99 and T1+. No estimated value or prices are given. Putting MGI in the same tender means competitive bidding at a Japanese national university. The award and prices will show up after Nov 2026.
items.why_new: The known list has no Japanese tenders and no MGI-versus-Illumina same-tender case.
items.verify_note: A Japanese university reagent tender lists brand-specific line items. NovaSeq X kits and MGI kits are separate items for different installed instruments, and distributors bid on each one. That is not head-to-head platform price competition. There are no prices or values yet. Re-check after the award (bids due 16 Nov 2026).

items.label: 2A
items.claim: UK university equipment capital is being narrowed to maintenance of existing facilities, which limits new sequencer purchases.
items.detail: From FY2026-27 RCIF goes only to sustaining current facilities, and the tapering path is reportedly 174 then 119, 121 and 124 (units unverified). Wonkhe puts the cut at £50m by 2029-30, and 35.6% of surveyed English universities are cutting support for facilities and equipment. Meanwhile UKRI's headline budget is up 4.6% to £9.2bn, so it is a mixed picture. It indirectly favours buyers squeezing vendor prices.
items.why_new: The known funding evidence is all US (NIH, NSF). No UK or EU funding data are listed.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: Natera's Medicare MRD cadence per patient rose and beneficiary counts grew ~70%, so MRD volume is deepening, not only broadening.
items.detail: 0340U services per beneficiary rose from 1.96 (13,783/7,028) in CY2023 to 2.16 (25,746/11,922) in CY2024, +10%. Beneficiaries rose +69.6% and services +86.8%. Combined 0340U+81479 beneficiaries were 22,511 (7,028 + 15,483) in 2023 and 32,820 (11,922 + 20,898) in 2024, +45.8%. This partly contradicts a known item saying the cadence barely rose. A code-migration caveat applies, since the 2023 draws sat more in 81479.
items.source_name: CMS Part B by Provider and Service
items.why_new: Gives a 0340U-only cadence of 1.96 to 2.16; the known list uses a blended ~2.2 and says it barely rose.
items.verify_note: Verified: 0340U was 7,028 beneficiaries / 13,783 services (1.96 per beneficiary) in 2023 and 11,922 / 25,746 (2.16) in 2024. The 2.16 figure and the 2024 counts are already known (F414/D037), so only the 2023 comparison is new. The combined 0340U+81479 beneficiary sum can double-count patients. The cadence change is modest (+10%) and Gb per draw is tiny (<1 Gb), so it barely counters 1C.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: Adaptive's MRD/immune-sequencing Medicare billing grew 57% in 2024, evidence that MRD sequencing is scaling.
items.detail: Adaptive Biotechnologies' only visible code in both files is 81479, with 3,258 services in CY2023 at $6,733 and 5,123 in CY2024 at $7,099. That is +57.2% in services and +5.4% in payment, giving ~$36.4M in 2024 vs ~$21.9M in 2023 (+66%). I could not confirm that 81479 is clonoSEQ, and 0364U returned no rows. The payment level is unusual for clonoSEQ, so treat the attribution as unverified.
items.source_name: CMS Part B by Provider and Service
items.why_new: Known list has Adaptive only from earnings, not Medicare claims.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: Combined Medicare FFS volume for the large therapy-selection and MRD labs grew only a modest ~25% in 2024, led by Natera, with the rest roughly flat.
items.detail: Summing Natera (0340U, 81479), Guardant (0242U, 0326U, 0334U, 81479), Foundation (0037U, 0239U, 81479) and Adaptive (81479): CY2023 total 36,295 + 41,185 + 23,219 + 3,258 = 103,957. CY2024: 56,069 + 43,735 + 21,601 + 5,123 = 126,528. Growth is +21.7%. Excluding Natera, the rest went from 67,662 to 70,459 (+4.1%). Natera's MRD adds ~20K services; others net near zero.
items.source_name: CMS Part B by Provider and Service
items.why_new: First cross-lab Medicare service-count aggregation. The known list covers dollars for individual labs only.
items.verify_note: Guardant (41,185→43,735, excluding 0422U) and Natera (36,295→56,069) were verified. Foundation and Adaptive were not re-checked. This is the CY2024 Medicare FFS mix. Natera's 81479 may include non-MRD tests. The useful point is that therapy-selection volume outside MRD was roughly flat (+4%).

items.label: 2A
items.claim: A further £50m RCIF cut is scheduled by 2029-30, about 29% of the £174m base, with reform starting in 2027-28.
items.detail: Wonkhe (10 Mar 2026) reports a £50m cut by 2029-30 and a further reduction from 2027-28. It also quotes UKRI's December explainer: 'After tapering in financial year 2026 to 2027, investment in RCIF will be reformed'. My arithmetic: 174 - 50 = £124m, which is -28.7%. This assumes the £50m is measured against £174m. The Wonkhe piece is secondary, and the Research England letter gives no taper schedule.
items.quote: its use focused on sustaining current facilities
items.why_new: The known file has no UK RCIF taper figure. It only says UK equipment capital is narrowed (F437).
items.verify_note: UKRI's explainer confirms RCIF tapers in 2026-27 and is reformed from 2027-28 to 'sustaining current facilities', but it gives no £ figures. The £50m/£174m arithmetic rests only on Wonkhe. RCIF is capital funding, so it bears on instrument purchases rather than consumables pricing. Relabeled from 2B to 2A (tight funding).

items.label: 2A
items.claim: UKRI curiosity-driven research is flat to down in cash through 2029-30, which means a real-terms cut for UK academic research customers.
items.detail: The UKRI budget explainer shows curiosity-driven research at £3,653m (2026-27), £3,581m, £3,612m and £3,638m (2029-30). 2027-28 is -2.0% nominal and 2029-30 is -0.4% vs 2026-27. Quality-related (QR) funding goes £2,258m to £2,161m (-4.3%) in 2027-28. Applicant-led grants go £815m to £821m (+0.7%). Inflation at roughly 2-3% a year (my assumption) would make these real declines. The UKRI total still rises, from £9,220m to £9,986m, but the growth goes to strategic and industry buckets.
items.source_name: UKRI budget allocations explainer, Tables 1 and 3
items.why_new: The known file covers NIH and US funding only. This is a UK funding time series by line.
items.verify_note: Verified: curiosity-driven £3,653m/3,581/3,612/3,638m; QR £2,258m→£2,161m; applicant-led £815m→£821m→£866m; UKRI total £9,220m→£9,986m. Applicant-led does rise to +6% by 2029-30, which softens the 'flat' framing. The real-terms decline rests on the item's own inflation assumption.

items.label: 2A
items.claim: MRC and BBSRC applicant-led budgets are about £113m and £112m a year and flat through 2029-30, well below earlier baselines.
items.detail: The UKRI explainer's Table 4 shows MRC at 113/113/111/115 and BBSRC at 112/113/111/117 (£m, 2026-27 to 2029-30). THE (via search) quotes MRC discovery research at 'close to £200m' per year in the 2022-25 plan, and BBSRC investigator-driven projects at 'over £150m'. My arithmetic is -43% (113 vs 200) for MRC and -25% (112 vs 150) for BBSRC, but the baselines are approximate and the lines may not be like-for-like. These are the two councils that fund most UK genomics-heavy biology and biomedicine, and the plan has them paused for grant applications. This is a UK-wide signal of tight funding, not sequencing-specific.
items.source_name: Times Higher Education / UKRI budget explainer
items.why_new: The known file has no UK council-level budget numbers.

items.label: 2A
items.claim: 35.6% of surveyed English universities are reducing support for research facilities and equipment.
items.detail: A Dec 2025 survey by the Innovation and Research Caucus covered finance leaders at 74 English universities. It found 35.6% cutting support for research facilities and equipment and 36.8% scaling back internal research consortia. The Academy of Social Sciences summary (Feb 2026) cites it alongside a £6.2bn loss on UK research grants in 2023-24. I did not see the IRC report itself, so the sample details are unverified. It is directionally consistent with F076 and F437.
items.source_name: Academy of Social Sciences policy update (citing IRC survey)
items.why_new: The known file has no university-finance survey on equipment support.

items.label: 2A
items.claim: UKRI infrastructure spending and the total budget rise through 2029-30, so UK research capital is not collapsing.
items.detail: The UKRI 'infrastructure' line is £486m, £502m, £485m, then £596m in 2029-30 (+22.6% vs 2026-27). The total budget rises from £9,220m to £9,986m (+8.3%). The RCIF core stays at £174m in 2026-27. The Delivery Plan page names UK Biobank proteomics on all 500,000 participants and Our Future Health at 3.75m participants as funded items. Neither carries a budget figure here, and neither is a clear Illumina volume.
items.why_new: It is a watch-out: the UK public budget is growing overall and the cuts are concentrated in curiosity-driven and capital lines.

items.label: 2B
items.claim: MGI's recurring reagent revenue grew 16.3% to RMB 645M while instrument revenue fell, so its installed base is generating more consumable pull-through.
items.detail: Sequencing reagents and consumables were RMB 645M (+16.28%, 60.77% of sequencing revenue). Instruments were RMB 289M (-6.37%) and other sequencing revenue was RMB 127M. These sum to RMB 1,061M against the RMB 1,062M reported. Backing out growth gives H1'25 reagents of about RMB 554.5M and instruments of about RMB 308.7M. Reagent revenue was 2.2x instrument revenue. A rival's consumable stream growing from a larger installed base supports a low-cost alternative for research buyers.
items.why_new: Known file has +16% reagent growth but not the RMB levels, the 61% mix, the instrument RMB figure or the derived H1'25 base.
items.verify_note: Reagents of RMB 645M (+16.28%, 60.77% of sequencing) and total sequencing of RMB 1,062M (+17.64%) were confirmed. The CSJ summary did not confirm the instrument decline of −6.37%. Domestic revenue (RMB 857M) is ~64% of MGI's main business, so this is mostly a China signal and only weakly bears on Illumina's ex-China research pricing.

items.label: 2A
items.claim: Illumina's contract revenue from Canadian federal departments (PHAC, NRC, AAFC, CFIA, DFO, Health Canada, ECCC) fell about 56% in calendar 2025, and order count fell about 31%.
items.detail: I summed the CKAN rows by hand. Calendar-year Illumina totals were about C$12.5M (2022, 175 rows), about C$12.8M (2023, 183 rows), about C$11.06M (2024, 165 rows by the search-UI facet; I counted about 170), and about C$4.88M (2025, 113-114 rows). The 2025 figure is 4.88/11.06 = 0.44, so −56%. If I drop the 2024 CFIA March NextSeq-package rows (C$2.61M, which include an original/amended duplicate pair), 2024 is about C$8.45M and 2025 is −42%. Average order size fell from about C$65K (2024) to about C$43K (2025). The 2022-23 totals come from the tool's own summing and are less reliable than the 2024-26 figures I summed myself. This is Canadian federal spending only, so it also reflects Canada's budget review. It is not a global read.
items.source_name: Government of Canada Proactive Disclosure of Contracts >$10K (CKAN datastore)
items.why_new: The known file has only individual Canadian orders (F051, F053, F411). It has no multi-year spend series, order counts or YoY decline.
items.verify_note: These are Canadian federal government buyers, so the item fits 2A (public research funding) better than 1C (global clinical volume). The tallies were summed by hand and include a known duplicate row. The decline probably also reflects the wind-down of COVID-era genomic surveillance (CanCOGeN, wastewater) and possible procurement through distributors or standing offers. Not verified here.

items.label: 2A
items.claim: At the Public Health Agency of Canada, Illumina's largest Canadian federal account, annual contract value fell from about C$9.6M (2022) to about C$3.4M (2025).
items.detail: PHAC totals were C$9.63M (2022, 87 rows in the tool's summary of that batch), C$7.26M (2024; total C$11.06M less C$3.80M non-PHAC) and C$3.35M (2025; total C$4.88M less C$1.53M non-PHAC). That is −54% from 2024 to 2025 and −65% from 2022 to 2025. H1 2026 PHAC was C$1.87M gross, or about C$1.24M if I drop a C$630K row that duplicates the C$645K amended row (same procurement ID 6D06353301). H1 2025 was about C$2.62M, so H1'26 is −29% gross or about −53% net. PHAC holds 813 of the 1,692 rows in the search UI. This is a government research and public-health buyer cutting Illumina spend, which fits tight-funding behavior.
items.why_new: The known file does not quantify any government research buyer's Illumina spend over time.
items.verify_note: This is a subset of F447 and has the same caveats. PHAC's 2022 spend was swollen by COVID genomic surveillance, so the −65% from 2022 overstates any funding-driven cut. 2024→2025 (−54%) is the cleaner comparison. Treat F447 and F448 as one piece of evidence.

items.label: 2A
items.claim: The National Research Council (NRC) cut Illumina purchases by about 90% between 2022 and 2025 and bought an Element AVITI in the same period.
items.detail: NRC Illumina contract value was about C$591K (2022, 22 rows), about C$251K (2023, Jan to mid-Sep, 10 rows), about C$120K (2024, 7 rows), and about C$57K (2025, 3 rows: C$26.8K, C$17.4K, C$12.4K). The 2025 figure is 57/591, so −90% vs 2022. H1'26 is C$74K across 3 rows (C$28.0K, C$20.8K, C$25.6K). NRC also awarded Element Biosciences C$337,265 in Jul 2025 and C$141,250 in Jun 2026 (the latter the upgrade already in F046). The Element contract is one item, but the NRC trend shows a research lab spending far less on Illumina.
items.source_name: Government of Canada Proactive Disclosure of Contracts
items.why_new: F046 shows NRC's Element upgrade only. The 5-year NRC Illumina spend decline is new.
items.verify_note: The row-level arithmetic is plausible: C$57K/C$591K = −90%. The headline overstates the case, though. F487 shows NRC moved most of this work to SickKids/TCAG and Génome Québec, which run Illumina instruments, so this is mostly a channel shift and not lost Illumina volume. The Element awards are real: C$337K in Jul 2025, and the C$141K award in Jun 2026 was already in F046. Read this as weak support that one research lab is diversifying vendors. It is not evidence of a 90% demand collapse.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: MGI's new sequencer placements fell and its instrument revenue per placed unit is low, so near-term price pressure on Illumina's high-throughput tier is limited.
items.detail: MGI placed about 410 sequencers in H1'26, fewer than in H1'25, when there were about 600 domestic placements. Instrument revenue of RMB 289M over 410 units is about RMB 705K per unit, or about US$105K at the GenomeWeb rate of 6.72. This is far below the ~$800K T7+ list price in the known file. The units figure may be defined differently from the instrument revenue line, because the revenue includes other items and benchtop units. Derived ASP is therefore only an upper-level sanity check. The data show no surge in high-throughput rival units.
items.why_new: Adds a derived revenue per unit; known file only lists the unit count.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: Illumina's October-December billings to Canadian federal buyers dropped two years running: about C$3.26M (Q4'23), C$1.94M (Q4'24) and C$1.20M (Q4'25).
items.detail: I summed the rows by month. Q4'23 = Oct 1.313M + Nov 0.927M + Dec 1.022M = C$3.26M. Q4'24 = 0.903M + 0.308M + 0.726M = C$1.94M. Q4'25 = C$1.198M (rows dated 3 Oct to 29 Dec 2025). The declines are −41% and −38% y/y. Calendar Q4 is also the quarter in which Illumina's H2 consumables push usually lands. The Apr-Mar fiscal year shows the same pattern: FY24/25 about C$8.56M against FY25/26 about C$4.58M gross (about C$3.95M net of the duplicate row), roughly −47%. Reporting lag is small for these quarters, so this is not a data-gap artifact.
items.source_name: Government of Canada Proactive Disclosure of Contracts
items.why_new: This gives quarterly and fiscal-year dollar series for a government account. Nothing like it is in the file.
items.verify_note: This mostly restates F447/F448 (calendar-2025 −56%, PHAC −54%) sliced by quarter. It is also mislabeled. Canadian federal buyers are government/public-health and research customers, so the item bears on 2A funding, not 1C clinical volume. At ~C$1–3M a quarter it is immaterial to Illumina's ~US$4.6B revenue. F454 also suggests the decline is budget-driven across vendors, and F487 shows some spend moving to cores. The 'duplicate row' netting adds noise. The quarterly cut adds nothing decision-usef

items.label: 1C
items.claim: The Canadian federal decline stopped in H1 2026: gross Illumina contract value was about C$3.19M, versus about C$3.29M in H1 2025 (−3%).
items.detail: H1'26 (46 rows to 29 Jun) is C$3.19M gross. H1'25 (79 rows) is C$2.37M for Jan to 25 Feb, plus C$0.92M for 4 Mar to 26 Jun, so C$3.29M. Gross dollars are flat even though order count fell 42% (79 to 46). Average order size therefore rose to about C$69K from about C$42K. About C$0.81M of H1'26 is two C$404,867 orders and one C$644,850 order, so large single instrument or contract buys drive it. Net of the likely C$630K duplicate, H1'26 is C$2.56M (−22%). Reporting lag could still add June 2026 rows. Read this as stabilization, not a rebound.
items.source_name: Government of Canada Proactive Disclosure of Contracts
items.why_new: This is a counter-trend datapoint for the same series, not in the known file.

items.label: 2B
items.claim: MGI says overseas rivals leaving China creates a replacement opportunity, so its growth is mostly domestic and policy-driven rather than a price attack on Illumina's research base.
items.detail: Domestic revenue was RMB 857M (+12.03%), about RMB 765M in H1'25, so +RMB 92M. Overseas was RMB 483M (+33.77%), about RMB 361M in H1'25, so +RMB 122M. High-throughput share of domestic public tenders was above 70% and share in the domestic medical sector was above 70%. MGI is entrenched in China, where Illumina's Greater China revenue is already shrinking and where it is not a US research competitor.
items.why_new: Known file has regional revenue but not the >70% tender share or the replacement framing.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: Oxford Nanopore's Canadian federal sales also fell in 2025, and Illumina's share of Illumina-plus-ONT spend barely moved (about 86% in 2024, about 83% in 2025). The 2025 decline looks like budget-driven, not share loss.
items.detail: ONT federal contract value was about C$1.83M in 2024 (50 rows, including a C$767,704 CFIA award on 25 Jun 2024). It was about C$0.98M in 2025 (31 rows), which is −46%, versus Illumina −56%. Illumina's share of the Illumina-plus-ONT total is 11.06/(11.06+1.83) = 86% in 2024 and 4.88/(4.88+0.98) = 83% in 2025. PacBio totals only about C$130K in 2025 (6 rows). Ultima Genomics has zero records, and MGI Americas has none since a C$3.03M pair at PHAC in Oct 2020 and two small 2024 rows. ONT's 346 records show no wave of rival awards at PHAC, the main account. ONT H1'26 is only about C$206K (11 rows to 8 Jun), but the file may still be catching up.
items.source_name: Government of Canada Proactive Disclosure of Contracts
items.why_new: The known file has no cross-vendor government spend comparison. It shows rival competitive pressure is not yet visible in Canadian federal dollars.
items.verify_note: The direction is right: the federal decline hit ONT too (−46% vs Illumina −56%), which points to budgets rather than share loss. But ONT is a long-read vendor, not one of the short-read price rivals in 1B. The share calculation also leaves out Element's C$337K NRC award (Jul 2025). Including it, Illumina's 2025 share of Illumina+ONT+Element+PacBio is about 4.88/(4.88+0.98+0.34+0.13) = 77%, against 86% on the Illumina+ONT basis alone. That shows some vendor diversification. Read this as neutral-t

items.label: 1B
items.claim: Illumina's largest 2026 Canadian federal awards were single-bid. The PHAC C$630K award cites a limited-tendering reason, and Health Canada and AAFC paid an identical price.
items.detail: PHAC procurement 6D06353301 (4 Feb 2026) was C$630,439.40 original plus C$14,410.12 amended, giving C$644,849.52. It has solicitation procedure TN, limited_tendering_reason 71 and number_of_bids 1. Health Canada (30 Jan 2026, HT28253534) and AAFC (17 Feb 2026, 20260485A) each booked exactly C$404,866.81, both single-bid TN awards. Two departments paying an identical price for an apparently identical item shows no negotiated differential. Across 2024-26 amendments the pattern is upward: +C$101,589 and +C$101,243 on the CFIA NextSeq package (Mar 2024), +C$58,280 (AAFC), +C$31,689 (Health Canada) and +C$14,410 (PHAC). I saw one negative amendment in about 330 rows (−C$13,169 on a C$7,251 CFIA row, 9 Dec 2024). The product behind the C$405K price is not stated, so it may be a NextSeq-class instrument.
items.source_name: Government of Canada Proactive Disclosure of Contracts
items.why_new: F040 and F050 say sole-source in general. This adds specific amounts, a limited-tendering code, duplicate pricing across departments and the amendment direction.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: CFIA, which bought a C$1.0-1.2M Illumina NextSeq package in March 2024, then diversified: ONT C$768K (Jun 2024), ONT license/warranty C$94.5K (Jun 2025) and Element C$300K (Feb 2026, open bid, 2 bids).
items.detail: CFIA's Illumina package was C$1,003,821 original plus C$101,589 amendment, shown as C$1,206,653 (5 Mar 2024). CFIA's 2026 Illumina rows are small: MiSeq Silver Support Plan renewals (C$31.6K on 16 Mar; C$32.2K on 6 Feb), a reagent kit and consumable reagents, each about C$24-32K. Elsewhere in the same department it awarded Oxford Nanopore C$767,704 (25 Jun 2024) and Element C$300,000 (18 Feb 2026, open bidding, 2 bids). The Element amount is likely the F047 award, so I count only the CFIA pattern as new: after a large Illumina buy, follow-on awards went to rivals. This is one department and one example of a buyer adding a second vendor.
items.source_name: Government of Canada Proactive Disclosure of Contracts
items.why_new: F047 covers the Element award only. The 2024 NextSeq package and ONT C$768K link show the department's multi-vendor trajectory.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: PHAC's recurring monthly Illumina reagent orders have stayed near C$22-25K per order for two years and show no growth in order size.
items.detail: PHAC orders (commodity N6640, 'Laboratory Supplies') include C$23,931 (the same value in Jun, Jul, Aug, Sep and Oct 2024), C$23,649 (Oct 2024 to Feb 2025), C$24,892 (Aug 2025), C$24,522 (Sep 2025), C$21,988.50 (twice in Jun 2026), C$21,585 (Jun 2026) and C$21,420 (Jan 2026). Six of the ten latest PHAC rows fall between C$21.4K and C$22.5K. The 2026 orders have delivery dates to 31 Mar 2027. The sample suggests a standing monthly buy of a fixed kit at a flat or slightly lower price. The product name is not disclosed, and the per-order value could simply be set by purchasing thresholds.
items.source_name: Government of Canada Proactive Disclosure of Contracts
items.why_new: This is new line-level time-series evidence for a standing reagent order.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: MGI's profit is still negative and its multi-omics line is growing 45%, which suggests rivals are monetizing non-sequencing volume rather than expanding clinical sequencing Gb.
items.detail: Multi-omics revenue was RMB 162M (+44.91%), with spatial +41%, single-cell +94% and pharma/drug-testing customers +115%. Automation was RMB 116M (+4.05%). Net loss attributable was about RMB 158M, narrowed 6.4%. This ties to the 10x CEO's view that single-cell/spatial counting demand is shifting toward cheaper sequencing and away from Illumina.
items.why_new: Adds MGI's multi-omics and pharma split, not in the known file.

items.label: 2B
items.claim: Federal research buyers have now awarded Element about C$0.78M across three contracts (Jul 2025, Feb 2026, Jun 2026), while Ultima has no Canadian federal records.
items.detail: Element Biosciences contracts at NRC are C$337,265.31 (30 Jul 2025, 'special industry machinery', advance contract award notice, 1 bid) and C$141,250 (1 Jun 2026). At CFIA it is C$300,000 (18 Feb 2026, open bidding, 2 bids). Total is C$778,515. This is about 16% of Illumina's 2025 federal total (C$4.88M), and large enough to place Element as a recurring federal vendor. By contrast, the CKAN datastore holds zero Ultima Genomics records. The file also shows no Roche or AXELIOS awards yet.
items.source_name: Government of Canada Proactive Disclosure of Contracts
items.why_new: This is a consolidated federal Element total and an Ultima null result. F046 and F047 are single items.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: PHAC has bought a competing high-throughput platform before (MGI Americas, C$3.03M in Oct 2020), but nothing comparable since. Its pandemic-era multi-vendor experiment did not become a lasting shift.
items.detail: MGI Americas Inc. has two PHAC rows dated 30 Oct 2020 of C$1,499,726 and C$1,534,376 (together C$3,034,102), described as laboratory equipment and supplies. The only later MGI Americas rows are C$28,250 (management consulting, Jul 2024) and C$11,606 (repair, Aug 2024). Meanwhile Illumina rows at PHAC continue every month. This shows a public buyer testing a lower-cost platform and then returning to Illumina. It is a small precedent, not a trend, and I could not confirm the 2020 item was a sequencer.
items.source_name: Government of Canada Proactive Disclosure of Contracts
items.why_new: The file mentions MGI only at the platform and BIOSECURE level, not as a government buyer's past choice.

items.label: 2B
items.claim: Several more European academic and medical buyers have bought AVITI-class systems in the past year, each at roughly €290–300K.
items.detail: MedUni Innsbruck (Neuropathology) awarded an Element AVITI system for €293,439 ex-VAT (tender V24-18r). Leiden UMC filed a voluntary transparency notice for an AVITI24 (L-EU-25-20, 7 Nov 2025). Helsinki reportedly stated the AVITI24 was the only instrument meeting its mid-output requirements. All are single-instrument awards of €290–300K. Combined with the Aachen buy, this is a repeated low-volume, mid-throughput pattern, not a flow-cell displacement. I opened the Innsbruck page but not the Leiden or Helsinki sources; those come from a search summary.
items.source_name: EU Publications Office tender record (Innsbruck); TenderNed (Leiden), BidSonar (Helsinki) via search
items.why_new: Adds three named European buyers (Innsbruck €293K, Leiden, Helsinki) beyond the Edinburgh, NHM and Czech AVITI buys already known.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: Helmholtz Munich, a large research centre, keeps awarding NovaSeq X kits to Illumina by price-only or no-competition procedures, so no visible discount pressure.
items.detail: Procurement 4500217555 (awarded Dec 2024) for 'various NovaSeq X kits' went to Illumina GmbH on a '100% price' basis, with a placeholder value of €1 (a framework, so the real price is not visible). On 19 Aug 2026 it published 'div. NovaSeq X Series 10B Reagent Kits' as a negotiated procedure without prior publication, with Illumina as the counterparty. The 2026 buy is the 10B flow cell, not the 25B, which fits the high within-X premium seen at cores. No quantity or value is disclosed, so it gives no price data.
items.source_name: Helmholtz Munich procurement notice; EU Publications Office record
items.why_new: A named German research centre buying 10B kits sole-source in Aug 2026. The known file has CIBER and IDIBAPS tenders but nothing on Helmholtz.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: Swiss and Danish public buyers purchased NovaSeq X Plus systems from Illumina without competitive tension in 2025–26, so opaque pricing is the norm.
items.detail: Univ. of Bern Vetsuisse NGS platform awarded 'NovaSeq X Plus including 1-year service' to Illumina Switzerland by direct award (closed 12 Mar 2026). The University of Copenhagen bought an X Plus by negotiated procedure without publication for USD 2,878,114 (awarded 28 Feb 2025). Both are 100% Illumina wins on non-competitive procedures. Copenhagen's value is a system, not consumables.
items.why_new: Quantifies two instrument awards ($2.88M Copenhagen; Bern direct award). The known file covers UK and Czech consumables buying but not these.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: Palacký University Olomouc set up a dynamic purchasing system in April 2026 for sequencing chemistry, so each future kit order is competed.
items.detail: The 8 Apr 2026 contract notice covers sequencing chemistry for NGS systems, DNA/RNA isolation kits and antibodies. Orders are placed through later competitions, with no committed volume or platform named. Competed call-offs let a public lab shop NovaSeq X, AVITI or MGI kits against each other, and that structure favours discounting. The article gives no value or quantity.
items.why_new: Known file lists Czech and Baltic framework buys, but not this DPS structure with competed call-offs.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: Japanese national universities buy sequencers and kits through reverse-auction tenders, and the University of Tokyo issued three sequencing-related tenders in July–August 2026.
items.detail: Tokyo notices: no. 21 (13 Jul 2026, 'next-generation sequencer set', delivery 26 Feb 2027), no. 32 (3 Aug 2026, 'high-precision short-read sequencer set', delivery 30 Oct 2026) and no. 36 (12 Aug 2026, library-prep kits on a unit-price contract to Mar 2029). All three use a reverse-auction system, and the platform vendor is not named in the page I opened (JETRO notice, item A). Osaka's Research Institute for Microbial Diseases lists X 10B kits (10 sets, Dec 2023) and, in a later notice, 10B (10) plus 25B (6), from a search summary I could not verify because the PDF would not parse. This is thin: no awards or prices were visible.
items.source_name: JETRO government procurement database; Univ. of Osaka procurement PDFs
items.why_new: Opens a Japanese university procurement channel not in the known file, other than the Osaka Sept 2026 MGI-plus-Illumina notice.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: GRAIL's spend with Illumina was small in H1'25, so Galleri adds little to Illumina's volume.
items.detail: GRAIL reported related-party cost of screening revenue paid to Illumina of $1.176M in Q2'25 and $2.687M in H1'25. It also reported $578K and $1.974M of R&D expense, respectively. Illumina stopped being a related party in Q4'25, so no 2026 figures are shown. These are cost lines, not a purchase total, so the Illumina share of GRAIL's sequencing spend is not established. Under the 4th amendment, GRAIL's perpetual royalty to Illumina is suspended until 24 Dec 2026. The rate is 9%, with anti-stacking down to a 7% floor, and drops to 5% after $1B cumulative.
items.source_name: GRAIL 10-Q Q2'26, Note 12 (via search-result and fetch summary)
items.quote: the perpetual royalty payment obligation to Illumina is suspended until December 24, 2026
items.why_new: The exclusion list covers GRAIL's 10-Q only as a source; these dollar amounts and the suspension and royalty-floor terms are not in it.

items.label: 2A
items.claim: Karolinska Institutet put its system-specific sequencing reagents out to open competitive tender in May 2026 with a small estimated value.
items.detail: KI published an open-procedure framework on 15 May 2026 for system-specific sequencing reagents and consumables, estimated at SEK 12M excl. VAT (about $1.1-1.3M, my conversion). Bids were due 12 Jun 2026. A major research university re-bidding reagents for existing instruments is consistent with price-led buying. Award criteria, platform and winner are unknown, so this is weak evidence only.
items.source_name: TED (Publications Office of the EU), seen via search-result snippet
items.why_new: This KI tender is not in the known procurement list (CIBER and IDIBAS only), and it gives a value and timeline.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: Guardant's Medicare FFS liquid-CGP dollars grew ~20% in 2024 on only ~5% more tests, because the 0326U payment rate jumped ~38%. Customer revenue growth here came from reimbursement, not sequencing volume.
items.detail: CMS Part B by provider and service: 0242U 21,416 services at $4,890 → 20,206 at $4,893; 0326U 16,798 at $3,533 → 19,695 at $4,892; 0334U 1,941 at $2,858 → 2,759 at $3,075; 81479 1,030 at $4,520 → 1,075 at $4,864. Medicare dollars are ~$174.3M (CY2023) → ~$209.4M (CY2024), +20%, while services rose +5.9% (41,185 → 43,735 ex-0422U). This matches Caris's revenue per case of +31% vs cost per case of +5% (F280): big Illumina customers' top-line growth overstates their sequencing Gb growth.
items.source_name: CMS Medicare Physician & Other Practitioners by Provider and Service
items.why_new: Known file has Guardant test growth but not its Medicare price-vs-volume split or the 0326U rate jump.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: Even at Natera's Q2'26 run-rate of ~1.13M MRD draws a year, MRD consumes only ~0.2–0.3M Gb a year on the classic assay (~0.02–0.03% of the ~800M Gb HT base), and ~2.5–3.8M Gb (~0.3–0.5%) if every draw were Signatera Genome.
items.detail: Clinical MRD units were 283K in Q2'26 (F267), or ~1.13M annualized. At the known 0.16–0.24 Gb per classic Signatera draw, that is ~0.18–0.27M Gb a year. At the known 2.2–3.4 Gb per Signatera Genome draw, it is ~2.5–3.8M Gb. Against the ~800M Gb HT base used in the known file, even all-genome MRD at the largest MRD lab is under half a percent of Illumina's volume. So MRD test growth of +50% adds well under 1 point of Gb growth. (Tumor-exome Gb, ~80–90% of per-patient Gb, is extra and scales with new patients, not draws.)
items.date: Q2 2026 run-rate; Gb/draw from known file
items.source_name: Natera Q2'26 deck units + known Gb-per-draw ranges (derived)
items.why_new: The known file lists Gb per draw and MRD counts separately but never aggregates them into a share of Illumina's Gb base.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: Natera's Medicare Signatera (0340U) payment per service fell ~8% in 2024 while services rose ~87%. MRD is growing as a high-count, low-Gb, falling-price line rather than a deepening one.
items.detail: CMS: 0340U average Medicare payment was $3,837.98 in CY2023 and $3,518.68 in CY2024 (−8.3%). Services went 13,783 → 25,746 (+86.8%) and draws per beneficiary 1.96 → 2.16 (+10%). Dollars rose ~71% ($52.9M → $90.6M). Combined with the Jan 2026 Medicare rate cut to $3,590 (known), MRD economics show payer price pressure alongside volume growth. That gives customers a reason to press Illumina for lower $/draw rather than run deeper sequencing.
items.source_name: CMS Medicare Physician & Other Practitioners by Provider and Service
items.why_new: Known items have only the 2024 0340U snapshot; the y/y payment-rate decline and cadence change are new.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: Roswell Park Cancer Center's March 2026 NGS solicitation asks bidders about trading in an existing NovaSeq 6000, an institutional 6000-to-X replacement signal.
items.detail: The NY State Contract Reporter notice #26-164 was posted 24 Mar 2026 with responses due 14 Apr 2026. It covers ultra-high-throughput NGS for the Genomics Shared Resource and Advanced Molecular Diagnostics. It requests 5-year consumable and maintenance pricing and mentions a possible NovaSeq 6000 trade-in. I saw this only in a search-result summary, and I did not open the notice. The award, the price and the sequencer model are unknown.
items.source_name: NY State Contract Reporter (via search snippet)
items.why_new: Roswell Park's solicitation and its 6000 trade-in clause are not in the known list, which does cover other 6000 retirements.

items.label: 2A
items.claim: NSF MRI awards for sequencers since 2023 are too sparse to show research buyers moving off Illumina on price.
items.detail: The NSF API returns one Element AVITI MRI award (Idaho, $584,845, Sep 2025) against two Illumina NextSeq 2000 MRI awards (Boston Univ. $639,794, Sep 2023; South Dakota State $495,290, Aug 2026). It also returns one PacBio Revio award (Texas Tech, $934,500, Oct 2024) and no Ultima or NovaSeq awards. The Idaho abstract has no cost language. The South Dakota abstract cites lower outsourcing costs as the reason to buy.
items.quote: significantly reduce costs and turnaround times associated with outsourcing sequencing services
items.why_new: The NSF MRI award tally by sequencer vendor is not in the known evidence; it shows a continuing Illumina mid-throughput purchase (NextSeq 2000, Aug 2026) and no price-driven switching.

items.label: 2A
items.claim: University of Leicester's 2025 sequencing framework went to four outsourced commercial providers including Novogene UK, Genewiz and Eurofins, not in-house cores.
items.detail: Award notice 031100-2025 (9 Jun 2025) for LUV01297 has one lot covering NGS, third-generation and Sanger sequencing, with an estimated value of £1.0M over 3+1 years (signed 20 May 2025). Winners are Randox Health London, Genewiz UK, Eurofins Genomics UK and Novogene (UK). Of 10 bids, 7 came from SMEs and 8 from non-EU foreign firms, so commodity sequencing sourcing is broad and price-competitive. The notice has no platform split (Illumina vs other) and no $/Gb.
items.source_name: Find a Tender OCDS API, University of Leicester LUV01297 award
items.why_new: The known list has no UK university framework award, no named lot winners and no bid count or price weights.
items.verify_note: Duplicate: F473 fully contains it (same Leicester LUV01297 award). The framework value (£1.0M over 3+1 years) is too small to matter, and the item has no price or platform data. 'Non-EU foreign firms' is a post-Brexit form artifact (UK buyer), not a sign of a global price race.

items.label: 2A
items.claim: UK academic sequencing frameworks weight quality well above price, so they do not formalise a price-only race to the cheapest lane.
items.detail: Leicester LUV01297 awards 75 points to quality (including 15 for social value) and only 25 to price. LSTM AF116 (tender 010265-2025, 19 Mar 2025) uses 70% quality and 30% price across two lots: Lot 1 NGS and third-generation at £280K, Lot 2 Sanger at £20K, total £300K. The framework values are small: £1.0M over four years at Leicester, and £300K for LSTM's first year.
items.source_name: Find a Tender OCDS API, LSTM AF116 tender notice
items.why_new: These are new quantified price/quality weights for UK academic sequencing procurement. They are a watch-out for the 'insane discounts' framing.

items.label: 2B
items.claim: Qiagen's Genomics/NGS group grew only 2% CER in Q2'26 (3% reported), to about $61M, which points to a soft research-linked sequencing-adjacent market.
items.detail: Per the search-result snippet of the press-release table, Genomics/NGS sales were $61M, +3% reported and +2% CER. Qiagen Digital Insights grew at a solid single-digit rate. The call said lower sales of other genomics products moderated the group's growth. Because panels on third-party sequencers grew >20% on a small base, the rest of the line (research-oriented genomics products) must have declined.
items.source_name: Qiagen Q2 2026 release (search snippet and call summary)
items.why_new: This is a quantified Qiagen Genomics/NGS growth rate. The known list only has the >20% panel figure.

items.label: 2A
items.claim: UK university sequencing-services frameworks are awarded overwhelmingly to low-cost outsourcers (Novogene, Genewiz, Macrogen), as research buyers shift work away from in-house Illumina cores.
items.detail: University of Edinburgh's EC0900 Lot 1 short-read framework (award published 14 Jul 2022, contract signed 21 Apr 2022, £1.0M) went to seven suppliers: Anthony Nolan HLA labs, Earlham Institute, GENEWIZ UK, Macrogen Europe, MicrobesNG, Novogene (UK) and CeGaT. Leicester LUV01297 (award notice 9 Jun 2025, £1.0M, 10 bids) has four winners, including Genewiz, Eurofins and Novogene (UK) and Randox. Novogene and Genewiz won both frameworks, which gives UK academic buyers a pre-approved low-cost outsourcing route. Edinburgh's 2022 rules also direct users to internal resources first, with the framework as the fallback on 'capacity or cost'.
items.source_name: Find a Tender OCDS API (Cabinet Office), University of Edinburgh EC0900; University of Leicester LUV01297
items.why_new: Names the winners and £ values of two UK academic sequencing frameworks. Known items only say Leicester's 2025 framework went to four outsourcers.
items.verify_note: Edinburgh (2022) and Leicester (2025) frameworks are new to the corpus. 'Overwhelmingly low-cost outsourcers' overstates them: Earlham Institute and Anthony Nolan are not commodity providers. Novogene and Genewiz mostly run Illumina, so outsourcing moves Illumina volume to large accounts and does not remove it. The item supports the consolidation and leverage mechanism, not lost volume. Both frameworks are £1M-scale.

items.label: 2A
items.claim: Quality outweighs price heavily in UK academic sequencing frameworks, which goes against the idea that research buyers run a price-only race.
items.detail: Edinburgh EC0900 weighted award criteria at Quality 90 / Price 10, and the lot sub-frameworks (Lot 12 and Lot 13) used the same split. Leicester LUV01297 weighted Quality 75 / Price 25, and LSTM AF116 (tender 19 Mar 2025) weighted Quality 70 / Price 30. The price weight rose from 10% (2021) to 25–30% (2025), so price matters more than it did, but it is still a minority factor. This weakens the claim that academic sequencing is bought mainly on price, although 7 of 8 Edinburgh bids were SMEs, so the supplier base is competitive.
items.source_name: Find a Tender OCDS API, Edinburgh EC0900, LSTM AF116, Leicester LUV01297
items.quote: Quality: 90, Price: 10
items.why_new: Gives the criteria weights for three frameworks and a trend in the price weight. The known item F471 only says quality is weighted well above price.
items.verify_note: The direction was mis-set. The claim itself says weighting quality at 70–90% cuts against a price-only research buyer, so this is 'against' 2A. The rising price weight (10% in 2021 → 25–30% in 2025) is a mild offset. These weights apply to choosing sequencing-service providers, not sequencer vendors.

items.label: 2B
items.claim: Edinburgh is re-tendering its whole sequencing and genotyping framework (EC1066) as a single lot with no stated value, which signals more open competition among outsourcers for research sequencing.
items.detail: Planning notice 053109-2025 was published 2 Sep 2025 for EC1066 'Sequencing & Genotyping Services'.
