It is one planned lot with no value and no award criteria, and the next notice is dated 30 Jan 2026. The predecessor EC0900 was a lotted family (Lot 1 short read, Lot 12 transgenic genotyping, Lot 13 DNA/RNA extraction, up to 10 participants per lot). Consolidating to one lot lets multi-platform outsourcers bid for everything, including Illumina short-read work. A Jan 2026 contract notice was not found, so scope and pricing remain unknown.
items.source_name: Find a Tender OCDS API, University of Edinburgh EC1066
items.why_new: Gives the structure of Edinburgh's replacement framework (one lot, planned Jan 2026), not previously known.

items.label: 2A
items.claim: The LSTM sequencing framework (AF116) is small and mostly outsourced NGS spend: £300K over up to three years, with £280K in Lot 1 and £20K for Sanger.
items.detail: The tender notice 010265-2025 (19 Mar 2025) estimated £300,000 including VAT for 1+1+1 years, which is about £100K/yr, split Lot 1 'Next Generation & Third Generation' £280K and Lot 2 'Sanger' £20K. Bids were due 22 Apr 2025 and the award decision was estimated 10 May 2025. No award notice or supplier names were found, and the OCDS record still shows only the tender stage. At £280K over three years, the NGS spend is about £93K/yr, which is immaterial to Illumina but fits a pattern of small institutions buying sequencing as a service.
items.source_name: Find a Tender OCDS API, LSTM AF116
items.why_new: Quantifies the AF116 lot split and value, and confirms that no award exists.

items.label: 2A
items.claim: Per-framework spend is small (about £1.0M per framework), and the incumbent outsourcers are broad service labs, so these frameworks are not a visible price attack on Illumina.
items.detail: Edinburgh EC0900 Lot 1 and Leicester LUV01297 each carry a £1.0M ceiling. Over the typical 3–4 year term that is about £0.25–0.33M/yr per university. Nothing in these notices names a non-Illumina sequencer or a price per Gb, and the notices do not show whether winners are shifting work to Ultima or Element. Some winners, such as Novogene, CeGaT and Macrogen, run Illumina-based production, so outsourcing may mean the same consumables bought in bulk rather than a lost Illumina sale.
items.source_name: Find a Tender, Leicester LUV01297 award notice; Edinburgh EC0900
items.why_new: Sizes the frameworks and says plainly that the notices carry no platform or price evidence.

items.label: 2A
items.claim: A Canadian public cancer research buyer renewed Illumina NovaSeq 6000/X Plus consumables by non-competitive direct award, with no competitor displacing it.
items.detail: PHSA (BC Cancer Research) issued a Notice of Intent to Direct Award to Illumina Canada on 29 Sep 2023 for NovaSeq 6000 and X Plus reagents, consumables and services. It was a one-year non-volume-commitment contract with an estimated value of $4.3M. The stated justification was compatibility with existing systems and Illumina being the sole manufacturer and distributor in Canada. This is a small buyer, and the notice is a 2023 estimate rather than payments. It shows research-lab consumable lock-in rather than price competition, and a single-year, no-commitment term leaves room for repricing.
items.quote: sole manufacturer and distributor of these platforms in Canada
items.why_new: This Canadian provincial direct-award notice with a $ estimate is not in the known procurement set, which has EU tenders and US cores. It is dated 2023, though, and says nothing about pricing.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: UConn's contract price for NovaSeq 6000 S4 kits fell about 3.9% in a year, and SP/S1/S2 kits fell about 5.2%, so legacy-platform prices are still being cut even as the X is held flat or raised.
items.detail: UConn's Center for Genome Innovation (CGI) rate sheet dated Jan 2025 lists S4 v1.5 300-cycle at $16,578, 200-cycle at $14,879 and 35-cycle at $11,192. The sheet current through Feb 2026 lists $15,938.08, $14,305.08 and $10,760.32. That is −3.86% on every S4 line (15,938.08/16,578 = 0.9614). S2-300 went $11,052→$10,473.28 and S1-300 $6,043→$5,726.08, both −5.24%. SP-300 went $3,454→$3,273.36 (−5.2%). Xp loading kits went $343→$324.76 and $690→$654.12 (−5.3%). These are internal contract prices that exclude a 6.5% shipping charge. The one tariff-bearing listing I found is a Honeycrisp SP-300 line at $3,649.80 for Jul–Dec 2025.
items.source_name: UConn Center for Genome Innovation service rates
items.why_new: Known list only has Jan 2025 S4 $16,578 as a level. This is a dated 12-month change on every 6000 kit tier, with SP/S1/S2 cut harder than S4.
items.verify_note: I checked the UConn page: the Feb 2026 prices match ($15,938.08 S4-300, $10,473.28 S2-300, $5,726.08 S1-300, $3,273.36 SP-300). The Jan 2025 comparison ($16,578) was not visible on the current page, so it rests on the agent's archive read. The page lists no NovaSeq X prices, so 'X held flat or raised' is not supported at UConn; it relies on other cores (TxGen, TGen). The finding that legacy 6000 prices are still falling is already known (Salk, EPFL). This adds a small, measured cut of −3.9% to −

items.label: 1A
items.claim: UConn's S4-300 contract price is only 73.5–76.5% of Illumina's published S4-300 list and the discount deepened over the year, which points to a persistent price gap between list and contract on the 6000.
items.detail: Illumina's published S4-300 list is $21,683 (known). UConn paid $16,578 in Jan 2025 (76.5% of list) and $15,938 in Feb 2026 (73.5%). On nominal 3,000 Gb that is $5.53/Gb and then $5.31/Gb. TxGen's 25B-300 at $3.20/Gb (Feb 2025) gives a cross-institution S4:25B ratio of about 1.73x ($5.53/$3.20). That is far below the 3.4x revenue-per-Gb gap Illumina reports. Part of the gap is that UConn's price is a contract price and TxGen's is a core recharge. The comparison is also cross-institution.
items.source_name: UConn CGI rates; TxGen price list Feb 2025
items.why_new: The ratio and the deepening discount (76.5%→73.5% of list) are new. Earlier work cites UConn only at $15,938 against the known S4 list and does not give the year-on-year path.
items.verify_note: This restates D026/F259 (UConn S4 ≈ 73.5% of the GSA price, $5.31/Gb). The $21,683 figure is the GSA distributor price, not Illumina's 'published list'. The 1.73x cross-institution ratio compares UConn's contract price with TxGen's core recharge price, which are not like-for-like. Core-level 6000/X ratios of 1.6–3.0x are already covered in D022/D025/D027/D029.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: TxGen raised its NovaSeq X flow-cell prices about 3% between May 2024 and Feb 2025 across 1.5B, 10B and 25B, so there is no visible X-side deflation at this core.
items.detail: From the TxGen v12 sheet (4 May 2024) to the Feb 2025 sheet (printed Apr 2025), 25B-300 went $24,224→$24,951 (+3.0%, $3.11→$3.20/Gb). 10B-300 went $15,192→$15,648 (+3.0%, $5.06→$5.22/Gb). 1.5B-300 went $3,998→$4,118 (+3.0%, $8.33→$8.58/Gb). The 10B:25B per-Gb ratio stayed at 1.63x in both sheets. The Feb 2025 25B-300 price is 3.3% above Illumina's published $24,155 list. The May 2024 price is about equal to list.
items.why_new: The known list gives a single TxGen/TGen 25B point. This gives a dated two-version history and a uniform +3% step across all three X flow cells, plus the constant 1.63x 10B premium.
items.verify_note: New core-level data point, consistent with TGen's +8.8% (F222). It is stale: May 2024 → Feb 2025, before the 35B launch and before AXELIOS/VITARI shipped. Per D019, core recharge rates mostly reflect core overhead and do not show Illumina's net price. The flat 10B:25B ratio of 1.63x contrasts with the compression in D018.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: In 2025 TxGen added a 3–5% surcharge to single-lane prices over flow-cell/8, on top of the 3% flow-cell increase, so effective per-lane prices rose 6–8% in nine months.
items.detail: May 2024: 25B lane $3,028 = $24,224/8 exactly, and 10B lane $1,899 = $15,192/8 exactly. Feb 2025: 25B lane $3,222 against $24,951/8 = $3,119 (+3.3% surcharge). 10B lane $2,059 against $15,648/8 = $1,956 (+5.3%). Lane price changes were 25B +6.4% and 10B +8.4% over the nine months. The 1.5B lane is listed at $2,162 against $4,118/2 = $2,059 (+5.0%). The snippets that gave me the lane figures may have mislabelled which flow cell they belong to, so treat the surcharge percentages as approximate.
items.why_new: A lane-vs-flowcell arithmetic check across two dated versions has not been done before.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: Per-Gb price of a top-end NovaSeq flow cell at one core fell from $8.61 (S4, 2019) to $3.11 (25B, 2024), about −64%, which sets the scale of the step 6000 labs face on conversion.
items.detail: TxGen internal Oct 2019: S4 2x150 $25,820.42 for 3,000 Gb = $8.61/Gb. A TxGen list dated Sep 2020 shows S4 2x150 at $20,448 = $6.82/Gb. That is −21% vs 2019, but the 2019 sheet is internal and the 2020 sheet's audience is unclear. Kentucky's 2022–23 handout has S4-300 at $17,132 = $5.71/Gb. TxGen's May 2024 25B-300 is $3.11/Gb. S4→25B is therefore −54% from the 2020 S4 and −64% from the 2019 S4. The top-flowcell series 8.61 → 6.82 → 5.71 (a different core) → 3.11 shows the 6000 itself was repriced downward before the X, which fits the claim that the remaining 6000 volume is the high-price tail.
items.source_name: TxGen price sheets; Univ. of Kentucky SRF handout
items.why_new: Gives a multi-year per-Gb path for the S4, which the known list does not (it has only the 2025–26 S4 points).

items.label: 1A
items.claim: MDC Berlin's SP v1.5 300-cycle price was unchanged at €3,096.50 between its 15 Nov 2020 and 15 Apr 2021 lists, so European core prices on the 6000 were sticky for at least that period.
items.detail: Search snippets of MDC media/38662 (dated 15.11.2020) and media/39029 (15.04.2021) show the same SP v1.5 300-cycle net price. The S4 rows were not readable, so the probe-note S4 v1.5 300-cycle €14,435.30 was not confirmed. The text of the MDC PDFs could not be extracted without a PDF tool.
items.source_name: MDC Berlin Genomics Platform price list
items.why_new: Unread until now. This is a single unchanged data point and it is old, so it is only context.

items.label: 2A
items.claim: Macrogen's Q1 2026 sequencing revenue was KRW 39.9B (88% of the KRW 45.3B total), and management says unit costs of analysis keep falling, so it must win volume to offset them.
items.detail: Edaily (26 Jun 2026) reports an operating loss of KRW 0.5B in Q1 2026, with sequencing profitability under pressure as unit prices fall. An official said service costs are decreasing and the company must secure volume that exceeds this trend. This is a large listed outsourcer confirming price deflation, but it gives no numeric price per sample or Gb and is not specific to academic customers or to Illumina platforms.
items.quote: we must secure a large volume of work that exceeds these trends
items.why_new: Adds Macrogen's Q1'26 sequencing revenue and operating loss, which the known list lacks. The known list only has a Macrogen quote on 'volume expansion for viability'.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: Macrogen runs about 300,000 samples a year and adds Ultima capacity, a low-cost rival platform.
items.detail: Edaily (23 Jul 2026) gives a current volume of 300,000 samples/yr at the new Songdo Global Genome Center. A separate search snippet (not opened) says Macrogen announced a collaboration with Ultima on the UG200 in April 2026. It also notes Macrogen already runs Ultima UG100 fleets at Macrogen APAC (Singapore) and Macrogen Europe. A service provider adding Ultima suggests Illumina's price pressure is rising, but the platform split is not disclosed.
items.why_new: Gives a disclosed sample-volume figure and a signal that Macrogen is adding Ultima UG200. The known list has only generic Macrogen commentary.

items.label: 2A
items.claim: The National Research Council (NRC) did not stop sequencing when its direct Illumina orders collapsed. It moved the work to outsourced academic cores, SickKids (TCAG) and Génome Québec, which run the NovaSeq X, so research volume is consolidating into larger accounts.
items.detail: NRC contracts with The Hospital for Sick Children (SickKids, TCAG): none from 2013 to 2023. Then 7 in 2024 (C$224.1K: 88,326 + 40,482.75 + 29,442 + 21,761.25 + 18,401.25 + 14,721 + 11,004), 7 in 2025 (C$213.1K) and 3 in H1'26 (C$110.3K). NRC contracts with Génome Québec: C$39.4K in 2023, none in 2024, C$68.6K in 2025 and C$106.3K in Feb 2026 alone. Total outsourced sequencing was therefore about C$39K (2023), C$224K (2024), C$282K (2025) and C$217K (H1'26, roughly C$430K annualized). Over the same period NRC's direct Illumina orders fell from 21 (2022) to 13, 7, 3 and then 3 (H1'26); FY25 direct Illumina spend was only about C$56.7K (26,829.35 + 17,433.21 + 12,428.33), so outsourced spend was about 5x direct spend in 2025. The roughly 90% NRC decline in F449 is therefore mostly a channel shift to big-core accounts that hold more negotiating leverage, not lost sequencing volume.
items.source_name: Government of Canada Proactive Disclosure, contracts over $10K
items.quote: 4 LANES OF ILLUMINA NOVASEQ X 25B 300 CYCLE SEQUENCING
items.why_new: F447/F449 recorded only Illumina-vendor declines; the substitution into outsourced X-core spending is new and quantified.
items.verify_note: I verified this on the search portal. The 2025 SickKids rows sum to C$213.1K (19,845 + 97,167 + 41,310.25 + 10,655.25 + 14,721 + 14,721 + 14,647.50), H1'26 sums to C$110.3K, and the 7 Jan 2026 row carries the quoted '4 LANES OF ILLUMINA NOVASEQ X 25B 300 CYCLE' text. Two caveats. First, every other row is generic 'Scientific services', and TCAG also sells PacBio and ONT, so not all of it is Illumina sequencing. Second, the portal shows 22 records against the 17 counted. The finding mainly correc

items.label: 1B
items.claim: A federal lab buying NovaSeq X 25B-300 lanes through SickKids/TCAG pays the core's list rate plus tax, about C$3.47–3.65 per lane-Gb (roughly US$2.5/Gb), with no volume concession visible.
items.detail: On 7 Jan 2026 NRC paid C$14,610.75 for 4 lanes of X 25B-300, or C$3,652.69 per lane. TCAG's April 2025 list price for a 25B-300 lane is C$3,470.00, so NRC paid about 5.3% above list, consistent with tax. At ~1,000 Gb per 25B lane (8 Tb per 8-lane flow cell), that is about C$3.47/Gb before tax. This is in the same band as US core 25B rates (US$2.6–3.5/Gb) and above Novogene's US$2,549 promotional lane.
items.source_name: TCAG NGS Price List April 2025; Canada Proactive Disclosure
items.quote: NovaSeq X Series 25B Reagent Kit (300 Cycle) $ 3,470.00
items.why_new: First Canadian core X price list (TCAG) and the first matched government purchase against it; not among the cores already logged.
items.verify_note: Verified: the TCAG April 2025 list prices a 25B-300 lane at C$3,470, in Canadian dollars. NRC paid C$3,652.69 per lane, +5.3%, which is consistent with 5% GST. This is a core resale price paid by an end user, not Illumina's price to a large account. A flat core list price with no volume concession goes against visible discount acceleration, not for it, so the item is relabeled to 'against'. At ~0.72 USD/CAD the lane is ≈US$2.50/Gb, which sits in the known US core band.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: Canada's largest pediatric genomics core (TCAG) prices every X flow cell per lane but lists the NovaSeq 6000 only as 'Contact facility', so the 6000 has dropped to an on-request legacy service.
items.detail: The April 2025 TCAG list publishes 9 NovaSeq X lane prices (1.5B, 10B and 25B at 100/200/300 cycles) and MiSeq run prices. The 6000 row carries no price. Human 30x WGS is quoted only on the NovaSeq X, at C$650 per sample including library prep (90–100 Gb).
items.quote: Illumina NovaSeq 6000 Sequencing Contact facility
items.why_new: TCAG has not been surveyed before; adds a large Canadian core to the 6000-delisting evidence (TGen, NCI, Rush).
items.verify_note: Verified: 'Illumina NovaSeq 6000 Sequencing — Contact facility', with nine X lane prices and human WGS at C$650 on the X. TCAG is mainly a research core, and research is already ~92% on the X, so this repeats the known pattern of research conversion (Dana-Farber, Novogene, UMN). It says little about the clinical 6000 tail that 1A is really about.

items.label: 2A
items.claim: Fisheries and Oceans Canada (DFO) roughly tripled its outsourced sequencing orders to Génome Québec, so federal research sequencing is moving from in-house boxes to core service providers.
items.detail: DFO contracts with Génome Québec: 9 (2022), 20 (2023), 31 (2024), 29 (2025) and 12 in Jan–Feb 2026 alone. The Jan–Feb 2026 orders run about C$11–40K each (e.g. C$40,167.20 twice in Feb 2026). DFO direct Illumina contracts stayed small: 5 in 2025 (~C$95.2K) and 5 by Mar 2026 (~C$139.0K, including one C$71.5K order).
items.why_new: Outsourcing-vendor time series for DFO not covered by F447–F460 (Illumina-vendor only).
items.verify_note: Only partly new. The move to outsourcing mirrors F487/D041 (NRC to SickKids). Order counts tripled from 2022 to 2024 but were flat in 2025 (31 to 29), so 'tripled' describes 2022–24 only. Génome Québec runs Illumina X instruments itself, so the work moves to a different channel but stays in the Illumina ecosystem. That shows a funding and efficiency shift, not price sensitivity as such. The Jan–Feb 2026 count of 12 is a run-rate signal, not a full-year figure.

items.label: 2A
items.claim: Agriculture Canada (AAFC), the largest federal buyer from Génome Québec, cut its outsourcing orders sharply while keeping direct Illumina orders steady and buying a ~C$405K Illumina instrument in Feb 2026.
items.detail: AAFC contracts with Génome Québec: 38–39 a year in 2020–22, then 19 (2023), 24 (2024), 16 (2025) and 9 (H1'26). AAFC direct Illumina contracts were 19 (2024), 24 (2025) and 9 (H1'26), including a C$404,866.81 equipment order on 17 Feb 2026. The shift to outsourcing is therefore department-specific, not a uniform research exit from Illumina.
items.why_new: AAFC instrument buy and its outsourcing trend are not in F447–F460.
items.verify_note: A useful counterweight. However, the C$404,866.81 instrument also appears as a Health Canada buy of the same amount in F510. It may be one procurement booked under two departments, or a duplicate row. Check before counting it twice.

items.label: 2A
items.claim: NRC's direct Illumina spend in H1'26 already exceeded its full-year 2025 total, and DFO's rose too, so the federal decline in F447/F449 is not deepening in 2026.
items.detail: NRC direct Illumina: about C$74.3K across 3 orders in Mar–Jun 2026 (27,962.52 + 25,603.20 + 20,771.10) vs C$56.7K across 3 orders in all of 2025. DFO direct Illumina: about C$139.0K by Mar 2026 vs about C$95.2K in all of 2025. This fits F452 (federal decline stopped in H1'26) and shows the 2026 bottoming is broad, not just at PHAC.
items.why_new: Department-level 2026 rebound figures for NRC and DFO were not previously reported.
items.verify_note: The absolute amounts are tiny (NRC C$74K vs C$57K; DFO C$139K vs C$95K), so these are noise-level changes. The 'bottoming is broad' wording conflicts with F509/F510: after deduplication, federal H1'26 is about −22% overall and consumable-type spend is down 70–77% at PHAC and AAFC. The narrower claim stands: NRC and DFO are no longer falling.

items.label: 2B
items.claim: The Canadian Grain Commission stopped buying from Illumina after 2022 and has bought only PacBio consumables and service since, a full federal research platform switch.
items.detail: Illumina contracts with the Grain Commission: C$42.8K (Jan 2021), C$161.8K instrument (Dec 2021) and C$15.6K (Oct 2022), then none. PacBio contracts: 11 from May 2022 to Jan 2026, including a C$182.7K service contract (Mar 2023) and steady C$17.7–23.9K consumable orders (4 in 2024–25, 1 in Jan 2026). The 10 PacBio contracts visible on the results page total about C$362K; the eleventh, on a later page, was not read.
items.why_new: PacBio substitution at the Grain Commission is not in F454/F459 (ONT and Element only).

items.label: 1A
items.claim: Illumina is monetizing a retired legacy platform: the Canadian Food Inspection Agency (CFIA) keeps renewing MiSeq support plans, and its spend on them is rising. That is a template for a sticky, revenue-producing 6000 tail.
items.detail: CFIA MiSeq Silver/Bronze support contracts totalled about C$92.4K (5 contracts) in 2024, about C$160.9K (7) in 2025 and about C$87.7K (3) in Q1'26 alone. The per-plan price rose from C$20,420.62 (Jul and Nov 2024) to C$21,237.94–22,856.07 (Nov 2025) and C$23,894.87 (Jan 2026), about +4–17%. This continued after the MiSeq's end of sale (30 Sep 2025). ECCC likewise renewed warranty on an Illumina sequencer (C$22,248.29, Feb 2026) after a C$32.8K repair in Jan 2025.
items.quote: MiSeq Silver Plan Renewal
items.why_new: Legacy-platform service pricing and persistence at federal labs was not in the corpus.
items.verify_note: These are service-plan dollars, not consumables, and the amounts are immaterial. The renewal price is still worth noting: C$20,420.62 (Jul 2024) to C$23,894.87 (Jan 2026) is +17% in about 18 months, or roughly +11%/yr, after MiSeq end of sale. So a legacy platform can carry price increases on service, but this says nothing about 6000 consumables volume.

items.label: 2B
items.claim: CFIA kept buying Illumina hardware even while it diversified to ONT and Element: it bought an Illumina sequencer for C$176.2K in Dec 2025, after its C$1.21M NextSeq package in Mar 2024.
items.detail: On 23 Dec 2025 CFIA bought a 'Sequencer' from Illumina Canada for C$176,193.21; the row was published late ('omitted from a previous proactive publication'). It also bought an Illumina 'Reagent Kit' (C$24,445.88, Feb 2026). Element (C$300K, Feb 2026) and ONT were additions, not replacements.
items.quote: This contract was omitted from a previous proactive publication.
items.why_new: F456 described CFIA diversifying after Mar 2024 but missed the Dec 2025 Illumina sequencer purchase.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: The only kit-level NovaSeq reference in Canadian federal contracts since 2019 names the NovaSeq X, and no federal row names a 6000 flow cell (S1/S2/S4/SP).
items.detail: A full-text search of the contracts database for 'NovaSeq' returns 1 record (NRC to SickKids, 4 lanes of X 25B-300, Jan 2026). Searches for '25B', '10B', 'v1.5' and 'reagent kit' return no 6000 kit lines. Illumina's own rows carry only generic commodity codes ('Medical supplies', 'Miscellaneous chemical products'), so the dataset cannot support a 6000/X dollar split.
items.why_new: Answers the strategist's 6000/X split request: the split is not available from this source.

items.label: 2A
items.claim: Federal use of the low-cost outsourcer Novogene is tiny and flat, so Canadian federal research is not visibly moving to cheap Chinese providers.
items.detail: Novogene has 14 federal contracts in total since 2020, all from AAFC and DFO, at C$10–25K each. Examples: C$24,308.73 (Jan 2026), C$24,718.23 (Nov 2025), C$19,797.63 (Mar 2025) and C$17,791.97 (Dec 2023). There is no step-up in count or size after 2021. Outsourcing goes to domestic academic cores (Génome Québec, SickKids, Dalhousie and others) instead.
items.why_new: Novogene's Canadian federal footprint was not previously checked.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: One Illinois core's Aug 2026 sheet prices a full wafer (assumed Ultima, labeling unconfirmed) at about the same as one 25B lane, implying roughly half the $/Gb.
items.detail: Carver DNA Services (effective 1 Aug 2026): NovaSeq X Plus 25B 2x150 lane $3,380 ($3,180 for 8+ lanes) versus Full Wafer $3,310, Split High $2,730, Split Low $1,990. Our $/Gb calc, using about 1.0-1.3 Tb per 25B lane and an assumed ~2.4 Tb per wafer, gives ~$2.6-3.4/Gb for the 25B lane and ~$1.4/Gb for the wafer. The page gives no output figures, so the gap is inferred. If the wafer rows are Ultima, a research core sells a cheaper-per-Gb alternative to the same user base at the same date.
items.source_name: University of Illinois Carver Biotechnology Center, DNA Services pricing
items.quote: All pricing is updated, effective Aug. 1, 2026.
items.why_new: The known list has other core 25B prices and Broad's Ultima listing, but not this same-sheet wafer-versus-25B comparison at Illinois.
items.verify_note: Checked on the page. The Full Wafer, Split High and Split Low rows sit under the 'ILLUMINA NOVASEQ X PLUS' heading. Ultima and UG100 are not named anywhere, and the page gives no output figures. The ~2.4 Tb wafer yield and the Ultima attribution are both assumptions, so the claimed ~2x $/Gb gap is unsupported.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: A European university-hospital clinical genetics lab with the X Plus live for under a year grew hereditary-disease samples about 40%, but the page ties this to in-sourcing capacity, not to lower prices or elasticity.
items.detail: Clinical Genomics Uppsala put a NovaSeq X Plus into clinical use in May 2024. Samples from patients with suspected hereditary disease rose roughly 40% in 2024 vs 2023, and many samples previously sent to external labs are now analysed in-house. Initial assays were rare-disease WGS and WGS plus transcriptome for paediatric leukaemia, with exome and gene panels still in progress. The page does not mention the NovaSeq 6000. The +40% is a sample count, not Gb, and it is partly in-sourced work. Clinical volume growth of this size is therefore not evidence of broad-based elasticity. If anything it shows that the pull comes from a capacity and in-sourcing step, which is one-time. It is also a single site, so weak.
items.quote: approximately 40 percent more samples
items.why_new: A hospital-level, dated go-live and sample-growth datapoint (X Plus May 2024, +40% samples in 2024) is not in the known list; the in-sourcing explanation is also new.

items.label: 2A
items.claim: Counting direct orders plus outsourced core work, NRC's Illumina-ecosystem sequencing spend fell only ~40–45% from 2022 to 2025, not 90%, and H1'26 is running near 2022 levels annualized. More of each dollar now goes to the core's markup instead of Illumina.
items.detail: Direct Illumina plus SickKids/Génome Québec outsourcing comes to C$591K + 0 (2022), C$251K + 39K = C$290K (2023), C$120K + 224K = C$344K (2024), C$57K + 282K = C$339K (2025, −43% vs 2022) and C$74K + 217K = C$291K in H1'26 (~C$580K annualized). TCAG's 25B-300 lane is C$3,470. Illumina's list is US$16,480/8 ≈ US$2,060 per lane, or ≈C$2,860 at 1.39 CAD/USD, so the core charges ≈21% above Illumina list. At most ~80% of outsourced dollars can therefore reach Illumina, and less once library prep and non-Illumina services are included. On that basis NRC's Illumina-attributable spend in 2025 was ≲C$57K + 0.8×282K ≈ C$283K, about −50% vs 2022. NRC also bought an Element system (C$337K, Jul 2025).
items.source_name: Government of Canada Proactive Disclosure; TCAG NGS Price List Apr 2025
items.quote: 4 LANES OF ILLUMINA NOVASEQ X 25B 300 CYCLE SEQUENCING
items.why_new: Nets F449's −90% against F487's outsourcing and TCAG's core markup to estimate a channel-adjusted decline.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: At TCAG (Apr 2025) the X 10B-300 lane costs ~1.6x the 25B-300 per Gb, above the 1.03–1.50x range at US cores in 2026. Not every core shows a compressing 10B premium.
items.detail: TCAG per-lane prices in CAD: 10B-300 C$2,080 for ~375 Gb = C$5.55/Gb; 25B-300 C$3,470 for ~1,000 Gb = C$3.47/Gb; ratio 1.60x. 1.5B-300 is C$2,485 for ~250 Gb ≈ C$9.9/Gb (2.9x the 25B). Against D018/D034/D035 (TGen 1.13x, Berkeley 1.38x, KUMC 1.03x in 2026), the TCAG sheet is a year older and matches TxGen's flat 1.63x (F481). Narrowing of the 10B premium may be a 2026 effect or specific to US cores.
items.source_name: The Centre for Applied Genomics (SickKids) NGS price list
items.quote: NovaSeq X Series 10B Reagent Kit (300 Cycle) $ 2,080.00
items.why_new: First non-US data point on the 10B/25B per-Gb ladder; it qualifies the D018 compression finding.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: A research core's all-in 30x genome on the NovaSeq X costs ~US$470 (C$650), of which Illumina reagents at core lane rates are only ~US$240, still well above rival marketing claims of ~$80–150 per genome.
items.detail: TCAG quotes human 30x WGS on the X at C$650 including library prep (90–100 Gb). Its PCR-free prep is C$140, and ~95 Gb at the C$3.47/Gb 25B lane rate is ≈C$330 (≈US$240). The remaining ≈C$180 covers QC and analysis. Ultima markets ~$80/genome and Roche AXELIOS lists $150 (duplex 30x, prep excluded). The sequencing component at a research core is therefore ~1.6–3x the rival list claims, which leaves room for pricing pressure in research. These are core resale prices, not Illumina's net price.
items.source_name: TCAG NGS price list; Roche Investor Day May 2026; Ultima marketing
items.quote: Human WGS (NovaSeq X), including library prep, 90-100 Gb (30X diploid genome) $ 650.00
items.why_new: Splits a published core genome price into prep, sequencing and residual components and compares the sequencing part with rival per-genome claims.

items.label: 2B
items.claim: Novogene's 10B lane price fell 8.8% from Q2'25 to Sep'26 ($1,699→$1,549), while the 25B lane price was nearly flat (−1.9%).
items.detail: The 10B lane (375 Gb) went $1,699 (Q2'25), $1,599 (Spring'26), $1,549 (Sep'26). The 25B lane (1,000 Gb) went $2,599, $2,599, $2,549. Per Gb, 10B is $4.13/Gb falling to $4.53→$4.27→$4.13 (-8.8% over the period) and 25B is $2.55/Gb. The 10B-to-25B gap is widening, which pushes customers to the larger flow cell and a lower Illumina revenue per Gb. Novogene's reseller price is a proxy for what Americas research buyers pay, though it is promotional.
items.why_new: The 2026 lane prices are known; the dated 2025→2026 series with percent changes is new.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: Carver's 'kit provided' fee shows how much of its lane price is Illumina reagent, which suggests the core marks reagents well above list.
items.detail: An 8-lane 25B run costs $27,040 at standard (8 x $3,380) and $25,440 on the 8+ tier. The 'Nova X, 8 lanes, kit provided' service fee is $4,860 ($608/lane), and 2 lanes is $1,420 ($710/lane). The implied reagent-plus-margin portion is $22,180 (standard) or $20,580 (8+ tier). That is 1.35x and 1.25x Illumina's published $16,480 25B-300 list, which comes from the exclusion list. The core appears to pass reagents through at or above list plus a markup, so core lane prices cannot show a vendor discount. Carver has not been shown to buy at list.
items.source_name: Univ. of Illinois Carver Biotechnology Center, DNA Services pricing
items.why_new: Decomposes Carver's lane price into labour and reagent using the kit-provided rows. None of the known items do this.
items.verify_note: The prices check out: 25B lane $3,380 / $3,180 (8+), kit-provided fees $4,860 (8 lanes) and $1,420 (2 lanes). The subtraction is correct. The main point, that core lane rates sit well above list, is already known (D019 has Carver at +64% per lane). What is new is only the split into a labor fee of about $608/lane and a reagent-plus-margin remainder of about 1.25–1.35x list. This is a research-core price; it does not show the vendor's net price.

items.label: 2A
items.claim: External users at Carver pay a 30.8% overhead uplift, so research price pressure on these lanes is cushioned by a big surcharge.
items.detail: The 25B 2x150 lane would be $4,421 for a non-Illinois external user ($3,380 x 1.308) and $4,159 on the 8+ tier. State-subsidised Illinois universities and agencies are capped at 20% ($4,056). That is about $4.70/Gb externally, against about $3.4-3.6 for internal users. This is a pass-through recharge that absorbs most discount signals and works against the claim that research buyers see steep price cuts.
items.source_name: Univ. of Illinois Carver Biotechnology Center, DNA Services pricing
items.why_new: Computes the external 25B price and $/Gb from the 30.8% and 20% overhead rules.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: Carver offers on-board DRAGEN secondary analysis at $188 per lane, about 5.6% on top of a 25B lane price.
items.detail: DRAGEN costs $939 per flow cell or $188 per lane. For the 25B lane at $3,380 that is 5.6% of cost, and about 9% on a 10B lane ($2,000). Illumina bundles analysis software into the workflow-cost story, so lab cost includes a non-sequencing line that rivals' bare reagent prices leave out.
items.source_name: Univ. of Illinois Carver Biotechnology Center, DNA Services pricing
items.why_new: Adds the DRAGEN price per lane and the share it makes up of a lane price.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: An Illumina oncology supply-agreement appendix awards instrument credits per installed system, valuing the NovaSeq X Plus above the NovaSeq 6000.
items.detail: A search-result snippet (not opened in full) of the 29 Sep 2022 addendum shows 'Table 3: Allocation of Instrument Credits': NovaSeq X Plus 13, NovaSeq 6000 Dx 11, NovaSeq 6000 10. This suggests contract customers get instrument-linked credits that favour the X. The unit (points, dollars or discount tier) and the link to consumable discounts are unknown. Newer 2024 versions with the same table layout were also listed.
items.why_new: The known list covers the Open Offer S-1 exhibit and the Natera amendments, but not these public Illumina-hosted appendices or their instrument-credit table.

items.label: 2B
items.claim: Novogene's 25B lane price has fallen about 12% per Gb since the Nov 2023 to Mar 2024 launch promo, and the 10B lane about 9% per Gb.
items.detail: Per-Gb arithmetic from dated Novogene pages: Nov 2023 to Mar 2024, 25B at 'as low as $2,799' on a ~950 Gb yield = $2.95/Gb, and that price needed ≥16 lanes. Q2 2025: $2,599 / 1,000 Gb = $2.60. Spring 2026: $2,599 = $2.60. Sep 2026: $2,549 = $2.55 single-lane. The full flow cell is $2.46. From $2.95 to $2.55 is −13.5%, and to $2.46 is −16.6%. The 2024 price needed the 16-lane commitment and the 2026 price is a single lane. The yield basis also changed (950 → 1,000 Gb). The 10B lane went $1,699 (Q2'25) → $1,599 (Spring'26) → $1,549 (Sep'26), which is $4.53 → $4.26 → $4.13/Gb (−8.8%). This is steady and modest erosion at a low-price research channel, with no cliff.
items.source_name: Novogene landing pages (Website_NovaSeqXPlus25B_PremadeLibrarySeq, Facebook_25Q2_Premade_X, Website_Premade_2026_Spring, Sequencing Savings 2026)
items.quote: as low as $2,799 per lane
items.why_new: The known list has only the Q2'25 to Sep'26 10B/25B moves. The Nov 2023 to Mar 2024 anchor and the per-Gb series from 2023 are new.
items.verify_note: The $2,599 and $2,549 25B promos are already known. The new parts are the 2023–24 launch price of $2,799 (with a ≥16-lane condition) and the 10B series. The claim's '−12%' does not match the detail's −13.5% / −16.6%; the like-for-like single-lane move is about −13.5% over about 30 months, or about −5.6%/yr (see derived item). This supports continued price erosion, but at a rate well below the thesis's 'accelerating' view.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: The Novogene 10B-versus-25B per-Gb premium has widened to about 1.6x, so within-X price steps are steep for smaller buyers and the 25B is the price-setting flow cell.
items.detail: Sep 2026: 10B $1,549/375 Gb = $4.13/Gb versus 25B $2,549/1,000 Gb = $2.55/Gb, a ratio of 1.62x. Q2 2025: $4.53 vs $2.60 = 1.74x. Spring 2026: $4.26 vs $2.60 = 1.64x. On the 4-lane tier, the 10B (4 lanes from $5,799 = $1,450 per lane, $3.87/Gb) vs the 25B 4-lane ($2.47/Gb) gives 1.57x. The steep step supports the view that mix migrates toward the largest flow cell and that a 35B (+40% output) priced on this ladder would reset outsourcers' $/Gb again.
items.why_new: The known list gives the 10B/25B ratio for cores (1.03-1.62x). A dated outsourcer ratio series is new.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: Novogene's full 25B flow-cell price of $19,699 is 18% below Illumina's GSA list of $24,155 for the 300-cycle kit, so the largest outsourcer is funding a retail price below distributor list.
items.detail: $19,699 / $24,155 = 0.816. Novogene's price also includes library QC, Q30 ≥85% guarantee, data delivery, lab labour and a margin. NCI's recharge is ~71% of GSA (~$17.15K), and IDIBAPS paid €16,000 for a 25B-300. Novogene's price is ~15% above NCI's level and ~23% above IDIBAPS's pre-conversion price. Rough implied reagent cost for Novogene is likely $14-17K (my estimate: it needs to buy at roughly the NCI/IDIBAPS level or better to earn a margin). It is not observable, but it means a mid-teens gross spread, consistent with its falling platform-service gross margin (32.5% in FY25). Novogene's volume buys give it purchasing leverage, a channel for extra Illumina discounting.
items.source_name: Novogene landing page vs known GSA/NCI/IDIBAPS prices
items.why_new: This compares Novogene's all-in full-flow-cell price with GSA, NCI and the tender. Margin inference is new but unobservable.

items.label: 2A
items.claim: After removing duplicate amendment rows, PHAC's Illumina contract value fell about 76% from fiscal 2024-25 to fiscal 2025-26, and its order count fell about 73%.
items.detail: The Public Health Agency of Canada (PHAC; it runs the National Microbiology Lab) contracts with ILLUMINA CANADA ULC were summed on Canada's April-to-March fiscal year. FY24-25 was about C$7.32M on 120 orders (Apr–Jun 2024 C$1.28M + H2'24 C$3.49M + Jan–Mar 2025 C$2.54M). FY25-26 was about C$1.76M on 33 orders (Apr–Jun 2025 C$0.078M + H2'25 C$0.734M + Jan–Mar 2026 C$0.948M). The FY25-26 figure counts the Feb 2026 C$630K equipment procurement only once, at its amended C$644.8K value. Calendar 2024 totals C$7.26M on 120 orders, against C$3.35M on 64 orders in 2025. The 2025 figure reconciles with the known ~C$3.4M.
items.source_name: Government of Canada Proactive Disclosure of Contracts (open.canada.ca)
items.why_new: F448 gave calendar 2022/2025 values only; this is a deduplicated fiscal-year series with order counts, including FY25-26.
items.verify_note: The deduplication logic is confirmed for 6D06353301: row 00425 has original C$630,439.40 + amendment C$14,410.12 = contract value C$644,849.52, i.e. cumulative. But the API comments show amendment rows are not reliably cumulative (C-2024-2025-Q4-00116 has original C$1.00M and contract value C$0.40M). FY24-25 may therefore hold similar distortions. Downgraded from strong. PHAC is a public-health and microbiology buyer, not academic research, so it is a weak proxy for 2A.

items.label: 2A
items.claim: F452's flat H1 2026 reading double-counts one PHAC contract. Deduplicated, PHAC's Illumina spend fell about 53% y/y in H1'26.
items.detail: Procurement 6D06353301 shows up twice: C-2025-2026-Q4-00424 (C$630,439, type C) and C-2025-2026-Q4-00425 (C$644,850, type A). The second row is an amendment whose contract_value is cumulative (C$630,439 + C$14,410). Counted once, PHAC H1'26 is C$1.244M on 20 orders, against C$2.621M on 46 orders in H1'25 (−53% in value, −57% in orders). If the earlier ~C$3.19M all-federal H1'26 total added both rows, the corrected figure is about C$2.55M, or about −22% vs C$3.29M rather than −3%.
items.source_name: Government of Canada Proactive Disclosure of Contracts
items.why_new: Corrects F452. Amendment rows (instrument_type A) repeat the cumulative value and were not removed before.
items.verify_note: Verified: row C-2025-2026-Q4-00425 (2026-02-04, PHAC, type A) has contract value C$644,849.52 = C$630,439.40 + C$14,410.12, so counting both rows double-counts. The corrected −53% PHAC H1 figure follows. The all-federal −22% depends on the earlier total having included both rows, which is plausible but unconfirmed.

items.label: 2A
items.claim: Excluding instrument purchases, consumable-type Illumina spend at PHAC and AAFC fell 70–77% y/y in H1 2026. The headline is propped up by new instruments.
items.detail: PHAC H1'26 without the C$644.8K equipment buy is C$0.599M, against C$2.621M in H1'25 (−77%); all H1'25 PHAC rows were 'Medical supplies'/lab supplies. At Agriculture and Agri-Food Canada (AAFC), H1'26 without the C$404.9K instrument is C$108.8K on 8 orders, against C$364.5K on 20 orders in H1'25 (−70%). About C$1.45M of the deduplicated ~C$2.55M federal H1'26 total (~57%) is three instrument buys: Health Canada C$404.9K, AAFC C$404.9K and PHAC C$644.8K.
items.source_name: Government of Canada Proactive Disclosure of Contracts
items.why_new: First split of federal Illumina spend into instruments and consumables. F452 treated H1'26 as one flat total.
items.verify_note: Relabelled from 1C. Canadian federal labs are immaterial to Illumina's global Gb volume; this is a government-funding and research-demand signal. Caveat: Health Canada and AAFC each show a C$404.9K instrument, which may be a duplicate. If so, the instrument share of the federal H1'26 total is about C$1.05M, not C$1.45M.

items.label: 2A
items.claim: PHAC's year-end (Jan–Mar) Illumina reagent buying collapsed by about 88% in 2026.
items.detail: Federal departments usually spend leftover budget before the 31 March fiscal year-end. PHAC's Jan–Mar Illumina buying was C$2.49M in 2024 and C$2.54M in 2025 (42 orders, including call-ups of C$394K, C$254K, C$230K, C$134K and C$132K). In 2026 the same window had only C$0.303M of supplies on 10 orders, plus the C$644.8K equipment procurement. Without that equipment, the decline is −88% y/y.
items.source_name: Government of Canada Proactive Disclosure of Contracts
items.why_new: F451 covered Oct–Dec only. The fiscal year-end budget flush is a separate, larger signal.
items.verify_note: This is a subset of F508/F510 (the PHAC Jan–Mar window), not an independent finding. It is useful only as evidence that the fiscal-year-end budget flush disappeared.

items.label: 2A
items.claim: PHAC's large-order Illumina channel through standing offer CW2237770 went quiet for 12.5 months, and orders of C$100K or more fell from 21 (2024) to 8 (2025) to 1 (H1'26).
items.detail: Call-ups against standing offer CW2237770 (a pre-negotiated government supply agreement; all Illumina, all PHAC) were C$2.01M across 21 orders in 2024. There were none between 31 Oct 2024 and 18 Nov 2025, then 2 orders worth C$0.25M in 2025 and 2 worth C$0.21M in H1'26 (C$63.6K and C$150.9K). Across all PHAC Illumina contracts, orders of C$100K or more fell from 21 in 2024 to 8 in 2025 to 1 consumables order in H1'26 (C$150.9K, 13 May 2026). The many small C$20–25K orders largely continue.
items.source_name: Government of Canada Proactive Disclosure of Contracts
items.why_new: F457 covered only small monthly orders. The large-order collapse and the standing-offer gap are new.
items.verify_note: New detail on the large-order channel: the standing offer went silent for 12.5 months and orders of C$100K+ fell from 21 to 8 to 1. Small orders continuing fits volume rationing rather than a platform exit.

items.label: 2A
items.claim: Much of PHAC's decline is the end of COVID-era genomic surveillance, not switching to rivals or price pressure.
items.detail: PHAC's procurement 6D06304822 (Illumina, 'Medical supplies') was a C$15.40M reagent contract dated 4 Jun 2021, amended by +C$3.88M to C$19.28M, with delivery through 31 May 2023. That single pandemic contract is about 2.5x PHAC's full FY24-25 Illumina spend. Most of the multi-year drop is therefore normalization after the pandemic surveillance build-out, so it is a weak read on Illumina pricing or share.
items.source_name: Government of Canada Proactive Disclosure of Contracts
items.why_new: The COVID master contract was not in F447–F460 and changes how the decline should be read.
items.verify_note: The proactive-disclosure dataset records a contract at its contract date. So the C$15.40M original (4 Jun 2021) falls in calendar 2021 and does not sit in the 2022–2025 sums behind F447/F448. Only the C$3.88M amendment could land in 2022, and its date was not shown. The point only weakens comparisons against pre-2024 baselines. It cannot explain the post-pandemic 2024→2026 declines (F508–F512, −53% to −77%). The '2.5x FY24-25 spend' ratio compares a multi-year contract with one year of spend, so

items.label: 2A
items.claim: Earlier federal baselines were inflated by duplicate amendment rows, so the measured 2022→2025 and 2024→2025 declines are overstated.
items.detail: Several contracts appear more than once with the same contract date. PHAC service contract 6D06315510 appears at C$2.80M and at C$2.88M (cumulative), both dated 29 Aug 2022. PHAC equipment 6D06325263 appears at C$609K and at C$850K, both dated 10 Feb 2023. CFIA 20240441A appears as an original row (~C$1.00M) plus two amendment rows (C$0.40M and C$1.21M), all dated 5 Mar 2024; AAFC and Health Canada have smaller cases. If those baselines were summed naively, PHAC 2022 (~C$9.6M) is overstated by ~C$2.8M (true ~C$6.8M, so ~−51% to 2025, not −65%), and 2024 all-federal is overstated by ~C$1.5M.
items.source_name: Government of Canada Proactive Disclosure of Contracts
items.why_new: Methodology correction to F447/F448 baselines.
items.verify_note: New: it corrects the PHAC 2022 baseline in F448 to about C$6.8M, so 2022→2025 is about −51% rather than −65%, and it trims the 2024 all-federal figure by about C$1.5M. It does not touch F508/F509, which were already deduplicated. The direction of the federal decline stands; only its size shrinks.

items.label: 2A
items.claim: The federal trough may be behind: PHAC's Apr–Jun 2026 Illumina spend nearly quadrupled y/y, and NRC's H1'26 already exceeds its full 2025.
items.detail: PHAC Apr–Jun 2026 was C$0.296M on 9 orders, against C$0.078M on 4 orders in Apr–Jun 2025 (+280%). That includes a C$150.9K call-up on 13 May 2026, the first consumables order over C$100K since Dec 2025. National Research Council (NRC) Illumina orders were C$580K (21 orders) in 2022, C$293K (13) in 2023, C$120K (7) in 2024 and C$57K (3) in 2025. In H1'26 NRC already had C$74K (3 orders).
items.source_name: Government of Canada Proactive Disclosure of Contracts
items.why_new: F449 gave only NRC's 2022–25 decline. The Q2'26 PHAC and H1'26 NRC rebound is new.
items.verify_note: The NRC part repeats F492 (C$74K in H1'26 vs C$57K in 2025). The PHAC Apr–Jun 2026 rise (+280%) is on a tiny base (C$0.08M→C$0.30M, about 4% of PHAC's FY24-25 spend of about C$7.3M), and it coexists with deduplicated H1'26 at −53% y/y (F509). A single C$151K call-up drives most of it. Not evidence that the trough has passed.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: Repeat federal Illumina orders show flat nominal prices for years, with only a ~1.2% step down at PHAC in Dec 2024.
items.detail: AAFC bought a C$24,040.80 chemicals order (commodity 6810) on both 16 Jan 2024 and 17 Jan 2025. AAFC's C$23,445.24 order recurs 8 times from Oct 2019 to Jan 2023. C$24,848.25 recurs at NRC (6 times, Feb 2022–Jan 2023; plus C$49,696.50 = 2x in Feb 2021 and Jan 2023) and at AAFC (Mar and Nov 2022). PHAC's monthly C$23,930.55 order (6 times, Jun–Nov 2024) became C$23,649.00 (Dec 2024–Jan 2025, 3 times) and C$23,648.99/23,648.59 (Feb and Oct 2025), −1.2%. Caveat: SKUs are not disclosed, and orders may be sized to a C$25K sole-source threshold.
items.source_name: Government of Canada Proactive Disclosure of Contracts
items.why_new: First repeat-order unit-price series from this dataset (strategist question 3).

items.label: 1B
items.claim: Illumina service contracts at federal labs renew at flat or higher prices, with no sign of service discounting.
items.detail: AAFC renewed an Illumina repair/maintenance contract (commodity JX66) at exactly C$12,625.04 on 17 Feb 2025 (to Mar 2026) and again on 4 Feb 2026 (to Mar 2027). Health Canada paid C$25,929.32 a year on each of two service contracts (4500415550 and 4500418242), renewed unchanged 2020–2025. In Dec 2024 these were replaced by HT28246602 at C$57,039, about 10% above the C$51,859 combined, later amended to C$88,728 (to Jan 2026). ECCC's renewals held at C$37,203.89 a year from 2022 to 2025.
items.source_name: Government of Canada Proactive Disclosure of Contracts
items.why_new: Service-renewal pricing was not covered in F447–F460.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: PHAC's sole-source Illumina fleet service contract runs to 31 Aug 2027 and was enlarged in early 2025, so the legacy fleet is under service for at least another year.
items.detail: Procurement 6D06315510 is a repair and maintenance contract for lab instruments: C$2.80M, 29 Aug 2022 to 31 Aug 2027 (about C$0.56M a year), limited-tendering reason 71, one bid. An amendment of +C$126.6K was reported in FY24-25 Q4, bringing it to C$2.88M. The instruments are not named, so this does not show 6000s specifically. It does commit the National Microbiology Lab's pandemic-era Illumina fleet to service through mid-2027.
items.source_name: Government of Canada Proactive Disclosure of Contracts
items.why_new: Answers strategist question 2 on service renewals. Not in F447–F460.

items.label: 2B
items.claim: PacBio long-read purchases at Canadian agriculture labs held steady through 2024–26 while those labs' Illumina consumable buying fell.
items.detail: AAFC bought PacBio at an identical C$21,864.00 five times (Mar 2024–Feb 2025), and the Canadian Grain Commission (CGC) bought C$18–24K PacBio orders through 19 Jan 2026. CGC also bought a C$679K PacBio instrument in Mar 2022. PacBio federal orders totaled about C$144K in 2024 and about C$130K in 2025, roughly flat. Over the same period AAFC's Illumina non-instrument spend fell 70% y/y in H1'26.
items.source_name: Government of Canada Proactive Disclosure of Contracts
items.why_new: Canadian federal PacBio spend was not covered. Earlier items covered ONT, Element and MGI only.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: A Danish university's 2025 award explicitly replaces an older NovaSeq 6000 and a NextSeq 500 with a NovaSeq X Plus, so 6000 retirement is still going on in 2025.
items.detail: University of Copenhagen TED notice 197476-2025 (a negotiated procedure with no prior publication) was awarded to Illumina Denmark ApS on 28 Feb 2025 at USD 2,878,114. It describes the X Plus as an upgrade that replaces the older NovaSeq 6000 and the NextSeq 500. This is a university, not a hospital. It is one instrument, with no kit data. This is search-result snippet level only, because the PDF fetch returned empty.
items.quote: replace the older Illumina NovaSeq6000
items.why_new: The notice was already seen, but the award date, USD value, supplier and the NextSeq 500 co-replacement were not recorded.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: Rigshospitalet's X Plus purchase is an addition to an existing X Plus with mutual backup, not a 6000 replacement. That fits dual-running or capacity expansion rather than a 6000 exit.
items.detail: The Capital Region of Denmark procurement is titled 'Whole genome sequencing apparatus for Rigshospitalet'. The final contracted value is DKK 8.5M excluding VAT. The notice says the two X Plus units 'can act as a backup for each other'. It does not mention the NovaSeq 6000 and gives no supplier or award date. It is no evidence that the hospital is leaving a 6000.
items.quote: the two NovaSeq X plus can act as a backup for each other
items.why_new: The notice was already seen, but the exact justification (capacity plus mutual backup between two X Plus units, no 6000 named) is now confirmed.

items.label: 2A
items.claim: A national Canadian research sequencing provider publishes all-inclusive per-sample prices and explicitly credits NovaSeq X and the 25B flow cell for lowering them.
items.detail: The Génome Québec standard price list (undated, 2026 footer) shows human WGS at C$525, exome 100x at C$316, and mRNA-seq at C$172 (25M reads) and C$237 (50M reads), library prep included. The same-source claim is that it 'introduced lower prices' through early X/25B adoption. This is a single snapshot with no earlier prices, so the pass-through rate is unquantified. For comparison, TCAG Toronto (Apr 2025) lists NovaSeq X WGS at C$650 including prep, so Génome Québec is about C$125 (19%) cheaper.
items.source_name: Génome Québec Centre d'expertise et de services
items.quote: introduced lower prices, thanks to our position as world leader
items.why_new: A per-sample all-inclusive Canadian price point; the known list covers per-lane or per-Gb core prices only.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: GEO shows the NovaSeq 6000's share of human sequencing submissions fell from 99.9% to 87%, then flattened between Q1 and Q2 2026.
items.detail: Human GSM counts by release quarter: 6000 was 26,287 (Q1'24), 27,542 (Q1'25), 29,447 (Q1'26) and 29,621 (Q2'26). X was 36, 1,761, 4,333 and 4,269. The 6000 share of the 6000+X total was 99.9%, 94.0%, 87.2% and 87.4%. The 6000 sample count is flat to up, not falling, and the share was flat quarter to quarter in 2026. This is research-heavy public data with a publication lag, so it shows a long sticky tail, not current conversion.
items.why_new: First public-dataset count of 6000 versus X sample submissions by quarter; none of the known evidence uses GEO.

items.label: 2B
items.claim: GEO data does not yet show a visible share shift away from Illumina in research, because only the X was measured.
items.detail: I could not find platform IDs for AVITI, UG100 or DNBSEQ-T7, so I have no non-Illumina share. Illumina's own X is still only about 13% of human GEO sequencing samples in Q1-Q2 2026. Any rival share is not measurable from this probe and needs the deep extraction described in how_to_mine.
items.why_new: New public-data baseline for the X's presence in research submissions.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: Public buyers are still signing sole-source NovaSeq 6000 service contracts in Aug 2026, which suggests 6000 sites are not retiring on the thesis timeline.
items.detail: NCI awarded Illumina a NovaSeq 6000 maintenance agreement worth $96,859 on 24 Aug 2026. The solicitation was posted 14 Aug 2026 as sole source, covering preventive maintenance for one 6000 system. Separate sole-source 6000 notices appear for Alberta and CanadaBuys in 2026. This is one site and one small contract, so it is a weak datapoint.
items.quote: MAINTENANCE AGREEMENT ON NOVASEQ 6000 SYSTEM
items.why_new: A dated 2026 federal 6000 service award with a dollar value; the known list has only vendor and core-facility 6000 retirements.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: Novogene's single-lane prices for the NovaSeq X are falling only about 5–7% a year, far slower than Illumina's blended revenue-per-Gb decline of about 15–19% a year.
items.detail: 25B lane: $2.95/Gb (Nov 2023–Mar 2024, $2,799 on ~950 Gb) to $2.55/Gb (Sep 2026, $2,549 on 1,000 Gb). That is −13.5% over about 30 months, or about −5.6%/yr. 10B lane: $4.53 to $4.13/Gb from Q2'25 to Sep'26, −8.8% over about 15 months, or about −7%/yr. Illumina's implied total revenue/Gb fell 15–19% (known), mostly from the 6000-to-X mix shift. A low-cost research reseller that is already fully on the X shows steady but modest erosion with no acceleration through Sep 2026.
items.why_new: The known list has only the two 2026 25B promos; this adds an annualized erosion rate and compares it with Illumina's blended $/Gb decline.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: Carver's Aug 2026 rate card puts the X 10B lane at about 1.4–1.6x the 25B per Gb, and Novogene's at about 1.6x, so the 10B-premium compression in D018 is not universal.
items.detail: Carver (eff. 1 Aug 2026): 10B 2x150 lane $2,000 ($1,710 for 8+ lanes) vs 25B $3,380 ($3,180). On ~375 Gb vs ~1,000 Gb per lane that is $5.33 vs $3.38/Gb (1.58x), or $4.56 vs $3.18/Gb (1.43x) on the 8+ tier. Novogene Sep 2026: $4.13 vs $2.55/Gb (1.62x). Both sit with TCAG's 1.60x (D042), above the 1.03–1.38x seen at TGen, KUMC and Berkeley. Carver gives a much larger volume discount on the 10B (−14.5%) than on the 25B (−5.9%).
items.source_name: UIUC Carver DNA Services pricing; Novogene pages
items.quote: All pricing is updated, effective Aug. 1, 2026.
items.why_new: Carver's 10B lane prices were not in any earlier item; this extends the 10B/25B ratio set with two more data points.

items.label: 2A
items.claim: After removing duplicates and instruments, Canadian federal consumable-type Illumina spend fell about 60–70% y/y in H1 2026.
items.detail: The deduplicated federal H1'26 total is about C$2.55M (F509). About C$1.05–1.45M of that is instrument buys: PHAC C$644.8K and AAFC C$404.9K, plus a Health Canada C$404.9K row that may duplicate the AAFC one (F510). That leaves about C$1.10–1.50M of non-instrument spend, against about C$3.29M in H1'25 (−54% to −67%; this assumes H1'25 was mostly supplies, as it was at PHAC). On PHAC's fiscal year, FY25-26 without the equipment is about C$1.12M vs C$7.32M in FY24-25 (−85%). The headline flat reading in F452 hides a sharp drop in reagent buying.
items.source_name: Government of Canada Proactive Disclosure of Contracts
items.why_new: Combines the deduplication fix with the instrument carve-out into one consumables-only federal decline, flagging the possible HC/AAFC duplicate.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: Illumina raised a legacy MiSeq service plan about 11% a year after end of sale, so a retired-platform tail can carry price increases on service.
items.detail: CFIA's MiSeq support-plan renewals rose from C$20,420.62 (Jul and Nov 2024) to C$23,894.87 (Jan 2026), +17% in about 18 months (about +11%/yr), and CFIA's total plan spend went from C$92K (5 plans, 2024) to C$161K (7 plans, 2025). MiSeq end of sale was 30 Sep 2025 (known). This concerns service, not consumables, and the dollars are immaterial. It is only a template for how Illumina may price a 6000 service tail.
items.quote: MiSeq Silver Plan Renewal
items.why_new: Annualizes the price increase on legacy service plans after end of sale; nothing in the known list covers legacy service pricing.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: NHS trusts still award single-source Illumina contracts for older-platform consumables through 2027, which shows installed older instruments stay in use.
items.detail: Guy's & St Thomas' NHS FT awarded Illumina Cambridge Ltd £156,200.91 for MiSeq reagents on 1 Sep 2026. The term is 1 year (to 15 Sep 2027) and the notice says no reasonable substitute exists. This is a MiSeq, not a NovaSeq 6000, so it is only indirect support for a sticky older-instrument tail.
items.source_name: Stotles (mirror of Find a Tender notice 082609-2026)
items.quote: no reasonable alternative or substitute exists
items.why_new: A new 2026 NHS single-source Illumina award on an older MiSeq platform; no NovaSeq 6000 or X data.

items.label: 2B
items.claim: Per-organism AVITI platform records are proliferating on GEO, showing a broad research user base spanning many species.
items.detail: A GEO title search for 'AVITI' returns 64 platform records, almost all one per organism (E. coli/MS2, Brachypodium, Cylindrotheca, Chlorocebus, Pan troglodytes, Octodon degus and others). The latest were created 14 Jul–29 Sep 2026 (GPL37215–GPL37604). New AVITI entries are appearing nearly weekly, so many labs are now submitting AVITI data, though most new records have 0–2 samples.
items.why_new: Gives a count (64 AVITI platform records) and creation dates not in the known list.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: Q3'26 human NovaSeq 6000 GEO samples jumped to 36,312, a 7-quarter high, so the 6000 tail is not visibly shrinking in published data.
items.detail: The 6000 series runs 27,542 (Q1'25), 29,509, 30,111, 30,855, 29,447 (Q1'26), 29,621, then 36,312 (Q3'26, +22.6% q/q). Months in Q3'26: Jul 15,621, Aug 10,617, Sep 10,074. The Q3 rise is not one giant series: 6000 series count rose from 1,408 to 1,647 (+17%), and samples per series were 21.0 vs 22.0. It is a lagged read of 2024–25 6000 sequencing, so it fits the 6000 tail being large.
items.why_new: Q3'26 count, monthly split and series-vs-sample check are new.
items.verify_note: I verified the Q3'26 count of 36,312 against NCBI eutils. But GEO is almost entirely published research data, sequenced 1–3 years earlier, while the thesis tail is clinical (about 80% of remaining 6000 Gb is clinical). It also lacks an X-platform comparison: if X GSMs grew faster, the 6000 share is still falling. At most, it is a lagged signal that research 6000 output persisted through 2024–25. Downgraded to weak.

items.label: 2A
items.claim: X-platform GEO series are growing faster than 6000 series, but each X series carries about as many samples, so newer data is not larger-scale yet.
items.detail: Q3'26 vs Q2'26: X series 251 vs 177 (+42%); 6000 series 1,647 vs 1,408 (+17%). X samples per series were about 21 (5,268/251) vs about 24 (4,269/177). X's share of 6000+X series was 13.2% in Q3 vs 11.2% in Q2. The research community is adopting the X, with no sign of bulk-lane megaprojects driving it.
items.why_new: Series-level counts were not in the earlier GEO work.

items.label: 2B
items.claim: AVITI reached 2.9% of human 6000+X samples in Q2'26 before slipping to 2.0% in Q3'26, so the rival's research share is small and lumpy.
items.detail: AVITI human 999 in Q2'26 vs 6000+X 33,890 = 2.9%; Q3'26 831/41,580 = 2.0%; Q4'25 389/33,385 = 1.2%; Q1'25 62/29,303 = 0.2%. The Q2 peak looks like a big batch release. Series for AVITI over Apr–Sep 2026 total only 87. The pattern is up from about 0.2% to about 2–3% in six quarters, but not yet at a scale that moves Illumina research volume.
items.why_new: Quarterly AVITI share of 6000+X is new.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: Illumina's IVDR roadmap, as of Oct 2026, shows the NovaSeq 6000Dx as the only high-throughput IVD sequencer, with no NovaSeq X Dx, so the EU regulated tail has no certified X path.
items.detail: The IVDR guidance page lists MiSeqDx, NextSeq 550Dx and NovaSeq 6000Dx as the Class A IVD instruments, and no NovaSeq X Dx. Its X references are only to the research NovaSeq X Plus roadmap. The DRAGEN Server for NovaSeq 6000Dx has a CE mark (IVDR). The NovaSeq 6000Dx page lists no NovaSeq X Dx or successor, and neither does a web search for 'NovaSeq X Dx'. Only the 6000Dx S2 and S4 reagent kits are IVD-compliant. EU labs needing certified high-throughput CE-IVD workflows therefore have no certified X to move to, which supports management's claim of a permanent clinical 6000 tail.
items.why_new: The known list covers US FDA PMAs (no X named) and the 6000Dx (2022), but not Illumina's own IVDR roadmap showing no X Dx and no dates.
items.verify_note: Largely known: no NovaSeq X Dx exists and only the 6000Dx (2022) does. The EU IVDR framing is the only new piece. Direction 'against' is correct, because it supports a stickier tail and so cuts against the ~5 points of conversion. However, most clinical 6000 volume runs LDT or RUO workflows rather than 6000Dx kits (see F534), so a missing X Dx does not bind most of the tail.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: The IVDR page gives no dates for Illumina's own planned IVDR products, so no near-term EU certified X path exists. IVDR deadlines (31 Dec 2027 Class D, 2028 Class C, 2029 Class B and sterile A) are generic.
items.detail: TruSight Oncology Comprehensive (EU) is Class C with a CE mark under the old IVDD, and its page says 'IVDR compliance in progress'. Targeted gene panels, the somatic interpretation platform and the germline insights engine are listed as in development or planned for IVDR submission, with no dates. The NovaSeq 6000Dx page puts TSO Comprehensive and VeriSeq NIPT under the NextSeq 550Dx column, not the 6000Dx. The Class C deadline of 31 Dec 2028 falls inside the thesis window. If a Dx X does not appear by then, certified EU workflows stay on the 6000Dx, 550Dx or other boxes. Absence of a date does not prove none is planned.
items.quote: IVDR compliance in progress
items.why_new: Gives Illumina's own IVDR timeline and the 'no dates, no X Dx' status for EU, which the known list does not cover.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: Illumina's IVDR assay table has no assay with an IVDR plan for the X, and its one flagship oncology panel is still on the old IVDD CE mark.
items.detail: TruSight Oncology Comprehensive (EU, Class C) is listed as 'CE mark (IVDD)' with IVDR compliance in progress. The page gives no date. The Class C transition deadline is 31 Dec 2028. The same product runs only on the NextSeq 550Dx, so oncology IVD volume in the EU sits on mid-throughput kit, not on the X. The implication for the thesis is that clinical lock-in on older platforms may last into 2028–29.
items.why_new: The known list covers the US TSO PMA (NextSeq 550Dx only). This adds the EU IVDR status, still on IVDD.
items.verify_note: TSO Comprehensive is a NextSeq 550Dx product, which is mid-throughput and not the 6000. 'NextSeq 550Dx only' is already known. Its IVDD/IVDR status tells us nothing about NovaSeq 6000→X conversion. If it showed anything, lock-in would cut against the thesis rather than support it.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: The NovaSeq 6000Dx's own product page lists only 6000-family kits and no assay, so the regulated tail has no named assay and no X migration path.
items.detail: The page lists compatible items as the 6000Dx Library Tube, S2/S4 Reagent Kits (300-cycle) and DNA Prep with Enrichment Dx plus the DRAGEN app. The comparison table names only 'Future Illumina assays' and 'Future partner assays' for the 6000Dx, with TSO Comprehensive and VeriSeq NIPT appearing only under the NextSeq 550Dx. In the US the intended use is targeted sequencing only and is explicitly not for whole-genome sequencing. Regulated 6000Dx volume is therefore small and limited to panels, and its use cases do not include the genome work that drives clinical Gb.
items.quote: Not intended for whole-genome or de novo sequencing
items.why_new: The known list has no 6000Dx spec or intended-use detail. This shows the Dx tail is panel-only.
items.verify_note: New detail: the US 6000Dx intended use is targeted sequencing only and not WGS, and the page names no assays. This implies little true 6000Dx-locked volume, so less of the tail is regulation-bound and more can convert. Caveat: FDA-approved tests such as F1CDx and Caris MI Cancer Seek name the RUO NovaSeq 6000 in their PMAs, not the 6000Dx. The regulated tail therefore extends beyond 6000Dx kits, and the inference that 'regulated volume is small' is overstated.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: Illumina's DNA Prep with Enrichment Dx support page lists MiSeqDx, NextSeq 550Dx and NovaSeq 6000Dx but not the X, so the IVDR enrichment workflow is tied to legacy architecture.
items.detail: The page says the kit is IVDR 2017/746 compliant and FDA-registered. Its sequencer compatibility list names only the three Dx instruments. No planned products or dates are given.
items.why_new: No IVDR-compliant library-prep workflow on the X is in the known list.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: Illumina's IVDR page shows its planned IVDR submissions are software and unnamed panels, with no dates and no instrument, so a certified X remains undated beyond 2027.
items.detail: Two unnamed software items, a somatic interpretation platform and an AI germline insights engine, are marked 'Planned for IVDR submission'. An unnamed targeted gene panel is 'in development for IVDR launch'. Potential Class B controls and Class C oncology panels are listed as future offerings. No instrument and no dates appear, while the Class C deadline is 31 Dec 2028.
items.quote: Planned for IVDR submission
items.why_new: The known list lacks the pipeline entries or the absence of any instrument in them.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: The regulated EU tail is probably small, because the 6000Dx is a panel-only IVD and most clinical volume runs under lab-developed or research-use workflows.
items.detail: The 6000Dx US intended use is targeted sequencing only and excludes whole-genome work. The page names no current assay. Management's clinical X share was already 78% in Q2'26. So the IVD-locked share of 6000 volume is likely a minor part of the tail, which weakens an IVDR-based case for permanent 6000 residence.
items.why_new: Gives a watch-out on the size of the IVD lock-in; not in the known list.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: In Illumina's own Open Offer catalogue, 6000 reagent list prices rose 15.1% between Sep 2022 and Feb 2024 while the X 10B stayed flat, so part of the tail's high price per Gb is a list-price effect.
items.detail: NovaSeq 6000 S4 300-cycle list was $14,400 (Sep 2022), $15,940 (Feb 2023, +10.7%) and $16,578 (Feb 2024, +4.0%), which is +15.1% cumulative. S2 300 went $9,600→$10,627→$11,052, SP 300 went $3,000→$3,321→$3,454, and NextSeq 550 HO 300 rose by the same +15.1%. The X 10B 300-cycle stayed at $9,600 in all three revisions, and the 6000 instrument stayed at $985K. Illumina raised the blade price on the legacy platform while holding the X, which widens the 6000/X gap independently of volume. Part of the reported revenue-per-Gb ratio drift (2.2x→3.4x) therefore comes from price moves on the 6000 side, and tail users have absorbed these rises. List prices only; net prices depend on the discount tiers.
items.source_name: Illumina Open Offer, Appendix 1 to Exhibit A (list-price catalogue), three revisions
items.why_new: The known list covers core and distributor prices and the 4% CNAG rise. This is Illumina's own contract catalogue, showing +10.7% (Feb 2023) and +4.0% (Feb 2024) on 6000 consumables against 0% on the X 10B.
items.verify_note: The PDF did not render, so I could not open it directly. It is corroborated independently: the UConn Jan 2025 rate for the S4-300 ($16,578, F479) exactly matches the claimed Feb 2024 Open Offer list. Correction: all the rises fall between Sep 2022 and Feb 2024, which is before or at the start of the Q2'24→Q2'26 ratio series (2.2x→3.4x). UConn's Feb 2026 price ($15,938, −3.9%) suggests the 6000 list was cut in 2025. So list moves do not explain the 2024–26 widening of the ratio. They explain the

items.label: 1A
items.claim: At published Open Offer discounts the 6000-to-25B gap is only 2.45–2.82x per Gb, well below the 3.4x revenue-per-Gb ratio in Illumina's disclosures, so reported X pricing sits 17–28% below the published schedule.
items.detail: Feb 2024 list per Gb, using spec outputs of ~3,000 Gb for S4-300 and ~8,000 Gb for 25B-300 (my assumption): S4 $16,578/3,000 = $5.53 and 25B $16,000/8,000 = $2.00, a 2.76x gap. Net at the top spend tier (≥$100M) is S4 $5.53×0.78 = $4.31 against 25B $2.00×0.88 = $1.76, a 2.45x gap. At $20–30M it is $4.97 against $1.86 (2.67x), and at $5–10M it is $5.36 against $1.90 (2.82x). Reported 3.4x implies X realized price per Gb 1 − (2.45 to 2.82)/3.4 = 17–28% below what the published schedule gives. That points to off-schedule discounts on X, or Gb shipped versus Gb consumed differences. This matches the 2.4–2.5x core-level result and is an independent contract-side check.
items.source_name: Illumina Open Offer Appendix 1 (rev. 31 May 2024), Table 1 and list catalogue
items.why_new: The known notes derive 3.4x from reported shares and cross-check it only with core rate cards. This computes the ratio from Illumina's contract list and discount tiers (my arithmetic, spec-output assumption stated).
items.verify_note: Mostly a restatement of D029 (2.4x at GSA/NCI prices) using the Open Offer schedule. Calling the gap 'X realized 17–28% below schedule' ignores the known alternative: the 6000 mix is skewed to small SP/S2 flow cells at 4–10x per Gb (D028/D032), and Gb shipped is not the same as Gb consumed. It also uses ≥$100M as the top tier, while F540 says ≥$50M, so the two items are internally inconsistent. The 25B list of $16,000 is the 2024 figure; it was $16,480 in Jan 2025.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: The 25B's published consumables discount tops out at 12% (≥$100M annual spend) against 22% for the 6000 and 10B, so the schedule leaves wide room for off-schedule deals with large accounts.
items.detail: Table 1 (identical in the 25 Jan and 31 May 2024 revisions): 25B discount runs 3% ($1–5M), 5% ($5–15M), 7% ($15–30M), 10% ($30–50M) and 12% (≥$50M). The 6000/10B column runs 0%, 3%, 5%, 10%, 13%, 15%, 17%, 20% and 22%. The 25B is richer below $20M and shallower above it. At the top tier the 25B nets $1.76/Gb (12% off $16,000) against $2.50/Gb for the 10B (22% off $9,600), a 29.5% drop in net price per Gb. Open Offer customers include US oncology labs such as Caris. Expert claims that big accounts pay 'half or a quarter' of small accounts therefore cannot come from the published schedule, so they must be bespoke contracts, which is where extra discounting would show up. Only the schedule is visible here, not the bespoke terms.
items.why_new: The known notes mention the Open Offer's MFN and price-only-falls clauses but none of the actual tier percentages by flow cell.
items.verify_note: I could not read the PDF to check the tier table. Internal arithmetic holds: 12% off $2.00 is $1.76 and 22% off $3.20 is $2.50, a drop of −29.5%. The top-tier threshold is inconsistent with F539 (≥$50M vs ≥$100M) and needs a check. The inference that 'half or a quarter' pricing must come from bespoke contracts is fair. This is schedule evidence only.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: Illumina's 25B list was set 37.5% below the 10B per Gb at launch, and the same price curve would put a 35B at about −15% per Gb versus the 25B.
items.detail: 10B-300 list is $9,600 for ~3,000 Gb ($3.20/Gb) and 25B-300 is $16,000 for ~8,000 Gb ($2.00/Gb), so the price went up 66.7% for 2.67x the output. That is a price-to-output exponent of ln(1.667)/ln(2.667) = 0.52. If a 35B (+40% output, per the roadmap) followed the same curve, price would be 1.4^0.52 = 1.19x, about $19.1K, or $1.70/Gb, which is −15% versus the 25B. That is milder than the known ~20% and ~25% estimates, so the 35B depends on Illumina choosing a steeper step than its last one. At the top Open Offer tier the net per-Gb path is 10B $2.50 (Sep 2022) to 25B $1.76 (Jan 2024), −29.5% in about 16 months.
items.source_name: Illumina Open Offer Appendix 1 (list catalogue); my extrapolation
items.why_new: The known 35B estimates are hearsay or UBS arithmetic. This derives a 35B price from the observed 10B→25B list step; the exponent is mine and spec outputs are assumed.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: The published discount tiers did not move between Jan and May 2024, and no 2025–26 Appendix 1 revision appears in the index, so the public contract shows no acceleration of discounting.
items.detail: The 25 Jan 2024 and 31 May 2024 revisions have identical Table 1 (consumables), Table 2 (hardware), Table 3 (credits) and Table 4 (service) percentages. Only the list-price base changed, from Feb 2023 to Feb 2024. The page's dated changes after Oct 2023 are new NovaSeq X and NextSeq XLEAP consumables becoming eligible, and a 18 Mar 2024 amendment for reduced NovaSeq 6000Dx pricing. Search returned no revision dated 2025 or 2026. The top X Plus/6000 tier has been 22% since Sep 2022. If large accounts are getting deeper discounts, it is happening off-schedule. A site that stopped being updated or an unindexed newer file would both look the same, so this is weak-to-medium.
items.source_name: Illumina Open Offer test-terms page and Appendix 1 revisions
items.why_new: It tests discount acceleration directly on the contract schedule, comparing revisions Jan 2022, Sep 2022, Jan 2024 and May 2024.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: The Open Offer's 'at least 43% lower' price-per-Gb commitment was already met on list by Feb 2024, so the contract does not force further cuts.
items.detail: The Jan 2022 catalogue has S4 v1.5 300-cycle at $14,400, about $4.80/Gb on a ~3,000 Gb spec, or $3.74 at the 22% top discount. A 43% reduction implies ≤$2.74/Gb. The 25B-300 at $16,000 is $2.00/Gb on list (−58% vs S4 list), or $1.76 at the 12% top discount (−53% vs S4 net). The 2025 commitment was therefore cleared roughly a year early. The known notes list the 43% clause and an unverified ~$4/Gb baseline but no check against actual catalogue prices. Whether Illumina measures against this 'S4 standard terms' baseline is unconfirmed. If the clause is already satisfied, it is not what drives the next price cut.
items.source_name: Illumina Open Offer Appendix 1 (Jan 2022 and May 2024 revisions); test-terms page
items.why_new: The known notes cite the 43% clause but report no remedy or measurement found. This tests it against the published catalogue prices.
items.verify_note: New check of the known 43% clause against actual catalogue prices. Caveats: it compares a 25B list price with an S4 baseline (the clause covers the highest-throughput product, which the 25B now is), and the March 2021 baseline (~$4/Gb in the known notes vs $4.80 on list here) is unconfirmed. The conclusion that the clause does not force further cuts holds either way, because the 25B is about 42–58% below on any baseline.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: The Open Offer discount tiers are keyed to annual consumables spend, so when conversion shrinks a customer's spend the discount percentage falls and cushions some of the price cut.
items.detail: Worked example: a customer spending $40M net on the 6000 (15% tier) moves the same Gb to 25B. List cost is 1/2.76 of the 6000's, so net spend falls to about $15.8M, which puts it in the 7% tier. Net price falls 60.4% ($40M→$15.8M), against a 63.8% list-to-list cut at equal discounts, about 3.4 points of cushion. Spend is defined as net invoiced sequencing consumables by contract year (15 Feb–14 Feb), with a refund or credit true-up within 60 days of the baseline period. Illumina's per-Gb revenue loss on conversion is therefore slightly smaller than a list-price comparison suggests, for tier-based customers. The reverse also applies: customers that grow volume rise through tiers and earn bigger discounts.
items.source_name: Illumina Open Offer Appendix 1, Table 1 and spend/true-up definitions
items.why_new: The known notes' conversion cost calcs use revenue-per-Gb ratios and do not model the contract's spend-tier mechanics.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: Instrument credits depend only on the installed instruments, not on consumables volume, and the program gives an X Plus 13 credits against 10 for a 6000, a small contractual nudge to swap boxes.
items.detail: Table 3 credits: NovaSeq X Plus 13, NovaSeq 6000Dx 11, NovaSeq X 10, NovaSeq 6000 10, NextSeq 500/550/1000/2000 3 and MiSeq 1, counted only for instruments under an active Illumina service contract in the customer's or affiliates' US facilities. The consumables discount (Table 1) uses annual spend and does not use credits. Credits drive the hardware discount (Table 2: 5% at 1–30 credits up to 24% at ≥900 for NovaSeq-family instruments, 20% for NextSeq) and the service-contract discount (Table 4: 0% at 1 credit to 22% at ≥201). Reaching the 22% service tier takes 16 X Plus (208 credits) or 21 6000s (210). A 50-box fleet moving from 6000s to X Plus goes from 500 to 650 credits, moving the hardware discount from 20% to 22%. The effect is small, but it favors conversion. The Sep 2022 addendum is the Open Offer Appendix 1 (the same program as Core Notes 17), not a separate one.
items.date: 2022-09-29 (Table 3 unchanged through 2024-05-31 except the NovaSeq X row added)
items.quote: For each Installed Instrument, Customer shall be entitled to a specific number of Instrument Credits
items.why_new: It answers the open question on credits: they scale with installed boxes, not consumables, and X Plus carries 30% more credits than the 6000.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: In the Aug–Sep 2022 revision Illumina switched service-contract discounts to instrument credits, which raised discounts for NovaSeq 6000 fleets by 4–12 points.
items.detail: The Jan 2022 service table used instrument counts: 5–10 instruments 8%, 11–30 10%, 31–50 12%, 51–75 15%. The Sep 2022 table keeps the same percentages but applies them to credits, and a 6000 counts as 10 credits.
