A single 6000 now gets 8% (was 0%), 3 6000s get 10% (was 5%), 10 6000s get 20% (was 8%), 21 6000s get 22% (was 10%), and 50 6000s get 22% (was 12%). The test-terms page describes the change as revised 'in customers' favor', dated Aug 19, 2022. It came during the GRAIL antitrust review, so it may reflect remedy pressure rather than competition. Illumina has deepened discounts for large fleets at least once when pushed. It affects service revenue (about 15% of revenue), not consumables.
items.source_name: Illumina Open Offer Appendix 1, Table 4 (Jan 2022 vs Sep 2022); test-terms page
items.why_new: It is a dated, quantified change in discount structure that the known notes do not cover; the known list says only that tiers were added.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: Illumina keeps refurbishing and selling 6000s, with a certified pre-owned 6000 at $785K and a 6000Dx list cut 21%, which extends the tail rather than shrinking it.
items.detail: The May 2023 revision made Certified Pre-Owned NovaSeq 6000 systems eligible, and the Jan and May 2024 catalogues list a CPO 6000 RUO at $785,000, 20.3% below the new 6000's $985,000. The NovaSeq 6000Dx instrument list was $1,080,000 (Sep 2022, Jan 2024) and $850,000 in the May 2024 catalogue, a 21.3% cut. The 18 Mar 2024 amendment is described as reflecting newly reduced 6000Dx pricing. For comparison the X list is $985K for the single-flow-cell X and $1.25M for X Plus. A cheaper 6000/6000Dx purchase path adds installed boxes that later pull reagents, which supports management's claim that part of the tail stays. The count of CPO and 6000Dx units sold is not disclosed.
items.source_name: Illumina Open Offer Appendix 1 instrument catalogue; test-terms page change log
items.why_new: The known notes mention a 79% lease price and '>10 new 6000s' but not the CPO list price or the 21% 6000Dx instrument cut.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: In May 2024 Illumina cut NextSeq 1000/2000 list prices 20–36% per read by moving to XLEAP-SBS kits, showing price-per-Gb deflation below the X as well.
items.detail: P3 300-cycle XLEAP is $4,305 for up to 1.2B reads against the legacy P3 300 at $6,150 for 1.1B reads: −30.0% per kit and about −35.8% per read ($3,587 vs $5,591 per billion). P3 200-cycle is $3,229 against $4,612 (−30.0%), and P3 100-cycle is $2,332 against $3,331 (−30.0%). P2 300-cycle is $2,722 against $3,628 (−25.0%) for the same 400M reads, and P1 300-cycle is $1,000 against $1,250 (−20.0%). Legacy NextSeq 2000 kits were left at their old list, so the new line is a price-cut-plus-upgrade path. Mid-throughput is where known notes find buyers losing to cheaper rivals. List only; it says nothing about volume response.
items.source_name: Illumina Open Offer Appendix 1 list catalogue (rev. 31 May 2024)
items.why_new: The known notes cover X-family steps and a 'harmonised' per-read cost, not Illumina's own XLEAP list cuts on NextSeq 2000 with the arithmetic.
items.verify_note: New: the NextSeq 1000/2000 XLEAP list cuts were not in the known notes. But they date from May 2024, so they are already in the reported price/volume history (FY24–25 revenue per Gb). They are mid-throughput, not HT consumables, and list prices only. They show the pattern of deflation, not acceleration.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: The posting asks for a 15+ year pricing leader and formal pricing governance with approval workflows, which suggests discount control is being centralized.
items.detail: The role requires 15+ years of experience in pricing, finance business partnering or commercial operations, and the ability to influence executives across a matrixed organization. It also covers maintaining approval workflows and compliance monitoring, and it frames pricing as 'ownership, consumption, and performance' models. This is consistent with management's statement that it will not do global pricing and will price emerging tests separately. The posting gives no sign of the scale or timing of any discounting. It could equally mean tighter discipline.
items.why_new: Adds the specific governance and seniority detail of the pricing build-out, which the known list lacks.

items.label: 2B
items.claim: An independent estimate puts AXELIOS run cost near $2,400 and calls Roche pricing 'competitive' but not aggressively low.
items.detail: The aseqer Substack (27 Feb 2026) estimates a run costs about $2,400 with a sensor module reused 20 times, and chip cost under $50 per run. It quotes $150 per 30x duplex genome and $0.06 per million simplex reads. This is a blog inference, not Roche data, and is not tied to any core rate sheet. If right, it implies research price pressure from Roche is less severe than the headline $/read gap suggests.
items.quote: competitive with Illumina, but it isn't aggressively low
items.why_new: Adds the run-cost and sensor-price estimate and an explicit 'not aggressively low' judgment; the corpus only has the $150/genome and $0.06 figures.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: The '$24,155 list' used in several items is the GSA distributor price, about 47% above Illumina's own catalogue list for the 25B-300. So NCI and KUMC pay roughly catalogue list, not deep discounts.
items.detail: Illumina's catalogue list for the 25B-300 is $16,000 (Open Offer, 2024) or $16,480 (Jan 2025), while GSA is $24,155 (1.47–1.51x). NCI's $17,196 (D023, '71% of GSA') is therefore ~104–107% of catalogue list, and KUMC's $23,872 (F386, '99% of list') is ~145% of catalogue list, which includes core markup. For the S4-300, GSA's $21,683 is ~1.31x the $16,578 catalogue list, and D026's academic net of ~$15.4K is ~93% of catalogue list. Large federal and academic accounts show no visible off-list discounting on the X.
items.source_name: Illumina Open Offer Appendix 1; GSA schedule; NCI and KUMC rate cards
items.why_new: It corrects the reference base in D023/D026/D029/F386, which treated the GSA price as Illumina's list.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: On list prices the 6000 S4-to-25B per-Gb gap narrowed from ~2.76x (2024) to ~2.58x (2025–26), so the widening reported 6000/X revenue-per-Gb ratio (2.8x→3.4x) comes from tail mix and discount structure, not list moves.
items.detail: The S4-300 list rose $14,400 (Sep 2022) → $15,940 (Feb 2023) → $16,578 (Feb 2024), then was cut to ~$15,938 (UConn pass-through, current through Feb 2026, −3.9%). Over the same period the 25B-300 rose $16,000 → $16,480 (+3%). Per Gb at ~3,000 vs ~8,000 Gb spec, that is $5.53/$2.00 = 2.76x in 2024 and $5.31/$2.06 = 2.58x in 2025–26. The reported ratio went the other way (2.8x in Q4'24–Q2'25 → 3.4x in Q2'26). That fits a residual tail skewed to small, high-$/Gb SP/S2 flow cells and less-discounted accounts (D028/D032), and so a higher revenue-per-Gb step when they convert.
items.source_name: Illumina Open Offer catalogue revisions; UConn CGI rate sheets
items.why_new: It splits the known ratio drift into list effects and mix/discount effects using dated catalogue prices.

items.label: 2A
items.claim: After deduplication, PHAC's Illumina decline from 2022 to 2025 is ~−51%, not −65%, and most of the remaining fall happened after 2024, outside the pandemic period.
items.detail: F514 puts true PHAC 2022 at ~C$6.8M (after removing ~C$2.8M of duplicate amendment rows), against C$3.35M in 2025 (F448), which is −51%. The 2021 pandemic reagent contract (C$15.4M, F513) is dated 2021 and is not in these sums. The post-pandemic FY24-25→FY25-26 drop of −76% (F508) still stands. So COVID normalization does not explain the recent decline, but the multi-year headline overstated it.
items.source_name: Government of Canada Proactive Disclosure of Contracts
items.why_new: Reconciles F513/F514 with F448/F508 into one corrected PHAC series.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: The cheapest public 25B lane price (Novogene, $2.55/Gb) is ~45% above the published Open Offer top-tier net ($1.76/Gb), so the largest accounts start well below any public reference price before bespoke discounts.
items.detail: Open Offer top tier: 12% off $16,000 for ~8,000 Gb gives $1.76/Gb (2024 schedule, F540). Novogene's Sep 2026 promotion is $2,549 for ~1,000 Gb, or $2.55/Gb (D044). Core lanes run $2.5–3.5/Gb. Expert claims that large accounts pay 'half or a quarter' of small labs imply net prices of ~$0.9–1.3/Gb at large clinical accounts, which sits below the published schedule.
items.source_name: Illumina Open Offer Appendix 1; Novogene promotions
items.why_new: Brackets the large-account net price against the published schedule and public lane prices.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: Human NovaSeq 6000 GEO samples in Q3'26 are not driven by one mega-series. The ten largest series cap out at roughly a third of the quarter.
items.detail: Q3'26 human 6000 (GPL24676) had 1,647 series. By series size (n_samples counts all platforms in the series): 0 series ≥5,000; 1 series at 2,000–2,999 (GSE305971); 1 at 1,000–1,999; 8 at 500–999; 67 at 100–499. The top 10 therefore total about 7K at the lowest and about 13K at the highest, i.e. 19–36% of 36,312. Excluding them leaves at least roughly 23K human 6000 samples, so the jump is mostly broad-based. This is bounded by size filters, not exact per-GSM attribution. GSE347972 (Crnic Institute Trisomy 21 atlas, released 30 Sep 2026) has a GPL field of 24247;24676 and is a large mouse and human series, so it may add to the Q3 mouse figure.
items.why_new: This is the requested mega-series test of F528 and none of the known notes did it.
items.verify_note: This only checks the robustness of F528, and it is bounded by size filters. GEO counts research deposits, which lag sequencing by a lot (see the derived item) and are dated by release. They say little about the current clinical 6000 tail, which is the 1A issue. The mouse/human Crnic series is a side note.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: Mouse 6000 spikes in Q4'25 and Q2'26 are series-driven, so they should not be read as a trend.
items.detail: Mouse 6000 samples jumped from 23,719 (Q3'25) to 45,314 (Q4'25) and from 25,326 (Q1'26) to 45,530 (Q2'26), then fell to 21,245 in Q3'26. Q4'25 had 1,295 mouse-6000 series. Nine of them had 1,000–4,999 samples (e.g. GSE181359, GSE181141, GSE181116, GSE169467), and none had 5,000 or more. Several large mid-sized atlases therefore explain the spikes. Excluding them, the underlying mouse 6000 run-rate is about 21–25K a quarter, which is flat to slightly down since Q1'25 (20.5K). The 6000's mouse deposit volume is not falling fast.
items.why_new: This is a new unit-of-measure check (series size) on the GEO series.
items.verify_note: The spike series carry 2021-era accession numbers (GSE169xxx, GSE181xxx). They are old data released late, not new sequencing. That confirms the spikes are artifacts, but it also shows that GEO PDAT does not measure current 6000 use. n_samples counts all platforms, so the run-rate of ~21–25K excluding them is approximate. The direction for 1A is ambiguous, because steady 6000 deposits fit management's 'stays' view as well as ours.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: The mouse X count has risen about 14x in two years in published data (713 to 10,120 samples), which fits a research base that is deepening on cheaper X output.
items.detail: Mouse X samples per quarter: 713 (Q3'24), 2,538 (Q1'25), 3,430, 5,326, 4,405, 7,414, 8,970, 10,120 (Q3'26). Over Q3'24 to Q3'26 that is x14.2. The 6000 count over the same span went 17,498 to 21,245 (+21%). Total mouse 6000+X samples rose from 18,211 to 31,365 (+72%) over two years. This does not support the thesis that research volume is flat. It may reflect more deposits and bigger sample counts per run.
items.why_new: This is a new mouse series with arithmetic that cuts against the research volume-flat claim.

items.label: 2A
items.claim: GEO mouse deposits on Illumina platforms grew about 72% in two years, so published academic sequencing activity is not shrinking despite funding strain.
items.detail: Total mouse 6000+X samples were 18,211 in Q3'24 and 31,365 in Q3'26 (72% higher). Q1'25 was 23,072 and Q1'26 was 32,740 (+42% y/y), a faster rate than the −7% R&A consumables drop. GEO is a lagging deposit measure, partly one-off atlases, and counts samples not Gb, so it is a weak watch-out signal.
items.why_new: New mouse y/y arithmetic and a contrast with R&A revenue.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: GeneDx's Q3'26 guide implies slowing sequential volume growth to about 8%, and its FY26 volume guide of 30% or more sits below Q2's +32%.
items.detail: Q2'26 volume was 30,785. Q3'26 guidance is 33,200 tests, which is about +7.8% q/q (my calculation). Q1'26 volume was reportedly 23,246, but the deck chart was garbled and this figure may be a misread of the Q2'25 base, so it is unverified. FY26 guidance is volume growth of at least 30% and exome/genome revenue growth of at least 20%, reiterated on 3 Aug 2026. That implies FY revenue per test falling by high single digits to about 10%. Customers are growing volume faster than revenue, and the Q3 sequential step is smaller than a +32% y/y pace implies.
items.why_new: The known list has no GeneDx guidance, Q3 volume guide or sequential growth figure.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: Illumina keeps winning Canadian federal mid-throughput sequencer buys by direct award, with no competitive pressure visible.
items.detail: A CanadaBuys award shows a directed NextSeq 2000 package worth CAD 404,860.78 to Illumina Canada ULC, running 2026/01/30 to 2027/03/31 in the National Capital Region. A separate non-competitive NextSeq 2000 award for Ontario ran 2025/12/19 to 2026/03/31. I read both in a search snippet only; the cw2436812 page returned 403 when I fetched it. Directed awards imply no tendered price cuts on the mid-throughput tier.
items.why_new: The exclusion list covers Canadian reagent orders, not these NextSeq 2000 instrument awards or their values.

items.label: 2B
items.claim: NHGRI's FY2027 GREGoR renewal is funded at only about $9.5M in FY2027, with no sequencing production budget, so it signals no growth in federal rare-disease sequencing buying.
items.detail: The GREGoRi renewal (NOFOs updated May 2026, posted Jun 2026) commits $7.5M in FY2027 to 8-10 innovation projects (up to $500K direct costs per year, up to 3 years). It also commits $2M in FY2027 to one data coordination center (up to $1.25M direct costs per year, 5 years). Neither NOFO sets genome counts or per-genome costs or names a platform. The original 2021 GREGoR funding level was not stated in either NOFO, so no change in dollars versus the prior cycle can be computed. The FY2026 NHGRI funding strategy page separately says resource grants (R24/U24/U41) may face further budget reductions.
items.source_name: NHGRI RFA-HG-27-013 and RFA-HG-27-011 via simpler.grants.gov
items.why_new: The GREGoRi FY2027 NOFO budget figures and the NHGRI reduction caveat on resource grants are not in the known list.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: Illumina's reagent-rental schedule adds about $10.4K to every NovaSeq X run to recover the instrument cost, so each rental X books roughly $520K a year of instrument payback as consumables revenue. That inflates reported X pull-through.
items.detail: Illumina's financing page (test-web mirror) lists reagent-rental per-run prices of $10,409 for the NovaSeq X Series, $8,378 for the NovaSeq 6000 and $9,045 for the 6000Dx, assuming 50 runs a year. Our arithmetic: $10,409 × 50 = $520K a year, and $10,409 × 150 runs = $1.56M over 3 years. The 36-month lease is $41,500 × 36 = $1.49M, so the per-run uplift recovers about the full instrument value. $520K equals ~42% of the ~$1.24M implied X pull-through in Q2'26 and ~63% of the $16,480 list price of a 25B-300 kit. Any rental placement therefore makes X consumables per box look ~40% higher than true reagent pricing. The page is undated and still lists the retired iSeq and MiniSeq, so treat it as an older schedule.
items.date: undated (pre-2026 schedule; page lists retired iSeq/MiniSeq)
items.quote: Reagent rental requires a reagent commitment. Per-run pricing assumes 50 runs per year.
items.why_new: Known notes only say rental 'may inflate X pull-through'. This is the first per-run dollar figure that quantifies the effect.
items.verify_note: Checked on the page. The per-run figures are 'as low as' prices, with the page saying it transfers 'the price of the instrument on top of reagents'. The MiSeq ($868) and iSeq ($227) figures are below kit prices, so the figure is an uplift on top of reagents, not an all-in price. The $520K/yr and the ~$1.56M vs $1.49M lease cross-check hold. Correction: the effect applies only to rental boxes (~5 of 100+ Q4'25 placements, known), so the fleet-level inflation of X pull-through is small (see the de

items.label: 1B
items.claim: Illumina's new Enterprise Pricing and Financing function is designing pay-for-consumption and pay-for-performance models by application, and it owns pricing for new product introductions, which would include the 35B launch.
items.detail: The Associate Director, Pricing Transformation posting (req ~42825, posted 28 Jun 2026, $170.6K–$255.8K, San Diego) describes a pricing vision 'by market, by customer type, and by application'. That vision spans 'pay for ownership, pay for consumption, and pay for performance'. The role also builds the 'New Product Introduction pricing process' and sets customer segmentation by tier. Application-level and performance-based pricing is the mechanism for giving price-elastic segments and large accounts deeper effective cuts without a list-price change. That fits a 35B priced per segment rather than globally.
items.source_name: Illumina job posting (resumegeni mirror of Workday)
items.quote: pay for ownership, pay for consumption, and pay for performance
items.why_new: F181 and F549 recorded the function and its governance role. The pay-for-consumption/performance models, by-application pricing and NPI pricing ownership were not recorded.
items.verify_note: This is a new source type (a job posting), but it restates known management statements on application-specific pricing. That it 'includes the 35B' is an inference. Pay-for-performance can also protect price, so the direction is not certain.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: Illumina's live financing page now offers an instrument 'Subscription' (12-month minimum, pay as you go) and no longer shows per-run rental prices. That is a new consumption-style option that makes the realized price per run less visible.
items.detail: The current illumina.com and sapac pages (©2026) list four options: reagent rental, Subscription ('access to the latest Illumina technology', minimum 12 months, pay as you go), leasing and instrument rental. The per-run reagent-rental column shown on the older mirror is gone. Starting 3-year leases are X $41,500/mo, 6000 $32,700/mo (79% of X), 6000Dx $35,900/mo (87% of X) and NextSeq 1k/2k $11,100/mo, 'for well-qualified buyers' with 0% offers. Dropping the published per-run figures and adding subscription matches the pay-for-consumption vision in the pricing posting.
items.quote: Subscription
items.why_new: F210 captured the 6000-vs-X lease ratio only. The subscription option, the removed per-run pricing and the 6000Dx lease were not recorded.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: Element earned ISO 13485 and plans an AVITI Dx Class A IVDR sequencer in 'select countries' in late 2026, so a rival may have a certified EU clinical path before Illumina has any NovaSeq X Dx.
items.detail: Element's 17 Jun 2026 release says ISO 13485 certification is the base for AVITI Dx, its 'forthcoming Class A IVDR sequencing platform', with availability expected in late 2026. Revvity is an IVD co-development partner for newborn screening. Illumina's IVDR roadmap shows only the 6000Dx in high throughput and no X Dx (F531–F536). EU regulated 6000Dx sites converting to a certified platform would therefore have a non-Illumina option first. Element also has an open Director, Regulatory Affairs role on Greenhouse (Oct 2026).
items.source_name: Element Biosciences press release; Element Greenhouse job board
items.quote: forthcoming Class A IVDR sequencing platform
items.why_new: Known material covers Illumina's missing X Dx and Element's general clinical intent. Element's ISO 13485 status and AVITI Dx IVDR timing were not recorded.
items.verify_note: Relabeled to 1B (competition). IVDR Class A is self-declared and a low bar. AVITI is a mid-throughput box, so it is not a like-for-like replacement for 6000Dx high-throughput sites. Being 'available in select countries in late 2026' is a plan, not a shipment.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: Element's open roles show a thin commercial build: 18 openings, only 3 in sales, and none for VITARI, clinical accounts or pricing, months before VITARI ships.
items.detail: Element's Greenhouse board (accessed 12 Oct 2026) lists 18 roles. Sales roles are a Channel Account Manager in Italy, a Country Manager in Japan and a Senior Inside Sales Rep in the Northeast. The rest are field service (2), field applications (1), R&D, software, operations and one reagent-manufacturing supervisor. No posting names VITARI, a strategic or key-account role, or pricing. VITARI is marketed for H2'26 shipment. Hiring this light does not point to an aggressive high-throughput sales push into Illumina's large accounts in the near term.
items.why_new: The known jobs work covered Roche AXELIOS hiring. No count of Element's commercial openings existed.
items.verify_note: This is a single snapshot of a job board, and Element may sell VITARI through its existing reps. It is a weak signal.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: Ultima posted a Phoenix-based field service engineer in Aug 2026 to serve 'customers primarily in the Phoenix area', which points to a local installed base in a city with big Illumina clinical customers.
items.detail: The Field Service Engineer II, Arizona role (posted 7 Aug 2026, on-site in Phoenix, $37–42/hr) covers installation, repair and lab inventory for Phoenix-area customers. Ultima's 16 open roles (Greenhouse, Oct 2026) also include a UAE field engineer, a NorCal sales manager, an Associate Strategic Accounts Director for pharma and biotech, and a Senior Commercial Operations Manager for 'lead-to-cash' ($150–190K, updated 23 Jun 2026). Phoenix hosts Caris's NovaSeq labs and Sonora Quest, a Quest/Banner joint venture (Quest has an Ultima MRD collaboration). Which customer the role serves is our inference; no source confirms a Phoenix Ultima site.
items.source_name: Ultima Genomics job posting (Khosla board / Greenhouse)
items.quote: Provide on-site service to customers primarily in the Phoenix, Arizona area
items.why_new: No known item places Ultima service capacity in Phoenix, and none counts Ultima's commercial openings.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: Ultima has no open clinical, regulatory or IVD roles, and only a 2025 reagent quality-engineer posting cites ISO 13485, so it is not building the regulated footprint needed to win validated clinical volume soon.
items.detail: Ultima's 16 open roles break down as R&D 5, Sales & Marketing 5, Engineering 2, Manufacturing 2 and G&A 2. None is in regulatory affairs or clinical. ISO 13485 appears only as 'preferred' in a Senior Process Engineer role (Apr 2026) and in a May 2025 reagent quality-engineer posting. Element, by contrast, has ISO 13485 and an IVDR product. This supports the known finding that no large US clinical customer runs production on Ultima.
items.why_new: First check of Ultima's hiring mix for regulatory and clinical build-out.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: Illumina was staffing a Bengaluru 'Value Engineering & Should-Cost' team (manager plus analysts) in May–Jun 2026, a cost-down program that could fund future price cuts.
items.detail: Postings for a Senior Analyst (dated 9 May and 6 Jun 2026), a junior analyst and a Manager (10+ years, leading a team of cost analysts) ask for should-cost models across plastics, metals, electronics and assemblies, using aPriori, SAP and CAD tools, on shifts that support US stakeholders. A dedicated should-cost function points to a structured COGS reduction on instruments and components. That would give room for 35B and large-account pricing while defending margin. It could equally be read as margin defense against tariffs and memory costs.
items.source_name: Illumina job postings (Simplify, Built In Bengaluru)
items.why_new: The Illumina cost-engineering hiring program was not in the corpus.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: GeneDx's Q2'26 revenue per test came in about 12% below its own guide even though volume beat, so its price per test is falling faster than the lab's own forecast.
items.detail: The Q1'26 deck guided Q2 to about 30,000 ES/GS tests and $110-112M, which is about $3,700 per test. Actual was 30,785 tests (+2.6% vs guide) and $100.3M (about $10-12M, or 9-10%, short), or $3,258 per test. Management had cut FY26 revenue guidance from $540-555M to $475-490M in May, and the deck named higher genome mix and lower parental-sample mix as the cause. Management now calls the $3,258 figure 'the new baseline'. A key Illumina customer is facing a structurally lower revenue per test while volume is delivered.
items.source_name: GeneDx Q1'26 earnings deck (EX-99.3) vs Q2'26 release
items.quote: We view this Q2 blended ARR as the new baseline
items.why_new: Quantifies a forecasting miss on revenue per test against GeneDx's own guide, which prior notes do not show.
items.verify_note: Misread. The $110–112M Q2 guide is TOTAL revenue. The same slide guides exome/genome revenue at '~$100 million' on ~30,000 tests (~$3,333/test). Actual ES/GS was ~$100.3M on 30,785 tests ($3,258), so ES/GS revenue met guide and revenue per test was only ~2% below the implied guide, not 12%. The FY cut ($540–555M to $475–490M) is already priced into the Q2 guide. This is also the customer's reimbursement, not Illumina's price.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: Verified: the FY26 guide floors imply ES/GS revenue per test falling about 7.7% for the year, and the H2 split shows the price-per-test drop is front-loaded into Q3.
items.detail: FY25 ES/GS revenue was $360.3M on 97,271 tests, or $3,704 per test. FY26 floors are volume +30% (126,452) and revenue +20% ($432.4M), giving $3,419 per test, or -7.7%. H1'26 was $190.9M on 58,273 tests, or $3,276. Q3 guide is $3,343 (-13.1% y/y). The floors imply Q4 revenue of at least $130.5M on at least 34,979 tests, or about $3,731, a +14% q/q jump. The guide therefore needs Q4 ARR to recover, which management ties to Carelon and collection gains from Q4 onward. If it does not, FY revenue per test is more likely -10% to -12%.
items.source_name: GeneDx Q2'26 deck and release (guidance table)
items.why_new: Completes the requested check on the guide-implied revenue per test and shows the Q4 recovery it depends on.
items.verify_note: The arithmetic is consistent with the guide: ES/GS volume 'at least 30%' and revenue 'at least 20%' give about −7.7% per test. This is customer-side reimbursement pressure. It links to Illumina discounting only indirectly, through the customer's push to cut reagent costs.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: GeneDx guides cost per test flat through H2'26 while revenue per test is down double digits and adjusted cost of services is growing faster than revenue, which sets up pressure on its reagent bill.
items.detail: Q2'26 adjusted cost of services was $33.9M vs $30.2M (+12.1%) against revenue +11.4%. Six-month adjusted cost of services was $66.1M vs $57.6M (+14.7%) vs revenue +14.2%. Adjusted cost per test across all tests (ES/GS plus panels) is about $539 vs $523 (+3%). Adjusted gross margin was 70.4% vs 70.6% in Q2'25, and 74% in Q3'25. On the call management said whole genome costs nearly twice an exome, 'almost entirely higher reagent costs', and expects reagent costs to fall as manufacturers improve technology. It also expects cost per test to be 'relatively flat for the second half of 2026' with step improvements in 2027. GeneDx is explicitly counting on lower reagent prices and has about 4 pts less gross margin than at its Q3'25 peak.
items.source_name: GeneDx Q2'26 call transcript (Webull) and 10-Q reconciliation tables
items.quote: The difference there is almost entirely higher reagent costs.
items.why_new: Adds the cost-of-services growth vs revenue, the margin path from 74% to 70%, and the 2027 cost-step expectation. Prior notes had only the reagent-cost-falls remark.
items.verify_note: Best of the GeneDx items. Management says genome costs about 2x an exome, 'almost entirely higher reagent costs', and expects reagent prices to fall, with cost per test flat in H2'26 and step-downs in 2027. That is a large customer planning on supplier price cuts. F239 (no validated alternative platform) limits its leverage, so the effect is pressure rather than a credible switch.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: GeneDx's own disclosed genome mix fell sharply from Q1 to Q2'26, which on rough Gb weights cuts sequencing Gb per test by roughly 20-30%. The mix bases differ, so this is indicative only.
items.detail: The Q1'26 deck says genome was 45% of the ES/GS portfolio. The Q2 call says genome was 32% of insurance-based outpatient volume, down from about 40% in Q1, and expects about 30% or lower in H2. With illustrative Gb of about 100 per genome and about 10 per exome, Gb per ES/GS test falls from about 54 (45% genome) to about 39 (32%), or -29%. Q1 Gb is about 1.50 Pb and Q2 about 1.19 Pb, so about -20% q/q even with volume +12%. The Q1 and Q2 mix figures use different bases (portfolio vs outpatient), so treat the size as uncertain. The direction is the point: the lab's biggest Gb-per-test product share is falling while volume is still rising. GeneDx's Gb growth therefore lags its test growth.
items.source_name: GeneDx Q2'26 call and Q1'26 deck
items.why_new: Puts illustrative Gb numbers on GeneDx's genome-mix reversal using the company's own mix disclosures. Prior notes had the general mix idea.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: GeneDx beat its own Q2 volume guide and says July's core-channel demand and reflex volume were healthy, a mild offset to the slowdown signal.
items.detail: Q1 guidance was about 30,000 ES/GS tests for Q2, and actual was 30,785 (+2.6%). Management said the Q3 volume guide of 33,200 reflects July trends, including healthy core-channel demand and reflex volume exceeding genome volume for the first time. Q3 volume is guided +29% y/y, not a collapse. An FY floor of 'at least 30%' has already been run-rated near 30% at H1 (+33% on 58,273 vs 43,808). The slowdown is gradual and consistent with the thesis's ~25-30%, not a break.
items.source_name: GeneDx Q2'26 call transcript and release
items.why_new: Shows how the Q2 volume beat compares with the earlier guide and what drives the Q3 volume guide.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: GeneDx's six-month volume grew +33% (58,273 vs 43,808), above the FY floor, and ES/GS is now 49% of its tests, so the high-Gb product is a growing share of the lab.
items.detail: ES/GS was 49% of all test results in Q2'26 and in H1'26 vs 40% a year earlier. Non-exome panel volume fell to 32,057 in Q2'26 from 34,510 in Q2'25 (-7%), and total test volume grew only +8.8% (62,842 vs 57,756). Almost all of the Gb sits in ES/GS, so GeneDx's sequencing needs are being driven by that line. The mix inside ES/GS (exome vs genome) is the swing factor, not panel decline.
items.why_new: Adds the panel-vs-ES/GS split and the 49% share from the 10-Q.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: GeneDx's capacity spending has leveled off and remaining equipment/software commitments step down over time, so it has bought ahead and has little scheduled capacity build left.
items.detail: Management said capex rose in Q2 to expand the sequencing fleet and 'has now reached a point of leveling out'. The 10-Q Note 9 shows commitments with software and equipment providers of $41.5M: $9.4M for the rest of 2026, $16.3M in 2027, $10.7M in 2028, $4.1M in 2029 and $1.0M in 2030. The 2027 amount is larger than H2'26, so the build is not over, but it declines after. With H2 volume guided to +26-29% y/y, the near-term fleet is sized for current growth. Equipment purchases are a leading indicator of consumables, and this one points to a plateau rather than acceleration.
items.why_new: Adds the dated commitment schedule ($41.5M, with $16.3M in 2027) behind the capex-leveling remark.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: GeneDx's revenue per test has flattened Q1 to Q2 (-1.2%) and management guides it flat at about $3,300 to Q3, so its pressure on supplier prices may ease rather than accelerate.
items.detail: ARR was $3,296 in Q1'26 and $3,258 in Q2'26 (-1.2% q/q). Q3 guidance implies about $3,300-3,343 per test (+2.6% q/q at the revenue midpoint). Management expects collection rates to stay roughly flat in Q3 and improve from Q4, plus Carelon uplift in Q4 and 2027. Adjusted gross margin was steady at 70% (69.5% for H1 vs 69.7%). Pricing and collection rates were 'relatively unchanged' per the Q1 deck. Its 10-Q names no sequencer supplier, and the largest supplier share of spend was 14% in Q2'26 vs 20% a year ago. The customer is not signalling a margin crisis that would force a discount demand on Illumina.
items.quote: Pricing and collection rates are relatively unchanged
items.why_new: Shows the stabilisation of revenue per test and flat gross margin, which is the watch-out to the revenue-per-test squeeze.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: GeneDx's initial FY26 plan was cut twice in four months, with the volume guide taken from 33-35% to 'at least 30%' and ES/GS revenue growth from 33-35% to 'at least 20%'.
items.detail: The Feb 2026 guide was 33-35% ES/GS volume and 33-35% ES/GS revenue growth, and total revenue $540-555M. In May it became volume 'at least 30%', revenue 'at least 20%' and total revenue $475-490M, a cut of $65M at the midpoint (-12%). Q1'26 revenue was $102M vs $114M expected. The revenue guide fell about 13 points while volume fell about 3 points, so the cut was mostly price per test and mix. Even so, volume was lowered, meaning a major customer's planning for sequencing demand dropped.
items.why_new: Quantifies the two-step guide cut and splits it between revenue per test and volume.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: Illumina prices its regulated NovaSeq 6000Dx reagent kits below the RUO 6000 kits, and the gap widened in 2024. The FDA/IVD-locked 'regulated tail' is therefore not the highest-priced part of the 6000 base.
items.detail: 6000Dx S4-300 kit list price: $13,876 in both the Jan 2024 (prices as of Feb 2023) and May 2024 (prices as of Feb 2024) catalogues. The RUO S4-300 went from $15,940 to $16,578, so the Dx kit's discount to RUO widened from 12.9% to 16.3%. Illumina cut the 6000Dx S2-300 from $9,600 to $8,976 (−6.5%) while the RUO S2-300 rose to $11,052, so the Dx discount widened from 9.7% to 18.8%. The NextSeq 550Dx HO-300 kit was held at $6,841 while the RUO 550 kit rose 4%. The 6000Dx instrument list cut from $1.08M to $850K happened in the same revision. The highest-price 6000 Gb are therefore RUO/LDT users (the labs that can most easily convert), not IVD-locked labs. The thesis's 'permanent regulated tail' is cheaper per Gb than the average tail.
items.why_new: The corpus has only the 6000Dx instrument list cut (F547). Dx versus RUO reagent kit pricing, and the 6000Dx S2 kit cut, are not recorded.
items.verify_note: These are list prices from the Open Offer oncology appendix. Many clinical 6000 users run LDTs on RUO kits, and the 6000Dx base is small, so the size of the effect is limited. It still undercuts the idea that the IVD-locked tail is the highest-priced Gb. It also means converting regulated sites costs less revenue per Gb than the blended 3.4x implies (see the derived item).

items.label: 1B
items.claim: Illumina's public Open Offer pages now appear to be withdrawn from its main site, so any post-2024 discounting to oncology accounts is no longer published.
items.detail: On 12 Oct 2026 the www.illumina.com cancer 'test-terms' URL resolved to the generic Terms and Conditions page with no Open Offer documents. The www illumina-open-offer.pdf link also landed on that generic page. The assets.illumina.com test-terms page, the 22 Apr 2024 Section 4(g) disclosure (emea and www hosts) and the tst-web 18 Mar 2024 appendix all returned HTTP 404. Only orphaned CDN copies (31 May 2024, 25 Jan 2024 and 6 Jan 2022 appendices) still load, and the staging tst-web index lists revisions only through Oct 2023. Together with the new Enterprise Pricing function (F181/F549), this is consistent with discounting moving to individualized, unpublished terms. It could also just be a site reorganization, so the evidence is weak.
items.source_name: Illumina website (Open Offer test-terms page and PDFs)
items.why_new: No corpus item records that the Open Offer page and disclosures are now unreachable or redirected on Illumina's live site.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: In GEO, the NovaSeq 6000's share of combined human and mouse 6000+X samples fell from 96.9% in Q3'24 to 82.4% in Q3'25 and 70.5% in Q3'26, still losing about 12 points a year with no plateau.
items.why_new: Earlier probes gave human-only levels and a Q1–Q3'26 human X ratio. This is the first combined human+mouse quarterly share series with y/y pace.
items.verify_note: The sums tie (Q3'26 6000 57,557 = 36,312 human + 21,245 mouse). The big caveat: GEO puts the X at only 29.5% of 6000+X samples in Q3'26, while Illumina reports research Gb at 92% on the X. GEO therefore lags actual sequencing by about 2+ years and reflects research publication, not the current clinical tail. Use it only as a lagged directional indicator.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: Counting series instead of samples gives the same result: the 6000's share of 6000+X GEO series fell 95.4% → 81.6% → 69.5% (Q3'24/Q3'25/Q3'26), so mega-series are not driving the trend.
items.detail: GSE counts by quarter: 6000 2,555 / X 123 (Q3'24); 2,816 / 636 (Q3'25); 3,149 / 1,379 (Q3'26). H1'26: 6,077 / 2,134 (74.0%). The series-level y/y declines (−13.8, −12.1 pts) match the sample-level ones (−14.5, −11.9). This stands in for the requested 5% per-series cap, which could not be run by hand (no script tool). A series that lists both platforms counts in each group.
items.url: https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/esearch.fcgi?db=gds&term=(GPL34284[ACCN] OR GPL34281[ACCN] OR GPL34290[ACCN] OR GPL34328[ACCN]) AND gse[ETYP] AND 2026/07/01:2026/09/30[PDAT]&retmax=0
items.why_new: F551/F552 only bounded the top-10 series. This is a full series-unit robustness check across three years.
items.verify_note: The series-count check is a sound defense against mega-series. It has the same lag and research-only caveat as F577. Series listing both platforms are double-counted.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: A linear fit to the Q1'25–Q3'26 GEO 6000 share (−2.6 pts/qtr) projects about 60% by Q4'27, with no sign of flattening toward a permanent floor.
items.detail: Ordinary least squares on 7 quarterly sample shares (87.6, 86.1, 82.4, 87.5, 76.2, 78.0, 70.5): mean 81.2%, Sxy −73.7, Sxx 28, slope −2.63 pts/qtr (~−10.5 pts/yr). Q4'27 is x=11, giving 81.2 − 8×2.63 ≈ 60%. GEO deposits lag sequencing by 6–18 months, so instrument use is probably further along than this. GEO is mostly academic research, where Illumina says ~92% of HT Gb is already on the X, so the level is not comparable. Only the direction and pace are informative.
items.why_new: First extrapolation of the GEO platform share to the 2027 horizon.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: Absolute NovaSeq 6000 deposits in GEO are still rising, with Q3 samples up 3.9% then 6.9% y/y and series up 10% then 12%, so the 6000 base still produces more published data even as its share falls.
items.detail: Q3 6000 samples: 51,824 (2024), 53,830 (2025), 57,557 (2026). Q3 6000 series: 2,555, 2,816, 3,149. Total 6000+X samples grew +22% and then +25% y/y (53,471 → 65,343 → 81,671), so the share loss comes from X growth on top, not a shrinking 6000 count. Because of the 6–18 month deposit lag, this partly reflects 2025 sequencing. It fits management's slow-tail narrative, but the data is research, not clinical.
items.why_new: F528 noted a single human Q3'26 high. This is a three-year same-quarter series and a combined species count.
items.verify_note: Verified: the Q3'26 6000 GSM count is 57,557 (E-utilities). The arithmetic matches F577 (X = 1,647 / 11,513 / 24,114). The human+mouse absolute series is new, since F528 covered human only. Q3'26 is lifted by the human jump (36,312) while mouse is volatile (F552). Because of D052's ~2-year deposit lag, this mostly reflects 2024–25 sequencing and says little about the 2027 clinical tail. Keep it weak.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: Published Illumina high-throughput research output in GEO is accelerating, with 6000+X samples up 25% y/y in Q3'26 after +22% in Q3'25, driven by X samples more than doubling.
items.detail: X samples (human+mouse): Q3'24 1,647 → Q3'25 11,513 → Q3'26 24,114 (+109% y/y). Over the trailing four quarters (Q4'25–Q3'26) there were 263,650 6000 samples and 73,301 X samples (336,951 total). Sample counts are not Gb, and GEO lags sequencing, but this does not show research usage slowing. It cuts against a 'research volume flat' reading for 2025 activity.
items.url: https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/esearch.fcgi?db=gds&term=(GPL34284[ACCN] OR GPL34281[ACCN] OR GPL34290[ACCN] OR GPL34328[ACCN]) AND gsm[ETYP] AND 2025/07/01:2025/09/30[PDAT]&retmax=0
items.why_new: F424 (literature flat) and F554 (mouse only) differ. This is a combined human+mouse HT Illumina growth rate from GEO.

items.label: 2B
items.claim: Non-Illumina short-read platforms (AVITI, Ultima, DNBSEQ-T7) rose from 0.75% of human+mouse HT sequencing samples in GEO in Q3'24 to 3.9% in Q3'25 and 4.5% in Q3'26.
items.url: https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/esearch.fcgi?db=gds&term=(GPL34295[ACCN] OR GPL34475[ACCN] OR GPL34762[ACCN] OR GPL36595[ACCN] OR GPL29480[ACCN] OR GPL28330[ACCN]) AND gsm[ETYP] AND 2026/07/01:2026/09/30[PDAT]&retmax=0
items.why_new: F530 covered AVITI human only. This is the first all-rival, human+mouse share with a 2024 baseline.
items.verify_note: The denominators check: 53,471+402, 65,343+2,680, 81,671+3,808. The rival share is understated because it excludes DNBSEQ-G400/G99 and other AVITI or Ultima GPLs. The DNBSEQ part is likely China-linked. Most of the share gain came in 2024→25 (+3.2 pts) and only +0.5 pts in 2025→26, so the rise is slowing in GEO.

items.label: 2B
items.claim: AVITI plus Ultima GEO samples grew 79% y/y in Q3'26 (834 → 1,494), against +25% for Illumina HT, so Element's research footprint is compounding faster from a small base.
items.detail: Derived by subtraction: rivals Q3'25 2,680 minus DNBSEQ 1,846 = 834; Q3'26 3,808 minus 2,314 = 1,494. AVITI+UG share of HT samples rose from 1.23% to 1.75%. Ultima is negligible (next item), so this is almost all AVITI, which fits the core-level AVITI adoption already in the ledger.
items.why_new: F425 gave AVITI literature-mention growth only. This is a GEO sample growth rate with DNBSEQ removed.
items.verify_note: The arithmetic checks (1,494/834 = +79%; 1.23% → 1.75%). Read it as an AVITI-led gain derived by subtraction. AVITI+UG captured only ~4% of the y/y increase in GEO HT samples (+660 vs Illumina +16,328), so it is compounding but not yet taking much of the increment.

items.label: 2B
items.claim: Ultima barely registers in public research data: only 187 human+mouse UG 100 samples were deposited in GEO in the four quarters to Q3'26, about 0.06% of Illumina HT samples.
items.detail: GPL34762 (UG 100, Homo sapiens, 564 lifetime samples) and GPL36595 (UG 100, Mus musculus, 27 lifetime) give 187 GSMs from 1 Oct 2025 to 30 Sep 2026, against 336,951 6000+X samples. Ultima's low $/genome has not yet shown up in academic deposits. Its use is concentrated in genome centers and population or atlas projects that may deposit elsewhere (SRA/dbGaP).
items.why_new: The UG100 GPL had never been identified or counted in prior probes.
items.verify_note: 187/336,951 = 0.055%, which checks. The caveat stands: Ultima's scale users (Broad, population and atlas projects) deposit in SRA/dbGaP or controlled access, and F611 could not resolve Ultima in SRA either. Absence from GEO is weak evidence of absence.

items.label: 2B
items.claim: DNBSEQ-T7, not AVITI, is the largest non-Illumina platform in GEO human+mouse deposits, at 2,314 samples in Q3'26 (+25% y/y), or 61% of rival samples.
items.detail: GPL29480 (human, 7,415 lifetime) and GPL28330 (mouse, 7,506 lifetime): 1,846 (Q3'25) and 2,314 (Q3'26). This is about 2.7% of Q3'26 HT samples. These deposits are likely China-heavy, which fits Illumina's Greater China declines more than the US. Our GPL list misses DNBSEQ-G400/MGISEQ-2000 and the new T7+ (GPL37606, 0 samples), so the true MGI share is understated.
items.why_new: No DNBSEQ GEO counts existed in the ledger.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: GEO's research 6000 share (~70%) is far above Illumina's reported ~8% of research HT Gb on the 6000, so GEO platform labels lag reality heavily and cannot size the tail.
items.detail: Q3'26 GEO 6000 share is 70.5% (samples) or 69.5% (series), against Illumina's statement that ~92% of research HT Gb was on the X in Q2'26. The gap reflects the 6–18 month deposit lag, submitters reusing the default 6000 GPL, and samples not being Gb (X runs carry more Gb per sample). Use GEO only for direction and pace, not as a level estimate of the tail.
items.source_name: NCBI GEO via E-utilities vs Illumina Q2'26 deck
items.why_new: This calibration caveat makes the prior GEO items (F523, F528) interpretable. It has not been stated before.
items.verify_note: This duplicates D052, which already establishes that the GEO X share lags Illumina's reported research X Gb share by about two years and cannot size the tail. No new data.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: A German university hospital (Aachen) was still procuring NovaSeq 6000 maintenance in March 2026, with no NovaSeq X named.
items.detail: Universitätsklinikum Aachen AöR published a notice on 10 Mar 2026 titled 'Wartungsvertrag für ein NovaSeq6000 System Firma Illumina', with document type AWARD. Contract length and value are not visible on the open page. The notice names only the NovaSeq 6000. This shows the 6000 tail is still being serviced in German clinical settings in 2026, but without term data it cannot be taken as evidence of multi-year stickiness.
items.why_new: The Aachen 6000 service tender is not in the known list; known 6000 evidence is mostly Siena, Providence and core labs.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: GEO's NovaSeq X share of deposits lags Illumina's own reported research X Gb share by roughly two years or more, so GEO 6000 counts (F528/F551/F577) cannot measure the current 6000 tail.
items.detail: GEO X share of 6000+X human/mouse samples was 3.1% (Q3'24), 17.6% (Q3'25) and 29.5% (Q3'26). Illumina reported research HT Gb on the X at 70% (Q3'24), 90% (Q3'25) and 92% (Q2'26), and even Q2'24 research was 59%. GEO's Q3'26 level sits below every research X share Illumina disclosed from Q2'24 onward. The Q4'25 mouse spike came from 2021-accession series (GSE169xxx/181xxx) released late. GEO tracks when data are published, not when they were sequenced. The rising Q3'26 6000 count reflects the publication pipeline, not 6000 consumables demand.
items.source_name: NCBI GEO vs Illumina earnings decks
items.why_new: No prior item compared the GEO platform shares with Illumina's disclosed research X share to measure the deposit lag.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: Reagent rental inflates fleet-average X pull-through by only about 1–3%, not ~40%, because rental boxes are a small share of placements.
items.detail: Illumina's schedule adds an 'as low as' $10,409 per X run on top of reagents, or about $520K/yr at 50 runs (F558). Rental was about 5 of 100+ X placements in Q4'25 (known). If 3–7% of the X fleet is on rental, the uplift is ~$16–36K per average box, or ~1–3% of the ~$1.24M implied Q2'26 pull-through. Rental cannot hide much X price erosion unless its share is far above disclosed anecdotes.
items.source_name: Illumina Financial Solutions page; Illumina Q4'25 call
items.quote: price of the instrument on top of reagents
items.why_new: This is the first estimate of the per-run rental uplift in dollars at fleet level. The known list only says rental 'may inflate' pull-through.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: At list, the regulated 6000Dx S4 costs only ~2.3x the X 25B per Gb, against ~2.8x for the RUO S4, so converting IVD-locked sites costs Illumina ~57% of revenue per Gb, not the ~70% implied by the 3.4x blended ratio.
items.detail: Feb 2024 lists: 6000Dx S4-300 $13,876 / ~3,000 Gb = $4.63/Gb, RUO S4-300 $16,578 / 3,000 = $5.53/Gb, and 25B-300 $16,000 / 8,000 = $2.00/Gb. That gives ratios of 2.31x (Dx) and 2.76x (RUO), so the per-Gb price cut on conversion is ~57% for Dx sites vs ~64% for RUO. List prices do not show net contract prices, but on list the 'permanent regulated tail' is the cheapest part of the 6000 base, and its eventual conversion is the least dilutive.
items.why_new: Known items computed RUO S4/25B gaps only. None priced the Dx kit against the X.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: GeneDx's guide implies ES/GS revenue per test falling ~8% in FY26 while cost per test stays flat, so its gross margin can only hold if Illumina reagent prices fall in 2027.
items.detail: FY26 guide floors (ES/GS volume +30%, revenue +20%) imply $3,419 per test vs $3,704 in FY25 (−7.7%), and H1'26 ran at $3,276 (−11.6%). Management guides cost per test 'relatively flat' in H2'26, with any 2027 step-down tied to lower reagent costs. Adjusted gross margin was already 70.4% vs 74% in Q3'25. A customer with ~8–12% annual revenue-per-test erosion and no validated alternative sequencer (F239) has strong reason to press for discounts, but limited leverage to get them.
items.source_name: GeneDx Q1/Q2'26 decks and Q2 call
items.quote: almost entirely higher reagent costs
items.why_new: This combines GeneDx's revenue-per-test path with its cost guide to show where pressure on its reagent bill comes from. Known items cover only GeneDx cost per test.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: BillionToOne's inventory and sequencing-related capex are rising, consistent with continued volume build.
items.detail: Inventories were $21.1M at 30 Jun 2026 vs $17.5M at year-end 2025 (+21%), and accrued inventory purchases were $5.3M vs $1.0M. 6M PP&E purchases were $8.5M vs $5.2M. It signed an Austin lease (220,000 sq ft, occupancy 2027) and a Union City lease (~62.7K sq ft, $3.6M/yr base, 12 years). The leases suggest capacity ahead of 2027 volume, though the filing names no sequencer count.
items.why_new: Inventory, accrued-inventory and lease figures are new for this customer.

items.label: 2B
items.claim: New GEO platform records for Element AVITI and Ultima UG 100 are being created at an accelerating pace, which shows more labs depositing rival-platform data.
items.detail: Count of GPL records with AVITI, 'UG 100' or 'Element Biosciences' in the title, by public-release year: 10 (2024), 24 (2025), 30 (2026 through 12 Oct). That is 2.4x from 2024 to 2025 and +25% in 2025 to 2026 on a partial year. Each record is created for a new organism or lab, so it measures breadth of adopters, not sample volume. These counts show only that adoption is broadening. They do not show it is Western, and I could not split by country.
items.url: https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/esearch.fcgi?db=gds&term=(AVITI[Title] OR "UG 100"[Title] OR "Element Biosciences"[Title]) AND gpl[ETYP] AND 2026/01/01:2026/10/12[PDAT]&retmax=100
items.why_new: The known GEO items (F582-F585) count samples. This counts new platform records and gives the first annual series for them.

items.label: 2B
items.claim: No GEO platform record exists yet for Roche SBX/AXELIOS, so Roche has no public research-data footprint to support the AXELIOS price-pressure thesis.
items.detail: The E-utilities queries Axelios[All Fields], 'Roche SBX'[All Fields], 'Roche Axelios'[All Fields], and SBX/Axelios/'Roche sequencing' in the title with the GPL entry-type filter, all returned Count=0 on 12 Oct 2026. AXELIOS has been commercially available since about May 2026, and Roche says about 1/3 of ~100 first-year placements were made by Sep 2026. Any research-pricing effect from Roche is therefore not yet visible in deposited data. GEO lags by months, and a platform may be filed under a generic or other name, so this is not proof that nobody has deposited.
items.url: https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/esearch.fcgi?db=gds&term=(Axelios[All Fields] OR "Roche SBX"[All Fields] OR "Roche Axelios"[All Fields])&retmax=20
items.why_new: The question of whether any SBX/AXELIOS platform record exists was open, and this answers it with the exact queries.

items.label: 2B
items.claim: DNBSEQ-T7 platform-record creation is far above the AVITI/UG 100/Element count and was not falling in 2026, so China-linked platforms still lead rival record creation.
items.detail: GPL records with DNBSEQ-T7 in the title, by public-release year: 38 (2024), 25 (2025), 51 (2026 through 12 Oct, which is already 2x the 2025 total). The most recent records, dated 1-9 Oct 2026, are organism-specific (Actinobacillus, Dendrobium, Lemna and others). Against that, AVITI/UG 100/Element is 30 in 2026, so DNBSEQ-T7 has about 1.7x as many new records. This reinforces F585 that the T7 is the biggest non-Illumina platform, and it is consistent with the rival-share gain in F582 being at least partly a DNBSEQ/China-style effect. I did not verify the depositor country.
items.why_new: Gives an annual new-record series for T7 versus AVITI/UG/Element. The known items count samples only.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: Illumina is advertising limited-time 0% financing and a no-reagent-commitment subscription for instruments, with NovaSeq X leases from $41,500 a month.
items.detail: The financial-solutions page lists reagent rental at 0% interest with the instrument price spread across reagent purchases, and a subscription (12-month minimum, pay-as-you-go, no reagent commitment). Leases start at $41,500/month for the NovaSeq X and $32,700/month for the NovaSeq 6000 (3-year terms, well-qualified buyers), with a limited-time 0% financing offer. A 6000 lease at $32,700/month is about $1.18M over 36 months. Cheap financing and consumption-based models lower the cost of entry and are a form of price concession. They sit alongside the new pricing function.
items.why_new: The exclusion list mentions reagent rental only as a count (~5 of 100+ placements) and not the public lease rate card, the subscription option or the 0% offer.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: In public SRA data the NovaSeq 6000 still accounts for about 73% of NovaSeq-class runs released in Q3'26, even though the X is a rising share.
items.detail: NCBI SRA esearch counts runs released in each quarter. NovaSeq 6000 runs were 551,041 (Q3'24), 410,548 (Q3'25) and 407,958 (Q3'26, partial). NovaSeq X-family runs were 16,351, 60,325 and 152,084. The X's share of 6000+X runs is therefore about 2.9%, 12.8% and 27.2%. The 6000 count has fallen only about 26% over two years. Run counts are not Gb and SRA skews toward public research data. Even so, this suggests the 6000 still carries most deposited sequencing, which is consistent with a long tail and with a slow shift of public data to the X.
items.source_name: NCBI SRA E-utilities esearch (run counts by instrument)
items.why_new: First direct SRA instrument-model run counts by release quarter; none of this appears in the known list.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: AVITI already appears in SRA at about 5,000 runs a quarter (Q3'25), roughly 1% of NovaSeq 6000 run volume.
items.detail: The "Element AVITI"[Instrument] filter returned 4,971 runs released between 1 Jul and 30 Sep 2025, against 410,548 for the NovaSeq 6000 and 60,325 for the NovaSeq X family in the same window. This puts a number on rival adoption in public data. It is small, and no Q3'24 or Q3'26 AVITI comparison was pulled, so growth is unmeasured. Ultima returned 0 under the filter string I tried, which says nothing about its true volume.
items.why_new: Gives an SRA-based measure of AVITI adoption, which the known evidence only has as anecdotes.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: Public SRA run releases tagged NovaSeq 6000 have stopped shrinking: Q3'26 is flat y/y at about 408K, and Q1/Q2'26 were above Q4'25.
items.detail: Entrez esearch counts for "Illumina NovaSeq 6000" by publication date were 551,041 (Q3'24), 410,548 (Q3'25), 385,046 (Q4'25), 456,759 (Q1'26), 475,081 (Q2'26) and 407,958 (Q3'26). Q3'26 vs Q3'25 is −0.6%, after −25% from Q3'24 to Q3'25. Counts are runs, not Gb, and the instrument field was not recognised, so the match is a text search. Still, the public 6000 tail is not visibly decaying in 2026, which fits a 6000 base that persists.
items.why_new: Quarterly SRA run counts (not GEO samples) show the 6000 plateau after a 2024-25 fall.
items.verify_note: Verified: Q3'25 = 410,548. These are text-match counts of SRA run accessions (per sample, not instrument runs) by public release date. They include embargo releases of older data and are sensitive to single mega-BioProjects. The 6000 count stops shrinking while total public runs grow ~24% (F611), so the 6000's share still falls. Research and public data only, not the clinical tail.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: The X's share of public SRA NovaSeq-class runs rose from about 3% to about 27% in two years, and conversion is still moving.
items.detail: X runs ("NovaSeq X" text match) were 16,351 (Q3'24), 60,325 (Q3'25), 110,675 (Q4'25), 111,707 (Q1'26), 118,865 (Q2'26) and 152,084 (Q3'26). X/(6000+X) works out to 2.9%, 12.8%, 22.3%, 19.7%, 20.0% and 27.1%. The Q3'26 share is +7 pts vs Q2'26 and +14 pts y/y. The 6000 is still about 73% of runs, so most of the public mix shift is still ahead, consistent with ~5 more points of conversion in 2027. The share is publication-lagged and counts runs, not Gb.
items.why_new: Gives a quarterly series of X vs 6000 run share, which neither GEO nor SRA notes in the corpus did.
items.verify_note: Verified: Q3'26 X = 152,084, share 27.2%. The direction is fine (+14 pts y/y, +7 q/q). The inference is wrong: a 73% public 6000 run share does not mean most of the mix shift is ahead, because Illumina reports 83% of HT Gb on the X (92% research) and D052 shows a ~2-year lag. It cannot support the '~5 points in 2027' level claim. Q4'25 → Q1'26 the share fell (22.3% → 19.7%), so the series is noisy.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: Combined public SRA NovaSeq run releases are roughly flat across 2024-26 despite the X ramp, so public volume is not accelerating.
items.detail: 6000+X runs were about 567K (Q3'24), 471K (Q3'25), 496K (Q4'25), 568K (Q1'26), 594K (Q2'26) and 560K (Q3'26). Q3'26 vs Q3'25 is +19%, but vs Q3'24 it is −1%. Run counts understate Gb because X runs are bigger, so this is only a weak read on volume and not a Gb estimate.
items.why_new: Run-level public volume trend; the prior GEO read showed +25% y/y for 6000+X samples.

items.label: 2A
items.claim: Twist's academic and government revenue rebounded sharply in the quarter ended Jun 2026, so US academic demand did not weaken in Q2 CY26.
items.detail: 10-Q Note 3 shows academic research and government revenue of $15,512K in FQ3'26 against $11,724K in FQ3'25, which is +32.3% y/y. Management put sequential growth at +21%, which implies about $12.8M in FQ2'26. The call attributed the rise to US accounts and 'several large customers' returning. This is a software-and-reagent supplier's customer line (synthetic DNA plus NGS), not sequencing consumables. It still matches the late-Q2 pickup in US funding releases and quotes that Illumina chose not to extrapolate.
items.source_name: Twist Bioscience 10-Q (quarter ended 30 Jun 2026), Note 3; call summary at allmind.ai
items.quote: several large customers return during the quarter
items.why_new: The known list has Twist NGS +12% only; this is the first academic-line datapoint, and it cuts against the research-weakness view.
items.verify_note: Verified in 10-Q Note 3: $15,512K vs $11,724K (+32.3%). Correction: Twist is a synthetic-DNA and NGS target-enrichment reagent company, not a 'software-and-reagent supplier.' It is a demand read on academic labs, not a price read. Partly offset by F599.

items.label: 2A
items.claim: The Twist academic rebound is a single lumpy quarter. The first half was flat, and management called the setting 'budget-constrained' and 'dynamic'.
items.detail: Nine-month FY26 academic revenue was $40,545K against $36,589K a year earlier (+10.8%). Subtracting Q3 gives H1 FY26 of $25,033K against $24,865K in H1 FY25, which is +0.7%. An analyst on the call cited growth of 3% in the prior quarter against 32% in this one. Management said 'order patterns may fluctuate' and described a 'budget-constrained environment' in which promotions into the segment are continuing. So the Q3 jump looks like returning large customers plus promotional pricing, not a broad recovery in research spending. That fits Illumina's 'too early to call a recovery' stance on research.
items.source_name: Twist FQ3'26 call transcript (allmind.ai, partly garbled) plus 10-Q Note 3; derived arithmetic
items.quote: budget-constrained environment
items.why_new: This is a quantified H1 vs Q3 split for an adjacent supplier. The exclusion list has only Thermo, Bruker and 10x funding reads.
items.verify_note: Verified: 9M $40,545K vs $36,589K. H1 is $25,033K vs $24,865K (+0.7%). The 9M figure is +10.8% including the rebound quarter, so the rebound is concentrated in one quarter. The 'promotions' point is from a partly garbled transcript, so treat it as soft.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: Twist's diagnostics line, its clinical NGS-heavy customer group, grew +15% in the quarter ended Jun 2026, with no sign of a clinical volume stall.
items.detail: Diagnostics revenue was $43,843K in FQ3'26 against $38,134K in FQ3'25, which is +15.0%. Nine-month diagnostics was $119,118K against $108,647K (+9.6%), so the quarter accelerated. Management guides NGS applications to 'return to growth above 20%' in FQ4 after +12% in FQ3, and total FQ4 revenue to $123–124M (+25%). This is weak evidence that clinical genomics customers are still buying NGS inputs. It also sits against the thesis that clinical volume decelerates toward 25% or less. It is a supplier-side proxy, not Gb.
items.why_new: The known list has only the NGS +12% headline and the 'return to 20%' target; it has no diagnostics-line growth.

items.label: 2B
items.claim: Twist's non-therapeutic, non-clinical lines are flat to down, so there is no broad research or industrial demand surge behind the academic bounce.
items.detail: Industry and applied revenue was $5,749K against $6,105K (−5.8% y/y). Global supply partners was $12,859K against $13,046K (−1.4%). Neither line grew in the same quarter as the academic rebound; the growth came from therapeutics (+49%) and diagnostics (+15%), plus the lumpy academic quarter. Management did not address NGS pricing on the call. I found no direct commentary on Illumina, Element, Ultima or Roche pricing.
items.why_new: This is a customer-type revenue split from a tools supplier, which the known list lacks.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: Illumina's pricing leadership comes from a medical-device background focused on limiting price erosion, so the company is managing price decline as an explicit goal.
items.detail: A Berkeley Executive Education faculty bio lists David Mok as Vice President, Pricing, Analytics & Insights, Illumina. He previously ran worldwide pricing at J&J's DePuy Synthes Spine, where the bio says he improved ASP erosion. He also led the pricing transformation at Xilinx and worldwide retail pricing at Seagate. The bio does not mention Illumina or give a start date, so the Illumina link rests on the directory title alone. This is only a weak signal about management intent.
items.source_name: UC Berkeley Haas Executive Education faculty directory
items.why_new: The VP of pricing is not among the known facts, and the profile shows a pricing-transformation specialist leads Illumina pricing.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: Mayo Clinic, a major clinical and academic center, went from zero NovaSeq X series in GEO in 2024 to 16 in Jan–Sep 2026, so its 6000 share fell from 100% to 60% and conversion there is still under way.
items.detail: Series submitted under the institute 'Mayo Clinic': 6000 had 21 in 2024 and 24 in Jan–Sep 2026; X had 0 in 2024 and 16 in Jan–Sep 2026. The absolute number of 6000 series has not fallen (~32 annualized in 2026, against 21), which fits the publication lag. Still, the arrival of X data shows the clinical-hospital segment converting rather than frozen.
items.source_name: NCBI GEO via E-utilities esearch (INST field)
items.why_new: First institution-level conversion reading from GEO, using the submitter-institute field.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: At Memorial Sloan Kettering, NovaSeq 6000 series in GEO are still rising in absolute terms, at 38 in 2024 and 52 in just Jan–Sep 2026, and the 6000 is still 71% of its 6000+X series.
items.detail: MSK 6000 series: 38 (2024) and 52 (Jan–Sep 2026, ~69 annualized, +82%). X series: 13 across 2024–25 combined and 21 in Jan–Sep 2026. Share in 2026 = 52/73 = 71%. The lag in release dates explains part of this, but a top-tier oncology hospital still turning out most of its public data on the 6000 in 2026 fits a slow, sticky hospital tail.
items.source_name: NCBI GEO via E-utilities esearch (INST field)
items.why_new: A named institution-level time series for a large clinical/oncology account. It has not been reported before.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: Stanford University's 6000 share of GEO series dropped from ~94% in 2024 to ~55% in Jan–Sep 2026, the fastest conversion among the institutions sampled.
items.detail: Stanford University 6000 series: 89 (2024) and 76 (Jan–Sep 2026); X series: 6 (2024) and 62 (Jan–Sep 2026). Share = 89/95 = 94% in 2024 and 76/138 = 55% in 2026. This academic flagship shows research converting faster than the hospitals sampled (Mayo 60%, St. Jude 68%, MSK 71%). That fits Illumina's research-ahead-of-clinical pattern, though the samples are small.
items.source_name: NCBI GEO via E-utilities esearch (INST field)
items.why_new: First split of GEO conversion into academic and hospital submitters.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: In the 2026 GEO data, hospital and cancer-center submitters still have 60–71% of their 6000+X series on the 6000, against ~55% at Stanford, so the clinical-leaning tail is visibly thicker.
items.detail: Jan–Sep 2026 series counts (6000 / X / 6000 share): Mayo Clinic 24 / 16 / 60%; St. Jude Children's Research Hospital 54 / 25 / 68%; MSK 52 / 21 / 71%; Stanford University 76 / 62 / 55%. Overlapping series were not netted out at institution level. This matches Illumina's disclosure that clinical work is less converted (78% X) than research (92%), but GEO lags both by roughly two years.
items.source_name: NCBI GEO via E-utilities esearch (INST field)
items.why_new: A named hospital-versus-academic cross-section of the 6000 tail in public data. It is new.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: Chinese universities are not visibly more 6000-heavy in GEO than US hospitals, so China's import ban is not the main reason the 6000 persists in GEO.
items.detail: Jan–Sep 2026 series (6000 / X / share): Fudan University 76 / 18 / 81%; Sun Yat-sen University 30 / 18 / 63%. These sit inside the 60–71% hospital range, except Fudan, which runs higher. The persistence of the 6000 in GEO is therefore broad-based rather than a China artifact (X sales into China have been constrained since the 2025 import ban). The sample is small: two institutions.
items.source_name: NCBI GEO via E-utilities esearch (INST field)
items.why_new: This tests whether China drives the GEO 6000 tail (raised as an open question in the probe notes). It was not tested before.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: Ultima's open-source analysis package ugbio-core is downloaded about 6–8K times a month on PyPI in mid-2026, but there is no baseline to show growth.
items.detail: pypistats shows ugbio-core at 5,784 downloads in May 2026, 8,432 in Jun, 8,135 in Jul and 7,849 in Aug, all with mirrors. Without mirrors the figures are 3,731, 6,430, 6,386 and 5,681. Elembio/bases2fastq on Docker Hub shows 16,954 cumulative pulls since it was registered on 2022-04-14. These counts include CI and mirror traffic and have no Illumina or prior-year comparison, so they can't show how many labs run rival platforms.
items.why_new: This is the first download-count read on the rival short-read tool ecosystem. It has no trend, though, so it only sets a baseline.

items.label: 2B
items.claim: Element AVITI SRA run releases grew 11x in two years: 966 (Q3'24), 4,971 (Q3'25), 10,838 (Q3'26).
items.detail: Y/y growth was +415% and then +118%. Quarterly 2026: Q1 7,071; Q2 11,750; Q3 10,838, so Q3 was -7.8% q/q after Q2 peaked. AVITI runs were 1.7% of 6000 runs in Q3'24, 1.2% in Q3'25 and 2.7% in Q3'26 (10,838/408,823). The rival is small but compounding. Run counts, not Gb. This is the run-level view that F582/F583 measured in GEO samples.
items.why_new: F594 gave only ~5,000 AVITI runs in Q3'25; this adds Q3'24 and the full 2026 quarterly path.
items.verify_note: Verified: Q3'24 AVITI = 966. Correction: AVITI as a share of 6000 runs in Q3'24 was 966/551,041 = 0.18%, not 1.7%. The path is 0.18% → 1.21% → 2.65%, which is steeper than stated. Note the 6000 denominator here (408,823, [Instrument] field) differs slightly from F595's text-match 407,958.

items.label: 2B
items.claim: DNBSEQ-T7 (MGI) SRA runs jumped 2.7x y/y in Q3'26 after being flat for a year.
items.detail: T7 runs: 12,394 (Q3'24), 12,873 (Q3'25), 35,144 (Q3'26), which is +3.9% then +173%. 2026 path: Q1 15,687; Q2 29,130; Q3 35,144, up 2.2x since Q1. T7 runs are 3.2x AVITI runs in Q3'26 (35,144/10,838). The low-cost Chinese platform is the larger price-competitive rival in public data. It is likely concentrated in China-linked submitters, which is a caveat.
items.why_new: GEO items (F585) show T7 samples +25% y/y; SRA runs show +173% in 2026 and a sharp H1'26 ramp.
items.verify_note: Verified: Q3'26 = 35,144. Relabeled 2B because public SRA deposits are research data, not large clinical accounts. The jump from 15.7K to 35.1K in two quarters could be a few large BioProjects, and DNBSEQ submitters are China-linked. Also, mainland China largely deposits to CNCB-GSA, so SRA understates and noises MGI. The price-competitor read is indirect.

items.label: 2B
items.claim: AVITI plus T7 rose from 2.3% to 7.6% of five-platform SRA run releases in two years.
items.detail: Share of 6000+X+AVITI+T7 runs. Q3'24: 13,360/581,731 = 2.3%. Q3'25: 17,844/489,660 = 3.6%. Q3'26: 45,982/606,789 = 7.6%. The rival share doubled in the last year and more than tripled in two. Ultima is excluded because its instrument string did not resolve, so the true rival share is higher. Run counts, not Gb.
items.why_new: First run-level rival share of short-read output; the GEO figures of 0.75%/3.9%/4.5% are samples and stop at human+mouse.
items.verify_note: The arithmetic checks (2.30% / 3.64% / 7.58%). Relabeled 2B because the data is research and public. About 76% of the Q3'26 rival count is DNBSEQ-T7 (35,144/45,982), so the caveats in F610 apply. This partly overlaps F609/F610 as a combination. Counts are runs, not Gb.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: Combined 6000+X runs fell 5.7% q/q in Q3'26, from 594,978 in Q2 to 560,907.
items.detail: Q2'26: 476,113+118,865=594,978. Q3'26: 408,823+152,084=560,907. That is -5.7% q/q, and the 6000 decline outweighed X growth. Run counts are release-date based and lumpy, and Q3 may be partly seasonal. It is a weak indicator of slowing public output.
items.why_new: Adds the Q1-Q2'26 sequential series.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: The Navy Naval Medical Research Center is buying a new one-year NovaSeq 6000 Silver Support Plan for serial A01716 in a notice posted Dec 2025.
items.detail: Notice N3239826Q4072 was posted 22 Dec 2025 and lists four line items of CAT# 20019988, 'NovaSeq 6000 Silver Support Plan'. It requires full OEM parts coverage and states intent to sole-source to Illumina. The notice is listed as Active, with responses due 31 Dec 2026, and it is not awarded. This is one government-owned 6000 being kept under paid service into 2026-27, not decommissioned. It suggests federal 6000 boxes are not leaving yet, but it is one box and no prior-year renewal is shown.
items.quote: NovaSeq 6000 Silver Support Plan
items.why_new: Not in the known list: the list has no federal 6000 service-contract serials. This is a 2025-26 notice, not one already mined (S147 not yet mined).

items.label: 1A
items.claim: NCI posted a sole-source preventive-maintenance notice in Aug 2026 for a government-owned NovaSeq 6000, serial A01064, and a separate NCI Frederick agreement covers a 6000 (A01063) on a Gold plan through Jan 2027.
items.detail: NIH/NCI notice 75N98026Q01014 was posted 14 Aug 2026 and closed 24 Aug 2026, as a firm-fixed-price sole source to Illumina under FAR 6.302-1. The Frederick solicitation M26-159 (period 1/21/26 to 1/20/27, proposals due 1 Dec 2025) lists a 6000 (A01063) on a Gold Support Plan, plus a MiSeq, NextSeq X Plus and NovaSeq X Plus. The Frederick agreement shows an agency running a 6000 alongside X Plus systems, which is a dual-running example. The Frederick details come from a search-result snippet, and I did not open the page.
items.why_new: Gives named 2026 federal 6000 serials (A01064, A01063) in service renewal, and an NCI site running a 6000 next to an X Plus. Neither is in the known list.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: SRA's 6000 tail by release date overstates current 6000 activity, because Q3'26 releases include runs registered about a year earlier.
items.detail: Of the 32 runs I read from four sampled offsets in the Q3'26 NovaSeq 6000 result set (407,958 runs), the ANU and Xi'an Jiaotong runs carry SRR345645xx accessions. Those numbers were issued far below the ~SRR4087xxxx range of fresh submissions in the same result set (Chinese Academy of Medical Sciences, SRR40869699), so I infer the data were sequenced and registered roughly 12 months before release. Public 6000 run counts therefore trail real sequencing by about a year, and the 'flat y/y' read (Q3'25 410,548 vs Q3'26 407,958, -0.6%) reflects 2025 activity, not the current tail. The accession-date mapping is my inference and was not verified against SRA submission dates.
items.why_new: Known notes treat SRA/GEO 6000 counts as lagging in GEO but not in SRA; this ties SRA lag to accession ranges and puts the Q3'25 vs Q3'26 comparison at -0.6%.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: At six named large sequencing centers, X runs outnumber 6000 runs at five, and none has zero X runs. The exception is HudsonAlpha, which is still 6000-heavy.
items.detail: I searched SRA free text for each center name (a text match, not a center_name filter). The 6000 counts are for Q3'26 and the X counts are for Jan–Sep 2026, so X is a longer window and the ratios are biased toward X. Q3'26 6000 / 2026 YTD X: New York Genome Center 74 / 1,902; Broad 3 / 55; Macrogen 511 / 995; Baylor 95 / 112; HudsonAlpha 130 / 12. Novogene is a same-window match: 7,575 6000 vs 5,802 X in Q3'26, so X is 43% of its NovaSeq-class runs against 27.0% for the whole SRA (150,561 X vs 407,958 6000). That points to outsourced providers converting faster than the average depositor.
items.url: https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/esearch.fcgi?db=sra&term="Illumina NovaSeq X"[ALL] AND "New York Genome Center"[ALL] AND 2026/01/01:2026/09/30[PDAT]&retmax=0&retmode=json
items.why_new: First center-level 6000-vs-X read; prior items covered only platform totals and GEO.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: The Q3'26 6000 releases I sampled come from academic, environmental and consortium submitters rather than clinical labs, and many contributing labs may never have an X.
items.detail: Sampled Q3'26 6000 runs come from the Leibniz plant-genetics institute (a GBS project), UCSDMI (Qiita microbiome, PRJEB11419), NGDC/Zhejiang University (soil and groundwater pathogens), the Chinese Academy of Medical Sciences, Essen University neurosurgery, ANU mouse RNA-seq, and Xi'an Jiaotong hospital. None is a clinical production lab. That fits the earlier point that SRA labels cannot size the clinical tail, which Illumina puts at ~80% of remaining 6000 Gb. The sample is 4 offsets of 8 runs (about 32 runs, clustered by project), so it is anecdotal.
items.why_new: Names the actual centers behind Q3'26 6000 releases, which prior GEO and SRA counts did not.

items.label: 2B
items.claim: Rival platforms (AVITI plus DNBSEQ-T7) took about 23% of the year-on-year growth in new-platform public SRA runs in Q3'26, up from about 9% in Q3'25, so challengers are capturing a rising share of incremental research sequencing.
items.detail: Q3'25 vs Q3'24: X runs grew by 43,974 (16,351 → 60,325) and AVITI+T7 by 4,484 (13,360 → 17,844), so rivals took 4,484/48,458 = 9.3% of the increment. Q3'26 vs Q3'25: X grew by 91,759 (→ 152,084) and rivals by 28,138 (→ 45,982), giving 28,138/119,897 = 23.5%. Ex-T7 (AVITI only), the share rises from 4,005/47,979 = 8.3% to 5,867/97,626 = 6.0%. The acceleration is therefore driven by DNBSEQ-T7 (likely China-linked), not Element. Counts are run accessions by release date, not Gb.
items.why_new: Measures rival capture of incremental runs rather than share of the stock, and shows the AVITI-only capture is falling.

items.label: 2B
items.claim: In GEO, rivals' share of the year-on-year increase in HT samples fell from about 16% to about 6.5%, which contradicts SRA's accelerating rival capture. The rival-momentum signal depends on the dataset chosen.
items.detail: GEO human+mouse: Illumina 6000+X samples grew by 11,872 (53,471 → 65,343) in Q3'25 and by 16,328 (→ 81,671) in Q3'26. Rival GSMs grew by 2,278 (402 → 2,680) and then by 1,128 (→ 3,808). Rival capture of the increment was 2,278/14,150 = 16.1% and then 1,128/17,456 = 6.5%; AVITI+UG alone captured ~3.9% in Q3'26 (660/16,988). The two public datasets disagree on direction, so neither is strong evidence of accelerating research share loss.
items.url: https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/esearch.fcgi?db=gds&term=(GPL34295[ACCN] OR GPL34475[ACCN] OR GPL34762[ACCN] OR GPL36595[ACCN] OR GPL29480[ACCN] OR GPL28330[ACCN]) AND gsm[ETYP] AND 2026/07/01:2026/09/30[PDAT]&retmax=0
items.why_new: Cross-checks the GEO and SRA rival series against each other and finds they conflict, which no item states.

items.label: 2A
items.claim: Public research sequencing activity rebounded in the latest year: five-platform SRA run releases rose about 24% y/y in Q3'26 after falling about 16% in Q3'25.
items.detail: 6000+X+AVITI+T7 runs were 581,731 (Q3'24), 489,660 (Q3'25) and 606,789 (Q3'26), which is −15.8% and then +23.9%. GEO HT samples rose +22% and then +25%. Together with Twist's academic revenue (+32% in the June 2026 quarter), this points to research volume recovering rather than flat. That cuts against a 'volume flat' research thesis, although the runs are publication-lagged and are not Gb or dollars.
items.why_new: Total public run growth and the triangulation with Twist are not stated in any item.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: Freenome, a cancer blood-test developer heading to a public listing via the Perceptive SPAC, names Ultima Genomics in its confidential draft registration statement.
