items.detail: Freenome's DRS (2026-01-12) and DRS/A (2026-03-30, accession 0001140361-26-011956) matched the 'Ultima Genomics' full-text query. The context is not yet read. It could be a sequencing supplier or a competitive mention, and either would show a large prospective Illumina customer with a second-source option. The snippet was not available.
items.why_new: Freenome's DRS filings are not in the sources used so far, and Freenome was previously noted only as an AXELIOS evaluator.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: NCI Frederick's NovaSeq 6000 A01063 is still on a top-tier Gold plan through Jan 2027, while the same federal lab also services two X Plus systems, so the lab is running both platforms at once.
items.detail: Solicitation M26-159 (proposals due 1 Dec 2025, period 1/21/26–1/20/27) lists NovaSeq 6000 A01063 on a Gold Support Plan and NovaSeq X Plus LH00551 on a Silver plan. It also lists NextSeq X Plus LH00236, a MiSeq and two DRAGEN servers. Separate solicitation M25-214 (period 3/26/26–3/25/27) services a second X Plus, LH00584. That makes at least 2 X Plus and 1 NextSeq X Plus against 1 NovaSeq 6000 in the NCI Frederick notices I found. The lab keeps paying for the premium tier on the 6000 even after buying X systems, which fits the dual-running tail rather than a clean swap. Caveat: these are service plans, not consumables, and the page does not say how much the 6000 is used.
items.why_new: Known list only says Frederick's core rate card shows no 6000 row. The service notices show A01063 still on a Gold plan to Jan 2027, next to two X Plus systems.

Solicitation M26-159 (period 1/21/26–1/20/27, due 1 Dec 2025, now closed) lists NovaSeq 6000 A01063 on a Gold plan with 1 PM, NovaSeq X Plus LH00551 on Silver, a 'NextSeq X Plus' LH00236 on Silver, a MiSeq and two DRAGEN servers. 'NextSeq X Plus' is not a real product. The LH serial prefix is a NovaSeq X-series prefix, so this is probably a second X Plus with a typo in the listing. That means the X count does not rely on M25-214, which I did not check. This is one federal re

items.label: 1A
items.claim: NIEHS moved its NovaSeq 6000 from a Silver to a Bronze service plan in 2025, which suggests lower-use tail instruments are being kept running on cheaper coverage.
items.detail: NIEHS bought a Silver Support Plan for the 6000 for 6/29/2023–6/28/2024. The 2025 notice (75N96025Q00037, posted 10 Jun 2025, period 6/29/2025–6/28/2026) is for a Bronze agreement. Illumina's brochure describes Bronze as the cheapest plan, aimed at low sample volumes without critical turnaround needs. I found no follow-on notice for 6/29/2026 onward, so I cannot say whether the box was renewed or retired. The 2024 tier was not confirmed because the page timed out.
items.why_new: The exclusion list only mentions generic 6000 service notices. A tier downgrade and the missing 2026 follow-on are new.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: The Navy NMRC is buying a new Silver plan for NovaSeq 6000 A01716, and prior-year NMRC awards of about $141K–$146K suggest the 6000 service plan is an annual repeat buy.
items.detail: N3239826Q4072 was posted 22–28 Dec 2025 (dates vary by aggregator). It is a one-year plan, with four identical line items of CAT# 20019988, for Silver Spring, MD, and is sole-source to Illumina. Search snippets mention NMRC Silver plan values of $141,313 and $145,522, but the year of each is unclear. Illumina's list price for the Silver plan at GovSci is $175,653, so the NMRC figures are roughly 17–20% below list if the plan is the same. The notice does not mention the X.
items.quote: NovaSeq 6000 Silver Support Plan
items.why_new: The serial and notice are already known. The NMRC dollar values and the discount against the GovSci list price are new, but the snippets are unverified.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: Federal buyers are still renewing NovaSeq 6000 service plans in 2026 across several agencies (Navy, NCI Bethesda, NCI Frederick), and the 2026 notices show no X swaps.
items.detail: The 6000 notices I found are NICHD (2/15/2025–2/14/2026, with a MiSeq), CDC (12/7/2024–12/6/2025, $144,910, 6000 plus MiSeq), NIEHS A? (6/29/2025–6/28/2026), NCI A01064 (posted 14 Aug 2026, FAR 6.302-1), Navy A01716 (Dec 2025) and NCI Frederick A01063 (Jan 2026–Jan 2027). That is 6 agency notices over about 20 months. Separately, NCI Frederick M25-214 and the NIAID solicitation covering X Plus LH00323 show X service plans are being bought alongside. No notice I read replaces a 6000 serial with an X serial.
items.why_new: This adds the NICHD, CDC and NIEHS periods, the NCI Frederick Gold line and the X Plus counterparts to the known A01064 and A01716 notices. The sample is small and federal only.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: The 6000 service-plan evidence is a small federal sample and says nothing about 6000 consumables volume or about the large clinical labs that drive the thesis.
items.detail: Service contracts are bought to keep installed boxes alive and often cover idle or low-use instruments, as the NIEHS Bronze tier suggests. A box under a plan can still convert its consumables to X lanes. Each notice covers 1 instrument, and the CDC and NICHD notices bundle a MiSeq. The 6 notices found sit against an installed base of roughly 1,360 6000s at end-FY25 (known list).
items.why_new: This is the sample-size and use caveat for the whole notice set, which the analyst should weigh before using it.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: Federal buyers pay about 20% below Illumina's list for the NovaSeq 6000 Silver plan, so even service carries a discount.
items.detail: GovSci lists the Silver plan (CAT# 20019988) at $175,653.32. Snippets put the NMRC Silver award at $141,313 and $145,522 (about 17–20% below list: 1 − 141,313/175,653 = 19.6%; 1 − 145,522/175,653 = 17.2%). CDC's $144,910 covered a 6000 plus a MiSeq, which would mean a steeper discount per box if the list price is comparable. The GovSci price carries no date and the NMRC values are undated snippets, so this is directional only. It touches service, not consumables.
items.source_name: GovSci; search snippets of NMRC and CDC notices
items.why_new: The exclusion list covers consumable and kit list prices but has no service-plan prices.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: Gold-tier service on the 6000 is listed as a 'warranty upgrade' at $113,750, below the Silver list price of $175,653, so the tail's service pricing does not line up cleanly with the 'premium' plan.
items.detail: GovSci shows NovaSeq 6000 Warranty Upgrade: Gold Support Plan (20020137) at $113,750 and Silver (20019988) at $175,653.32. The Gold item is a warranty upgrade, so it is probably priced differently from a stand-alone Gold plan. I could not tell whether the two are comparable, so no conclusion is drawn on tier pricing.
items.why_new: Service price points were not in the known evidence.

items.label: 2A
items.claim: The University of Colorado system added Illumina to new system-wide master agreements in Dec 2025, usable for purchases under $250K.
items.detail: The CU Procurement Service Center post (15 Dec 2025) lists Illumina among new master agreements and says the PSC is updating its contracts page. It gives no discount, contract number or term. It shows that more academic systems are pre-negotiating Illumina pricing, but it is not price evidence.
items.why_new: No CU or other system-wide Illumina academic master agreement is on the known list.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: Measured in gigabases rather than run counts, the NovaSeq X's share of public NovaSeq data released in INSDC (ENA/SRA) more than doubled in a year: about 4.6% in Q3'24, 15.7% in Q3'25 and 32–34% in Q3'26. The conversion is not slowing.
items.detail: Method: we counted runs with ENA portal /count, which mirrors SRA, by first_public quarter and base_count bin (<3, 3–15, 15–60, 60–150, ≥150 Gb). Gb was estimated by giving each bin a midpoint of 1 / 7 / 30 / 90 / 220 Gb; Q3'24 and Q3'25 used a single ≥60 bin at 110 Gb. The resulting Gb: 6000 2,062K / 2,774K / 2,489K and X 98K / 517K / 1,191–1,261K, so the X Gb share was 4.6% → 15.7% → 32.4–33.6%. The share rose about 11 points, then about 17–18 points, so the pace is not decelerating. Run share is lower and rising more slowly: 2.4% → 11.2% → 24.2%.
items.url: https://www.ebi.ac.uk/ena/portal/api/count?result=read_run&query=(instrument_model="Illumina NovaSeq X" OR instrument_model="Illumina NovaSeq X Plus") AND first_public>=2026-07-01 AND first_public<=2026-09-30 AND base_count>=15000000000
items.source_name: EMBL-EBI ENA Portal API (INSDC mirror of SRA)
items.why_new: This is the first Gb-weighted (not sample- or run-count) public series. Earlier items F577–F596 used counts only.
items.verify_note: The ENA bucket arithmetic is consistent with F644. 'Not decelerating' is only true in share points. In logistic odds the multiple slowed from 3.9x to 2.7x, so conversion is decelerating. Release dates (first_public) lag sequencing by months to years, and SRA is research-heavy, while ~80% of the remaining 6000 Gb is clinical and never deposited. This is not evidence on the clinical tail, which is the subject of 1A. Known D052 already covers the deposit-lag point for GEO.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: In Gb, the 6000's public data output fell for the first time: down about 10% y/y in Q3'26, even though its run count rose about 21%. The 'tail not shrinking' read from run counts (F580, F595, F528) is a counting artifact.
items.detail: 6000 runs: 388,682 (Q3'24), 421,447 (Q3'25), 511,741 (Q3'26). Runs of at least 15 Gb went 25,629 → 38,045 → 30,305 (−20% y/y), and runs of at least 60 Gb went 4,451 → 6,359 → 5,198 (−18%). Estimated 6000 Gb went 2.06 → 2.77 → 2.49 Pb, about −10% y/y. In the same period X Gb rose about 2.3–2.4x.
items.url: https://www.ebi.ac.uk/ena/portal/api/count?result=read_run&query=instrument_model="Illumina NovaSeq 6000" AND first_public>=2026-07-01 AND first_public<=2026-09-30 AND base_count>=15000000000
items.why_new: It reverses the earlier run- and sample-count reading that 6000 public output was still rising.
items.verify_note: Duplicates F644: same endpoint, same quarters, different bins. Keep F644 as the primary item. The 6000 Gb fall comes out at −10% to −13% under either binning, so the direction holds. Also note that ENA's 6000 run count (511,741, +21% y/y) conflicts with known F595 (Entrez SRA, 407,958, flat). The two use different date fields, so neither run series should anchor anything.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: For deep, genome-scale runs (60 Gb or more), the X's share of public 6000+X runs went from 8.6% (Q3'24) to 20.3% (Q3'25) to 39.8% (Q3'26). High-Gb work is converting fastest.
items.detail: Runs of at least 60 Gb, 6000 vs X: 4,451 vs 417 (Q3'24), 6,359 vs 1,623 (Q3'25), 5,198 vs 3,437 (Q3'26). Within Q3'26, 1,044 X runs were at least 150 Gb against 802 for the 6000. So 30% of the X's ≥60 Gb runs are 150 Gb or more, against 15% for the 6000.
items.url: https://www.ebi.ac.uk/ena/portal/api/count?result=read_run&query=instrument_model="Illumina NovaSeq 6000" AND first_public>=2026-07-01 AND first_public<=2026-09-30 AND base_count>=150000000000
items.why_new: No earlier item splits the public data by run depth.
items.verify_note: Consistent with the F644 buckets. A caveat on reading it: SRA base_count is per run accession, which roughly means per library or sample, not per instrument flow cell. 'Runs of 60 Gb or more' therefore means deep samples (WGS-scale), not large flow cells. That is valid for 'genome-scale work is converting', but the data is research-weighted and lagged.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: The work left on the 6000 is shifting toward shallow, low-Gb samples. That fits a tail of low-volume users who are less volume-elastic.
items.detail: Average Gb per 6000 run went 5.3 (Q3'24) → 6.6 (Q3'25) → 4.9 (Q3'26). Runs under 3 Gb rose from 259,973 to 367,640 (+41% y/y) and are now 72% of 6000 runs. X runs average about 7.3–7.7 Gb in Q3'26, roughly 1.5–1.6x the 6000. The deep work leaves the 6000 first, and what remains is amplicon, 16S and low-depth RNA-type work.
items.url: https://www.ebi.ac.uk/ena/portal/api/count?result=read_run&query=instrument_model="Illumina NovaSeq 6000" AND first_public>=2026-07-01 AND first_public<=2026-09-30 AND base_count>=3000000000
items.why_new: This is the first per-run depth profile of the public 6000 tail.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: Growth in combined 6000+X public Gb slowed sharply, from about +52% y/y in Q3'25 to about +14% in Q3'26, while run counts still grew about 42%.
items.detail: Estimated combined Gb: 2.16 Pb (Q3'24), 3.29 Pb (Q3'25), 3.68–3.75 Pb (Q3'26). Runs of at least 60 Gb grew +64% (4,868 → 7,982) and then only +8% (→ 8,635). Caveats: the data is release-dated and research-heavy, and the release lag runs 6–24 months, so this reflects 2024–25 sequencing more than current demand. It also differs from F581, which counted samples (+25%).
items.url: https://www.ebi.ac.uk/ena/portal/api/count?result=read_run&query=instrument_model="Illumina NovaSeq 6000" AND first_public>=2025-07-01 AND first_public<=2025-09-30 AND base_count>=60000000000
items.why_new: This is the first Gb-weighted growth rate for public deposits. Earlier items were run or sample counts.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: Public deposit data lags Illumina's own conversion by more than two years, so it cannot calibrate the ~5 points of 2027 mix shift. Its trend only shows that conversion is still moving.
items.detail: Public X Gb share was ~34% in Q3'26, against Illumina's reported 55% (Q3'24) and 83% (Q2'26) of HT Gb shipped. On the logistic fit the public share has an odds multiple of 3.9x in the first year and 2.7x in the second, which would put it at ~58% by Q3'27. Illumina's own series added ~+5 points over three quarters (78% → 83%), which extrapolates to ~88–89% by end-2027. That leaves about 5 points of Gb share to convert. Because the 6000 carries ~3.4x the revenue per Gb, that is far more than 5 points of revenue mix. The last two calculations use already-known Illumina data, not SRA.
items.url: https://www.ebi.ac.uk/ena/portal/api/count?result=read_run&query=(instrument_model="Illumina NovaSeq X" OR instrument_model="Illumina NovaSeq X Plus") AND first_public>=2024-07-01 AND first_public<=2024-09-30
items.why_new: It quantifies the size of the public-data lag in Gb terms. D052 did this only for GEO samples.
items.verify_note: This restates known D052 (public deposits lag Illumina's reported share by about 2 years) for SRA instead of GEO. It is a methodological caveat, not evidence against 1A. Its own extrapolation is also inconsistent: +1.7 pts per quarter from 83% gives about 93% by Q4'27, not 88–89%. The revenue-mix point is already known (each 5 pts of X share ≈ −8.5% of HT revenue).

items.label: 2B
items.claim: Measured in Gb, Element AVITI is under 1% of public short-read output (6000+X+AVITI) in Q3'26. Its fast-growing run count is mostly small samples.
items.detail: ENA AVITI runs in Q3'26: 10,684, of which only 1,797 (17%) are 3 Gb or more. Our rough estimate is ~8.9K Gb from runs under 3 Gb plus ~18K Gb from runs of 3 Gb or more (assuming ~10 Gb each), about 27K Gb in total. That is ~0.7% of the ~3.7 Pb on 6000+X. On run share AVITI is ~1.6%.
items.url: https://www.ebi.ac.uk/ena/portal/api/count?result=read_run&query=instrument_model="Element AVITI" AND first_public>=2026-07-01 AND first_public<=2026-09-30 AND base_count>=3000000000
items.why_new: F609 and F611 gave AVITI run counts only. This is the first Gb-weighted share.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: EDGAR full-text search finds almost no rival-platform disclosure at the large US clinical labs, so there is no filing-level sign of a credible price threat at Illumina's biggest accounts.
items.detail: For 1 Jan 2025 to 12 Oct 2026, the exact phrase "Ultima Genomics" returned only four operating filers in 10-K, 10-Q and 8-K filings: Guardant (10-K FY24, FY25), PacBio (10-Ks and all five 10-Qs from Q1'25 to Q2'26 for "Ultima" + sequencing), 10x (8-K, 12 Feb 2025) and the Freenome DRS/A. The other hits were SolarEdge, which is noise. "AXELIOS" and "Complete Genomics" returned 0 hits in 10-K/10-Q/8-K/S-1/DRS. "Sequencing by expansion" returned only the Freenome DRS/A. Natera, Tempus, Caris, GeneDx, Myriad and BillionToOne do not appear for "Ultima Genomics", but the index may miss variant spellings. The Guardant 10-K FY25 mentions Ultima once, only as a platform that "could be used for liquid biopsy".
items.why_new: Quantified negative result across EDGAR (only 4 operating filers name Ultima; 0 for AXELIOS and Complete Genomics) was not in the known list.

items.label: 2B
items.claim: 10x Genomics sued Element in May 2026 over the AVITI24, which puts legal risk on the rival's single-cell research push.
items.detail: The 10x Q2'26 10-Q (filed 7 Aug 2026) says it sued Element in May 2026, alleging AVITI24 and its kits infringe four US patents (11,021,737; 11,566,276; 11,566,277; 12,264,358). A second suit in the UPC Munich Local Division alleges infringement of EP 4249605 and EP 4491741. Element filed a partial motion to dismiss in July 2026 and an EPO opposition against EP 4491741. No schedule is set. An injunction would hit Element's research single-cell and spatial positioning, which is Element's main route into the academic market, so it would cap the research price pressure from AVITI.
items.quote: Element filed a partial motion to dismiss in July 2026.
items.why_new: Known list covers only Illumina's suits against Element; 10x's suit against AVITI24 (US and UPC) is new.
items.verify_note: Verified in the 10x Q2'26 10-Q. The D. Del. suit was filed May 2026 on US 11,021,737 / 11,566,276 / 11,566,277 / 12,264,358 against AVITI24. The UPC Munich suit asserts EP 4249605 and EP 4491741. Element filed a partial motion to dismiss and an EPO opposition against EP '741 in July 2026, and no schedule is set. This is new, since the known list covers only the Illumina–Element suits. The impact on research pricing is speculative: it is early-stage, covers AVITI24 single-cell and spatial only, a

items.label: 1B
items.claim: Roche is a large shareholder and lender in Freenome, which is moving to a public listing and is evaluating AXELIOS, so Freenome has a captive route away from Illumina.
items.detail: The Freenome/Perceptive SPAC DRS/A (30 Mar 2026) says Roche will own about 18.11% of New Freenome common stock after closing. A Roche convertible note converts at $12.00 and Roche receives 12,778,058 merger-consideration shares. I read about 326K characters of the document and found no mention of Illumina, Ultima or sequencers in the proxy/transaction section. The business and supplier sections are not in this file, so the DRS/A does not confirm an Ultima supply deal. The ownership link makes a Roche-sequencer shift at Freenome more plausible, but that is inference.
items.quote: Roche will own approximately 18.11% of New Freenome Common Stock.
items.why_new: Known list notes Freenome evaluating AXELIOS and naming Ultima; Roche's 18.11% stake and $12 convertible note are new.

items.label: 2B
items.claim: Element is being built into the research workflow ecosystem: Twist expanded its collaboration to put its library prep and target enrichment on AVITI flow cells.
items.detail: Twist's FQ3'25 release (4 Aug 2025) lists an "expanded collaboration with Element Biosciences" for AVITI workflows on Trinity flowcells. Twist NGS revenue was $55.3M (+27% vs $43.4M) and the CEO cited "deepening our reach into the long tail of the academic market". It shows Element compatibility work, not any price effect on Illumina.
items.quote: Expanded collaboration with Element Biosciences to enable Element's AVITI systems
items.why_new: Known list has Twist NGS growth but not the AVITI/Trinity workflow collaboration.

items.label: 2B
items.claim: A small US genetic-testing program (Virotek/Kala Bio) names Element as a sequencing vendor in its cost-of-goods schedule.
items.detail: The Virotek-Kala Bio exclusive distribution agreement (effective 3 Sep 2026, 8-K Ex. 10.1) lists Element Biosciences in the "Sequencing / reference laboratory fees" row for the Eye-Gene tests. The fee is redacted and no volume or commitment is stated. It is a tiny example of a US genetic-testing program using Element capacity, but there is no price evidence.
items.why_new: A new named Element clinical-testing user not on the known list.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: Illumina's published 2022 US oncology contract template capped the NovaSeq v1.5 consumables discount at 22% at $100M+ annual spend, and NovaSeq discounts began only above $5M.
items.detail: Appendix 1, revision of 6 Jan 2022: the NovaSeq v1.5 column runs 0% up to $5M, then 3% ($5-10M), 5%, 10% ($20-30M), 13%, 15%, 17%, 20% ($75-100M) and 22% at $100M+. The NextSeq 550 TG column gets 40% at the top, and NextSeq 1000/2000 gets 15%. This is the published pre-X baseline against which the 2024+ X schedules and the redacted Natera and Caris tiers can be compared. It also implies that formal template discounts on the 6000 were modest, so most of the extra discounts now reported for large accounts are negotiated outside the template. I could not read any 2024+ schedule to measure escalation.
items.source_name: Illumina Appendix 1 to Exhibit A, Universal Consumables and Instruments Discount Schedules
items.why_new: The known list covers Natera/Caris/Guardant contract terms but not Illumina's own public tier table; it is old (2022) and has no X column.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: In Jan 2022, 6000 S4 v1.5 300-cycle list was $14,400 per kit, and the template credited each installed NovaSeq 6000 as 10 instrument credits.
items.detail: The 6 Jan 2022 appendix catalogue lists S4 300cyc at $14,400, S2 300cyc at $9,600 and S1 300cyc at $5,250. The 6000 system was $985,000. Hardware discounts reached 24% at 900+ credits. Snippet-level only (not verified by opening the file): the Jan/Mar 2024 versions give X Plus 13 credits and X 10 credits, so the X counts for more than the 6000 in credit tiers. This is an older price anchor for the 6000's per-Gb price before the later Salk-style list cuts of 16-24%.
items.why_new: It gives the 2022 official 6000 kit list-price anchor (S4 $14,400). The known list has only 2025-26 S4-300 prices ($52K→$39.7K at Salk, $21,683 from GSA).

items.label: 2B
items.claim: AVITI single-cell runs are mostly shallow, so by Gb its share of single-cell output is far below its run share.
items.detail: Runs of at least 20 Gb as a share of all single-cell runs, Q3'26: AVITI 25/1,008 = 2.5%; X 952/4,362 = 21.8%; 6000 4,216/20,931 = 20.1%. Among runs of at least 60 Gb in Q3'26, AVITI has 9, X 350 and 6000 1,731. Of the 5,193 runs of at least 20 Gb (6000+X+AVITI), AVITI is 0.48%. In Q3'25 the same floor-bin share was 14/4,898 = 0.29%. The base_count cutoffs are only a proxy for Gb share.
items.url: https://www.ebi.ac.uk/ena/portal/api/count?result=read_run&query=instrument_model="Element AVITI" AND library_source="TRANSCRIPTOMIC SINGLE CELL" AND first_public>=2026-07-01 AND first_public<=2026-09-30 AND base_count>=20000000000
items.why_new: This is a Gb-based cut of single-cell data, which the all-library items do not provide.
items.verify_note: Plausible and new, but per-accession base_count partly reflects AVITI's lower output per flow cell and different multiplexing, not only shallow experiments. Single-cell is one counting application. This does not show Illumina pricing power.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: Deep single-cell runs on the 6000 and X combined fell as a share of runs, so the Q3'26 rebound is shallow.
items.detail: Runs of at least 20 Gb on the 6000 were 3,900 in Q3'24, 4,467 in Q3'25 and 4,216 in Q3'26 (-6% y/y), against all-run growth of +54% for the 6000 in Q3'26. The 6000's deep-run share of its own runs fell 14% → 33% → 20%. X deep runs were 417 → 952 (+128%). Combined 6000+X runs of at least 20 Gb went 4,884 → 5,169 (+6%) while all runs rose +72%. Gb per run is falling, which matches volume growth lagging run counts (F631).
items.url: https://www.ebi.ac.uk/ena/portal/api/count?result=read_run&query=instrument_model="Illumina NovaSeq 6000" AND library_source="TRANSCRIPTOMIC SINGLE CELL" AND first_public>=2026-07-01 AND first_public<=2026-09-30 AND base_count>=20000000000
items.why_new: Single-cell deep-run counts. The known Gb items (F627-F633) cover all libraries.

items.label: 2B
items.claim: Single-cell runs on the T7 (MGI) fell in Q3'26 and Ultima has almost none, so cheap-rival capture of single-cell research is not visible.
items.detail: T7 single-cell runs: 59 (Q3'24), 484 (Q3'25), 382 (Q3'26, -21% y/y). UG 100 single-cell runs: 0 (Q3'25) and 15 (Q3'26). Ultima's single-cell push has so far left no mark in public deposits.
items.url: https://www.ebi.ac.uk/ena/portal/api/count?result=read_run&query=instrument_model="UG 100" AND library_source="TRANSCRIPTOMIC SINGLE CELL" AND first_public>=2026-07-01 AND first_public<=2026-09-30
items.why_new: Ultima and T7 single-cell counts, which are not in the known items.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: In ENA public data, estimated NovaSeq 6000 output (Gb) fell about 13% y/y in Q3'26, and the NovaSeq X share of 6000+X Gb about doubled, from ~17% to ~36%. So by data volume the 6000 is shrinking and conversion is still moving, even though 6000 run counts are rising.
items.detail: I used ENA count-endpoint run counts in base_count buckets (<1, 1–10, 10–50, 50–100, 100–200, ≥200 Gb), assumed bucket means of 0.3/3.5/20/70/135/300 Gb, and filtered by first_public. 6000, Q3'25: buckets 210,735/146,999/55,560/4,878/2,892/383, about 2.54 Pb. 6000, Q3'26: 322,724/134,975/47,466/3,910/2,379/287, about 2.20 Pb (−13%). X/X Plus, Q3'25: 16,478/24,581/10,375/1,048/776/130, about 0.52 Pb. X/X Plus, Q3'26: 76,490/60,682/21,987/2,184/1,382/713, about 1.23 Pb (+138%). The X Gb share (~36%) is far below Illumina's 83% shipped-Gb share, so public deposits lag. What matters here is the direction and the y/y change, not the level. The bucket means are my assumptions.
items.source_name: EMBL-EBI ENA Portal API (read_run count endpoint)
items.why_new: Earlier GEO/SRA items counted runs, samples or series only. This is the first Gb-weighted public estimate, and it shows 6000 Gb falling y/y while 6000 runs rise.
items.verify_note: Verified: 6000 Q3'25 total = 421,447, 6000 Q3'26 ≥10 Gb = 54,042, X Q3'26 ≥200 Gb = 713. The bucket sums reconcile exactly to the totals, and my recomputed Gb is 2.535 Pb → 2.199 Pb for the 6000 (−13%) and 0.516 → 1.228 Pb for the X. X Gb share: 16.9% → 35.8%. Caveats: first_public lag, research-weighted, assumed bucket means. Downgrade to weak if used to argue about the clinical tail.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: The public 6000 tail is increasingly small runs. 6000 runs of 10 Gb or more fell 15% y/y while sub-1 Gb runs rose 53%, which fits a residual base of low-volume users who pay the highest per-Gb prices.
items.detail: 6000 runs, Q3'25 → Q3'26: total 421,447 → 511,741 (+21%); ≥1 Gb 210,712 → 189,017 (−10%); ≥10 Gb 63,713 → 54,042 (−15%); ≥50 Gb 8,153 → 6,576 (−19%); ≥100 Gb 3,275 → 2,666 (−19%); ≥200 Gb 383 → 287 (−25%). Sub-1 Gb runs rose 210,735 → 322,724 (+53%). Core rate cards (D028/D032) show small 6000 flow cells cost 4–10x the X 25B per Gb. A tail of small-run users is therefore the high-price tail behind the 3.4x revenue-per-Gb gap.
items.why_new: This is the first run-size breakdown of the public 6000 tail. Earlier SRA/GEO items (F595, F580) showed only flat or rising totals.
items.verify_note: The counts are right, but the inference is overstated. Sub-1 Gb 'runs' are small libraries (amplicons, small RNA), usually multiplexed on S4 flow cells. They do not identify low-volume users on small, high-price flow cells. Sub-1 Gb runs also carry only ~4% of 6000 Gb (~97K of 2,199K Gb). See the derived item: in Gb terms the 6000 tail is not turning into a small-run tail.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: Genome-scale work has largely left the 6000 in public data. The X share of runs of 200 Gb or more rose from 25% to 71% y/y, so the 6000 work that remains is small runs with little per-Gb reason to convert. That fits management's 'long tail' framing.
items.detail: Runs of 200 Gb or more, Q3'25: 6000 383 vs X 130 (X 25%). Q3'26: 6000 287 vs X 713 (X 71%). Runs of 100 Gb or more: X share 906/4,181 = 22% → 2,095/4,761 = 44%. Runs of 10 Gb or more: 16% → 33%. The price-motivated, high-Gb movers have mostly converted. What is left looks like low-volume users, Thaysen's cohort 1 'never-convert', which caps how many more conversion points 2027 can deliver.
items.why_new: This is the first public split of 6000 vs X by run size. It shows the high-Gb cohort has converted and the remainder is small-run.
items.verify_note: The run counts duplicate F629/F644. The inference is wrong in Gb terms: 74% of public 6000 Gb in Q3'26 still sits in libraries of 10 Gb or more (77% in Q3'25), and 54K such 6000 runs remain against 26K on the X. The remaining 6000 work is not mainly tiny runs. Run size also does not identify Thaysen's cohort 1, which is clinical and not in SRA.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: Public NovaSeq high-throughput output is growing only about 12% y/y in Gb, and large-run counts only about 6%. That is well below the '>30%' Gb growth Illumina reports.
items.detail: Runs of 10 Gb or more, 6000+X: 76,042 (Q3'25) → 80,308 (Q3'26), +5.6%. Runs of 100 Gb or more: 4,181 → 4,761, +13.9%. Estimated total Gb (item 1 method): ~3.05 Pb → ~3.43 Pb, +12%. Public deposits are mostly research and lag usage, so this is a weak read on clinical volume. Still, it shows no acceleration in research HT output.
items.why_new: F581/F597 were sample and run counts (+25% / flat). This is a Gb-weighted and large-run read.

items.label: 2B
items.claim: MGI's DNBSEQ runs of 10 Gb or more grew 52% y/y in ENA. The rival share of large short-read runs rose from about 11% to about 16%, though the gain is DNBSEQ, not Element or Ultima.
items.detail: Runs of 10 Gb or more, Q3'25 → Q3'26: DNBSEQ 9,856 → 14,976 (+52%); Element 440 → 462 (+5%); Illumina NovaSeq 76,042 → 80,308 (+5.6%). Rival share of NovaSeq+DNBSEQ+Element large runs: 10,296/86,338 = 11.9% → 15,438/95,746 = 16.1%. This is likely China- and Asia-weighted (BIOSECURE and 1260H limit US uptake). It shows a low-cost platform taking incremental large-run research output.
items.why_new: F610 counted all T7 runs in SRA. This restricts to runs of 10 Gb or more on ENA and compares directly with NovaSeq large-run growth.
items.verify_note: Verified: DNBSEQ Q3'26 ≥10 Gb = 14,976. The NovaSeq figures reconcile (6000 63,713 + X 12,329 = 76,042; 54,042 + 26,266 = 80,308), and the share math is correct. This extends known F610 (T7 run surge) to large runs. The activity is China- and Asia-weighted with little bearing on US/EU research pricing, and Illumina's Greater China revenue is already −19%. Indirect for 2B.

items.label: 2B
items.claim: Element's footprint in large runs is flat y/y and below 1% of NovaSeq, so AVITI's fast SRA run growth is small runs, not high-throughput research volume.
items.detail: Element runs of 10 Gb or more: 440 (Q3'25) vs 462 (Q3'26), against 80,308 NovaSeq runs of 10 Gb or more in Q3'26 (0.58%). This contrasts with F609 (AVITI SRA runs up 11x in two years). That growth must be sub-10 Gb runs (amplicon, small RNA-seq), where Illumina's mid-throughput boxes, not the X, are exposed.
items.why_new: This is the first run-size split for Element. It reframes the known 11x SRA growth as a small-run phenomenon.
items.verify_note: Verified: Element Q3'26 ≥10 Gb = 462. This is a useful correction to known F609/F583 (AVITI run growth). Large-library AVITI activity is flat, ~0.6% of NovaSeq large runs and ~3% of DNBSEQ's. Same caveats on per-accession base_count and lag apply.

items.label: 2B
items.claim: Ultima is nearly invisible in ENA: 778 runs in total since Jul 2025 and only 19 runs of 10 Gb or more in Q3'26.
items.detail: ENA instrument_platform=ULTIMA, first_public ≥ 2025-07-01: 778 runs. Q3'26 runs of 10 Gb or more: 19, against 80,308 NovaSeq. Ultima's large customers (Broad, NISC, UK Biobank proteomics) may not deposit, or may deposit elsewhere, so this understates real use. Still, there is no public research-data footprint of Ultima price-driven share gain.
items.why_new: F584 was GEO samples. This is the ENA run count, including a large-run cut.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: Medicare-only Signatera (0340U) volume is roughly 26K draws, so Medicare draw counts are checkable and small relative to Natera's roughly 283K quarterly MRD tests.
items.detail: CMS Physician & Other Practitioners by Provider and Service lists Natera 0340U with 11,922 beneficiaries and 25,746 services, about 2.2 draws per beneficiary. Average allowed amount is about $3,519 per service, so about $90M Medicare allowed in the file year (year not confirmed). That is a small share of Natera's Q2'26 run rate of 283K MRD tests, so Medicare is a minor share of MRD Gb and the volume story depends on commercial and other payers. Prior years are needed to measure growth.
items.date: file year unconfirmed (latest available CMS release)
items.source_name: CMS Medicare Physician & Other Practitioners by Provider and Service
items.why_new: First Medicare claims-based Signatera draw count and draws per beneficiary; prior notes only had company test counts and cadence assumptions.

items.label: 2A
items.claim: Wellcome Sanger's public NovaSeq runs of 10 Gb or more fell 54% y/y, and Sanger still deposits 79% of them from the 6000. So one of the largest research accounts shows shrinking public Illumina output and a slow move to the X.
items.detail: center_name matching *Sanger*, runs of 10 Gb or more. 6000: 4,449 (Q3'25) → 1,838 (Q3'26), −59%. X/X Plus: 621 → 492, −21%. All platforms: 6,189 → 3,372, −46%. Non-NovaSeq: 1,119 → 1,042, roughly flat (likely PacBio and other long-read). NovaSeq share of Sanger large runs: 82% → 69%. Release timing (project batching) can swing one center's quarterly deposits, so this is suggestive, not conclusive.
items.why_new: This is the first center-level 6000-vs-X read for Sanger, a known AXELIOS buyer, from ENA.

items.label: 2A
items.claim: Fred Hutch's genomics core raised NovaSeq X Plus lane rates about 3% for both internal and external users, which is not the price pressure the thesis expects.
items.detail: The live page (last modified 3 Sep 2026) lists the 10B lane at $1,494 internal / $2,629.44 external and the 25B lane at $2,472 / $4,351, all up to PE151. A search snippet of the same page showed the 10B at $1,450 / $2,552, so both tiers rose about 3.0%. The snippet's date is unknown, so the timing of the increase is unconfirmed. The external premium is about 76% on both lanes. One core is a single data point, and a rate increase could reflect the core's costs or Illumina list-price increases rather than research demand.
items.source_name: Fred Hutch Genomics & Bioinformatics Shared Resource rates page
items.why_new: Fred Hutch is not among the core rate cards already used, and no source in the corpus shows a core raising X Plus lane rates in 2026.

items.label: 2A
items.claim: Outside users pay about 76% more than internal and consortium users at Fred Hutch, which shows how much research pricing depends on internal subsidies and tiering.
items.detail: The 25B lane is $2,472 internal/consortium vs $4,351 external, and the 10B lane is $1,494 vs $2,629. Per Gb, the 25B is about $2.05-2.64 internal and $3.60-4.65 external, using the page's 3.1-4B read pairs at PE151 (my calc). The internal 25B rate is at or just above the $2.50-3.14/Gb core range already in the corpus, so cores are not pricing near the $2.00/Gb floor that a 35B-driven reset would imply. The page gives no X Plus lane rate for 6000-era comparison. This fits the known 35-50% internal discounts.
items.source_name: Fred Hutch Genomics & Bioinformatics Shared Resource rates page
items.why_new: This is a new core with 10B and 25B internal and external lane rates and a computed 76% spread; the corpus already has internal rates running 35-50% below external.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: Deep human WGS runs (30 Gb or more) on NovaSeq 6000 and X combined collapsed in Q3'26.
items.detail: Runs with base_count ≥30 Gb. The 6000 had 227 (Q3'24), 495 (Q3'25) and 192 (Q3'26), which is +118% then −61%. The X had 63 (Q3'25) and 14 (Q3'26), which is −78%. Combined 6000+X deep runs were 558 and then 206, a fall of 63%. Genome-depth public release is not speeding up. Caveat: it may be a few big consortium batches landing in Q3'25.
items.why_new: Gb-threshold split of human WGS; F627-F631 used all-organism run data, not human WGS only.

items.label: 2B
items.claim: DNBSEQ-T7 is the only rival with fast growth in public human WGS, while AVITI and UG 100 show nothing in this slice.
items.detail: DNBSEQ-T7 human WGS runs were 174 (Q3'24), 14 (Q3'25) and 1,038 (Q3'26), which is −92% then +7,314%. That is 16% of all 6000+X+T7 runs in Q3'26, and mostly a China-linked batch. Element AVITI and UG 100 human WGS counts were 0 in Q3'26, though AVITI has 5,664 human runs since 1 Jan 2026 across all strategies. A rival share is appearing in public data, but it is T7, not Western low-cost players.
items.why_new: Human-WGS-only T7/AVITI/UG 100 counts; the lumpiness warns against reading a rival trend.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: At Fred Hutch the 10B lane costs about 1.5x the 25B lane per Gb. Within-X price steps are steep, so a 35B flow cell priced on the same curve would pull the 25B price down.
items.detail: A 25B lane is 3.1–4B read pairs. At PE151 (302 bases per pair) that is about 936–1,208 Gb. At $2,472 internal that is about $2.05–2.64/Gb. A 10B lane is 1.25–1.5B pairs, about 377–453 Gb. At $1,494 that is about $3.30–3.96/Gb. The ratio is about 1.5x internal. External: 25B $4,351 is about $3.60–4.65/Gb and 10B $2,629 is about $5.80–6.97/Gb, also about 1.5x. Output is nominal and not measured. These are cores, not Illumina's net prices.
items.source_name: Fred Hutch Genomics core rate page
items.why_new: A new core's 10B/25B ladder. Known ladders include Pitt 1.5x and KUMC 1.03x, but not Fred Hutch.
items.verify_note: Checked on the page (last modified 3 Sep 2026; it gives no effective date for the rates). Internal 10B lane $1,494 for 1.25–1.5B pairs and 25B lane $2,472 for 3.1–4B pairs; external $2,629.44 and $4,351. The ~1.5x per-Gb ratio holds at both tiers. This is only one more core inside the known 1.03–1.6x within-X range (D034/D035/D042/D045), so it adds little. The claim that a 35B 'would pull the 25B price down' is an inference, not evidence. Output figures are nominal, and these are core recharge r

items.label: 1A
items.claim: The University of Oregon GC3F core's NovaSeq 6000 S4-300 price has risen about 4.5% in a short window and about 13% since launch, not fallen. A 6000 tail lab is not seeing list cuts here.
items.detail: The GC3F rates page now shows S4 300-cycle at $5,070 internal and $6,903 external. A search snippet from the same session showed $4,852 / $6,606, so +4.5% on both tiers (5070/4852; 6903/6606). The July 2022 table showed $4,612 (+9.9% to now) and the launch table $4,500 (+12.7%). The page has no revision note. The cause is unknown, since I did not find a rate memo for FY26–27. This conflicts with the known Salk and UConn 6000 price cuts.
items.source_name: University of Oregon GC3F rates page
items.why_new: Known: F393 notes Oregon's 6000 price at ~2.3x the X, and F479 notes UConn cuts. This is a dated 6000 price increase series at Oregon.
items.verify_note: The live page confirms only the current rates: S4 300-cycle $5,070 internal and $6,903 external. That row is priced per LANE (2–2.5B pairs, ~600–750 Gb, ~$6.8–8.5/Gb internal), not per flow cell. The earlier $4,852/$6,606, $4,612 and $4,500 come from snippets or older tables and were not checked. The page has no date. A core's recharge rate includes labor and overhead, so the rise may reflect core costs rather than Illumina's list price. It is a mild counterpoint to the known Salk/UConn cuts and

items.label: 1A
items.claim: At Oregon the 6000 S4 costs about 6.8–8.5 dollars per Gb, which is 2.6–4x Fred Hutch's 25B internal per-Gb price. A 6000 lab that converts would get a deep cut.
items.detail: S4-300 is $5,070 internal for 2–2.5B read pairs. At 300 bases per pair that is 600–750 Gb, or $6.76–8.45/Gb. Fred Hutch's 25B is $2.05–2.64/Gb internal. The cross-core ratio is about 2.6x (6.76/2.64) up to 4.1x (8.45/2.05). The overlap is wide because the two cores state nominal ranges, not measured output. Smaller flow cells are higher: SP-300 is $2,318 for 325–400M pairs, or $5.8–7.1/Gb.
items.source_name: University of Oregon GC3F rates page; Fred Hutch rate page
items.why_new: This pairs a new X core with Oregon's S4. The known list has the Oregon-to-Berkeley ratio only.

items.label: 2A
items.claim: Oregon's external premium on the 6000 is only about 36%, much smaller than Fred Hutch's 76% on the X. External research users here are not paying a wide premium.
items.detail: S4-300: $6,903/$5,070 = 1.36x. S1-300: $5,305/$3,897 = 1.36x. SP-300: $3,158/$2,318 = 1.36x. The NextSeq 2000 P4-300 premium is 30% (5,496/4,228). MiSeq Classic external is about 1.49x. The premium is set per core.
items.source_name: University of Oregon GC3F rates page
items.why_new: New measurement of an external-premium spread across cores (36% vs 76%).

items.label: 1A
items.claim: Neither Oregon nor Fred Hutch can show a 6000 tail shrinking by price. Fred Hutch lists no NovaSeq 6000, so the sequencing sits in the X Plus at a core that has dropped the 6000.
items.detail: The Fred Hutch page has X Plus 10B and 25B, 1.5B on request, NextSeq 2000, MiSeq i100 Plus, PromethION, and Revio via Seattle Children's. There is no NovaSeq 6000. Oregon still lists 6000 S4/S1/SP, and no X Plus or AVITI. That is a split between one core on the X and one on the 6000.
items.source_name: Fred Hutch Genomics core rate page
items.why_new: Fred Hutch is a new core. Oregon's no-X list is a new data point of the two-core split, though 'most research cores no longer list a 6000' is known.

items.label: 2B
items.claim: Fred Hutch lists no AVITI, Ultima or Roche sequencer, so there is no sign of a rival-priced research option at this core.
items.detail: The only short-read platforms priced are NovaSeq X Plus, NextSeq 2000 and MiSeq i100 Plus. Long-read is PromethION and Revio. Oregon also lists no AVITI. The core page carries no price-comparison language.
items.source_name: Fred Hutch Genomics core rate page
items.why_new: Adds Fred Hutch and Oregon to the list of cores with no rival short-read platform. Pitt is already known.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: In public ENA data, about three-quarters of remaining NovaSeq 6000 Gb still comes from libraries of 10 Gb or more, so the 6000 tail is not shrinking to small runs and convertible work remains.
items.detail: From the F644 buckets (assumed means 20/70/135/300 Gb), 6000 Gb in libraries of 10 Gb or more was ~1,957K of 2,535K Gb in Q3'25 (77%) and ~1,630K of 2,199K Gb in Q3'26 (74%). Sub-1 Gb libraries, which grew +53% in count, are only ~4% of 6000 Gb. There are still 54,042 6000 runs of 10 Gb or more against 26,266 X runs (Q3'26). This cuts against reading the run-count mix (F645/F646) as a permanent low-volume tail. Caveats: research-weighted, release-lagged, and the bucket means are assumptions.
items.why_new: Gb-weighted composition of the public 6000 tail. Prior items used run counts only.

items.label: 2B
items.claim: Gb-weighted public NovaSeq output grew only ~12% y/y in Q3'26 while run counts grew ~42%, so the run-count 'research rebound' overstates research volume growth.
items.detail: 6000+X estimated Gb was ~3.05 Pb in Q3'25 (2,535K + 516K) and ~3.43 Pb in Q3'26 (2,199K + 1,228K), +12%. Runs went from 474,835 (421,447 + 53,388) to 675,179 (511,741 + 163,438), +42%. Known D058 (five-platform SRA runs +24%) and the GEO sample growth (+25%) are therefore count-inflated. Gb growth of ~12% sits well below Illumina's total '>30%' Gb, which fits muted research volume. The data lags actual sequencing, and the bucket means are assumptions.
items.why_new: First Gb-weighted public research volume growth. Known D058 is run-count based.

items.label: 2B
items.claim: In large public runs, the rival pressure is almost entirely MGI. DNBSEQ has ~32x Element's count of runs of 10 Gb or more, and Element's large-run presence is flat.
items.detail: Q3'26 runs of 10 Gb or more: DNBSEQ 14,976 (+52% y/y), Element 462 (+5%), NovaSeq 80,308 (+5.6%), all verified on the ENA count API. Western rivals (Element, Ultima, Roche) together show no measurable large-run share gain in public data. The DNBSEQ gain is China/Asia-weighted and constrained in the US by BIOSECURE/1260H. So public data does not yet show the US/EU research price competitor that 2B relies on (AXELIOS is not yet visible).
items.why_new: Combines verified DNBSEQ and Element large-run counts into one rival-mix read. Known F611/F583 are run-count shares dominated by small runs.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: Whole-genome-sequencing interventional trial starts have fallen every year since 2022, so WGS is not a growing source of new clinical-use momentum.
items.detail: Interventional trials with 'whole genome sequencing' starting in each year: 32 (2021), 38 (2022), 34 (2023), 29 (2024), 25 (2025), 19 YTD in 2026 (annualized ~24, about -3% vs 2025). That is -34% from the 2022 peak to 2025. The count is small and the query is broad, so it is a weak proxy. It still shows no acceleration in WGS clinical research, which fits the view that WGS is too small to offset slowing volume.
items.why_new: No known item uses a registry-based count of WGS trial starts.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: Calgary's internal NovaSeq 6000 S4 v1.5 300-cycle price rose about 4.9% from the June 2024 list to the 2025 list, so 6000 list prices did not fall there.
items.detail: S4 v1.5 300-cycle PE150 (10,000M read pairs, 3,000 Gbp) was $21,371 in the June 2024 list (item 8120.60) and $22,420 in the 2025 list (item 8120.70), up 4.9%. The one-lane S4 price rose from $5,600 to $5,820 (+3.9%). That is about $7.1/Gb in 2024 and $7.5/Gb in 2025 on spec output. This is a rise in the 6000's list price, which runs opposite to the Salk and EPFL list cuts already known and matches CNAG's roughly +4%. Currency is probably CAD.
items.source_name: University of Calgary Cumming School of Medicine, CHGI internal price lists (June 2024 vs 2025)
items.why_new: Calgary CHGI is not in the used core list, and this is the first year-over-year S4 price pair, a rise rather than a cut.
items.verify_note: Duplicate of F672, which covers the same Calgary lists with the fuller 2023-24→2025 path. Read alone, it misleads: the two-year path is a net CUT of ~22.6%, not a rise. The 2025 figures are verified from the PDF (item 8120.70 S4-300 C$22,420; 8125.10 one lane C$5,820).

items.label: 1B
items.claim: The NovaSeq X 25B one-lane price at Calgary, run in partnership with BC Genome Sciences Centre, was $4,100 in both the 2024 and 2025 lists, with no cut.
items.detail: The 25B flow-cell lane at 300 cycles PE150 (item 9000.00) is listed at $4,100 in the June 2024 list and the 2025 list, so it was flat year over year. The S4 lane at $5,820 in 2025 is about 42% above the X lane. The X lane is therefore not being discounted for existing core customers within a year. The flat price may reflect Calgary's pass-through of Illumina list prices or the partner's pricing, and I could not tell which. This is snippet-level evidence from a single core.
items.source_name: University of Calgary CHGI internal price list June 2024
items.why_new: This is a new core price point (an X lane run through a partner), and it shows X pricing flat across two lists.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: Registered interventional trials mentioning ctDNA have started at a rising rate every year since 2021, with 2026 year-to-date already above full-year 2025.
items.detail: Interventional trials with start dates in each calendar year and the term 'ctDNA': 2021 = 116, 2022 = 140, 2023 = 153, 2024 = 167, 2025 = 188. 2026 through 12 Oct = 195. That is +62% from 2021 to 2025, a compound rate of about 13% a year. The count is of trials, not patients or Gb. It points to MRD/ctDNA clinical-use momentum continuing, which cuts against the idea that MRD cannot add volume. Counts came through WebFetch's summarizer, not raw JSON that I opened.
items.why_new: The known notes cite MRD guideline and coverage events but give no registry time series of trial starts.
items.verify_note: Re-checked on the API: 2025 full year = 188 and 2026 YTD (1 Jan–12 Oct) = 195. The 2021–24 counts were not re-checked. 'ctDNA' as a term matches many drug trials that use ctDNA as a biomarker or endpoint. These are trials, not commercial MRD tests or Gb. It says little about 2027 Illumina volume, so it is only a weak counterpoint.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: On a like-for-like window, ctDNA trial starts in 2026 are running about 29% above 2025.
items.detail: Start dates from 1 Jan to 12 Oct: 2026 = 195, 2025 = 151, so +29% (195/151 − 1). Late registration affects 2026 more than 2025, so the true gap is probably larger. The growth rate is faster than the 2021–25 trend of about 13% a year. It suggests MRD research activity is accelerating, a watch-out for the 'MRD too small' argument. It is a leading indicator of clinical-use evidence, not of Gb.
items.why_new: This is a new quantified YTD-versus-YTD registry comparison.
items.verify_note: The 2026 count of 195 is verified; the like-for-like 2025 count of 151 was not re-checked. Same caveats as F666: it is a research-activity indicator, not a Gb or test-volume indicator. Some 2026 start dates may be estimated rather than actual.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: Industry-sponsored ctDNA trial starts fell from 2021 to 2025 but jumped in 2026 year-to-date.
items.detail: Industry-led interventional ctDNA starts: 2021 = 30, 2023 = 22, 2025 = 21. For 1 Jan to 12 Oct, 2025 = 17 and 2026 = 27 (+59%). Pharma and diagnostics sponsors are the ones who fund large sequencing-linked MRD programs. The 2026 rebound is a possible sign of MRD-guided drug trials restarting. The 2021–25 dip fits a plateau, so the signal is mixed.
items.why_new: No sponsor-class split of MRD trials is in the known notes.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: Phase 3 ctDNA trial starts, the late-stage trials that change practice, rose from 13 in 2021 to 21 in 2025.
items.detail: Phase 3 interventional ctDNA starts: 2021 = 13, 2025 = 21 (+62%). 2026 through 12 Oct = 17, so 2026 is on pace to pass 2025. Phase 3 trials matter more than early-phase ones because their results can set guidelines and reimbursement. Small counts mean this is directional only.
items.why_new: The known notes cover individual trials (DYNAMIC-III, ALTAIR) but not aggregate Phase 3 counts.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: Interventional trials with genome sequencing as a term have fallen since 2022, adding numbers to the known WGS-trial decline.
items.detail: Starts with the phrase 'genome sequencing': 2022 = 45, 2023 = 36, 2024 = 32, 2025 = 33. For 1 Jan to 12 Oct, 2026 = 24 versus 2025 = 26 (−8%). From 2022 to 2025 that is −27%. The pattern fits the thesis that WGS is not a growing source of new clinical-use momentum. The phrase is broad (it includes non-WGS uses) and the counts are small.
items.why_new: F663 states a decline without numbers. This gives a year-by-year series with an equal-window 2026 check.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: Natera appears in 18 interventional trial records started from Jan 2025 to Oct 2026.
items.detail: A term search for 'Natera' among interventional studies starting 2025-01-01 to 2026-10-12 returns 18. This shows Natera is still funding or supplying MRD evidence generation, which supports a durable Signatera volume pipeline. The term search matches any field, so it mixes sponsor and supplier roles. I did not split by sponsor or MRD relevance.
items.why_new: This is a new registry count of Natera-linked trials.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: Calgary's internal NovaSeq 6000 S4 price path is a 26% cut in 2024 followed by a 4.9% rise in 2025, so the tail is not being repriced downward.
items.detail: The CHGI internal list (CAD) shows S4 300-cycle full flow cell (3,000 Gb) at $28,960 in 2023-24 (item 8120.5), $21,371 in June 2024 (8120.60) and $22,420 in 2025 (8120.70). That is -26.2% (21,371/28,960) and then +4.9% (22,420/21,371). Per Gb it is 9.65 → 7.12 → 7.47 CAD. The 2023-24 row is not labelled v1.5, so part of the first step may be a kit-generation change. The 2025 list is a re-issue, not a cut. All numbers are from search snippets, not the PDFs.
items.source_name: University of Calgary Cumming School of Medicine, CHGI internal price lists
items.why_new: F664 gave only the +4.9% 2024→2025 step. This adds the 2023-24 baseline and a 3-point price path.
items.verify_note: Corrected reading. The 2025 list (verified in the PDF) has S4 v1.5 300-cycle at C$22,420 for 3,000 Gb (C$7.47/Gb). The 2023-24 (C$28,960) and Jun 2024 (C$21,371) rows come only from snippets. If they are right, the two-year path is −22.6% net (−26.2% then +4.9%). So the tail IS being repriced down, which fits the known 'list cuts continue' point (Salk −24%). It does not show the tail holding its price. Part of the first step may be a kit change to v1.5. Currency is CAD.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: Calgary's smaller 6000 flow cells are also being repriced upward or held flat, not cut.
items.detail: The S2 300-cycle price was $18,480 in 2023-24 (8100.5), $14,301 in June 2024 (8100.60) and $14,810 in 2025 (8100.70): -22.6% then +3.6%. The SP 500-cycle price was $9,030 in 2023-24, $9,290 in June 2024 and $9,290 in 2025: +2.9% then flat. The 2022-23 SP 500 price was $8,290, so SP is +12% over three years. Only the 2023-24 to 2024 S2 step is a cut, and kit versioning may explain it. These are snippet-level readings.
items.source_name: University of Calgary CHGI internal price lists
items.why_new: The known list covers only the S4. S2 and SP three-year paths are new.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: Medicare-FFS tissue and liquid CGP volume at three of Illumina's big oncology customers is growing slowly or not at all, at a CMS-fixed price. That fits a saturated therapy-selection market.
items.detail: Foundation Medicine's tissue code 0037U went from 15,551 services to 13,787 (−11.3%), and its liquid code 0239U was flat at 7,188 vs 7,181 (+0.1%). Combined that is 22,739 → 20,968 (−7.8%). Tempus's genomic-panel services (81455/81456 in the older file; 81455/56/59/64, 0473U, 81450/51/63 in the latest) rose 44,896 → ~50,900 (+13%). Allowed dollars rose $128.3M → ~$145.2M (+13%), with every Tempus panel at ~$2,857. The Tempus comparison is inflated or deflated by a CPT code restructure (81455 fell from 30,175 to 3,203 services), so treat it as approximate. The Medicare-age slice need not match total test growth.
items.source_name: CMS Medicare Physician & Other Practitioners by Provider and Service (data.cms.gov API)
items.why_new: The known list has the FMI −7.8% figure only. The Tempus time series and the FMI tissue/liquid split are new.
items.verify_note: The Foundation half (0037U −11.3%, 0239U flat) is already in known F440 (Foundation 23,219→21,601), so only the Tempus Medicare series is new. Tempus services rose ~+13% (44,896→~50,900), but a CPT code restructure (81455 30,175→3,203) makes this approximate. Tempus +13% is moderate growth, not stagnation. Medicare FFS covers only part of each lab's volume.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: Medicare-FFS volume at the established hereditary and broad-panel labs is flat or shrinking. Caris, the one large oncology lab in the file that is growing, grew about +17%.
items.detail: Services on code 81479 (the catch-all molecular code, so a proxy only): Caris 25,033 → 29,370 (+17.3%, price $3,382 → $3,421). Myriad 17,148 → 17,612 (+2.7%). Invitae 40,806 → 22,979 (−44%), though Labcorp Genetics now bills 11,242, so the combined drop is −16%. Ambry rose 22,535 → 29,300 (+30%) and CareDx was flat at 35,002 → 34,671. BRCA code 81162 across all labs went 6,676 → 6,532 services (−2%). Caris's Medicare growth sits below its own ~+18% total case growth and below the +35% Natera shows in the same code. Hereditary and other mature lines are therefore not adding Gb.
items.source_name: CMS Medicare Physician & Other Practitioners by Provider and Service
items.why_new: Lab-by-lab 81479 and 81162 series for Caris, Myriad, Invitae/Labcorp, Ambry and CareDx are not in the known list. Only Natera and Adaptive Medicare series are.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: Medicare billed almost no whole-genome or exome sequencing in this file. WGS is too small a share of mix to offset slower NIPT or CGP volume.
items.detail: Exome code 81415 returned no rows. Genome code 81425 returned one row, Baylor Miraca Genetics, with 127 services at $4,931 allowed (~$0.63M). Signatera's 0340U alone had 25,746 services (~$90.6M) in the same file. NIPT code 81420 has 50 services in total (Labcorp 39, Quest 11, $744 each). Medicare is an older population, so this understates pediatric and prenatal WGS. Still, the largest clinical payer shows no WGS mix to speak of, which matches the thesis that WGS and MRD-WGS are not yet meaningful.
items.source_name: CMS Medicare Physician & Other Practitioners by Provider and Service
items.why_new: The known list has 81420/NIPT as negligible but has no exome/WGS claims count.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: Guardant's Medicare liquid CGP (0326U) volume grew about +17% in the latest year, not flat or +5%. The price also rose 38.5%, so this customer's Medicare volume is still expanding.
items.detail: Services went 16,798 → 19,695 (+17.2%). Beneficiaries went 15,346 → 17,856 (+16.4%). Average allowed went $3,533 → $4,892 (+38.5%), so allowed dollars went ~$59.4M → ~$96.3M (+62%). This conflicts with the known D038/F429 readings (~5% more tests; essentially flat). The cause could be a different year pairing or a different row, so the analyst should reconcile before using either. A strong Guardant liquid book would support Illumina clinical volume.
items.source_name: CMS Medicare Physician & Other Practitioners by Provider and Service
items.why_new: It updates or contradicts the known Guardant Medicare growth figures with exact row values. Reconcile before use.
items.verify_note: Not new. Known F429 already has 0326U +17.2%, and D038 already has 0326U 16,798 at $3,533 → 19,695 at $4,892. The 'conflict' with F429/D038 is not real: those figures are 0242U+0326U combined (+4.4%), and 0242U fell 5.7%.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: Natera's Medicare MRD cadence per patient rose about 10% on code 0340U, and unique patients rose about 70%. Test growth there is real.
items.detail: Code 0340U: 7,028 beneficiaries and 13,783 services (1.96 services per beneficiary, $3,838) → 11,922 beneficiaries and 25,746 services (2.16, $3,519). Services +87%, beneficiaries +70%, price −8.3%. Code 81479 for Natera went 15,483/22,512 → 20,898/30,323 (+35% services), and its cadence was flat at 1.45. Adding the two gives ~$133M → ~$196M allowed (+47%). The services-per-beneficiary ratio is partly a partial-year artifact of newly enrolled patients, so it is only a loose proxy for draws per year. The per-year Gb-per-draw logic is unchanged, but MRD test counts are growing fast.
items.source_name: CMS Medicare Physician & Other Practitioners by Provider and Service
items.why_new: The 0340U cadence delta (1.96 → 2.16) is quantified. D037 and F438 give only the 2.2 level and a direction.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: Medicare pays a single administered rate for CGP panels across all labs, about $2,857 per panel. Customers' revenue per test is therefore set by CMS, which leaves the sequencing-cost line as their main lever.
items.detail: Tempus's 81455/81456/81459/81464 all price at $2,846–$2,858 allowed. Circulogene, Bostongene and NeoGenomics sit at $2,853–$2,861 on 81455, and FMI's tissue and liquid codes sit at $3,418–$3,424. A Medicare rate that does not move with labs' sequencing cost, followed by the known CY2027 CLFS cuts of −22/−23% on sequencing codes, puts the pressure on lab margins. That is the inference for why large labs press Illumina on reagent price. It is the analyst's inference, not a customer statement.
items.source_name: CMS Medicare Physician & Other Practitioners by Provider and Service
items.why_new: The known list has the CY2027 cuts but not the uniform ~$2,857 administered CGP rate across labs.

items.label: 2B
items.claim: Open-access Methods mentions of rival sequencers (AVITI, Ultima UG, AXELIOS) are not gaining on NovaSeq X in academic papers.
items.detail: Europe PMC METHODS+OPEN_ACCESS hitCounts: rivals combined were 62 vs 656 NovaSeq X (9.5%) in H1'25, and 373 vs 4,230 (8.8%) for Jul'25–Sep'26. AVITI/AVITI24 alone was 54 vs 410 across periods, a stable ~8% of X. Publication lag means 2026 rival placements are not yet visible.
items.url: https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/search?query=(METHODS:"AVITI24" OR METHODS:"AVITI") AND OPEN_ACCESS:y AND FIRST_PDATE:[2025-01-01 TO 2026-09-30]&format=json&pageSize=1&resultType=lite
items.why_new: First publication-based count series of rival vs X usage in academic Methods; not in the known list.

items.label: 2A
items.claim: Academic Methods mentions of NovaSeq X grew about 2.6x per month while rival mentions grew in step, so research use is still Illumina-dominated.
items.detail: NovaSeq X Methods mentions rose from ~109/month (H1'25) to ~282/month (Jul'25–Sep'26). AVITI rose from ~9 to ~24/month. AXELIOS/SBX total only 8 and UG-series 17, so the rival threat in research is still negligible in published work.
items.url: https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/search?query=(METHODS:"NovaSeq X") AND OPEN_ACCESS:y AND FIRST_PDATE:[2025-01-01 TO 2026-09-30]&format=json&pageSize=1&resultType=lite
items.why_new: Quantifies academic usage lag; no prior publication-count series.

items.label: 2B
items.claim: nf-core shows only a trickle of Element AVITI support activity and none for Roche SBX or Ultima, so no pipeline-demand signal of research volume leaving Illumina.
items.detail: A search of the nf-core org (Jul 2024 to Oct 2026) for AVITI, Ultima, AXELIOS and SBX returned 17 hits. Only 3 were genuine Element items, all in nf-core/demultiplex: a bases2fastq image update for AVITI OS 3.4.0 (PR #343, 8 Oct 2025), an out-of-date elembio docker image (issue #341, 30 Sep 2025) and empty Undetermined FASTQs in the bases2fastq workflow (issue #395, 11 May 2026). There were zero Roche SBX/AXELIOS items and zero Ultima platform items. This is weak, tiny-sample evidence that pipeline-level demand for rival platforms is still small.
items.quote: Upgrading bases2fastq image from Element Biosciences for Aviti OS 3.4.0 sequencer outputs
items.why_new: No GitHub or pipeline-support signal for rival sequencers is in the known list.

items.label: 2B
items.claim: A large academic core launched a dated, 10x-specific Ultima UG 100 discount in Aug 2026, steering single-cell and spatial research volume to a non-Illumina platform.
items.detail: UMGC's news item, dated 2 Aug 2026 on its news-events index, offers 'preferred' UG 100 pricing for 10x Genomics single-cell and spatial projects. The saving is $500 per wafer (10–12B reads) and $250 per half-wafer (5–6B reads). The fetched page gave about $2,704 UMN and $3,188 external per wafer, which is roughly $0.22–0.27 per million reads at 10–12B reads. The search snippet quoted $2,409 and $2,712 instead, so the figures conflict and need re-checking. No NovaSeq X price appears on the page, so the discount against the X is not yet computed.
items.quote: savings of $500 per wafer or $250 per half-wafer
items.why_new: The dated, 10x-specific subsidy and its 2 Aug 2026 date are new; the corpus had only generic UMN Ultima pricing (~$12/50M reads).
items.verify_note: Numbers checked and the conflict resolved. Preferred rates are full wafer $2,704 UMN / $3,188 external and half wafer $1,857 / $2,175. These equal the standard Savings tier ($3,204 / $3,688; $2,107 / $2,425) minus $500 or $250 exactly, so the snippet's $2,409/$2,712 is wrong. Eligibility runs through 10x account executives, which suggests 10x co-sponsors the steer toward Ultima. The fetched page itself carries no date; the 2 Aug 2026 date comes from the news index and was not re-checked.

items.label: 2A
items.claim: UMGC has made repeated, dated price cuts and promotions on non-Illumina platforms, and its news index shows no matching Illumina price move.
items.detail: The 15 Sep 2025 AVITI upgrade gave a 50% output increase on certain kits and cut AVITI sequencing cost per million reads by 33%. The 1 Nov 2025 Parse offer gives free sequencing with Evercode kits. The 2 Sep 2026 seminar is titled 'Rethinking the Cost of NGS with Ultima Genomics'. The index of 15 items (Sep 2025 to Sep 2026) shows no NovaSeq X price cut or UG 200/AXELIOS item.
items.why_new: The dated sequence of UMGC alternative-platform price actions across Sep 2025 to Sep 2026 is new; the corpus has the AVITI cost fall only in aggregate.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: BillionToOne's prospectus describes sole- and single-source sequencer and reagent suppliers with a 1-9 month replacement time.
items.detail: The risk factors say BillionToOne relies on a limited number of suppliers, some sole- or single-source. They estimate that replacing a supplier could take about 1-9 months, and the company aims to hold at least 3 months of inventory. They also say that if the FDA required clearance for the RUO-labelled sequencers, it 'would have to find an alternative sequencing platform'. The filing does not name Illumina, so this is only weak evidence of lock-in. It implies that volume growth in NIPT is tied to Illumina supply and has no near-term alternative.
items.quote: we would have to find an alternative sequencing platform
items.why_new: The known list notes only the Illumina patent suit against BillionToOne. It does not include the prospectus's supplier-concentration language.

items.label: 2B
items.claim: On UMGC's preferred pricing, Ultima reads cost about $0.25 per million, roughly 3x to 4x cheaper than the 25B lane prices at cores that publish them.
items.detail: $2,704 / 11,000M reads (mid of 10-12B) = $0.246 per M reads (preferred UMN). Standard UMN is $3,204 / 11,000 = $0.291 and external standard is $3,688 / 11,000 = $0.335. A 25B lane carries about 3.1-3.25B clusters. Published lane prices are Missouri $2,317, MD Anderson $2,595, TGen $3,137 and Northwestern $3,000-3,750. That is about $0.74, $0.83, $1.00 and $0.96-1.20 per M clusters. The gap is roughly 3x to 4x per read before read-length and quality differences (UG 100 reads are single-end ~300 bp). The Missouri, MD Anderson and Northwestern figures came from search-result snippets I did not open. Per-read parity is not per-Gb parity.
items.source_name: UMN Genomics Center UG 100 rates; Missouri, MD Anderson, TGen and Northwestern price pages (search snippets)
items.why_new: Gives a per-read comparison from a single university core's published Ultima prices against peer 25B lane prices. The known list has Ultima at about $0.24/M from a secondary post and Broad's $0.50.
items.verify_note: UMN prices verified: standard $3,204 → $0.29/M reads; preferred $2,704 → $0.25/M. The known list already has Ultima at ~$0.24/M reads and UMN-style evaluations at ~$12 per 50M reads, so the per-read gap is largely known. UG 100 reads are ~250 bases after filtering vs 300 bases per PE150 cluster, so the per-base gap is somewhat smaller than 3–4x. See the derived per-Gb item. The other cores' lane prices are snippet-level.

items.label: 2A
items.claim: UMGC, a large academic core, has stopped running the NovaSeq X Plus in-house because outsourcing is 'faster and less expensive'.
items.detail: The UMGC X Plus service page (© 2026) says it 'has determined that for the time being' X Plus access is 'both faster and less expensive when outsourced' through unnamed partner facilities. It lists no price table and only a project quote. It offers the 10B and 25B flow cells only in 300-cycle format. The core instead runs the Ultima UG 100 in-house (service launched 2 Jan 2025) and AVITI. That fits cores consolidating Illumina volume into cheaper outsourcers while installing rival platforms for their own in-house capacity.
items.quote: access to the NovaSeq X Plus will be both faster and less expensive when outsourced
items.why_new: Adds UMN to the cores that outsource X lanes (Georgia, Berkeley, Cornell, Mainz). The core states its rationale in writing.
items.verify_note: Duplicate of previously verified F376 (UMGC X Plus is outsourced because it is 'faster and less expensive'). The only addition is the UG 100 launch date of 2 Jan 2025.

items.label: 2B
items.claim: UMGC's AVITI upgrade in Sep 2025 delivered 50% more output at the same price, a 33% cut per million reads.
items.detail: UMGC news item of 15 Sep 2025: the upgrade gives 'a 50% increase in output for 150-cycle and 300-cycle kits, while AVITI pricing remains the same.' The page says AVITI is 'now 33% less expensive per million reads'. The check is 1/1.5 = 0.667, a 33% cut. This is a hidden $/read cut with no list change. Together with the Ultima preferred pricing 11 months later, it shows UMGC repeatedly cutting rival-platform prices. The known list has UMN's 62-71% AVITI decline since FY24 but not this dated step.
items.quote: AVITI sequencing is now 33% less expensive per million reads
items.why_new: Gives the dated step (15 Sep 2025, -33%/M reads) within the known 62-71% AVITI decline. The detail came from the news-index summary, because the item's own URL returned 404.
items.verify_note: Correction: this is Element's own kit upgrade (+50% output at the same kit price) passed through by the core, not UMGC choosing to cut rival-platform prices. It is a dated step inside the known UMN 'AVITI costs fell 62–71% since FY24', so it adds only the timing and mechanism of a hidden per-read cut.

items.label: 2B
items.claim: UMGC's news cadence shows only non-Illumina price actions in 2025-26: Ultima preferred pricing, an AVITI cut, a Parse free-sequencing offer and an Ultima seminar.
items.detail: Index entries: 2 Sep 2026 seminar 'Rethinking the Cost of NGS with Ultima Genomics' (held 15 Sep 2026; UMGC speaker cites about 18 months of UG 100 experience); 1 Nov 2025 Parse free sequencing at 10,000 reads per cell; 15 Sep 2025 AVITI upgrade; 2 Aug 2026 Ultima preferred pricing. No NovaSeq X price news appears on page 1 of the index (15 items, Sep 2025 to Sep 2026). Vendor-sponsored promotions use the core as a channel for competitor platforms. Page 2 of the index and Illumina-side pages were not checked.
items.source_name: UMN Genomics Center news and events
items.why_new: Extends the known UMGC price-cut pattern to a second dated item (Parse free sequencing) and the Sep 2026 Ultima seminar.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: UMGC's standard Ultima UG 100 wafer price appears to have risen, not fallen, from an earlier table. Ultima does not price like a chain of cuts at this core.
items.detail: A search snippet of an older UMGC UG 100 table gave a full wafer at $2,909 UMN / $3,212 external and a half wafer at $1,709 / $2,012. The fetched live page now shows $3,204 / $3,688 (full) and $2,107 / $2,425 (half) in the Savings tier. That is +10% and +15% for the full wafer, and +23% and +21% for the half wafer. The older snippet was cached and undated, so the timing is unverified. A related UMGC webinar page says about $2,600 for 10-12B reads after the Solaris upgrade. The page also adds Speed and Priority tiers at +4.7% and +9.5% over Savings for UMN. This is the cheaper platform raising its own list, so the 'preferred' $500 off may be restoring the earlier price level (2,704 vs 2,909).
items.why_new: A watch-out the known list lacks: a rival platform's core price rose or recovered. The older snippet is undated and was not opened, so treat it as a lead.

items.label: 2A
items.claim: UMGC speakers say the center has about 18 months of Ultima production experience, yet UMGC still lists X Plus only via outsourced Illumina capacity, not as an exit from Illumina.
items.detail: The UMGC X Plus page keeps the 10B and 25B 300-cycle products on offer, via partners, so Illumina consumables still flow to UMN users, but at partners' prices. Ultima and AVITI sit alongside as in-house options. The core's own news index shows 15 events and news items over a year and no announcement dropping Illumina. This is channel shift (a cheaper Illumina route), not displacement of Illumina volume. The first-order effect for Illumina is lower realized price per lane through an outsourcer such as Novogene.
items.why_new: Frames the UMGC finding as outsourcing, not abandonment of Illumina.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: Human NovaSeq X GEO series (GPL34281) rose from 35 to 123 to 251 in Q3'24, Q3'25 and Q3'26, but the X is still only about 13% of human 6000+X series on this one platform record.
items.detail: GPL34281 is assumed to be the human X Plus platform; I did not verify its name. Share of human 6000+X GSEs: 35/(1,380+35)=2.5%, 123/(1,441+123)=7.9%, 251/(1,647+251)=13.2%. X series grew +251% (2025) and +104% (2026). This conflicts with the known 70.5% 6000 share (F577), which covers human plus mouse and probably several X records. It therefore likely understates the X, because X Plus has many per-organism GPLs.
items.why_new: Shows that the GPL used affects the apparent conversion curve, which is a caveat on F577.

items.label: 2B
items.claim: The GEO platform-title search finds 64 AVITI platform records but no Ultima records, so Ultima has no GPL footprint under the title 'Ultima'.
items.detail: esearch 'AVITI[Title] AND gpl[ETYP]' returned 64 platform records. 'Ultima[Title] AND gpl[ETYP]' returned 0, although other items report UG 100 records, so the title string may differ (for example 'UG 100'). NovaSeq X title search returned 634 per-organism records. Platform-record counts do not measure sample volume.
items.why_new: Gives a count of platform records: 64 AVITI vs 634 NovaSeq X.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: A Japanese regulated NGS test, FoundationOne Liquid CDx, was still labeled for the NovaSeq 6000 in a Sep 2026 package-insert revision, which supports a persistent regulated 6000 tail.
items.detail: A search-engine summary of the PMDA package insert (approval 30300BZX00074000) says the 7th edition, revised Sep 2026 (6th edition May 2024), names Illumina's NovaSeq 6000 as the sequencer. The same summary says the insert sets NovaSeq 6000 run-quality criteria: at least 60% of clusters passing filter per lane, mean read 1 and read 4 error of 2% or less, and at least 85% of bases above Q30. It did not show the NovaSeq X. This is a second jurisdiction beyond the US where a regulated test is still locked to the 6000 about 3 years after the X launched. I could not tell whether the Sep 2026 edition changed the sequencer. This is snippet-level evidence; the PDF text was not read.
items.source_name: PMDA package insert search (FoundationOne Liquid CDx)
items.why_new: This is a Japan PMDA label clock. The known list covers only US FDA PMAs and supplements.
items.verify_note: This is new: Japan is a regulated jurisdiction not yet covered (the US PMA and EU IVDR cases are already known). I fetched the PMDA PDF but could not extract its text, so the sequencer naming and the Sep 2026 7th-edition date are still unconfirmed and rest on a search snippet. The run-QC thresholds (≥60% PF, ≤2% error, ≥85% ≥Q30) are typical NovaSeq 6000 spec language, which makes the claim plausible. Downgraded to weak. Direction 'against' is correct: a test that stays locked to the 6000 limits

items.label: 1A
items.claim: Ten major Chinese institutions deposited zero NovaSeq X human series in GEO in both Q3'25 and Q3'26, while they kept depositing 6000 series, so the Chinese 6000 tail shows no conversion.
items.detail: Series (GSE) counts by submission quarter, filtered with exact-phrase Submitter Institute terms (Peking, Fudan, Zhejiang, Sun Yat-sen, Shanghai Jiao Tong, CAS, Tsinghua, Sichuan, Nanjing Medical, Wuhan). Human 6000 platform GPL24676: 80 series in Q3'25 (5.6% of 1,441) and 73 in Q3'26 (4.4% of 1,647). Human X platform GPL34281: 0 in both quarters, against 123 and 251 X series overall. So these institutions have 6000 share of 6000+X = 100% in both quarters, versus 92.1% (1,441/1,564) and 86.8% (1,647/1,898) for all submitters. China is a small share of 6000 deposits (4–6%) and Greater China was already weak (−11% y/y in Q2'26), so it does not explain the global 6000 tail. Caveat: exact-phrase lists miss institute-name variants, and the 6000 count includes non-human series only if they use the human GPL.
items.why_new: Known GEO items give global 6000 share only; this is the first institution-group (China) split, and the X count there is zero.
items.verify_note: Three problems. (1) Zero NovaSeq X series from Chinese institutions is explained by China's 2025 ban on Illumina sequencer exports (unreliable entity list), not by sticky customers. (2) Illumina's reported X-share and Gb metrics exclude China, so this says nothing about the tail the thesis is about. (3) GPL34281 is only the human NovaSeq X platform; GPL34284 (X Plus) is not counted, and X Plus is about two-thirds of human X series. Also, the known list has Greater China at −19% y/y in Q2'26, not

items.label: 1A
items.claim: At ten large US academic and cancer-center submitters, the 6000 still held 75% of 6000+X human series in Q3'26 (84% in Q3'25), converting slower than the all-submitter pool is converting.
items.detail: Institutions: Harvard Medical School, Stanford, Johns Hopkins, MSK, Mayo, UCSF, Broad, WashU, Yale, Penn (exact INST phrases). Q3'25: 6000 = 54 series, X = 10, so 6000 share 84.4%. Q3'26: 6000 = 49, X = 16, so 75.4%. That is a fall of about 9 points in a year, against about 5 points for the global pool (92.1% to 86.8%, using series counts of 1,441/123 and 1,647/251). Absolute 6000 series at these sites only fell from 54 to 49, so a quarter of their output is still on the 6000 and the decay is slow.
items.why_new: Adds a pooled US-institution group with Q3'25 and Q3'26 series counts; earlier items looked at single institutions (Mayo, MSK, Stanford) over different windows.

items.label: 2B
items.claim: Per Gb, a 10x single-cell project on UMGC's preferred Ultima UG 100 rate costs roughly 2–3.5x less than an Illumina 25B lane at Fred Hutch's core.
items.detail: UMGC preferred full wafer is $2,704 (UMN) / $3,188 (external) for 10–12B reads at ~250 bases after filtering, about 2.5–3.0 Tb, or ~$0.90–1.08/Gb internal and ~$1.06–1.28/Gb external. Fred Hutch's 25B lane is $2,472 / $4,351 for 3.1–4B pairs at PE151, about 936–1,208 Gb, or ~$2.05–2.64/Gb internal and ~$3.60–4.65/Gb external. That makes Ultima ~1.9–2.9x cheaper internally and ~2.8–4.4x cheaper externally. The comparison is across two cores, uses nominal output, and ignores differences in read structure and quality (single-end vs paired). For counting work such as single-cell, the 10x-backed discount widens a gap that already favors Ultima.
items.source_name: UMN Genomics Center UG 100 pages; Fred Hutch Genomics core rates
items.quote: savings of $500 per wafer
items.why_new: The known list has Ultima per-read prices only; this is a per-Gb comparison at the 10x-preferred rate against a named core's 25B lane.

items.label: 1A
