items.claim: At Calgary's core (2025, CAD) the NovaSeq 6000 S4 costs only ~1.6–1.7x the outsourced X 25B lane per Gb, far below Illumina's ~3.4x revenue-per-Gb ratio, so a small academic 6000 user there saves only ~40% by switching.
items.detail: Calgary's 2025 internal list prices the S4 v1.5 300-cycle flow cell at C$22,420 for 3,000 Gb (C$7.47/Gb) and one S4 lane at C$5,820 for 750 Gb (C$7.76/Gb). It prices the X 25B lane, outsourced through the BC Genome Sciences Centre, at C$4,100 for 900 Gb (C$4.56/Gb). The ratio is 1.64–1.70x, below Salk's 2.3–3.1x (D028), Pitt's 3.7x on S2 (D032) and Illumina's reported ~3.4x. Part of the compression is the markup on outsourced X lanes. The savings from converting are small for academic 6000 users who can reach the X only through partners, which may slow conversion in that part of the tail. The tail is mostly clinical, though, so the weight is weak.
items.source_name: University of Calgary CHGI Internal Price List 2025
items.quote: In partnership with BC Genome Sequencing Centre
items.why_new: This is the first core in the corpus that lists 6000 and X prices together where the X is reachable only by outsourcing, and it shows the smallest 6000/X gap seen so far.

items.label: 2A
items.claim: UNC School of Medicine funded 19 core vouchers of up to $10,000 each in FY26 to keep investigators using its cores.
items.detail: The UNC SOM Core Voucher Program awarded 19 applications in FY26 (announced 8 Dec 2025), each worth up to $10,000 and usable only for core services. The program is still described as a pilot, and an FY27 round has opened. The pages give no total budget, no prior-year counts and no sequencing-specific breakdown. A search snippet said grant-termination applicants could qualify, but I did not verify this. It shows institutions subsidizing core use during the funding squeeze, but it is not quantified for sequencing.
items.source_name: UNC School of Medicine Core Facilities
items.quote: Core vouchers worth up to $10,000 will be awarded
items.why_new: Dated, quantified university subsidy to core usage; not in the known list.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: In ENA, the NovaSeq X share of 6000+X runs of 10 Gb or more rose from 7.9% to 17.6% in a year, so the public 6000 base is still big and converting only slowly.
items.detail: Runs of 10 Gb or more released in Q3'25 numbered 63,713 on the 6000 and 5,481 on the X, so X was 5,481/(63,713+5,481)=7.9%. In Q3'26 they numbered 54,042 on the 6000 and 11,567 on the X, so X was 11,567/65,609=17.6%. The 6000 count fell 15% y/y and the X count rose 111%. That is +9.7 points of run-share a year in the public record. This is runs, not Gb, and ENA release timing lags the actual sequencing by up to a year. Public data is mostly academic, so it measures the research tail, not the clinical tail.
items.url: https://www.ebi.ac.uk/ena/portal/api/count?result=read_run&query=instrument_model="Illumina NovaSeq 6000" AND first_public>=2026-07-01 AND first_public<=2026-09-30 AND base_count>=10000000000
items.why_new: Exact ≥10 Gb run counts for both platforms and both quarters. The known items give the 6000 −15% but not the X count or the share path.
items.verify_note: The numbers are wrong because the query on instrument_model="Illumina NovaSeq X" leaves out "Illumina NovaSeq X Plus". I checked on the ENA count API: X Plus runs of 10 Gb or more were 6,848 in Q3'25 and 14,699 in Q3'26. Combined X+X Plus is therefore 12,329 and 26,266, so the X share of large runs goes from 16.2% to 32.7%, not 7.9% to 17.6%. These totals reconcile exactly with F648 (NovaSeq 76,042 and 80,308). The 6000 counts duplicate F645, and the corrected X share is close to F644 and F629.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: Per-center mix-shift tracking is impossible from ENA: about 75% of large-run rows carry a blank or SUB-ID center_name. Only Sanger-type named centers can be tracked.
items.detail: In a 3,000-row sample of Q3'26 X runs of 10 Gb or more, 1,063 rows had a blank center and 1,201 had an anonymous SUBxxxx ID. That is 75%. Only 736 rows (25%) carried a named center, and 190 of those were Wellcome Sanger. A 1,100-row 6000 sample for Q3'25 showed the same pattern, with NISC and OKIMBS as the only named centers. So the strategist's 40-center converted/mixed/6000-only labeling cannot be built from ENA. It would need bioproject-to-center mapping, which is a heavy job. The clinical-versus-academic split of 6000-only centers is therefore unobservable here.
items.url: https://www.ebi.ac.uk/ena/portal/api/search?result=read_run&query=instrument_model="Illumina NovaSeq X" AND first_public>=2026-07-01 AND first_public<=2026-09-30 AND base_count>=10000000000&fields=center_name&limit=3000&format=tsv
items.why_new: This is a methodological limit that stops anyone repeating a center-level conversion study from ENA metadata.
items.verify_note: This is a methods limitation (ENA center_name is mostly blank), not evidence about the 6000 tail. It does not support or cut against 1A.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: Public large-run volume on 6000+X rose only about 0.2% y/y in run count, from 69,194 to 65,609, a drop of 5.2% in Q3'26.
items.detail: Q3'25 6000+X runs of 10 Gb or more were 63,713+5,481=69,194. Q3'26 were 54,042+11,567=65,609. That is −5.2% y/y. Large runs are the closest proxy here for deep-sequencing activity. This is a decline, not the >30% Gb growth Illumina cites. Caveats: the data is public research deposits with release lags and is not Illumina's connected-instrument metric.
items.url: https://www.ebi.ac.uk/ena/portal/api/count?result=read_run&query=instrument_model="Illumina NovaSeq X" AND first_public>=2025-07-01 AND first_public<=2025-09-30 AND base_count>=10000000000
items.why_new: The known items show 6000 runs of 10 Gb or more −15% and run growth +6%. This adds a combined 6000+X count down 5.2%, which differs from the earlier +6% figure, so the earlier figure may rest on a different definition.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: NISC, a US federal sequencing center, still released 13 runs of 10 Gb or more on the 6000 and none on the X in Q3'26.
items.detail: NISC (NIH Intramural Sequencing Center) had 23 6000 runs of 10 Gb or more in Q3'25 and 13 in Q3'26, with zero X runs in Q3'26. It is a small count, but it is a named federal center that appears to be 6000-only. That is consistent with the known federal 6000 service-plan renewals. NISC also bought an Ultima, so its mix is not purely Illumina.
items.url: https://www.ebi.ac.uk/ena/portal/api/count?result=read_run&query=instrument_model="Illumina NovaSeq X" AND first_public>=2026-07-01 AND first_public<=2026-09-30 AND base_count>=10000000000 AND center_name="NISC"
items.why_new: Gives NISC's run counts on both platforms, which are not among the known items.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: Registered NIPT/cfDNA-prenatal trial starts on ClinicalTrials.gov have trended down since 2021, with no sign of rising research momentum.
items.detail: A broad query (prenatal/pregnancy/fetal AND cell-free DNA/cfDNA/NIPT/NIPS) returned 26 (2021), 23 (2022), 21 (2023), 22 (2024) and 17 (2025) trials by start year. 2025 is down 35% from 2021 (17 vs 26). The 2026 year-to-date figure (to 12 Oct) is 21, against 14 for the same 2025 window, so 2026 is up 50% like-for-like. That makes the trend a decline to 2025 followed by a rebound. Counts are small and noisy, and I did not check the raw JSON because the WebFetch summarizer returned them.
items.why_new: No prior item counts NIPT or cfDNA-prenatal trial starts by year. The existing list only has the ctDNA and WGS trial counts.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: Industry-led prenatal-cfDNA registrations fell sharply in the broad query, and the narrow NIPT-term query shows only 2 starts in 2025.
items.detail: The industry-sponsored count in the broad query was 17 for 2021–23 (about 5.7 a year) and 8 for 2024 through 12 Oct 2026 (about 2.9 a year over 2.8 years). That is roughly half the rate. The narrow query (NIPT / non-invasive prenatal / noninvasive prenatal / cell-free DNA prenatal) returned 10, 4, 7, 9, 2 for 2021–2025 and 8 for 2026 YTD (2 for the same 2025 window). Both queries are noisy because many matches are non-NIPT cfDNA or pregnancy trials, so this is a weak maturation signal.
items.why_new: This is a new sponsor-class split of NIPT research activity. Nothing in the known list measures NIPT trial pipeline.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: Interventional prenatal-cfDNA trials are being registered at a lower rate in 2024–26 than in 2021–23.
items.detail: The broad query gives 32 interventional trials for 2021–23, or about 10.7 a year. For 2024 to 12 Oct 2026 it gives 20, or about 7.1 a year over 2.8 years. That is a 34% lower annual rate. Most 2024–26 'interventional' hits are not NIPT at all, such as neonatal physiotherapy, hydrogen inhalation and an LCH drug trial. The true NIPT interventional pipeline is therefore smaller still. Where the hits are real NIPT, they are decision-aid and consent studies (Cleveland Clinic NCT06382636, Case Western INFORM NCT07557303, Rhode Island prenatal chatbot NCT07077707), not new test-volume drivers.
items.why_new: This shows the shift of NIPT research toward counseling and consent, which fits a mature market. None of it is in the known list.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: Industry NIPT players are registering expanded-scope prenatal studies. Monogenic and fetal-cell tests raise sequencing depth per sample, so they could lift Gb per test.
items.detail: Natera's EXPAND (NCT06808880, start 2024-01-25, n=4,000) covers prenatal cfDNA screening across monogenic disorders. BillionToOne's ADVANCE (NCT07643896, start 2026-01-10, n=1,000) uses circulating fetal cells for non-invasive fetal risk assessment. Zhejiang Women's Hospital is running prenatal cfDNA with targeted and whole-exome sequencing (NCT07106853, start 2025-09-16, n=1,600). Gene Solutions has a preeclampsia and obstetric-disease prediction study using NIPT data (NCT06385366). The known list puts NIPT at about 1–2 Gb and deeper for microdeletions. If expanded panels become standard, Gb per NIPT could rise even as test growth saturates. The enrollments are small.
items.why_new: These are named industry studies of expanded-scope NIPT. The known list only has NIPT as mature, with a plateau in BillionToOne costs.
items.verify_note: New, but weak. Enrollments are small (1,000–4,000), and all of these are studies, not commercial launches. Monogenic cfDNA screening (Natera, BillionToOne) uses targeted amplicon panels, and fetal-cell assays sequence few cells, so the gain in Gb per test is likely modest compared with a shift to WGS. The Chinese WES-NIPT study (n=1,600) is the only clearly Gb-heavy design. It falls outside Illumina's ex-China metrics.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: Baylor's SRA deposits show the X at only 6% of 6000+X experiments in 2025 and 12% in 2026 year to date. A genetics-heavy center is therefore still mostly on the 6000.
items.detail: Center name containing BAYLOR. 2025 to 2026 totals: 6000 = 1,159, X = 134. 2026 alone: 6000 = 829, X = 112, so X share = 112/941 = 11.9%. By subtraction, 2025: 6000 = 330, X = 22, so X share = 6.3%. The 'BAYLOR' string matches several Baylor centers, which may include Baylor Genetics, but I did not separate them. The share roughly doubled in a year, but the 6000 still held ~88% in 2026.
items.why_new: This is a named clinical-adjacent center's 6000 vs X split; known GEO/SRA items are platform-level or academic.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: NYGC, Garvan and Regeneron show a very thin X footprint in SRA, which fits a clinical or population-scale 6000 tail that is slow to convert.
items.detail: NYGC 2025: 6000 = 827, X = 4, so X share = 0.5%. NYGC 2026 H1: X = 0. Its 2026 6000 count to 12 Oct is 121. Garvan 2026: 6000 = 270, X = 11, so X share = 3.9%. Regeneron all-time: 6000 = 5,448, X = 0. NYGC's all-time X count is 1,906, but only 4 are dated 2025 and 0 in H1 2026, so the all-time figure looks like a date-field artifact I did not resolve. Treat these as release-date counts, not production.
items.why_new: The tail is shown at named population-genomics and clinical-research centers, not just in aggregate.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: Extending the linear trend puts the human X series share near 19% by Q4'27, a gain of about 5.4 points over calendar 2027.
items.detail: The fit is y=7.24+1.345*(t-4). Q4'26 (t=9) is 13.97% and Q4'27 (t=13) is 19.35%, so the 2027 gain is 5.4 pts. That is close to the thesis's roughly 5 points of 2027 mix shift. The fit is linear, so a logistic curve would give a similar or slightly faster path at these low levels. The caveat is that this is a share of published series, a lagging proxy, and it is not a Gb or revenue share.
items.why_new: This is the first projection of the 2027 pace of conversion from public data, and it lands on the thesis's 5-point figure.
items.verify_note: This is built on a human X series count that excludes X Plus. I checked GPL34284: 515 human X Plus series in Q3'26, against 251 on GPL34281. The true human X share of 6000+X series in Q3'26 is therefore 766/2,413 = 31.7%, not about 13%. The '+5.4 points in 2027' match to the thesis is an artifact of the undercount. GEO also lags Illumina's own share figures by about 2 years (D052).

items.label: 1A
items.claim: Outside China and the EU/Japan list (mostly US-led), the X share of series jumped from about 10% to about 17.5% in a year.
items.detail: Residual cohort = all minus China minus EU/Japan. Q3'26: 6000 1647-438-145=1064, X 251-8-18=225, share 225/1289=17.5%. Q3'25: 6000 1441-362-168=911, X 123-4-14=105, share 105/1016=10.3%. That is +7.2 pts a year. Continuing it five quarters gives about 26% by Q4'27, which is faster than the global fit. The cohort is a residual, not a clean US list.
items.source_name: NCBI GEO via E-utilities; derived by subtraction
items.why_new: This gives a cohort-level slope, where F696 gave only a share for ten named US institutions.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: The EU/Japan institution list is converting at about +3.3 points a year, slower than the rest of the world.
items.detail: For a list of Japan, Germany, France, Karolinska, Oxford, Cambridge, Tokyo and Munich, X series were 18 against 145 6000 series in Q3'26, a share of 11.0%. In Q3'25 it was 14 against 168, 7.7%. The 6000 count there fell 14% y/y while the X count rose 29%. A keyword list is only a proxy for country, and the list is not the T591/T588 cohort.
items.why_new: No earlier item gives a regional X-share slope.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: Absolute human 6000 series counts are not shrinking, so the share gain comes from X growth on top of a flat to rising 6000 base.
items.detail: 6000 series per quarter were 1342, 1485, 1380, 1392, 1522, 1460, 1441, 1340, 1837, 1408 and 1647 from Q1'24 to Q3'26. Q3'26 is +14% y/y against Q3'25 and the series is noisy, with a Q1'26 spike. X series are growing 2x y/y (123 to 251) on a much smaller base. A 6000 share that falls by 1.3 pts a quarter while 6000 output stays flat is a weak sign of tail erosion.
items.why_new: This gives the full quarterly 6000 series line; earlier items cited only Q3 comparisons (F580).
items.verify_note: This restates the known F580 (6000 series up 10–12% y/y, share lost to X growth). It also repeats the X-undercount error: X series are 766, not 251, in Q3'26.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: Taiwan's NHRI paid about 58% less in NT$ per NovaSeq 6000 S4 v1.5 300-cycle kit in Dec 2023 than in Dec 2020, and bought far fewer kits.
items.detail: Dec 2020 (09GD-0002): 25 kits for NT$10,797,000 is NT$431,880 per kit, or about US$14.6K at the record's 29.5 FX. Jul 2020 (09GD-0001, S4 300-cycle): NT$17,337,600 for 32 kits is NT$541,800, or US$18.0K at the record's 30.1 FX; this assumes 32 kits is the real quantity, since the award notice lists 1. Dec 2023 (112A0C0676): 16 kits for NT$2,929,920 is NT$183,120, or about US$5.9K (my FX estimate of ~31) and about $2/Gb on 3,000 Gb. Kits fell from 57 in 2020 to 16 in 2023, and each purchase was a single-bidder award direct from Illumina. Caveat: the 2023 notice may define a 'set' differently, because a per-kit price this low is far below the $11–14K list prices the analyst already tracks. Treat the cut as indicative until the unit is confirmed.
items.source_name: Taiwan e-Procurement (PCC) via openfun API; NHRI awards
items.why_new: First dated per-kit 6000 award series from a public research institute; the known list covers core rate cards and tenders only for the X.
items.verify_note: I checked the 2023 notice: 'NovaSeq 6000 S4 v1.5 試劑組 (300 循環) 16組' (S4 v1.5 300-cycle reagent kits, 16 sets), award NT$2,929,920, floor NT$2,980,000, sold direct by Illumina Taiwan, awarded 18 Dec 2023. Quantity 16 is labelled 預估需求數量 ('estimated demand'), which suggests a unit-price framework. The award total may therefore not map to 16 delivered kits, and ~US$5.9K per kit (about 64% below the $16,578 Feb 2024 list) is implausibly low. Indicative only. This is 6000 legacy repricing, so it fits t

items.label: 1B
items.claim: Taipei VGH paid the identical NT$201,000 per P4 XLEAP-SBS reagent set in Apr 2025 and Apr 2026, so there was no discount acceleration at this hospital.
items.detail: 1140134V (award 10 Apr 2025): 9 sets at NT$201,000 each, total NT$1,809,000, floor NT$1,827,000, one bidder (Genetech). 1150157V (awarded 29 Apr 2026): 18 sets at NT$201,000 each, total NT$3,618,000, floor equal to award, one bidder (Genetech). That is flat unit price over 12 months with estimated quantity doubled (9 to 18 over 2 years). The P3 set was awarded at NT$235,000 (15 sets) on 7 May 2026. This is mid-throughput NextSeq-class, not NovaSeq, so it only partly tests the thesis.
items.source_name: Taiwan e-Procurement (PCC) via openfun API; Taipei VGH
items.why_new: Known evidence covers core rate cards and list prices; this is a same-buyer, same-SKU award price repeated a year apart with quantity doubling.
items.verify_note: New, but this is NextSeq 2000 P4 XLEAP, mid-throughput, sold through a distributor (Genetech) with a single bidder, so it is a weak test of high-throughput discounting. The P3 set at NT$235K is priced above the P4 at NT$201K, which suggests different cycle counts. Per-read comparisons are not possible without the kit spec.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: Hospital buyers are setting budgets well above what they pay. Awards land at the floor price with a single bidder after repeated failed tenders, so buyers are extracting concessions from the Illumina distributor.
items.detail: Taipei VGH P3 set: budget NT$293,750 (4,406,250 / 15) vs award NT$235,000, 20% below. P4: budget NT$228,750 vs NT$201,000, 12% below (both 1150157V). Taichung VGH 115A018 (Sep 2026, P1-P4 300-cycle kits): total budget NT$23.39M vs award NT$19.92M (−14.8%), with P3 NT$12.0M budget vs NT$9.48M award (−21%) and P4 −15%. Almost every tender here failed (流標) at least once before a single bidder accepted the floor: 1140134V twice, 1150157V twice, K114031, 115A018, TD14E170, M11476V three times, and M11405V cancelled after two failures. This reads as buyer leverage, but the budgets are estimates, not past prices, so the gap is only a proxy for a discount.
items.source_name: Taiwan e-Procurement (PCC) via openfun API; Taichung VGH, Taipei VGH
items.why_new: Quantifies buyer-set price floors and the failed-tender dynamic at hospital level, which no known item covers.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: NTUH's whole-genome 'reagents with instrument' contract was flat at NT$32.5M per 2 years through Oct 2025, then jumped to NT$297M over 3 years in Feb 2026 (about 6x the annual run-rate).
items.detail: TD13E080 (Sep 2024): NT$32.5M for 2 years (about NT$16.25M/yr), against a NT$40.57M budget. TD14E170 (Oct 2025): the same NT$32.5M for 2 years, against a NT$36.8M budget (a budget cut of 9.3%, award flat). K114031 (award 4 Feb 2026): NT$296,999,880 for 1 Mar 2026 to 28 Feb 2029, about NT$99M/yr, awarded to Genetech at the floor. That is about 6.1x the earlier annual commitment. The notices name no brand, only US origin, and the earlier two went to a different distributor (Genomics BioSci), so K114031 may be a different platform or a bundled capex and instrument deal. A price per genome cannot be derived from the notices.
items.source_name: Taiwan e-Procurement (PCC) via openfun API; NTUH
items.why_new: A new, dated hospital WGS volume signal; the known list only covers NHS and Western genome programs.
items.verify_note: No brand is named, the distributor changed, and the contract may bundle capex or instruments. NTUH is in Taiwan, which falls inside Illumina's ex-China metrics (Greater China includes Taiwan, but the China carve-out is mainland). This is one account, so it is anecdotal for 1C. Keep as a weak signal of large WGS program demand.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: For NTUH WGS reagents, the award held at the same NT$32.5M floor in Sep 2024 and Oct 2025 even as the hospital cut its own budget estimate by 9%.
items.detail: Budget NT$40.574M (Jul 2024) vs NT$36.804M (Aug 2025). The award was NT$32.5M both times, 80.1% and 88.3% of budget. A fixed award with a shrinking budget means the price ceiling the buyer will pay is tightening. Illumina's share of these awards is unconfirmed, because no brand field is given.
items.source_name: Taiwan e-Procurement (PCC) via openfun API; NTUH
items.why_new: A hospital-level tightening of budget against a fixed award; not in the known list.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: Taipei VGH's 'high-throughput reagent set' price was roughly unchanged between Dec 2023 and May 2026 (about NT$230K vs NT$235K).
items.detail: 1120652Y (Dec 2023): 29 sets, budget NT$250,000/set, award NT$6.67M, which is NT$230,000/set. 1150157V P3 (May 2026): NT$235,000/set, about 2% higher. The product match is assumed (the 2023 notice says only 'high-throughput reagent set'), so a like-for-like read is not confirmed. Taipei VGH's NT$3.94M lot award in 1140732E item 1 (Nov 2025) was 15% below its NT$4.635M budget, with quantity unspecified.
items.source_name: Taiwan e-Procurement (PCC) via openfun API; Taipei VGH
items.why_new: A 2.5-year price comparison at one hospital; the known list has none for Taiwan.

items.label: 2A
items.claim: NHRI, Taiwan's main public research institute, stopped issuing NovaSeq-titled reagent and maintenance tenders after Dec 2023 and instead outsources whole-genome work.
items.detail: Searching the PCC API for 'NovaSeq 6000' returned 17 records, none later than 21 Dec 2023. NHRI bought S4 kits in Jul 2020, Dec 2020 and Dec 2023. It renewed 'NovaSeq 6000 4-system' maintenance every year from 2018 to Dec 2023. From Sep to Oct 2024 NHRI issued two 'NGS WGS sequencing, 150 samples' tenders (1113MG1722, 113B0C0270), which are outsourced services. A query for 'NovaSeq X' returned 0 records. This could reflect retitled tenders rather than retirement, so it is weak evidence of 6000 retirement or reduced research purchasing.
items.source_name: Taiwan e-Procurement (PCC) via openfun API; NHRI
items.why_new: Procurement-title evidence of a research institute's 6000 fleet (4 units) and the absence of later purchase notices.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: Taiwan hospitals' sequencing tenders in 2025-26 are mostly mid-throughput (P1-P4) kits with large estimated quantities, so volume demand is intact at mid-throughput.
items.detail: Taichung VGH 115A018 (award 15 Sep 2026) covers estimated quantities of 30 P1, 69 P2, 60 P3 and 12 P4 300-cycle kits over a contract from 1 Oct 2026 to 30 Sep 2028 (note: the award notice itself lists 1 EA per item, so these come from the tender notices). Taipei VGH's P4 estimate doubled from 9 to 18 sets and P3 is 15. No NovaSeq-class (S4 or 25B) reagent tender appears at Taipei VGH, Taichung VGH or NCKU in 2024-26. Some NovaSeq-class demand may be in outsourced or bundled contracts such as K114031.
items.why_new: Names buyers and quantities for Taiwan hospital mid-throughput demand.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: Medicare FFS genome-sequencing code 81425 volume is negligible, and NIPT code 81420 volume is small and falling.
items.detail: 81425 (genome sequence analysis) shows 131 national services in the newer release vs 13 in the older one. The base is tiny, so Medicare claims show no WGS mass market. 81420 (NIPT, trisomy) fell from 183 to 150 services (-18%), and 81507 fell from 34 to 13. Medicare covers few pregnancies, so the NIPT figures are only weak evidence of NIPT maturing. Year labels are unverified.
items.source_name: CMS Medicare Physician & Other Practitioners - by Geography and Service
items.why_new: Known list has WGS and NIPT growth from company and expert sources, but no payer claims counts.

items.label: 2B
items.claim: Public human+mouse expression-profiling sequencing series released on GEO are growing, not flat. Q3'26 jumped +42% y/y after +5% to +16% y/y in every quarter since Q1'25.
items.detail: I counted GSE series with DataSet Type 'Expression profiling by high throughput sequencing' (the type filter that worked; Genome-binding and other types are excluded), organism human or mouse, by release quarter. Counts were Q3'23 3,719; 2024: 3,765 / 3,827 / 3,646 / 3,690; 2025: 4,156 / 4,009 / 4,238 / 4,025; 2026: 4,711 / 4,435 / 6,036. The y/y changes were Q3'24 -2.0% (3,646/3,719), Q1'25 +10.4%, Q2'25 +4.8%, Q3'25 +16.2%, Q4'25 +9.1%, Q1'26 +13.4%, Q2'26 +10.6% and Q3'26 +42.4% (6,036/4,238). The count is series released, not Gb. GEO release lags sequencing by about 6-12 months, so this reflects 2025 lab activity. A Q3'26 spike of this size may be lumpy and needs a per-submitter check.
items.why_new: Earlier GEO work counted 6000 and X platforms. This is the total human+mouse sequencing series count across all platforms, with its y/y path.
items.verify_note: This is partly new because it is specific to RNA-seq (counting) series. It overlaps D058, the known public research rebound. Counts are series, not Gb. D060 shows Gb-weighted public NovaSeq output grew only about 12% while run counts grew 42%, so a +42% series spike overstates volume. There was also no per-submitter check. Release lag means this reflects roughly 2025 lab activity.

items.label: 2B
items.claim: Series that mention a non-Illumina short-read platform (AVITI, DNBSEQ/MGISEQ, Ultima UG100) more than doubled in two years. Their share of all series rose from about 4.3% to about 5.9%.
items.detail: Series matching AVITI, DNBSEQ, MGISEQ or UG100 were 162 (Q1'24), 191, 163, 151 (Q4'24), 170 (Q1'25), 220, 235, 269 (Q4'25), 341 (Q1'26), 324 and 357 (Q3'26). As a share of total series that is 4.3%, 5.0%, 4.5%, 4.1%, 4.1%, 5.5%, 5.5%, 6.7%, 7.2%, 7.3% and 5.9% over the same quarters. Q3'26 rival series were +52% y/y (357/235) against +42% for the total. Rival series were 6.8% of the Q3'26 y/y increase in series ((357-235)/(6,036-4,238) = 122/1,798). The share peaked at 7.2-7.3% in Q1-Q2'26 and fell back to 5.9% in Q3'26.
items.why_new: Earlier items reported rival samples and runs on specific platforms. This is a keyword-based series share across the whole human+mouse GEO base, with a quarterly path.

items.label: 2A
items.claim: Series that mention Illumina grew +15% y/y in Q3'25 and +39% in Q3'26, so published Illumina-based research output is not flat.
items.detail: Series with the keyword 'Illumina' were 3,166 (Q3'24), 3,648 (Q3'25) and 5,061 (Q3'26). That is +15.2% and then +38.7% y/y. The Illumina-keyword share of all series was 86.8%, 86.1% and 83.8%, so Illumina's share slipped about 3 points in two years. The remaining (non-Illumina-keyword) series were 590 in Q3'25 and 975 in Q3'26 (+65%). The 'Illumina' keyword also matches text mentions such as kit names, so this is only a proxy for platform.
items.why_new: This gives a direct Illumina-share and growth series across all platforms. Earlier items covered only 6000 vs X shares.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: Used NovaSeq 6000 units are listed at $30K-$99K, 90-97% below the $985K list price, so decommissioned units are being resold.
items.detail: MSU Surplus lists a retired, working 6000 at $30,000 (was $60,000), local pickup, wiped computer, image timestamp ~Aug 2025. REUZEit (a broker in Temecula, CA) lists two units, serials A01351 and AO1257, at $99,000 (was $200,000, -51%), described as 'Excellent', near-new, with a 90-day warranty and 14 S4 buffer cartridges on one. No listing date or manufacture year is shown, so this is not a retirement-pace measure.
items.quote: used and in good physical condition
items.why_new: Not in the known list: adds resale asking prices for 6000s, but undated and anecdotal.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: Cheap used 6000s (as low as $30K) lower the cost of keeping a 6000 tail running, though buyers still need an Illumina service contract.
items.detail: The REUZEit listing says the buyer 'will need Illumina Service and Support contract' and that consumables must be replaced. The 6000 tail's economics therefore stay tied to Illumina reagents and service even when the instrument is nearly free. This weakly supports a permanent low-volume tail.
items.quote: will need Illumina Service and Support contract
items.why_new: Not in the known list: resale-market view of instrument cost versus the Illumina service tie.

items.label: 2A
items.claim: The NCI intramural sequencing core charges non-NCI users exactly 2x what it charges NCI users on every NovaSeq X Plus flow cell.
items.detail: NCI CCR's published table (undated) lists the 25B 300-cycle flow cell at $17,196 for NCI users and $34,392 for non-NCI users. The 25B 200-cycle is $15,131 / $30,262, and the 1.5B 100-cycle is $2,042 / $4,084. The NCI internal 25B-300 price is about 29% below Illumina's published GSA list of $24,155, but the 25B-200 internal price ($15,131) is slightly above the $14,500 Jan 2025 list price, so the core's rates likely include recharge overhead. The 2x internal/external gap shows how far price is policy and negotiation rather than reagent cost. That fits research buyers' leverage, but it does not show a price decline.
items.source_name: NCI CCR Frederick sequencing core pricing page
items.why_new: The NCI CCR core price table is not among the core rate cards already listed, and the 2.0x internal/external ratio is new.

items.label: 2A
items.claim: A no-minimum $50/sample academic RNA-seq service on Illumina is drawing 'unprecedented demand', which shows research buyers move fast on price.
items.detail: Plasmidsaurus launched 3' RNA-seq at ASHG 2025 at $50 per sample for academia and $80 for industry. It delivers up to 10M deduplicated Illumina reads in under 3 days within the US and Europe, with no minimum order and no quote process. Per a GenomeWeb search summary, CEO Mark Budde cited 'unprecedented demand' and 'hundreds of samples' a day. He also said the service is only 'barely' profitable. Counting work like this is the segment Roche AXELIOS targets. The reads stay on Illumina, but the revenue per sample is a small fraction of core-level pricing.
items.quote: There is no minimum order size or quote process.
items.why_new: The exclusion list has no Plasmidsaurus. This is a new, quantified low-price counting service on Illumina with a demand datapoint.
items.verify_note: New anecdote, but the direction is mixed. It shows research buyers will flock to a very low price per sample, which supports price sensitivity. It also shows volume responding to price, which cuts against 'less volume-elastic'. The GenomeWeb quote is a snippet (the article returned 403), and 'barely profitable' is the CEO's claim. The reads stay on Illumina, so Illumina's per-Gb revenue depends on the provider's own negotiated price, which is not disclosed.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: Medicare whole-genome volume is tiny: 131 genome claims nationally in 2024, 127 of them from Baylor.
items.detail: Code 81425 (genome sequencing) had 131 national services in 2024 (127 from Baylor Miraca Genetics) at $4,931 each. That is roughly 15,700 Gb at an assumed 120 Gb per genome, or about 0.002% of a ~800M Gb high-throughput base. Counts under 11 are suppressed, so the true total is slightly higher. The 2023 national figure was 13, so growth was ~10x, but from a negligible base. WGS is therefore growing fast but is nowhere near enough to offset slower NIPT or CGP volume in Medicare. This is Medicare fee-for-service only, so commercial rapid-WGS volume is not captured.
items.source_name: CMS Medicare Physician & Other Practitioners (data.cms.gov API)
items.why_new: This quantifies WGS in Gb terms, with the 13 → 131 change. F720 and F676 say only 'negligible'.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: The Medicare beneficiary count for Natera's Signatera MRD code is about 51 times that of the one Guardant MRD-like code, whose identity I did not confirm.
items.detail: Natera 0340U had 11,922 beneficiaries and 25,746 services. Guardant 0422U ('Onc pan solid tum alys DNA') had 232 beneficiaries and 243 services at $1,897. I did not confirm that 0422U is Guardant Reveal, so treat that as unverified. MRD Medicare volume is concentrated in one vendor. Outside Natera, MRD is still tiny, which supports the claim that MRD is not yet a broad Gb pool.
items.source_name: CMS Medicare Physician & Other Practitioners (data.cms.gov API)
items.why_new: The competitor MRD code magnitude and the concentration ratio are not in the known list.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: Some Medicare code counts moved sharply, which may mean volume growth is hidden by coding shifts. The 'against' reading is ambiguous.
items.detail: 81455 (51+ gene panel) fell from 41,582 to 13,895 services, while 81419 (epilepsy panel) rose from 6,072 to 30,385. Adaptive's 81479 line holds 5,123 services at $7,099. These swings look like billing or coding migration between codes, not real volume change. Code-level Medicare series are therefore unreliable for per-test trends unless the codes are tied to a lab. I did not verify the cause.
items.source_name: CMS Medicare Physician & Other Practitioners (data.cms.gov API)
items.why_new: This is a data-quality caveat for the Medicare claims reads used so far, with the specific code swings quantified.

items.label: 2B
items.claim: AVITI is a fast-growing but tiny presence in mouse research series, and Ultima is absent.
items.detail: Mouse series naming AVITI: 0 (Q3'24), 19 (Q3'25), 45 (Q3'26), up 137% y/y. This is 2.0% of 6000+X+AVITI series (45/2,254) in Q3'26. Ultima returned 0 in Q3'26. NextSeq 2000 rose 130 → 210 → 234 (+61% then +11%), about 10.6% of 6000+X volume.
items.why_new: Mouse-only rival counts; known items are combined or human-focused.
items.verify_note: This mostly restates F582, F583 and F584 (AVITI ~1.75% of GEO HT samples, Ultima negligible), cut down to mouse only. An 'AVITI[All Fields]' keyword count is a weaker method than the GPL-based counts already accepted. The NextSeq 2000 series path is new but does not bear on 2B.

items.label: 2B
items.claim: Rival platforms are not yet taking meaningful mouse research volume from Illumina.
items.detail: Illumina 6000+X mouse series grew +25.5% y/y (1,760 → 2,209) in Q3'26 against 45 AVITI series. Total mouse high-throughput expression-profiling series were 1,830 / 2,255 / 2,571 (+23%, then +14%). The 6000+X series equal 86% of that total in Q3'26 (2,209/2,571) versus 72% in Q3'24 (1,320/1,830), so Illumina's share of the series count is rising. The DNBSEQ/MGISEQ keyword returned only 1 / 1 / 0, which looks like a keyword gap rather than true absence, so MGI is not measured.
items.url: https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/esearch.fcgi?db=gds&term="Mus musculus"[Organism]+AND+"Expression profiling by high throughput sequencing"[DataSet Type]+AND+gse[ETYP]+AND+2026/07/01:2026/09/30[PDAT]&retmax=0&retmode=json
items.why_new: Shows total mouse research volume is growing and Illumina's share of it is rising.
items.verify_note: The denominators do not match. The 6000+X series count is not limited to the expression-profiling dataset type, but the 'total' (2,571) is, so the 72%→86% 'Illumina share' is an artifact of the method. It also likely misses X Plus GPLs (D065). The useful part (rivals small in mouse) is already covered by F582–F584 and D057.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: Published mouse research volume is growing rather than flat, and growth is mostly X-driven.
items.detail: Total mouse HT expression series rose +23% (Q3'25 vs Q3'24) and +14% (Q3'26 vs Q3'25), so growth is decelerating but positive. X series grew +110% y/y in Q3'26 against 6000 +7.4%. This conflicts with a flat research volume assumption, though series count is not Gb.
items.url: https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/esearch.fcgi?db=gds&term="Mus musculus"[Organism]+AND+"Expression profiling by high throughput sequencing"[DataSet Type]+AND+gse[ETYP]+AND+2025/07/01:2025/09/30[PDAT]&retmax=0&retmode=json
items.why_new: Mouse total-series growth rates by year, with deceleration from +23% to +14%.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: Rat series show the same direction, with the X share of 6000+X rising from 18% to 24% in a year.
items.detail: Rat series on 6000 / X: Q3'25 62 / 14 (X 18.4%); Q3'26 80 / 25 (X 23.8%). Small counts, so noisy. The 6000 count rose +29% y/y.
items.why_new: Rat conversion data not covered elsewhere.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: Mouse HiSeq 4000 series were flat at 148 between Q3'24 and Q3'26, so legacy-platform decay is not visible in this count.
items.detail: HiSeq 4000 mouse series: 148 (Q3'24) and 148 (Q3'26). Identical counts could be a coincidence, so treat this as weak. It suggests older-instrument use persists in published research, as with the HiSeq-to-NovaSeq tail of 2019-20.
items.why_new: HiSeq 4000 legacy count not in known list.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: With X Plus included, the NovaSeq X share of public ENA runs of 10 Gb or more doubled from 16.2% in Q3'25 to 32.7% in Q3'26, while 6000 large runs fell 15%.
items.detail: ENA count API, runs of 10 Gb or more by first_public quarter. In Q3'25 there were 63,713 runs on the 6000, 5,481 on the X and 6,848 on the X Plus, so the X family was 12,329/76,042 = 16.2%. In Q3'26 there were 54,042, 11,567 and 14,699, so the X family was 26,266/80,308 = 32.7%, a gain of +16.5 pts in a year. X Plus is about 56% of X-family large runs in both years. Public data is research-heavy and lags, so this tracks the research tail more than the clinical one.
items.url: https://www.ebi.ac.uk/ena/portal/api/count?result=read_run&query=instrument_model="Illumina NovaSeq X Plus" AND first_public>=2026-07-01 AND first_public<=2026-09-30 AND base_count>=10000000000
items.why_new: Corrects F698, whose X-only filter halved the share. These run-count shares reconcile exactly with the F648 NovaSeq totals.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: Any public-repository mix-shift count that filters only on the plain 'NovaSeq X' platform misses one-half to two-thirds of X output, so the X-only GEO and ENA items (F695, F698, F708, F711) are invalid as stated.
items.detail: X Plus accounts for 6,848/12,329 = 55.5% (Q3'25) and 14,699/26,266 = 56.0% (Q3'26) of X-family ENA runs of 10 Gb or more. In GEO human series for Q3'26 it accounts for 515/766 = 67% (GPL34284 vs GPL34281). With X Plus included, the human X share of 6000+X series in Q3'26 is 766/2,413 = 31.7%, consistent with F578's 30.5% for human plus mouse. The projected '~19% by Q4'27' path is therefore spurious.
items.source_name: NCBI GEO E-utilities; EMBL-EBI ENA portal API
items.why_new: This is a data-quality correction confirmed against live counts. It prevents the corpus from taking in understated X shares.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: In public GEO series, the X share gain is slowing but is still about +12 pts a year, and a simple extension gives roughly +9 to +11 pts for 2027 in research-heavy public data.
items.detail: From F578 (human plus mouse series), the X share of 6000+X was 4.6% (Q3'24), 18.4% (Q3'25) and 30.5% (Q3'26), which is +13.8 then +12.1 pts. If the gain keeps shrinking by about 1.5–2 pts a year, the X share reaches about 40–42% by Q3'27. GEO lags Illumina's reported research Gb share (92% on the X) by about 2 years (D052). This is therefore a lagging read on research conversion, not a forecast of clinical points, and it does not directly validate the thesis's +5 points.
items.why_new: Replaces the rejected F708 projection with a trend that includes X Plus.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: If NHRI's Dec 2023 award really covers 16 S4-300 kits, this 6000-only account paid about US$2.0/Gb, roughly 64% below the 2024 S4 list and level with the 25B's own list per Gb.
items.detail: NT$2,929,920 / 16 = NT$183,120 per kit, about US$5.9K at ~31 NT$/US$, or about $1.97/Gb on ~3,000 Gb. The Feb 2024 S4-300 list was $16,578 ($5.53/Gb), and the top Open Offer net was about $4.31/Gb (22% off). The 25B-300 list was $16,000 / 8,000 Gb = $2.00/Gb. The notice labels quantity as 'estimated demand' (a framework award), so the per-kit price is unconfirmed. The account's kit purchases fell from 57 (2020) to 16 (2023).
items.quote: NovaSeq 6000 S4 v1.5 試劑組 (300 循環) 16組
items.why_new: First per-Gb comparison of a direct Illumina 6000 award in Taiwan against list and the Open Offer tiers.

items.label: 2A
items.claim: Baylor's internal 3' RNA-seq price fell about 21% in 2025 and was then flat into Feb 2026, a core repricing toward outsourced rates.
items.detail: Baylor's Genomic & RNA Profiling Core price lists show 3' Quant RNA-Seq (SR75, ~10M reads) at $250/$220 (Aug 2022, batches <24 / ≥24), $190/$180 (Mar 2025), and $160/$150 (Sep 2025). The Feb 2026 list is unchanged at $160/$150. Arithmetic: 190→160 is -15.8%, and 180→150 is -16.7% across Mar→Sep 2025. 250→160 is -36% from 2022. This is an in-house cut inside the window where Plasmidsaurus pricing appeared. The cause is not stated, and the Sep 2025 date predates the Oct 2025 launch.
items.source_name: Baylor College of Medicine GARP core price lists
items.why_new: Not among the core rate cards already used (Baylor is not listed). It gives a dated time series for a research assay.
items.verify_note: Correction: the 2025 cut is ~16–17% (Mar→Sep 2025: $190→160 and $180→150), not ~21%. The larger step is Aug 2022→Mar 2025 ($250→190, −24%). The docx was not opened, so the numbers are unverified. This is a core's service price, not Illumina's reagent price, and the cause is not stated. It predates the Plasmidsaurus launch, so it cannot be a response to it.

items.label: 2A
items.claim: GenomeWeb reports the Plasmidsaurus service is an order of magnitude cheaper and faster than alternatives and is causing unease at academic cores.
items.detail: A search summary of the paywalled article (GenomeWeb, Huanjia Zhang, 24 Nov 2025; the article itself was not opened) says the service launched at ASHG, takes under 3 days, and poses 'stiff competition' to academic core facilities. Cores are described as having longer timelines and higher price points. This is snippet-level evidence only.
items.why_new: The known list has the F377 and F376 core outsourcing items but not this named GenomeWeb piece.

items.label: 2A
items.claim: Plasmidsaurus's founder describes demand as unlike anything seen, which suggests research buyers move to the lowest price quickly.
items.detail: Founder Mark Budde, in a 14 Oct 2025 SynBioBeta launch article, said demand so far was unlike anything he had seen. The page also reports 'hundreds of samples' a day (per the probe notes, not re-verified here). At $50, 100 samples/day is ~$5K/day, or ~$1.3M/yr at 260 working days. This is a small revenue figure but shows price-led demand.
items.quote: The demand that we've been seeing so far is unlike anything I've ever seen
items.why_new: Gives a quote and dated launch. F727 has no quote or date.

items.label: 2B
items.claim: The cheap research RNA-seq service still runs on Illumina (NovaSeq X Plus), so the price gap is captured by an Illumina customer's margin, not by a rival platform.
items.detail: The Plasmidsaurus page states it uses the Illumina platform, and GenomeWeb's summary says NovaSeq X Plus. At ~20M raw reads for $50, revenue is $2.50/M raw reads, or $5/M dedup reads. The Illumina reagent cost at ~$0.7-1.0/M clusters on a 25B lane (known Illumina and core numbers) is roughly $14-20 per sample, 28-40% of $50. Illumina keeps the volume but the buyer's all-in cost is far lower. That cuts against the idea that Roche or Ultima are needed to drive research price down. These per-read figures are my own derivation, not disclosed.
items.why_new: Quantifies the Illumina reagent share of a $50 research assay. This was not in the known list.
items.verify_note: Verified: the page says 'We utilize the Illumina platform', ~20M raw / up to 10M deduplicated reads, $50 academic / $80 industry. The page does not name the NovaSeq X; that rests only on GenomeWeb. The 2B relevance is that research volume is concentrating in high-volume aggregators that can demand top-tier discounts (the large-lab leverage mechanism), not rival-platform pricing. The reagent-share figure (28–40%) is the author's derivation at core-level $/M, and the aggregator's net price is like

items.label: 2A
items.claim: Cornell's plate-based 3' RNA-seq library prep alone costs about $76 per sample internal, above Plasmidsaurus's full $50 price.
items.detail: Cornell BRC lists a quarter plate (max 23 samples) at $1,755 internal and $2,880 external, with one blank well: $1,755/23 = $76 per sample internal before sequencing, and $2,880/23 = $125 external. Plasmidsaurus's $50 all-in is 66% below the internal prep-only cost and 60% below external. The Cornell page is undated.
items.why_new: Cornell BRC is known only as a no-NovaSeq core. This is a library-prep price comparison.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: NHS's central Illumina WGS stream (Hinxton) is being moved to a distributed model in 2026, and the 300K-genome contract target was missed and extended.
items.detail: Genomics England extended its 2019 short-read WGS contract with Illumina Cambridge to 31 Mar 2027 for £4.67M (notice 13 Jun 2025). The notice says the target of 300,000 WGE could not be met in the original five-year term because sample supply fell short (delays largely outside the buyer's control, including Covid). The extra payment covers lab and staff costs only and 'does not cover any additional volumes'. This is a small, public-sector volume stream that under-delivered against plan, consistent with clinical WGS being slower than hoped. It is not evidence of a volume decline at Illumina overall.
items.source_name: Find a Tender (OCDS), Genomics England Ltd
items.quote: more time is required to enable the target number of samples to be met
items.why_new: Known list cites NHS WGS volumes (42K rare-disease genomes) but not the contract's missed 300K WGE target or the £4.67M extension.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: Genomics England says the Illumina contract extension is needed to manage the move to distributed WGS in the NHS during 2026; this is a dated transition of a large clinical WGS stream, but the notice names no platform.
items.detail: The notice says the NHS is 'transitioning from a central location for WGS in Hinxton to a distributed model' and the extension 'is necessary to manage the move to distributed WGS'. It covers short-read services only and argues that data consistency requires Illumina's own equipment and materials. Contract value is £4.67M against a 300K WGE target, so a rough ~£15.6 per WGE (my calculation, not stated, and it may not cover reagents). The notice does not say whether the move is to NovaSeq X or the 6000, so it cannot be tied directly to the 6000 tail.
items.source_name: Find a Tender (OCDS), Genomics England Ltd
items.quote: The extension is necessary to manage the move to distributed WGS within the NHS.
items.why_new: Gives an official dated NHS WGS transition from Illumina's own lab to regional labs; not in the known list.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: UK public research buyers still sign 14-month Illumina sequencer service plans without competition in late 2025, keeping legacy instrument tails alive (NextSeq 2000, MiSeq).
items.detail: UKRI-5363 (signed 23 Oct 2025): GBP 54,984 gross for a NextSeq 2000 Silver plan, 14 Jan 2026 to 23 Mar 2027, below threshold and without competition. Cefas CEFAS25-129 (signed 3 Nov 2025): GBP 55,083 gross for MiSeq and NextSeq 2000 service for 2026. This is mid- and low-throughput, not 6000, so it is weak support for the 6000 tail.
items.why_new: Not in the known list; the NextSeq 2000 and MiSeq service amounts are new but adjacent to the thesis.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: Three separate 2025–26 Taiwanese hospital WGS awards all landed at exactly NT$12,800 per genome (~US$410), and one includes blood extraction, so outsourced clinical genome pricing has settled at a low common price.
items.detail: Kaohsiung VGH bought oral-cancer WGS for 210 samples at NT$2,688,000 (Dec 2025, ST1411027), which is NT$12,800 each. Its OB/GYN WGS including blood extraction cost NT$3,200,000 for 250 samples (Jan 2026, ST1412017), also NT$12,800 each. Both match Taipei VGH's NT$12,800 (Feb 2025). In the Kaohsiung OB/GYN tender, CENTOGENE APAC (Centogene is a named AXELIOS buyer) bid NT$3,498,750 (~NT$13,995 each) and was disqualified on paperwork. At ~NT$31/US$, an all-in clinical genome near US$410 leaves little room for Illumina reagent pricing at the service lab.
items.source_name: Taiwan Government e-Procurement (g0v mirror), Kaohsiung VGH ST1411027 and ST1412017
items.quote: 高通量全基因體定序檢測分析(含血液樣品萃取服務)
items.why_new: The convergence of awards at one price, and an AXELIOS-owning lab bidding on Taiwan clinical WGS, are not in the corpus.
items.verify_note: Verified for ST1412017: NT$3,200,000 for 250 samples, including blood extraction, awarded 29 Jan 2026 to 基龍米克斯 (Genomics BioSci & Tech). CENTOGENE APAC bid NT$3,498,750 and was not awarded on specification documents. Caveat: all three NT$12,800 awards (Taipei VGH, both Kaohsiung VGH tenders) went to the same vendor, so this is one vendor's price point, not market convergence. Downgraded from strong. The quantities are estimated demand under open contracts.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: When Taipei VGH's WGS price nearly halved, its contracted WGS volume almost tripled (173 to 490 genomes per two years), which is evidence of strong price elasticity for clinical genomes.
items.detail: The estimated WGS quantity rose 183% between the 2023–25 and 2025–27 contracts, while WES rose only 15% (576 to 663). WGS spend rose 51% (NT$4.15M to NT$6.27M) despite the 47% unit price cut. So in this one hospital, WGS is substituting for exome and expanding in Gb terms. That cuts against the view that sequencing cost no longer constrains volume.
items.source_name: Taiwan Government e-Procurement (g0v mirror), Taipei VGH X11204H vs X11326H
items.why_new: This is a quantified price-cut and volume response at a named clinical buyer, with no equivalent in the 1C evidence.
items.verify_note: Verified: X11204H (awarded 20 Jul 2023) WGS 173 @ NT$24,000, WES 576 @ NT$12,700; X11326H (awarded 20 Feb 2025) WGS 490 @ NT$12,800, WES 663 @ NT$9,600, both won by 基龍米克斯. The WGS cut is −46.7%. WES also fell −24.4%, which the item omits. The quantities are estimated ceilings in open contracts, not realized volume. This is a single hospital and immaterial in size.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: Taichung VGH awarded a NT$117.6M (~US$3.8M) three-year outsourced high-throughput WGS contract in Aug 2025, a large new clinical genome volume source in Taiwan.
items.detail: Tender 114Y-R5 had a budget of NT$145.45M and was awarded on 27 Aug 2025 to Genomics BioSci & Tech (基龍米克斯) at NT$117,550,800, for 28 Aug 2025 to 27 Aug 2028. There were two bidders; 台基盟 bid NT$122.7M. No unit count is disclosed. At the prevailing NT$12,800 per genome (items 1–2) it implies roughly 9,200 genomes, about 3,000 a year (our derivation). That is several times Taipei VGH's ~245 a year.
items.source_name: Taiwan Government e-Procurement (g0v mirror), Taichung VGH 114Y-R5
items.quote: 高通量全基因體定序檢測委外代檢
items.why_new: This Taiwan clinical WGS program is new. F715 covered only NTUH's reagent contract.
items.verify_note: Verified: budget NT$145,454,400; award NT$117,550,800 to Genomics BioSci & Tech on 27 Aug 2025; runs 28 Aug 2025–27 Aug 2028; second bidder 台基盟 at NT$122,734,656. No quantity or test type is given, and the notice is flagged as security-sensitive. The ~9,200-genome figure assumes NT$12,800 per genome, which is unverified for this contract. It is ~US$1.3M/yr, immaterial to Illumina (see the derived item).

items.label: 2B
items.claim: Element has built a Taiwan research base through its channel 亞洲準譯 (Asia Pathogenomics): four instrument or reagent awards at Academia Sinica and National Taiwan University worth ~NT$54.8M (~US$1.8M) since Nov 2024.
items.detail: The awards were: Academia Sinica Biodiversity Research Center AVITI24, NT$15.31M (Nov 2024; a correction names Element Biosciences, Inc. as vendor); NTU College of Medicine AVITI24, NT$17.0M (Jul 2025, NT$12.35M Ministry of Education subsidy); an NTU AVITI24 reagent open contract, NT$13.32M running to 31 Dec 2028 (Dec 2025); and Academia Sinica Institute of Molecular Biology 'AVITI mid-throughput platform', NT$9.2M (~US$295K; May 2026). All were single-bid restricted tenders under Procurement Act Art. 22(1)(2)/(4), which reads as a deliberate platform choice by Taiwan's top research institutions.
items.source_name: Taiwan Government e-Procurement (g0v mirror), awards to 亞洲準譯股份有限公司
items.quote: AVITI中通量定序平台01套

The amounts and the single-bid procurement article were not checked; the search page shows no amounts. Context: 亞洲準譯 is mainly a pathogen-NGS service lab (APGseq contracts at several hospitals), so its role as Element's channel is a side line. The total is ~US$1.8M,

items.label: 1B
items.claim: Chi Mei Medical Center, a large Tainan hospital, bought a NT$9.96M 'high-throughput NGS sequencer' in Feb 2026 from Element's Taiwan channel, probably an AVITI-class box entering a clinical medical center.
items.detail: Tender 114B01342H1 had a NT$10.0M budget (NT$7.61M Ministry of Health and Welfare subsidy) and was awarded on 3 Feb 2026 at NT$9.96M to 亞洲準譯, the single bidder. Origin is listed as the USA. Brand is not stated. The price matches the Academia Sinica AVITI (NT$9.2M), and Illumina instruments in Taiwan list Singapore as origin and come through 均泰 (Genetech): the CGMH Illumina system was NT$2.245M (Aug 2025) and the NTUH Yunlin 'high-throughput sequencer' NT$5.05M (May 2025). So the AVITI identification is an inference.
items.source_name: Taiwan Government e-Procurement (g0v mirror), Chi Mei Hospital 114B01342H1
items.quote: 高通量次世代定序儀採購案
items.why_new: This is a clinical-hospital rival instrument buy in Asia funded by the government's Healthy Taiwan program. It is not in the corpus, and none of the nine large US labs showed one.
items.verify_note: The award to 亞洲準譯 (24 Feb 2026, Chi Mei) is confirmed in the vendor list. The brand is inferred, not stated. 亞洲準譯 runs pathogen-NGS services at many hospitals, so the box may serve infectious-disease mNGS rather than an oncology or genome workload that displaces Illumina.

items.label: 2B
items.claim: Taiwan CDC's 2026 nanopore spend (~NT$15.0M) now exceeds its flat Illumina library-reagent spend (~NT$10.2M).
items.detail: The Illumina library-prep reagents and chips lot via 均泰 was NT$10,180,000 (Aug 2025, KA114045) and NT$10,199,000 (Aug 2026, KA115051), so it was flat. In 2026 the CDC also awarded ONT consumables at NT$11,590,000 (Jun 2026, KA115024, vendor ANTEC, EU origin) and a 'high-throughput nanopore long-fragment sequencer' at NT$3,450,000 (Aug 2026, KA115057, UK origin, a PromethION-class price). It also opened a further nanopore instrument-components quote (KA115075, Sep 2026). Incremental public-health sequencing budget is going to ONT, not Illumina.
items.source_name: Taiwan Government e-Procurement (g0v mirror), Taiwan CDC KA114045, KA115051, KA115024, KA115057
items.quote: 高通量奈米孔長片段定序儀
items.why_new: This is a year-on-year same-buyer comparison of Illumina vs ONT spend at a national public-health lab. The prior ONT items were Canadian (F454, F456).
items.verify_note: Not opened. This is a like-for-unlike comparison: the Illumina lot covers library-prep reagents and chips only and may not be the CDC's whole Illumina spend, while the ONT total mixes a one-off NT$3.45M instrument with consumables. ONT consumables alone (NT$11.59M) slightly exceed the Illumina lot. This is public-health/applied spend, and long-read is not a direct short-read price substitute.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: NTUH, Taiwan's flagship hospital, multiplied its Oxford Nanopore reagent contract about 3.5x, and two other Taiwanese medical centers also buy ONT flow cells, so long-read is taking hospital genomics budget.
items.detail: NTUH's R10.4.1 nanopore chip unit-price contract was NT$5,435,490 for Mar 2024 to Mar 2026 (TD130050). The 'high-throughput nanopore reagent set with instrument' was NT$19,054,200 for Sep 2025 to Aug 2027 (TD14E130), and a separate nanopore chip contract followed (TD140310, Jul 2025). New chip-set quotes followed in Jun and Aug 2026 (PK2600074, PK2600108). Taichung VGH bought UK-origin 'nucleic acid analysis chips' (ONT flow cells) for NT$4.0M over 2 years (May 2025, 114A08). All of these were single bids via ANTEC.
items.source_name: Taiwan Government e-Procurement (g0v mirror), NTUH TD130050/TD14E130; Taichung VGH 114A08
items.quote: 高通量奈米孔三代定序試劑組(附儀器)開口合約
items.why_new: The corpus has no hospital-level ONT spend growth in Asia.
items.verify_note: The '3.5x' compares a chips-only contract (NT$5.44M) with one that includes an instrument (NT$19.05M), so it is not like-for-like. This is long-read budget competition, not evidence on Illumina discount rates. It is better read as share pressure than discount acceleration.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: Taichung VGH's Sep 2026 two-year NextSeq 2000 kit contract shows mid-throughput Illumina prices holding near US$13–14 per Gb, with one bidder and awards only ~15% under budget.
items.detail: Tender 115A018 was a joint procurement covering Oct 2026 to Sep 2028 at NT$19.92M against a NT$23.39M budget. Implied per-kit prices are P1 NT$46,000 (30 kits), P2 NT$93,000 (69), P3 NT$158,000 (60) and P4 NT$220,000 (12), all 300-cycle; quantities are from the tender and the per-kit prices are our division. Taipei VGH paid NT$201,000 for a P4 XLEAP kit (Apr 2026), so a sister VA hospital pays ~9% more for the same class of kit. That is dispersion, not convergence toward lower prices. At ~540 Gb per P4 and ~360 Gb per P3 (spec, our assumption), that is ~NT$407–439/Gb (~US$13–14/Gb).
items.source_name: Taiwan Government e-Procurement (g0v mirror), Taichung VGH 115A018
items.quote: P1定序試劑組等4項單價開口契約
items.why_new: This is a new Sep 2026 award with per-kit prices across all four NextSeq 2000 flow cells, plus a cross-hospital comparison. F713 covered only Taipei VGH P4.
items.verify_note: Verified: budget NT$23,386,500; award NT$19,917,000 (−14.8%) on 15 Sep 2026; period 1 Oct 2026–30 Sep 2028; the first round failed (流標). Corrections: the sole bidder and winner is 基龍米克斯 (Genomics BioSci & Tech), not Illumina's channel 均泰, and origin is listed as USA. Item discounts vs budget are uneven: P1 −6%, P2 −6%, P3 −21%, P4 −15%. The per-kit prices are award ÷ estimated quantity and the Gb/kit figures are spec assumptions.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: NTUH's two-year 'human WGS and WES reagent set with instrument' contract fell 33% in value between the Feb 2022 and Jul 2023 awards, both single-bid with Genomics BioSci & Tech.
items.detail: TD10E290 was awarded on 8 Feb 2022 at NT$29,796,000 (budget NT$34.4M) for Feb 2022 to Feb 2024. TD12E060 was awarded on 19 Jul 2023 at NT$19,890,000 (budget NT$23.56M, the bid cut to the floor) for Aug 2023 to Jul 2025. Both list US origin. Quantities are not disclosed, so the drop could be fewer tests rather than a lower price. Read it alongside F715 (the later NT$32.5M and NT$297M contracts).
items.source_name: Taiwan Government e-Procurement (g0v mirror), NTUH TD10E290 and TD12E060
items.why_new: These earlier points in the NTUH WGS reagent series predate the F715/F716 awards.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: Counting every human X GPL (15 accessions incl. X Plus), the X share of human 6000+X GEO series was 4.3% in Q3'24, 19.3% in Q3'25 and 31.6% in Q3'26, so the 6000 share is still falling about 12 pts a year.
items.detail: Human X union (15 GPLs) series counts for Q3'24/Q3'25/Q3'26: 62/345/762. Human 6000 (GPL24676): 1,380/1,441/1,647. X share = 62/1,442=4.3%; 345/1,786=19.3%; 762/2,409=31.6%. The y/y step was +15.0 pts then +12.3 pts, so it is slowing but not flattening. The 6000 share is 68.4% in Q3'26. Some GPLs (35012, 35268) are human+mouse and are counted once.
items.why_new: Sums all 15 human X and X Plus GPLs, per the D065 fix; earlier GEO items used only GPL34281 or the plain X platform.
items.verify_note: The arithmetic checks out (4.3%, 19.3%, 31.6%). This is mostly the human half of the known F578 and D066 series: human plus mouse 6000 and X series add up to roughly the F578 totals. The only new part is the human-only split, which tracks the combined path. D052 still applies: GEO's X share lags Illumina's reported research X Gb share (90%+) by about two years, so this measures publication lag as well as mix.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: Mouse GEO series show the same shift: the X share of mouse 6000+X went 5.1% to 17.6% to 29.4% over Q3'24, Q3'25 and Q3'26.
items.detail: Mouse-only X GPLs (13 accessions, X and X Plus) gave 66/306/643 series. Mouse 6000 (GPL24247) gave 1,233/1,432/1,542. X share = 66/1,299=5.1%; 306/1,738=17.6%; 643/2,185=29.4%. The 6000 share is 70.6% in Q3'26. The y/y step was +12.5 pts then +11.8 pts, the same migration pace as the human series.
items.why_new: This is the complete mouse X and X Plus GPL union; earlier mouse items used a narrower platform set.
items.verify_note: The arithmetic checks out (5.1%, 17.6%, 29.4%), but this is the mouse half of the known F578 and D066 human-plus-mouse series. It adds nothing beyond 'same pace in both species', which F753 already shows.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: By contact-country proxy, the US X share rose 5.1% to 25.0% to 34.5% in Q3'24/'25/'26 and China's rose 1.8% to 12.3% to 23.6%. Neither shows a stalled 6000 tail.
items.detail: US series (text match 'USA'): X 32/207/404; 6000 590/621/767. US X share = 32/622=5.1%; 207/828=25.0%; 404/1,171=34.5% (y/y +9.5 pts, prior +19.9). China: X 7/51/136; 6000 375/363/440. China X share = 1.8%, 12.3%, 23.6% (y/y +11.3 pts, prior +10.5). China is accelerating, which fits the idea that its 6000 tail does not hold. The US is decelerating but still moving. Caveat: the country is a free-text 'All Fields' match, not a verified contact-country field, so it is noisy.
items.why_new: This is the first regional split of the GEO 6000-to-X shift, using a text proxy for country.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: The residual rest-of-world group (everything not matching USA or China) is converting fastest, from about 5% to 16% to 33% X share. That points to EU, Japan and other sites, not a permanent floor.
items.detail: Residual = total minus USA minus China, assuming no overlap. X: 23/87/222. 6000: 415/457/440. X share = 5.3%, 16.0%, 33.5% (y/y +17.5 pts). Overlap between the USA and China text matches would bias this, and the sign is uncertain. This conflicts with earlier institution-list reads that EU/Japan sites convert at about +3.3 pts a year (F710). Treat it as directional only.
items.why_new: The residual-region split is new and contradicts the earlier EU/Japan slow-conversion read.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: The 6000's absolute series counts are still rising and the rate of share loss is easing, which fits a tail that stalls.
items.detail: The human 6000 count rose 1,380 to 1,441 to 1,647 (+4% then +14%). The mouse 6000 count rose 1,233 to 1,432 to 1,542 (+16% then +8%). The human X share step eased from +15.0 to +12.3 pts, and the US step from +19.9 to +9.5 pts. Management can read the US slowdown as the 6000 floor forming. GEO measures publication timing, not Illumina consumables.
items.why_new: The US-specific deceleration (+19.9 to +9.5 pts) is a new watch-out.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: At Taipei VGH, contracted Gb rose ~140% between two-year contracts because WGS replaced exome after WGS's price premium over WES shrank from 1.89x to 1.33x.
items.detail: The WGS/WES price ratio was NT$24,000/12,700 = 1.89x in the Jul 2023 contract and NT$12,800/9,600 = 1.33x in the Feb 2025 contract. At ~100 Gb per 30x genome and ~10 Gb per exome (known), estimated contract Gb went from 173×100 + 576×10 ≈ 23.1K Gb to 490×100 + 663×10 ≈ 55.6K Gb, +141% over the two years, or ~55%/yr. Contract spend rose only from NT$11.47M to NT$12.64M (+10%), so the service lab's revenue per Gb fell ~54%. The quantities are open-contract estimates, and one hospital is immaterial to Illumina, but this is a clean case of price-driven exome-to-genome substitution.
items.source_name: Taiwan Government e-Procurement (g0v mirror), Taipei VGH X11204H vs X11326H
items.quote: 人類全基因體定序服務委外
items.why_new: It combines the WES and WGS legs into a Gb-weighted volume and a price-premium path; F745 gave test counts only.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: Even Taiwan's largest public hospital WGS contract is only ~0.04% of Illumina's annual HT Gb, so new clinical genome programs of this kind cannot move volume growth.
items.detail: Taichung VGH's 114Y-R5 is NT$117.55M over three years (~NT$39.2M/yr, ~US$1.26M/yr). At the NT$12,800 per genome seen in three other VGH awards, that is ~3,060 genomes a year, or ~0.31M Gb at ~100 Gb each. Against a ~800M Gb HT base (known), that is ~0.04%. Even combined with Taipei VGH (~245 genomes a year), Taiwan's VGH WGS outsourcing is a rounding error, consistent with the known NHS figure (<1% of HT Gb). The per-genome price for this contract is assumed, not disclosed.
items.source_name: Taiwan Government e-Procurement (g0v mirror), Taichung VGH 114Y-R5

items.label: 1B
items.claim: An all-in outsourced clinical genome at NT$12,800 (~US$410, including blood extraction) leaves room for only ~$1.8–2.5/Gb of Illumina reagent if reagents are 45–60% of price, so the dominant service vendor must buy near top-tier net pricing.
items.detail: NT$12,800 at ~31 NT$/US$ is ~US$410 per ~100 Gb genome, or ~$4.1/Gb all-in, including extraction, prep and analysis (Kaohsiung VGH ST1412017, Jan 2026; Taipei VGH X11326H, Feb 2025). That is below TCAG's research 30x genome (C$650, ~US$470, excluding extraction; D043). At core 25B lane rates of $2.5–3.0/Gb, reagents alone would be ~$250–300 (61–73% of price). At the Open Offer top tier ($1.76/Gb, D051) they are ~$176 (43%). One vendor (基龍米克斯) won all three awards, so its negotiating leverage with Illumina is the price-setting factor.
items.quote: 含血液樣品萃取服務

items.label: 1B
items.claim: Taichung VGH's Sep 2026 NextSeq P3 XLEAP 300-cycle price (~US$5.1K) is ~18% above Illumina's US list ($4,305), so mid-throughput kit pricing in Taiwan shows no discounting, although the highest-output kits got the biggest cuts against budget.
items.detail: 115A018 awarded P3 at NT$9,480,000 for 60 kits (NT$158,000, ~US$5.1K at 31 NT$/US$), against Illumina's May 2024 P3 300 XLEAP list of $4,305 (F548), about +18%. Award-vs-budget cuts were P1 −6%, P2 −6%, P3 −21%, P4 −15%, with one bidder after a failed first round. That suggests negotiation concentrated on the higher-output kits rather than a broad price fall. FX and local margin (the vendor is a service lab reseller) explain part of the premium.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: Outsourced 30x-genome prices in Taiwan have converged on NT$12,800 (~US$400) at three VGHs, and a research institute paid only NT$9,800 (~US$305).
items.detail: Kaohsiung VGH paid NT$12,800 per genome in both of its awards. The oral-cancer WGS contract (ST1411027, 30 Dec 2025, one bidder) was NT$2,688,000 for 210 genomes. The women's-medicine WGS contract, including blood collection (ST1412017, 30 Jan 2026), was NT$3,200,000 for 250 genomes, and the rival bidder, Centogene APAC, was disqualified on specs. Taipei VGH also pays NT$12,800 (2025). At ~US$400 all-in, including library prep, analysis and vendor margin, the sequencing-reagent share is a fraction of that. This implies very low effective $/Gb at the two vendors (Genomics, Taiwan Genome Alliance) that dominate Taiwan's market.

items.label: 2A
items.claim: Taiwan's National Health Research Institutes (NHRI, a research buyer) bought outsourced WGS at NT$9,800 per genome in Oct 2024, 23% below the hospital rate. The winning bid came in 19% under NHRI's own base price.
items.detail: Tender 113B0C0270 was for 150 next-generation genomes. Budget was NT$2.25M and the base price NT$1.82M. It was awarded on 29 Oct 2024 to Taiwan Genome Alliance at NT$1.47M (NT$9,800 per genome). The rival, Genomics BioSci, bid NT$1.90M (NT$12,665). The research institute captured a price 23% below the NT$12,800 hospital rate and 19% below its own base price. This happened through a two-bidder price fight after NHRI stopped buying NovaSeq S4 kits for its in-house fleet.

The rival 基龍米克斯 bid NT$1,899,750 and was not the lowest bid. Two caveats: (1) the hospital comparison is across periods (the NHRI award is Oct 2024, the hospital awards are 2025–26) and across scope (the hospital awards include clinical work and blood draw); (2) the price fight is between two Illumina-based service vendors, so the discount comes out of vendor mar

items.label: 2B
items.claim: Taiwanese research buyers write Illumina into tender qualifications: a government livestock institute requires bidders to own a NovaSeq X Plus in Taiwan, which excludes rival platforms by design.
items.detail: The Livestock Research Institute (Ministry of Agriculture) required proof of purchase of an 'Illumina NovaSeq X Plus' in Taiwan, plus serial number and maintenance reports, in tender 114B006-2 (2025) and tender 115B005-2 (Feb 2026). The 2025 award drew three bidders and went to KIMFOREST at NT$1,595,880, 28% below the NT$2.22M base price. The 2026 award drew a single bidder and went at NT$2,499,500 against a NT$2.5M base price. Competition among Illumina-X service vendors pushes price down, but Roche, Element and Ultima are excluded from these research tenders.
items.quote: 位於臺灣地區Illumina NovaSeq X Plus定序設備購買證明
items.why_new: This is the first evidence of tender specs that lock in the Illumina platform at research buyers.
items.verify_note: Verified for 115B005-2: the tender is a chicken (紅羽土雞) NGS service. Budget NT$2.6M, base NT$2.5M, one bidder, KIMFOREST at NT$2,499,500. The qualification clause requiring purchase proof for an X Plus located in Taiwan is quoted as stated. The 2025 award (NT$1,595,880, 28% under a NT$2.22M base, three bidders) was not re-checked. It is a small agricultural research buyer, so this is lock-in evidence, not a volume datapoint.

items.label: 2B
items.claim: Taipei Medical University's Sep 2026 research WGS tender required at least two Illumina high-throughput sequencers plus a PacBio Sequel IIe, again specifying Illumina into research outsourcing.
items.detail: Tender TMU115-029 (subsidized by the Ministry of Education with NT$3.37M) failed once for lack of bidders. It was then awarded on 24 Sep 2026 to the single bidder, Taiwan Genome Alliance, at NT$3,057,600, exactly the base price, against an original bid of NT$3,346,512. The vendor qualification read 'two (or more) Illumina high-throughput NGS instruments' and required MOHW LDT certification. The notice gives no sample count.

The clause requires two or more Illumina high-throughput sequencers. The page does not disclose the budget, so the NT$3.37M MoE subsidy and the 'original bid' figures could not be confirmed. There is no sample count, so no $/genome can be derived.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: Taipei VGH's two-year service budget for its Illumina high-throughput system rose 17.6% between the 2024 and 2026 tenders, so there is no sign of service discounting at this pathology lab.
items.detail: Contract 113A2019M (May 2024, single bidder Genetech) carried a NT$2.096M budget and was awarded at NT$1.89M for Oct 2024 to Oct 2026. The renewal tender 115A2A55M (5–6 Oct 2026, award pending) carries a NT$2.465M budget, 17.6% above the 2024 budget and 30% above the 2024 award. The instrument model is not named.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: Illumina instrument buys in Taiwan in 2025–26 went to its distributor as single bidders, at only 1–2% below budget, so these buyers show no competitive price tension.
items.detail: Four awards went to Genetech Biotech (均泰), each with one bidder: NTU Yunlin high-throughput sequencer at NT$5.05M vs a NT$5.35M budget (May 2025); NTU College of Life Science 'NGS upgrade' at NT$3.98M vs NT$4.70M (Apr 2025, restricted tender); Linkou Chang Gung 'ILLUMINA' NGS system at NT$2.245M vs NT$2.264M (Aug 2025); and the Veterinary Research Institute NGS instrument at NT$2.295M vs NT$2.35M (May 2026). The origin is mostly listed as Singapore, which suggests Illumina mid-throughput boxes. The vet institute's follow-on library kits and chips cost NT$1.246M (Oct 2025) and then NT$1.595M (Oct 2026), also from a single bidder.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: Taiwan's outsourced clinical WGS market is effectively a two-vendor contest (Genomics BioSci vs Taiwan Genome Alliance), and prices fell sharply once both bid.
items.detail: Across seven WGS service awards from 2023 to 2026, every winner was one of these two firms. Where both bid, the spread was 4–29% (NHRI 2024: 9,800 vs 12,665 per genome; Taipei VGH 2025: 12,800 vs ~13,980; Taichung 2025: 117.6M vs 122.7M). The 2023 single-bid award at NT$24,000 per genome was nearly halved once a second bidder appeared. Centogene APAC tried and was disqualified (Jan 2026). Genomics listed on Taiwan's Innovation Board in May 2026 and also runs an instrument-distribution business, so it may supply rival platforms (lead).
