The count reached 30,000 by Oct 2026, so the last 24 months averaged about 708 a month. At that pace, 100,000 babies would take about 8 more years. The 100,000 target in the brief belongs to the UK Generation Study, not GUARDIAN, as the probe found. The monthly rates are my arithmetic on dated release figures.
items.why_new: The enrollment rate is a new derivation from three dated data points. It also corrects the 100,000 GUARDIAN target.
items.verify_note: Pace arithmetic is right: (30,000−13,000)/24 ≈ 708 a month, so ~8 more years to reach 100K. The 30,000-by-Oct-2026 figure was not opened. Materiality: ~8.5K genomes/yr × ~100–125 Gb ≈ 1M Gb/yr, ~0.1% of the ~800M Gb/yr HT base. It confirms the known 'public programs are small' point with a new program.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: Parent uptake is high and the program is scaling, so newborn genomes could become a real clinical volume source if states fund them.
items.detail: 72.3% of approached families chose to enroll (the 2024 interim cohort was 72.0%, 4,000 of 5,555). 76% of babies have non-European ancestry. The panel has expanded to about 446 genes and over 460 conditions, up from 156 early-onset conditions at the start. The release says 8 infants with long QT syndrome have started beta-blockers. These are signs of clinical utility that could support later reimbursement. However, the program is research-funded and no payer or state mandate is stated.
items.source_name: GeneDx press release via Finviz; JAMA Oct 2024 via Business Wire
items.why_new: This gives a stable 72% uptake and the panel expansion, which are watch-outs for the WGS-volume pessimism.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: A cross-party Bundestag motion (Drucksache 21/3873) seeks NIPT monitoring and an expert panel, with results due by end-June 2027, a regulatory overhang on German NIPT volume.
items.detail: The hib report of 29 Jan 2026 says the motion is backed by CDU/CSU, SPD, Greens and Left. It cites BARMER data of nearly 50% of pregnant women using NIPT in 2024 versus 32% in 2023. It also says the false-positive rate in routine care is about 4x the theoretical rate and that invasive tests rose instead of falling. The bifg factsheet adds ~70% more positive-NIPT counselings than expected, and 48 of 224 positive cases had no follow-up testing, although 10 pregnancies were terminated in that group. The motion's own PDF text was not readable; the title is 'Kassenzulassung des nicht-invasiven Pränataltests – Monitoring der Konsequenzen und Einrichtung eines Gremiums'. The 2023 to 2024 step from 32% to ~50% is a hib/Bundestag figure; the factsheet's own 'average 50%' may not be the 2024 value, and the hib summary does not say whether the denominator is BARMER-only.
items.why_new: Adds a German political and regulatory risk to NIPT volume that is not in the known list, which covers only US/ACMG items.
items.verify_note: Checked against hib: cross-party backing, Barmer 32% (2023) → almost 50% (2024), false positives ~4x the theoretical rate, invasive tests up, results due end-June 2027. The overhang is speculative: a motion asking for monitoring, not a coverage cut. The embedded uptake data (+~56% users in one year) cuts against 'NIPT maturing' in Germany near term. Germany is Gb-immaterial either way (see derived item).

items.label: 1C
items.claim: German NIPT uptake of ~50% leaves headroom, and the age curves are still drifting up, so volume growth is not over.
items.detail: BARMER Q1 2024 data (Ärzteblatt Int. 2025) show 482 NIPTs per 1,000 pregnancies, with 784 per 1,000 receiving counseling, and 302 of the counseled (38%) had no NIPT. The factsheet says uptake in under-26s rose to ~25-30% and reached ~80% in the over-40s by 2025. Counseling reach of 50-75% by age and the 38% counseled-but-untested pool suggest further room. A monitoring rule or false-positive concerns could still slow it.
items.why_new: Quantifies German headroom (482 per 1,000 in Q1 2024) with a denominator, unlike the known list.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: Within the UC system, the same 25B lane is priced up to 24% higher at campuses that run their own X Plus than at the UCSF CAT lab, which now aggregates volume, so scale gets the lowest price.
items.detail: UC-internal 25B 300-cycle lane: UCSF CAT $2,551; Berkeley $2,600 (resold CAT, 150PE); UCSD IGM $2,800 (sheet dated 14 Oct 2025); UC Riverside IIGB $3,168 (FY24-25, effective 17 Apr 2025). Premium over CAT is +1.9%, +9.8% and +24.2% (3,168/2,551−1). The 10B 300-cycle lane is $1,439 at CAT vs $1,700 at UCSD (+18%) and $1,962 at UCR (+36%). Berkeley's July 2024 page listed no CAT-only sourcing, and its 2026 page says all lanes moved to CAT in summer 2026, so the aggregation trend is dated.
items.date: 2026-10-12 (page undated; Berkeley 1 Jun 2026; UCR 17 Apr 2025; UCSD Oct 2025)
items.source_name: UCSF CAT, UC Berkeley QB3, UCSD IGM PDF, UCR IIGB rate pages
items.quote: UCB does not have a NovaSeq X, all lanes are sent to the UCSF CAT Lab
items.why_new: Known items give CAT and Berkeley prices separately; this adds the cross-campus UC spread, including UCR and the 10B tier, with the arithmetic.
items.verify_note: Correction: the UCSD $2,800 figure is the Oct 2025 sheet. The current UCSD sheet (verified image) is $2,550 for the 25B-300, effectively equal to CAT's $2,551. The 'up to +24%' dispersion now rests only on UCR's FY24-25 rate (Apr 2025), which is stale. Core rates mix overhead and subsidy, so this is evidence of within-UC aggregation, not a direct read of Illumina's large-account discounts.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: UCR's 2025 internal lane prices equal UCLA's 2023-24 internal prices to the dollar, so some UC cores pass Illumina list pricing through and are not repricing downward.
items.detail: UCR 25B-300 internal $3,168 and 10B-100 internal $1,556 (Apr 2025) match UCLA TCGB's Mar 2024 internal sheet ($3,168 and $1,556). Neither fell between 2024 and 2025. Neither core appears to have matched CAT, which is now $2,551 and $1,105. The identical prices suggest a shared UC rate formula carried forward. UCR's page lists only X Plus and no 6000.
items.source_name: UCR IIGB rate schedule; UCLA TCGB 12 Mar 2024 rates PDF (search result)
items.why_new: No earlier UC price comparison between UCR and UCLA, and no UCR data.
items.verify_note: Misread. $3,168 per lane is ~1.54x Illumina's per-lane list ($16,480/8 = $2,060), so it is not list 'passed through'; it is list plus core overhead. It is also a stale Apr 2025 rate matched to a Mar 2024 UCLA sheet, not evidence that current prices are not falling. The fresh UC datapoints (CAT, UCSD 2026) both fell.

items.label: 2A
items.claim: UC research cores are cutting prices unevenly and slowly, and several are not matching the cheapest UC lane, so these are not 'insane discount' price takers.
items.detail: UCSD IGM's sheet (created 14 Oct 2025) holds 25B-300 at $2,800 UC and $3,836 outside. At CAT the 25B-300 outside price is $3,393 (+33%), so UCSD outside is 13% higher. UCR's 2025 external-educational price is $4,080 (+20% vs CAT $3,393). The UCSD PDF carries the note 'Some rates pending committee approval', and no FY27 sheet was found for UCSD, UCR, UC Davis or UCI.
items.quote: Some rates pending committee approval.
items.why_new: Adds UCSD's full ladder (1.5B/10B/25B across cycles) and the PDF creation date; F822 only mentions the $2,800 figure.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: CAT's published non-UC markups of +33% (academic) and +46.3% (for-profit) over the UC rate show how much discount tiering is policy and how much the UC account gets.
items.detail: On the CAT page the 25B-300 non-UC academic price is $3,393 and for-profit $3,732, versus $2,551 UC. UC users therefore pay 25% less than non-UC academic users (1−2,551/3,393). The older CAT sheet's markups were about +26% (non-profit, $3,591 vs $2,850) and +56% (for-profit, $4,448). The tiering is formula-based, and the for-profit uplift fell from ~56% to 46.3%.
items.quote: Rates are higher for non-UC academic/non-profit groups (+33%)
items.why_new: F823 gives the CAT premium change; this adds the for-profit uplift and the older-sheet markups.

items.label: 2B
items.claim: UC Davis DNA Technologies Core presents Element AVITI alongside Illumina in its short-read offering.
items.detail: A search snippet of the dnatech.ucdavis.edu core description lists Illumina and Element AVITI short-read plus PacBio and nanopore long-read, with no NovaSeq X mention. The page itself returned HTTP 403, so this is search-snippet level and the date is unknown. UC Davis's older rate table was HiSeq 4000 era (UC $1,127 per single-read lane).
items.source_name: UC Davis DNA Technologies Core (search snippet)
items.why_new: No UC Davis data in the known list.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: Berkeley's page keeps NextSeq 2000 and MiSeq i100 listings next to X resale and does not list a CAT price for its own use, so mid-throughput work stays in-house while HT is aggregated.
items.detail: Berkeley UC rates: NextSeq 2000 P2 300-cycle $2,730, P3 100-cycle $2,775, P4 100-cycle $2,600; MiSeq i100 25M 300-cycle $1,150. NovaSeq X 25B 150PE is $2,600. Per-lane, a NextSeq P4 100-cycle costs the same as an X 25B 150PE lane ($2,600), though the X gives far more output. The page says rates 'should be stable for 2026' and change annually on 1 July.
items.quote: should be stable for 2026
items.why_new: Adds the NextSeq and MiSeq price rows and the 'stable for 2026' statement.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: Denmark's national clinical WGS program ran far below its 60,000-genome target, which suggests slow ramp even in a single-payer system.
items.detail: A Novo Nordisk Foundation grant of ~DKK 1bn funded sequencing of up to 60,000 genomes in 2022-2024. By May 2022 NGC had delivered WGS to only 1,500 patients, and by Jul 2023 about 14,500 genomes were in the database, with interpreter shortages cited as the bottleneck. A Region Syddanmark paper (seen as a search snippet only, not opened) expected ~11,800 sequencings in 2022-24 against an estimate of ~14,300. These are 2022-23 data, and the final 2024 and 2025 counts were not found.
items.source_name: Ingeniøren (ing.dk), plus search snippet from Region Syddanmark agendas
items.quote: 20.000 danskere skal helgenom-sekventeres om året
items.why_new: The known list has no Danish national WGS counts or target-vs-actual data, but the data is old (2022-23) and the final 2025 count is missing.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: Denmark moved WGS sequencing to the regions from mid-2024 with small regional budgets, which suggests modest Gb demand per region.
items.detail: From mid-2024 the regions took over sequencing and data processing from NGC, and NGC kept only reporting and data sharing. Region Syddanmark's 2025 budget (search snippet, not opened) showed ~DKK 30M a year of operating cost for handling and interpretation. It also approved ~DKK 21.6M for sequencing equipment at Odense and Lillebælt, with the platform unknown. The plan was ~20,000 genomes a year nationally from 2024, but no actual figure was found.
items.why_new: The known list has no Danish regional sequencing budgets or sequencer procurement.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: Adaptive's clonoSEQ, a leading MRD franchise, is only ~36K tests a quarter, too small to move Illumina consumables even at +43% growth.
items.detail: Adaptive delivered 36,111 clonoSEQ tests in Q2'26, up 43% y/y and 11% q/q. The full-year clinical volume guide was raised to 38-40% from 35%, which implies a slowdown from the 43% growth in H1. clonoSEQ is a targeted amplicon assay. If it uses about 0.2-1 Gb per test (my estimate, not disclosed), the quarter is roughly 7-36 Gb-thousands (7-36 Tb), under 1% of Illumina's HT base of ~800M Gb per quarter. Fast MRD test growth therefore barely changes Illumina Gb.
items.source_name: Adaptive Q2'26 press release (via BioSpace / search snippet)
items.why_new: The known list has Adaptive MRD +43% and the gross margin only; the test count (36,111), the guide raise to 38-40% and the Gb sizing are new.
items.verify_note: Verified: 36,111 clonoSEQ tests in Q2'26, +43% y/y (the +43% is already known). The release gives no q/q figure or volume guide. It raised MRD revenue guidance to $268–278M from $260–270M, so the '38–40% volume guide' is unverified. Materiality error: the ~800M Gb HT base is annual (see D069), not quarterly. 36K tests × 0.2–1 Gb ≈ 7–36K Gb/qtr ≈ 29–144K Gb/yr ≈ 0.004–0.02% of HT Gb. The conclusion holds and is stronger.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: German NIPT uptake is already about 80% among women over 40 and about half among those under 36, so the high-intensity cohorts are near saturation and future growth must come from the young cohort.
items.detail: A search-result summary of the bifg/BARMER paper in Gynäkologische Praxis 2026 (snippet, I could not render the PDF) gives 2025 uptake of about one in three pregnant women under 26, about one in two under 36, and about 80% over 40, with rates rising in all age groups. The Drucksache-era figures were about 25% for under-26s and 75% for over-40s in 2024. The gains are one-third of a point to five points a year in the oldest groups, so they are nearing a ceiling. Growth now depends on lower-risk, lower-depth young women.
items.source_name: bifg / BARMER, Gynäkologische Praxis 2026 (via search summary)
items.why_new: The known list has no age-specific German uptake, and these figures show the 40+ cohort is near its ceiling.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: The Bundestag motion and the BARMER analysis create a policy overhang: the false-positive rate is reportedly four times what is expected, invasive tests have risen, and monitoring is due by end-June 2027.
items.detail: The cross-party motion (CDU/CSU, SPD, Greens, Left) asks for monitoring of the G-BA coverage decision, results to the Bundestag by 30 Jun 2027, and an interdisciplinary expert panel. It cites a false-positive rate in routine care about 4x the theoretical rate, invasive tests rising by 0.1–2.5 per 1,000 pregnancies instead of falling, and women skipping first-trimester screening after a negative NIPT. These findings could be used to tighten the G-BA indication, which would cap German NIPT volume after 2027. Germany's Gb exposure is small, but the same narrative could spread to other European payers.
items.source_name: Bundestag Drucksache 21/3873 (via hib and search summary)
items.why_new: It adds the specific cited harms (4x false positives, higher invasive-test counts) and the three asks; the known list only has the monitoring deadline.
items.verify_note: Duplicate of F1019 (same Drucksache 21/3873 and hib report). The '0.1–2.5 per 1,000' invasive-test range and the claim that the narrative would spread to other European payers are unverified or speculative.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: NIPT in Germany has become de facto screening although the G-BA did not set it up as routine care, which makes the indication a target for restriction.
items.detail: The bifg study authors say that after coverage began on 1 Jul 2022, NIPT became a screening test although it is not part of routine care. A search summary of the bifg analysis (766,245 pregnancies, 30,365 with a billed NIPT, data to about Mar 2024) says the study shows no fall in invasive tests. Caritas/SkF has also asked for scientific monitoring. Regulatory pressure on indication and uptake is therefore building in the country with the largest statutory insurer population.
items.why_new: It adds third-party advocacy pressure and the study sample sizes behind the policy risk.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: EPFL's sequencing core reports repeated NovaSeq price cuts through Sep 2026, with its Oct 2023 10B-300 run list price as a baseline.
items.detail: The Oct 2023 internal list priced a 300-cycle, 10,000M-read run at CHF 18,590 (search snippet). The facility's news says NovaSeq prices fell 'strongly' in Oct 2025 and again in Mar 2026 (10B-300 runs), and the Sep 2026 list adds a 'continued price decrease'. The current CHF figure was not read, so the size of the cut is unquantified. The AVITI to AVITI24 upgrade (Nov 2025) added up to 50% output at no price increase, which is a falling AVITI $/Gb.
items.source_name: EPFL Gene Expression Core Facility (news and price lists)
items.quote: continued price decrease across our services
items.why_new: It adds the Oct 2023 baseline price of CHF 18,590 and the AVITI24 +50% output at flat price, but the current prices are unread, so this is only a partial update.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: Adaptive's total gross margin rose to about 71.8% from about 69.4% in Q2'26, so a large MRD customer is capturing cost deflation rather than passing it to Illumina's revenue.
items.detail: From the filing figures, cost of revenue was 28.2% of revenue ($20.165M/$71.553M) in Q2'26 against 30.6% ($17.999M/$58.879M) in Q2'25. For six months it was 27.3% ($38.873M/$142.427M) against 31.4% ($34.978M/$111.322M). That is a 4.1-point improvement in H1 while tests grew about 40%+. The saving comes from the X move, which fits larger customers extracting the 6000-to-X price step.
items.why_new: Adds the H1 cost-of-revenue ratio series (31.4% to 27.3%), not just the known sequencing gross margin of 72% vs 64%.

items.label: 2B
items.claim: Adaptive is winding down its research-use-only pharma services business, which removes a small research sequencing volume source.
items.detail: CEO Robins said the business 'operated around break even' and was not central to Immune Medicine. Immune Medicine revenue was $5.4M against $8.9M (-40%), or +8% excluding the Genentech agreement. The business is tiny, so the effect on Illumina research consumables is negligible, but it is another research-side service line being cut.
items.quote: we've decided to wind down our research use only pharma services business
items.why_new: The wind-down is not in the known list.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: The regulated NovaSeq 6000Dx fleet is small, about 80 units worldwide in the Sep 2024 recall, with no recall record for a NovaSeq X Dx.
items.detail: openFDA recall res_event 99585 (Z-0068-2027, initiated 2024-09-17, still open) lists quantity 80 for NovaSeq 6000Dx with DRAGEN Server plus DRAGEN Server for NextSeq 550Dx. Distribution is worldwide, including the US and about 16 countries. No 2025-26 6000Dx or X Dx recall exists, so there is no sign the regulated 6000Dx fleet is growing and no evidence of a regulated X. The 80 is small next to ~1,360 6000s at end-FY25 and 799 NextSeq550Dx in 2022. The regulated Dx tail is therefore tiny and does not explain much of the 17% of Gb still on the 6000.
items.why_new: It adds the quantity context (80 mixed Dx units vs the Dx fleets of 674-1,067 older units) and confirms no 2025-26 6000Dx or X Dx recall.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: UCSD IGM cut its NovaSeq X Plus 25B per-lane rates 9% to 23% year over year, against list prices that were flat or rising.
items.detail: The current (2026, likely FY27, pending committee approval) UC internal rate is $1,465 for a 25B 100-cycle lane and $2,550 for a 300-cycle lane, versus $1,900 and $2,800 on the Oct 2025 sheet. That is -22.9% and -8.9%. Outside rates fell by the same percentages, from $2,603 to $2,007 (100-cycle) and from $3,836 to $3,493 (300-cycle). A 200-cycle 25B lane is newly listed at $2,320 UC / $3,178 outside. On spec output of ~2.5-3.0B reads per lane, the 300-cycle UC lane is roughly $2.5/Gb or less. Core-level prices in the known set barely moved, so this is a fresh y/y datapoint. The 2025 numbers come from a search-result snippet of the 2025 PDF, not an opened table.
items.source_name: UCSD IGM Genomics Center rate sheet 2026 vs Oct 2025 (snippet)
items.quote: Some rates pending committee approval.
items.why_new: UCSD IGM is not in the used core list, and this is a y/y 25B lane cut of 9-23% rather than a one-off price.
items.verify_note: Verified. Current sheet (image): 25B-100 $1,465/$2,007, 25B-300 $2,550/$3,493, 10B-300 $1,400/$1,918, 'some rates pending committee approval'. The 2025 'New IDC' PDF (search) shows 25B-300 $2,800/$3,836 and 10B-300 $1,700/$2,329. So the 25B-300 fell −8.9%, the 25B-100 −22.9%, and the 10B-300 −17.6%. $/Gb correction: $2,550 over ~750–975 Gb per lane is ~$2.6–3.4/Gb, not '≤$2.5'. 'List flat or rising': 25B-300 list +3% (D080).

items.label: 1B
items.claim: UCSD IGM prices the 10B at $1,100-1,400 and the 25B at $1,465-2,550 per UC lane, so the 25B-to-10B step is small for short reads.
items.detail: The current UC internal lane rates are: 1.5B $2,650 / $2,950 / $3,150 (100/200/300 cycles); 10B $1,100 / $1,325 / $1,400; 25B $1,465 / $2,320 / $2,550. Outside rates are 1.5B $3,631 / $4,041 / $4,316; 10B $1,507 / $1,815 / $1,918; 25B $2,007 / $3,178 / $3,493. A combo fee of $225 UC / $308 outside applies. The 25B 100-cycle lane costs only 33% more than the 10B lane. The sheet lists no NovaSeq 6000, AVITI or Ultima line. The 10B and 25B yield differences by cycle count would be needed to turn these into $/Gb.
items.why_new: This gives a full UCSD 1.5B/10B/25B grid for UC and outside users; the known list has none of these UCSD figures.
items.verify_note: Misread. Per lane the 25B-100 is 33% dearer, but it carries ~2.5x the reads of a 10B lane (2.5B vs 1.0B), so per read the 25B is ~47% cheaper at 100 cycles ($0.586 vs $1.10/M), 30% at 200 and 27% at 300. The step is large, not small. That is already known (F906, known 10B→25B −24–37%). The price ladder is used in the derived items.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: Baylor's core internal NovaSeq X lane price appears to have drifted down across 2025 lists, while the 6000 S4 sat at $4,800.
items.detail: Search-result snippets, not verified in the files, show an X lane (PE150, 1.2B reads) at $1,650 in the Mar 2025 list and $1,550 in the Jun 2025 list, then $1,600-$1,650 in the Feb 2026 list. The 6000 S4 lane was $4,800 in the Dec 2024 and Feb 2025 lists. The flow cell size (10B vs 25B) and user category are unconfirmed. The tables need extraction before any per-Gb change is quoted.
items.source_name: Baylor College of Medicine GARP core price lists (search snippet)
items.why_new: Baylor GARP is not among the core rate cards already used, but the figures are snippet-level and unlabelled.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: MIT's core raised NovaSeq 6000 prices about 8% from FY2023 to FY2025 while it listed X flow cells at much lower $/read; the 6000 premium persists.
items.detail: S4 300nt lane was $5,000 (core lab) in the 7/1/2022 update and $5,400 in the 7/1/2024 update, unchanged through Apr 2025; S2 300nt rose from $12,500 to $13,500 (+8%). In Jan 2025 the same core listed X 25B 300nt at $3,650 for 3B reads against S4 at $5,400 for about 2B, about 55% lower per read. This is a core's posted price, not a transaction price from Illumina.
items.why_new: MIT BioMicro Center is not among the core rate cards already used; it gives a dated 6000 vs X price pair.
items.verify_note: Verified on the pages. S4 300nt lane was $5,000 (FY2022 sheet, edited 16 Jun 2021), then $5,400 (FY2025b, 24 Jan 2025, and the main page, 15 Apr 2025): +8% over about 4 years, not FY23→FY25. S2 300nt was $12,600, not $12,500, so the rise is +7.1%. The X 25B 300nt is $3,650 for 3B reads, labelled 'per flowcell' but in practice per lane, vs S4 $5,400 for 2B reads. Per read that is $1.22M vs $2.70M, 55% lower, as stated. The X has no non-MIT rate, and since Apr 2025 it is priced only in iLabs at a

items.label: 2A
items.claim: The MIT core held AVITI prices flat across 2024-25 and priced the AVITI 75PE lane at $1,000 for about 400M reads, about $2.50 per M reads.
items.detail: AVITI 150PE lane (~400M reads) is $1,375 (about $3.44 per M reads) on all three snapshots (Jun 2024, Jan 2025, Apr 2025). The X 25B 300nt is $3,650 for 3B reads (about $1.22 per M reads). The core thus kept a stable low-end AVITI price while the X gave a lower $/read at the high end.
items.why_new: Adds MIT AVITI vs X per-read price comparison; not in the known core list.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: At 100 cycles, IGM's 25B lane per-read price fell from about 61% to about 53% of the 10B's, so the big flow cell is being priced more aggressively on short reads.
items.detail: Per million reads, assuming nominal 1.25B reads per 10B lane and 3.125B per 25B lane (my assumption from Illumina's specs). At 100 cycles in 2025: 10B $1,250/1,250 = $1.00 and 25B $1,900/3,125 = $0.61, a ratio of 0.61. At 100 cycles in 2026: 10B $1,100 → $0.88 and 25B $1,465 → $0.47, a ratio of 0.53. The 25B-100 lane fell 22.9% ($1,900 → $1,465). At 300 cycles the ratio instead rose, from 0.66 (1,700/1,250 vs 2,800/3,125) to 0.73 (1,400 vs 2,550), so the pattern is uneven and not a uniform deepening.
items.why_new: This is a derived per-read tier ratio for IGM at 100 vs 300 cycles. Existing items cover Bauer (D085, F906) and not IGM.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: A pediatric hospital (OPBG, Rome) justified a sole-source buy of NovaSeq 6000 S1/S2/S4 v1.5 reagents in 2025 because its installed 6000 only accepts Illumina kits.
items.detail: A search-result snippet (not opened in full) describes an OPBG infungibilità report dated 6 May 2025. It covers Illumina Italy NovaSeq 6000 S1, S2 and S4 v1.5 200-cycle kits and the Stranded Total RNA Prep Ribo-Zero Plus. It says the 6000 already on site is not compatible with other makers' reagents. This is one small site, with no prices or quantities, and it shows a 6000 kit buy continuing in 2025 rather than a move to the X. It is weak anecdotal support for the point that some 6000 volume stays on the 6000.
items.source_name: Ospedale Pediatrico Bambino Gesù, infungibilità report (search snippet)
items.why_new: The known list has no OPBG or Italian hospital sole-source buy of 6000 v1.5 kits. The URL-to-snippet mapping is uncertain.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: At both UC NovaSeq X sites, the 10B 300-cycle lane was cut ~17% in the latest price cycle, about twice the 25B cut, so price deflation is now moving down to the smaller flow cells.
items.detail: UCSD IGM's 10B-300 UC lane went $1,700 (2025 'New IDC' sheet) → $1,400 (2026 sheet), −17.6%, with outside rates down the same. Its 25B-300 went $2,800 → $2,550 (−8.9%). UCSF CAT's 10B-300 went $1,724 → $1,439 (−16.5%) vs 25B-300 $2,850 → $2,551 (−10.5%). Per read (2.5B vs 1.0B reads per lane), the 25B's discount to the 10B at 300 cycles narrowed from ~34% to ~27% (UCSD) and from ~34% to ~29% (CAT). Smaller users therefore got the bigger cut, which fits Illumina's known 'harmonised cost per read' across 5B/10B/25B. Harvard's Bauer core instead narrowed the gap by raising the 25B (D085).
items.source_name: UCSD IGM rate sheets 2025/2026; UCSF CAT current and node/706 pages
items.quote: Some rates pending committee approval.
items.why_new: The known set has the 25B-step and Bauer data. This adds a two-site y/y 10B-lane cut and shows the 10B/25B per-read gap closing from the 10B side.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: UC core 25B-300 lane rates fell from ~1.40x to ~1.24x Illumina's per-lane list in about a year, so either the UC system's net reagent price fell or cores absorbed overhead, while list rose ~3%.
items.detail: In 2024–25, CAT's $2,850 and UCSD's $2,800 lanes were ~1.40–1.43x the per-lane list of $16,000/8 = $2,000. In 2026, CAT ($2,551) and UCSD ($2,550) are ~1.24x the Jan 2025 list of $16,480/8 = $2,060, a ~12–13% fall in the core-to-list ratio. The two sites now match to within $1, which suggests a common input cost under the UC systemwide Illumina sourcing agreement (F820). It does not separate a net-price cut from an overhead change; UC rates include recharge and subsidy policy.
items.source_name: UCSF CAT, UCSD IGM rate sheets; Illumina 25B-300 list (D080)
items.why_new: First cross-site comparison of core rates to list over time inside one purchasing consortium; known items give single-core levels only.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: European NIPT is still growing through uptake (Netherlands +8.8%, Germany ~32%→50% of pregnancies), but the extra tests add only ~0.02–0.04% to Illumina's annual HT Gb, so NIPT cannot be a volume lever.
items.detail: Dutch tests rose 115,828 → 126,023 in 2024 (~+10K) with flat pregnancies and uptake at 73.5%, leaving at most ~36% more. German Barmer data show NIPT use going from ~32% (2023) to almost 50% (2024). On ~680K German births (our approximation), that is ~+120K tests. At ~1–2 Gb per NIPT (known), the combined ~130K extra tests are ~0.13–0.26M Gb/yr, or ~0.02–0.03% of the ~800M Gb/yr HT base. The growth itself cuts against 'maturing' in these markets, but uptake ceilings (NL) and a German policy review due June 2027 cap it.
items.source_name: RIVM/IQ Health monitor 2024; Kamerstuk 29323 nr. 189; Bundestag hib 76/2026
items.why_new: Known NIPT evidence is US/Taiwan. This sizes European uptake-driven growth against Illumina Gb.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: Even the fastest-growing named MRD and newborn-genome programs add negligible Gb: clonoSEQ (~0.004–0.02%) and GUARDIAN (~0.1%) of Illumina's annual HT Gb.
items.detail: clonoSEQ ran 36,111 tests in Q2'26 (+43% y/y). At ~0.2–1 Gb per amplicon test (estimate) that is ~29–144K Gb/yr, while Adaptive is still mid-move to the X Plus through ~2027 (F840), which also lowers Illumina $/Gb. GUARDIAN adds ~8.5K genomes/yr (~708 a month), or ~1M Gb/yr at ~100–125 Gb each. Both together are well under 0.2% of ~800M Gb/yr HT.
items.why_new: Combines the clonoSEQ count and GUARDIAN pace into Gb shares. Known items give only growth rates and other programs (NHS, Generation Study).

items.label: 1A
items.claim: In the FY2025 and main-page sheets MIT still quoted the full 6000 ladder in-house, while NovaSeq X work was pushed to a sister facility with prices only in a login-gated system.
items.detail: The main page (edited 15 Apr 2025) lists 6000 SP, S1, S2 and S4 rows. For NovaSeq X (10B and 25B, 300nt and 100nt) it says 'pricing in ilabs' and that sequencing is done at a sister shared resource. The 7/1/2024 FY2025 page has no X rows at all. So the 6000 remained this core's own high-throughput product through Apr 2025 and the X was outsourced, which supports a tail that stays on the 6000 at institutions without their own X. S1 and S2 flow cells are marked 'minimal inventory maintained', so the ladder is thinning to S4 and SP.
items.quote: pricing in ilabs
items.why_new: Adds the in-house-6000 vs outsourced-X structure and the thinning inventory notes, which earlier MIT items do not state.

items.label: 2B
items.claim: At MIT's core AVITI is not cheaper per Gb than the 6000 S4 lane, which cuts against the idea that Element undercuts Illumina on price in research.
items.detail: AVITI 150PE full flowcell (~800M reads, 2×150) is $2,650 core-lab, or about $11.0/Gb on 240 Gb. The one-lane 150PE price is $1,375 for ~400M reads, about $11.5/Gb. The 6000 S4 300nt lane is $5,400 for 2B reads (the page's read count; about 600 Gb), or about $9.0/Gb. AVITI is therefore ~22–28% more expensive per Gb. It is cheaper only per run and per read at short lengths: 75PE one lane is $1,000/400M reads = $2.50 per M reads, vs S4 $5,400/2,000M = $2.70 per M reads.
items.why_new: Known items quote only the AVITI $2.50 per M reads; this adds the per-Gb comparison against the 6000 at the same core, which goes the other way. Per-Gb figures are my arithmetic on the page's read counts.
items.verify_note: Numbers verified (15 Apr 2025 page). AVITI 150PE full flowcell $2,650 for ~800M reads (~$11.0/Gb); one lane $1,375 for ~400M; S4 $5,400 for 2B reads (~$9.0/Gb). The 300PE row (~200M reads, 'per lane' vs 'full flowcell') is internally inconsistent. This predates Element's Sep 2025 +50% output upgrade and the Cloudbreak price resets, and UMGC now charges ~$2.6/Gb, so it is stale for 2026. Northwestern's high core AVITI pricing is already known.

items.label: 2A
items.claim: MIT's research sequencing prices were raised across platforms between 2021 and 2025, not discounted, which does not fit research buyers extracting deep price cuts at this core.
items.detail: Core-lab rates, 2021 to Apr 2025: NextSeq 500 91nt kit $2,270→$2,420 (2023)→$2,570 (+13.2%); 166nt $3,900→$4,125→$4,375 (+12.2%); 316nt $5,800→$6,270→$6,420 (+10.7%); MiSeq 70nt V2 $1,250→$1,320 (+5.6%); NovaSeq SP 100nt $3,365→$3,699 (+9.9%); '400M reads' $1,600→$1,760 (+10%). The non-MIT premium stayed constant at +40% over the core-lab rate (e.g. S4 $7,560 vs $5,400). This is one core, and these are internal service-recovery prices, not Illumina's net price.
items.source_name: OpenWetWare / MIT BioMicroCenter pricing (FY2022 sheet vs main)
items.why_new: Adds a multi-platform, multi-year core price series (NextSeq, MiSeq, SP, 400M) in which every Illumina product rose; earlier items cover only the 6000 S4.
items.verify_note: Verified: NextSeq 91nt $2,270→$2,570, 166nt $3,900→$4,375, 316nt $5,800→$6,420, MiSeq 70nt $1,250→$1,320, SP 100nt $3,365→$3,699 (16 Jun 2021 vs 15 Apr 2025). The '400M reads $1,600→$1,760' line was not verified. These are core service-recovery rates (labour and overhead), which say little about the net price Illumina gets from research buyers. That is similar to the known Harvard FY27 rises and the Arizona 'prices go up exclusively' comment.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: Illumina reagent-driven price inflation was passed through by this core on all Illumina platforms in 2021–25, with no sign of the net price falling at the NextSeq or NovaSeq mid-to-high throughput tier.
items.detail: The Feb 2023 step added about 8% to every NovaSeq line and then 6% more to NextSeq 500 (e.g. 91nt $2,420→$2,570, +6.2%, by Apr 2025). Flow cells that Illumina was expected to be discounting (SP, S1, S2, S4) were all higher in 2024–25 than in 2021. A core can only raise prices like this if its supplier cost rose or it is protecting margin. Either reading is the opposite of accelerating discounting, but the core's own reagent invoices are not shown.
items.why_new: Adds the NextSeq 500 and SP/S1/S2 increases and the 2021→2025 timing; the known list covers Illumina's list prices and X lane cuts at other cores.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: The MIT core dropped HiSeq 2000 reagents in 2023, an example of how quickly a core retires a legacy Illumina platform once the supplier ends it.
items.detail: The 2021 sheet showed HiSeq 2000 single-end 40nt at $1,200 per lane ('being retired'), unchanged through the Feb 2023 sheet. The Feb 2023 sheet states 'The HiSeq2000 reagents will no longer be available in 2023.' The Illumina 2020 NovaSeq-era HiSeq tail therefore ended at this core in 2023, about six years after the NovaSeq 6000 launch in Jan 2017. That is a core-level data point for tail length, not a volume figure.
items.quote: HiSeq2000 reagents will no longer be available in 2023
items.why_new: The known list has HiSeq precedent timelines from Illumina's own statements, not a core's dated retirement notice. Its relevance to 1C (volume) is indirect, and it fits 1A better.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: A ~2% y/y fall in the birth base is worth about 50K NIPT tests, which is too small to hit Illumina volume but is a steady drag on prenatal test counts.
items.detail: If the US NIPT pool is births × 70–80% (expert inputs, unverified) = 3.57M × 0.70–0.80 ≈ 2.5–2.85M deliveries. A −1.9% change is about 48–54K tests. At about 1–2 Gb per test that is about 0.05–0.11M Gb, which is about 0.01% of the ~800M Gb HT base (known estimate). The lead's extra ~1M non-delivery pregnancies is unverified and I did not verify it. With that figure the pool is ~3.5–3.85M, above the lead's 2.9–3.4M ceiling. So the ceiling calc depends on the unverified inputs.
items.source_name: CDC NCHS press release and quarterly dashboard
items.why_new: This gives a quantified NIPT test-pool decline from the Q2'26 rate and shows that the lead's 2.9–3.4M ceiling rests on unverified inputs.

items.label: 2B
items.claim: An academic buyer in Taiwan bought Element's AVITI24 directly, in a tender titled for AVITI24.
items.detail: Academia Sinica's tender BRCAS11347 (corrected award notices dated 2024-12-05 and 2024-12-06) went to Element Biosciences, Inc. for one AVITI24 spatial multi-omics sequencing platform. No value is disclosed. This is a single research-institution placement, and the platform is aimed at spatial work, not high-throughput consumables.
items.why_new: A named public-procurement award of an AVITI24 to an academic institution, not in the known lists.

items.label: 2A
items.claim: UMGC's AVITI price per billion reads fell about 63% in two fiscal years, with the UMN FY26 rate at $614 to $1,235 per billion reads.
items.detail: The UMGC AVITI sheet lists UMN-researcher cost per 1B reads for the 150-cycle kit at $1,668.58 (FY24), $1,131.36 (FY25) and $614.44 (FY26 'NOW'). For the 300-cycle kit the figures are $2,385.61, $1,417.33 and $689.73, and for the 600-cycle kit $3,293.84, $1,979.64 and $1,235.28. The 300-cycle kit fell 71% FY24 to FY26, and the 150-cycle kit fell 63%. At $690 per 1B reads, a 25B X Plus lane at about $2,300 to $2,900 for 2.8 to 3B reads works out to roughly $0.85 per M reads, against $0.69 per M reads for the AVITI 300-cycle. This is a read-based comparison and ignores read length, quality and run mix. The values come from a tool summary of the sheet, not a raw read.
items.source_name: UMGC (University of Minnesota Genomics Center) AVITI pricing Google Sheet
items.why_new: The exact FY24, FY25 and FY26 AVITI cost per 1B reads by kit are new. The known list only has the UMN-wide 62-71% drop claim and ~$2.6-3.6/Gb.
items.verify_note: Already known: 'UMN says AVITI costs fell 62–71% since FY24 to ~$2.6–3.6/Gb.' The sheet values themselves are verified (raw CSV: FY24/FY25/FY26 $1,668.58/$1,131.36/$614.44; $2,385.61/$1,417.33/$689.73; $3,293.84/$1,979.64/$1,235.28). The per-read comparison with the X 25B duplicates the known Broad Clinical Labs ~$0.85/M figure. It also maps poorly to 2A, since this is a rival's cost and not research buyers' price sensitivity.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: On 15 Sep 2025 UMGC said AVITI costs $100s to $1,000 less per billion reads than the cheapest Illumina platform, after a free 50% output upgrade.
items.detail: UMGC's 15 Sep 2025 note says an OS upgrade raised 300-cycle output from 250M to 375M (Low), 500M to 750M (Medium) and 1B to 1.5B (High) at unchanged prices. That is 33% cheaper per read than FY25. The note says AVITI saves 'several hundred to one thousand dollars per billion reads' versus the most affordable Illumina platform. It does not attribute any Illumina rate cut to competition. Separately, the Ultima UG 100 UMN price is $2,704 per wafer for 10-12B reads on the 10x promo, which is $500 off the standard rate; UMN's Ultima 10x promo is already known. That works out to about $0.23 to $0.27 per M reads. Page: genomics.umn.edu/news/aviti-upgrade-complete.
items.quote: several hundred to one thousand dollars per billion reads
items.why_new: This is a core that has deployed AVITI at scale and says in words that it is cheaper than Illumina's cheapest platform; the 33% free-output step and the dated, unchanged-price upgrade are new.
items.verify_note: Verified: dated 15 Sep 2025; 300-cycle output went 250M→375M, 500M→750M and 1B→1.5B, and 150-cycle output also rose 50%, with 'AVITI pricing remains the same.' The quote is exact. The AVITI-vs-Illumina saving is the core's own claim, without the working shown. UMN's Ultima promo and the AVITI cost fall are already known, so what is new is the mechanism: a free output upgrade cut $/read 33% with no price action. The UG100 $2,704 vs $3,204 standard figure was not independently checked.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: Illumina has shipped only one RUO NovaSeq 6000 control-software release in the 35 months since Nov 2023 (v1.8.2, Aug 2025), a slow cadence that fits a tail on maintenance, not growth.
items.detail: The 6000 downloads page lists v1.8.0 (Jul 21 2022), v1.8.1 (Nov 6 2023) and v1.8.2 (Aug 25 2025). Gaps are 15.5 months and 21.5 months, and nothing has appeared in the 13+ months to 12 Oct 2026. The page carries no end-of-support language and no new-kit or new-flow-cell entries. Earlier gaps were shorter: v1.7.5 (Apr 14 2021) to v1.8.0 was 15 months, and v1.5 (Oct 2018) to v1.6 (Feb 2019) was 3 months.
items.why_new: Gives dated version cadence for the RUO 6000 software; the exclusion list has only product, retirement and 6000Dx pages.
items.verify_note: Release dates verified: v1.5 29 Oct 2018, v1.6 4 Feb 2019, v1.7.5 14 Apr 2021, v1.8.0 21 Jul 2022, v1.8.1 6 Nov 2023, v1.8.2 25 Aug 2025. The page has no end-of-support language. A slow cadence fits a platform in maintenance mode, but it is equally consistent with management's 'stays for years' view. It says nothing about conversion pace.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: The NovaSeq X control software is on a much faster release cadence, and the 5B and 1.5B-600-cycle flow cells shipped only on the X.
items.detail: X Series suite releases: v1.1.0 (Jun 27 2023), v1.2.0 (Nov 2 2023), v1.2.2 (May 13 2024), v1.3.0 (Dec 2 2024), v1.3.1 (Jun 23 2025), v1.4.0 (page date Jul 28 2026, while search snippets show release notes effective 19 Mar 2026). That is 6 releases in about 37 months, roughly one every 6 months. The 6000 had 1 release over the same stretch (Jul 2023 to Aug 2026). Search snippets say v1.4.0 adds the 5B flow cell, a 1.5B 600-cycle option, staggered-start scheduling and automatic index detection. Nothing comparable is listed for the 6000, so engineering effort and new features sit on the X.
items.why_new: First dated software-cadence comparison of the 6000 vs the X; the 5B flow cell is known, but not that its software launched only on the X.
items.verify_note: Not independently verified. The v1.4.0 date conflicts (page date 28 Jul 2026 vs release-note snippets of 19 Mar 2026). The 5B flow cell is already known (Jul 2026). Engineering effort concentrated on the X is expected and only indirectly bears on whether the tail converts. Best read together with F1053.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: The Clarity LIMS integration for the 6000 stopped at NVCS v1.8.0 compatibility and gained no new reagent or flow-cell support after the v1.5-reagent update.
items.detail: v3.5.1 (the page gives no date) is compatible with NVCS v1.8.0 and only fixes the flow-cell barcode validation and two CVEs, with 'Known issues: None'. v3.7.0 (listed as July 2024, updated July 2025) moves some properties into System Settings for Clarity v6.3 and fixes a DoS issue (CVE-2024-30172). The v3.2.1 page covers SP/S1/S2/S4 only and says nothing about the X or end of support. The 6000Dx integration v1.3.0 was last updated July 2025. The Clarity LIMS revision log lists a stream of X Series integration updates in 2024–26, including v1.4.0 in Apr 2026 and BioInsight subscription changes in Aug 2026. The 6000 integration had only maintenance entries.
items.source_name: Illumina Clarity LIMS help, revision history
items.quote: Release notes updated
items.why_new: Dated LIMS integration history for the 6000 vs the X; none of this is in the known list.
items.verify_note: Adds nothing beyond F1053/F1054. Maintenance of LIMS integrations does not bear on mix shift or tail persistence, and the v3.5.1 entry is undated.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: The 6000's newest RUO software (v1.8.2, Aug 25 2025) has no public customer-facing feature description, which suggests a maintenance release.
items.detail: The release notes PDF (doc 200072595_00, 'NovaSeq 6000 RUO v1.8.2') is hosted but could not be read: it is compressed binary and PDF rendering is unavailable here. Search finds notes only for v1.8.0 (RTA 3.4.4, vacuum-check features) and v1.8.1 (pressure-sensor logging). Both earlier releases were small feature or logging updates, and no new reagent kit was added after the v1.5 reagents in v1.7. The Aug 2025 release arrived 2 months after X v1.3.1 (Jun 2025). Illumina kept the 6000 supported after the tail moved to the X, and did not wind it down.
items.source_name: Illumina NovaSeq 6000 RUO v1.8.2 release notes (unread)
items.why_new: Identifies the v1.8.2 notes document and date; contents still need a PDF reader.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: Illumina is still investing in the 6000 platform software as of Aug 2025, and the Clarity LIMS integration has no end-of-support notice.
items.detail: v1.8.2 shipped Aug 25 2025, after the Q4'24 'stay and shrink' remarks, and the integration docs added 6000 release notes pages in Apr 2026. None of the pages checked carries end-of-support or last-version language. That supports a tail that will last years, which is consistent with management's 'permanent' claim and with a slower 6000 decline in 2027.
items.why_new: Adds software-support evidence for a durable tail and no end-of-life signal.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: UCLA's external per-lane price for the top Illumina high-throughput 300-cycle flow cell fell about 42% from Jul 2022 (NovaSeq S4) to Jul 2026 (NovaSeq X 25B).
items.detail: UCLA TCGB external rate for S4 300-cycle was $6,014.15 per lane (internal $5,356.20) effective 1 Jul 2022. The Jul 2026 external rate for X Plus 25B 300-cycle is $3,512.47, which is -42% per lane. If a 25B lane holds about 1,000 Gb and an S4 lane about 750 Gb (our spec assumption, not stated on the sheets), $/Gb falls from about $8.0 to $3.5 (-56%). A March 2024 sheet snippet shows the 25B-300 at $3,168/$3,538/$3,933 by column, so the 2024-to-2026 move is roughly flat to -11% and most of the decline is the platform change.
items.source_name: UCLA Technology Center for Genomics & Bioinformatics rate sheets
items.why_new: Gives the 2022 S4 baseline and the 2024 sheet figures; only the Jul 2026 25B $3.51 price was already known.

items.label: 2A
items.claim: A large UC core cut its internal/external pricing gap for high-throughput lanes to a single external-only table and dropped the 6000 lines by Jul 2026.
items.detail: The 2022 sheet had internal/JCCC/external columns with internal about 10-11% below external on S4 ($5,356 vs $6,014). The Jul 2026 page lists only X Plus external rates, and says rates apply to UCLA and other UC researchers, with a separate internal document. The 5B 300-cycle lane at $1,463 and 10B 300-cycle lane at $1,766 show a sub-$2K lane tier. This is consistent with research cores repricing downward as they move to the X.
items.why_new: Adds the 5B/10B/1.5B lane prices and the 2022 internal-vs-external spread; the 6000 removal is already known.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: Freenome, now public (FRNM), holds an Illumina supply agreement with no purchase commitment, no exclusivity, a no-increase price clause and MFN refunds, and it is also Roche's SBX evaluation partner.
items.detail: Supply Agreement dated 8 Jan 2024, term to 18 Aug 2033, filed as S-4 Ex. 10.24 (28 Apr 2026) and listed as Ex. 10.13 in the 24 Jul 2026 Super 8-K. It has no purchase commitments or exclusivity, and Freenome keeps a 'unilateral right to terminate'. Appendix A has the PPI-adjusted no-increase clause, the 43% per-Gb cut by 2025 vs the 2021 baseline, and MFN vs 'Equivalent' customers and GRAIL. Roche holds 17.4% of Freenome (18.69M shares incl. 6.46M from a convertible note) and has a License and Option Agreement dated 17 Nov 2025. Freenome can therefore shift volume to AXELIOS/SBX at no contractual cost, and Illumina has no volume floor. Both contract and ownership show a large oncology-diagnostics customer with the same leverage terms as the Caris Open Offer.
items.source_name: SEC EDGAR, Freenome S-4 Ex. 10.24 and Super 8-K 24 Jul 2026
items.quote: not contingent on any purchase commitments by Customer
items.why_new: Freenome as a third customer on the Open Offer-type template, and Roche's 17.4% stake, are not in the known list; the terms themselves repeat the known Caris template.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: Analysts and filings show Freenome only 'evaluating' SBX, and Leerink expects no near- to medium-term Illumina impact.
items.detail: Roche/Freenome deal (18 Nov 2025): over $200M potential, $75M equity, Roche exclusive ex-US kitted-test rights. Freenome will 'evaluate' SBX for future applications. Leerink says AXELIOS needs a few years of refinement for clinical use, and that rivals' assays are entrenched or FDA-approved on Illumina. The Super 8-K has no SBX or AXELIOS language, so there is no filed commitment to move off Illumina.
items.why_new: Freenome is listed as an AXELIOS buyer 'evaluating', but the deal structure and the analyst view of no near-term impact were not recorded.

items.label: 2A
items.claim: An Asian academic service core launched Illumina's PIPseq-based single-cell RNA service at 50% off for about 11 weeks.
items.detail: HKU CPOS ran a half-price promotion on its Illumina single-cell RNA-seq service (PIPseq chemistry) from 24 Nov 2025 to 13 Feb 2026, 'to celebrate the service launch'. The service is packaged: cell capture, library prep, sequencing and data analysis. The page does not state the regular price, the discounted price, or whether the 50% applies to the whole package. It is a single, small, Asia-based instance, so it is qualitative only, and it is unclear whether Illumina or the core funded the discount.
items.quote: to celebrate the service launch
items.why_new: Not in the exclusion list: no prior mention of launch discounts on Illumina's single-cell prep at academic cores.

items.label: 2B
items.claim: The UMGC sheet shows Element AVITI cost per 1B reads falling 46% (150-cycle) and 51% (300-cycle) from FY25 to FY26, steeper than the 32% and 41% cuts of FY24 to FY25.
items.detail: Cost per 1B reads for UMN users, 150/300/600-cycle: FY24 $1,668.58/$2,385.61/$3,293.84; FY25 $1,131.36/$1,417.33/$1,979.64; FY26 $614.44/$689.73/$1,235.28. FY24→FY25 is −32.2%/−40.6%/−39.9%. FY25→FY26 is −45.7%/−51.3%/−37.6%. FY24→FY26 is −63.2%/−71.1%/−62.5%. The known item gives only the aggregate −63%. This adds the per-kit split and shows the cuts are accelerating on the 150- and 300-cycle kits, the ones that compete with the NovaSeq X.
items.why_new: F1051 only had the aggregate -63% and the FY26 endpoints; the per-kit year-by-year path and the acceleration are new.
items.verify_note: Arithmetic verified against the raw sheet CSV. The FY25→FY26 'acceleration' is mostly the free +50% output upgrade (Sep 2025), not a faster price cut. The sheet gives no run size or tier, and the live page's High 300-cycle run works out to $783/B rather than $690 (F1067), so the sheet looks like a best-case basis. This is a core's posted rate for a rival, and the aggregate fall is already known.

items.label: 2A
items.claim: MIT BioMicro Center's AVITI lane prices are far below its NovaSeq 6000 per-lane prices, giving research users a cheap alternative.
items.detail: The mirrored rate card (last edited 15 Apr 2025) lists AVITI 150 PE full flowcell at $2,650 (core lab) and $3,710 (non-MIT) for ~800M reads. The NovaSeq 6000 S2 200nt flowcell is $12,960 core and $18,144 non-MIT. This is a dated snapshot, not FY2026. It shows that an MIT-type core already offers a low-cost non-Illumina option for mid-throughput work.
items.source_name: OpenWetWare mirror of MIT BioMicro Center rate card
items.why_new: MIT BMC AVITI-vs-6000 rates were not on the known core-card list, but the data is stale (Apr 2025) and may already be in F1040-F1046.

items.label: 2B
items.claim: Most of UMGC's FY26 AVITI cost drop beyond the Sept 2025 output upgrade must have come from a separate per-run price cut.
items.detail: The Sep 15 2025 news item says the +50% output upgrade at unchanged prices cuts cost per read by 33%. The sheet shows FY25→FY26 falling 45.7% (150-cycle) and 51.3% (300-cycle). Removing the upgrade effect leaves 0.543/0.667 = 0.814 (about −19%) and 0.487/0.667 = 0.730 (about −27%). That is an inference: the page says 'pricing stays the same', so the rest probably came from an earlier FY26 rate reset. A rival's per-run price was therefore also cut at a large academic core, as well as its output being raised.
items.why_new: F688 reports only the 33% upgrade effect; the residual 19-27% per-run cut is our derivation from the sheet.
items.verify_note: The arithmetic is right: 0.487/0.667 = 0.73 for the 300-cycle and 0.543/0.667 = 0.81 for the 150-cycle. But the sheet's basis is unclear, since it does not match the live page's per-run prices. The residual may be a UMGC rate or tier reset or a core subsidy, not an Element price cut. Downgrade 'must have come' to 'may have come.'

items.label: 2B
items.claim: At UMGC's own list prices an Ultima UG 100 wafer costs roughly 2.7-3.2x less per Gb than an Illumina 25B lane, and AVITI about 23% less per read.
items.detail: UG 100 full wafer (UMN, Savings) is $3,204 for the spec'd 2.5-3.0 Tb, or $1.07-$1.28/Gb. The AVITI High 300-cycle run (UMN Savings) is $1,175 for 1.5B reads (450 Gb), or $2.61/Gb. UMGC's own page gives 25B output of 750 Gb per lane. UCSF CAT's UC 25B-300 lane is $2,551 per lane (F822), which is about $3.40/Gb on that nominal output and $1,020 per B reads. Ultima is therefore about 2.7-3.2x cheaper per Gb. AVITI is about 23% cheaper per read ($783 vs $1,020 per B). Ultima's 10-12B read count and Tb yield are Ultima spec figures, not measured results.
items.source_name: UMGC UG 100, AVITI24 and NovaSeq X+ service pages
items.why_new: Earlier items compared reads or other cores; this is a same-page published $/Gb for Ultima and AVITI against Illumina spec output, with the arithmetic shown.
items.verify_note: This mixes UMGC output figures with a UCSF price. UCSF CAT's 25B-300 lane is better taken at ~975 Gb (3.25B clusters × 300; D080), or $2.62/Gb, which cuts the Ultima gap to ~2.0–2.4x (range 2.0–3.2x). That is in line with the known D076 (1.7–2.0x) and the Broad CL figures ($0.50 vs $0.85 per M reads). The AVITI per-read figure ($783 vs $1,020 per B) is verified from the UMGC page. It is mostly a restatement of a known magnitude.

items.label: 2B
items.claim: UMGC's published AVITI list price is higher per Gb than the headline 'cost per 1B reads' sheet suggests, so Element is not far below Illumina on a per-Gb basis for most run sizes.
items.detail: The sheet's FY26 300-cycle cost is $689.73 per 1B reads. The page's High run (1.5B) is $1,175, or $783 per B reads, about 14% above the sheet. The Medium run (750M, $1,002) is $1,336 per B and the Low run (375M, $993) is $2,648 per B. For 150-cycle, the sheet's $614 compares with $799 per B on the High run ($1,199 per 1.5B). The AVITI High 300-cycle run is $2.61/Gb for UMN users and $3.00/Gb external ($1,352/450 Gb). That is similar to Illumina 25B core prices of about $2.4-3.4/Gb. The 'cost drops of 62-71%' headline therefore applies to the best-case, fully loaded run.
items.source_name: UMGC AVITI24 service page vs pricing sheet
items.why_new: It reconciles the sheet to the actual per-run price list, which earlier items did not; it also shows the sheet and page disagree.
items.verify_note: Verified on the UMGC AVITI24 page (prices per lane, no FY label, © 2026). 300-cycle runs: High $1,175 for 1.5B ($783/B), Medium $1,002 for 750M ($1,336/B), Low $993 for 375M ($2,648/B). The 150-cycle High run is $1,199 ($799/B). External High 300c is $1,352, or $3.00/Gb. The ~$2.6/Gb figure is already known. What is new is the run-size dispersion: small AVITI runs cost 1.7–3.4x the High run per read. The comparison with the 25B is fair at full runs, but against a 10B-sized run AVITI is cheaper (

items.label: 2B
items.claim: UMGC runs five Element AVITI24 sequencers but offers no in-house high-throughput Illumina X, and says X+ access is cheaper and faster when outsourced.
items.detail: The Sep 2025 news item says the center upgraded 'five Element AVITI24 sequencers'. The Illumina side offers NovaSeq X+ (10B/25B, 300-cycle only) via partner facilities 'for the time being', plus NextSeq 2000 and MiSeq. Illumina pages carry no prices and say 'contact us for a project quote'. The AVITI and Ultima pages carry full public rate tables. A large Midwestern research core has put its own capital into five rival boxes, plus Ultima, instead of a high-throughput Illumina box.
items.source_name: UMGC news and NovaSeq X+ service page
items.quote: faster and less expensive when outsourced
items.why_new: Box count (five AVITI24) and the in-house vs outsourced split at UMGC are new; F691 only noted X Plus is outsourced.
items.verify_note: Verified on the X+ page, which says access 'will be both faster and less expensive when outsourced… for the time being'. It offers only 10B/25B at 300 cycles, with no prices ('project quote'). The known list has UMN's AVITI cost cuts, but not that UMGC has no in-house HT Illumina box. Caveat: outsourced X+ work still buys Illumina reagents through partner labs, so this is a price and channel shift more than lost Illumina volume. The 'five AVITI24' count comes from the Sep 2025 news item and was

items.label: 1B
items.claim: UMGC sells a 30x human genome on Ultima at $192 (UMN) all-in, less than half its AVITI price of $407, with 90x at $329.
items.detail: 30x PCR-free WGS including QC, prep and analysis: Ultima UG 100 $192 UMN / $221 external (24-sample batch). AVITI is $407 / $469 (4-sample batch). AVITI Ultra Q is $1,015 / $1,168. Ultima 60x is $238 and 90x is $329. Going from 30x to 90x adds only $137 (+71%) for 3x the data, or about $68 per extra 30x. That is a marginal-cost signal that deep Ultima sequencing is very cheap. The page lists no Illumina WGS price. This is the all-in price a research customer sees, and it sits near the $200 Illumina list genome the UBS expert cited, which is a sequencing-only figure.
items.source_name: UMGC human whole genome sequencing page
items.why_new: F794 only says AVITI is about twice Ultima; the 60x/90x ladder and marginal $/30x arithmetic are new.
items.verify_note: All prices verified: Ultima 30x $192/$221 (24-sample batch), 60x $238/$274 (18), 90x $329/$379 (12); AVITI $407/$469 (4); Ultra Q $1,015/$1,168 (2). All include QC, PCR-free prep, sequencing and analysis. No Illumina WGS is listed. The batch sizes differ, and the comparison to the $200 Illumina figure mixes an all-in price with a sequencing-only price, as the item says. The marginal-cost reading is better done per wafer (see the derived item): each batch fills about one wafer.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: Library prep is a second Illumina revenue line at risk: UMGC charges $103.00 for Illumina DNA Prep vs $60.09 for Ultima PCR-free WGS prep (UMN Savings).
items.detail: Illumina DNA Prep is $103.00 / $133.13 / $186.21 across Savings/Speed/Priority for UMN users. Ultima PCR-free whole-genome prep is $60.09 / $81.62 / $117.16, which is 42% lower. Illumina Nextera XT 1/4 reaction with QC is $59.61. Ultima 'library conversion' of non-Ultima libraries is $52.51. The Ultima prep is 31% of the $192 all-in genome price. Switching sequencer for a genome therefore removes both Illumina flow cell revenue and Illumina prep-kit revenue, and the core's price for a competing prep is much lower.
items.why_new: No earlier item compares Illumina and Ultima prep prices at one core or counts prep revenue at risk.

items.label: 2A
items.claim: UMGC's external premium is a uniform ~15% over UMN rates on every sequencing platform, so research tiering here is mild and not an 'insane discount' structure.
items.detail: AVITI 150-cycle Medium: $900 UMN vs $1,036 external (+15.1%). AVITI 300-cycle High: $1,175 vs $1,352 (+15.1%). UG 100 full wafer: $3,204 vs $3,688 (+15.1%). Library prep is similar (Illumina DNA Prep $103.00 vs $118.54, +15.1%). Fred Hutch charges outsiders 76% more and NCI 100% more, so a gap of 15% suggests pricing at UMGC is cost-plus policy, not leverage-driven discounting. The Savings-to-Priority step is +38% on AVITI 300-cycle High ($1,175→$1,617) and +9.5% on Ultima.
items.why_new: Adds a third data point on internal/external research gaps (15%) against the known 76%, 100%, 40% and 33%.

items.label: 2B
items.claim: UMGC's Aug 2026 Ultima preferred rate for 10x projects cuts the wafer price about 12-16%.
items.detail: The savings are $500 per full wafer and $250 per half-wafer. Against UMN Savings prices that is $500/$3,204 = 15.6% and $250/$2,107 = 11.9%. Against external prices it is 13.6% and 10.3%. Eligible are both UMN and external researchers. The news item (2 Aug 2026) gives no reason, and it targets single-cell and spatial work that Illumina sequences today. Combined with the $3,204 base, a 10x project wafer comes to $2,704 UMN, or about $0.99/Gb on 2.75 Tb.
items.why_new: F683/F689 note the offer exists; the percentage discounts and resulting $/Gb are new.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: Roche had not delivered an SBX/AXELIOS instrument to Freenome as of 30 Jun 2026, so Freenome's volume can't move off Illumina for a long time.
items.detail: The post-close 8-K/A financials (Note 8) say Roche Sequencing 'has not exercised the Option and has not provided the SBX Platform' as of 30 Jun 2026, about 7.5 months after the 17 Nov 2025 deal. Freenome's evaluation runs up to two years from delivery. If delivery happened in Q4'26, the evaluation would end around Q4'28 at the earliest. An AXELIOS-driven loss of Freenome's Illumina volume therefore cannot show up in 2027 consumables. This is a timing watch-out for the 'Roche pressure' leg of 2B.
items.quote: has not provided the SBX Platform to the Company
items.why_new: First dated read on whether an AXELIOS customer has the instrument yet; the known list only says Freenome is 'evaluating'.
items.verify_note: Verified: 'has not exercised the Option and has not provided the SBX Platform', as of 30 Jun 2026 and through the issuance date. The evaluation runs ≤2 years from delivery. Relabeled from 2B to 1B: Freenome is a diagnostics (MCED) developer, not academic research demand, so this bears on the Roche threat to large clinical accounts. A related known item already lists Freenome as 'evaluating' AXELIOS, but the non-delivery is new.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: Freenome's S-1/424B3 names Illumina as its sole supplier of certain sequencers and reagents, and says switching is slow and costly.
items.detail: The risk factor says 'Illumina, Inc. is our sole supplier of certain sequencers and related reagents'. It adds that moving to a new supplier 'would be time-consuming and expensive' and may require revalidating tests. The 8-K/A Note 1 repeats the sole-supplier dependence. This is the customer's own statement of lock-in, which weakens the idea of an imminent large-account walk-away, though the Illumina agreement has no minimums (already known).
items.quote: Illumina, Inc. is our sole supplier of certain sequencers and related reagents
items.why_new: Post-close public-company language; the known list covers only the Illumina supply contract terms (Ex. 10.24).
items.verify_note: The 424B3 risk-factor quote is verified, including 'time-consuming and expensive' and 'require that we revalidate our tests'. Correction: the 8-K/A financials do NOT name Illumina; they mention only unnamed 'sole suppliers'. This is boilerplate risk-factor language from a small, pre-scale customer, so it carries little weight as evidence of lock-in at large accounts.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: The Roche agreement does not require Freenome to move its sequencing to SBX, and the SBX migration terms are redacted.
items.detail: Ex. 10.16 (effective 17 Nov 2025) has Freenome and Roche 'investigate' running assays on SBX and transition them 'if certain conditions are met'. The conditions, evaluation timing, performance study (§4.3–4.6) and milestones are redacted. Freenome's licence to SBX IP is non-exclusive and royalty-free (§5.6). No SBX cost-per-sample target appears, and no clause bars other sequencers. Roche may terminate on a Change of Control involving a listed third party (Exhibit C, redacted).
items.source_name: Freenome S-4 Ex. 10.16 Roche License and Option Agreement
items.why_new: First read of the Roche–Freenome contract mechanics; no exclusivity or switching obligation was previously documented.
items.verify_note: Not re-fetched, but it is consistent with the verified 8-K/A, which says there are no enforceable rights until the option is exercised or SBX is delivered. It overlaps heavily with F1073/F1076; treat the three as one Freenome-Roche finding. Relabeled to 1B.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: The full SBX migration clock is long: if Roche doesn't exercise its option, the agreement ends three years after all Freenome commercial assays are on SBX.
items.detail: Roche paid a $75M upfront (a convertible note, 5% interest, of which $15.0M was allocated to the licence). It can pay a $10.0M option exercise fee, with up to $100M in milestones, up to $24M in SBX R&D milestones, and royalties from low single digits to mid-teens. The evaluation runs up to two years from delivery, and a not-exercised term then runs three years after full assay availability on SBX. A complete Freenome move would likely land in 2028–2031. That is slower than the 2027 timeline in the thesis, but it shows Roche is paying for an AXELIOS foothold with a diagnostics customer.
items.why_new: Dollar terms and the termination clock of Roche's incentive to an AXELIOS evaluator are new.
items.verify_note: Verified: $75.0M note at 5%, $15.0M allocated to the licence, $10.0M option fee, up to $100.0M in milestones plus $24.0M in SBX R&D milestones, low-single-digit to mid-teens royalties (on non-US sales), and a term that ends three years after all commercial assays are on SBX if the option is not exercised. The 2028–31 full-migration window is our inference. This is mixed evidence: slow timing, but Roche is paying to win a diagnostics account. Relabeled from 2B to 1B.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: Freenome, a large MCED/CRC developer and Illumina customer, has cash well short of its burn, which limits how much sequencing it can buy.
items.detail: Freenome's net loss was $132.6M in H1'26 (FY25 $219.3M, FY24 $274.4M) against about $102M of cash and short-term securities at 30 Jun 2026 (search-result summary of an Aug 2026 registration filing). R&D was $106.4M in H1'26 vs $197.1M in FY25, so the H1 pace is about $213M annualized. Laboratory sequencing sits in R&D, and cost of services is only $0.94M. Funding, not sequencing cost, looks like the volume limiter here.
items.why_new: Freenome's post-close financials are not in the known customer list; the $102M cash figure comes from a search snippet only.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: UIUC Carver Biotechnology Center sole-sourced a five-year Illumina reagent contract with a $25M estimated ceiling starting Jul 2024.
items.detail: The Board's May 16, 2024 purchase recommendations list Illumina reagents for the Carver Center's DNA Analyzer Systems. The term is 1 Jul 2024 to 30 Jun 2029 with one 5-year renewal option, and the estimated cost is $25,000,000. The justification is that the items are patented and required for research, and the center's six Illumina sequencers need Illumina reagents. This is a snippet-level read. The text on discounts or price terms was not seen, and the prior term (about $5M) points to a roughly 5x larger ceiling, which could be volume and the NovaSeq X rather than price.
items.source_name: University of Illinois Board of Trustees, Purchase Recommendations
items.why_new: A university sole-source Illumina contract with dollar ceiling and term is not in the known list of procurement sources.

items.label: 2A
items.claim: A prior UIUC Illumina sole-source renewal (term Jul 2023 to Jun 2024) carried tiered discounts of 5%, 10% and 12% on most items.
items.detail: The March 2018 Board purchase and renewal report lists a sole-source renewal of about $5,000,000 (estimated) from Illumina with a 5%, 10% and 12% discount on the majority of items. This is a snippet-level read, and it is old (2018) and unconfirmed. If the 2024 file lacks a comparable discount line, that would show a change in terms. Only the 2018 snippet shows tiered academic discount levels in the 5-12% range, which is shallow compared with the 'insane discounts' large accounts reportedly get.
items.source_name: University of Illinois Board of Trustees, Purchases and Renewal Report
items.why_new: No public-university contract-level discount percentages are in the known list.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: A Taiwan medical-center NIPT tender is small and covers only a few hundred tests over two years, which fits a mature, low-growth NIPT niche.
items.detail: NCKU Hospital awarded NIPT outsourced testing (tender Y11363, 21 Jan 2025) to Bionet for NT$5.58M. The estimate was 420 tests over 21 Jan 2025–20 Jan 2027: 120 basic at NT$9,000 and 300 advanced at NT$15,000. The tender failed several times in Oct–Nov 2024 before award, and only 2 bidders took part. This is one hospital's service outsourcing, not Illumina kit demand, and there is no prior-year NCKU count to show a trend.
items.why_new: Taiwan hospital NIPT tender counts and unit prices are not in the known evidence; the data is only loosely tied to Illumina volume.

items.label: 2B
items.claim: At comparable run sizes (~375–450 Gb), an AVITI24 High 300-cycle run at a university core costs ~30–40% less per Gb than an Illumina NovaSeq X 10B 300-cycle lane at peer cores, so Element's real undercut is in the mid-size runs where research labs buy.
items.detail: UMGC's UMN rate for an AVITI High 300-cycle run is $1,175 for 1.5B read pairs (~450 Gb), or $2.61/Gb (2026 page; F1067). X 10B-300 lanes at university rates are UCSF CAT $1,439 and UCSD $1,400 for ~375 Gb, or ~$3.73–3.84/Gb (F817, D092), and Harvard FY27 $1,314 for 300 Gb, or $4.38/Gb (F775). That puts AVITI 30–40% below the 10B. Against a full 25B lane ($2.5–3.4/Gb) AVITI is only at parity. So the pressure lands on the 10B and smaller Illumina outputs, which are also where the latest UC price cuts were deepest (D092).
items.source_name: UMGC AVITI24 page; UCSF CAT, UCSD IGM and Harvard Bauer rate cards
items.why_new: Known items compare AVITI with the 25B or the 6000; none sets it against the 10B at a matched run size.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: At MIT's core, users saw only a ~2.2x per-Gb gap between a NovaSeq 6000 S4 lane and an X 25B lane in Jan 2025, against ~3.1x at Illumina list prices, because the core marked up the X lane more. That blunts the price signal pushing core users off the 6000.
items.detail: MIT charged $5,400 per S4-300 lane (~600 Gb, $9.0/Gb) vs $3,650 per 25B-300 lane (~900 Gb, $4.06/Gb), a 2.2x ratio (FY2025b sheet, 24 Jan 2025; F1040). Illumina's per-lane list was ~$4,145 for the S4-300 (Feb 2024 kit list $16,578 ÷ 4; D067) and ~$2,000 for the 25B-300 ($16,000 ÷ 8; D093). On the same Gb per lane that is a ~3.1x list ratio. The core's markup over list was ~1.30x on the S4 and ~1.83x on the 25B. MIT's 25B price is also above other cores ($2.5–3.4/Gb), and its X runs sit at a sister facility. This is a single research core, and research is already ~92% converted, so the effect on Illumina's tail is small.
items.source_name: OpenWetWare / MIT BioMicroCenter pricing; Illumina list prices
items.why_new: No known item measures how core markups compress the 6000-vs-X user price gap compared with Illumina's list gap.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: The Ultima wafer at UMGC carries a ~16% 'promo' discount ($2,704 vs $3,204), and AVITI got a free 33% $/read cut. That gives two separate rival price levers at one core within a year, and Illumina's posted prices at peer cores fell only ~9–17% over a similar period.
items.detail: UMGC's UG100 wafer is $3,204 standard and $2,704 on the 10x promo (−15.6%; F1052, F1066), and AVITI output rose 50% at unchanged price in Sep 2025, cutting $/read by 33% (F1052). Over a similar 2025–26 window, UC cores cut X lanes by 8.9–10.5% (25B) and ~17% (10B) (D092). The rivals' combined per-read moves are therefore roughly 2–3x larger than the Illumina lane cuts seen at cores. These are core-posted prices, not vendor net prices.
items.source_name: UMGC news and service pages; UC core rate cards
items.why_new: Sets the size of the rivals' price moves at one core against Illumina's core-level cuts over the same window.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: Public human WGS-scale (>=100 Gb) runs on the NovaSeq 6000 rose rather than fell from 2025 into 2026, and the X share did not rise.
items.detail: ENA human runs with base_count>=1e11, counted by first_public date: 6000 had 821 in 2025Q1, 771 in 2025Q3, 1,391 in 2026Q1 and 2,177 across 2026Q2-Q3 (about 1,090 per quarter). NovaSeq X had 113, 103, 77 and 278 over the same periods. The X share of the 6000+X total was 12.1%, 11.8%, 5.2% and 11.3%. No quarter shows the 6000 share falling. These are public research and consortium deposits that lag sequencing, so they say little about clinical consumables.
items.why_new: This is a new public-repository measure of 6000 versus X high-output human runs. None of the known items used ENA.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: Taiwan hospital WGS/WES kit contract awarded at 11% below budget and 10.6% below the original bid in a lowest-price tender.
items.detail: NTUH awarded Genomics BioSci a 2-year unit-price contract (Aug 2023 to Jul 2025) for a human WGS/WES reagent set with instruments at NT$19.89M. The public budget was NT$23.556M and the original bid NT$22.25M. The first round drew too few bids, so it had to be re-tendered, and the rebid cleared well under budget. This shows price-led award dynamics at a hospital buyer. No Illumina platform is named and no per-genome price is listed.
items.url: https://pcc-api.openfun.app/api/searchbycompanyname?query=基龍米克斯生物科技股份有限公司&page=2
items.why_new: Award, base and bid figures for TD12E060 were not in the known list; novelty versus the S724 set is unchecked.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: Genomics BioSci appears on a Taipei Veterans General Hospital 2-year human WGS service unit-price open contract (July 2023).
items.detail: Title: 人類全基因體定序服務等二項委外二年單價開口契約, job X11204H, dated 2023-07-21. Only the title and buyer were seen; I did not open the award value or unit prices. It is a candidate for a per-genome price datapoint.
items.url: https://pcc-api.openfun.app/api/searchbycompanyname?query=基龍米克斯生物科技股份有限公司&page=2
items.source_name: Taiwan PCC via pcc-api.openfun.app (Taipei VGH X11204H)
items.why_new: Not checked against the 49 S724 items; the unit prices are unread.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: German NIPT use under statutory insurance is still rising into 2025, not maturing.
items.detail: A bifg analysis (Gynäkologische Praxis 2026, search snippet only) reports 2025 uptake of roughly 1 in 3 pregnant women under 26 and about 1 in 2 under 36, with the trend rising in all age groups. Its observed cohort had 55,441 NIPTs (GOP 01870) against 301,945 NIPT consultations (01789), a ratio that suggests many consultations do not become tests. This extends the known 32%->50% (2023->2024) Barmer figure into 2025, but Table 2 was not read, so the quarterly growth rate is unverified.
items.why_new: Adds 2025 age-band uptake and cohort service counts, not the earlier 32%->50% figure.

items.label: 1C
items.claim: The German NIPT fee was cut about 19% from 1 Jul 2026 to track falling test costs, and the test is concentrated in 20 labs.
items.detail: Bewertungsausschuss decision 833 lowers GOP 01870 from 1642 to 1326 points, effective 1 Jul 2026. The decision cites the Institut des Bewertungsausschusses evaluation: use is 'significantly more than expected', done in 20 labs, and the fee is adjusted to current test costs. This points to lab-level unit cost deflation and buyer concentration, which fits the large-account leverage argument. It does not show an Illumina price effect, and the payer cut could also squeeze lab margins.
items.why_new: Not in the known list: a payer-mandated 19% German NIPT fee cut and the 20-lab concentration.

items.label: 1A
items.claim: Over Oct'25–Jun'26 the X share of ≥100 Gb human runs was only 8.5%, and 6000 releases stayed high, so ENA does not show a clean 6000 decline.
items.detail: For the nine months Oct 2025–Jun 2026 there were 4,028 6000 runs and 373 X runs at ≥100 Gb. The X share is 373/4,401 = 8.5%. Those nine months already contain 6000 releases of about 1,340 per quarter, against 610 in Q3'26. The series is very lumpy, so the Q3'26 decline may reflect batch timing rather than a trend. This warns the analyst not to over-read single-quarter ENA shares.
items.why_new: Shows consortium batch volatility in the same series and rules out a simple monotonic read.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: Illumina's Taiwan distributor has settled single-bid research reagent lots about 15% below its opening bid every year from 2022 to 2025, so discounts are formulaic and not speeding up.
items.detail: NTU College of Medicine sequencer-reagent lots, opening bid → award: 1113A004 (Apr 2022) NT$11.424M→9.655M (−15.5%); 1112A012 (Jan 2023) 3.05M→2.5896M (−15.1%); 1124A012 (Jul 2023) 8.5475M→7.265M (−15.0%); 1134A016 (Sep 2024) budget 5.79875M→4.92M (−15.2%); 1142A007 (Oct 2025) 6.79999M→6.12003M (−10.0%). The Veterinary Research Institute (農業部獸醫研究所) library-prep reagent and chip lots show the same pattern: Sep 2024 1.324375M→1.125M (−15.0%) and Oct 2025 1.467375M→1.246M (−15.1%). Every lot had one bidder (均泰生物科技). The 2025 concession was the same or smaller, not larger.
items.why_new: Earlier findings covered single lots. This is the first multi-year time series of concession size from the same buyer and distributor.
items.verify_note: Not re-verified (PCC API returned 429). The consistent ~15% gap between opening bid and award is mostly a Taiwanese procurement artifact: a single bidder opens at budget and is negotiated down to the buyer's secret floor (底價), which is typically about 85% of budget. Taiwan CDC's −15.4% (F983) shows the same pattern. So the gap reflects the buyer's floor-setting habit, not Illumina's discount policy. It still shows no acceleration through 2025, and the 2025 NTU concession (−10%) was smaller.

items.label: 2B
items.claim: National Taiwan University College of Medicine's annualized Illumina reagent contract ceiling fell about 80% from 2022 to 2025, and the latest lot is almost entirely grant-funded.
items.detail: Annualized award ceilings: Apr 2022–Jun 2023 NT$9.655M plus a NT$2.59M top-up over about 14 months ≈ NT$10.5M/yr. Jul 2023–Jun 2024: NT$7.265M over 11.4 months ≈ NT$7.6M/yr. Sep 2024–Dec 2025: NT$4.92M over 15 months ≈ NT$3.9M/yr. Oct 2025–Jul 2028: NT$6.12M over 33 months ≈ NT$2.2M/yr, with NT$5.44M (89%) subsidized by the science ministry. Two caveats: these are open-contract ceilings, not invoiced spend, and the 2025 lot is titled 'NGS sample prep reagents' only, so sequencing reagents may have moved to another vehicle or to outsourcing. A separate ministry-funded Illumina lot (1111A009, NT$2.15M, May 2022–Feb 2024) has no visible successor.
items.why_new: This is the first spend series for a Taiwanese university research core. Earlier findings covered NHRI and hospitals only.
items.verify_note: Not re-verified (429). The figures are contract ceilings, and the 2025 lot's scope changed to sample-prep reagents only, so this is not a like-for-like spend decline. Relabeled from 2A to 2B. The more likely explanation is substitution: the same NTU College of Medicine bought an AVITI24 and signed a NT$13.3M AVITI reagent contract from Dec 2025 (F885, D084). See the derived item.

items.label: 1B
items.claim: At Taipei Veterans General Hospital, the negotiated discount on the renewed Illumina tumor CGP reagent-plus-instrument contract shrank from 20% to 7.5%, even though the contract value fell 11%.
items.detail: The 8-cancer CGP contract (v1, M11109K, Apr 2022, 3 years) had a budget of NT$38.88M. The single bid was NT$38.88M and the award NT$31.104M (−20.0%).
